_childDocuments_.review: There is a lot to like about Wintermoor Tactics Club, and I'd give it a neutral or not-for-everyone rating if I could. The reason I'm rating it down is because it's not really a strategy or even a tactics game, despite its title. The game pretends to be one thing but is actually another. It presents itself as a tactical, story-driven, pseudo-rpg (the store page mentions 'upgrades' and unlocking characters, giving a false sense that there's progression). In reality, it's a visual novel with incidental puzzles disguised as tactical battles.Now, if you like puzzle games, and if you like visual novels, Wintermoor Tactics Club is probably right up your alley. But if you're an XCom, Battle Brothers, or Battletech fan, the "tactical" part of this game will feel very, very hollow. If you're a D&D nerd you may appreciate the atmosphere of the story, but you'll also notice how vastly more simplified WTC's gameplay is compared to D&D.As an homage to nerds, then, WTC succeeds. As a critique of hoighty-toighty private schools, their often arbitrary governance, and the ridiculous exclusivity of their students, WTC more or less works. The writing is legitimately funny at times, and the tactical puzzles are satisfying for a little while. But, for me at least, the game ran out of steam well before I was finished with it. I wanted to like it, and I appreciate it as an artistic effort, but the gameplay was just not what I expected - it was too shallow - nor what I prefer.If you want relaxing, simplistic puzzles punctuating a more-or-less charming and cozy story, WTC is for you, but if you like complex tactical decisions, deep emergent storytelling, and an expansive world, you'd be better served looking elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Super quick review because I don't feel like writing a bunch of stuff.  Wintermoor Tactics Club is a very nice surprise.  It's a tactical turn-based combat game with a visual novel wrapper, but you already knew that from the store page description.  The visual novel part is a LOT, LOT, LOT more interactive than your standard read and click to the next thing to read.  There are a lot of side quests to go on, which mostly involve just walking around searching for things and talking to the right people in the right order.  But, that process is enjoyable and not tedious at all so far.  The overarching story is fairly compelling, well written, and definitely caters to the inner geek in me as a D&D fan.  There is also some super mysterious stuff going on in this school, and I can't wait to see how it plays out.The combats are small, single screen maps at least so far as I've played.  Hopefully they expand to some larger maps.  But, maybe this isn't even necessary.  I am getting an "Into the Breach" feel to these combats.  Puzzley, positioning is very important, as is using the right dude with the right attack/skill at the right time in the right order is key to success.  There are upgrades each of your dudes get during the game, and you can change them out at ANY time.  So, if one combat is giving you trouble, maybe swap out your upgrades and try again.  You will find the right combination of party members and equipment/upgrades for any combat.You gain more party members as the game progresses, and you can swap them out as needed at the start of each combat.So . . . a very nice surprise.  It's definitely on the easier side, at least so far.  But, to get perfect scores on each combat will require some thought and good tactics.It says there are Steam achievements, but I haven't received any yet.  Either it's bugged, or the stupid "Steam is learning about this game" is still preventing achievements from being awarded.  And, there are no emoticons for completing card sets.  What the heck?!?  Give us some emoticons!!Jake and Elwood are too cool to play D&D, but they still think this is a very fun game, and the developers did a wonderful job of designing something just a little different.  Which is nice.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: What an excellent game. Really fun and cute from start to finish, which I honestly beat over two days playing for hours and hours at a time.Wintermoor Tactics Club is about Alicia and her friends in a copyright-avoiding DnD analogue and the year they got pitted against the other school clubs in a snowball fight for their survival. While one of the more apt words to describe this game is "simple" I don't mean that even remotely negatively. Wintermoor Tactics Club aims for a very chill experience where you can enjoy the fights, smile or laugh at the story and grow to like the characters. This is not Final Fantasy Tactics. But it's not trying to be.The gameplay itself is a very simple SRPG; you field three characters on a map who have 2-3 skills and you later get items that can modify what certain skills can do (make an attack magical instead of physical, change from a chain lightning attack to a cone of fire, stuff like that). As the game progresses you add more characters to your club and get to know them and use them in combat. While I wouldn't call the combat hard (except for one specific fight at the end of the game, jesus) there is a lot of strategy you can play around with based on characters, customizations and enemies. I was never really bored or going through the motions during the fights and enjoyed trying to get the best rank I could (even though I don't think it unlocked or did anything).The plot, writing and characters are all very strong. I would compare this to a good YA novel or softer Stranger Things. The plot isn't complicated or intricate but still has it's fun climaxes, cool reveals and still manages to touch on some important or more serious topics without coming off too heavy. The feelings it evokes and that certain characters feel can certainly be relatable to anyone who went through school as a bit of an awkward kid. The writing is very cute and fun, with each character feeling like their own unique person as the school is filled with named students with individual sprites and portraits who always have new things to say. The people who join you are pretty great as well, though as a shorter game unfortunately the ones who join later get much less development than the earlier ones; there's not much that can be done about that. If you put them all in the beginning, you front-load your game and never feel like you're progressing or gaining anything. There is fantastic representation as well, many different ethnicities, LGBTQ representation and even furries in a positive light! I'd also say that a big unfortunate part is that one character who I was all ready to be my favorite actually...didn't change at all, or go through any development and often didn't have an attitude or motive that matched up with the other characters. They seemed to be there to be that type of character, but as a character also felt like they never would be there or stick around. They were a funny and cool character just not one that fit well or felt natural in the club. Super broken skills tho.The art is great too. As an indie studio, it is limited in what it can do but the characters, backgrounds and battle units that are there are fun to look at. You won't have tons of animations or characters performing sick backflips but it's fine. I don't think it ever feels "cheap" simply a good execution on what a talented artist could do within a small budget.The game won't take that long, a solid 13 hours when I did everything on offer in the game but I 100% feel I got my money's worth. More than that if I look at how much I paid for longer games I enjoyed less. If you're looking for the next Final Fantasy Tactics; you won't find it here. Tamper down your expectations some and if you want to play a mediumish relaxing SRPG with a chill and fun story, this won't disappoint.Buy it at 15 bucks, it is completely worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game I wanted to love but just didn't. It has two big problems that drag the experience down.First is that they walk back their own premise. The idea of snowball fights using the framing of wargaming is a fertile ground for unique twists on familiar concepts. But in the game every fight is framed as if it literally was a tabletop fight so all the characters are just using their usual set of magic abilities. How those abilities translate to reality is handwaved away. So there is just a huge disconnect between the core gameplay and the narrative This is especially bad near the end of the game because The second problem is a lack of atmosphere. Walking around Wintermoor is a completely disengaging experience without a good sense of place or of mood. This is further harmed because the characters in the school are inconsistently zany. Some characters are supposed to be over the top, but the world doesn't back them up so most often these characters just become broad caricatures of their archetype. This is a problem because every interstitial quest involves walking all around the school and talking to people and the lack of atmosphere makes these sections drag and ruins the pacing of the game.The game has some great ideas and some good moments that capitalize on those ideas, but overall there is nothing here in narrative or in gameplay that hasn't already been done better elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Back in 1981, a particularly snowy winter settled down upon the area that those attending a boarding school called Wintermoor Academy won’t ever forget. Did that particular winter set a new record or were the students snowed in that made it memorable? No, something worse. Like many other schools, Wintermoor Academy lets their students form and be a part of clubs so they can meet people with similar interests and do activities alongside their schoolwork. The clubs here range from the normal Knitting Club to the strange Psychic Detectives Club. However, this all changed one day.As we’re going through what happened during the fateful winter of 1981, we follow one student named Alicia and the club she was involved with called Tactics Club. Tactics Club, made up of Alicia, Collin, and Jacob, revolves around playing a tabletop role-playing game called Curses & Catacombs (or C&C). However, one day Principal Enfield called for an assembly for all of the clubs and, you guessed it, it wasn’t good. He announced a snowball tournament that all clubs must participate in. If your club is the one that lost, it must disband permanently. With only one club able to be win and be deemed as the Ultimate Club, the Tactics Club is dedicated towards winning so their sense of belonging can stay with them throughout their school years.The majority of battles in Wintermoor Tactics Club takes place in the club’s C&C campaign that Collin runs (and occasionally Alicia). Thus, combat takes place on small, tile-based maps the replicates what it would look like if it was drawn on paper. Every turn gives each active team member and enemy a chance to move and attack if they’re able to. Each character and enemy type has their own abilities and quirks that goes along with their design. Each enemy type (including enemy club members) also has their own qualifications for who they’re targeting (like targeting whoever is closest) and will show you who it’ll be. Though, your team in particular has special combat abilities called Tactics Power. However, Tactics Powers can’t always be used as they have a one turn cooldown timer and you need enough Tactics Points, gained by successfully injuring enemies. Going over our main three: Alicia plays the mage Anjaya who can cast a ranged chaining electric attack with a strong line attack Tactics Power; Jacob plays Rogey the rogue that is quick on his feet with the ability to kick away or pull enemies as well as throw a damage reducing smoke bomb as a Tactics Power; and Collin is the paladin Eodwald with the only character with armor, can taunt the enemy with his attack, and does a skull cracking Tactics Power slam that dazes enemies caught up in it.When it’s time to go head to head with another club for the snowball tournament, the school field where it takes place is re-imagined as a C&C board. So while your characters would be throwing snowballs in reality, you’ll still have access to each character’s abilities as well as a familiar set up.Your club does get more members over time, so you won’t stay with only having three characters to choose from for long. Each time someone new joins, you’ll be able to introduce their C&C character and hopefully help out with their personal problems with a campaign Alicia writes (with the help of you choosing between various options). Not only giving that new club member a sense of belonging despite just joining, but also introducing the player to their character abilities. The new characters are pretty helpful, unique to the others, and comes with their own pros. For example, the first new club member has a ranged, AoE attack that lowers magic resistance and a chaining Tactics Power that forces an enemy to target their own teammate.After you complete a battle, you’ll be awarded medals based on your performance in various categories like how many turns it took you or how much damage your party took overall. The maximum/minimum amounts vary depending on the battle, but if you’re planning on getting all medals, you’ll be up to a challenge as some later battles does get a bit tricky. On the other side, if you’re having trouble with a particular battle, you’ll also get the option to activate a No Fail Mode so you can continue on with the story if you so wish. Of course, you could also mess with enemy/party health in the options as well.Unlike other turn-based tactical RPGs, Wintermoor Tactics Club does not have a leveling/experience system in place. While there are going to be people that won’t pick this up based solely on this, I honestly didn’t miss it. It was nice playing a casual tactical game for once where you don’t have to worry about keeping everyone’s levels up or worry about permadeath if a character is defeated in battle. So how are the characters going to get more powerful later on if not by leveling up? Well, each character has unlockable equipment and an unlockable Tactics Power.As you’re going through the story, Challenge Levels will pop up for individual characters. First Crucible Battles and then Mastery Battles. These challenge battles gives you a challenging scenario, like not letting anyone but this one character take damage, and you’ll get a reward if you manage to win. You’ll first be given Challenge Levels that grant you new equipment for the target character, but later on you’ll be rewarded with a new Tactics Power (although they require double the points to activate).Between C&C campaigns and participating in the snowball tournament, you have free reign over where you want to go within Wintermoor Academy. In each location, you’re able to talk to your fellow classmates as well as examining anything that gives you the option. Sometimes, a character will have a side quest for you to do (which you’re alerted by both the map and the equipment list). These side quests do mostly involve you running between locations and talking to characters, but you’re rewarded with new equipment and new interactions (well, if you enjoy the characters in Wintermoor). Equipment can give an ability a new affect or even give that character a new ability to use. Since Wintermoor Tactics Club doesn’t have a leveling system where you have to choose between abilities or specialties that a certain character will be stuck with, it lets you swap equipment as you see fit. So if you find that a certain equipment won’t necessarily help you in a battle, you can easily switch it out with one that will when you reset the battle. Not to mention that later on, you’ll be given access to Specializations.The artwork Wintermoor Tactics Club has is wonderful, but there is a mismatch of styles. The character sprites for the main characters are wonderfully designed, but the other minor characters rely on their in-game model for a small sprite beside their dialogue. Some minor characters look better than others. This isn’t a big deal, but it was particularly weird for characters like Jania where her in-game model looks significantly different than their in-game model. So much that I originally thought they were two different characters until I did a double take when I was looking back at my screenshots.Other than characters, the environment are wonderfully done and feels like a school that you most likely won’t be mad at having to live at. I particularly loved how the environment all the battles takes place on was designed. I love how it looks like it was drawn on paper by Collin or Alicia and how it easily tells you which tile can’t be stepped on. Not to mention how you and the enemy looks like they’re actually miniatures both with how they look and how they move.

_childDocuments_.review: This is being marketed as some kind of tactical RPG or at least tactical strategy game. There is a battle system, but it's just a series of deterministic tactical puzzles. That could be good, but even those are extremely same-y and simplistic. All but a handful of them are "solved" by maximizing damage output per turn, which you can do using the same broken combo of "magimist" and "spark" on nearly every level. There are no new mechanics introduced between roughly Chapter 2 and the final boss., so the only variation is that the enemies are in different places until they all run directly at your characters on their first turn, then the levels are all identical.In an effort to be positive, here's a short list of games that you can buy on steam that actually do the kind of tactical gameplay you might be looking for:The Disgaea seriesPhantom BraveWasteland 2The Valkyria Chronicles seriesBanner of the MaidBattletechXCOMXCOM 2Warhammer 40,000: MechanicusSpace Hulk: TacticsDvinity Original SinDivinity Original Sin 2Baldur's Gate 3The King's Bounty seriesExpeditions: ConquistadorThe Shadowrun Returns seriesAnd I'm sure there are many, many more.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Wintermoor Tactics Club piqued my curiosity several months before the official release. I did not know what exactly to expect: a dark story about corrupted Academy that hides vicious experiments behind innocent snowball fights? or just a slice-of-life adventure of a young girl on her quest to find friends? or a hidden magical world on the verge of a major snowball conflict? Or maybe I just play too many games with sudden plot twists… Whatever it is, though, the true attraction for me was the mere image of The Psychic Detectives (could it be an actual pun towards one of South Park’s episodes?!) with its lovely characters’ design. So, not thinking twice, I decided to give this game a chance. You will play as a shy school girl Alicia who has a heart of gold and her favorite Tactics Club. She loves playing tabletop fantasy games with her two friends, and everything was going calmly and smoothly until one day. The day when the Principal of this prestigious Academy decided to find the one Ultimate Club. Announcing the start of the grandiose snowball tournament, Principal Enfield doomed various clubs to fight each other, and each lost match meant elimination of yet another creative group. Never being the one to fight, Alicia feels hesitant about the whole thing. But she has to join the battle to save her beloved club from being disbanded. Will this quite girl be able to save everyone from the strange plan? And will she find out the real reason why the bizarre Principal is so fixed on the Ultimate Club idea?Wintermoor Tactics Club has a pleasantly cozy atmosphere and presentation. Nothing outstanding or breathtaking, but the one that gives you the warm fuzzies during the whole time you play the game.Each location is carefully designed and quite bright. While the Academy is not a big place by any means, it is still a nice one. The amazing winter setting is what designers did the best, in my opinion. Maybe I am just missing normal snow after the lackluster winter, but Wintermoor Academy’s grounds covered with this white delight looked surprisingly refreshing and heartwarming.  While there are various monsters that you meet during club’s activities, none of them are scary at all. Which suits the general atmosphere perfectly. Some Tactical Club’s enemies get special designs during fights, which was also a really nice touch. The last but not least: music. There are not that many tracks, and, to be honest, I started getting tired of some after several chapters. The music in general is good, but I really wish there was a greater variety to it. Speaking of the characters’ design, they are very easy on the eye. The artwork looks quite cartoonish and soft in general, but still sports interesting details. Each person is unique in their own way, whether it is just an accessory on their clothes or beautiful long flowing hair of the self-appointed queen. Most characters belong to some clubs, so you will notice them wearing attributes associated with their activities. Well, except for the three main ones: you would have never guessed that Jacob is among the fans of fantasy adventures and not a rebel fighting against the corrupted school system. Well, he is actually both, but these are just silly details! I really liked not only characters’ looks, but also their personalities. You can find absolutely all kinds of people around this impressive (yet somewhat small) Academy – fans of horses and riding, sport fanatics, literal jerks, a crazy guy who treats books as fragile and invaluable creatures, a queen bee, a scary School President with a…sword? Yeah, that is just the short list of students who inhabit this snowy kingdom. We also should not forget about the Principal who seems to be the main villain of the story. This guy might look innocent and hippy, but his actions speak for themselves. And the intrigue behind his *evil* plan is quite fascinating. While, once again, there is nothing groundbreaking, this game is a really enjoyable one. The gameplay is very simple to navigate and to learn – *user-friendly* will be the best word to describe it. There are three main parts: first, you will need to explore various locations to interact with people, complete the main quest and some side ones, to check out different objects and to collect equipment. This includes walking around the campus, quite a lot of it, to be precise. Second, here we have a lot of tabletop battles. The main characters have their own avatars in this fantasy world, and their tasks focus on fighting monsters to progress through the campaign. In addition, all snowball fighting also takes place in the form of a turn-based encounters. So it is like having a game inside another game, I guess. Still, these battles can become repetitive at some point because you technically do the same thing every time. Third, there are visual novel elements. You can make some choices from time to time (for example, what kind of essay to write during the third chapter), a well as either take or reject side quests. Other parts are quite linear, though. All character interactions take part in this mode too, so be ready for a lot of reading. But that is not all! I was surprised to find mini-games too – none of them were mentioned on the store page, after all. I had fun drawing my horrendous version of a horse for sure. And you can also write fantasy campaigns for your avatars’ adventures, which, in my humble opinion, is a great gameplay design. I am not speaking about anything major, of course, only about some battles and Alicia’s story, but this is still amazing. What else…Strategy does matter here. I made several mistakes during one of the battles in chapter 2, which resulted in the OK-ish score, and this still bugs me a lot (achievements hunters should pay particular attention to this part). So you will not be able to just run through thoughtlessly – after all, enemies have their own special moves too, and each chapter introduces more and more difficult challenges. However, if you are more focused on the story and do not need to complete any achievements, then you will be happy to play in the easy mode, which allows you to move forward even if you lose some battles.  I think Wintermoor Tactics Club can become a good game for teenagers with its cartoonish style and friendly atmosphere. But I advise parents to check it on their own first, because some characters like using foul language (even though all bad words are hidden), and one guy is quite aggressive towards his school by literally calling it a ‘fascist authority’.  There is also this mystery case that .Adults will most probably like Wintermoor Tactics Club for the tabletop gameplay and tactical challenges. Depending on which mode you play, you can get either a very relaxing experience or something to test your skills. So, to sum up, I think Wintermoor Tactics Club is a curious story-and-strategy-focused game that has a lot of potential. It might feel repetitive because of the constant turn-based battles, but the plot is interesting enough and almost each chapter brings something new. Mini-games are a lot of fun too.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think it's actually a polarizing game, and yet I'm weirdly polarized by it.Wintermoor Tactics Club is a loosely dnd themed trpg puzzle game. It's mostly cozy and low stakes with a wild escalation in the final act, and overall feels like a playable Faith Erin Hicks comic.The characters are kind of caricature-y, kind of fleshed, and there's a lot of warm humor that lands only occasionally, but the art and soundtrack are consistently lovely.My problem---and this is a me problem---is the combat.Your characters mostly don't improve, except for a handful of sidegrades that are unlocked by time gated fetch quests and some move unlocks that are stuck behind optional battles.This means that every fight is basically just a puzzle, sometimes with fairly narrow criteria required to solve it, and the feeling of advancing and getting stronger and mastering the game that come with rpg territory mostly aren't here. There's some tech you can do, but mostly it felt like fiddling with a lock rather than playing a squad of combatants.Now, if you're in the mood for cozy, you want some dnd nostalgia, you don't mind low stakes, and you don't mind combat puzzles, you'll probably have a good time here. It's a decent length, and the characters and plot do grow on you by the end.But if you like your rpgs crunchy, and edgy, and character advancement as a core part of play, you're going to be better off trying Tactics Ogre or Triangle Strategy or the like.For me personally, this game wasn't really my thing, but I don't think that means it's bad, just that I had different expectations going in from what it actually was.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Wintermoor is a visual novel with acceptable puzzles that masquerades as a tactics rpg and a less then stellar story that ultimately undermines and lessen the experience.Wintermoor Tactics Club is not a horrible game just from the gameplay.But it's selling itself as a tactics rpg when it's more so puzzles structured like a tactics rpg.You don't level up or become better, you simply equip a few pieces of gear that changes a character abilities to solve whatever puzzle fight your currently doing.Only at the end when getting an S rank no longer matters and you're free to do whatever is when you realize just how shallow and abusable some of the mechanics really are without those restrictions.So as a puzzle game it's fine and does have some satisfying puzzles and solutions and I honestly can't complain that much about it.However the game is less of a puzzle game and more of a Visual Novel and here is where I think the game really dropped the ball.It takes place during the 90's which is briefly mentioned at the start of the game and yet it only makes a very small selection of references at the beginning and then promptly forgets about it's setting.The characters are mostly kids in their early teens but they all have the "modern sensibilities" of a 2020 twitter user which I wouldn't mind if it didn't take place during the 90's.I think the setting would have been much better suited if it took place in the 2010's when kids actually acted like they do in this game.The characters are also mostly written to be quirky, nerdy, funny and relatable, but I think all of that felt very flat.This is subjective but non of the jokes to me where funny and I really think the moral messages of the game about inclusion and equality get's lost in translation when the main character is universally liked by all the students.Overall I think this game is a little all over the place, I think it really would have helped to make this a little more true to it's 90's aesthetics and tell a slightly harsher story about overcoming adversity.Or make this a modern game about acceptance. As it is now the games tonal shifts don't mix well and makes the story and characters sadly not that relatable or very interesting.You could do a lot worse then this game but it's just not a game I can recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game so much. The characters are diverse and interesting. I love the sense of humour. I wish I could play more games like it. Turn based tactical RPGs on a grid are a genre i've always found difficult to dip my toe into, but wintermoors difficulty felt just right for me, and Id love to explore the genre more in the future. I would die for Jania

_childDocuments_.review: This is a simple but very moving tactical rpg, where you play Alicia, a teenager with a passion for tabletop games and writing. The gameplay is easily accessible (maybe a bit too simple for hardcore gamers) and quite fun for an introduction to the genre, but the real value here is the story. Alicia is a loveable character and she will write different roleplaying stories to introduce her new friends to the game. The player will chose how those stories unfold (to a certain extent) and how they are tailored for each character's strengths and weaknesses. Want to introduce a very shy friend to your tabletop group? Well, write a story in which they will be able to display their qualities and save the day, so they can feel confidence. The whole game revolves around these very personal and touching moments, and it definitely leaves a warm feeling in your heart! Plus the overall story is fun.An overall simple tactical rpg, great for introducing your kids to tactical games, with a touching story and absolutely loveable characters. Fans of the genre can appreciate it too, but don't expect much of a challenge.8.1/10 Nice discovery
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a tactic or a strategy game. This is a a visual novel with puzzle solving elements.From a tactical perspective the game is shallow. It gives you a lot of options which you unable to apply because of a little number of encounters: around 25 or 30 battles on the main story line. Like you have 7 character, who have about 6 abilities per character. In the first half of the game you able to select only one ability for each class, and there is some variaty in the second half. New clubmates are stronger than older ones. There's no time to test different ability combinations. In addition battles are turn-to-turn reproducable: AI always reacts the identical way on an identical sequence of your actions. Sometimes the game decides to be a video novel with miles of typical indie-style graphomaniac texts and questionable design patterns from the generation before last.Wintermoor is better to play on phones.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Overall? An enjoyable experience from a game that is clearly a love letter to video games like final fantasy tactics and to TTRPGs of the D&D variety. The characters were well written and likable - falling into stereotypes somewhat, but having enough care and though put into that by the end of my 8.5 hour playthrough I was invested in the main cast. The actual combat is engaging if not bit lop-sided when it comes to difficulty. There were battles that felt like they should have been easy that ended up being surprisingly difficult whereas battles implied to be difficult ended up being somewhat of a cakewalk. The characters' abilities are all interesting and have enough options in build variety that won't get bored with one set-up, though balance between each character was a bit...unequal. Though no character is useless by any stretch and I think you could make any combination you find fun work. Also, if you care about diversity and games not randomly having some wild racist/sexist/etc. thing pop up out of nowhere I think this one hits it out of the park. You've got a diverse cast of characters on a lot of different axes and those identities are worked into their stories organically. And thankfully without any cloying, preachy bits thrown in that would take you right out of what is a fun, and somewhat surprising story.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the loveliest games I've ever played. It is a mix of adventure/visual novel and turn-based tactics set in a school during the 80s (being a child of the 80s like myself certainly will help your enjoyment, but it is not necessary). You help Alicia by meeting other students and playing a computer version of D&D. The tactics part is not very taxing - I have played several turn-based strategy games, but I do not consider myself an expert and I get easily frustrated: this game did not frustrate me, and kept me engaged through most of my time with it. I did skip some optional "mastery" battles since I wasn't interested in them.The story, however, is just fantastic - comic, heartwarming without being sappy. I didn't like a couple of plot developments towards the end, and some characters inevitably are weaker than others,  but that doesn't diminish my admiration for it. I genuinely looked forward toward more opportunities to talk to everyone. Just very well told, with "simple but nice" graphics and great music.I don't write reviews often, but I feel this game deserves all the exposure it can get. Great work, devs!
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: A very charming, lighter weight game about (essentially) a D&D club tackling a real life adventure.It's sort of like a western version of Persona, but bite-sized, with your time spent split between talking to people / making friends and turn based combat battles.I say 'lighter' and 'bite sized' because the game isn't super deep. It's an enjoyable experience, to be sure, and it has a diverse and interesting cast of characters, but don't expect anything to be as fleshed out as you might find in a full-blown, larger RPG game.The story and writing is good, and the characters are interesting, diverse, and mostly well-realized, although not in a super deep way. The game is fairly easy, the quests leaving little to do apart from walking around and talking to people, but for what it is (a lighter experience), there's nothing wrong with that.The tactical part of the game, the combat, isn't difficult to win, but a little more difficult to optimize. You get medals for completing the battles while fulfilling certain conditions, which leads to some tactical puzzle solving throughout the battles. "Okay, if I use this character to attack here, that gives me enough tactics points to use this ability here, which means i'll kill any enemies who are close enough to attack me this turn..."If you're only in it for the story, you'll have an enjoyable, breezy time as you flow through the majority of the game. If you're someone who enjoys creative puzzle solving via combat, you'll have fun chasing all the medals in combat.Overall, I think this was a very enjoyable game. My playtime is a bit bloated, and I expect my single playthrough (replaying battles for all the medals and doing all the side quests) was probably 13 hours or so. If you just blast through it, it would be much shorter... probably 8-10 hours or so.

_childDocuments_.review: This is...  A pretty darn good game actually.  It is a tactics game, but...  It's not hard!  You can actually make it easier or harder, so don't be discouraged...  As in: all enemies can have 10% HP while you have 200% HP...  XD...  You wont get most medals at this rate, but you can just blow through the story?  I actually didn't try the 10%, but I can imagine the last boss can be owned with one hit...  Super overpowered club for ya!Oh yes, this game is about clubs...  And "C&C" (you get the reference) and friendship and quirky humor.  My favorite part was the Cat Calendar...  It was adorable...  Wait, it still is!The story is good, absolutely nothing is forced onto you, and it just makes you understand and think and not to give up when everything seems hard or ...  Well, if you are not a people person: you will still find a place to belong.  It was nice.I made sure to play with every available character on the battlefield.  They all had something unique to offer.  You can also do upgrades and change their classes!  Later on that is.  I thought "Duncan" was the most adorable...  but that is because he is written to be like a puppy...Seriously, did not call the twist with the "Butterfly Girl"...  Actually, I didn't even think about twists, so this way it happens and surprises me.  Best way to do it.  Okay, I also kinda thought that "Alicia" would end up with "Jacob"?  That was in the back of my head...  But!  I liked the pairing choice in the end regardless.  :DSo thank you and it is very fun and I can play it again sometime and rock out to the fun tunes!!! :D :) =)

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent game. Its strengths are its humor, its plotting, and its diversity. The gameplay is a little on the easy side, but that's in keeping with the relaxed and fun nature of the game itself. If you'd like to spend a pleasant day or two in a fantasy school world, I can't recommend anything more than this. I really did laugh and cry.

_childDocuments_.review: It´s not a bad game. I understand what they are trying to do here and it´s pretty cool. However, as a fan of the ´tactics´ genre I cannot fall in love with Wintermoor Tactics Club, though I tried...The graphics are not bad but I tend not to be very critic on graphs as it usually don´t matter to me if the gameplay is good.Story is cool. They are trying to recreate those "nerd" kids that want to be something powerful instead of just the nerds, but I had the feeling that I was taken out of the fantasy part all the time, with cool characters and powerful spells. The emphasis here is on characters and story and not the combat, so dont go expecting anything crazy or complicated. Or Difficult. _childDocuments_.review: Great game! Low-stress tactics - not super duper challenging, but getting perfect grades is enough of a brain tickle to keep you entertained. Short (~10-15 hours), but a good time. Main complaints: no New Game Plus with harder battles or opportunities to see more of the writing (you make choices that customize the stories-within-a-story; it would be nice to be able to see more of them without having to start all the way over); no 'endgame' lobby where you can replay the last few special battles. It might also be nice to be able to load chapters. Great art!

_childDocuments_.review: Wintermoor tactics club is both a visual novel and a puzle game (rather than a tactics one)It is subpar in both cases, and while the writing starts great it becomes increasingly worse as the game progreses. You can find better visual novel, better tactics or puzzle games and worse of all... the combination of both.Utawarerumono (or however its written) is a better tactics game and a better visual novel. Ultimately, it's not a bad game, but its not good either. A loss of time.

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely turn-based game, with lots of references to D&D. The story is about a few students from the Tactics Club, who regularly play boardgames together. Suddenly the principal of their school orders them to fight the other clubs of the school instead, forcing them to expand their club and train their abilities.The combat is surprisingly good. Each character has a unique class, and has a selection of possible upgrades and special attacks. You can only use 3 of your characters in battle, so picking your characters and their upgrades heavily impacts your chance to win. Most of the battles are rather easy for experienced players, but the game is still fun until the end. Definitely recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: I played **Wintermoor Tactics Club** earlier this year but forgot to review it, so I thought I'd add some quick thoughts now.First off, it was fully Steam Deck compatible, which was nice. No adjustments were necessary and it was generous with the battery life as well.Alright. So....Wintermoor Tactics Club was a fun mix of Saturday Morning Cartoon graphics and feel with solid, isometric free roam gameplay and concise turn based tactical combat.The story is your group, the aforementioned Wintermoor Tactics Club, comprised of students at a boarding school with a love for tabletop RPGs is pitted against the schools other recreational clubs in snowball fights. Whoever wins the snowball fight tournament will be allowed to continue while all other activities clubs will be disbanded.With that as the backdrop, there is also a parallel story wherein a mystery surrounding the founders of their favorite TTRPG needs to be solved while an ancient evil also threatens to consume the school and must be stopped. As your group defeats other clubs, you are able to recruit new members to your club, and they adopt role playing personas which also become their characters during the turn based battles. You can use three characters in any battle, and all characters earn upgraded abilities and magical buff items as they progress. There are also training battles you can participate in to earn new items. The battles themselves are not too complicated and rely heavily on character placement and map obstacles.There was a funny reveal at the end that had me chuckling, and I thought the story in general resolved in a cool and fun way. Ultimately, this was a game with an eye towards good wholesome fun. I quite enjoyed it.I think cost to value was there for the asking price, although it's been out for a little while now, so buying it on sale is of course optimal. It took me right at 11 hours to complete with all side quests finished and only a handful of crucible/mastery battles remaining. Definitely worth a look.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Huge fan of this game! I don't normally like visual novel style gameplay as I would prefer to read a book if I'm going to read that much. However, due to the fact that it was mixed with some really fun tactical combat, I really thought that this game was quite fun. I almost 100%'ed it (missing a few S rank battles) and I don't regret it. The stories were great, the characters felt real and interesting, and I loved the ending! Make sure, if you play it, to talk to everyone in the epilogue bits!
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really delightful, wholesome game. There's a subtle (?) underlying message about inclusivity if you want it, but ultimately it's a cute Saturday morning cartoon about the Power of Friendship! The tactics are not super difficult and suffer a little from being imbalanced (I found myself using the same three characters through the game), and while you can't skip battles you can enable a god-mode to ensure you just win to get on with the story. I am slightly ashamed to admit I did not realise how wholesome the game really is so
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure if I was going to like WTC when I bought it.As it turns out, I love it. The game has some of the best YA writing I've ever seen in terms of theming and messages, and in a way that feels very modern and aware of what the world is like today. The world and the characters are engaging, and the strategy combat is light and approachable, and good for people like myself who don't tend to get too heavy into the genre.The only QoL adjustment I think I would want to see if a chapter select menu for trophy hunting... and even that, there's an abundant amount of auto-saves as you progress through the story to go back through.All in all, this game was a great pleasant surprise, well worth the purchase, well worth playing through. Great job team!
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: The artwork is absolutely delightful, the writing is better than most RPGs, and the game lasts just about the right amount of time to avoid reaching the point where the limited mechanics would start to feel repetitive. If you're looking for challenging turn-based tactical warfare, this isn't it, but if you just want a heartwarming and slightly goofy story combined with battles you'll rarely have to save-scum your way through, Wintermoor Tactics Club is well worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Wintermoor Tactics Club is not a game that will wow you with its combat system, or art style, or storytelling. All of those aspects are good, don't get me wrong, but they aren't the crux of this game. Where this game shines is not in any of its technical aspects but rather the heart it brings to its wonky coming-of-age story. This is a game that's approachable, interesting, unexpected, and will try to restore a bit of whatever faith in humanity you still have in these troubled times. There's something for most types of strategy gamers here. Those who come for the story will find a pleasing change of tone and pace. Those who come for the gameplay will find their tactical insights rewarded. Perhaps the most interesting aspect of the game is for those who approach it with tabletop gaming experience, as this is what's at the core of Wintermoor Tactics Club's vision. One part celebration and one part examination, Tactics Club touches on a broad array of topics from creative freedom and community among players to tricky terrain like gatekeeping, competitiveness, elitism, and inclusion. A playful bite-sized romp with some though-provoking perspectives and zany twists, Wintermoor Tactics Club is a must-play for anyone with even a passing interest in turn-based strategy titles or tabletop gaming.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed this game immensely; a fun story, entertaining characters and a unique art style. I also really enjoyed the tactical turn-based combat, particularly toward the end when you have lots of different abilities and there's no obvious best strategy. In the final battle I even used one of the characters which I'd completely discounted previously as being too weak. I also liked the side quests and optional challenges since you can tell that there's been real thought put into them and they aren't just tacked on like in a lot of triple A games. Would recommend to anyone who enjoyed Persona or XCOM
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, a short and sweet RPG.  7/10The tactical portion of the game is simple enough that those not used to such games can pick it up without much difficulty.  For those players who are used to tactical games, such as myself, it is still intricate enough to hold your attention with only a few missions being difficult if you are trying to ace all of them. The overworld portion of the game is simple but fine, although I will admit that towards the end of the game I was starting to find it to be tedious. I wish there was an ability to pull a map and instantly travel to a different building instead of having to walk to the exit of the one you are currently in. If such a feature does exist I never figured it out or found it. At any rate that's more of a personal gripe than anything else.  The story is quaint, in a young adult novel sort of way. if you are purchasing this game for your pre-teen or teenager you can rest assured that they will learn some nice life lessons. If you are an adult, the story can seem a little childish at times. If you take it for what it is, you'll enjoy it. For the characters that do get fleshed out, they are likeable, especially your party/club members. Even the students who are just around give enough of a middle or high school halcyon days vibe. The music is nice, and you will likely find yourself humming the academy's tune as you are going about your day. The sound effects are on par. My biggest issue is that they get reused for clearly different attacks. WIhat is there is passable, i just wish there was more variety. In short, the game knows itself. It presents its' gameplay and story without overstaying it's welcome (much). For those new to RPGs I would say this is not a bad introduction, for those used to the genre, its a nice short romp.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished this amazing game. I recommend not using any guides for this one (even if you're the type who usually does) as this is more of a puzzle game than tactics RPG. Make no mistake, it's challenging to get top marks on all levels, especially if you don't use guides.Nothing missable, and overall a great experience. No replay value, but looks to be deliberately designed that way.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: It's a simple, but loving game. It's short (~6 hrs), and not specially hard. Most of the good this game has goes from the "visual novel" part, rather than the "tactics" part (too easy). Anyway, nowadays it's very uncommon to  me to even finish a game (most of them doesn't keep my attention for more than a couple of hours). Anyway, loved the story and the characters :)
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game, very fairly practiced. You get an 8-hour campaign. I was happy to play it, brought back memories of final fantasy tactics and similar games I've played in my childhood. Notice that the story is targeting children, so it gets cringy a lot.... My only complain is that the tactical depth of the game isn't that much. But again, this is an extremely fairly priced game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Wintermoor Tactics Club is a delightful combination of the Turn-based Tactics and Visual Novel genres, both in the form of a hard-as-you-want-it game of hand-drawn art and clever writing. You take the roles of a group of kids at a boarding school who play a form of Dungeons & Dragons, all brought together by the fact that other cliques and their own anxieties have ostracized them from other kids. Brought together under one banner, that of the Tactics Club, they find ways to apply the lessons they learned in their games to real life.Despite the game being more similar to a puzzle game in some ways (the characters don't really level up, so much as they get new abilities and specialized equipment), it never crossed the bridge from Challenging to Impossible. Each level starts with allowing you to placeWhat really surprised me was the willingness of the writers to do more than just make a tactics game, though.  Within Wintermoor's halls I discovered a dark mystery, as well as several characters in need of help. Though you start with only three, others joined my group as the game went on and like normal kids (and D&D characters) they didn't just slot into the team without issues. Through side quests and dialogue, I found out more about them, and wanted to make it work. None of the side quests really felt forced, and some even had some excellent examples of real-world issues (making friends, getting over yourself, anxiety) that were handled with equal amounts of humor and heart. I'm nearing up on the end of the game, I think, after about 10 hours of play, and I wish I had taken my time. The music, the characters, the writing...it's all been wonderful. I look forward to seeing what other amazing works this team comes out with in the future, and am really glad I jumped on it early to have a good time. I highly recommend this game as a relaxing, fun, and very enjoyable Tactics-lite game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: This is the most wholesome gaming experience I've ever had. Seriously. This game is just so, so PURE and beautiful and lovely I want to hug it and kiss its forehead. It's not a hardcore tactical game - I'm a veteran of this sort of SRPG games and let me tell you, it is not Fire Emblem on Maddening - but, well. I don't think it would be better if it was harder. With the current difficulty (for me it's "I sometimes need two tries to get a perfect mission clear") it just makes it all the cozier and lovelier and sweeter.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: The captivating tabletop story, interesting characters and charming art are undoubtedly the highest selling points of the game.The turn-based combat is solid enough to keep you entertained as you go and I recommend you to try and clear everything you can to unlock all the skills for the characters.You should think of it as a visual novel complemented with a satisfying dose of tactical RPG.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really good. The entire idea of it to begin with is great, and when you combine that with the underlying message of finding where you belong, and being able to bond with others is executed well. Using pseudo d&d as a tool for bonding with others is the main crux of the plot, with the gameplay being fun combat puzzles. Good ♥♥♥♥
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Simple tactics game wrapped inside a visual novel about diversity and inclusion. Starts out easy, then started to get challenging until I realized I missed something important: the enemies tell you who they are going to target next turn and why (e.g., closest, fewest hit points, etc.). They will ignore a character right next to them in order to get to their target. Once I used that information the game became trivial, other than the final few battles.I enjoyed it. Simple, but entertaining. 80's and D&D references were fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: The tactical part was pretty simple and constantly felt constrained in terms of actual decisions, but it wasn't bad per se.  I kept wishing for fights that let me play with more than 3 characters at a time or on bigger maps that would justify that, but alas, no.  The requirements to S-rank every fight can also be quite aggravating, especially since 1) there's no way to see what the requirements are within battle to see how close you can be to par and 2) using X tactical powers in a fight was really annoying for some fights since they would end before I had the opportunity to use the 2-3 that the game wanted me to make.What ultimately makes this worth playing is A) it's relatively short and B) the characters and overall message of the story are both pretty good.  Nothing mindblowing or anything, but it's just really pleasant and charming and I don't think the world is oversatured with stories about the need for and power of empathy, so why not enjoy one?
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Jesus H Christ this is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ delight to play. Just complicated enough to scratch that tactical itch, with an easy difficulty curve and settings to adjust. But that's not what made me love this game. Rarely do I finish a game and feel happy that I made it through the story. Maybe satisfied, or sort of 'oh that happened cool'. Perhaps a sense of sadness its over. This made me feel geniunly happy I got a chance to experience it. IF you get the chance, play this now.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Oh my gosh, this game is so cute and funny! A lot of games that try to be "comedic" fall flat, but the quirk levels in this game just work. The in-game world is small enough that the "missions" on the world map get a bit tedious, what with having to go from one place to another place, then back to the first place, but all the dialogue is so fun that it barely counts as a quibble. The characters' personalities are all unique, the tactical battles are interesting and again the player characters all do something completely different, and the story being an homage to D&D is just so meta and cool. It is pretty short for this kind of game, but there are side-challenges that you can complete to stretch out the fun. Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Wintermoor Tactics Club (WTC) is a delightful strategy game with a fun story. It's wholesome, impactful, and the characters are immersive (yes, both the ridiculous ones and the 'normal' ones that YOU, the player, may sympathise with most). I'll get into hours invested near the end.As someone who dabbles sin the odd turn-based tactics game, but not too frequently outside of the big regular ones (Divinity, Civ, XCOM), things were easy to understand and the gameplay loops and concepts were never too much. On the other hand, as someone who HAS played the games aforementioned, I can say that things never stayed still long enough to make the combat dry and undeserving.There are additional things you can explore and do, and you can challenge yourself to perform better in the combat (beat it without X damage, X deaths, having Y character do X damage in a turn, etc.) throughout the campaign that features repeatable battles. Additionally, you there are challenge scenarios available to the player if they want to level their characters up or unlock a certain spell for them to use.And that's the other thing: the player progression.The story is fairly linear and character-driven (well), but there are additional side quests or things to explore that can help you on your journey. Some of the things I unlocked I never used, but as a completionist at heart, it made me happy to know that there were extra things for me to do.As you can see, I have 6.9 (nice) hours put into the game. But I guarantee you that unless you're a speedy perfectionist like me, you'll have many more hours. I beat Horizon: Zero Dawn with all side activities and the main story completed within 30 hours, while taking pauses to make videos for it. In other words -- I play very fast, and my play hours into games don't equal the average play time you'll get out of it.Lastly, yes, I did receive this for free, but it has no bearing on my review -- I was a .I don't really review many games, because not a lot of games are impactful to me, same with movies, tv shows, etc.. But when I am impacted, I get really excited because it does generally take a lot. So please, take a look into WTC. It's a fantastic game and I can't wait for more from the dev team.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: It's a neat idea, but the combat is too easy to be interesting. Enemies broadcast their targeting priority, which would be fine except that they're so brainlessly locked into that priority that they won't attack at all if they can't hit their preferred target. This means you can just stand so their target is at the back and they'll all conga line in front of your lead unit without attacking, which sets them up to all get killed by the main character's chain lightning spell the next turn. Add in some enemies that also have nonsensical priorities (*highest* HP?) and I just didn't find it satisfying to win these battles. Admittedly I didn't play for very long, but there's nothing in the mechanics, screenshots, or other reviews to suggest it's going to change much.The story seemed like it's going for the "everyone is a caricature" thing that's common in high school stories. I'm lukewarm on that, but mileage may vary. I obviously didn't play enough to evaluate the story beyond the initially cliched characters. Give it a try if the story appeals to you or if you're new to tactics games. It wasn't for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Want to experience the highs and lows of high school in a special way? It was hard enough for Alicia at the famed Wintermoor Academy before the Principal declared a snowball war between clubs! Now her club's only hope is to transform from nerdy nobodies into fantasy heroes. Unravel a reality-bending mystery with your friends and test your strategic mettle against an avalanche of colorful characters. And remember! High School is all about learning and making friends!Wintermoor Tactics Club is a very charming, turn-based game about (essentially) a D&D club tackling a real life adventure. There's an underlying message about inclusivity and being true to yourself, but ultimately it's a cute Saturday morning cartoon type of game about the Power of Friendship! The tactics part of the game is not overly difficult, but some parts of it can offer a slight challenge.The game offers a huge emphasis on characters and story, though the combat is also important. It's a wonderful little game that I spent a good chunk of time in, and I think it's fully worth it in the end. The story was intriguing and kept me on the edge of my seat, where as the characters were all lovely and unique, with their own little quirks and styles.The game is very much worth it even at full price. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Wintermoor Tactics Club is a fairly simple and easy but still enjoyable tactics game.Story and Characters:Wintermoor Academy's principal orders all the student clubs to participate in a snowball tournament, with defeat spelling the dissolution of your club. The tabletop tactics club comes to realize they can incorporate their tactics know-how into their fights, and fight to win in between tabletop game sessions and uncovering the truth on why the tournament had to occur. The story is lighthearted in tone and is quite short, at least compared to much more longer contemporaries, but contains likable enough characters to carry the story to its end. Gameplay:Outside of the visual novel elements for the story, most of the game's combat, be it snowball fight or tabletop battle, takes place as an isometric grid based game, similar to something like Final Fantasy Tactics. Wintermoor Tactics Club, with its lack of tactics game staples like items or even leveling, feels more like a gateway game into the genre rather than its pinnacle. The game's fights tend to be easy, with the actual challenge being completing a battle in metrics such as minimal damage or turns taken, and you'll have to mix and match character loadouts to make the most of your kit.Technical:Wintermoor Tactics Club is reasonably polished, but still has some flaws. It crashed for me a few times, which is extremely odd for both an indie game and a game in this sort of genre. Several quality of life features, like more easily swapping the place of characters during placement or more easily selecting a tile behind a character would have been very helpful to me. None of these were enough to prevent me from finishing the game however.TLDR: Wintermoor Tactics Club is not a very challenging strategy game, but is very welcoming to newcomers of the genre and uses its lighthearted story and decent enough characters to carry itself to its end.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: So far, Wintermoor Tactics Club has been a delight!+ Fun puzzle-combat that feels fresh each fight+ Well written characters and scenario+ "Kids playing games" is our favorite genre of game!+ Post fight score cards are fun to max out+ Each sidequest feels rewarding and nicely made- The combat hasn't been challenging yet, and it's relatively easy to get perfect scores- There's a bit of quest-log-itis, where one gets in to a mindless trance of talking to people to move quests forward- Lots of scene transitions
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: This review is specially made for those who like to get all the achievements in games (minor spoilers ahead).Wintermoor Tactics Club is an indie low budget point and click visual novel with turn-based tactics combat. You will explore the world, complete quests and side quests and battle monsters and enemy teams.The story takes place in a college where magic events are taking place and where there are a lot of different student clubs. The one you belong to is the Tactics club where everyone plays D&D, and you and your teammates will have to figure out what is wrong. The side quests offer insight into the motivations of the secondary characters and their motivations and personalities. The graphics and animations are where the low budget of the game can be seen more clearly: while not being terrible, the hand drawn backgrounds and characters aren’t very elaborate or detailed and the walking animation of the main character is very choppy… still, you’ll get used to it quickly and it's not that bothersome. There are 3 different types of heroes you can play with initially, but more will be available as the story progresses. The same is true for the abilities they can use, but to unlock some of them you have to complete mastery battles. Regarding difficulty, the game will be very easy for a turn-based tactics veteran, especially in the beginning, where getting S, SS, or SSS ranks can be done at your first try without much effort. Later on I had to restart some battles to pick the optimal team, but after that getting a good rank was almost always guaranteed, so you don’t have to worry about getting the rank related achievement.    29 Achievements. 8 hours, with a guide just for one or two last achievements. Easy, most battles will be easy to finish with a S rank or better. Easy, most are not missable as long as you keep saving often, but two require completing tasks that are spread out in several chapters:. Wintermoor Tactics Club is an interesting indie low budget visual novel set in a college where magic events are happening. The turn based combat is fun and there are a lot of tactical options but not many different kinds of enemies and most battles end up being too easy to be a challenge. Still, it’s an enjoyable game if you like the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Not done yet, but I'm almost there. It's a great story that's about the experience of playing D&D when you were young. Salt shakers for minis, managing group conflicts, writing stories that will excite your friends. It's clear that a lot of love went into this game, and it's funny to boot. Combat is really solid, and the character build options are pretty varied.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: I was expecting a cute little tactics game, and instead I've found one of my favourite gems of all time. Simply put the writing is absolute perfection. The side quests and characters are all brilliantly thought out, have their own motivations and feelings, the tactics gameplay usually feels fun and fair and achievable. And Alicia is just the perfectly characterised teenage nerd; oblivious, generous, clever, with an excellent bookshelf.  I don't know how this game ends, but I am itching to find out.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: For tactics game short and sweet but not too short (I got like 3+ hours from having game paused due to being interrupted while playing :p), it has its cheesy moments but lot of heart, its more of story about D&D/roleplaying and how it can help people. It does have some unity data leak slowdowns though, but yeah enjoyable game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: I must admit I initially picked this up because of the art and also that it was said to be D&D-inspired. But it ended up so much more than that. Not only everything beautifully drawn, but the narrative has so many layers to it because, to an extent, every character significant - emphasised by how every single character has a little written epilogue post-WTC. I find Alicia so relatable in how she writes her stories via campaigns to reach out to people through the love of tabletop gaming, which reminded me to why I loved writing so much. Really, I couldn't recommend this game enough!
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: This game caters well to teens, given its themes and difficulty level. For the older or more experienced turn-based tactics player, I can recommend this for when you're craving to scratch the itch but don't have a lot of energy. It's often very close to feeling like a puzzle game but, thankfully, does not really cross that line.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: With a charming art style and a entertaining premise, this game fails to deliver in a few minor errors. The tactics portion of the game feels a bit underwhelming, with small, simple maps and a lack of options that limits actual "tactics" However, the story is engaging and enjoyable, and as the game progresses a few new options are unlocked through challenge maps which provide a bit of depth to the core mechanic. Overall, an enjoyable game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: There are some issues with the game. For one the turnbased combat is way to easy. The maps are always really small and so tactical positioning rarely required. The only way to pump up difficulty is to decrease player health which is really the worst way to make it more difficult. The over arching story is ok. But the ingame story (the d&d campaign) is a complete mess. You are constantly unlocking new characters which all need their own tutorial missions that constantly interupt the flow of the game game. As such the made up ingame story doesn't matter and I eventually just skipped through it. So yeah, as a visual novel with very light game play interludes it is ok. As a tactical rpg it is trash.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Thumbs up! This was a nice mix of a visual novel and turn-based tactics. I liked the overall story and experimenting with different combinations of characters in the battles. It’s shame they never made a sequel.The Wintermoor Tactics Club consists of three high school students who just want to play Curses and Catacombs, a reference to Dungeons and Dragons. However, all the school clubs are forced to compete in a snowball fight tournament. At first, the tactics club doesn’t want to be in it, but they then realize that their knowledge of tactics could help them win. Eventually they discover the real reason for the tournament.The visual novel aspect mostly consists of walking around the campus and talking to other students. Side quests usually involve passing messages from one student to another. Students tend to stay in the same spot, so it’s that not that hard to find somebody you’re looking for. The travel map is very helpful. It takes you from building to building, and shows where there are side quests. You can skip the side quests if you want, but you can get rewarded with bonus items that help in combat. Also, there are achievements for completing all the side quests.The turn-based aspect consists of roleplaying brief skirmishes. The snowball fights are shown in the same way as Curses and Catacombs battles. The original three club members play as a mage, a paladin, and a rogue. As the story progresses, you get new club members. You can only have three members in a battle though, so figuring out which characters to include is important. As you might have guessed, I kind of like rogues and the rogue has some rather useful abilities. He has a grappling hook, so he can pull targets closer. He can also shove targets away. This can put a monster in range of an attack from a different character. You can actually look at the monsters and see who their target is. Monsters have several possibilities to choose from. For example, least health, most health, or the closest. A monster who is targeting the character with the least health won’t attack anybody else even if they are in range. So, sometimes it helps to move the character with the least health away from the actual fighting. The battles might seem on the easy side if you’re familiar with turn-based tactics, but this game was meant to be accessible to newcomers. The biggest negative about the game is the missable achievements. Just Kitten Around requires playing nearly the whole game again if you missed it the first time. That includes the epilogue/closing credits. Fan Favorite is not as extreme, but it does require replaying a few chapters. There are guides available if you want to get all the achievements on one playthrough, but I usually like to first try without spoilers and see how much I can figure out myself. Note. I did get a key for this game, but not from the developers.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great, light, cozy indie experience, that hits on some tactical play, good storytelling, and memorable aesthetics. While I wish it had a little more depth to its tactical elements (or at least, made all party members a little more viable in play), I think this game shines by the brevity of its combat with its snappy dialogue.Delivered in its episodic format, it's well worth the price - especially if you're a fan of visual novels or tactics games.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Wintermoor Tactics Club is a fun and charming short tactics game - and one that I can recommend without reservation.  Its game play is easy to get into, friendly to genre newcomers, and lays down some solid game fundamentals which it builds upon throughout the 12 hour or so game time.  The story is also very engrossing with enjoyable characters, many of whom show development over the course of the campaign.  Overall, this is a great game and one I hope more folks play.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: A relatively simple but enjoyable turn-based tactics game. The writing is sharp and enjoyable, and the characters are quirky and fun. I enjoyed the game's message of positivity and inclusiveness in gaming. The battles themselves are not terribly difficult - I didn't "lose" a battle, although I did replay a number of them to get the best rating. The game is not overly long (took me about 18 hours for a full playtrhough, including replaying battles) which I appreciate, as this is one of the few games I have actually completed recently. Overall, I would say it is worth the price of admission, and I'll be interested to see what the designers work on next.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Wintermoor Tactics Club is what happens when you tell folks it'll be a game about tactics, and then you reveal a game about compassion and childhood courage and loving yourself even when you're not sure you deserve it. And a cat calendar that gets its own epilogue. There's so much to appreciate here. I hope this game encourages new people to feel welcome at a gaming session, both online and tabletop : ) Pick this up!
