_childDocuments_.review: After getting frustrated playing XCOM 2, I swore off of turn-based tactics. I was  Chryssalids and timers. However, when I saw Wintermoor Tactics Club and the praise it was getting, I decided to take a look. I not only liked the concept, with turn-based battles taking place at a boarding school in the midst of a D&D-like game (and later in the midst of snowball fights), but I heard that it was a more simplified and accessible take on turn-based tactics.For the most part, this is correct. There are fewer decisions both during combat and outside of it than in a game like XCOM, and to be honest, I mostly didn't miss them. However, there are challenge missions that require a very particular strategy and approach to complete. Although I did most of them, I didn't finish them all.The story that wraps around these combat encounters was satisfying as well, and was enhanced by the gorgeous visual design of the characters and setting. I went to a residential high school myself and remember my peers playing D&D in their dorm rooms, so much of the setting felt oddly familiar. In many ways, Wintermoor Tactics Club is a story about fitting in and finding a home away from home. However, I didn't like Alicia's habit of trying to trying to deliver some sort of proxy therapy through personalized D&D-style adventures. While it's certainly possible for us to learn what we're capable of and test out new ways of being/acting through role-playing (certain therapists, such as Katie Lear, specialize in offering D&D therapy), it felt "off" that these lessons would be offered by a fellow high school student. Why exactly would Alicia be any wiser than her peers? Although this practice comes back to bite her on at least one occasion, the game never really conveys that this is inappropriate. Even so, I generally liked the dialogue and writing in the game.But on balance, my experience with the game was much more positive than negative. If you're looking for a fun, turn-based tactics experience that is less demanding and punishing than your XCOMs or Battletechs, Wintermoor Tactics Club has you covered. Give those "Dorklings" what for!
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: Two parts, the visual novel elements and the tactics battle elements.VN:Characters are one note but charming, the writing is pretty good, and I found myself laughing a lot.  You'll do a lot of talking to get all the upgrades in the game, but I didn't really mind all that much.Tactics Battle:This is not a hard game until it is.  Particularly if you get the various upgrades as they become available, the story missions in particular are a breeze.  It's a nice way to sit back and relax.  That said, when the difficulty spikes, it spikes hard.  The last two Master Missions in particular are far more challenging than the rest of the missions in the game.It feels like certain missions were designed to be done with certain characters using certain upgrades.  When I got stuck, it felt I only had to keep switching until I found that magic combination.I found the Hellion character to feel notably stronger than the rest of the party.  Outside of the last mastery missions that felt like they needed a particular setup, the Hellion never left the party and contributed more than the other characters.At the end of the day, I really enjoyed my playthrough of the game.  It may seem like I have a lot of critiques about the Battle part of the game, but its only because I got into it.  While I would have liked to see a more even ramp up in difficulty and more equal characters, that didn't detract from the game enough for me not to like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Although the game feels somewhat plain at first it really opens up into a marvelous story with solid puzzle gameplay.The art and music are distinctive enough to give the game a unique feel, although many of the characters are presented as being somewhat ordinary at first the consistency and depth to their writing is really there. The way the story is paced along with how well it keeps the conceptual themes of the plot relevant are exceptional. Admittedly the ending felt overly mythical but beyond that the writing as a whole is superb.Although it is presented as a tactical role playing game it's more puzzle based. Each combat scenario feels much more like a somewhat flexible puzzle than an actual combat encounter. It's still fun and engaging but it's not what the game is labelled as. There is some customization along with different selectable characters though.Some of the hiccups in the game as a whole included the transition between a tournament fight ending and the protagonist sleeping being too abrupt, character sprites don't have legs and you can see that whenever they bounce up during a conversation, the very few time gated side quests are quite annoying, ultimate abilities generally don't feel worth using and having to reach a certain quantity of special ability uses per fight to get a good rank was bad. Optimal strategies can be formed which complete a stage fast enough that players don't even have enough time to charge their special multiple times, so reducing the players rank for not using it basically punishes the player for being too efficient. Especially since rank is also based on speed, so having to balance getting the speed rank and charging specials up for the special rank is an arbitrary balancing act. It's not required since rank accomplishments are cumulative so players can try to same stage multiple times to reach different rank thresholds, but it's necessary for successfully getting max rank in one try. Consequently the characters with the highest mobility and damage are generally the most used ones since it's needed to complete the level as fast as possible to get a good rank.Considering that it's a linear campaign the length of the game is solid compared to the price; with a fantastic story, lots of great dialogue and engaging puzzle combat.

There is a character for everyone to be able to connect with.If you enjoy story-driven games with deep character interactions (and the occasional TTRPG session), wintermoor Tactics Club will be perfect for you. Defintiely a big recommendation from me.

_childDocuments_.review: Warning and TLDR: I don't have many nice things to say about this. If there was a "Mixed feelings" rating then that would be my choice. Recommended by a barely passing margin but recommended nonetheless if you're fine with a simple tactical experience with questionable optimization, clunky interface, subpar writing and an irritating amount of lost potential in the art department. Wintermoor Tactics Club is about an ever-growing group of high school students with varying degrees of passion for fantasy and role-playing through a stripped down D&D campaign as part of their after-school club activities and applying their collective experience in life's daily whatevers, including a decently sized tournament in which every other school club takes part. 	The story is either acceptable or sucks major throbbing wiggly Johnsons, depending on how much you're able to turn your brain off at the time of playing. Sadly I'm unable to run my ♥♥♥♥ on low-power consumption mode and I tend to overthink ♥♥♥♥ so I had the displeasure of processing the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I was reading through and it wasn't great. As such, I'll just give you the short of it. It feels as if whoever wrote it made an active effort to make every character more interesting than the one you're actually playing as, which is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up because every other character is archetypal and conceptually dry. Aside from maybe smirking at like 3 Twitter-esque gags don't except the dialogue to be engaging or funny.	But yeah enough about the story, who gives a ♥♥♥♥? What about the gameplay?	Meh. 	The gameplay consists of the actual tactical rpg combat shtick and the hub exploration which is really just a point and click experience on its own. The combat is just good enough for me not to dread booting this game up and for the casual unfortunate game enjoyer stumbling upon this mess it shouldn't be too much of a pain since it's easy enough but not totally ♥♥♥♥♥♥ proof.	Here's the problem though. The account from which I'm laying down my jaded old man ramblings (which you shouldn't heed btw but you're already in deep) was made out of my autistic urge to see integer values go up. This is my achievement hunting account, so I played with the intention to 100% it. This game ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ kicks bricks for achievement hunting. It's either because the game is too piss easy or because the devs simply didn't think some literal who on Steam would try to milk it dry but God is this ♥♥♥♥ a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ drag. Being efficient at level clearing is genuinely detrimental for getting the medals you need for 100%. If you have more than two synapses firing in your brain at any time, then it's likely you can beat most of these levels in a turn or two, which means you don't get to use your super tactic moves or whatever, WHICH FOR SOME ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ REASON ARE A REQUIREMENT FOR GETTING ALL THE MEDALS. So here I am essentially skipping turns because the game punishes me for being good at it.	I'm getting too riled up so I'll try to machine gun the rest of my thoughts on this before I punt it somewhere back in my mind where I'll hopefully not have to reach for. The art direction is genuinely good, which works against it because there's not enough actual art for me to enjoy it. Like some character designs are well thought of and clearly build upon with passion and good ideas but then some of them are just lazy carbon copies. It's not consistent in any way either. Like the three main characters have some pseudo idle animations but then the rest of the squad doesn't. Some characters fit the style and then some look like family guy extras. The walking animation consists of four boring frames which is a travesty considering how much walking and talking to people the game expects me to do. There's next to no enemy variety in the art department. Like yeah I get it, they're broke school kids doing their D&D club activity with some old miniatures that they keep using despite not fitting into the setting, while imagining they're something else. They even do the classic salt shaker as enemy joke haha ♥♥♥♥ you. You have separate sprites for the characters in their fantasy canon, so why is it that you can't have fitting enemy designs as well?	The more I write about it, the more I feel like urging you to stay as far away as possible, but I'll refrain from budging from my original rating.	If there's more to add it's the possibly cluttered coding, where running the game for extended periods of time starts to slow down loading times drastically and the amateurish interfacing in combat, where the UI might be intrusive and cover your vision of some tiles in range of attack and whatnot. 	Possibly the actual worst thing about this game is that not only does it not actively make fun of furries, you actually have to take one in your party and put up with his ♥♥♥♥. Make of that what you will. Hello I like to bleed games dry and get each and every achievement they have to offer. With this I have [1] 100% completed game. May there be many more.

_childDocuments_.review: Wintermoor Tactic Club is one of those games I wanted to love, but a lot of the times it just didn't hit the spot.Negative: The travel function between areas made me groan with frustration when I'd pop into an area for 1 minute, then out again. _childDocuments_.review: Wintermoor Tactics Club aims to find the sweet spot between visual novel and turn-based tactics.  While the writing is fairly clever and the concept is fairly-well polished, this love song to high-school nerdery meets supernatural conflict doesn't  quite manage to do either of them as well as certain other titles.The GUI is intuitive and lean but well-designed for what it is; I'd have preferred a quest menu to the text in the bottom right but can live with it.  Art is fairly good but the walking animation and "go to sleep" animation for the main character looks somewhat janky.  The music is good enough for this sort of title but not really what I came for anyway.The "tactics" sequences representing play of the tabletop roleplaying game or the game's 'combats' are fairly well done, and are generally fun, but many of these levels play a lot more like simple chess puzzles than what I'd think of as actual "turn based tactics."  The battles could be played a few different ways and the number of potential character and power combinations is enough to be interesting but the game's replay-ability is minimal at best.  Overall, a little too casual for me, but that's okay.The writing starts off very good, it's fairly humorous, and clearly having a little bit of fun with the setting.  Clearly a lot of effort went into it, but degrades around the halfway point of the game and continues to get worse.  A lot of plot twists were fairly obvious, later characters start and remain fairly one-dimensional, and the last two chapters are about 80% too eye-rollingly woke.  Whomever thought the furries-as-a-stand-in was subtle was very, very mistaken. While I was wishing for voice acting in the early part of the game, I was thankful there wasn't any by the end.  While I won't go so far as to say I wish I didn't buy it, I sort of just wanted the game to be over and to move onto the next thing; not unlike my personal high school experience.Heads Will Roll is a better VN with combat, Symphony of War is a better turn-based tactics game, and Legionary's Life is a good example of trying to land in the middle of those two.  Wintermoor Tactics Club, while okay, isn't as good as any of those three.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: The art is passable (characters don't blink, for example) and the majority of the tactics are honestly easier and more generic than expected for a tactics game. But a group of kids in the 80's wouldn't have had access to a variety of miniatures, would they? So of course the monsters would be similar from fight to fight. Of course they would put most of the effort into the PCs and the writing, because that's what makes sense for a tabletop club from the 80's. And besides, the snowball fights are unique enough to make up for that.All that leads in to what makes this game great: the compelling characters. The game really pushes you to understand what each character's motivations, foibles, and idiosyncrasies are. Each piece of gear, each part of their kit, ties into some aspect of who they are as people. The writing is competent enough to convey everything you need to know, while still being funny. Especially notable are the inclusion of various queer/racial minorities (because people like that existed back in the 80's, too) as well as the portrayal of Colin. Play the game and you'll see what I mean.There are some bugs! The game can crash if left idling for too long then changing scenes, and occasionally attacks will display or work incorrectly. But most of the time the game runs smoothly, and nothing persists past a restart.Overall: good game, simple mechanics but complex writing... like the AD&D it pulls from

_childDocuments_.review: All this doing you could describe by one word - primitive. Everything here is out of date. At the first glance I could say that graphics resembled me about old Anastasia cartoon, but without attention to details. It is just pictures here. Not cinematic scenes and even no animations. Like in visual novels. And, you know, I had a feeling about of drawn game from 2000th. As the Freddy Fish for example. But Wintermoor Tactics Club lost in that comparison.Plot is awful and silly. Principal of Wintermoor school has decided that students live too carefree and easy. So, he arranged a snowball battle royal between school clubs, where only one must survive and reborn as an ultimate club. Defeated clubs will no longer exist. Why? You'll know if you play the game. Our heroes are members of board games club, and they use their tactical skills from DnD sessions (here it is CnC) to fight with other clubs. It feels as stupid as it is in fact. Quests here are like "go there and talk to somebody". And here we came to TBS element of the game. If that's what you're here for - NEVER buy it. Really. Worst tactical thing I ever saw. As simple as that and boring. Tactics here only in the title of the game. I was disappointed when played the first battle. It's not a main feature here, and even not a second plan thing. Seems developers wanted to make a visual novel and attached TBS element for nothing. I wasn't interested, but bored.Music tracks are well-made. But there aren't enough. Just approximately 10 melodies, which you'll hear for 10 hours about. I was tired because of them after 2-3 hoursAn atmosphere here has vibes of frosty morning of winter student campus near Christmas holidays. And it really does. Even if the game disappointed me in other moments, here I felt the presence of New Year celebrations.  Christmas spirit feels better in the second part of the game. You can buy it in December. Probably it'll help you catch the right mood. The question is - will you endure a boring game for it? Is it worth for you?Verdict. I love board games, and that could be fun to play because of its theme. But wasn't. UnEpic was much better.  Here we've got a visual novel with artificial gameplay and dull story.P.s. _childDocuments_.review: This game is fun for it's nostalgia that it inspired in memories of my own real life in and around my school age years and how much I also had friends that enjoyed the same things and how outcast that enjoyment seemed to make us. It's fantasy, but based very much in real life and it's subverted into making real life into something it isn't. It's a clever device that I thought was fun. As far as other games like this in genre, it's far less complex than I am typically attracted too, and I do see that as a draw back, as with the limited exploration and the complete absence and I mean ZERO customization and that is taken to an extreme when you see very early they don't even have gear in this game. It's annoying and feels like a hugely stupid thing not to include. I do like this game, I have enjoyed it but It would be SOOOOOOOO much better if they had just included the standard elements that are available in literally every other game of the type. I think it's even fair to say that the things they leave out are what makes games like this identifiable and beloved and intentionally leaving them out seems willfully ignorant and with no clear benefit for doing so deliberately. if you like games like this but would prefer them with out any of the most interesting parts 10/10 if your an actual person who likes games like this 4/10. If you try to enjoy parts of everything you play and and appreciate it based on the merit of it's story and like the genre I would recommend this. I don't regret buying it but I think alot of refunds would be requested if this game was more widely known. Persona score 5/10 without prejudice.

_childDocuments_.review: Wintermoor Tactics Club is a console ported E-book with a lightweight turn based tactical combat game tacked on.  I guess on the upside, I was very surprised to see these developers did the right thing and hired an artist.  The hand drawn art for the E-book sections is very well done.  That's good stuff.  Unfortunately, that's in the E-book section, so let's all go over this again... developers must learn to tell their story through the mechanics and narrative of the game itself.  Gamers don't want to be drowned in walls of text... or worse, endlessly click through text to try get to the game to find out if the game is any good or not.The turn based combat portion does work, but it's pretty shallow stuff, of secondary importance to the E-book component.  Unfortunately, my gaming rig is not a Kindle.  This isn't nearly as good as more serious turn based strategy games, games where the gameplay is front and centre. From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.Because this is designed for consoles, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the inferior console gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the console-centric developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for consoles forces upon a game.  Once more, console peasants have made gaming worse for everyone.This looks and feels like a mobile app, but it doesn't seem to have made it to the app stores, just consoles and PC.  It's unclear why this was put on Steam instead of the app stores it seems to have been designed for.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).  Maybe the developer just didn't understand who their target audience is. Regardless, for all intents and purposes Wintermoor Tactics Club might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps. These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.Reviewing SteamDB to check how popular this game was with players reveals a surprise... there's a very healthy spike in player counts for the game.  But this only appears around the same time that trading cards were applied to the game... so this is just card idlers getting their cards and moving on.  A closer look at the numbers shows the game just has a couple of players every week running up the game and idling it for cards, then deleting it.  We must ask how it benefits gamers for there to be so many games like this, with no merit as a serious game, that only generate sales from people idling and selling the trading cards.Wintermoor Tactics Club has the comically over-optimistic price of $15 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  This is also competing with over 9,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.  If this was like a $1 game (like most mobile apps should be), I might even consider a "maybe", but the pricing here is just insulting.

_childDocuments_.review: I had such a great time with Wintermoor Tactics Club! The combination of tactical gameplay with high school storytelling is unique and super charming. The characters are written with care, and each one has their own personality and backstory that make you want to get to know them better. The battles are fun and well-paced, and the whole game has this cozy, welcoming atmosphere. Whether you’re a fan of tactics games or just enjoy good storytelling, Wintermoor Tactics Club is a gem worth playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those rare games; a fast, fun, complete story that's lightweight enough to finish in a reasonable time, but heavyweight enough to challenge and engage. The narrative through-line is well-handled and the entire format of the game is structured around alternating rounds of combat and slice-of-life RPG. It doesn't overstay its welcome, nor does it drag. It last long enough to give you all the tools you'd need, and then gracefully bows out when it's shown you everything. An incredible effort and a truly wondrous game, cannot recommend it enough; a perfect shorter game.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game fun? Yes. Is it worth 20 bones? Nah. Get it on sale if you enjoy tactics games, especially if you're newer to them and want some more experience before bashing your head against Final Fantasy Tactics or Tactics Ogre.The meat of the game are grid-based tactics levels that are more like puzzles: you only have 3 characters to control and they have no more than 3 abilities each. Battles only last a few turns and are extremely easy, even if you're going for the highest possible score. The levels are bite-sized but the core gameplay is fun, especially later on when you have more characters and abilities to choose from.The other half of the game is adventuring around the school. This is not so impressive. There's only a handful of locations and you'll see most of them within 20 minutes of play. All there is to do is get sidequests, virtually all of which are "go here, talk to this person" or "and then talk to a third person (or the questgiver)" if the devs are feeling rambunctious. I quickly grew tired of these sidequests but they're how you unlock new abilities for your units.The writing is... okay. The plot's strongest moments are all in the first half, but the premise is wishy-washy and the pay-off to the mysteries is pathetic. My interest in the game bottomed out in the third act, to the point I nearly didn't finish it. Most of the characters are reasonably likable. In addition to the lack of payoff,  the writing gets steadily worse (as well as more cringe) as it goes on, with far too many characters and cliches. Nevertheless the game has enough charm, wit, and fun tactics gameplay to be worth playing for fans of the genre. I dunno if I'd recommend it to anyone else.A note to the devs: if you're going to make your game a period piece, then don't bury that fact. This game takes place in the 80s, something I was utterly unaware of until the last half-hour of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: While I think long time tactics fan will enjoy this one, it’s definitely a great starter game for the genre. _childDocuments_.name: Wintermoor Tactics Club

_childDocuments_.review: If you are a dungeons and dragons player and love tactics games, this game has a very wholesome story which plays off D&D. The game can be played over a few day being concise. The characters are lovable and endearing. I especially loved the MC of Alicia and side character Jania. Some characters can rub you the wrong way at certain parts of the story but it's part of the story. The game play is a traditional turn based combat system. Your turn and then the opponents turn. There is not a lot a depth but the simplicity and ease of understanding for a short title was perfect for me. You can utilize your favorite characters in combat in a party of 3. Each character has clear specializations. The only gripe I would have is you can see that the later characters got more cool/stronger abilities than earlier characters. I believe they are all still viable but wish that was balanced more.Overall, I recommend this great tactics RPG for any that want something quick to pick that can scratch your tactics itch.

_childDocuments_.review: Wintermoore Tactics Club is a story driven turn-based tactics game which plays out more like a point-and-click high school adventure with tactical combat on the side. There is a lot of reading, with simple tactics combat that focuses on team composition. While this can make the game feel a bit slow, and made it a slow burn for me, by the end I was enjoying this lighthearted story about inclusivity. The game really plays out in two different parts: Real world narrative “drama” and in-character fantasy combat. I’d say the split is 1/2 narrative, 1/4 team composition, and 1/4 tactical combat. You’ll spend most of your time in-game walking around the campus and talking to students to advance the story and complete little quests. There is a lot of optional side dialogue, but all of the purposeful side quests reward you with upgrades for your characters. The campus is fairly small, with 6 areas to visit on the world map. There’s no exploring, or secret chests to find. It’s all character and dialogue driven.I found the combat to focus heavily on “choosing team composition” on my first play-through. The battle maps are fairly small, and can be treated more like puzzles instead of tactical reactions to enemy AI. If you want to get S rank, you’ll need to think your moves ahead of time, and this really translates into choosing your team. On my second play-through, I was able to cruise through the prep process.If you're just trying to beat the level, there’s still reason to choose which units you’ll bring into combat. You have space for 3 members per battle. Each member can have 1-2 powers equipped to them, which can vary from damage based abilities, to passive status effects. The limitation of units and powers among all the choices really makes you think about what composition will work best for the situation.Combat is turn based: your characters act, then the enemy’s. Each party member is quite unique. Attacks are either physical or magical, and can cause lingering status ailments or buffs. There are a few tile-based persistent effects they can leave behind. There is also physical and magical defense to consider.Before a level begins, you will be presented with the map and enemies, and you will have to choose who to use, what to equip, and where to place them. Taking all of this into consideration, you can spend time planning out your moves and preparing accordingly. Most levels should only take 3-4 turns to resolve. If you don’t plan properly, it could take longer. Overall the combat is pretty simple and straight forward. There aren’t any terrain or height advantages, no cover systems, and no chance-to-miss. I feel this limited scope is appropriate for the game.While the gameplay is fun enough, and is more of an accompaniment to the story, I found I couldn’t play for more than a few levels at a time. Personally, I’m just not very interested in such a heavy focus on team composition. For example, I’m not a fan of card based games where you craft a deck and then play with it. I’d rather have a team either given to me, or pick a few characters I like to stick with. But this game really encourages you to think about who to use every time. I’m not that interested in that specific type of strategy. If you like building decks, or enjoy planning out synergies, I think you'll enjoy the otherwise simple combat.By the end, once I got familiar with everyone and had my go-to abilities, I warmed up to the combat. I found the user interface in combat to be very helpful. Movement tiles or shown in green, and attack range is shown in red. Selecting an attack and hovering it over the enemy will show who is in range and how much damage they will take. It made it very easy and intuitive to plan out a strategy.(FYI, in case you don’t notice this tool tip, you can hold shift over a green movement tile to turn it into an attack tile. I foolishly didn’t pick up on this right away, and thought I was forced to move before I could attack a space within my movement range.)One thing I didn’t like about the combat UI is that the menus that show all the info when you hover over a person can overlap the map, causing certain titles to be blocked from visibility. So sometimes you can’t see the full extent enemies can move or attack. There’s no way to pan the camera, so whatever ends up blocked is just blocked.The menus and character sheets all look like they’re written out in a book, which blends nicely with the overall aesthetic.Under options you can set player and enemy health handicaps, as well as a “no fail” mode. Controls wise, everything is done with the mouse, point and click style. Spacebar is used to speed up time, tab is used to open the character sheet, and enter is used to end turn. But overall, this is a point and click control scheme. Wintermoor Tactics Club is a lighthearted story about friendship that doesn’t take itself too seriously. For example, you and your friends are obsessed with C&C (Curses and Catacombs), which is the kind of on-the-nose charm that's used throughout. The premise is kind of ridiculous, but in a good and fun way. Clubs at this school must compete in a snowball fight tournament, and losers have their clubs disbanded. The different characters and cliques are all unique and can be rather outlandish. But overall it’s about kids saving the day by banding together. So it has a nice message, and it doesn’t mind being a little cheesy.There’s no spoken dialogue or narration, but there are text prompted grunts and gasps from the characters that add a bit to their personality. In general, everyone at the school has their own personality, even if is a simplistic or silly one. Wintermoor doesn’t really feel like a school because no one seems to take any classes. It’s more like a summer camp in the winter for kids to geek out over their niches. Like I said, it’s not too serious, but it’s pleasant and a little silly.The art style and animation is 2D and largely stiff, focusing on poses to portray character. Tactical combat is played with pieces on a board, which sort of wobble from tile to tile. The animation is minimal, and the budget shows, but the game is visually nice to look at.The SFX are pretty one-to-one with what you’re seeing happen on the screen. I did enjoy the pen-on-paper SFX for the text dialogue boxes. It was much more enjoyable to listen to instead of the digital booping and beeping that’s common. There are really no ambient soundscapes, leaving it all to the music instead, which is largely music tracks designated for certain emotions, with some catchy but repetitive battle tracks. Overall, the sound feels kind of simple, but appropriate.With a lighthearted atmosphere throughout all of its facets, I certainly felt like there was a world with characters fighting a problem and learning along the way. I think the portrayal works well, and benefits significantly by not taking itself too seriously. Simple of effective atmosphere. Wintermoor Tactics Club is a nice lighthearted adventure that celebrates nerdy RPG culture. Though it’s largely a reading-heavy experience, its cast of characters and choice of abilities makes its combat moments engaging in the larger narrative. Just be ready for some pre-planning before any action actually happens. Overall, I give it a lighthearted recommend.
