_childDocuments_.review: A gripping enough game. UI is very smooth, better than many high budget games, but do constrain your expectations for the overall experience. I would say it's probably not worth the full purchase price at this time, even for a mecha fan, due to the sort of repetitive nature of its gameplay and nothing special in the plot department. It gives the impression of not a whole lot of development (Possibly understandable with such a small devteam) followed by tons and tons of polish (Unusual for such a small devteam). It shines in the balance department, being bug-free, fantastic UI. It has some cool robots so you should pick it up on a sale.My playtime is representative of finishing the campaign and allocating no time to multiplayer or map editor so you may want to consider those in your valuation of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: WARBORN

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Maybe, it is definitly a good looking sci-fi hex-grid turn-based strategy game in anime aesthetics. You command small teams of mechs over small maps, moving and/or using their weapons and abilities every turn. Terrain gives boni and refineries generate income to purchase additional troops. There are three types of attack (kinetic, energy and explosive), and units have different defence statistics against them. This requires you to use rock-paper-scissors tactics to inflict the highest damage to your enemies. Later in the battle it is possible that your hero joins the fight. Don't let him die, though.Throughout the 40 mission campaign you play with four different factions, all having the same units but a unique hero. The story is a bit strange at first, but becomes better when you understand more of the universe. In most missions you have to wipe the enemies off the map.The game is supposed to be a Mech game, but to be honest, I first assumed that I was commanding single commando units. I thought they were just drawn big to give you a better overview when they walk through the forest or a city. Well, they are mechs, and the characters you see in the cutscenes are obviously their pilots. The game does lack options to upgrade mechs and when they receive damage they loose health points, but never an arm, cannon or a leg. So they could be just be soldiers wearing armor.A local/online 1v1 multiplayer mode allows you to play vs a friend, a skirmish mode vs the CPU, and an editor to create your own maps.Turn-based strategy game inspired by Advance Wars that is a lot of fun to play.
_childDocuments_.name: WARBORN

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely terrible!Extremely buggy, simplistic AI, TERRIBLE UI, unbalanced, and uninspired story. I love the graphics and the look of the game. It really reminds me of old school games and some anime, but you’re really better off just playing an older game, or at least a different one.  At most this game is worth $1-$2 but really just skip it.(There are many more examples, I’m just listing the ones that bothered me the most. This game isn’t worth the time to list them):Bug examples: If you have a dual monitor setup and click outside the game you usually have to force close the game because when you select the game again and click anywhere except the dead center of the game (even then sometimes) the game will minimize and you can’t get back into it.If you try to save a map in the map editor before placing start locations, you get an error telling you that you need start locations (great!), however you can never save that map even if you add the locations.  Your only option is to close everything and start again. Add the locations and then save. Even with battle animations set to skip all you have to watch animations every time a unit is destroyed.Achievements don’t trigger properly Ex: s rank on all missions does not properly fire.  I even tried playing the final mission again (yes I got s on it again) and it still didn’t fire. AI example:Enemy units that need to move one square to fire at your units just sit there on some maps.  Even if a unit can destroy yours in one shot it will always try to capture points even if you have multiple units surrounding it. So instead of you losing units you just put your guy next to the capture point and mow down the AI.The AI will just let units stay where they are and fight one at a time, in multiple situations, instead of moving and attacking.The AI doesn’t seem to know how to use abilities properly.  UI examples:You have to always hold down your left mouse button to speed up the gameplay. Instead of keeping the camera where you have it, it resets every turn to where it decides your base is and goes there.You cannot load checkpoints even though you can save them.There is no next/previous units button.  There is also no way to select unmoved units so you have to search the map to make sure you moved everything.The units don’t auto capture points if you end your turn on them accidentally(the end unit turn and capture buttons are right next to each other, I have clicked the wrong one multiple times).There are no tool tips on skills. A number of abilities just say they will apply something, like virus, overcharge ect… but the only place that tells you what those abilities do are deep in the menu under help files.  You can’t really zoom out and even if you do it forces info boxes on the top and bottom of the screen so you can’t really move around the map quickly.You can’t just select a unit and right click to move it or use a hot key, you have to first select the unit that actually click the move button then click where you want it. (IE no hotkeys for many useful things)Unbalanced: Unit balance is a joke.  It’s really sad that unit the last couple missions your commander can solo all the maps.  About 60% of the units can be one shot by a number of the other units.The buff/degen system is a joke. EX: If you cast armor, aim, and overdrive buffs on a unit and the enemy casts an armor negative instead of canceling out the armor buff it just goes negative and removes all positive buffs. As for the story…. If you like it great but I couldn’t find anything redeeming about it.
_childDocuments_.name: WARBORN

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game on Steam sale 30% discount for $17.50. It was worth it. It had a very good 41 mission campaign package with interesting story. I did like the characters. The mech design and gameplay mechanics were good. Yes, there were some issues regarding variety of units. Lack of Air or Naval units. I would have love for the pathfinders to have capture ability and even an assault mechs that could hop over mountains. Also, enemy commanders do not have commander mechs or commander powers. This was disappointing. I would have loved to see Pirate Leader or Lyssander Orswell with Commander Mechs and Power like the protagonists. I was able to create simple maps from the Map Editor. It's not as robust as Wargroove's Map Editor that allows for conditions and triggers for custom game modes and maps. I think it is ok. Overall, I had fun playing this game.
_childDocuments_.name: WARBORN

_childDocuments_.review: I usually only review a game I completed or a game which doesn´t have an ending, like it is endless or online, however I am not sure I will play this to the end.I love the idea of a simple and clean turn based mech game, really great idea, however it falls short from there.Story/narrative: Yay for a female lead on a mecha game, but sadly she goes for the whole cliche of superpowered/enhanced pilot which I highly dislike - they try to say it has counter effects to her health but meh, I like my heroes being normal people who earn everything they have through sheer effort and experience. Other characters so far seem quite bland too. The political background feels interesting with many factions but I feel it is less expored than it could.The art: Now that is my area and I think the mechs are a mixed bag - some look too industrial, others too humanoid and light to a point they don't even look like they are from the same universe - also movement is beautiful, but a bit too human at times. That being said I love the pathfinder design xD Settings and maps look nice enough.Now one thing which is hideous as hell are the character portraits, I wonder  if those were made with those bland looking face editors people used in the early 2000"s for rpgmaker games, really inexpressive.The gameplay: I like the simplicity, really do, however the game fails on prontly informing you what  each status do, or for exemple when enemies lay mines - I was wondering why enemies where shooting to the sky with their pistols and only found those were mines by stepping into them. Another issue is how easily it is to have a unit be one-shot killed - I know it happens a lot in gundam and I hated that about the franchise - you are talking really tall, heavy and expensive vehicles, they should be able to withstand some punishment, even lighter ones.The protagonist mech is tottally broken which also gets back to my issue with the plot and her being "the chosen one".So yeah, negative review, but to be fair I´d give it a five for the idea.

_childDocuments_.review: Audio: Good music, some of the sound effects are lackluster. Some weapons make sad little "pew" noises instead of something more imposing.Visual: Mostly good, the art is a bit off sometimes. In game, there is little distinction between buildings for cover and  buildings to capture. Also, the first faction you play is red, but the UI always has blue for your team's map icons and dialogue, and red for the enemy's. The other factions have other varied colors, why make the first group you play as the UI color for the enemy?Gameplay: Very reminiscent of Advance Wars. Your commanders level up, which is nice, but you get no choice in the level up process, it's on rails upgrades. And speaking of the upgrades, they aren't very exciting. +X% to Y stat makes up 90% of them. Leveling up does not grant new abilities or units, so it's not particularly exciting. Also, every commander has a super move that they can use when the super meter is filled. What sucks is that the super meter fills up more when your units get killed. So if you are doing really well and destroying lots of enemy units, the enemy commander gets their super move. I thoroughly dislike this, because it punishes you for having a good strategy. Then again, the super moves are fairly uninspired (get +X to Y bonus for one round), so I guess it's trivial if you don't use it much. Regardless, the mechanic is not fun.Good idea, falls short in execution. I would give it a "medium" if that was an option.
_childDocuments_.name: WARBORN

_childDocuments_.review: Easily recommended for fans of turn-based tactics, Advance Wars, robots, and strategy. For the amount of content it is worth the asking price, and a steal on sale. Most of the issues are just nitpicks, the gameplay is great. Also worth checking out Sunrider, Wargroove, BattleTech, and the Front Mission series if you haven't already.+Visuals, art style, animations, UI+Music+Difficulty options+Variety of options overall+Mechs+Turn-based tactics battles+Variety of units and special skills+Deploy/build units and heroes+Map Editor-No key rebinding-Unlisted hotkeys (WSAD - camera, H - objectives, Space - commands, Esc - options)-Lacking hotkeys for move, attack, end turn, advance dialogue-Story/characters not well developed-No upgrades/progression-No voice-No camera zoom except to view objectives-Mechs can't change/lose parts, act as soldiers only-Speed up must always be held (no toggle)-Some missions drag due to hunting straggler units-Statuses can't be refreshed until they expire-Some status unclear/lack tooltips-Later chapters can get repetitive / lack new units-Same units for all 4 commanders/factions
_childDocuments_.name: WARBORN

_childDocuments_.review: A fun romp into turn-based combat, much in the vein of Advance Wars or the more recent Wargroove. There is a much more unique dynamic here though given the hex-based nature of the levels, meaning you really have to strategise and plan your route to victory.Lengthy campaign that I'm 7 hours into and about a third of the way through. The art-style is very anime. The game's biggest asset is how polished it is - rare on day one, even rarer for an indie title.I personally am not a huge multiplayer person, but it's there and it's cross-platform and you can design your own maps for it! There's a lot here for your money, so if that's your concern, don't have that concern.
_childDocuments_.name: WARBORN

_childDocuments_.review: Not too shabby turn-based strategy game that might just be a bit too easy. I love the unit variety, and gameplay is pretty streamlined I would say, while still providing enough depth in my opinion. It's not very complex, which I for one welcome very much. Of course there are some rough edges here and there but nothing major.Except there is one big elephant in the room:Playing through the campaign it never really got difficult, even though I changed the difficulty up to "Hard". The enemy AI would still take very obvious sub-par choices (e.g. using the weaker attack that debuffs a unit when the other attack would have killed it outright; or giving a unit that can only heal a crit-chance buff (well maybe heals can crit, but I've never seen that happen), sending in units one-by-one to die... etc.). Surely less frustrating when you are first starting the game, but if I deliberately turn the difficulty up, I want it to actually get difficult.Also I would have liked more missions that pull a trick on you, most of them are pretty straight forward skirmishes.Well, having a weak AI is not much of an issue when you have online multiplayer, however I have yet to find a match via quickplay. But I can imagine a small dedicated community emerging around the game.So in summary, a good game that I just have nobody to play it with.
_childDocuments_.name: WARBORN

It's a solid turn based tactics game that's also super fun and accessible to players of any level.  The 80's anime art-style only makes it that much better and visually appealing.Just wish it had a split-screen local multiplayer mode.Check out my full review here:

_childDocuments_.review: Takes an Advance Wars style foundation and builds upon it. Mechs have different resistances to various types of damage and performance doesn't degrade as they loose health, which emphasises the importance of buffs and debuffs. Every unit has three abilities, many on short cooldowns, and ranged attacks usually only have line of fire in straight lines along the hex grid which makes positioning important, especially when units can physically screen an ally.Each commander has a bunch of buffs that unlock as you go through the campaign, along with a special meter that lets them either activate an Advance Wars style army-wide buff or (re-)deploy in their personal mech. These hero units can be very powerful when properly supported, but aren't win buttons either.Some of the missions, especially early on, can be quite easy, but the challenge really ramps up at about the halfway point, and there's a good mixture of scenario types. There's also a bunch of skirmish maps to play against AI and proper multiplayer as well.A solid and enjoyable game. I'd love to see a follow up with more unit types and commanders building atop everything already here.

_childDocuments_.review: WARBORN is a Nintendo Switch game that somehow also got put on Steam (in what feels like an afterthought).  It's an anime/mecha themed turn based strategy game where you give instructions on a small hex map to a bunch of painfully generic looking Japanese giant robots.  Okay.  There's some plusses here, like a map editor, multiplayer (but no players, we'll get into why later), and, well, the game "works" if you try to play it (but not many did). One important note is that even though this is an amateur project, it does seem to be sincerely and genuinely made.  I couldn't find any flipped assets, plagiarism or any other kind of insincere actions from the developer, but unfortunately genuine intentions alone are not enough to produce a brilliant PC gaming experience.As mentioned, there's no-one around for the multiplayer feature.  Why not?  Because, from a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.While there are options to change the resolution for the game, all this does is scale up the simplistic 2D art assets used to make the game, which makes little or no difference to the graphics quality.  It's nice that the robot models look 3D at least, but they're just 2D animations of 3D renders.  It's 2024, you know, computers are capable of rendering their own 3D graphics now!  Oh yeah, this is a Nintendo Switch game.  Without any other substantial graphics tweaks, it's not possible for gamers to improve the lacklustre 2D visuals.The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just point and click stuff like a browser/Flash game.  The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction.  You'll get none of that here.Because this is designed for handheld/portable gaming appliances, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the low power handheld gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the mobile game developers.As a matter of fact, I was surprised to see this wasn't available on app stores, because that's the kind of experience the game provides.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for low power handhelds forces upon a game.  While this might run well on a Steam Deck, we must remember the vast majority of gamers here are gaming on PC.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.The game never really caught on with the millions of gamers on Steam, with a very low peak player count close to launch, and then just a handful of players launching this game every couple of days.  This is undoubtedly caused by factors such as those raised in this review.  It's always helpful with buying decisions to consider how popular and successful the product is, and unfortunately while this did accumulate a few participation trophy reviews, overall, people just aren't using it.So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?WARBORN has the farcical price of $25 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.  For comparison, the $25 asking price for this game could get you games like "Alien: Isolation", "Subnautica" or "Disco Elysium".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.

_childDocuments_.review: I suppose this is meant for people looking for an Advance Wars game. I don't remember much of AW, played it but wasn't that much into it.  I went into this just looking for a decent mech turn based game and did not get that experience it from this. The units might look like mechs, but they lack any gameplay related to the units being mechs. For example, there is no mech customization, not even changing weapons, and no localized damage, or even performance degradation due to damage other than when hit with specific debuff attacks. The mech theme is only superficial, you could mod the game unit graphics into other setting and it would work just the same. Therefore, not what I was looking for.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great, and I can't believe how few reviews it has. It's like those older Gameboy Advance games like Fire Emblem or Advance Wars but with a twist, using mechs instead of tanks or infantry. There are four factions, each with unique hero mechs and abilities. The game also includes a map editor for creating your own skirmish games. The campaign and story are quite fun and reminiscent of the Gundam universe.The balancing could use some work, but overall, this is a really fun turn-based RTS that will remind you of those older handheld turn-based strategy games with a lot of fun and character.
_childDocuments_.name: WARBORN

_childDocuments_.review: If you miss Advance Wars or wish it had mechs, Warborn might be the game for you.My video will give you the best idea about what Warborn is like. For those who played Advance Wars (I didn't), you already understand the concept of spawning in units to conquer a turn-based map. Warborn uses a hex-grid, and attack lines go down a line of hexes, making for an interesting (and sometimes annoying) twist. This isn't a turn-based strategy about specific characters--although you can summon in your commander--or a variety of heroes. It's about building an army to take over a map by out-positioning your opponent.The map editor and multiplayer will offer replay value for those who fall in love with Warborn. It's a shame there's not more variety in tiles to vary user maps.The writing is poor. The music is decent but not good. But you're here for the gameplay.Hardcore fans of Advance Wars might prefer to stick to their old copies, but it's been more than a decade since we last saw an entry into that series. For a generation of gamers who have never heard of it or missed it entirely (like I did), Warborn reminds us what we're missing out on.
_childDocuments_.name: WARBORN

_childDocuments_.review: Warborn: Variable Armour Command stimulates long-forgotten memories of a 90’s pop culture phenomena that swept over Japan and the Western Hemisphere. Giant mechanized robots fighting to the death has been a staple in the animated entertainment industry for decades, as the rise of Transformers, Voltron, and the legendary Gundam series captivated the minds of children and adults alike. Warborns’ salute to the fanbase is a refreshing experience that compels you to appreciate a genre that felt lost, but ultimately falls short as a holistic turn-based strategy gameThe Good: * Variety of unit types with 3 different damage types that allow for dynamic gameplay. * 20+ Hour campaign including 40 missions * Kick-A 90's Mecha-Inspired animations and Sountrack* Mutiplayer support* In-Game Map Editor* Long-Term value with updated Multiplayer functions and expanded Map editorThe Bad: * Lackluster story that fails to draw any emotional connection with the characters. * Background Information and Story Dialogue are told through conversational text. * Limited Mission types and objectives* Commander Units and Traits are boorishly overpowered, causing you to plow through any AI. Verdict: Warborn: Variable Armour Command is a fleshed-out, turn-based tactics game that is limited by its overall simplicity. At a $19.99 price point, there is enough value here to justify the entertainment. Once you complete the Main Campaign it will be difficult to find any replayability in Warborn without future updates to multiplayer, so keep that in mind.
_childDocuments_.name: WARBORN

_childDocuments_.review: Superb turn-based strategy game. Perfect balance of story, beautiful art, inspiring music, and challenging gameplay. I perfected the first few levels and after that things get a bit harder. I'm going to go back and perfect them all eventually. It's extremely satisfying when you think you're going to fail but then work out a way to destroy them all - normally involving the  . OOOoo it's so good.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a turn based 'mech combat game on the surface, but it plays very much like the old GBA Advance Wars or SSI's Panzer General series in reality, which is no bad thing.  You get to play 4 different commanders throughout the 40 odd mission campaign, each of which has their own perks and power skills. There is also a fully functional multiplayer option, but don't expect to find many players around these days. You can still setup a game easily enough with a steam friend though. I got this game at 90% off during a sale, and there is around 25-30 hours of gameplay so would recommend it whilst discounted.

_childDocuments_.review: Warborn is a great introduction to the Advance Wars-style tactical strategy game. It has crisp anime-like graphics, a boppy soundtrack, and enough variation of units, tactics, and factions for multiple playthroughs. It also has a custom map editor and multiplayer if that's your jam. I wouldn't say it's the deepest of this genre, other Advance Wars-style games have more tactics or units etc..., but I bet you will enjoy the time (and money) you'll spend it on it. Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: WARBORN

_childDocuments_.review: If you like a very simple turn-based strategy game with mechs, warborn is for you. The 2D graphics look like japanese robot cartoons from the 70's/80's and I rather like it that way. The AI is stupid as mud even after the september 2020 update. Unfortunately every military strategy game I know of from the last 30 years or so is more complex and challenging than warborn (think Battle Isle 1/2/3, crescent hawk revenge, java mechwar, android uniwar etc.). Warborn definitely is not worth the 20 bucks at the moment.

_childDocuments_.review: Gundam like TBS + skirmish + 40 missions = Pick 1 of 4 unique commanders to battle. Call for reinforcements to capture resources and bases. 3 types of attack and defense to mix up the strategies.Rock-paper-scissors type mechanics with variety of unit types. Charge up SP by capturing resources, which will aide in calling reinforcements to your base. The tactics is a bit more streamlined for a wider audience, but still fun.
_childDocuments_.name: WARBORN

_childDocuments_.review: WARBORN. A turn-based mecha strategy battle game created by Raredrop Games and published by PQube. According to the developer's mention in the store page, the graphic visual was inspired by the Japanese anime style in the 90's, but it seems to be well ported in western anime style and has a good mood in the actual impression. Moreover, gameplay is more exciting than expected.There are 3 modes in this game. Single campaign, online multiplayer, and level editor. About 40 campaigns including stories are available in single mode, and it also includes a basic tutorial. In each campaign, goals are set, and the result rank is displayed according to the player's achievement. Gameplay is easy to play, but difficult to master. Since most mecha units will be destroyed after getting 2-3 attacks, as the commander, you should take good care of your units. There are 4 commander types, each with unique skills and mechas. They are quite powerful, but they can consume a lot of resources. In other words, your strategic judgment will dominate the game stages. Each stage consists of hexagonal tiles, which contain facilities and various terrains. Some of them affect units and resources, so you need to take them properly. The battles are rather simple, but gameplay has some strategic depth, considering the above elements. With a built-in level editor, you can create custom maps, and also use them in online PvP mode. The game experience is pretty good overall.WARBORN. It's a nice turn-based tactical mecha battle game with some simplified strategy elements. Players can fully enjoy the single campaign mode, and the built-in level editor can further expand such fun. Best of all, it supports cross-platform online multiplayer, so we expect that this game will keep the user base well. Things to polish up still remain, but with future updates it will get better and better. Let's dive into this cool mecha strategy game! Recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: WARBORN

_childDocuments_.review: I played through the entire campaign on Normal mode in around 16.5 hours and loved every minute of it! This is the sort of game that the world needs a LOT more of. It's a welcome fusion of so many great ideas, ranging from 90s Masaya games, Starcraft, hex-based strategy, and Famicom Wars, among other things.In particular, I would suggest that fellow fans of Masaya's 90s games will love Warborn. There are lots of parallels, whether intentionally or not, between Warborn and Masaya's 90s catalogue: a protagonist (Luella) who resembles Lucia Cabrock from Gley Lancer, the 10 HP system from Langrisser (retooled to 1000 HP to allow for more variance), the turn-based, mission-based format of Guyframe, and an interesting take on mech-based strategy which surprisingly doesn't take any influence from Front Mission or Super Robot Wars -- Masaya's Vixen 357 followed this same premise, too. (I say this is "surprising" because those two series are the granddaddies of mechs within the context of Strategy RPGs/Turn-Based Strategy.) Oh yeah, then there's the often rock-based music of Warborn, which will likely resonate with any fellow fan of Noriyuki Iwadare's music. I don't usually get too much into traditional Turn-Based Strategy because sometimes, it feels like battles can drag on for way too long, essentially boiling down to a glorified tug-of-war capture game; this is one problem I had with WarGroove, and perhaps the main reason I don't enjoy that game as I should. Warborn, on the other hand, somehow manages to avert this, at least during its campaign mode. Most of the battles, particularly towards the endgame, are pretty challenging, even on normal mode. I can't imagine what hard mode would look like, so I definitely need to replay the game on hard at some point. Hooray for replayability!Balance in the game seems really well done. I didn't find myself relying on just one troop type throughout the campaign, and in fact, every type has its uses. Havoks and Pathfinders are useful for their high mobility, with Havoks doubling as your "capture" units. On the other end of the spectrum, slow-moving Insights and Farsights aren't going anywhere anytime fast, but they've got lots of applications for tower-defense type battles due to their long-range nukes. Invaders are lowkey great, due to their strong damage, decent mobility, and crippling debuffs. Throughout the campaign, I found I actually had to think about how to approach these battles. It's such a refreshing change of pace from all these grind-based FFT clones which insult your intelligence with their "lol just grind more" philosophy. Warborn's UI could've probably used at least a LITTLE tweaking. There's no way to view enemy move/attack ranges, and there's also no easy way to tell which damage type each attack does. Even so, I found the game to be completely bug-free, which is a rarity for a game with such a small development staff. The soundtrack is spectacular in all aspects. It's got more soul and excitement than just about anything that AAA games are putting out these days, and I find it a shame that the composer hasn't even uploaded it on any of his platforms. There's a good blend of rock, metal, orchestral, country, and a genre which I can only describe as "Cowboy Bebop-esque space western-inspired blues," which perfectly befits Warborn's atmosphere. The basslines throughout the  soundtrack are splendid -- aside from vintage Wishbone Ash (like "Vas Dis" or "Handy"), I usually don't hear such high basslines, and it's a real refreshing treat. In particular, I found that Luella's B Theme, Izol's C Theme, and Vincent's A Theme were standouts. Then you have a song like the Shadow Wolves' theme, which sounds eerily similar to the Enemy Battle (Swift Attack) theme from Front Mission 2. All in all, Warborn has the best soundtrack I've heard in quite a long time. There's also multiplayer, in case that sort of thing tickles your fancy.

_childDocuments_.review: Warborn is a bit of a hidden gem of a strategy game. It features mech combat, with each mech have 3 skills, usually relating to different weapon systems. Each mech has armor rating for each of the 3 weapon types. Attacks always hit, which is something I love, no random misses. The difficulty can be a bit unbalanced. I played on hard mode, and most levels were fairly easy. But some were pretty difficult. The final mission seems impossible on hard mode, I had to switch to normal mode to beat it. It is also fun to go back and try to get S ranks on the missions, although even on hard mode I got them most of the time on my first try. The story is a grounded sci-fi military tale. It reminds me of Front Mission in that way (and other ways too, obviously). Great game.

_childDocuments_.review: Decent turn based tactical game. Though I don't think this is worth the full price tag. I got this at $5 on sale and I think that's a good price to spend about 15 hours in a game. The strategies required for the campaign aren't exactly mind blowing though. You can pretty much brute force each level. Yeah you'll lose a lot of your own units but there's a bunch of missions where you'll have to sacrifice them anyways. Each commander "ultimate" doesn't actually do much to turn any sort of tide except the main bad guy's one where you can't even play as him. I played the campaign but didn't pay much attention to the story. It's basically following 4 factions that end up fighting each other due to misunderstandings until they find the big bad guy causing the actual ruckus.
_childDocuments_.name: WARBORN

_childDocuments_.review: 1) StoryIt's boring and bad. It's mostly simple talk betwen main commander/protagonist, general type character who is rank above and few grunts while nothing interesting is happening.First 10 missions are the most poor exposition dumps about lore and setting I did see in a while. Just skip whole conversation cutscenes. Litteraly nothing worth of your time is happening for majority of the game anyway.2) Visuals and musicGraphics and art is alright but you will get tired of those boring animations and that units from both sides look the same unlike games like Wargroove.Music? What music? Oh there was music in this game? I didn't even notice lol3) GameplayIt's pretty.... dull version of Advance War or Wargroove without any sort of depth or tactics. Units mostly have two or three moves, there is no difference in units design, abilities or stats between sides and most of missions is just the lamest kind tug of war I did see in a while where the most expensive units are so strong that AI cannot do anything about that because its way too busy purchasing only the cheapest units.Don't get me wrong - this game will definitely satisfy casual audience of this genre but it just didn't work for me who spend almost entire life time playing this genre.4)  Traits, super moves and commandersThose three are the only difference between sides of conflict and they all depend on selected commander.Traits are small passive changes that affect mostly the army. Most of them are boring nothing stuff but some of later ones are indeed powerful.When energy bar is filled by attacking, killing and losing units player can use super move (also depend on selected commander) or summon commander unit.Super move buffs all units with specific thing that last for a turn and commander unit is just a powerful version of a generic unit that last until it dies.5) The good, the bad and the uglyThe game have a very slow start, first 20 out of 40 missions are really boringly easy as heck where no tactics required yet take a while to finish anyway.The gameplay is extremely sluggish - units have very limited movement distance (often moving only single tile right after they spawn in their next turn).Every single time to move you need to select unit then click move button and then select location and click "end unit turn". What is this - Warcraft 1?Enemy units not only takes their sweet time but also the game need to show you for a second their movement range first. Why the heck not just do the action like in any other turn based game before? Enemy AI? What AI? Its dumb as rocks. Constantly purchasing cheap units, doesn't summon commander when should, using super move with only 3 units alive that cannot attack anything... Seriously, Advanced Wars on Game Boy Advance was more intelligent enemy than that.Wargroove, Advance Wars, Divinity, Ancient Empires? Those games are way older and yet did that 10 times better.Not even in game setting to speed up enemy turn movement or skip it entirely? CMON!Is that hard to implement hold right click or hold right+left click and move your mouse to quickly move around camera? Nope, you need to put mouse on side and wait ETERNITY for camera to move. Is there a way to increase the camera scroll speed? Of course not.At least using WSAD buttons does move camera a little bit faster but then again - what is the point of saying that Warborn can be played with mouse only in the first place if doing so is far inferior experience.Why zoom out button does hide UI but displays objective and defeat conditions? I would gladly play WHOLE GAME on zoom out but what the heck is this design decision? Why auto hiding UI and display instead game conditions that are basically the SAME on EVERY single mission.6) So how long the game is?There is multiplayer but considering that this game combat is not as good as Wargroove I rather stay far away from it.Singleplayer is 40 missions long (most of them are boring or copypasted that takes less than 10 turns to finish), 10 for each different commander. Around 35 hours to beat those.7) ConclusionI will rate this game 6/10. After finishing Warborn it just left me with feeling to replay Wargroove. I did exactly that and boy that game is so awesome. Never again Warborn. Never again.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I'm surprised this game isn't more well-known, and doesn't have a higher positive review ratio. This seems like a great game for anyone who likes both mecha anime, like Gundam, and turn-based strategy games similar to Advance Wars. I'm sure there are plenty of other people out there who are in both of those camps, and would enjoy this game as much as I have so far. Admittedly, I haven't played really far yet, so I don't know if the game actually gets frustrating later on (as some people claim), but so far it's been fairly easy but fun.Also, for any Deck owners wondering about it, this game runs PERFECTLY on a Steam Deck. At the time I bought this, there was no official Deck compatibility rating yet on Steam, nor any reports at all on ProtonDB, but I really wanted to play a game like this on my Deck so I gave it a shot, and was very pleased with the results. I also added the very first entry for this game on ProtonDB.

name: Encased: A Sci-Fi Post-Apocalyptic RPG
detailed_description: A tactical sci-fi RPG set in a dystopian environment allowing you to fight enemies, explore the hostile wasteland, level up your character and join one of the factions – made up of survivors - in the shattered world and cut off from the rest of society. Enrolling in one of the five wings of the CRONUS Corporation - each with its own features, mechanics and game options - and embark on a one way trip inside the Dome in the quest for unique artifacts as you avoid radiation, anomalies and a whole host of creatures out to do you harm. You may start as an ordinary company employee but you will eventually become the driving force behind the narrative that takes place before, during, and after the disaster known as ‘The Incident’. Crafting, combat, negotiation; you’re going to need all your wits about you if you want to survive. Once you’re familiar with the basics, you are thrust into an open world filled with riches and danger. The old ways are gone – ground into dust by the powerful Maelstrom – and rising from the ashes are six powerful factions, vying for control over the ravaged landscape under the Dome. Will they be allies or enemies? That choice – and the future of the Dome – is in your hands. Not everyone under the Dome is your friend; quite the reverse in fact. If you’re a smart likeable character (with a high charisma rating) you might be able to talk your way out of things. But more likely it’s time for a bit of ultra-violence. And that means weapons; lots of weapons. And there’s no shortage of choice: from high tech beam weapons through to a solid right hook, there’s loads of way to bring down a hostile group of foes. Of course, you can be a pacifist and use non-lethal force but that’s a story for another day… The hostile and unforgiving world can be a lonely place; so why not team up with some like-minded individuals and face the challenges together. From hardened criminals built like mountains or scientists with a shady past, there’s a host of different potential companions to journey with, each replete with their own unique personality and skills. Or you can just go “Lone Wolf” and face everything alone; it’s not an easy road but you can play this way too if you so wish. Encased is full of choices: from what sort of character you will be, what wing you will join and how honourable a person you are. What equipment do you take? How will you fight? Do you craft better weapons or armour? And it doesn’t stop there. You will hold lives in the balance and will have to choose who survives and who perishes. And every decision you make will impact the story and your gaming experience. Well, no one said surviving Armageddon was going to be easy…

_childDocuments_.review: is an isometric, turn based RPG created by Dark Crystal Games and currently in development with early access release. It partly succeeds in emulating the nostalgia of Interplay’s  games, encased in a brand new setting. Mechanically, it treads similar paths to the classics and familiars with little twists of its own. This by no means is a bad thing, as old fans of the post-apocalyptic simulators will delve into the game almost like newly polished old shoes, comfy and fit but looks fresh.  truly has the potential to morph itself into a great successor, but as for now there are some design and technical hurdles to overcome.  There are 5 different ‘classes’ players can take. Black (soldier), Blue (Mechanic), Orange(Rogue), White(Medic), Silver(Scientist). Each role players take offer exclusive routes and dialogue in solving the multitudes of problems inside the dome. Upon leveling up, player characters are assigned skill points and perk points, in which they can spend improving some of the dozens of abilities and perks available. Combat works with AP as a resource to manage their actions. It does spice things a little bit compared to its predecessor by having combat skills a lot more involved. You don’t only increase a weapon type’s proficiency, but also dozens of active skills that achieve different effects such as various debuffs or manipulating enemies’ positions. I have little qualms with the non-combat skills in the game. They provide ample, mostly balanced solutions to quests players find in the world. The lethal side of your skillset is a separate matter, as I feel it funnels you into the typical ‘rifle’ build as the most effective method of culling the dome’s population. I started with a knife wielding orange suit, ended up with a trusty rifle hanging on her back. My recruited companion, Crump molded into a similar path. Crump is a brute with a pair of hammers for fists, that ended up deadlier using my leftover guns as soon as I found a better piece for myself.  It seems they have no concept of ownership under the dome. It’s unknown whether it’s yet to be implemented or a design decision. Pretty much everything that isn’t nailed down is free for you to plunder. No matter if it’s a trash can or someone’s locker. This completely breaks the economy and you end up with a literal mountain of junk in your inventory. The inventory is a jungle of trash you collect during your adventure. The junks can’t be sorted by their weight or value, which makes barter and organizing harder that it should have. The loot on most containers are also randomized and I am not really a fan of random loot. They are still mostly junk so the element of uncertainty isn’t that much detrimental to the overall experience.  In the current version, I feel like companions are more of a liability than dependable allies. They block your ways, run into hot steam, and kill themselves in ways I can’t even imagine they can. The auto-docs cannot be used on companions so unless you want to invest in medicine skills, don’t bother unless you just want meat shields that can be discarded when it’s all used up. In this current version, they don’t have too much to tell either. They have their introduction quest, and after that they become hound dogs that follow order and constantly screw things up. They do feel more like a template for more content to add and dimension to their persona, so it all could be tentative. The overall state of the game is akin to a prototype of a car. There’s an engine, there are  wheels and steer. The car does run but that’s it. There’re not yet features that make it market-ready. At this state, I wouldn't recommend spending your time playing it, but keep an eye on it if you’re a fan of the genre. It won’t revolutionize the genre nor it will magically be appealing for people that aren’t into RPGs, but it can at least be a decent fallout clone. In some areas the game struggles to maintain 60 FPS on 1440p with almost all settings turned high. The game has some minor bugs spread around here and there, but i didn’t find anything game breaking. My major complaint about the technical side of the game is the lack of QoL features especially in companion behavior and interaction outside combat. There are also several lines of untranslated texts in the game. Worry not, they are minor so they don't hamper non-russian speakers to complete all the available contents.  In the heights of The Cold War The Dome suddenly burst into existence, carrying wealth and discoveries within it, bringing the war into a sudden halt. World’s leading power diverted their attention into stripping the secrets of the dome bare. With that, like a maelstrom, The Dome swept the globe by its feet unleashing endless prosperity and ushering humanity into a golden age. In the center of that storm is CRONUS, the international organization in charge of cracking The Dome open. Players are thrust into a new member of CRONUS, ready and eager to tame the mysterious beast and within the center of it all, suddenly thrust into a dire situation that put the fate of The Dome on their shoulders.While the story of  is obviously not finished, there is already a unique identity in the setting they have built. It’s not wholly original, but more of a blend of ingredients borrowed from multiple familiar sources. It does its job well as a backdrop for player’s adventures. I am definitely looking forward to what they have in store for The Dome. offers sufficient fidelity relative to its distance from objects to the camera. The models and landscape of The Dome won’t surprise anyone, but built with a strong vision of its direction. The result is varied, but thematically consistent environments and setpieces that are overall pleasing to see. It is increasingly harder to nail retrofuturism style in the wake of saturation brought by fallout’s popularity. In my opinion, the game nailed their identity through their choice of style.In stark contrast to its excellent visual style, I found the soundscape of  wholly unremarkable. It does serve its purpose providing audio feedback to players action’s in the world. Otherwise, both music and sound effects don’t really stand out in any way.  is currently still a little bit premature for you to invest in. However, any fans of role-playing games should keep this on close watch at least.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. The first act is absolutely amazing, writing, voice acting, story, completely engrossing. 80% of the attention to detail is concentrated into this first act. Once you get past that, the game feels spread thin like butter scraped over too much bread. Every location you visit has one or two interesting features, then a lot of nothing. Compared to a game like Wasteland 3, where exploring every corner of the world is rewarded. Every map feels barren. One of the first locations I visited was a swamp the locals talked up to be a amazingly dense zone full of anomalies. I found a small grouping of about 5 anomalies with no purpose, easily walked around. Then some over-sized roaches and a big crab. Very little environmental story telling at all. Very little to see.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is almost fun. It is a bit of a Wasteland knock-off. The game also forces you to save-scum constantly. As you will die often in combat, unless you build a combat specific character, and then you will miss out on 90% of the game since it all revolves around the non-combat skills. The "exhaustion" from using skills is broken, as you will be running around the game exhausted, (from picking locks?!) and suffering stat deductions, as well as being overloaded with crafting items that you can't use, but really need, if only you could find that one rare component. After 11 hours, and fighting my way 90% through a level, only to die and realize that I forgot to save, and have to start all over again, I have decided to just give up and play something more enjoyable. I did enjoy the game, so I will recommend it, but understand that it requires a lot of patience and micromanaging.

_childDocuments_.review: Some useful advice, with mild spoilers:Best weapon shop I found was the the Bradbury Weapon Store located near the middle right of the map (And by best I mean its the earliest good weapon store, you can go there immediately after Nashville)You can "reset" merchants by making a save before talking to them, then talking to them and going back to the save if you don't like what they are sellingBefore you actually start playing make a dummy character and check out the list of perks by clicking C and looking at the bottom right, then adjust your actual characters starting stats to fit perk requirementsI would highly recommend going to Junktown then Magellan immediately after finishing Nashville to recruit companions, my personal favorites were Fox (strongest psionic companion, has ok melee capabilites) and Katarzyna (lots of different damage types and DoTs, very easy to recruit and is a medic)If your having a hard time fighting groups a tedious way you can beat them is by using phase shift from psychokinetic gloves to teleport a enemy away while you are stealthed, this will let you 3v1 and kill them easilyCriminal is extremely powerful and I find playing without it to not be a good idea, I find money hard to obtain in this game due to enemies not dropping much loot and even if they do your going to need that loot for crafting anyway, also not many quests pay you and the ones that do don't pay much. The best way to acquire goods is by pickpocketing them from merchants.For unarmed the best weapon is probably Discord, not much resists energy damage and even with a critical build it has a better ap to damage ratio than HerculesDon't craft Weapon Upgrade Kits unless you have tons of weapon parts, its more efficient to just buy them instead (4 weapon parts requires 800 combonds while a kit costs 400)It might be a good idea to not use permanent skill books until you have maxed out a skill, since doing that will let you hit 165 in a skill instead of just 150Temporary skill books stack, letting you reach high numbers temporarilyRight click a weapon to open the upgrading menu, this requires either tech or science depending on the weapon

_childDocuments_.review: Encased is an RPG that I've taken to listening to a podcast to while I play.  The central conceit is neat and the writing is decent. The main character isn't really well established, and the friends that join your party do so on the flimsiest of pretexts.  It's not sim-y enough to be a survival sim and the narrative isn't hooky enough for a pure RPG.  Encased is in this weird middle ground.  It's a mechanics heavy RPG where the mechanics aren't well explained, An ok-writtenly RPG that chides you for skimming over the dialog of forgettable NPCs, and a crafting and survival system that's just shy of being a stand-alone offering.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those things where Encased is by no stretch a bad game; it's just a painfully mediocre game that clearly made a lot of decisions out of tradition rather than playability. There are a lot of mechanics pulled from terrible games like dexterity based AP pools, a bunch of alternate attacks nobody ever uses,  Skills that are functionally useless for most of the game, adding eight companions but only letting you use two, the list goes on. While billed as a "post apocalyptic" RPG, the apocalypse is very much in progress during Encased. Essentially an alien dome structure appeared in the alternate 1970's, a mysterious corporation named CRONUS is sending massive amounts of people inside that by whatever mysterious reason are now trapped inside that dome cut off from the world and CRONUS. For whatever reason, you are capable of surviving the psionic feedback in the dome and set out to find out what is going on. Where the story loses me is how psi is essentially just magic in this setting, there is zero effort made by the game to explain why everybody inside the dome can use magical powers. There are five wings of CRONUS, which make up the five main professions you may choose to formulate a character. While these are not hard and fast classes, they do lean towards predetermined pathes. For instance you basically have to be psionic to be a Silver, you need good science to be White, etc. Oh by the way, Security is Black and Science is White. So you will often see statements like "The Blacks hate the Whites so much for their bad attitude", it's terrible, cringey, racially charged writing that really has no purpose in game. All they had to do is refer to Black as Security or Dome-Sec instead. Paranoia also uses white and black as ranks, but instead refer to it as Infrared and Ultraviolet. There are several skills in the game, many of which are completely useless. Piloting in practice sounds like a useful skill right? I want to be able to drive around and save time. There does not seem to be a single drivable car in the entire game, the only use for the piloting skill is the servoshell power armor and the land train you get in the last act of the game. Imagine my shock when I realized that I wasted one of my skill choices on something that does not even have purpose in the game! Combat is zero effort, you have a bunch of action points and you left click on enemies until they die. While they did add 5-8 extra buttons for every weapon, these are all useless. They usually deal less damage in return for a status effect; but why do that when we can just end this miserable fight? There is also non-lethal, but it's just there for the handful of pacifist players and serves no in game purpose. I always chose social options that avoid combat, otherwise most of the game will be spent waiting for boring combats to end. Also god help you if you chose the psionic glove like I did, because it costs more AP to fire than a gun and every glove is HARD LOCKED to one set of elemental attacks. So if you suddenly fight cryo enemies with a cold glove, you simply lose, all you can do is hope you equipped a different weapon in your other slot. If you ever wondered what happens when you just copy down mechanics from other rpgs without any testing or balancing, you end up with stuff like Encased. Action point bags are not fun. Allowing you players to pick useless skills is not fun. Bad combat systems are not fun. Hard lcking your brain magic by the glove is not fun. Encased is not fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I've  played it twice now and didn't finish it either time.There are good things but the bad makes it too frustrating.I'll give 2 examples of many- 1. your companions can disappear a few times. It's scripted. Then , for some stupid reason, the devs hide them in the environmentsand give you no clue about finding them. There is no hotel or bar they congregate at. It's one of the dumbest unfriendly mechanics I've ever encountered in an rpg. What does that add to the game?2. Why I just quit the second time. There is some kind of damage called delayed toxin. Combat is turned based. I guess you can get rid  of the effect in combat. It says its on a 15 second timer. If you wait till after combat the timer kicks in and if you don't get in your inventory and quickly cure yourself - for instance if you try and check what the status effect means - you die.  So it goes from turn based to some race against the clock and there is no note to explain it. I died several times from this effect repeating the battle because I honestly thought the first 2 deaths were some anomaly. Or even a glitch. I have never played a game that expects you to go from turn based to countdown timer with no warning or precedent - there is no other mechanic in the game like it. How that passed the testing  and review I have no idea but it's a hint about the sloppiness of the game. It's a pretty good fo2 simulator. The writing is decent, and the plot, though no great, is serviceable. The skill tree is good and the  variety of  builds is good. A lot of good, but you can't treat the player like a lab rat and force them to waste lots of time on the devs little "cute" quirks. I feel bad if there were devs who weren't trying to be cute and "sassy" by wasting the players time. Wasteland 2 had a lot of garbage like this too but it was a bigger deeper game so they could do that - though I had to quit that nightmare also after some good hours. If you've played a lot of these types of rpgs you know what I'm saying. I don't know why the devs think it's cute to frustrate the player. I  think there is some small minority of players who are masochists and like to figure out these stupid in game quirks because maybe it's like knowing  a secret or something. I'm not one of those. I don't enjoy broken bits and needless frustration.

_childDocuments_.review: There are a lot of comparisons to Fallout 1 & 2 and some to Wasteland 2 (or 3), but this game is actually a bit more clever than the games it is most similar to.  The skill system forces the player to put some thought into where to spec and put point for actions that are freebies in other games.  Tossing a grenade, even badly, is pretty available in other systems while with Encased you have to build up contraptions to 30.  Medical treatment is dependent on other skills to fully realize and some abilities don't become available without prerequisite ability scores.  This is in addition to some  perks that are also dependent on minimum skill and attributes.  For me, this is a depth of complexity that encourages really looking at the mechanics and planning out is advance in a way I usually only do for achievement hunting.  Will it float your boat?  Maybe.  It depends if you like shifting through the interface to find out that there are some things you didn't realize for the first few hours of game play.  I find it very rewarding and give this a warm endorsement (my holdback are a few bugs that aren't game-breaking but are irritating).

_childDocuments_.review: A short premise: since the release of Planescape Torment back in the day i've played mostly crpgs and rpgs in general, it is by far my favourite genre and i have played the vast majority of these games. So now that you know where i'm coming from, here are my general thoughts on the game.THE SETTINGThe setting as it is presented to you during the initial hours of the game is good. It is a different take on the post apocalyptic theme that tries (and succeedes) in doing something different. It is a much needed coat of fresh paint and fresh new ideas. Sci-fi post apocalyptic in the 70s with weird unexplainable tech sprinkled on top? Sign me up. During the character creation you're introduced to the concept of "wings", which are essentially branches of this corporation that is leading operations in "the Dome". Each wing is specialized in a specific aspect necessary for the whole operation to run smoothly: you have the managers and leaders (the silvers), you have your scientists and researchers (the whites), you have your general choiche of convicts "pardoned" and forced into manual labor (the oranges), mechanics, builders and engineers (the blues) and the police/security (the blacks). The wings are an interesting concept and they give a playthrough unique dialogue options and ways to solve things depending on the wing you choose: character identity and not limiting your skills based on what you pick (you get some bonuses to some skills depending what you choose) is great and adds a lot of replay value.STORY The story during the Act 1 is great. You get a general view of how things are, how the factions (the wings) work together, the political scenario at play, the different locations, and every area of the game is filled with npcs, some of which have a lot of dialogue, but even those who don't still have interesting inputs that are essential in giving the game a believable and immersive atmosphere.There's also an overarching mystery that is quite intriguing in the way it is presented. I will not spoil the story itself, but at the end of Act 1 there is a big climax of sorts and the some things change. I was very excited to see where the story would go and how the game would evolve under the new premises but alas, if Act 1 is a fantastic start with incredible potential, the rest of the game is, without any grey margin, largely bland and unfinished: the new locations and areas feel empty, most of the npcs outside of those directly linked to the main questline have northing or just one liners to offer. The story is unfortunately held back by the lack of atmosphere and the barren and personality deprived areas. If in the first Act exploring was an exciting experience, in the rest of the game after a while you just stop trying to interacting with random npcs, knowing full well that there's nothing for you, neither dialogues, nor quests, just a lot of one liners. It is sad because the ideas are there and the overall story is quite interesting, but it's just not finished.COMBATCombat is nice, nothing stellar or ground breaking, it's your standard action point system tied to movement, attacks and other actions in combat (reloading, using items, etc). You have both melee and ranged combat, the first divided in bare hands and weapons, while the latter is divided in light, heavy and high tech weapons, each with their own pros and cons. There's also "psychic wizardry", which is quite nice from a lore prospective too: essentially gifted individuals can use psychic powers with the aid of special gloves (your weapon essentially) that allows you to use fire, lightning, ice or psionic crowd control/buffing/debuffing. The combat isn't exciting like Wasteland 3, or Divinity OS, but it has a certain depth and it's satisfying in its own right, especially considering that there are a lot of different possible character builds given the variety of skills you can acquire. There's also a decent amount of enemy variety and although you can only have two party members at any given time, there is quite a bit of strategy involved depending where you choose to fight: many different maps have different ways you can engage an enemy if you have the right skills; sometimes you can find a secret passage to ambush enemies from the back, avoiding turrets, other times you can lure enemies into a minefield you spotted, and so on.VOICE ACTINGThis is another very important part linked to a good story, immersion and general suspension of disbelief. The quality is good, the narrator in particular does a good job with the exposition, although sometimes it can be a bit verbose, but it is an overall enjoyable thing. In general, voiced characters have a fitting voice and good performances.COMPANIONSAs mentioned above, you can only have two active party members at any given time, out of a total of six possible ones. Forcing you to choose only two isn't necessarely a bad thing, on the contrary it forces you to make a decision and choose who fits best your team comp and your character. The builds the companions come with are varied enough to allow you to have some wiggle room: you're not obligated to choose a character for his stats, you have options.The various characters are decently written with some highs and lows, but they generally feel like people, with maybe one a couple of exceptions in which the whole personality of a character revolves around one single aspect. The voice acting of the companions is generally well done, especially when it comes down to Katarzyna and Yoko, on the other hand although he did a good job, i really think that Crump's voice doesn't fit the character and its avatar at all. MUSIC AND SOUNDTRACKI would define the overall experience as "meh". Some of the music or sound effects in general are bland and repetitive to the point which sometimes i would just turn off the music completely. Also, hearing the same voice lines over and over in determinate areas is quite tiring after a while, especially since it's just two lines repeated constantly.CONCLUSIONIn conclusion the game clearly has potential. The creative setting, coupled with the strong start embodied by Act 1 really makes me want to see this game succeed and possibly have sequels, but as things stand right now it's an unfinished product that amazes in the first act just to fizzle in the two that follow. It's not an early access game and in good conscience i cannot recommend the game in its current state. I will still check the progress though and as i did for Pathfinder: Kingmaker, will update my review when the game will (hopefully) feel feature complete, or at least be as good as what is shown in Act 1 in its entirety.

_childDocuments_.review: (NOTE: Recommendation is not unreserved)Encased is one half of of one of the best games ever. Act 1 is utterly brilliant. It's everything that a revival of the isometric RPG  would want to be. It's the Fallout 3 that fans of Fallouts 1 and 2 wanted, it is damn near perfect. An interesting system powering everything with twists on how builds work that encourages you to play interesting characters over middle-of-the-road 'safe' choices, a fun combat system, and incredibly deep reactivity. Every corner has some brilliant quest, every NPC something unique about them, and throught it all you constantly have choices to make, unique strategies to pursue, and things to explore. The companions are great and promise great things adventuring with them. Then you complete the first act and the game just sort of... stops. What used to be incredibly intricate becomes bland and threadbare, what used to offer options, offers none. From one point in the main story one of the best classic RPGs ever, becomes a tedious paint-by-numbers exercise. Why is this review still a 'recommend?' The game absolutely does not stick the landing. In fact, I'd not recommend beating the game at all. The reason that it is still a recommend despite this horrible problem is that the point where the game becomes a mediocre-to-bad slog is some thirty hours or so in and those thirty hours are going to be exquisite fun, If you are willing to just stop the game when it is no longer fun and abandon it midway in order to get about thirty hours or so in a classic RPG  in the vein of Fallout, then Encased is absolutely worth a purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: The Good: Cool theme and setting, good exploration, lots of hidden secrets to find, combat is good, does not feel grindy.  What needs improvement: the English translation/localization.  You'll notice a slew of errors from small things like incorrect pronouns, to Russian words that were simply typed in Latin characters. For instance, 'Canalization' means something completely different in English than it does in Russian (the correct English translation would have been 'sewers').  However, single word errors pale in comparison to garbled sentences, non-sequiturs and dialog that falls on its face.  The amount of enjoyment you will get from this game now [PRE RELEASE] will be proportional to your exposure to Slavic languages, idioms, and culture.  These will define your ability to correct and make sense of the translation.  However, I believe that the themes and mannerisms presented, which are faithful to the Strugatsky setting, are an asset to the game.  Deciphering a complex sentence that presents a novel idea can be euphoric.  Whereas, deciphering a mess of errors is just frustrating.  I hope that the developers will ensure the translation is up to the standards of the source material, Roadside Picnic, by the time this game is released.

_childDocuments_.review: You will either love it or hate it. And if you do love it, you will likely also hate it.As far as the story and setting goes, it is incredibly unique, and the world feels thoroughly realised and lived in. The NPCs react how you would expect them to react. Put bluntly, if you're a fan of the old fallouts, and want to play a similar game with some quality of life improvements, this is a must buy. _childDocuments_.review: "This looks like Fallout 1 and 2. Is it Fallout?"Yeah, pretty much. A little more precisely: It's Fallout, minus the satirical 1950s Jet Age aesthetic. Instead, the touchstones here are early 70s dystopian brutalist sci-fi like Logan's Run, 2001, The Omega Man (the Charlton Heston version), Soylent Green; probably a lot of Soviet and French cinema I haven't seen; and a hint of the Paranoia RPG."Is it good?"If it were bad, I wouldn't compare it to Fallout. I'm not that far in, so I can't say if it's as good as Fallout yet, but I don't think fans will be disappointed."It just came out, how stable is it?"The worst problem I've encountered so far is a few low-importance objects being placed poorly so they can't be searched. In other words, it's pretty solid."So, basically..."If you liked Fallout 1 and 2, it's a no-brainer.Edit to add:A lot of reviews: "This fails at being tight tactical RPG like XCOM, Shadowrun, and Troubleshooter."Well, yeah. It's a different type of game. Hardcore tactical RPGs have to more or less railroad you through a series of linear scenarios, to control the difficulty curve. Encased is a much less linear game, where a major element of gameplay is wandering around the board and figuring out which challenges you can take on now and which ones to leave until later. It also gives you multiple paths through challenges (a LOT, if you count replays with different builds). That means a tradeoff against tactical complexity. It's not a failure, just a difference.If you want a hardcore tactical RPG, let me recommend Troubleshooter. That game is pure gold. Encased is pretty great too, though.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing it in Early Access, I was patiently waiting for the full release. Once it did so, I of course downloaded it again and started playing.There is good and there is bad, but in my opinion there is mostly good. Let's start with that.The story is decently entertaining and between choosing your Wing, your attributes, and deciding which faction(s) to support, your story can be quite different in terms of events and dialogue. For example, if you have no Brains, everyone assumes your character is a bumbling idiot and you have fun dialogue options like eating paper or licking people. If you are in the Orange Wing, you get treated differently since you're a criminal.The combat is nice, you slide right into it seamlessly and can even stealth past a number of enemies if you don't want to fight. In fact, I think you might be able to avoid killing anyone if you have the right skills. You can upgrade weapons and craft a lot of stuff with the random items you get in the world as well.Now for the bad. There were three major things that I disliked.1) Some towns were just too large and the exits too far, so it would take a long time to go where you needed to go and then leave the town so you could continue your journey. My suggested solution to this would be to have an option somewhere to just exit the town from anywhere.2) Some of the quests were really tedious, especially near the end. Specifically a few that were just going from town to town to talk to people or get a single item and then going back. These are the worst kinds of quests, and it was made infinitely more insufferable when you would have to do 2-3 quests like these back to back because the quest giver didn't give you all of them at once. For example, the quests for Phalanx to do the main story. Their base sucks, as it takes forever to get from the entrance to the leader to turn in the quest. Then he wants you to go back and forth between two different towns that are quite far away basically just to talk to people. My suggestion to fix this, would be to just give the player all the quests from the single quest giver at once.3) #2 leads me to number three. Travel. At first, exploring around and getting into random encounters was fun. But near the endgame it became just a huge waste of time, even though I had a vehicle. My suggestion to fix this, would be for you to be able to turn off the random encounters once you have a vehicle. None of them are ambush things, you always have the option to do them or not. So, you could just as easily have some option that basically makes your character ignore everything.Anyhow, it has some decent replayability, since you can change your playstyle, Wing, and the faction(s) you side with. I personally don't replay games, but if I did I would definitively try a no-kill run.

_childDocuments_.review: It is very reminiscent of Fallout 1+2 style game with a new and novel concept for how this part of the world is so dysfunctional/ has it's own apocalypse. Character variety/customization is quite good and voice acting is well done for the parts that are voice acted. Skill variety is nice but lots of content if gated to a few key skills (criminal for lockpicking comes to mind.)Now the bad experience is derived from lots of different actions not just combat. At first this novel idea seemed wonderful as it allows you to be rewarded without having to murder everyone you meet. The detriment of this system is XP is tied to looting containers more than anything else so you will find yourself trying to loot the hundreds of containers for their mediocre loot just to level up. What should be novel and fun turns into tedium very quickly especially since Encumbrance is very much a concern in the game.Another novel idea is Fatigue your character gets slightly more tired with many different actions whether it's just walking around, picking a lock, breaking machines into components, or using any of your special attacks to name a few. This resource management part of the game seemed reasonable as a gate to stop you from being too strong compared to the NPC's however it turns into a uninspired resource management game. To make matters worse looting locked containers which as previously mentioned is a great source of experience in game will also make you tired which leads to having to deal with the fatigue system. The Hunger / Thirst mechanics are fine as they just slowly increase over time and are easily managed without being tedious but the amount of things that add fatigue is overwhelming and constantly forces you to stop having fun and deal with it whether you just drink some caffeinated beverages or find a place to sleep.Another major issue is the companions you meet that can join you lack depth. They all have a very short and not incredibly deep story the reputation system seems to mean very little to their interactions with you. I think every 25 reputation unlocked a single non branching dialogue response from each companion and that's it. They lack a meaningful reactivity to the environment and the things you encounter. Without interjections or feedback from them they just fall flat and turn into stat sticks that occasionally walk into a trap or pull an encounter you tried to avoid.My last major complaint is the story just isn't compelling enough to make me deal with the quest format. Many quests want you to do these five things or acquire 4x super critical plot device. The problem is over half of these quests turn into other small quests before you can get them which sounds fun as it forces you to explore but quickly turns to tedium. For example a part of the main quest in the second act asks you to go pick up a part from this settlement. Okay no problem but in order to get this part you have to put up campaign posters first for the quest target. Okay no problem you go and do that and then he wants you to solve the town's water crisis which requires you to go to a different map and that's not even the last step. Branching quests are fine but branching quests that branch get frustrating and tedious when overdone.Overall the game has some good qualities and great concepts but it's not worth your time or your money due to it's numerous flaws.
