_childDocuments_.review: This game tries to be Fallout so much that the developer missed the fact that Fallout was released 25 years ago and that there were games like Original Sin or Pathfinder in the meantime.The good things:- story (in Act 1) - it feels like Fallout. Lots of choices and possibilities to avoid most if not all combat situations. Many quests have a number of possible solutions. There are interesting factions and locations. In general, despite many flaws, it would be a solid 6-7/10 game if there was only act 1- the sci-fi/apocalyptic setting is kind of nice - at least in act 1 - a nice refreshment in the world flooded by fantasy RPGsThe bad:- act 2 - as many have already mentioned - Act 2 in its entirety. All the side quests are gone and 90% of NPC have just one liner responses and the game kind of becomes pointless. The game would be much better if it just ended at act 1.- ending - I don’t want to spoil the game, but in the end it seems like 90% of what we did is pointless anyhow and the choices you make during the epilogue matter the most (and you can’t make some of that choices if you don’t have the right skills)- combat - it is dull and kind of a "click to kill" combat style. It is turn based and there are various skills, but in general it is mostly about having good weapons and lots of medpacks. In many cases the combat is tiring and uninteresting but unavoidable (in particular in random encounters - you can skip those only if you have the right skill). Fun fact - your character can’t use grenades unless you invest in a particular skill.- way too many chests, lockers etc. - after like 3-4 locations I got so fed up with opening tenths of various containers that it kind of killed much of the exploration fun. To make it even worse some of them require "searching" which takes the form of a time wasting progress bar on the screen), most of which contain some random rubbish.- gear upgrade/levelling - not sure why, but the developers thought that actually having to upgrade your knife 10 times is a nice mechanic and having limited resources to do so is even better. As good as it may sound on paper it is actually not fun in game - you have to constantly hoard resources to be able to upgrade and in many cases you can invest lots to upgrade a weapon which you will find upgraded (yet as you already spent most of the resources on upgrades you can’t upgrade the one you found). For some reason you can't upgrade armour -  which is kind of ok as you don’t have to worry so much whether it will be useful during combat. You can actually find a level 1 unique weapon by the end of the game - stealth is way overpowered (e.g., most of the time you can sneak the enemies by walking 1m in front of them) and at the same time useless - you get no XP for sneaking on enemies = less levels

_childDocuments_.review: So I initially posted a bad review after losing several hours of gameplay to some bugs (described thoroughly below) However, despite the errors (which are annoying!) The excellant writing, atmosphere, environment, and non-grindy levelling still makes Encased worth playing. I kept my complaints below, primarily to warn people from making the same mistakes, and also to inform the devs who I hope read the reviews.I will update this later with the pro'sSome of the more glaring problemsTLDR-A couple completely broken perks/features (DONT PICK AMPLIFIER!)-Overly complex character design, I don't need 30-40 different stats/subs-stats to track, especially when many overlap, and many of them have unintuitive layouts. Why does muscle effect my tech skill? Why does fortune impact my combat speed?-Errors in tooltips, or blatantly unclear skill/perk descriptions (Add proper brackets to your equation tooltips, ask any mathematician whats wrong with them)-Occasional serious bugs (some glitch caused several dots to be applied several dozen times per round instantly killing one of my characters in a particular battle)Long VersionI started playing, and I did really like it! The setting is cool, the dialogue is enjoyable, the combat looks okay so far (I only got a few combats in) the freedom of choice on how to handle tasks is really good and refreshing.I was really stoked to be playingUntil I picked a perk called "Amplifier" (a major level up reward granted once every 3 levels) which stated it that it gave my character +5 to my psionic damage, as well as some buffs to companion psionic damage. Turns out that the +5 damage for my abilities component just doesn't work. The biggest bonus of the ability just isn't in the game period.I went online to search for possible solutions, because as it was my first time playing I didn't notice the problem until a couple combats later, as my character is not a huge combatant this was several hours of playtime into the game. Once I realized what had happened I started trying to look for ways to fix it. There are none... They have reported, broken perks (this issue was reported over 4 months ago on their reddit page, and via steam) in their 1.0 release. Something that could be fixed with a few lines of code, and there is no response about hte problem. The perk is a popular one, and its very easy to run into the problem. I doubt this is the only issue either...The game has too many broken features not to include a respec option. Unless your game is solidly bug free, you need an undo. Especially for a game designed to promote optimization and punishing tactical decision making. I play on the hardest difficulty, and have completed X-com, X-com2, DOS 1, and DOS 2 on the hardest difficulties and enjoy the strategy. But l'm also a parent and have very little time for recreation. So losing 5ish hours of my progress or continuing onward losing one of only 4 or 5 perks I am likely to spend the game with, just really took the wind out of my sales.What's worse, the dev's have even gone so far as to adjust the console commands so that the currently discovered ones are outdated. I cannot even use the dev-console to pick a new perk, or replace the broken one.There are other issues as well:I constantly have to refer to online explanations of what things do. One example Perk-Mysterious Patronage Description"Perks -1"What the hell does Perks -1 mean as a description? Is it removing one of my perks? Are there bad or negative perks in the game that I may need to remove later on? What is this? Well, turns out it reduces the number of levels between getting a new perk from 3 levels between perks, to 2 levels between perks. How hard is it to explain that?The dev's did include formulae in their tooltips (Which is awesome!) however they fail to properly include brackets in many places which makes the order of operations ambiguous. For those familiar with the gameplay and with math it is usually relatively easy to infer the intended design of the formulae, but why do I need to solve a puzzle just to know what 1 of the 40 governing stats on my character sheet do?If you fix the Amplifier Perk, and include a method for respeccing attributes until things are running smoothly, I will change my review.This game is absolutely playable, but if you are an optimizer (like myself) or plan to play on a high difficulty, then sadly, you will probably need to google each major perk choice to determine what they do and if they work.

Right click enemy to find out what they're weak to - use that. done. Even tactical difficulty mode won't provide much challenge to people who play the genre frequently.- The Survival System (hunger,thirst,fatigue,radiation). Pretty inconsequential. I could see this being a real con for people who don't collect/craft a bunch of supplies, though.- Weapon upgrades - for the most part it was fun to find the right resources to upgrade. _childDocuments_.review: Weak non-recommendationEncased is an isometric western rpg in the vein of fallout or the recent wasteland games.  Players control a character from one of five factions investigating an anomalous dome on behalf of the entire world in a concerted international effort in the 1970s, making choices and improving their character's skills and gaining or losing favour with the various factions and comrades.Unfortunately, polish is low or at least lacking in some very key areas.  It's always hard to place games like this as non-recommendations, because there is some genuine great stuff in here, but it's just mired in problems.The short of it: Encased has, for the most part, a terrific first act, impressive voice acting and characters, a good setup for faction dynamics, interesting character creation and a time-schedule system as well as a massive 7-floor main area and the rest of the dome to explore.  Unfortunately, bad balance, awkward UI choices, slow transitions, poor combat, encounter design and combat AI, baffling progression and a very boring second and third act mar what would otherwise be a very good sister game to the wasteland series.The long of it:Encased has a lot of things going for it, so let's start by talking about those.  Character creation is a lot of fun and you can make very different characters.  Some of the perks have a lot of character and some are specifically made to benefit characters with some hilariously low statistics.  The Concord area is an excellent tutorial with a lot to do, the intro ends dramatically and the world really unfolds after that.  The Magellan area is easily one of the best single hubs of any game I've ever played- and if the entire game was just a really really big Magellan, I think it honestly would have worked better.  Some of the companions are pretty likable and very well voice-acted, getting involved in a lot of different interactions and stating their feelings on a number of different things, particularly within Magellan itself.  There are many places to go and quite a few quests to do.  After the intro you can pretty conceivably get seven or so levels without fighting at all.  There's a stealth system and a crime/punishment system, theft and factional responses to wanton killing, a robust weapon upgrading system and non-lethal options as well as many different useful consumables.Unfortunately, there's a yin to each yang.  The full importance of character creation will be lost on a first-time player.  Certain specializations are much better than others, while others hold no merits at all.  Skill points are extremely important, and builds that forego them will struggle considerably more.  Some substats are very difficult to qualify for.  Stats essentially will not change over the course of the game (though you can respec for a moderate fee), but some unexpected limitations will become clear after character creation.  Low AP builds will suffer, and low strength builds can be easily made redundant (the easiest partner to permanently obtain is absurdly strong and comes with a really good unique weapon).  Finding other partners that use most ammo types is quite difficult or easy to miss, and the rewards are rarely worth the effort.You will basically need to specialize in a single weapon type, and due to the game's extremely suspect loot pools, you will be lucky to get much of anything over the course of the game even with a decent fortune stat.  I didn't find a single hand-to-hand weapon after the first 8 hours, and I never found a flame psi-hand for the game's entire runtime.  Shops are extremely limited- at least for weapons- and although they can be refreshed over time, I found it pointless to even try.  Even once the game opens up completely, the only consistent vendors are medical ones and chefs.  Furthermore, many consumables you might feel tempted to try are restricted until you put a number of points into a consumable combat tree, further eating precious skill points.  On top of that, it's extremely easy to put points into a tree for the weapon or discipline you like and get strange results- what skills you get at what tier and why seem almost entirely random, and the rewards for closing out a tree could be mostly unrelated like in the influence tree, or actually kind of a detriment like in the medical tree.Even if you manage to find the weapons you want, it's unlikely you'll find many good upgrades.  You can upgrade them yourself, but the material cost is quite prohibitive- and again, getting enough can involve repeatedly refreshing shots.  I barely upgraded anything over my run but a suit of power armour, but the improvements aren't that considerable anyways; I felt like whatever weapon I was using was doing about a tenth of an enemy's health in a standard situation where I was not overpowered after the midgame.  While this does bring home the concept of scarcity for the setting, a game with as much combat as Encased shouldn't have this in such a state.On the subject, the combat is more or less broken.  I played on the third difficulty level of four, and I can say firmly without a doubt that most of my struggles and successes were for the wrong reasons.  Many skills that cost fatigue as an extra resource might have been a good idea, but the rewards for using them are rarely commensurate.  Determining what status effects work on what enemies often seemed like an exercise in futility- matriach hyenas are immune to lacerations... why?  Why can't the necrobe's hands be disabled?  Why is there nothing indicating that the red necrobes shoot?  I just wasted AP or exhaustion on that?  Sometimes, the AI just seizes up and does nothing- Hyenas being the biggest offenders on this, but far from the only ones.  This can be helpful considering how spongey many enemies are or how hard they hit.  In particular, enemies with a defense value or brutal to fight.  "35%" chance to miss sure seems like "66%".  Not that the difficulty of any given encounter really matters 90% of the time- stealth allows you to easily crush enemies one at a time.  Heck, even unstealthed a lot of enemies will fight out one at a time, allowing you to defeat enemies twice your level.  Damage forecast is not great at explaining when your attack will heal enemies, and this is occasionally very relevant information.  Thankfully- or perhaps not- many of the enemies are fairly trivial mindless creatures, or singular targets.  Often, the same tactics work really well on them- shoot them from stealth with a rifle multiple times before the start of combat, and then finish them off with a high initiative character.  Most speciality tactics were pretty worthless or not worth forgoing damage- although credit where it's due- the psionic multi-stun, psi-confuse, leg shot, castling, teleportation, karate chop and headbutt all had their place.  This review is too long so I'll sum up. Human enemy encounters are unbalanced the other way.  Companions are likable but lack quests or significant connection to the setting. Quests and dialogue suck in part II and there are better (even co-op) rpgs of this ilk out there- wasteland II and III are just better at almost everything this one tries.

And there have been overall 5 relics in flower pots during my second and last run. The amount of lootable things combined with the 3 second delay to loot it and the imho slow walkspeed of the characters makes it tedious instead of exciting. Looting is about 50% of your time and maybe 80% of your click actions in some locations.I tried it without looting _everything_ on my second run, but the missing xp and money was quickly noticable.RandomnessDid I mention the relics in the flower pots? On my first run my char hat at level 12 the same torso armor as with level 1, since neither loot provided anything better for my playstyle nor did the merchants sell anything better. On the second run I found a plate armor in a crate and never changed this one till level 21 (where I quit playing). Winning or loosing may depend on your luck here. Merchants should have some basic stuff for you at least.Unclear goalsAt first I thought those might be translation errors. But nope... a npc told me he gave me coordinates for a tank to find. But no new marker popped up on the map. For the main quest I need to go to the "first settlement", but I have no idea where it is. All in all 4 quests now which tell me to do stuff in a certain point, but I have no idea where to go (unless combing through the whole area...)The last quest told me to get special fabric, which was used in landing pods. Luckily I found a landing pod already so I went there. Can't interact with the landing pod. To be fair, there is a chest I can't open since I have no skills in lockpicking...And there is a lot of stuff you won't notice until you do it... sounds pretty normal, but that a knuckle duster needs only half of the AP your char has per turn compared to a glove, is no part of the description. So only after you buy the expensive weapon, you see it. Damn waste of money at that point.FatigueAnd here comes the worst point. You have too take breaks while traveling for resting since fatigue is rising. Ok, realistic but a bit boring since you are able to basicly camp everywhere. You basicly hit the camp button, walk over to the sleeping bag, sleep some hours (no quest I had was time sensitive) and march on. Additional to this boringness, there are attacks which rise your fatigue by a large amount. Like 400 points of fatigue provide the first malus and one hit does 100 fatigue to your char. And the enemy I encountered could attack 4 times in one turn. And this enemy wasn't alone... At 1200 fatigue it is game over for the char. I lost more fights to fatigue-attacks than to normal damage. Until they balance that a bit, there is no way I play this game again, even if it has its good points.PS: Some enemies are able to use the high end melee attack "Your are already dead". It doesn't do any damage on impact, but deals 500 true damage three turns later. Not even winning the fight stops that. There is no counter (at least not that I found one). Onliest tipp from the steam community: Get enough hp to survive and heal afterwards. That one really hit the nail for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Update on this review posted below after playing through some of the content of the third massive update. Ok, I believe I've played enough to make a review on this game. I'll just list things down to make it easier.+ The main story and game premise itself is pretty interesting, small side quests and characters are also well made and directly interact with your character's choices through out the game.+ Character customization as well as being able to choose which "Wing" your character originates from.+ Replayability is strong, since the world and it's NPCs react differently depending on which "Wing" you choose. Making different play styles and story choices available.+ Remappable keys as well as a quick save and load system which makes the game way easier.- Is definitely combat, as it is the weakest part of the game. The "cover" system does not actually function as an actual cover system like in games like Xcom, instead it uses the characters left over AP to increase defense level which doesn't make a big difference. Accuracy is also questionable, since I can understand missing from 2 feet away at 83% chance to hit but I also miss sometimes at literal point blank distance at 100% chance to hit, I mean how can you miss at 100% chance to hit? That's just nonsense. Basically, I advise people to use food and drink items to increase your stats before any combat encounter and try to stack up on as many medkits and explosives as possible beforehand.  - Lots of small bugs which are expected since the game is in early access but I hope they get stomped out before the full release. An example of this is, is the glossy/miscolored textures for certain character hair/facial hair options.Overall, it's a pretty good game and a great game narrative wise. I just hope they rework the cover system to actually function as a proper cover system before release, as combat is what you're going to be doing a lot in this game and it's just personally annoying.After 3rd Massive Content Patch+ Devs are considering changing the cover system mechanics in a future update, so I look forward to that hopefully happening.+ Miscolored hair options are now fixed but some of them still have a low poly texture look.- Stealth is broken, most of the time your character is stuck on "in sight" status even when there are no NPCs around or when none are in your line of sight.- Some NPCs speaking Russian instead of English, which I wouldn't have a problem with if I actually spoke Russian and didn't have my language option set to English.- Graphic options keep resetting on game exit. I have to go to graphic settings and switch them back to Ultra everytime I run the game.- As usual, lots of other small bugs which I'm too lazy to list down.Basically, the update did add a lot of content and certain bugs were fixed but it also broke a lot of other stuff. So I would advice waiting till the devs push out some more hotfixes, until they get a fairly stable version going.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the new companions, however the AI tracking seems to get in the way and blocks free movement. I have seen in other games, where the AI would typically allow an companion NPC to move out of the way. Additionally there can be a dialogue option to ask the companion to move out of the designated spot so one is not trapped.Fast forward to May 4, 2020 the devs have improved on pathfinding and easier to progress the game. Although I share the frustration of many of the players about restarting, this is early release and can be expected. One of the areas I would like to have access to is the ability to talk to an NPC/console to re roll my character. it is unfortunate where you get into the game and find that unless you picked specific charisma or have some items that boost that stat significantly you are locked out for more companions in the game. Having this option does give some latitude and can be tiered with a cost to make sure it is not abused too much in game.Update to the game post release as of October 2022.The game has come along way to being complete as of Act 1 of my play through.Pros:Encounters are now more balanced and playing various builds are more viable such as SilverWing and Psionics/Charm.The world is more integrated and allows both for linear and open world exploration.Vehicles are purportedly going to be available in a recent update, however I have not run into as of yet.NPCs are more flushed and developed and causes a balanced approach in interactions especially when two do not necessarily agree on the type of approach.  This would be nice to see in the dialogue window potential +/5 to a given companion to help with dialogue choices. NPC pathfinding is finally fixed and no longer blocks you or locks you in spots.Item selections, and relics are more flushed and varied.very low game crashing bugs.Cons:As of Act 1, the cons are greatly reduced.NPC count in your team at a given time could be increased with certain perks/charisma, however this seems to be absent now and caps you at 2 regardless of your influence level.Lots of running, meaning, lots of running.....where are the pack mules? (not companions)Certain missions that present the main player to go solo, suddenly makes you greatly encumbered since the party pooled inventory suddenly drops all your encumbrance onto you. It would be nice to have a stash box near by to alleviate this.There seems to be a lack of armor types still in game, and I find myself wearing the same clothing minus an upgrade of the same type with slightly better stats.  If there was an armor improve button, I must have missed it also.Overall impressions:This game has improved from its initial early access release and has come closer to what was promised in the roadmap. _childDocuments_.review: TL:DR combat system is terrible. It's not hard, just extremely barebones and basic. The story seems quite good and I will play through it. If you don't care about combat in these games, it's a buy. If interesting combat systems make you happy, skip it.Common complaint about steam reviews: I wish I could give a 'middle of the road' rating.I go into these kind of games expecting an enjoyable combat system which goes beyond "point and shoot, tank damage" or "rush and bash, tank damage." Unfortunately, those last two scenarios define the combat system in this game. You'll want to leverage your standard mmo crowd control techniques because cover is pointless, everything rushes suicidaly to get into firing distance of you, and everything can kill you.On that last point, it gets real 'suspension of disbelief' destroying. Very early in the game, you find for yourself a suit of what is essentially power armor. Despite this giant suit of fully enclosed metal, normal office workers can punch you to death.   That should say a lot about the combat system in and of itself, but it the game always devolves into 'point and shoot' without any real interesting decisions happening. Age of Decadence has proven that these games can feature little or no combat and still be triumphant (and that game has optionally a lot of combat), but what combat there is must be satisfying. This game goes through the motions. A random crit will pop up and you'll 'ho' and 'hum' in boredom because you did nothing to set that up. A random crit will happen to you and you will be one shot by an office worker while wearing power armor and you'll stare blankly at the screen, sigh and reload. It's not like good combat systems in these sorts of games don't exist. Hell, just copy paste one page rules combat systems and you're already off to a more interesting start. Heck, you could even keep the same boring perk/combat system and just program more interesting scripting into enemy encounters ("pop into and out of cover instead of relentlessly advance towards you").A word of praise: I played the game on the hardest difficulty because I was excited to discover that the game doesn't fudge numbers for or against you. I dug that a lot: let the good times roll. The story is as described and even from the beginning drew me into the setup. I thought I'd hate the '1970's' feel, but it doesn't feel dopey like in Fallout. I'd say that, if you were on the fence, get the game for the story but hard pass for the combat system. Like another reviewer mentioned: even shadowrun felt deeper.

_childDocuments_.review: Putting aside the goofy plot and lack of enemy variety and all the other game design details that are admittedly kind of annoying, what I really wanted out of this game was explosive, over-the-top turn based isometric combat reminiscent of Fallout 1 and 2, and on that respect Encased absolutely delivered. This game has a crazy array of big explosive guns, absurdly overpowered perks, hours and hours worth of character build tweaking options that feel empowering without ever seeming unfair or punishing, and  to slow combat down (thank god). You can absolutely break the RPG system in this game in half and become a one-man army if you want to- or collect a bunch of companions, or play as a stealth ninja pretty much avoiding combat the entire game if you feel like it. There are level up perks designed to make just about every type of character build feel incredibly powerful, even one to massively boost characters with their attribute points spread evenly across the board instead of min-maxxed in a few specific areas. I love how far the developers were willing to go with this. There isn't even a level cap to "reign in" your character progression in the endgame, so if you play through every single sidequest like I did you're going to be an unstoppable wrecking ball of destruction even on the hardest difficulty. This style of combat, the massive amount of customization options, the Relic system and all the unique usages of skills is one of the most fun experiences I've ever had in an isometric RPG, and for me is enough of a selling point to justify buying and playing through the game. Encased does a much better job recreating that old school Fallout combat feel than other isometric RPGs like Wasteland 3. There are definitely some balance issues with how certain guns are tweaked but it was never enough to seriously hinder my enjoyment of the game.What in the heck happened with the location/character design in the second half of this game? It's like whoever made the City, the Phalanx HQ and Carmine Heights areas just never finished programming the NPC interactions or creating sidequests. It's crazy to me because Junktown and especially Magellan Station are loaded with interesting characters, unique building designs and tons of stuff to do, and after all this hype and buildup in-game about how you're going to unlock all these new locations after you complete that big first main quest- you find out that most of these new locations are filled with pointless generic NPCs and copy-paste boxy building designs with absolutely nothing of interest inside of them. The Fops headquarters is at least kind of cool, but Carmine Heights in particular is just so dry and generic despite having so much potential and buildup plotwise during the early parts of the game.The sidequests and random interesting locations you can stumble on on the world map made the second half of the game not feel like a total wash, but it's a shame how the actual main quest itself ends up feeling like a bunch of boring fetch quests and running around through locations I don't care about just to unlock the final area of the game. Because of how massive these endgame cities are despite having basically nothing to do in them I really believe the developers must have run out of time or resources at some point. I would love it if this game got some patches or a DLC expansion in a future update that really fleshed out some of these factions that felt grossly underdeveloped.I still recommend playing this game because of how fun the core combat and character customization is, but if you're in it more for the story and dialogue- well, you might consider passing this for another title.

_childDocuments_.review: You can really tell how hard they worked on the prologue and act I - the worldbuilding, setup, difficulty curve, everything is pretty well done and makes a lot of sense, had me very engaged. However, beyond act I the game really feels a lot less incredible, and the sense of awe i had about it kinda wore off. The biggest example of this is the complexity of the locations:In act I, you're going to spend *a lot* of time in Magellan station. It's a huge location, there's tons of quests, there's tons of loot, there's just a lot to do and see and enjoy. But when you compare the complexity of those interactions with the environment to what you encounter later in the City, or Carmine Heights (Phalanx was a pleasant surprise, it was more what I expected from it), there's a big difference. It just feels like the team kinda lost steam after their initial push to make an amazing first half of the game, it feels like maybe this needed another year or so of work before the second half was up to the standard the first half set. That being said, I'm still in act II, so maybe there's more to look forward to... but I doubt it. I had a lot of fun with the first part of this game, only to be disappointed as I got further in. I hope future games from these folks can be more consistent about the level of quality.I still recommend this game because I found the first like 60-70 hours really great. But it just seems like it's lost it's shine after that point.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty damn good - it looks and runs great, and I'm impressed how slick the game-engine is. The story starts off really well, and the first 8-10 hours are very enthralling, but as the game progresses cracks begin to show - it's a bit incomplete in areas, and bloated in others - some things seem like placeholders put there until a better idea/asset is implemented, or too over/under-engineered to truly enjoy engaging with. Don't get me wrong, I've still enjoyed playing it, but it needs some polish. I think the dev's have released it earlier than perhaps they should have, hopefully to get the funds they need for further development.The combat is particularly bothersome - AI Npc's tend to run around attacking randomly, blocking choke-points, shooting somebody point-blank, then sprinting to melee attack someone else several squares away - if there's any more than 4 or 5 Npc's then fights tend to devolve into long-winded John Woo Parodies of flailing arms and bullet-time shenanigans. In fact I mostly try to avoid combat, it really isn't very appealing. Enclave is not alone in this, Atom's combat was a bit crap, and so was Wasteland 2's until the Directors cut, but InExile had a better base to work from - they had cover-mechanics and map areas designed with tactical manoeuvring in mind. People might say: "Enclave is an RPG not X-Com!", but I will retort: Half the skills are "Combat", and many of the "Applied" skills are combat buffs! So I'm sorry, combat is just too integral to the game's core for it to be so unenjoyable. Non-lethal aproaches just draw out the combat even longer as you try to "beanbag" someone unconscious with your shotgun while someone else karate-chops, with another guy zapping them with tasers and pepper-spray - it's like watching Bumfights! It's strange, but I think if the game were uglier, jankier, and more obviously indie-developed I probably would've been more forgiving - but it's a nice looking game, so its flaws (especially the combat) are more jarring. Overall I'm glad I bought it, because it's an impressive game in many ways, and a non-violent or stealthy approach is totally viable. I know games like this are hard to make, so I hope the devs continue to work on it and make the most of its potential - it needs the games-development equivalent of a "movie-editor" to tighten things up a bit! I like Sci-Fi RPG's, and I want to see more of them - I'm sick of dragons, elves, and bloody wizards!

_childDocuments_.review: WHAT I HAVE BEEN WAITING FOR, FOR A LONG TIME.Preface:My particular "geekiness" is intelligent science fiction I also like getting lost (when I have time) in a good, intelligent, Sci-fi movie, Novel, or game. I have been looking for a good Sci fi RPG for a long time and I haven't found any since the Mass Effect games and Deus EX HR. Good: -Good Graphics, great soundtrack-Controls are perfect-Performance is superb on my laptop (950m) haven't even bothered on my desktop.-Even though I have hardly entered it at the time of writing this the world is a fascinating cocktail of Roadside Picnic (S.T.A.L.K.E.R) the alternative universe type thing from Fallout and the Dome concept from the Stephen King novel. Sounds odd but so far it's working.- Combat isn't XCOM 2 but it works well and it is really related to who you are\build ( I made a charming executive and then tried to punch someone in the face, needless to say it didn't work out well)- Good and easy to understand mechanics (some are not available at present)-NPC's with personalities who seem like actual human beings, very good writing ( with one or 2 caveats) - So many choices you can do what you want people react to you differently depending on who you are and who you build.- Huge influence from the brilliant recent Shadowrun games from the great little hand painted images of people to the style of writing\storytelling.-For me the tone is perfect. It's got humour but it's not too "wacky" it also treats you like an adult there is swearing when you would expect it, not for the sake of it.- a half dozen ways to survive a broken lift (elevator)-It's a REAL rpg if you know what I mean.To Improve\bad:- The writing as I mentioned is very good but you would not mistake this for a US,UK,European or AA production. There are some grammar errors and missing or superfluous articles (articles don't really exist in Russian as far as I know) which should be corrected. There is nothing that stops you from understanding anything  major but in a CRPG the writing is the immersion and as such should be a major priority to fix.- It's in EA, it's missing some stuff. Including (no spoilers) something that will really be fun to use.-Due to the fact that it's missing stuff some of the attributes are useless (at time of writing) apart from discussions with NPC's.-The UI is far too small.-a cover system in combat would add a heck of a lot of extra complexity to the combat (personal preference). -The roadmap (development schedule) needs to be more specific and have some estimated dates. We've all been burnt by EA games that gave up or did not fulfil their potential.Conclusion:This is a very good CRPG, it has a unique world, clearly talented developers and has the potential to be something very special.If you have read this I'd buy it if this sounds like your cup of tea but if you're looking for a fully complete game I'd wait a few months but I'd definitely keep an eye on this.From hours played,  I really like this game, highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good post apocalyptic crpg, mechanics and gameplay are the usual but this game has a good roleplay component. Your job and your skills come up a lot in dialogues and, honorable mention, because for me it’s the sign that a game has a good roleplay, you can do a “special person” character with tailored situation, dialogues and its own “understanding” of the story. The game Is a mix-up of mechanics and clichés of other rpgs or post-apocalyptic games, you have vehicle combat like Wasteland, throwing metal bolts to anomalies to scan them and get strange relics, like Stalker, and of course there are tons of citation from every post-apocalyptic source from books to movies.This is not a game where you can do a jack-of-all-trade. Like ATOM and similar games with the grouped skills system, you need to specialize and keep specializing or in the lategame you will suffer a lot. It's not a bad thing, you can see all the skills and perks you gain at character creation, so you can do the character you want without surprises.Companions are not for granted, some will not join if you act in a way they don’t like when you meet them the first time, some can hate your guts for your jobs and they track how you act during the game. Too bad devs never expanded their stories or interactions so they are barebones and sterile.This is clearly not an AAA game but it gets the job done, it’s not the longest or more polished game you’ll ever play but considering it’s basically an indie it’s a very good work.

_childDocuments_.review: No spoilers. If you like Fallout 2 or Wasteland 2, then this game is more of what you like. I definitely like both of those, and this game gets a high recommendation from me. All the motivations of the NPCs make perfect sense. All events and encounters are very much in the character of the world as advertised. For Early Access, their software build is very polished. No crashes at all. Minor glitches include not being able to throw grenades, not being able to use a short-range personal teleportation device, and not being able to use a short-range jet-pack (though it is possible that I was not using these devices correctly). 99.9% of everything else worked as intended, which means the developers have really done a great deal of work putting this together. _childDocuments_.review: At first, I had very high hopes for this game. It struck me as a nicely modernized version of the original "Fallout," and it features an opening act that's a fantastic example of both writing and pacing.Near the end of that opening act, the quest requires you to solve a puzzle involving a power control panel and a generator. The puzzle doesn't initially show any signs of trouble, because it's presented in a relatively compact space. Plus, it's "readable:" You can figure out what you have to do. At first.When you get the puzzle to a certain point, you're told that the system can't engage without you enabling an emergency generator. When you do that, it seemed to me that you were no longer in danger from the dark...but I still couldn't reach the objective. I legitimately thought that the quest was bugged. It turns out, though, that the expectation is for not much to happen after you start the generator. You're supposed to go back to the control panel to get the power back on.The thing is that, in my mind, I had done everything I needed to do at the control panel, so going back wasn't at all something I saw as being required.I saw this as just a fluke, a bit of odd puzzle design, and moved on.I got to the main game (where the world opens up), and went into the first major quest and puzzle. I progressed a bit of the way into it, and became stymied. I finally started searching the web to see what needed to happen, and it was a case of, "First you select this, then say to pull a lever, and after that you can get an item from so-and-so, which you put into this box which isn't marked as interactable in the normal way, and then..."It was there that the realization hit me. The devs had mixed "Fallout" with "Myst." Put another way, this was going to be a slog through obtuse, fiddly, bull-feces. An isometric pixel-hunt where you use all the things on all the other things in hopes that you'll get a result, with resource intensive and unrewarding combat when the action kicked in.That's probably great for someone else, but it's not at all what I want out of an RPG. I don't mind challenge - "Fallout" wasn't exactly the easiest thing to see the end of - but I did have fun and see the end of that game.With "Encased," though, I stopped caring and put the thing down.It's not a bad piece of software as such, but I simply wasn't enjoying myself.

_childDocuments_.review: I have a weak spot for post-apocalyptic stories. Fallout 2 has been my favorite game for years now, and I am always on a lookout for anything that even remotely resembles it. Last year I was extremely lucky to receive a copy of ATOM RPG, which Early Access build brought me hours of fun. And before it I had a pleasure to enjoy Underrail, which is also an awesome old-school-styled RPG. Anyway, when I read the description of Encased and saw these words: “…inspired by Fallout 1 and 2, Divinity Original Sin and Wasteland”, I knew it was love at first sight. Now, EA can be a major turning point for many players, but let me tell you more about the game so that you could decide whether you want to get it right now and support the developers or wait until the full release. Let us begin! As I have already said, there is hardly anything I like more than post-apocalyptic settings (high fantasy is the only exception). If writers can create a unique world full of its own amazing lore, then they can just shut up and take my money. Judging by what I can currently see in Encased, there is a good base for a truly splendid story with dark motives and lots of crazy science. The writing itself feels a bit dry at times, but the lore got me interested for sure. Also, the humor is nice – just read description to some skills, for example. I do love games where your position in the society actually matters. Encased has a system of five groups called “Wings”: Whites are doctors and scientists, Blacks are security and military people, Silvers are bureaucrat and administrators, Blues are technical personnel, while Oranges are criminals who were given a second chance (read: they do all the dirty work others do not want to). Depending on your Wing, you will have different options in many dialogues and people will treat you differently. You can check your progress with different Wings and people at the Reputation page. People will have different attitude to you depending on your actions. Helping one Wing can worsen your relationships with others; committing crimes can also change how people see you – some will become friendlier while others will be more suspicious or outright hostile. The hierarchy also plays an important role here, so, for example, being an Orange can make your life difficult sometimes. The Reputation page will also explain how your past actions affected people’s attitude.  You can look through various containers to find some useful (or not so useful) stuff. You can simply open most of them but others should be searched thoroughly. Maybe you will find something unique? Or just another pile of dirt…which is not too bad as there is a crafting system, so any kind of junk can eventually turn out to be useful – who knew that broken scissors can be turned into a lockpick? There are also secret places and hidden items, as well as some containers that need a good burglar. I definitely recommend checking out the ventilation system – it can bring you to some very interesting rooms, you know.And the best part: there are books that can help improve your character’s skills. They are well hidden, but so worth finding! I really appreciate the simple fact that you can look in the mirror and get a Charisma bonus. Or wash your face in the basin and feel Invigorated. This adds a new level of buffs that can be received without the usual food, medicine, or drinks. As well as a certain level of realism. Also, sometimes it is a good idea to look around you to find new solutions. For example, if you find the first fight difficult, there is one certain round thing in the room that can solve everything without even a single hit. It is a bit difficult to judge whether they are really good or bad right now while a lot of features are still locked and the story has no ending, but I already like what I see. Yes, there is a Fallout vibe during fights; yes, most options are quite easy to lean and navigate; yes, character stats can be confusing at first, but you will learn more about them in the prologue. Speaking about the general balance, once again, it is difficult to say something right now. I think developers will change a lot of things before the full release depending on the feedback from players. The only thing I can say is that you should be careful while creating your character: mine definitely was not good during fights, but I built her for talks and trades, not killing, in the first place.I love and hate it at the same time. One the one hand, it reminds me of Arcanum: Of Steamworks and Magick Obscura as every item has both weight and size that occupies slots in your inventory. On the other hand, I cannot carry as many items as I could – even if I am strong enough, as soon as my inventory runs out of space, the looting has to stop. The good thing is that you can actually buy backpacks to get more slots, but gosh are they expensive! I did not put this feature in the pros part because I am quite indifferent to it – I always play as a female so that I could associate myself with the character. But I think other players can find this unique character creation feature a pleasant surprise. There are a lot of items, skills, and features that are not available right now. Technically, there is only prologue and an open world to explore after it. I do understand that we are talking about EA here and it is not an issue for me, but some players will most probably find the current content lacking and start complaining about it. To avoid such situations, please, decide right away whether you can buy the game and wait until it gets finished or would rather stay away for now.As you choose your character’s appearance, there is an option to select some special features for them. The sad thing is that these decorations are very small and you simply cannot zoom in on the model’s face, so you will barely see any changes. I noticed that some of the options added piercing, but that is all – I also could not distinguish their colors (you can change them with another button). For now, I see no use in this feature – unless developers make it possible to have a closer look at your character’s face. I will be honest here: usually I am quite suspicions of Early Access games because you never know what might happen with them. However, in this very case, I would give Encased a chance. Looking at the current content, I expect a high quality RPG with the true old-school feeling about it. People did not believe in ATOM RPG and look at it now! I think that developers of Encased can be successful too, so my answer is yes, I would recommend this game to my friends and readers. There is a lot to be done before the full release, but it will be worth the wait.

_childDocuments_.review: So before I get to my review, I've heard that the devs kind of just... disappeared, so I'm not sure if they have anything else planned for this game, or if it's just completely done. But there's been no word from them since last year (the last update was in May 2022 and it was a hotfix update), and at this point, without any word from them, I assume there will be no more updates.With that said, I enjoyed my time playing this game. There have been others saying things feel incomplete, or just downright unfinished, and I do agree to a certain extent. Some questlines feel rushed or lacked a satisfying ending, like they were trailing off and expecting to come back to give more. But overall, everything felt complete, and I finished the game with a lot of the quests done and not seeing anything that looked incredibly off or unfinished.However, there are some issues with certain puzzles or clarity with the quest dialogue. One puzzle expected you to look at a sign and be able to determine the order through color coding. I don't know if they gave this puzzle enough quality testing because I could not figure it out at all. The colors I was seeing were not right, and maybe it was because of the lighting or something else messing with things in the area I was in. But at a certain point I got frustrated and looked up a walkthrough for the puzzle.Turns out, I DID do the puzzle right, but this puzzle might have some kind of bug affecting it if you talk to an NPC and resolve their issue first. I think I managed to fix it by reloading my save, but it was annoying enough that they didn't do enough testing to see if the color coding was good enough, and now there might be a bug hampering it. I think this was the only serious issue that I came across involving bugs (thank goodness), but this was only my experience. I have no idea what other bugs there might be out there that still exist.Unfortunately, clarity with the quest dialogue was something I had to keep fighting against throughout the entire game. While there are general spelling and grammar mistakes still present, and not that big of a deal, some of the quest instructions and dialogue could've gotten another pass. At one point, you're told to go to southeast of a city for something but it's not clarified what exactly that is. You're told what to interact with, but not if this item is in another location you're supposed to visit, or if it's in the southeastern part of the city.And then it turns out it's barely registered anywhere near the location of where you got the quest. Turns out, the place you're supposed to go to is not just another location you have to visit, but it's also MUCH MORE CLOSER TO A DIFFERENT CITY. This is just one example of a weird lack of quest dialogue clarity, I have encountered a few others but enough time has passed and I (unfortunately) have a poor memory so I cannot remember them off the top of my head lmaoI think my biggest gripe is how slow everything is outside of combat. In combat, you're able to fast forward by holding down the SHIFT key, but outside of combat you're at the mercy of the natural clock. There's no fast forwarding long stretches of walk time and every container you loot has to incur a small process before you're able to see what's inside. So if you see a lot of containers around an area? I hope you have the patience to loot them all!Speaking of combat, yeah I didn't have any major problems with it. You have access to 2 different toolbars: one's for weapon skills and the other's for items or skills learned from expertise like medical healing or robot repair. As far as I know, you can't organize anything from the weapon skills, which is very weird since you can switch things up for the other toolbar. It might not be an issue for most but it was something that definitely bothered me, especially since I hyperspecialized in hand-to-hand and my weapon skills bled into the 2nd layer, and I barely used most of the weapon skills on the first toolbar layer. Other than that, sometimes it was annoying trying to target enemies, but your mileage may vary and this is also a small gripe.I think that's pretty much it other than some other small gripes. If you're a lockpicker type, know that your skill won't have a cooldown, but if you were bruteforcing things like I was, for SOME reason, there's a cooldown for that, and it lasts a few seconds before you can use it again. Sometimes followers can act wonky and you can't transition off a level until they're near the doorway, so you'll have to select them and round them up like a lemming. I was a servoshell user (read: power armor guy), and you can upgrade your servoshell a few times... IF you run into the servoshell manuals, which I NEVER DID, so I finished the game with basically a mk.0 servoshell acting like a tanky fisto for my followers lmaoThere are some balancing issues with that, and at the beginning of the game past Concord. I was having a lot of trouble fighting roaches because there so many, but I was just simply not equipped well enough to do some of the new quests, so I basically made due from exploring, scanning, and looting stuff until I was ok enough to buy items and gear up my character. I had a very particular playstyle though, so it might be better for people who were ranged or don't do a lot of combat and sneak around.TLDR, like I mentioned before I enjoyed my time playing this game despite its issues. It has plenty of rough edges though, and it wouldn't be right to ignore them while making my review. Best case scenario I recommend this game if you are interested in checking out more CRPGS, because I thought the story in this game was nice! However, I would buy it on a discount, especially because I'm not sure if the devs are still around or not. If any of the issues I talked about might concern you, it might not be addressed ever if they disappeared. But still, it was a nice time for me, so maybe it might be a nice time for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr - Very good, story heavy, cool build possibilities, lots of alternative ways to do things. Makes me hungry for more content, and very hopeful for more perks and skills. A modding scene would also bring an insane amount of possibilities to the title as far as character possibilities.Encased is a CRPG in the old-school vein. They're backed by Larian, and have a lot of talented and competent folks on their team. As a heads up, I went in on the Kickstarter at the Founder tier maybe a year ago and have been keeping a close eye on this.The backer early access was very promising. Despite only having a few levels available, most of the problems that I noticed were centered around collision meshes on lootable containers and missed translations. The public early access is much larger (by more than three times, from what I can tell), and the bugs have been  mostly narrowed down to collision issues with lootables, and those are relatively few and far between.Content wise, there's still a lot more to go. Performance seems to sit stable at 60 on high settings even on older hardware, (1050ti, i5 6600k). What is there is very good, well written and interesting. In a word, the plot after leaving the starting zone can be described as "intense", and I'm really looking forward to seeing where things go.Obviously I've got interest in the product. I paid a little bit more than what's on the price tag, and I don't regret that. Even with the content that's currently there, it's easy to see how a bunch of runs through the content are viable. The different wings and different character builds offer a lot of variability both in accessible content as well as in play styles, which is certainly of merit. A lot of recently released titles cannot say the same, despite being in the same genres and being released by more well known developers.The title has got a lot of promise, and there's a lot currently there to play with. To say that I'm excited is an understatement, and while there's a lot coming up soon to keep me distracted, their release, patching and update history has got me feeling very good about their early access update cycle and release.If you're a fan of strong RPGs, I recommend this highly. I can't wait to see where it goes, whether mod support gets built in and how accessible that is, and what future content will contain.

_childDocuments_.review: Usually I don't do reviews, but this one definitely deserves it. It will be a quick one as I still didn't finished what is available to play in EA version. It was almost an instant buy for me with the decision made within 5 minutes. I grew up with early Fallout games and Divinity was also my piece of cake. So was definitely hooked up the moment I saw it. I built my first character just to skip through the playtime and try to see the wastelands as soon as possible and also to get myself familiar with the game mechanics, especially Skills system. Then I started the game with slightly new build and actually was trying to leave no stone unturned. The amount of time I could spend on every floor was insane and it didn't feel boring, I have read every bit of the dialogue etc. Absolutely loving the game so far! On my second run I have 6 hours and I still didn't leave the vault as I'm far too busy doing the quests inside. And there's good few of them! Dying to get back to it and see what else is out there!Pros:- Fallout 1/2 feel at its best!- Xcom/Divinity combat mechanics!- interface/Skills system- music (The Thing inspired?)- runs good on my 5YO gaming laptop!- amount of loot items to be picked up,- reputation system feels like it may cause the difference,- lots of reading and plenty of dialogue options,- Nashville area, great visualisation of well-known Vault,- within the first main location there were about 22/23 quests!- Space Odyssey 2001 fans will definitely notice what they need to notice!Cons:- lower FPS performance in some areas (still playable),- you can get overburdened easily (I mentioned to devs that I need Sulik obviously),- no voice overs even with the important NPCs,- prologue is quite short, but leaves so much to hope for!Bugs:- nothing game-breaking encountered yet,- few random spelling/font errors,- rag-doll effect of certain dead bodies,- built-in tool that enables you to share the feedback with the devs, used it few times already!I may edit it once I'll complete it. So far, it's absolutely fun to play! Would love to help the devs to make it a gem, it already has a great potential!

_childDocuments_.review: This is by far the best spiritual successor we've gotten to the original Fallout games, Atom RPG is close but has far too much jank, this is a very polished and easily played game. Can't recommend it more. That being said, I also think the XP curve is a bit scuffed, leveling is a bit slow at the start but once you hit level 20-ish it snowballs something crazy and you're leveling every 2-3 fights with enemies, not sure what happened there. That being said, I adore the wing system, felt like it actually mattered through the game and the wing system alone might make me do a second playthrough to try different weapons/companioins. Game length is also great, although I do feel like the story loses steam about halfway through act 2. The different factions could've been stronger and every hub (Carmine heights, phalanx base, fop base) felt small and barely had anything to do. I was expecting each new ''town'' to have a new series of missions for me to embark on but this was rarely the case. Fantastic, we need more turnbased tactical RPG's, especially post-apocalyptic ones. Hope to see a lot more from you guys in the same vein.

_childDocuments_.review: If you listen closely, you can hear the murmuring of lazy devs on the wind. It makes a big deal of the skills, attributes and perks but then makes utilizing those skills both rare, often pointless and occasionally objectively negative. It's not intuitive and the puzzles don't provide enough feedback to figure out in a timely manner. I'm not spending hours flipping switches that I can't tell are on or off, Then transitioning to another area entirely to go check, then running back etc. There are many things that you will spend your time on, only to get experience points out of it. Just xp. Nothing of note happens. Just xp. You will have submenus, even if they aren't necessary, just so that the game can know if you want to use your item that increases your skill for whatever action you are taking, unnecessarily. The text dialogue for quests is both lengthy an uninformative so you just run around and click things because talking to people is pretty pointless. every zone can be worked out like a maze where you just hug a wall and then circle in once you've clicked on all clickables.There's no incentive to go forward in the world. I won't do spoilers but, things happen and then you go for a long walk.  No connection to anything story-wise on a macro level or micro level. They keep things mysterious whenever it would advance the story and the payoff? It's not a payoff. It's just some mumbo jumbo. It really feels like someone sabotaged this project. It seems like every time they could have gone a little bit farther if they understood or cared about the player experience.  It's always one step short of satisfying though, the entire time, in every aspect of every mechanic.

_childDocuments_.review: Aloha, this is my review of Encased, a post-apocalyptic tactical RPG. Set in a anomalous land encased by an impassable dome in a thrilling homage to the soviet sci-fi novel: Roadside Picnic. The combat is action point based, with the standard RPG gameplay loop of kill mutants [or robots, or cultists, or bandits, or roaches/rats], level up, acquired loot, repeat.The Good: I played a high intelligence scientist expecting that I would not be viable for combat, but was happily surprised, the combat system is a fun with plenty of cool weapons and abilities to use. The companions are interesting and you recruit a buddhist bruiser, a robotic japanese school girl sniper, a washed up alcoholic actor,  a trenchcoat wearing edgelord, an insane furry, and a disgruntled scientist. The world is decently sized with plenty to do and fourteen different endings, many random events, a ton of side areas, with some events only open to certain builds. The sound design was decent, music is used sparingly; good graphics and artwork.The Bad: some of the questlines are quite convoluted and I needed to use a guide; when you zoom too close some of the characters have awful doughy droopy eyed facial features! YUCK!The Ugly: the pit side area, I was unprepared for the amount of body horror. *shudders*

_childDocuments_.review: Encased is a generally well-written and put-together Fallout 1 clone throttled by Bethesda-style inventory management. It's another one of those games that makes me curse the binary nature of the steam review system. It's a 5/10. I don't recommend this, and yet it could be something you like.But anyway, standard opening for context. Who the hell am I? I'm the guy who:-First fell in love with RPGs when he played the Fallout 1 demo, back in the mid 90s.-Absolutely loved Fallout 1, and Fallout 2 even more so.-Was something of a hoarder even in those games-Liked Morrowind and New Vegas for while...-...but ultimately fell out of love with inventory management as a primary gameplay mechanicI like to make nuanced reviews of the games that I play. I read other people's reviews and Steam's downvote/upvote system just doesn't feel like a good way of judging how good a game is. So I generally do my best. However, full disclaimer, reviewing Encased is going to be hard. I've not touched it for several weeks, and very little of it sticks in the memory.When I started playing Encased I thought that its character creation system was reasonable. It was the first thing that leapt out at me, honestly. It's an old-school system with little in the way of visual customisation but a reasonable level of depth, and seemingly a focus upon multiple ways of solving problems. It isn't on course to win any originality points, but it seemed to handle itself well. I liked the idea of coming into the world from an existing faction rather than tagging on as we went.The world building I would describe, again, as reasonable. There's a nice alternative history fantasy going on, and the writing was generally sitting in that positive space of interesting enough to follow, but never falling down the road of pretentiousness. The story, or what I recall of my emotions when playing it, was told well enough and even though I only encountered the start I felt relatively invested in this world and where it was taking me.Discussing the gameplay will necessitate ignoring the elephant in the room. Broadly speaking it's standard isometric RPG stuff but well-executed. Pick stats that make you specialise in certain things, and you will have access to additional options to solve problems. Stats allow your character to bypass computer systems, charm those around them, or sneakily achieve things without notice. Sometimes the game will pull the player in with this. Computer systems may require specific instructions in order to work, or stealth may be used to get past certain points. All this is done inoffensively and is casually engaging.Of course you are balancing these non-combat skills against their combat brethren. I don't want to harp onto the combat too much here because I suspect the combat increases the further into the game you get. As it was, I faced off against my fair share of radioactive, mutated invertebrates in a combat system not a million miles away from Fallout 1. Thus far, it lacked anything like the impact, but there is time for that to improve.The Graphics you will see from the photos, and there's little more to say, really. A less stylised version of Disco Elysium, but then you were never playing Disco Elysium for the graphics.The sound is, thank the Gods, wholly customisable and with good reason. The game has full voice over including a narrator who describes everything that isn't directly spoken by a character and if they hadn't given me the option to turn that infuriating thing off my playthrough would've been 11 hours shorter.But that, alas, is not the elephant in the room.Of those 11.5 hours, I spent around 8 hours trudging round maps picking up dirt from plant pots, wires from bins, and detergent from janitor's trolleys.Now, on reading that, you may know where you sit with things like this already. You may, in fact, say that I am to blame for the experience, and it is not the game's fault if I cannot show the discipline to not check a plant-pot that has a non-trivial chance of having $10-$50 in it. Let's be honest, we've been here before. Bethesda have had most of us searching through container after container for more valuable spoons since Morrowind (maybe even Daggerfall for some). Who didn't enjoy Fallout 3 onwards, where searching through endless filing cabinets might result in value/weight treasures like Toy Cars, or even Packs of Cigarettes!I am not here to convince people of the value of extended inventory management to the genre. I am here to say that Encased features an absurd amount of it, and that even by Bethesda's standards it is teeth-pullingly dull. In the first ten hours you will generate far more money from searching every single container on the map than you will from quests, and with ammo scarce you will likely need that money if you didn't go down the melee path. And there are SO. MANY. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. CONTAINERS. Every. Single. Map. You don't even have the utterly asinine Bethesda mechanic of value/weight considerations because your inventory is essentially infinite.I know that Fallout 1 and 2 had lots of containers, but they were almost all empty and only a select few held anything of value that wasn't telegraphed. Practically every container in Encased has something insi......oh, the name is a pun. I just got that. Oh...Well. Don't I feel like an idiot.Encased, then, is a superb piece of commentary about how inventory management and looting is tearing apart the modern RPG and how easy it is to pad out a game with bland non-mechanics in order to artificially inflate its length. It also goes to show that early Fallout fans are quite literally willing to search through endless bins if you give them a suggestion that it might replicate those glory days.Recommended to all the RPG fans who Prime Matter are presumably taking the piss out of with this. 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This quick review is based on the EA content patch 4. The game as of right now is very much playable and enjoyable. The UI is very smooth in its current state, and visually the game is very well detailed. Playing on Ultra settings I had very little stutters throughout my quick run. The game currently feels like a cross of the original Fallout games and Wasteland 2. There's also a dab of Pillars of Eternity in there as well as some Underrail.The story telling and dialogue with NPCs is by far my favourite part of the game right now. As someone who's played a lot of CRPGs throughout the years, this element is very important (I think) to the success of the game like this. And so far it's looking really good in that regards.Combat still needs some work as it feels clunky at times and things don't work the way they should on occasion. There's a lot of abilities to use but I'm not sure it's needed. I guess we'll see in the end how this evolves in later builds and I am hopeful it will all work out.My time played at review time is from one playthrough. I completed about half the quests so there's definitely a lot to do in content patch 4. Overall this is an easy recommend as an Early Access game for those craving a sci-fi CRPG.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this since it first arrived as early access, and I'm done. Game play is plagued with confusing plot points, bugs in quests, crafting is a joke, the NPC sidekicks constantly trap you into corners, and the story line continues to go nowhere. I'm leaving out the language issues of confusing misspelled words, grammatical errors and responses still in Russian. I don't feel this game is improving, if anything it has attempted to improve by going off in multiple directions but not truly progressing in quality. I will attempt to explain some issues: 1. the story line continually goes no where, the basic prologue still ends after you use the emulator and interaction with anyone is pointless. Scanning objects is useless unless you like an amazing detailed database that adds nothing to the story line or if anything creates an even more unclear picture of what is going on. Looting anything is tedious and provides less reward as you attempt to scrape anything useful from what ever ruins or containers you find (seriously I have found just dirt in containers you would think would have components) . 2. Bugs in quests are rampant, either the character does not allow you to interact with them or the conversation choice never appears to progress in the story line ( after using the emulator the scientist disappears so further interaction isn't possible) locations are present in the southern half of the dome but are inaccessible even after telling the maelstrom to move to the center of the dome, so you die if you attempt to move south to any locations you find from the observation deck.  3. Crafting, you carry around massive amounts of pieces/parts/components and cant build anything, literally hundreds of upgrades to weapons and I can never buy or find any of the the full list of components to complete any of them. Workbenches are scattered throughout the dome and  you cant upgrade a weapon on a chemistry bench or science bench etc. NPCs are worthless, they cant hack for you, disarm mines or open containers, but they will trap you into a corner or narrow area and cause you to re load games constantly. Graphically the game has come forward but when you mix all the difficulties with the attempted improvements it becomes more annoying than enjoyable. I feel like this game has an incredible amount of potential, but continues to fail as we re promised more in worthless weekly news updates that give us nothing but promises and rainbow ponies. I'm removing this game from my account and moving on.

_childDocuments_.review: I would give this game a 6/10 and recommend it when it goes on sale.  This game is a Fallout Like with some nice twists. This results in the strategy of pumping dexterity for action points as not being the only optimal option.  The world building is good and there is a lot to explore.  The negatives of this game are that the companions are not very fleshed out, the quests can be very fetch oriented and finally the pacing is not good.  When I say the pacing is not good, I mean that the difficulty in the game starts off good, but you become godlike very early on and there is no challenge after that.  Finally, the main story ended very weakly I felt.  Overall, still a positive experience.  Although it could have been much better.

_childDocuments_.review: So much potential, and close to being great, but too unpolished for my tastes.The concept and setting are very original. That's a plus.The animations are all clunky, floaty and slow. Combat should be punchy, but its weight is robbed by the slow movements. In addition, your enemies do battlecries, similar to games like Divinity: Original Sin 2, but they're just kind of... lame. Some better ones are undercut by very lame shouts like "Whatchu think you doin?"In addition, the combat really, really feels like it needs a cover system, similar to Shadowrun.The writing seems great at first, but part of the problem is it's so verbose when it needs to be concise, and concise when it needs to be verbose. NPCs say so much stuff, but your character never makes a personal connection with them, so it feels oddly sterile. The voice acting is really hit or miss. In general the voice actors are good, but most of the time there isn't voice acting.Finally, it's all just kind of clunky in a vague way that's hard to capture. An example: A few hours into the game you start a quest to fight in an arena. After you win, you don't get any reward, no special item. None of the NPCs (except the fight coordinator) even say anything different. No one says "Wow, you're the champion of the arena pit!" or whatever. It's like it never happened. Again, it creates that sterile feeling, and breaks immersion.Compare this to the arena in KOTOR or Divinity Original Sin 2. The world feels alive because people react to your wins and losses.All that said, if this game had a few more months in the oven it could be really, really fantastic. Its concept and design are so original, there really isn't much else like it right now. But it's just a little underbaked.

_childDocuments_.review: Bearing in mind that this game is in an Early Access state and that only the prologue (approximately 10 hours) of the game is currently available, I can overlook bugs if the core game is enjoyable, which this one is. If you like games such as Divinity: Original Sin 1/2, Tyranny, BG2, and other isometric RPGs -- or even Bioware's RPGs -- take a look at this one at some point. Some aspects of this game are reminiscent of much older sci-fi RPGs, such as Knights of the Old Republic, so I'm hoping the devs complete this and give it the polish it needs, unlike so many EA titles.  I have played Neverwinter Nights, Planescape Torment, and Baldur's Gate 2, and out of the more recent RPGs, I've played the Dragon Age series, Mass Effect series, KotOR 1/2, D:OS 1/2, the Shadowrun series, Tides of Numenara, PoE 1/2, and Tyranny, just as a point of reference/context. In particular, if you liked Shadowrun or D:OS 2, you should give this one a look.As the preceding paragraph probably indicates, I prefer text-heavy, thought-provoking games with a degree of player freedom (e.g., the capability to steal and non-linear quests) and this one seems to be sating that need so far, and I'm hoping this trend continues through release.At the very least, keep Encased on your watch list until it releases. There are too few sci-fi RPGs as it is, so this is a rare gem.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me correct a lot of incorrect assumptions or misunderstandings.  First off, I have seen entries about lack of info from the devs, but that is erroneous.  They have a fun twist on their updates that appear to be in game like with the same style as the game, but they do provide info to the community quite frequently if you take the time to read it.Second - Some people are talking about the game mechanics and how they can't kill a single creature.  You have to READ the info you are dealing with before trying to use an action/weapon in combat.  For example the range on a weapon has a big impact to accuracy and damage, so you cant use  a shotgun which is a close combat weapon to shoot someone 50 feet away...You just wont hit them.  The same applies for using fully automatic weapons, they are not accurate on will auto at range, so you should default to the 3 round burst mode which is why in real life the US Army switch to the from the fully automatic to the 3 round burst fire, so the barrel doesn't keep going up and up and you just waste ammo.Third - The game does a great job recognizing your starting Wing (background class) and responds to you with different responses, which I thought was really cool and labor intensive for the devs to develop conversations based on each Wing, so kudos to the devs for this feature.Fourth - The game could use a bit more options for character appearance during creation or post creation.  It is almost impossible to create a character that looks like the portraits associated with it.Finally, this game is very fun to play!!!   The story is good.  The combat is good if you understand it and read the tool tips.  Itruly encourage everyone to buy this game and enjoy it.
