_childDocuments_.review: A note to everyone who is concerned about gamepad experience.I had the same concerns after seeing some other reviews stating that the game is only playable with keyboard and mouse, while my plan was to play it on a Steam Deck, and in general I prefer to use a gamepad for this kind of games.Now after beating the game with 100% completion I can assure you, that the game is not only perfectly playable with a gamepad, but it's also an extremely satisfying experience.Some other reviewers wrote that with a gamepad you can only smash sticks and buttons and hope that it accidentally works the way you expect. This is true during the first 1-2 hours while you learn, since the movement mechanics in this game is quite fresh and unfamiliar even for seasoned metroidvania players.But after your muscle memory has been built - you start flying across the map and slicing through enemies like a hot knife through butter.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOMBLADE

_childDocuments_.review: Fun metroidvania! The movement and combat are a bit different from what you'd usually expect, but there is a demo that gives you a chance to try and see if it's your cup of tea. Additionally, I think the map felt decently big with enough things to find to make it interesting. The story and character are just alright, but the combat and exploration do enough to make it worth playing.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOMBLADE

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10I like the game and had mutch fun zooming across the screen and trough my enymies. The artdirection is also pritty nice and the soundtrack is perfect.The problems I have are, navigation; it is somitiomes to hard to find your next objective, reaper; the abbillity seemes to be buggy and sometimes not to do what is advetised, and deep spawn the range is to short for my taste, but that are all the problems i had with the game.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOMBLADE

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game. Reminds me of an aggressive, metal, gory Hollow Knight. Amazing art, sound, and game design make this around 8-10 hour game an amazing experience. If you like fast paced movement and exploring a world with a ton of lore that is easy to find, I highly recommend. Not an easy game but not one that you are pulling your hair out trying to beat either. Amazing experience for the price, wish I could upvote twice.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOMBLADE

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, the good old metroidvania! I was a bit skeptical at first because I prefer less acid color schemes and I was a bit wary about the unusual controls. But the game was very enjoyable overall, with lots of backtracking and unusual abilities, just as I like. Gloomy atmosphere is also quite cool when you get used to it.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOMBLADE

_childDocuments_.review: it is a fully functional (if somewhat basic) game. the difficulty is high, and challenges punishing (but only your first time through). what problems it does have tend to stack on top of each other to create flaws much greater than the sum its parts (patience will prove enough to deal with most of these). when the map opens up though you can really start to play (even if its constant loading and poor optimization will make your processor heat up quite a bit and even lag sometimes).save often... especially after anything you dont want to have to do again, even if it means backtracking
_childDocuments_.name: DOOMBLADE

_childDocuments_.review: I like a good challenge but I also know when something burns me out, this game is not perfect and I doubt it will ever come out of its niche, polished or not; this is the first game I rage quitted in over 25 years of gaming; I know it should have happened sooner or later, I just wished it didn't happen bc of something I was hyped for.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOMBLADE

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of action and fun.The genre is quite new to me, but it feels like old school jump 'n' run game. Game has its own style in design which I like. Sounds are also cool. For me it was quite difficult at times, but that makes you work even harder. If you like the genre and design, I recommend doomblade :)
_childDocuments_.name: DOOMBLADE

_childDocuments_.review: While I do greatly recommend this game and I'm having a very fun time,My main complaint is how short your i-frames are after being hit, you can easily get battered around by the horde type encounter rooms and take 3-4 hits in a few seconds and that really doesn't feel very fair in a game where you have no dodge action to give yourself i-frames.Although you have i-frames while performing an attack, you can often end up flinging yourself into other attacks. Then getting ping-ponged around. It really interrupts the pace of the game imo. While this is probably also a skill issue, I've only played a few hours at time of review, a little more "feedback" when getting hit would have improved the experience for a new player. Even if it means Gloomgirl gets knocked back a little more away from the hit you took, or slightly longer grace-frames after being hit.I think if you're going to do a completely different combat from other metroidvanias, which is GREAT breath of fresh air in what's becoming a very stagnant genre, you need to keep in mind that not every player is going to have the experience with twin-stick style games.Also interact being "L-stick up" by default can lead you to accidentally interacting with the many, many lore tablets or NPCs placed in areas you have to platform. Which is a little annoying when there's so many unused buttons, like pretty much all the face buttons.I know this review doesn't sound glowing or anything, these are really small issues in the grand scheme of things and I didn't see anyone else bringing it up. Just things to keep in mind. :)Other than my small gripes, the game is amazing, fluid, great atmosphere and music. AND OH GOD THE MUSIC IS A BOP!!
_childDocuments_.name: DOOMBLADE

_childDocuments_.review: The blade has me, and I can't let go. polished, fun & challenging metroidvania gameCurrently about 2,5 hours in, and the progress tracker shows around 25%, so I'm guessing there's a good 10+ hours of gameplay.The world is very atmospheric, with the sounds and visuals blending together nicely. There are bits that are quite tricky to navigate, and have me dying and running through them over and over.The main controls of clicking on enemies is something I like, and adds a nice puzzle element to running through the world. It also allows you to hack away and fly through the screen, which feels fun. Gameplay overall is smooth and everything feels polished.I would wholeheartedly recommend this game to people who like Hollow Knight and similar games.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOMBLADE

_childDocuments_.review: I don't have a lot of experience with Metroidvania games so I wasn't sure what to expect going in. I have to say, I have been really impressed so far with what I have seen. I was a bit confused when starting off, as the game felt a bit slow. This very rapidly shifted into an exhilarating and fast-paced experience that completely pulled me in. The movement system makes gameplay feel fresh and easy to handle. You always feel on the move and can quickly get across the map. I have gotten lost a few times, but this is also part of the game and takes some getting used to. The art style is also extremely beautiful. While I have not seen all the biomes yet, each one so far has had a distinct feel with pleasant music to top off the atmosphere. I would really recommend it to newcomers to the genre, as it both a blast, and a challenge, while also feeling quite accessible to the average gamer.
_childDocuments_.name: DOOMBLADE

_childDocuments_.review: Deep underground, Gloom Girl discovers DOOMBLADE, a sentient weapon hellbent on escape after eons in chains. Together, "Doom and Gloom" embark on a brutal quest to unlock the powers of The Void and destroy the Dread Lords once and for all in this 2D Action Metroidvania.

name: Max Mustard
detailed_description: Immerse yourself in the world of Max Mustard, a made for VR platformer meticulously crafted to deliver top-notch gameplay and unforgettable experiences. Combining the best of first-person power-ups with the timeless charm of classic third-person platforming, Max Mustard offers an irresistible blend that will keep you hooked from the moment you step into its virtual world. Embark on a heroic quest alongside our fearless protagonist Max to rescue adorable mudpups from the clutches of the devious Stubbins. Journey through immersive landscapes, facing tough challenges, unexpected twists and moral dilemmas, forcing you to make difficult decisions that will shape the course of your journey. Max Mustard is a thrilling odyssey paying homage to the classic platformers of yesteryears while offering a fresh and innovative gaming experience. With 40 hand crafted levels, each bursting with surprises, inventive mechanics, and endless variety, Max Mustard is an epic adventure that will capture your imagination and keep you coming back for more! Note - In-game language is limited but not localised and will display in English unless other stated.

_childDocuments_.review:
Max Mustard is an inventor on the dying plant Krunch, who witnesses small creatures being captured and caged by an unscrupulous businessman and his mechanical workforce. He's making a fortune selling them as an elitist vanity product to the super wealthy. You and Mustard team up to save as many creatures as you can.

Along the way, you are faced with a surprise dilemma when a friend reveals a secret about who they really are and imposes an impossible decision on you. One which could have monumental consequences.

Max Mustard is a made-for-VR platformer with a timeless, delightful art style. Each of the 40 hand crafted levels are their own unique adventure, designed for intense gameplay, exhilarating surprises and constant variety. No boring bits! It's the perfect combination of first-person power-ups and classic third-person platforming. This is a VR platformer you'll find impossible to put down!

name: Harold Halibut
detailed_description: Harold Halibut is a handmade narrative game about friendship and life on a city-sized spaceship submerged in an alien ocean. It’s been 250 years since your home - an ark-like spaceship - fled an Earth on the verge of cold war to find a habitable planet to preserve the human race. You are Harold, a young lab assistant for the ship’s lead scientist, Jeanne Mareaux. While most of the ship’s inhabitants have reconciled themselves to a life lived aboard the sunken ship, Mareaux still works tirelessly to find a way for the ship to leave the planet and find a new, dryer home. But the weird, wonderful and diverse people of the FEDORA I keep Harold busy too… Until one fateful encounter plunges Harold into a world no one could have imagined - and one that may hold the key to Mareaux’s re-launch plans. Join Harold as he explores a vibrant retro-future world in his quest to find the true meaning of ‘home’. Features: Unique Stop-Motion Aesthetics: Every element in Harold Halibut is a tactile and meticulously hand-crafted using traditional sculpting and model-making techniques. Full Voice Acting: All of the Fedoras' wonderful inhabitants come to life with full English voiceover, elevating the game's narrative to cinematic proportions. An expansive Character Ensemble: Meet a variety of unique characters and get to know their personalities, quirks and stories through meaningful conversations. A riveting cinematic storyline: Journey through a captivating narrative, underscored by a carefully orchestrated script that blends drama, humor, and suspense.

_childDocuments_.review: Very unique game. It's like being in an animated Wes Anderson film, the visuals and sound design are incredible. Loving the experience so far!Update 6-7hrs in: For those who are looking for an exhilarating game that involves you doing many different puzzles etc, this is not it. As other reviews have stated, you mainly just walk from A to B. But I think a better description of the experience is an interactive stop motion film, where you can just sit back and enjoy the story, visuals and music. I am thoroughly enjoying just exploring the world and appreciating the details. Props to the developers for creating such a different and special game.
_childDocuments_.name: Harold Halibut

_childDocuments_.review: This was hard to write, but I gotta follow my gut.With 5% gameplay and 95% storytelling, the story better be good, yet I can't fathom who or what age range this game was written for.The philosophical human themes are examined through relentless pondering by the main adult protagonist, yet this 'Adventure', having only fetch or 'Walk to X quests' seems that it's designed for very patient children to play? It's all very...wishy washy too? Huge themes whittled down to, 'Yeah, I suppose you're right..' reactions. It's stunning for sure, with ooodles of glorious Stop Motion to watch, however, with 4 minute long unskippable cutscenes and minimal game play, I found this a laborious trial to finish.The voice acting is hit and miss, and only English Language which is a shame. The music is fine with a bit of a nod to Phillip Glass, though it still feels half-effort in comparison to the visuals for me. Tonally confusing.Sorry to say it, and as an Adventure Game lover, it's extremely frustrating to see such a commitment to art be so 'nicy nicy', and safe, almost childish in it's writing, and still fails to bring home any specific message, coating everything in 'A that's nice isn't it!?', thus losing all impact, and for me a game that simply fails to cater to a specific audience thus failing both Child and Adult gamers. Maybe a good game for free thinking parents with lots of time to play with their inquisitive children? I'm glad I bought the game and supported the Dev's, and I truly hope this game finds it's niche, but it just wasn't for me.TLDR: It's like asking a 9 year old to watch Koyaanisqatsi (1982) and expecting them to comprehend it, or an Adult to play  Noughts and Crosses for ten hours and enjoy it, but both at the same time.
_childDocuments_.name: Harold Halibut

_childDocuments_.review: I love and adore this game.However, I don't think that it is a game for everyone.It is a slow game, with a lot of running around, finding stuff.It feels more like a book you can walk through than a "game".I LOVE IT!The game tells the story of a sad little man, who seems to suck at everything he does. He is pretty much a nobody at the beginning of the story.I love the story of Harold. How a sad, lonely and uninspired guy becomes someone who knows who he is and what he wants form live. I love the little storylines of the other characters, they help to make the world feel lived in.The story is quite weird but at the same time very thoughtful.You have to accept the weirdness of it all and you need to be open to the slow concept, then you can love the story as much as I do. If you don’t, you will get frustrated by the game.However, if there is the slightest chance that you could be interested in the game, pleas try it. Walk around the fedora, talk to everyone you come across and learn about their silly little lives. Follow Harold as he grows as a person and finally finds his passion, his will to live.Warning: IT THAKES A WHILE. Pleas be patient with Harold, after all in the beginning he is simply a sad little man (that I have grown really found of).
_childDocuments_.name: Harold Halibut

_childDocuments_.review: I spent a long time pondering over the question of "Would you recommend this game to other players?". It's not like there aren't aspects of this game that I thoroughly enjoyed; the unique, hand-crafted art style, the intriguing set and setting, the diverse cast of characters with some pretty decent voice acting, the soundtrack. Not to mention the curiosity I had to see the finished product of what sounded like a long and arduous development cycle. However, the main problem I did have with the game was unfortunately a very big one:It's not fun to play.In fact, there are times during Harold Halibut's extremely lengthy playtime (15 hours) that playing felt like an absolute chore.There are moments throughout the experience that are charming, clever, funny, even weird and trippy. But the overall experience feels like a slog.I've seen this game categorized as an Adventure Game and I really don't think that is an accurate description. Harold Halibut is more of an interactive movie. The gameplay (and I hesitate to call it that) is just walking back and forth and talking to people. There are a handful of minigames, but they are extremely basic; a lot of them are in fact just doing monotonous chores (i.e. unscrewing panels from a machine, washing graffiti off a wall, moving items on a conveyor belt). They lack fun and engagement. There's an arcade with cabinets you can play, but even these are boring, as 2 of them are the exact same game (where you fly a plane through some rings) and the 3rd is the same exact game just with a different skin.Frustratingly there is extremely little to interact with. I remember walking into the botany room, seeing tons of weird contraptions and alien-like flora all over the walls, and feeling flabbergasted when no interaction icon popped over my head as I walked by everything. It feels like a giant missed opportunity, a hallmark trait of an adventure game simply ignored.The walking and talking wouldn't be so bad if the story and dialogue were deeply engaging, however the game fails on both of these as well. While the overall story is unique and seems set up for grand ideas, it never goes in a direction you want or expect it to. There seems to be a noticeable lack of conflict or consequence. Dialogue with the patrons of the Fedora (the sunken starship you are stranded on) is extensive but ultimately uninteresting. Conversations also feel ham-fisted with an "after school special / lesson learned" style which just feels unnecessary. I have no issue with a "slice of life" approach to a story, but to experience it for 15 hours with no interesting or engaging gameplay is quite rough.I keep mentioning the playtime because I truly find the length a bit shocking. Harold Halibut absolutely overstays its welcome. The middle 5 hours of the game were the absolute worst for me, I was finding it hard to get myself to sit down and continue playing. The game even seems to be self aware of its own monotony. At one point Harold is in need of an item and is inquiring about it from a shop vendor. The vendor begins to say something along the lines of "I don't know where this item is, you need to talk to every person in this area to--oh wait, never mind, I have it right here". There was also an instance where you have a quest to go pick up an item from a character, so you laboriously walk to her location, only for her to tell you that no, she doesn’t have it, she mailed it to you, so you have to again laboriously walk back to where you started. Oh, and don't get me started on the "cleaning out the storage room" quest...It doesn't help that Harold moves excruciatingly slowly, even if you press the "jog" button.Thankfully, the final act does pick up in an interesting way, including some strange and trippy, existential moments. Again, there are some fun, unique and interesting moments to be had here; they are just few and far between. I truly believe if Harold Halibut was condensed into a 5 hour game instead of a 15 hour game I would have much higher remarks for it. I'm happy I purchased the game to support the developers and their large undertaking of putting this game together, I just don't feel we share the same vision.TL;DR - Art style and setting are clearly the games highlights. Everything else falls kind of flat. Beautiful to look at, not fun to play, and just too long.

_childDocuments_.review: Relieved to see that the full game fixed all the issues I had with the demo! Runs without framedrops now and the image quality in general is better with the smearing gone. Been following the development of this game for what felt like ages because I adore the art style so much, the word and characters just ooze with atmosphere and I love everything about it. Really hope this game gets the attention it deserves, this game truly has "cult classic" written all over it.
_childDocuments_.name: Harold Halibut

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know what I thought this game would be. I suppose I thought it would have more depth than walking from point A to point B and back. There is no inventory. There is barely any backstory to get you engaged or involved. You're just plopped in and start walking, which I suppose has worked in other games, but this one feels like they forgot I was here. I've followed this game for a while based on it's art style, but ♥♥♥♥ me, the ONLY things I can interact with or do is click A when I'm on a quest person and listen to rough dialog. I guess I knew I liked Wallace and Gromit and other clay-mation style things, but this wasn't enjoyable at all. Wife sat beside me watching me 'play' it and I was just making excuses for an hour and a half for it. I feel terrible writing this as I'm sure this was a passion project but I just didn't enjoy it. The visual style is cool and the music has a nice vibe to it. I suppose at the end of the day, I thought it'd have more puzzles or interactivity in the narrative and not just 'turn the page' mechanics. I don't think they ever misrepresented the game, I just went off of other games I'd played with similar descriptions. Hope this helps decide if this game is for you or not. To the Devs, sorry to leave this review, but it would've helped me decide whether or not to get it so I'm hoping it does the same for someone else. Best of luck.
_childDocuments_.name: Harold Halibut

_childDocuments_.review: Loved, loved, loved this game.  One autosave that saves frequently.  Minimal puzzles and lots of dialogue, cut scenes, and exploration.This game is a beautiful piece of art, with beautiful music and voice acting and storytelling. The story made me laugh at times and a bit weepy at times.  I was completely invested and enjoyed it immensely.  What I got from my 15 hours of play time trying to speak to everyone and explore everything in each act was well worth the price of admission into this wonderful world.
_childDocuments_.name: Harold Halibut

_childDocuments_.review: Just over an hour and this world has already stolen my heart <3I recommend you make yourself comfy, prepare a nice drink and some snacks. Take your time and relax, this interactive movie/book feels like a "once in a life time experience/story" Update: So far has nothing changed, just finished chapter 3 and it felt magical owoHere is some feedback:I noticed that the game has a bit of a pacing problem in Chapter 2 and that walking and running might become a bit tedious for some as you continue to complete all the tasks and try to find secrets/achievements etc. (especially when you're not that much of a fan of the art style and charm of the game, love to detail). I know first hand that it's not unrealistic since you're playing a handyman/janitor, but that doesn't mean it probably should have been handled differently.This is special, u feel the love to detail and passion. A game, story, world in work since 2010 and it's actually real and finally here. The character, voiceactor and sound designe, outstanding for being the first game of an small german studio.Oh and 30 usd/35 euro are fine in comparison to games like Suicide Squad and Star Wars Outlaws which cost between 70 and 120 usd/euro lmaoWhat can i say, 2024 gaming is somehting else.
_childDocuments_.name: Harold Halibut

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not through, yet. But to this point, i think this is a very nice game with interesting setting, characters, locations and overall catching story. The stop motion art style is exceptionally unique and well made. Music is nice. There is some humour. Runs well technically (on Linux). It's from a likeable small german studio. Enough reasons for me to recommend this game.It's not without some minor "flaws". I actually would have expected some more gameplay than walking slowly from A to B to A all the time doing fetch quests and some linear dialog. Some puzzles maybe. Something that forces you to think a bit. There is no inventory. You can only interact with the things you have to interact with for the quest at hand. Oh and there is no mouse support.So if you don't mind playing a visual novel without much challenge. The novel itself is good so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Harold Halibut

_childDocuments_.review: I told myself not to be swept up by "neat ideas" after I got burned by Broken Age, and yet here I am. I absolutely love a good point and click, but it needs to DO something in those regards. The puzzle solving is non-existent, it's just fetching. At one point a side-quest objective that was in my log for ages, was unavoidable during the main story, why was it labeled as a side objective at all? Everything just falls into place on it's own. There's even a minigame where you have to avoid one obstacle, and I'm not even sure you need to avoid it. You can actually see the start and finish on one screen, it takes longer to load it than to play it. I'm not exaggerating I was still getting vocal explanations as it was fading out cuz it was done already.There's a severe lack of music and sound effects that makes this very, VERY slow paced game even more grueling. I only recall one in game music track, and it was a whistling tune that sounded like I was in a Western about to go to a showdown, it was very confusing. There's a random minigame that starts with moving two small boxes one by one before suddenly being a "the room is now on the side and you're dropping everything in from the top without explanation" - again all silent. It's odd. It's a very unpolished game leaving Harold falling through the floors, slowly glitch sliding thru vents, etc that makes it feel like it was rushed, which is surprising in this case. The story is why I ended up giving this a shot, and it's really letting me down. The characters are pretty one note, and the idea that all of them knew Harold for so long and treated him so poorly, but within literal days come to love him, it's a bit weird. It leads to a large portion of the dialogue just telling a pretty simple guy who is inept that he is simple and inept repeatedly but then going "luv ya tho" after a while. The entirety of the first chapter is pretty much that, mixed with "Harold accidentally walked into a situation that wasn't his fault but now he has to fix it oh no" - exhausting.And don't get me started on the complete lie of "choices" - many games act like choices matter and they fail. But this is possibly the worst. It basically has many choices list polar opposite answers in theory, but literally result in the *exact same dialogue line* which is neither what you could say, is just infuriating honestly. This is 100% a visual novel, hardly a point a click, mostly a fetch quest at best. I rather it just be a movie. The idea is very intriguing but I fell asleep 3 times playing it yesterday and I wanted --- really wanted to love this. I'm finishing it eventually just cuz, and if things change I'll update this. But this game has been on my mind... with how disappointed I am in it and how much I don't want to get back to it.Also, devs, if you're gonna be cute about 4th wall breaking, be smart about it. Having a character send an item you need to the destination for you - but only doing this once ever - is a bad idea when you have instructed the player to do otherwise for *hours* at this point. To put in a line about "hueh hueh we would get nothing done if we had to go pick up everything by hand the all the time *wink*" doesn't work when that's the *only time*. And what's worse, is to assign achievement for making that mistake, is so counterproductive that I have no idea what the intention of any of this was.
_childDocuments_.name: Harold Halibut

_childDocuments_.review: This interactive story is gorgeous, it is very obvious that a ton of work went into it and it really is very pleasing to look at. I loved this cozy world, its characters and the music. I even found myself getting a bit attached to it. The voice acting was very nice as well.However, there is one big minus that overshadowed all the good for me. It was too long for what it was. I took my time with the game at first, really soaking up the environment, but by chapter 5, I just wanted it to be over. I'm not sure if it's because the world is relatively small and you go back and forth between the same spaces over and over, but after a while you've just seen it all. In my opinion, this would have been a much better experience if it was a game that could be finished in one day/one sitting. Just a cozy short experience. But unfortunately, it had me skipping dialogue by the end because I was over it.The story was okay, I personally don't mind when a story is simple. But there were quite a few times where I felt like I wasn't the right age group for the game. I can see what they were trying to do by including conversations about existence, decisions, feeling useless, alone, etc. But the way these topics were presented felt like they were meant for kids.Overall, I'd say the art was great, the writing not so much. In my opinion, it's not worth your money.
_childDocuments_.name: Harold Halibut

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a fan of walking simulator/narrative games AND long slow-burn films, and I still can't imagine anyone not getting bored of this by Chapter 3. At the current price, I genuinely feel kind of ripped-off. $35 for this is actually kind of insane considering how little there is to do, and what IS here is extremely tedious and repetitive.This isn't the place for me to just rant about things I would have done differently if I were the one who made it, so I won't do that, but it's clear that this was just not working for me at all - which is unfortunate given how much I was interested in the original trailer, and how much the demo seemed like it was working for me.This game is SLOW. Like, often very aggravatingly slow. At 6 hours in I had just finished chapter 2 (out of 6), and I felt like I had really played about 90 minutes of actual content. There is so much back tracking that it truly feels like a chore, and the 'gameplay' boils down to just walking from place to place and then pressing A occasionally. I only decided to finish it so that I could say it was done and not have to come back to it. Maybe the stupidest aspect of this is the achievement whose description says to play the game at a 'leasurely pace' (their typo, not mine), which just equates to 15 hours of playtime - somehow encouraging you to spend even longer playing it.With a game like that, you'd better hope the story is enough to hook you, because that's literally all there is - and the story here feels self aggrandizing at best, and quite mundane at worst. There's just not a lot being said here despite just listening to people talk the whole time. There have been other reviews I've read on here that go into more detail about how the story kind of struggles thematically from beginning to end, and I do agree with those. It's just so boring. I contemplated giving up 4 hours in. The Adult Swim scene (if you play the game you'll know what I mean) was maybe one of the dumbest things I've seen in a game.So what IS here to justify the cost? Some would say the art/design, but again I kind of disagree. I do think that the claymation style is charming, but it's not enough to sell this as a package. The voice performances were also all either utterly bizarre or just actually not good, but again I didn't direct it so it doesn't seem helpful to be nitpicky about that.I would say that this could be worth checking it out if on sale a good amount, but frankly I still think it's in desperate need of significant quality of life overhauls, and even then I don't think the story is all that worth it

_childDocuments_.review: Harold Halibut is a genuine, heartwarming story told in a clever and endearing way. Obviously, it looks great too. You already know that. I 100% recommend it.I found out about the game many years ago when a spotlight article was posted about it on the Unity website. I checked in on its development a few times every year, and bought it on release day. Even though I was intrigued from the start and this kind of game is right up my alley, I'll admit I was concerned going in. Artsy games like this are notorious for looking pretty, but having little substance in the actual story or gameplay. Now that I've played through it, I'm happy to say that Harold Halibut did not end up in that group.The gameplay is admittedly very simple, but I found myself super engaged with the story and characters, and immersed in the world. The game is super straightforward overall, with the primary objectives usually involving the player going from point A to point B, completing simple tasks and engaging in dialogue, but it really shines if you just take your time in the side objectives, and enjoy the characters. I never felt that I wanted to skip any dialogue or cutscenes because I just loved the characters so much and was genuinely interested in the story.Every single character in the game is developed with care. Everyone felt like they had a life of their own, and the story treated every one of them with respect. Even the employees of the big bad corporation were just good people doing their jobs or trying to help. Nobody's just evil just for evil's sake. I found myself growing attached to the little cast of characters, and I was always excited to see more of them.I also love how effectively it places you in Harold's shoes. I found him to be a very relatable character, and I never felt put off by the way he interacted with other characters, as I often do with the protagonists in more poorly written games. He's a simple, somewhat absent-minded man who just wants to be helpful and please everybody. he doesn't understand technology so well, so all of the interfaces with technology in the game are presented as strange incomprehensible symbols and shapes. That way, you know exactly how he feels when he has to deal with it. The menial gameplay in the beginning reflects the menial nature of his job, so you feel the same way he does about it. So much of the game is cleverly designed to make you relate directly to what it's like to be Harold.All of the love and care put into the design of the game and story makes Harold Halibut into a really unforgettable experience. It's somehow warm, cozy and nostalgic despite the cold, uninhabitable setting. It's just so darn appealing. My favorite thing about it is definitely the aliens, but I don't want to spoil any of that for those who haven't seen anything of them yet. I just resonated with every part of the game. The ending is brilliant and surprisingly effective, emotionally. And, to the developers, if you're reading: (spoilers)Tidemo!

_childDocuments_.review: Played the game through on Xbox, then I bought the game on Steam to support the developers and play again!          Harold Halibut is a slow-paced, but heavily story-rich game. A last-ditch effort to save humanity occurs and a spaceship, the Fedora I, is sent to a foreign planet in hopes of saving mankind. Unfortunately the ship crash lands and becomes stuck in the ocean. Time to figure out how to relaunch.          On the Fedora I holds many unique characters with incredibly different personalities. You grow to love every single one of them - seriously. Harold Halibut starts off pretty slow, allowing you to explore the play-space, and to get to know everybody.          The graphics are absolutely stunning! I read that the entire game (I believe) is modeled and recorded in stop-motion. The game has amazing voice acting throughout it's entirety as well. I find myself constantly doing some of their voices along with them. They're all very unique.           Please, if you want a one of a kind story game, play Harold Halibut! If you can't muster up the $35, it's on Game Pass!, but it's worth every penny. Absolutely no reason for you to not try it!Negatives: (the only thing i think is a negative is a possible spoiler, but no specific details)Eagerly waiting for Slow Bros. next release

_childDocuments_.review: There's something quite charming, quaint, and comforting about Harold Halibut. It feels like something pulled straight out of a Wes Anderson stop-motion catalogue. However, this game is NOT for everyone.As far as video games go, Harold Halibut feels akin to a point-and-click visual novel with a tiny bit more interactivity. But, if you're OK with an undemanding, easy-going experience, you'll find that there is a lot to love about this decade-long endeavour.

_childDocuments_.review: I was going to say recommended at first, but when I remembered this cost $35 I had to change it.I had a friend tell me once he hates these kind of games because "I would rather just watch the movie." And that's how I feel about this game -- you could condense the story into an average length feature film that I would enjoy watching, but it doesn't make for a great game.At first I loved the slow pace. It fit thematically. But after 8 hours of walking back and forth between a very limited set of points in order to advance the story... I have had enough. I wasn't expecting to be battling sea monsters, but I thought it would gain some gameplay elements as the story progressed. Nope. Just walking back and forth to talk to the same handful of people to get to the next chapter.I will admit I have not finished the game, but I don't think I am going to. It's like a book I'm not enjoying at this point. I'm not sure whether I should just finish it because I've already invested the time, or if that's just wasting more time. And it was $35.Hard review to write because the artwork and style is truly amazing. I love the atmosphere of the game. But the actual gameplay and story are a real let down in comparison.

_childDocuments_.review: Admittingly, I struggled to get into the game for the first chapter. It felt like a lot, but nothing at the same time; although through a slow first chapter, the game is worth pushing through. As I continued dedicating more time I've been finding myself more curious and intrigued of the goings on. My favourite chapters that I experienced were chapters 5 and 6.  I appreciated that it does touch up on the characters throughout the chapters, you see their development as you continue playing through each chapter, including Harold's.It is a VERY story based game.So expect a lot of story telling cut scenes, lots of walking/running back and forth  There isn't a whole lot of "gameplay" but that does not make this a bad game in any way. If you are patient and sit and listen to each dialogue you truely do grow some attachment to the creative story.You can see the time, creativity and effort that has been put into this game.I appreciate and love the art style. I can only imagine the sweat and tears put into a stop-motion clay animated game, and I feel like it was portrayed beautifully.EDIT: The only issue I had experienced was during the different story cut scenes for the day skips, where it would glitch a little (pixelise on a frame then go back to normal), otherwise playing the game and any other normal cut scene for tasks I didn't experience any issue.

_childDocuments_.review: Harold Halibut" is just something else, isn't it? I mean, that stop-motion animation mixed with 3D graphics is like a feast for the eyes. And the story? Man, it's like diving into this whole other world – literally, since it's set on this weird oceanic planet. But it's not just the looks that got me hooked – the characters are so fleshed out, each with their own quirks and wisdom to share. And the game isn't afraid to get deep, Like, it's got these moments that really make you stop and think about life and stuff.Gameplay-wise, it's a nice mix of exploring, solving puzzles, and chatting with folks. It all flows together nicely, keeping you engaged without feeling overwhelmed.Overall, "Harold Halibut" is an extraordinary achievement in game design, offering a captivating journey that lingers long after the credits roll. With its stunning visuals, engaging storytelling, and thought-provoking themes, it's no surprise that this game has the potential to inspire future game developers and redefine the boundaries of interactive storytelling. Whether you're a fan of adventure games or simply appreciate artistry in gaming, "Harold Halibut" is an experience not to be missed.☻

_childDocuments_.review: I only reccommend for the artistic aesthetics.  And I have a lot of complaints and comments.  I still played it all the way through and I think its a bit of a marvel for what it is.  But it is not particularly enjoyable.So many people keep repeating its like a Wes Anderson film.  It is not.  I think someone on youtube said it and its just getting parroted.   I mean it really has nothing in common with W.A films which are primarily styled to embody theater dramas.  So if you are  fan of his, dont expect this to be in his style.  It is not.  It really is its own thing.  But a basic Disney pixar film comes closest.  It is though, basically a movie with  buttons needed to progress it.  It was excruciatingly slow at times.  I found myself spamming buttons as conversations drolled on and on.  Every now and then, in the middle of a very long conversation, an option to choose a response popped up but I usually missed them from spamming the buttons.   They just talked so damn slow.   And walking is incredibly slow.   This is the kind of game where your hand starts to hurt because you keep pushing the joystick harder and harder hoping for the character to speed up. I like walking sims, I have played a lot of walking sims.  And typically they center on a mystery and finding clues.  This does not follow that design. This is instead just basically following a kind of boring character discover themselves and some philosophy stuff thrown in.  By boring I mean that Harold is sort of boring as a personality.  Not as "he isnt interesting".  He is interesting but from the standpoint that he is a boring person.  He has nothing really going for him.  He seems rather complacent and just goes along with whatever because there is no reason not to.  And he realizes he doesn't want to be that person.  But also, who could he be?  Not a lot of options.  He isn't really a big hero or anything of the story.  At the end *Spoiler WARNING*At the end he just decides he'd rather do something different than stay with the humans who are heading back to earth.  But even this role is kind of bland.  Its not like there is a role for him there.  But also its not like he really had a strong relationship with any of the humans.  And in the game they keep emphasizing that Harold had a strong relationship with the mailman, but I only had the chance to meet him once so it was weird that this relationship was emphasized so much as Harolds main squeeze.    Harold has no back story.  No forward story.  Nothing about family.  When he later says he is in his 20s I thought maybe they were going to talk about him transitioning from lonely child to lonely adult with routine leading his life.  I thought that could be interesting.    But they never touched on that.  The conspiracy part of the company was kind of flat.  I thought they were going to learn that it hadn't been 200 years since they left earth but that the people on the ship now were the earth people, but they forgot somehow.  And they were all there to do something nefarious.  Or some other big plot twist.  Nope.  Nothing really interesting there.   And the bad guy's rational for freezing the ocean is just silly.  And makes no sense. Also, So they say the journey to earth will be 200 years.  But like, no one on the ship seems to care that they wont be alive by the time they get back.  No one else decides to stay.  Even the mentor lady says something about looking forward to standing on the ground, but she wont be alive to do that. THAT SAID:  The game is really rather unique.  And I do enjoy something new and original.  Although the story was rather bland there was some parts that were interesting.  Some of the philosophy stuff was interesting but also a lot of it felt like they were talking in circles and not saying anything (to be fair a lot of philosphy does that).    The soundtrack was pretty good.  Performance: meh. I had a few crashes near the start.  And I updated my GPU and that seemed to mostly fix it.  I fell through the floor once.  A few times, even near the end, the conversation ran on auto super fast.  Like faster than I wanted and it just auto went through it so fast I barely could tell what they said and this was not due to me pushing buttons.    The sprint button seemed to not work very well in the last 2 hours of game play. There is this part in the game where you say good bye to all the fish people and its all cinamatic. And in slow mo.  ITS ALREADY SLOW AND THEY SLOWED IT DOWN MORE!   It was insane.  I actually just held the joystick and made myself some dinner  in the kitchen and when I came back it still hadn't finished the walk.  No joke.  It takes like 3 minutes to walk a short distance.There was a side mission to deliver mail to people but I wasn't able to do it.  I got to the major's letter but it would not let me deliver it to him. It wouldn't let me interact with him to give him the letter (while he was at the school area).  Also the few options you get in conversations seem like they dont make any difference.There are a few times in the story where it seems like you are going to be presented with two options to resolve an issue. Like with Rafi.  Giving her a music tape or black mailing her into compliance with a request.  But when you go to her, you just give her the tape automatically. These things might be bugs. I dk.  Play the game for the aesthetics and for a unique game play experience.  Dont play for the story, the characters, or puzzles.  It was like 6-8 hrs in until I got to interact with the alien. I mean, common.   You just fart around until then.  And then do some more farting around afterwards. Id say buy it to support the dev team who did something bold and new.  E for Effort. And I think effort counts for a lot.  But I did not really enjoy the game.  I hope to see more games with this style in the future.  Games that are more enjoyable though.  Its a good start though.  A lot of potential.   Also this game is huge!  its like 50gb. wth?

_childDocuments_.review: Harold Halibut is a gorgeous visual novel. Do not go in expecting puzzles, there aren't any.There are some big problems with it.Firstly: the devs have crafted a very interesting and detailed world - but almost none of it is interactive. You can only interact with things that you HAVE to interact with to advance the plot. If there's some interesting device on a table or poster on the wall that you're curious about, tough luck. All you can do is stare. Harold may not know much, but he definitely knows more than the player does, and he ain't talking. For a game with such a compelling and beautiful environment, this is really frustrating.Secondly: the writing is frequently painfully awkward. There's some attempts at comedy in there - at least I think they're supposed to be jokes - but it hasn't managed to make me crack a smile yet; there's no sense of comic timing. Relatedly, the voice direction is AWFUL - the emotion in the actors delivery frequently does not match the lines, and there are frequent problems with mispronunciations (I can forgive 'Brigitte' as 'Bridget', but 'communique' is not pronounced 'commu-neek').Thirdly: for a narrative game, where the things people say to you are important - if you miss something, you're screwed. There is no 'conversation log' as you might find in other visual novels.Fourthly: it's minor compared to the other things, but jesus ♥♥♥♥ do something about Harold's animation when walking up and down stairs guys, it looks SO BAD in contrast to how good everything else looks.I bought the game so I'm going to try and keep going with it, but all in all I cannot recommend it at its current price point, which is a damn shame because $45 CAD feels like an reasonable amount to ask for the amount of work that has gone into the visuals - but actually playing it is just too frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: I was initially drawn to this game because of its unique and wonderfully weird art style—it’s unlike anything I’ve seen before, in the best possible way. _childDocuments_.review: Stop motion is a challenging technique to use in video games. Neither is it in the world of animation tout court. Still, the problems are multiplied for video games, considering the environmental interactions and the different presence of characters in space, so much so that we have seen it applied primarily to a static genre such as graphic adventures. The most famous examples are The Dream Machine and The Neverhood, but there are others, such as the lesser-known Tanita: Plasticine Dream, which we cite to get a slightly broader picture.In Harold Halibut's review, we will see whether it was worth waiting ten years, the time of the game's development, to play this narrative adventure that exploits this style to seek its own identity.Let us begin by specifying that Harold Halibut is a pure narrative adventure; that is, it is a game in which interaction is entirely functional for the story. So, there are no big puzzles to solve or complicated puzzles to overcome. There are mini-games interspersed within the entire experience, such as some arcade-like arcades that you would find in an arcade or a small musical mini-game used to put Harold in contact with the aliens, which, if you will, is a nod to the philosophy of Steven Spielberg's Close Encounters of the Third Kind.One can follow various objectives, which are very simple and listed in the wrist-mounted laptop computer, which serves as a journal and communicator for text messages, which usually require going to a particular place, and that's it. You talk a lot with the other characters, you listen to Harold's inner monologues, and there are several related storylines, but it's all played out from a narrative point of view. So, nothing is designed to challenge the player in the classical sense. The mini-games almost have a rhythmic function, i.e., they are there as punctuation of the experience to break the linearity of the narrative, with which, however, they are perfectly integrated.Don't expect chickens with pulleys and gold nuts to be found, but an extremely fluid narrative in which progress is made without any stops due to a precise choice of the development team, which wanted to make the game accessible to everyone and did not want the story to stop or risk, even worse, stopping players, leading them to terminate the experience prematurely. Harold Halibut, therefore, bets everything on his style and on how he depicts this underwater world of an alien planet, made up of fleeing humans who suddenly come into contact with the indigenous population, from which then arises a series of frictions of which we do not want to anticipate anything. The authors have put much of their spin on it, playing the whole experience on an intensely melancholy and meditative note. Harold eventually finds his dimension, evolving from being an extremely passive character to becoming the linchpin of a radical change. The play's take on reality is not cut with a hatchet but, however strong, appears nuanced and delicate, in this sense, extremely authorial, as is the entire experience.As mentioned, the story of Harold Halibut tells of the escape of some humans from Earth in the 1970s amid the Cold War. Many are convinced that the world is about to end, so they build a vast spaceship divided into living modules resembling an actual city and begin a journey to a distant planet that is supposed to be the new home of our species. Unfortunately, upon arriving there, after 200 years of crossing and several generations born and living inside the spaceship, they find themselves on a planet entirely made of water, where they are forced to establish an underwater city despite themselves. They are stuck there, surviving for another fifty years in harsh conditions and moving from one living module to another via human-sized hydraulic pipes. The whole thing is run by a multinational corporation, All Water, which makes the best of the situation. However, launching a probe on the planet's surface early in the adventure allows them to pick up a message from Earth that the planet is not dead. Naturally, hearing it rekindles the hopes of everyone eager to return home.Unfortunately, it is difficult to succeed because the city's power is running out, and there is no practical way to leave. However, what seems like an adventure about escaping a desperate situation will become something else in the game when the contact mentioned above with the planet's indigenous species brings out all the contrasts within the city of humans.The narrative is constructed in a decidedly skillful way, with a prolonged start in which the various pieces begin to fit into the puzzle and then go on to define the framework of the story, the setting, and the characters without ever forcing the issue too much. Some will consider it far too slow, but Harold Halibut is one of those games that aims to be different, with characters who sing beautifully. At the same time, they think they need to be heard, with professors who love to teach children about the history of our planet and with postal workers who keep ancient letters that have never been delivered from which they derive stories out of collective memory and whatnot.On closer inspection, the underwater world of Harold Halibut is a kind of aquarium in which each housing module represents an aspect of our society that is put on display when described in an ironic way, when emotional, or when connoted in such a way as to make references to facts of reality obvious, going on to form a more complex and fascinating overall picture. The initial solid contextualization is appropriate where the game events make sense precisely based on how the narrative has been constructed up to that point. Rushing to the turning points would have resulted in debasing the narrative fabric, producing unrecoverable tears within it. So we have a first chapter devoted essentially to letting us experience this underwater world in Harold's shoes, letting us get to know who inhabits it, the various perspectives in the field, the key characters, and also those who are part of the protagonist's love life, there where in later chapters the contact with this world that becomes deeper and deeper begins and still produces those frictions will be resolved in the second part of the game.Harold Halibut is also a joy to watch. As also explained by the development team, the game's graphics are in stop motion, but not in the classic way in which this style is understood; that is, all the models were created by hand - we are talking about characters, scenery, and individual objects - so they exist in reality in the form of sculptures, and then are scanned and transformed into 3D models. This choice was probably made as a matter of practicality because handling this amount of content using only pure stop motion would have been prohibitive for such a small team, despite the ten years it took to make it all. The technical problems they would have had to overcome would have been enormous, and they would undoubtedly have had to limit certain aspects of the storytelling, making compromises they did not want to suffer.So they found an intermediate solution that still achieved very high visual quality, accompanied by a soundtrack of original and other licensed songs of the highest quality, contributing distinctly to the atmosphere. As a result, Harold Halibut is very beautiful to watch and listen to. The developers have also added a zoom function to allow you to admire the details of the various models and environments. At the same time, it gives the impression of being an utterly handcrafted product, thus handmade, from which a strong passion exudes. The results show and embellish a work that deserves to be played.

Oh, Harold..I was looking for something relaxing to unwind to before bed and this was great for that.I've never really played a game like Harold Halibut. In fact, not sure I'd even call it a game. If you're okay with pressing WASD and Space for 12-15 hours and not much else in the way of player control, then you'll get to experience one of the best, most emotionally impactful narratives about self-discovery, social ties and the human condition. _childDocuments_.review: Harold Halibut is an absolutely beautiful game, and definitely one of the more unique experiences I've had in gaming, even if the pacing of the story and gameplay is a little off sometimes. This game is definitely a slow burn, and chapters 2 and 4 (out of 6 total) drag on especially long with a lot of backtracking. It's about 12 hours long and frankly should probably have been half that length, but I enjoyed getting to know the residents of The Fedora and exploring everything. If you like walking sims or weird artsy adventure games, this one's for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Your enjoyment of Harold Halibut completely hinges on how open and willing you are to being Harold. If you allow yourself to completely let go of any preconceived notions on games and "go with the tide" I think you'll find at least a somewhat enjoyable experience. Stepping into Harold's shoes, you'll be frustrated, annoyed, awestruck, intrigued, confused, and excited throughout this roughly 10 hour journey. I see a lot of people saying this could just be a movie, and while it could, it wouldn't be as successful. We need to allow games to let us into their world, uncompromisingly, and recognize the effort developers put in to make you feel things (even if those things are banality, or frustration). What I mean is, it all makes sense if you let it! I had a really interesting and engaging time with this game, and I'll definitely be following the developers with whatever they do next. I'm glad people like this exist to take gigantic risks and give us something nobody has really done before. I think everyone can agree the artistry on display here is pretty incredible, and I can at least applaud them heavily for their time well spent. The game is not without it's issues though, primarily in the realms of design and performance. Performance is a more obvious issue: the things on screen may not move quickly, but they are DETAILED. Playing this in 4K is pretty much impossible at 60fps, and even 2K dips from time to time. Normally this wouldn't be a huge cry, but in a game that emphasizes it's detail and realism (things in this game are literally real models after all) it's a real shame I can't see it in all it's glory without a super powered machine. There are some minor bugs here and there, nothing too jarring from what I found, and only 1 bug that forced me to reload (thankfully to only 20 seconds earlier). This, and the performance, I feel like could be ironed out, but it's not necessary. The gameplay is mundane and banal, on purpose! And no, that's not a cop out. It's intentionally done like this to put you in Harold's shoes. Around the 1/3 point when life changes forever, things start to get super interesting. The final act is maybe my favorite part of the game, as Harold himself takes a deeper inner look as to why he's been feeling things (and as such, we the player are forced to do the same). I thought that was great! That being said, I would've liked a stronger arc swing around the midway point. The heist with the kids is really one of the only examples I can think of where Harold truly goes off course. Otherwise, it's menial tasks as usual, even when thematically it doesn't make sense. The puzzles are maybe my weakest point. I understand they're intentionally obtuse, but when your forced to complete them to progress (looking at you filter room) it's just sort of obnoxious from a player perspective. Later on they did away with this by having them automatically end (or in one instance where a character literally tells you exactly what to do) but I can't really deny how weak that is. We could've gotten some pretty great puzzles from a game like this, thematically and gameplay wise. I'd genuinely recommend this, but not if you're a person without patience. This game isn't really like other games, and while it isn't perfect, I think if you allow the game to be what it is you'll find some value in it. Please keep making different, risky things like this!
_childDocuments_.name: Harold Halibut

_childDocuments_.review: I cheated a little bit and read some reviews ahead of writing my own and I have to say I'm a little surprised. When looking at the trailer and tags for the game (one of which literally says 'walking simulator') did people not understand that this would be an almost exclusively narrative driven point & click game? I suppose not, judging by some of the reviews, so let me get this out of the way first and foremost: THIS IS A NARRATIVE DRIVEN, SLOW BURN GAME. If you're looking for intense gameplay I can suggest hundreds of games better suited for you, so please don't waste your money and/or time and then give this absolute masterpiece a "Do not recommend" just because it wasn't a game it never claimed to be. For the love of all that is good please do not buy this game expecting to be vastly challenged with tons of puzzles or combat or anything else other than an absolutely lovely narrative experience. Now, with that out of the way, let's review this game.Personally, I loved it. I adored every minute. It is, by far, one of the most visually stunning games I've ever played. It's no wonder it took so long to make this game; it's extremely obvious the passion that went in to every single second of this game. Once finishing this game I would highly suggest looking into the making-of; it's so impressive what has been done here and with what techniques. There are stop motion games out there and I have to say I've never seen one executed this well. From the clay models to the motion capture of the cutscenes to every single environment that's been built it's just stunning. **I will say there were some moments where, during a cutscene, the transition to another scene would artifact like crazy. When the visuals of the game are the main selling point I'd really suggest that get updated as soon as you can muster. It didn't take me out that much, but I would have had a much better time if I was never taken out of the story like that.**The story really sucks you in, that being said. If you're unwilling to care about the characters in this game then I'm sorry to say but you probably won't enjoy this game much at all. It's extremely narrative driven and said narrative is very VERY character driven. It's a lot of walking to and from places to simply talk to someone, or watch them do something they love, or get a little lore about the world you're in. If you're unwilling to engage with the feelings and emotions of the characters within the game then there just isn't much point in you even playing. The game NEEDS you, BEGS you, to care about the story and it's characters and how they feel and why they feel that way. If you're just going to get bored because they're normal people talking about their normal lives then you just will not engage with this at all. I know a ton of people have already likened it to a Wes Anderson film, but I cannot stress just how true that is. If you've ever watched a Wes Anderson movie and thought to yourself "God this is boring" or "Why is there so much talking?" AVOID THIS LIKE THE PLAGUE. It aint for you friend I'm so sorry. Everything about this game is emotion and the interactions you have with people and I 100% understand that will not keep each and every person engaged, which is why I post this as a warning. This is a very artsy game, from the visuals to the music down to the very narrative of the game, including its ending. Artsy people know who they are, I'd say, and that is who this game was made for. The music is a great example of this. Gorgeous soundtrack, absolutely cannot wait to own this one way or another (please god do a vinyl release I'll give you all my money) but it comes in the strongest during its most 'artsy' moments. This game wants you to FEEL something above all else. It wants you to walk around in this world and feel what Harold is feeling because you had to make every move yourself. If you don't want to engage with everyone around you, you don't have to; but if you don't you're going to miss out on a lot of the emotional elements and the turmoil that is so important throughout the game. That's the point of making it a game - it isn't forcing one story on you, you can decide how much you engage with it and, thusly, how much it will emotionally effect you in the end. Honestly I just can't sing the praises of this game enough. I know it isn't for everyone but I really think it's something emotional and beautiful and, if you're willing to let yourself be taken for a ride, it can really make you think about life or the world or even just your day to day experiences with people differently; and I think that's something really special. I highly recommend this game to anyone and everyone I can possibly recommend it to. You know yourself and you should know if this sounds interesting enough or not to you. Please give this game a chance, it's a work of art, truly, but don't give unjust criticism if it just isn't for you. *****************I'd like to give just a few more positives that didn't really fit in with my above rant but that I feel really need their praises sung:OMG whoever designed the UI (the little PDA) GIVE THEM A RAISE. What an absolutely genius way to keep the player engaged throughout the story and excited for every new interaction. I was constantly anticipating another Harold Drawing(tm) and every time the notification popped up saying I had a new one I rushed to the PDA to check it. The messages were also a great way to do additional story telling at a different pace. I loved when multiple days would pass and I'd get to check a plethora of messages, especially after the longest time skip; it was so emotional! Just amazing, I loved this element the most out of the whole game.Also wow the voice acting was so good. I also saw quite a few reviews saying the voice acting was bad? I genuinely have no idea what other people were hearing. I was very impressed with the performances and the emotions that each actor was able to project, especially Jeanne's VA during the "party" scene (WOW!!). There were a lot of actors at play here and they all did phenomenal, imo. I mean, even the body actors did an amazing job with the mo-cap. After a AA/AAA title like Baulder's Gate 3 had the mo-cap it did people should be kissing the feet of the mo-cap done in this game; it's genuinely impressive for such a small studio.Okay I'm officially running out of room but let me real quick say these:Lighting and cinematography were amazing. Seriously, idk where this team of people came from all of a sudden but there's a lot in this game that takes industry professionals years to do. Very impressive stuff.Writing was also good. Was seeing reviews saying the writing was bad or even milktoast but I just cannot disagree more. It was not the most intelligent thing ever to be written, but I think that’s the point. A good portion of dialogue is written purely to confuse Harold and, by proxy, you the player. The rest of the writing is simply there for you to engage with emotionally. It isn’t trying to be super smart, it just wants to make you feel something, and I think it’s done that perfectly.--------------I will note my ONE gripe with the game. Why can’t I see Coco dance? Zoya specifically mentions she dances, why was that not put in the game? I’m mostly being hyperbolic but I was actually a little sad getting to the end of the game and not getting a little cutscene of Zoya and Coco. If there were to ever ever ever be an update to the game I would hope that would be included.
_childDocuments_.name: Harold Halibut

_childDocuments_.review: In short, this game succeeds at painting Harold as a punching bag, an outcast, and a victim of his surroundings, but it does so at the expense of the player that controls him.Before buying this game, I read some of the reviews, and decided to wave off the warnings about pacing and tedium. I usually really enjoy story-based games, and figured that a slower experience would fit well with that. Unfortunately, at the 2-hour mark, I now realize I was sorely mistaken.I think my core issue with this game is that it simply doesn't respect the player's time. There's something to be said for narrative pacing and giving a game room to tell its story—that's the main reason I ignored the negative reviews at the outset. But when one of the first minigames requires you to move Harold's hand to unscrew twenty-four individual screws from a panel, only to be electrocuted and laughed at by an NPC because you fell for his prank? To me, that's not storytelling—that's wasting the player's time.The game frequently, and seemingly at random, disables your ability to run, locking you into a sub-leisurely walking pace. When your only task is to travel across two maps, talk to someone, then travel all the way back and go to sleep, having your speed capped to that of a geriatric birdwatcher almost makes it feel like the game is messing with you on purpose.At one point near the end of my play time, the game abruptly started to ramp up. Suspenseful music played. A new mystery was revealed. Harold started piecing things together. I, as the player, started getting excited. And then, just as quickly, Harold's NPC boss interrupted: "Harold, it's late. We've had enough excitement for one day. Let's leave the theories for tomorrow."I feel this is a pretty good example of how the game treats its protagonist, and by extension, the player that controls him. After enduring that almost nonstop for two full hours, I was ready to be done.
_childDocuments_.name: Harold Halibut

_childDocuments_.review: There are so many positive things to list out here -- Visually this is one of the most interesting games I've ever seen. The warm style of characters mixed with the colorful lived in environments make for an immersive and 'homey' feel. The audio in this game is genuinely good. Voice acting feels natural and non-forced, and the OST accompanying it is the sort of thing I would listen to on its own. See the sights, meet the people, have a grand old time. This is really the epitome of a walking simulator. With the playable areas being so much smaller than other games in that category, the story really has to pull its weight. And it does! You can tell that there was a lot of thought that went into the how / what / where / why. The story highlights the 'human experience' in a relevant, relatable, and non pretentious way while still managing to add a few twists here and there.There are however some aspects that not everyone is going to like. While there is some action, it really is far and few between. I got great satisfaction running around filling out the to-do list, but I understand why some would find that tedious. There is no shame if you aren't the patient type - but you might find this not super fun. This is a slow game, with a slow story.
_childDocuments_.name: Harold Halibut

_childDocuments_.review: This game is warm, visually interesting, at times bizarre, and unique. I think Harold Halibut might not appeal to everyone due to its slower pace, lack of action-y elements, and abundance of weird - but I truly enjoyed the experience. At times it felt more like playing with a miniature toy set than controlling a video game character; it felt more like walking through someone else's imagination than exploring a video game environment. I don't think this is the game for everyone, but if you appreciate small details in games and artfully crafted visuals while not minding a slower pace, I highly recommend this wonderfully strange piece of interactive art.
_childDocuments_.name: Harold Halibut

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is really unique and we won't see a game like this for a very, very long time. I've really liked the game. You can understand the work that was put into this game easily, with it's artstyle and animation being claymation.The world the game is takes in is really cozy and cool, there are vast majority of different characters with different personalities and attitudes. The story wasn't anything complex but it was still good to keep me going. The music is especially really good!I think the gameplay will be the main point where people will be divided, and that's okay. The gameplay loop mostly consists of fetch quests with a little bit of puzzle sprinkled on top of it. So it's mostly a "walking sim" type of game. I do not mind games like these so I didn't have any issues with it.All in all, I think this is a game that should be experienced at least once and I recommended it if you don't mind "walking sim" type of games.

_childDocuments_.review: Blown away and deeply moved by this dreamy, thought-provoking, Kafkaesque Sci-Fi world about connection and purpose. Meticulously crafted characters and wondrous vistas, this is a story of community and uncertainty, and ways we may navigate themes involving culture, bureaucracy, conflict, hope, and mortality. Happy to support the beautiful soundtrack and would purchase an artbook in a heartbeat. An absolute technical and artistic marvel.

_childDocuments_.review: is a game that has captivated me with its unique charm and exceptional craftsmanship. The art style, crafted entirely in claymation, is nothing short of stunning. The dedication of the developers, Slow Bros., is evident in every frame; after all, it took them 12 years to bring this masterpiece to life. Their meticulous attention to detail truly pays off, making every scene a visual delight.The story and characters are where  truly shines. The narrative is a slow burner, but if you push through the initial pacing, you'll find a rich, rewarding experience. The characters grow with you, becoming an integral part of your journey. They are memorable and impactful, leaving a lasting impression long after the game is over.Graphically, the game is a feast for the eyes. The claymation work is a testament to the developers' dedication to their craft. The painstaking effort put into every detail shows through, creating an immersive and visually arresting world. The soundtrack complements the visuals beautifully, enhancing the overall atmosphere and drawing you deeper into the story.I highly recommend  to those who feel lost in their lives and are seeking a sense of purpose. It's perfect for fans of slow burners and slice-of-life narratives. However, be prepared for a dialogue-heavy experience. The game involves a lot of talking and interacting with NPCs, which may not be everyone's cup of tea.In conclusion,  is a unique gem in the gaming world. Its craftsmanship, attention to detail, and heartfelt storytelling make it a standout experience. If you're willing to embrace its leisurely pace, you'll find a game that is as fulfilling as it is beautiful.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow.....I mean......WOW. Where do I even begin? This is a masterpiece! I wish I could tell the whole team their faces how absolutely beautiful this game is and hug them! The sound design, stop-motion, visuals, character design, side stories, voice acting etc. I mean literally all of it is top quality!! 14 years in development and boy does it show. Like other reviewers have said, it's more of a "walking sim" with some interactions here and there and a good amount of listening, exploring and watching cut scenes. 13 hours it took me to complete, I tried to look in every nook and cranny I could find and do all the side quests, each very enjoyable and so rewarding. I honestly wish I could erase my memory of playing it and do it all over again. It was emotional, funny, thought provoking and just absolutely so wholesome. It's going to be hard to top this game for me. Highly recommended!
