_childDocuments_.review: Now this is how you do a remake Square Enix. Good job. Square Enix made quite the blunder with Secret of Mana by describing it as a remake instead of a remaster, and we gamers crucified them for that mistake and a missed opportunity to give some much needed love to the Mana franchise. Well, apparently they listened because Trials of Mana is actually a remake of the original, and improved upon it in almost every way. While the classic is still worth playing, this game is now the de facto way to experience it. None of that is to say the game is perfect, it still has a few flaws, but the overall experience is wonderful. The aesthetics and presentation of the game are quite nice. Sure, they aren't going to rock your world, or put fire to your graphics card. However, what is here is a nice, colorful anime-esque aesthetic that lends itself quite well to the game. That said, the character models can be a bit janky at times, and some of the environments are very bland (yeah I'm looking at you Castle Laurent) but the beautiful portions far outweigh then handful of blemishes. The music is also top notch. The new soundtrack is a very faithful rendition of the originals chiptunes. Several occasions I remember pausing before what I knew what was going to lead to a musical transition to see if the remastered song was going to be as good as what I remember the original sounding, and I was almost always pleased or blown away. That said, there was one noticeable exception - Splash Hop - also known as Vuscav's Theme. The lack of that strong, synthetic drum in the background is sorely missed, but I digress. Gameplay is a bit more of a mixed bag, but I'd still argue an improvement over the original. The ability to chain combos is a nice touch, even if what is available is quite rudimentary. Also telegraphed AoEs and the ability to dodge and manipulate their positions is a nice touch from the original where you just had to take the hit, and dust yourself off. That said, the AI is quite thick. They will constantly stand in AoEs, and make little effort to dodge oncoming attacks. They also have quite an issue with using their Class Skills, seemingly doing it whenever the feel like it, often forcing you to switch to them to use the attack when necessary. The battle system desperately needs more strategy and tactical options than what is given to you. Okay, so let's address the big gripe most players have with this game - the voice acting and delivery. Yes, it can be bad, atrocious even. I'm not sure if the blame should be put on the voice actors, of which most of them are new or otherwise inexperienced, or the director for giving poor instructions. Could be a bit of column A and a bit of column B. We'll never know. That said the poor delivery is the exception rather than the norm. I think a lot of people forget that the Mana series is very cartoony in it's fantasy aesthetic, bordering on kitschy. When you stop to consider that, most of the voice acting falls into place. Overall, the remake of Trials of Mana is fantastic, and the preferred way to experience this classic gem.

_childDocuments_.review: Trials of Mana is a fun experience and I recommend it, but it definitely isn't perfect or as good as I hoped it would be. I am extremely in favor of keeping the Mana (or Seiken Densetsu if you prefer that title) series alive, and remaking the SNES classics is a fine way of accomplishing that if done right. However, Trials of Mana felt like it chose an awkward middle ground between the classic experience it was based on and the modern experience it was trying to be. Environments were fully rebuilt in 3D, but just like the original version's maps, they're all small and primarily consist of narrow paths with few branches or options. That layout felt fine in the classic 3D context, but the experience feels cramped by modern 3D standards and a little more open space would have really helped. Speaking of the added third dimension, you can jump in this version, but the ability adds very little to the exploration since invisible walls and objects you simply can't jump on for no reason are absolutely everywhere. On top of that, exploration mostly yields money you don't need or common consumables that aren't very exciting anyway, which takes even more punch out of exploring the world.Combat was spiced up from the original game, but it still feels very mindless and button mashy compared to good modern 3D combat and while there are a lot of passive abilities, active abilities are really lacking. Expect to use the same simple light and heavy attack combos for the entire game. (Or at least until near the end when you can get a passive ability that automatically charges the super move meter so every non-boss battle is an instant win. Which was very much a good thing at that point.) I definitely would have preferred slightly slower combat that took a little more thought, and more active abilities. And ditching the old-fashioned non-regenerating MP system for magic/special moves, so that you could use active abilities on a more regular basis.Aside from the game design issues though, the game does have its strengths, and the greatest is the art direction. As someone who both prefers their games stylized and colorful AND likes the capabilities of modern hardware, it's an all too rare treat to get a 3D game with an even half decent budget behind it that goes as cartoony and stylized as this game. That cute colorful Mana look is the single style I'm the most nostalgic for, and Trials of Mana comes pretty close to recreating it in 3D. With that said though, I still don't feel like the game really nailed the classic Mana look - most simply put, I'd imagine the characters closer to their original big-headed in-game sprite proportions and detail level. Not precisely that look, and certainly not pixelated, but closer than what Trials of Mana gave us. For comparison, I'd point to the enemies, which by and large stuck much closer to the original sprite designs. Rabites are still just as cute and simple, and the robots in particular are about as identical to the original sprite designs as 3D versions could be. I wish the PCs and NPCs had skewed closer to that design philosophy. But, with that said, I'll admit that interpretation of what old sprite graphics were supposed to represent is a subjective matter, and the Mana series never had absolutely precisely defined singular art direction. (But nonetheless, Secret of Mana specifically is the correct style because I say so.)Of course, characters aren't the only thing to see, as there are also environments to walk around in. (But not really interact with at all, unfortunately.) They're a similar story to the characters though, looking nice and pleasantly stylized, but still don't quite feel like a perfect recreation of what the original game was going for. However, while the characters feel pretty well crafted technically, the environments feel comparatively weaker and less polished, and in particular tend to have bland flat lighting, especially at night. Which really stands out for those of us who always go with Kevin for our main, since he's at his strongest at night. I'm pretty sure Trials of Mana didn't exactly have a AAA budget, so I get why the backgrounds didn't get the most love and care possible, but still, they do detract from the experience a little. The dreaded Unreal Engine shiny plastic look also rears its ugly head in the backgrounds here and there, especially in dark places, and that doesn't help either.So having established that the visuals in Trials of Mana aren't my personal idea of perfect, I'll readily admit that these subtle issues are probably totally irrelevant to people new to the series. For those without the baggage of older Mana games, it's likely you either like the looks of Trials of Mana for what they are, or hate them for what they are, depending on how much you think gritty realism is the only mark of good graphics. There is, however, one big creative flaw that will stand out to anybody: The voice acting. Most of the voice acting in this game is bad, and I say this is a person who has never cared about voice acting enough to complain about it before. Ever. A few characters are okay to good, but so much of the voice acting just plain hurts, and I will never forgive Trials of Mana for the voice it gave the light elemental Illumina. My favorite main character Kevin also sounds all wrong, but at least that voice isn't guaranteed to annoy every player since I don't think many people choose him. Anyway, if you have strong feelings about voice acting, know that the complaints aren't overblown. Trials of Mana really does have awful voice acting.Luckily, the voices are the only audio problem, as the music and sound effects leave no complaints. The game includes both remade and original versions of all the music, which is a very nice touch. Also kind of unnecessary though, because unlike that terrible 3D version of Secret of Mana, I feel like the remade music is superior the the original music across the board this time. The worst I can say is that I still think Secret of Mana had better music in the first place, but fixing that would require replacing the music entirely, not updating it.So, with graphics and music covered, it's time for the most exciting feature of all: PC version quality! And on that note, I'm happy to report that Trials of Mana is mostly pretty good. It never crashed once and has almost all the graphic options you could ask for. My only complaint is that there is no field of view adjustment available. You have the somewhat unusual option to alter the camera distance, and pulling it back helps, but adjusting the field of view would have been the preferred solution. Still, the default FOV isn't the narrowest around, so it's at least tolerable if not ideal. Square Enix really needs to get over its inexplicable hatred for FOV adjustments though.And finally, it's a little thing, but Trials of Mana has the best New Game+ implementation that I've seen in a LONG time. First, everything but key items rolls over - levels, abilities, items, gear, and money, which is great. (And should be how New Game+ always works for that matter.) But on top of that, completing the game unlocks new additional abilities for subsequent playthroughs, so you aren't just keeping what you had but starting over with even more. It makes playing again with a different party so much worthwhile than it would otherwise be and this is the first time I've ever played Seiken Densetsu 3 twice in a row. Or played a party other than Kevin, Angela, and Reisz. Trials of Mana may have its faults, but it's the new gold standard for New Game+ implementation if nothing else.So, that's my rambling take on Trials of Mana. It falls a little short by modern game expectations, and falls shorter still as an interpretation of a classic game by my obsessive fan standards, but it's still a solid game worth playing. And an important step to finally getting the new AAA Mana game of my dreams, so buy it! Twice!

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent piece of art!The remake of the old snes game "Seiken Densetsu 3" finally released and I couldn't be more happy about how it turned out! To be honest I would even go out and say, that this remake is better than the original! For those who haven't played the original game: Seiken Densetsu 3 is a JRPG that never left Japan. The game allows the player to choose from 6 characters one main and two side characters. Picking the main character actually effects your playthrough! The final boss and the side story changes depending on the characters that are in your party. This means that you may want to play this game for a second or third time to see what the other final dungeons and bosses look like. I always prefered to have Charlotte as the main character since I think her story is the best and the end dungeon is just amazing! You can change your class and learn spells depending on your class. The Bosses are sweet and the story about the Mana Tree and the Mana Sword is alright. Everything that I just mentioned can be found in this remake too! So, let's talk about the new stuff that they added!After a level up you gain skill points. You can spend those skill points on different abilities like stronger attacks, party heal after defeating an enemy or poison if you land a critical hit. The player can choose which playstile he likes the most! Resi can be a killing machine and support class while Hawkeye casts non elemental magic spells and Charlotte is in the back and heals the team. The combat is soooo much fun! After changing your class you can do new combo attacks and new "Special Moves" (I don't actually know what this move is called). The class outfits are also pretty sweet! Now, why I prefer the remake over the original game is because the combat is just waaay more fun! You can dodge attacks and you can jump now! These little things make fighting way more interesting. The new cutscenes and voice acting are nice additions and it helps making some dramatic and sad moments. Speaking of voice acting...Yeah, it kinda sucks. Some of the characters have pretty good voice actors. I thought that Hawkeye sounded alright, but then there are the bad voice actors. Each time Salamander spoke I cringed to death. The grafics are also hit or miss. This games Artstile is beautiful! Some places look awsome like the ghost ship, every end dungeon or the desert! But then there are the not so beautiful looking places like the beastman forest which name I forgot. Pretty much all of the caves look bad. The stone texture doesn't look good BUT there is even a stone texture in the game that looks amazing, so why not using this one? I know, that this was a low budget game, since literally nobody knows the original game so why spending a ton of money on a game that won't do so well? The extra end dungeon  that you unlock after beating the main story is also a joke. I like that they made an extra story that wasn't in the original game, but the story is kinda dumb. Basically, there is a book that tells you that the world will end because of some witch and the only way to defeat her is to reach class level 4. Don't get me wrong, I love getting a new class, but the class outfit of the dark side for Resi, Duran and Angela look awful. And the dungeon itself just consists of stone platforms and places that you already visited. I still like how these places look destroyed and I think this isn't so bad as everyone says  it is. Ah yes, the game is very easy even on hard mode, just sayin'.Trials of Mana is a wonderful game! I completely ignore all of these flaws becaue this game is just so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fun! For the older generation this is a awsome game, however I don't think the younger generation will like this game as much because there are literally no side quests and the hole game is just fighting. If you don't like Trials of Mana then you can try out Seiken Densetsu 3, because it still looks better and it is way harder. This review may contain a ton of grammar mistakes but whatever.8/10 Points!Farming the ???-Seeds is still f#cking annoying tho

_childDocuments_.review: A great remake of a great game, which had not been sold in central europe. Many people in europe never have heard of the sequel of the great "Secret of mana" for SNES. As soon I had my SNES / ♥♥♥ copy of the sequel (Seiken Densetsu 3) I was fixed on the characters (especially of Angela, because you could feel her grow during the game) as my favourites. Still looking for one, haha... Anyway, what will you get for a full price game? --- Gameplay--- ,sadly 8/10The gameplay changed heavily from SNES. In the former version each boss had a unique pattern, which you should abuse or die (For example using NOT a special kind of attack on Ludger, as he would wipe your party in that combat). The remake did not only introduce visible area attacks, which can be dodged, but also a much easier gameplay as on SNES. If you had played the SNES and were confident with the difficulty, you should try "Hard". If not you should at LEAST go on "normal". "Easy" and "Story" should be avoided if you actually want a good, lightly challenging, game.--- Audio --- 9/10 Optional SNES-music and the remade version with the better sound, done everything right, but could sometimes need some more "pep". Voices often wait a little delay before speaking the next line, which feels unnaturally slow for such young girls and lads. --- Video --- xx/xx It is a downsized, non-reality driven, anime-like look. The animations are fluid, but feel sometimes slow, especially in dialogues. I decline the rating in this review, as I had mixed feelings. It is a very good, fitting video setting, the animations are good and the combat is not easily overcrowded and feels very fluid. Nearest guess would be 8,5/10--- Combat --- 10/10Now we are talking! Combat and out of combat movement is the biggest change from SNES, as the characters can jump and often have to. new Combo-attacks, reworked KA-attacks, Magic and items make this game a little jewel. the only downside is, the bosses loose their unique " I wipe your party, if you use magic"-mechanics, or use their primary attack with a timer in which you can stun them (which resulted in the lower overall difficulty)--- Utility / Community / Stability --- 10 / 10There are already a lot of mods changing aspects of the game, like other costumes, (also more revealing ones, too). There are mods to increase the difficulty of the game even further or adjust the new level up mechanic (skill STR on Angela for using a Fireball-magic, just feels wrong, you know?). The game is so far very stable, a full run from beginning to the end with no crash on first try. There was one minor glitch of the voices cut from speaking by interacting with something. After the game completed, there is BONUS Content allowing another class change and to fight against an even greater evil, with several cutscenes complementing the story of the 6 Chars.--- Summary --- * 9/10 * I just love what their vision was with the game. The combat feels fluid and a great improvement of the stiff, harsh combat of the SNES, if they just would not kill some of the unique Boss mechanics... The audio is nicely redone, the voices and characters are great additions to the already nice story.Sadly there is a lack of difficulty through QoL-improvements (lol). Also i would love to achieve class 4 in the main game, meaning a real new game + with tougher enemies I would prefer. Do I recommend to buy the game? --> Yes, even on full price, you get 6 fully written mainchar stories, and it changes by which companions you take with you, increasing the replayability. One playthrough to the normal end takes around 20-25 hours on normal-difficulty.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best JRPGs / ARPGs of all time, and the remake is actually done well, plus includes some new content. If you played the original Seiken Densetsu 3, there's tons of nostalgia to be had: you can switch between original and remake OST at any time, there's still a world map and you can freely travel by sea / air, and most importantly you can still become busted as hell by the endgame.If you haven't played the original, this is the definitive version in my opinion. As far as JRPGs go, it's on the shorter end (just shy of 20 hours for me to finish one playthrough + post-game), but between New Game+ and the central gimmick of the game having 3 stories based on who your main party member is, there's room for replayability if you want more. Each of the characters gets access to a Light / Dark class system meaning each of the 6 characters has 4 different build options by the end of the game, plus 6 different stats to level up and tons of passive abilities to use. You can definitely min-max if that's your thing, but this isn't the hardest game on a first playthrough, even if you play on Hard. Also the OST is incredibly good (both the original and the remake version).Overall, easy recommendation. If you like ARPGs, go for it. If you like JRPGs, go for it. If you like being able to customize your character's stats / build / abilities, go for it. If you've played Seiken Densetsu 3, why are you still reading this go play the game.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: If you like action RPGs, this is a modern take on an old classic.Graphically, this game is gorgeous. Unreal Engine is Square Enix's weapon of choice (also used in FF7 Remake), and this game is like a 3D anime adaptation of the original. Characters are modeled according to their original designs, animations for the most part are well-executed (with some caveats), and the world is believable fantasy without looking too realistic or too otherworldly. Lighting and particle \effects are top-notch, but Unreal Engine makes those look fantastic out of the box.When the characters are zoomed in, however, you might start to notice a few things. Canned poses that might pass as one-offs, but are repetitive and used in just about every situation, and so exaggerated that a mime would seem bland by comparison. Lip syncing that looks like old-school Hong Kong kung fu films. It's as though the animation team could've played more with the models, but either didn't have enough time or the animation was not a priority. Some of the poses (angry girl) are used in place of the character threatening an NPC with a weapon in the original, which makes the NPC's "OMG don't kill me with your death glare" reaction rather stupid. When they're using a graphics engine this good and models this vibrant and expressive, one wonders why they didn't work on this more. I could storyboard a much better animation sequence for Riesz and a certain merchant in Beisel, but they had her in "angry girl" pose which is honestly much more cute than threatening.In the original, whenever a character went to bed, the shoes magically teleported to the foot of the bed and the character sprites don't have hats or armor on. In the remake, everyone goes to bed fully dressed, which can break immersion. There are also invisible walls in the game, some understandably (jump off here and drown or get stuck forever), some not so much (can't jump off a stairwell even though falling damage isn't modeled).Story wise, the game is a carbon copy of the original with voice acting and random banter added. Only key scenes are voiced and fully animated; the rest you'll have to read old-school. For those of you unfamiliar with the original Seiken Densetsu 3, there are three distinct main stories with separate antagonists all vying for the power of mana, and whoever you pick as the leader or main protagonist determines a number of story elements, including the arch-rival and final boss. There are many subtle changes that can happen depending on who is in your party and even who is in which position when you select them at the beginning, so you might end up using all 12 save slots to check out every possibility. However, the remake's contribution is just voice acting and some banter between characters.The game's core mechanics received a modern overhaul. Previously, you can build up your special move meter by landing hits on your enemies; now there are a number of ways to build up the SP meter, mainly hitting your enemies with heavy or charged attacks. Special moves are based on the original game and pack a decent punch (I'm up to the first class change, halfway done with meeting the spirits), and abilities contribute a nice mix of attack power, support, and defense. The timing of attacking, dodging, special moves, spells, etc. are different from the original, and honestly I can't really say which I prefer. The remake does provide a few quality of life improvements over the original: item management is a bit easier, with ring menu items automatically replenished from the stash and come with the restriction of 9 items in combat. Instead of shuffling around as though their bodies suddenly developed rigor mortis when enemies are close, you can maneuver much more easily, which is good because some attacks are more effective from the enemy's flank. Many attacks no longer hit the entire playing field, making it a bit easier on the glass cannons in the party like Angela.Two fairly significant updates to combat are QoL improvements. First, you can knock down the enemy as in Secret of Mana, but you can also continue pummeling the enemy while they're down (be warned, however: the enemy can probably do the same to your characters). This is loads of fun in boss fights, as in FF7R, albeit only half as dramatic. Second, the hardware limitations of the Super Famicom are removed, so there is no skill/spell timing or queuing bug that allows an enemy to fire off 2 super powerful skills in quick succession because of the length of the skill's animation.The companion character AI isn't that smart, though. If a boss throws a wave-like ground attack, they'll probably be hit every single time.I liked the collection mechanics of finding every item in the various regions, and the cactus minigame is a nice challenge. However, the "talk to NPCs to learn new skills" minigame is rather silly, because (a) the Japanese player base will have every location, NPC, and unlock conditions on a wiki before the third day of sales, and (b) there are better ways to encourage players to talk to every NPC. To be fair, the NPCs who have skills tend to be memorable or significant ones, and the skills they provide aren't game-breaking OP skills by any stretch of the imagination.The new skill development mechanic is a nice improvement on the original, suggesting that boss fights will be much harder than the original. The item pot development... Honestly I don't see the point of boosting item drops that way, but I guess if they don't want to add a crafting component, this is the next best thing.Finally, the audio. The music generally builds upon what is a fantastic soundtrack to begin with, with the title screen booming with the key melody to Meridian Child arranged for orchestra. That's great, but the rest of the music sounds like the original tracks re-scripted for MIDI with the best instrument banks; it doesn't sound like anyone put in the time and effort to arrange and perform with live instruments and musicians, which is a bit of a shame. Then there's the voice acting. In Japanese the characters sound all right; not ear-clawingly awful, not instant moe addiction, but "good enough for government work". All the main characters' voice actors are unfamiliar to me, but there are a number of voices you may recognize, off the top of my head there was Ikumi Nakagami as the voice for Wisp/Lumina who also voiced Yukari from Girls und Panzer (though unfortunately she was acting much like Yukari).In English, however... the script they have is, again, "good enough for government work"-- not particularly accurate, not exactly flowing in English, good enough to get the point across. But it sounds like there was either no direction given by the production team from Japan, or very bad direction. Riesz sounds like Starfire from the first Teen Titans animation: like a space alien just learning how to talk to Earth friends. Charlotte sounds like a 30-year-old unsuccessfully trying to act like a 5-year-old with an Elmer Fudd speech impediment. Kevin doesn't sound like a boy who spent most of his time in a forest away from civilization. This is why I don't watch anime with the English audio, the cadences are all too often unnatural and forced, like they're trying too hard to act like the character rather than letting the moment shape the voice, or the directors just have no idea how to give good direction. This, sadly, could be a budget thing: FF7R probably had every need filled and every resource thrown at it, and it shows-- the English acting, particularly among the men, outperforms the Japanese acting. Trials has nowhere near the audience of FF7, even though this was a beloved game with a cult following, and Square Enix probably allocated resources accordingly. Even though the Japanese audio is at worst mediocre, it's probably best to set the audio to 日本語 and the text to your native language.

_childDocuments_.review: For players who are new to the Mana series, Trials of Mana is a remake of the beloved SNES classic, Seiken Densetsu 3, which was never released outside of Japan (until Nintendo Switch). This remake changes the game from a 2D action RPG to a 3D one and brings many quality of life changes. Due to the change to 3D, the game is significantly different from the original. The biggest strength of this title is definitely in the music. The catchy tunes of the original have been rearranged and I really like it (both the new and old). Not to mention, this game includes both version of music tracks which you can switch in game - really nice! The graphics is okay by modern standards although I do like the art direction. One issue with it is the textures and there are noticeable texture pop-ins every now-and-then. An important thing to note is that there is basically no in-game configuration for graphic settings apart from choosing resolution and fullscreen/window mode. As such, if you wish to change graphical settings, you may have to use a mod.The combat (which you will be doing majority of the time) is just serviceable; it doesn't have a visceral feel to it nor do the controls feel tight. Needless to say, I didn't find it to be very engaging. Apart from controls, the combat is essentially a basic combo system; even more basic than most hack-and-slash games in the market. To make matters worse, the party AI isn't good and multiplayer (which had been in earlier titles of the Mana series) is absent. The combat does get better past the 2nd class change (i.e. after level 38) thanks to the harder enemies, interesting boss fights and more available skill options. However, it should be noted that the character progression in this game is gated by class changes and past the 1st class change (at level 18), they have additional requirement (like needing specific class items which are acquired based on RNG and are consumables) that are beyond simply character level. What this means is that you cannot switch between classes at will because the class change/reset items is difficult to come by, and by the time you can do that would probably be when you're almost done with the playthrough. I think the game would have been a lot better if they had made class changes more accessible (like making class change/reset items purchasable) and keep training point respec as it currently is - which would at least make it easier to recommend the game to a casual player.I can overlook the simplicity of the combat as I'm rather fond of the Mana series itself (that being the only thing that is keeping me going). However, the story is a major letdown and this is my biggest gripe with the game. I don't think that it's a fault with the story itself but rather the execution of it. The unpolished story cutscenes do a very poor job of story-telling; the voice-acting is kinda meh, dialogues are rushed, character animation doesn't look good and the transitions in-and-out-of cutscenes are abrupt. While I haven't played tons of JRPGs, I can't recall another title which makes it so difficult for me to find emotional connection with my characters (and their motives) like this one. An example of a JRPG which I felt that the story wasn't compelling but still felt was well-delivered, would be Tales of Vesperia.To be fair, Trials of Mana is not a bad game if you're looking for a simplistic action-based JRPG - it is, at least, very functional. Also, due to its branching story based on the characters you choose in your party, the game definitely offers replayability. However, it's a difficult game to recommend to any JRPG fan because the game is so average in nearly almost every aspect that matters to an RPG; made even harder in consideration of its asking price and its level of polish. Sadly, I can only recommend the game to players who wish to revisit the classic in a new light and only when the game is heavily discounted for 50% or more.After having played through all characters, I'm having seconds thoughts about my earlier impression of the game - but I thought I'll leave what I had previously written (above) as-is for reference. I do enjoy the game more now than I did when I wrote that review, so I felt the need to do it more justice. First, I'd like to reaffirm that the combat feels really good when you can access the better parts of it at the earliest in NG+ (since I don't have to grind for class items). The tightness of control varies somewhat depending on which character(s) you are playing with - Kevin felt great, Duran not so much even though I liked him more. The problem I had with combat, was the pacing of the game due to the progression gating with class change mechanics. While the combat is still largely button-mashing (if you play melee), it is straightforward and certain characters do play better at early game than others. Paired along with the harder enemies and fun late-game boss fight mechanics (which includes potentially damaging but not necessarily fatal DPS checks), the combat past mid-game was a lot of fun. The devs should really consider making a game mode for doing boss fights that supports multiplayer as a DLC.However, I've not changed my mind about the inaccessibility of class change mechanics in this game. If you want to reset a character's class in order to experience a different class route, the item required (Goddess Scale) is limited to 6 acquisition per playthrough (through opening specific chests) and you have 3 characters in your party with 4 possible routes for each. As such, experiencing the different character builds in this game is going to require multiple playthroughs either way - whether you choose to amass large quantities of the reset item for NG+ or choosing a different class path for each character in each playthrough. I really hope the devs would update so that the item is at least farmable, if not purchasable. And better still, make class change items not be consumables and that class 4 items can be carried over to NG+. The tedium of class changes makes it really hard to recommend to players who can afford time to do 1 or 2 playthroughs. While it's a huge step forward compared to the original (in terms of QoL), it really feels like they went halfway with it. Class change was an issue for me in the original, and sadly, it still is in this remake - it's a legacy of the classic that doesn't need to stay. As a side note, if you are an achievement hunter, this game will require at least 3 playthroughs with different party composition.I think players, who have never played Seiken Densetsu 3 before, may enjoy this game if you:- Don't mind a slow start.- Fancy combat that feels akin to Musou-style games (minus juggling enemies) or say, Genshin Impact.- Aren't too bothered with the depth / polish of the story in an RPG.- Prefer a relatively shorter RPG.- Don't mind / Enjoy spending time grinding for items.- Don't mind the tedium of exploring the game through repetition, with multiple playthroughs.Lastly, regardless of my second thoughts, I still think this game (even in the current ver. 1.1.0) is only worth getting during a discount (preferably 50% or more) for both new and old players alike. If you're the type that doesn't do NG+ in any JRPGs, then I definitely don't recommend this game or you'd definitely want a much deeper discount because this game is relatively short - I completed my first playthrough (on Hard) in sub 30 hours and at least a third of that time includes grinding for items and max level.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never played the original game, so I wasn't sure what to expect. I've heard a lot about it, but I have 0 nostalgia about it compared to a lot of people.This game, it's basically a 3D version of it, made with a super small budget and amateur voice-acting. It's super cheaply made, the animations aren't great, the plot really show its age, but I enjoyed it a lot. I finished it 3 times. I 100% it.It's like, a complete remake of a 2D game made with a shoe-string budget. It shows, it really shows. Despite its jankiness, its cheapness, I greatly enjoyed it.The combat is super simple, and yet quite satisfiying. The markers really cheapens the game, but it makes it way easier to play. You do get attached to a few characters, and it's nice being able to make your own party choice in the beginning. There's 3 "main" scenarios depending on your main character choice, with 3 different middle dungeons, 3 different end dungeons, and 3 different final bosses. That's definitely not something you would see in a RPG in this time.It's a great cheap game that really smells like a 90's RPG. It's good.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get the bad out of the way first.* A lot of the English VA is difficult to listen to, so select the Japanese VA.* The AI is not great, and you might find yourself soloing a handful of bosses with certain party compositions.* What are Riesz's shoulder guards attached to?* The pink bird of Palo will no longer follow you.* Some late-game passive abilities are overpowered, so you will break the game at the end.But overall, it's an excellent remake of Seiken Densetsu 3.  The game stays true to the spirit and atmosphere of the original game, and it fixes so many friction points.  As an incomplete list:* You don't have to "grind" to feel like you can keep up in power and level.  Skipping most random encounters is generally safe.* You are less likely to go broke, and going broke (and missing upgrades) is not punishing like in the original game.* The remake (in contrast with the original) does not "punish" you for promoting late.* You can actually experience the second and third classes earlier in the game.* There is no Pedan/Pedda grind for ??? Item seeds.* Most equipment is still character specific and are basically still just stat sticks, but there are status-protecting and damage-resisting accessories you can find that reward planning.* Enemy moves are generally avoidable, so combat rewards doing more than just facerolling.* The remake doesn't punish/counter you for using high-level charge combos (in contrast with the original game).* The game will point you where you can go next to advance the story, so there's no more getting lost.The story is still what it is (not super deep, mostly light), but the gameplay absolutely gives what you would realistically expect a remake to deliver, and it adds some other features (passive abilities, lots more treasure, in-town intra-party dialogue) to give you something new to experience.tl;dr: It's a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been aware of Seiken Densetsu 3/Trials Of Mana for several years now, ever since I first heard about it through a Youtube video around 2012. Though I never got around to playing it, it's something I've always kept my eye on, due to it having a massive cult status among RPG and SNES fans.Fast forward to last year's E3 event, and I was surprised and ecstatic to hear that not only was it getting localized in the form of the Collection Of Mana release, but it was also getting a remake on top of that. I planned on going through COM as anticipation for TOMR (Trials Of Mana Remake as I'm gonna call it from here on) but uh... that fell through since Doom Eternal and Final Fantasy 7 Remake were coming out beforehand, and then Sakura Wars 2020 was coming out a little after, so I prioritized going through the Doom series, OG FF7, and the fan translated first game of Sakura Wars first. Still, I was excited for TOMR nonetheless, so I went and preordered it anyway, and ended up loving it. Since I never went through the original, this review is mainly gonna be about my experience with the remake, though I'll make some clarifications on stuff I do know was added and changed.I picked Angela as my main character, and for her story, I was actually surprised at how much I ended up liking it. I went in knowing that Mana was a series of RPGs that placed much more emphasis on gameplay rather than the story, but even still they did a nice job fleshing both her and her villains' personality out, and in general detailed a fine backstory of the universe, made even more enjoyable due to adding Duran to my party, making him and Angela interact a bit more since the two share the same set of villains. Speaking of interactions, I've heard that they added some new dialogue stuff for the other party member(s) not connected to the *main* MC's story, the other three that weren't picked at all, and even the two other villains you don't face. While I don't know which were newly written and which were already in the original, I'm nonetheless glad to see that everyone outside of the MC's story have a fair amount of depth to their story (as abridged and shortened as they can be) and their personality, making it so that you WANT to see their POV in the next run. The new post-game story content, the Epilogue, is done after beating the game once, and overall it was good. I do think some people won't like how the dungeon is handled, but the conclusion for my three character's arcs in terms of both their individual quests and their new Class 4 status, as well as the boss for it, more than made up for it to me.My party for the whole game was Angela as Light Class magic attacker, Duran as a Light Class tank, and finally Kevin as a Dark Class physical powerhouse, and all of them filled their roles magnificently. While I'm not too sure about the specific workings of a character's build and stats in the original (though I've heard Angela has been buffed  in comparison, and Kevin, already being insanely powerful in my playthrough, is supposedly even better and literally game-breaking in the original?), I do know that the style of combat changed from attacks done via how much percentage was in the charge meter and other uses like magic and items being done through the Ring system, to an actual action-oriented battle, alongside new stuff such as dodging and (assuming these weren't in the original) Class Strikes and a tab that will allow you to fine-tune the AI's ability in battle to your liking. All of these were executed greatly here, though maybe a bit too great since outside of a few instances, I never felt any challenge, even when I played through the *entire game* on Hard. At the very least, though, the Epilogue's dungeon and especially the superboss that can be done after beating the main game deliver on the challenge front (though that being said, I can also see some people really not like the superboss due to it being a tad demanding).As for technical aspects, the game looks great. Though the seams of it being a budgeted title is noticeable due to the short draw distance and how textures are loaded, the overall art direction and presentation is great, and in some instances gives an even greater sense of atmosphere. In terms of sound effects, all the ones pertaining to combat (magic, hits, etc etc) sound punchy and satisfying, though the main star for this part, for me, is the soundtrack. I've listened to some of the original's music here and there for comparison, and almost all of the tracks got a wonderful rearrangement, my favorites being High Tension Wire, Rolling Cradle, Meridian Child (<3), and Decision Bell. The only notable flaw for sound is, probably the most infamous part of the remake, the English dub. I know that, since Mana is a budgeted series in comparison to something like Final Fantasy, Dragon Quest, and Kingdom Hearts, the English dub didn't get that much of a priority, but man... it's still awful. Though I've used JP audio for my entire playthrough, I did play the demo with the ENG voices as well as hear other bits from various clips online, and while I do like some of the ENG voices, such as Belladonna's, Hawkeye's, and Angela's, everyone else either had bad vocal delivery (Riesz, Duran, Crimson Wizard), weren't good to begin with (Charlotte, pretty much a majority of the side NPCs), or a mixture of both (Kevin). I just stated there's JP audio, but even still I'm disappointed SE just didn't put much effort for the dub to begin with.The only other flaw I can think of is that I think the late game dungeons fall flat. While the bosses for them - especially the final three bosses for my story - are all at least great, and the atmosphere for each are equally good, most of the dungeon design themselves ramp up the linearity and fighting rooms to a degree that made it a chore to go through, but that being said I still liked a decent chunk of them (Crystal Desert, Woods Of Wandara, Gemstone Valley, and Shimmering Valley specifically).All that said, I've very much enjoyed my time with TOMR. While I don't think it's something everyone will enjoy, due to it being a near 1:1 remake of the SNES original, instead of something like Resident Evil 1 and 2 remakes or the recently released Final Fantasy 7 Remake of being a wholly different experience while still keeping the tone, theming, and core parts of the original, it's loving charm, characters, and combat more than satisfied me. I'll definitely make sure to play the original - as well as finish up my progress in Final Fantasy Adventure and replay Secret Of Mana - sometime soon.

_childDocuments_.review: Update @ 3rd Playthrough:TL;DR: Disappointed in the game. I played through it 3 times, got most of the achieves already (will obtain the last couple on completing this playthrough), and finished the challenge bosses already. Just not that impressed with the Story, Characters, AI, or QoL aspects of the game. Needs work still, IMHO. Changed from Recommend (when discounted) to Not Recommended (until they update to improve AI/QoL - if they even will).It seems like the remake hasn't gone as well as I would've hoped. Several aspects of the game that need some QOL don't seem to have been addressed with the update:1) Magic/Support Caster AI: I still find that my Angela w/ the Black Rabite (0 magic cost) skill still likes to run up and hit things instead of cast magic at it. My Charolette also didn't like to cast any of the saber spells on my melee character in any of the battles (I had to manual cast these if I wanted that support). Both casters were set to use skills to their max without regard for mana, they were set for all out attack or support (as appropriate), and otherwise given the permissions they need (e.g. Charolette also had permission to use items and wouldn't use support items at all either). 2) ???? Seeds: These items are not randomized when planted, but are set when they are picked up. They will change to the classes of the new characters selected on NG+, but they are fixed at the start of the game. This means that if you do not go the direction that the ???? Seeds have predetermined for class items, you are stuck at a single class upgrade until you get the next few ???? Seeds and have to hope they plant like you want. This causes the seeds to be more of a waste of time then anything. With 8 seeds carried over, I have only 1 item drop that would allow me to progress a character to their 3rd class - both my lvl 99 Angela and my Hawkeye both have to wait till I get more ???? Seeds.The following is my initial review:TL;DR -- I would give the game 3 out of 5 stars. Definitely playable, but might want to wait for a sale.Pros: Good game play/controls (Kingdom Hearts-esque); reasonable over-arching storyCons: Horrible voice acting for some characters (e.g. Kevin, Charlotte); Character story translation/localisation team failed hard when doing the character scripts (i.e. some characters react in odd ways to events in the game); the 4th wall aspects of the game break with characters knowing they have to "change their class" in order to obtain power or instances where you are offered "candies and cups of wishes" to help you out in a direct manner - both of these would seem kind of ridiculous in a real fantasy setting; game encourages xp mismatch between characters  which can be a little annoying (or absolutely infuriating to the OCD crowd).FYSA -- The rabbite medallion that gives extra xp to lvl 10 is for only 1 character... kind of a chump move. Should've been wearable for stats by 1 character, but xp apply to all characters.

I know earlier Mana games used Benevodons too, but damn, that name is stupid. Are they Spanish speakers saying "welcome"? Are they actually good? God-Beasts fit better and it fits with SoM's Mana Beasts anyways. That out of the way, the combat is far above what I was expecting out of a remake of a 20+ year old game, there are dancing innkeepers like in SoM, the menu sounds take me back to happier times, the game looks great (and runs at 120 FPS!), and I sat listening to some music in a forest for like 20 minutes because it's great and CLEARLY sounds like Secret of Mana. _childDocuments_.review: I'd been looking forward to the release of Trials of Mana remake since I'd heard it was being worked on roughly half a year ago. I've played through the game twice now. I would be lying if I said I didn't enjoy the game over all, but that is not to say it doesn't have a host of problems-Lack of Multiplayer. Now I wouldn't include this if the games predecessor didn't actually include Multiplayer as one of it's core features. Finding out that it was removed in this one, and that they had no intention of adding it in, in future updates, was a pretty big let down. For me, that was the biggest draw. There's not a lot of co-op arpg titles on the market. The only one aside from the Tales of series that comes to mind is Secrets of Grindea, which is still incomplete.-Jank Voice Acting. There are very few cases where a voice actually fits a character or rather feels like they just took the first recording of a line and went with it every single time. The voice acting is alright at best and pretty bad at worst.-New Game Plus keeps character levels without increasing difficulty level or providing more options. Chain Skills do plenty to break the next run already mind you. But, quite frankly unless you're just looking to over power everything in your next run you're better off just playing on a new file altogether rather than New Game Plus.-Incredibly easy. I played the first few hours on normal difficulty before raising the difficulty to hard. And then, I still didn't manage to get myself wiped a single time throughout the game. Even with minor exploration the game will toss you item after item. You should never run out of anything that is commonly used in your inventory. A higher difficulty setting would be nice.-----+You can switch between the new music and the original tracks from the game on the fly through the options menu.+Amusing Branching story with variants based on the characters that you pick+Combat feels incredibly fluid and easy enough to get used to. Mechanically very enjoyable.+New Content as well as post game content not in the prior game.+Diverse enough class system allowing you to experiment with different ways to play the game on each play through.+The shop Keeper's are always dancing.+In a world where everything is fantastical and everyone's got your stereotypical fantasy name. You can have a guy simply named 'Kevin' in your party.-----Overall, it has it's problems, but it still stands up pretty well.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - Trials of Mana is a great remake of a classic, important game that suffers from being made WAY too easy in the transition, but thankfully this is PC and there are mods for that. Easy recommend if you just want a bright, cheery fantasy beat 'em up RPG though.At Length - Seiken Densetsu 3 is one of the more important games of the SNES/Super Famicom era though not for obvious reasons. First, it was an early attempt at making a JRPG where the story was highly variable and you had to play through it multiple times to see all of the variations it could take - extremely rare at the time and still a rare feature today. Second, in the US, due to the fact that it never got a port as Secret of Mana 2 for the longest time, this game was one of the biggest drivers for the SNES ROM scene back in the late 90s and early 00s (along with Tales of Phantasia and Star Ocean 1). As a lovingly crafted remake of that classic game, this version does an overall great job in bringing that experience to modern platforms, all in glorious 3D! No scrimping was done in terms of lovingly making the game's environments, characters, monsters, varying story paths and especially the genuinely amazing soundtrack. It's all here, all brought back to life at (almost) modern AAA standards as well as some extra bonus features including a whole extra post-game dungeon and a New Game + mode. All in all, you've got a great looking if fairly simple Action-JRPG that basically plays as a really bright and cheery fantasy anime in this package. (Pick Duran, Angela, and Riesz as your characters for a harem anime!)That said, there are some pretty big flaws to warn you about, big enough that were this not on PC I wouldn't recommend the game.First, the voice acting is . . . well, when they decided to make a game from the mid-90s apparently they also decided to bring back the terrible VA direction for English dubs from that era too. Duran, Angela, Hawkeye and a couple other characters are OK, but basically all the secondary characters and Riesz especially are just . . . wow they're bad. You have the option to turn on the Japanese audio and I 100% recommend that unless you want to revel in the cringe of some of this stilted, bizarre dialogue delivery.Next, this game is atrociously easy. Playing on hard feels like the easy mode for any other game. And it's bizarre because this game could be decently challenging enough to be interesting in its simple but decent brawling combat system, but the game just gives you WAY too much help. You have pots scattered about that heal you for free, as well as tons of free healing items if you do some basic exploration that make buying any at all pointless. There are huge telegraphed attack indicators for every attack that might possibly hurt, a guide marker to your next objective you can't turn off, and they dole out far too much experience and money, so you're always over-leveled as you progress through the game even if you do zero grinding and just explore each area thoroughly.I know difficulty is a preference thing, but this is a game tailor-made for very young children with poor reflexes at its current tuning level. If that's your level of capability or you just want to mindlessly bash cute monsters, well then this is your game. But for anyone else, I'd honestly say the low difficulty makes the actual gameplay so frightfully dull that on another platform I'd give this a pass. But, this is the PC version and thankfully, mods exist. They don't turn off achievements either. So I highly recommend hopping online and picking up at the very least the Difficulty Rebalance mod and optionally the ones that turn off attack indicators and the Map Quest Marker (there's none that erase the magic newb pots, yet). It's necessary if you want to enjoy this game at any level of challenge. It's not perfect, since this isn't official support from Square-Enix or anything, but its miles better than the current level of difficulty tuning.All in all, with some basic modding, this is an absolute blast from the past and highly recommended for anyone, but without modding stay away unless you're a game journalist.

_childDocuments_.review: I got a cart of the fan translation for the SNES many years ago, and at the time I actually didn't think much of the game. I barely got past the intro and just kind of stopped, and only came back to it months later from shear boredom since the initial impression I got was that it was a low effort, badly translated sequel to follow in the wake of secret of mana. I couldn't have been happier to be wrong. The game was phenomenal. The writing was simple but effective, the visual presentation was some of the best of the era, the real time combat with casting queues was vastly superior to any turn based system even today, the progression was almost perfectly structured, I could go on and on.Back then, I had always imagined what it would be like if there was a remake. But it was like a pipe dream, as it didn't seem nearly popular enough to warrant one. Once again I was happy to be wrong, and when I heard this was in the works, I knew that entire year was going to be fantastic. It looked and sounded exactly what I imagined a modernization would be like, quite literally a dream come true.Fast forward to now, I actually have a lot more playtime since I only got it on steam to stream. It is just as phenomenal as I had imagined. The aesthetic style and soundtrack covers are just perfect, not to mention the option to replace them with the original versions. But through all the gushing I can do, there are some few and far between gripes I have.Some of the character animations are very off, sometimes stiff or being too short before repeating. The voice acting is also probably the weakest of the artistic elements of the game, it often doesn't match the character animations or is too exaggerated in a way that breaks immersion.As for the gameplay, there are 2 key points in combat that don't really mesh together. The queue system has been removed and adapted into real time, and strong boss spells have been made disruptable. Having them on a queue with a special animation gave you time to think about what to do in response, and having them be undisruptable was to break the rhythm if you just went in guns blazing. Now, you get much less time to think about what to do if you get bonked, but it also became unnecessary. This is part of why a lot of people found the remake significantly easier.Those are just general gripes that are throughout the game, but there are also some changes in specific parts that were for the worse.Despite some ultimately minor problems, the game as a whole is still as close to what I once dreamed of. Always remember that before playing, take your mind back to the days of the SNES.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played the ♥♥♥♥ out of Seiken 3, 16 years ago back when the fan-translation was out, I feel like I had to write this review, since this game is very important to me and a considerable large part to my childhood. Let me start off by saying this game is a decently solid experience, and seems to hit nearly all the right notes as a long time Mana Series fan. It seems this game was made mostly for old fans for people who played the original game, since it seems to  be intentionally retain its authenticity as a remake. However I believe it draws in newcomers to the series with gorgeous art and honestly beating out a certain game that attempted to do dynamic story progression. So if you're an old time Mana fan, Someone who played Seiken 3 or someone who played Octopath Traveler and was severely disappointed with the lack of character development and dynamic storytelling, then this game is probably for you.Let me start off by saying this game is extremely faithful to the original game, for the most part. The majority of the overall plot as well as a large majority of the original script was kept intact. In my experience it sometimes came off as dated and even outright lazy at times (I'm looking at you Kevin....). A lot of the events in most the characters main story come off as awkward, as the original game did as well but this is especially amplified in 100% voice acted cutscenes. If you find yourself busting out laughing or cringing really hard, you'll know what i mean.  I feel like this could've been a positive change for the remake had they rewrote the script a bit more but its not too bad. Some of the game events have been changed, losing quite a bit of the comedic flavour Seiken 3 had. For example, there were various scenes where if you had Charlie and Kevin on the same party, they would often interact very comedically, with Kevin either knocking her out of the way to talk to a priest or holding back an angry loli with a flail from bludgeoning an old man to death for giving them the run around for seemingly no reason. In Trials these scenes which i was looking so forward to seeing in the remake was changed to a small shove (if even that) and a scolding gesture, which was disappointing. The overall plot is more or less the same, which can be a good or bad thing depending on who you ask. Unfortunately this means plotholes and questionable character motivations are still a thing in this game. However the flavour of the game never was the character motivations in the first place. It was always the journey and interactions between the cast you chose at the beginning of the game. This was something I was hoping to get from Octopath Traveler a few years back but was tragically disappointed and ultimately dropped the game.The original game took a top down cooldown based action RPG  approach with a rather wonky levelling and stat system that didn't really make a lot of sense, hell some stats didn't even work properly due to a bug that prevented crit and evade procs. In the remake all of this is reworked in someways bad and in MANY ways good. Starting off with the bad, the game drops the cooldown based gameplay on your melee attacks for a full on action JRPG battle system, meaning no cooldowns and spacing enemies is more or less an actual viable strategy now that your movespeed isn't impaired. The battle system retains it simplicity and remains fun to play. This is however, partially ruined by the addition of the dodge/roll button, essentially letting you pretty much never take damage for the most part (Ben & Bill and Zehnoa will still ♥♥♥♥ you up in this game, thankfully this hilarious difficulty spike was kept intact). In Seiken 3, spells casted by both party members and enemies did not have an AOE, they would just do damage and were unavoidable. In Trials however, thanks to the dodge button you can essentially dodge every single spell with little to no issue. It's broken. Now for the good. This game reworks how stats work completely. In the old game, you had your attributes in each stat that you could increase every time you levelled up....that's it. In this game however, when you level up not only does it increase effectiveness of each attribute, but when you put points into an attribute it comes with a learned skill/perk system that unlocks essentially passives that buff your characters in varies ways. For example, there's a passive that increases the amount of meter you get for your special attacks every time you finish a battle. This leads to a lot of variety in building your characters in a certain way, especially since some of these passive can be shared and equipped across your entire team, giving you a reason to invest points into otherwise completely unrelated stats to a certain characters playstyle. Battles essentially work as they did in Seiken 3, where as you enter the aggro range of a group of enemies, you beat them up and move on. In the remake this is more or less kept the same but enemies have less aggro range and now there's a small arena indicator where the fights actually take place, where if you run against the borders of said arena it lets you run from a battle. This is a huge quality of life change compared to slowly strafing away from the enemy who, nine times out of ten have double your movement speed, just to leave the whole area to skip a fight and I'm glad they added it. The remake now as a system in place that lets you set items and spells on a quick cast menu. (Which is especially important for Mage characters like Charlie and Angela who usually chain AOE's together.) There are 3 quick cast options allowing 4 slots for each. One for Special Attacks, one for items, and one for spells. It can't be understated how much of a quality of life change this is and how annoying it was to open the mention and scroll through the item ring just to use an item or spell in Seiken 3.You've probably heard this in other reviews but I'm here to tell you its all true. As someone who can typically play either sub or dub when it comes to JRPG and appreciate English voice actors and their work when done right and can recognize a good dub when I hear one (I.E Persona 4, Persona 5, Dragon Quest VIII, Dragon Quest XI, Final Fantasy VII Remake, Fire Emblem: Three Houses, Nier), I can confidently say this. Besides Chaos Wars, THIS IS THE WORST ENGLISH VOICE ACTING I HAVE EVER HEARD IN MY ENTIRE LIFE. My jaw absolutely dropped to the floor when I booted up the demo and played through Charlie's story and heard her voice. I have never closed a game so fast and switched to sub that quickly. It's THAT BAD. For context, Charlie in the original game had a LISP speech impediment. In this game however, (and the Switch port) she now speaks in uwu for some god forsaken reason. This problem isn't only unique to Charlie either, it's EVERYONE. Kevin and his lazily done caveman-like dialect, Duran and his lack of emotion, Riesz and her awkward pauses. Everyone has ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ voice acting. I wouldn't wish my worst enemy to listen to that monstrosity of voice work. If you play this game, do yourself a favour and switch to sub, TRUST ME. The Japanese voice acting is fairly decent this however comes at the  cost of missing out on a lot of banter between the cast after a battle if you don't speak or understand Japanese since this isn't subbed, which was extremely infuriating for my playthrough of the game.The music in this game isn't particularly hit or miss, as most of the soundtrack is really nice. Some songs are actually BETTER than Seiken 3's soundtrack, while some just lose all its flavour thanks to the lack of SNES soundfonts. (A lot of the bass and kicks are non-existent in the remake. See "Different Road" in both games and you'll see what i mean.)Overall this game is honestly, a good game, but not without quite noticeable flaws.If you're still on the fence about getting this game, I'd definitely recommend picking this up.

_childDocuments_.review: The original release of this was one of the reasons I paid way too much for a super famicom even though I can't read a word of Japanese. I even remember being excited for the English patch for the rom, so yeah I love this game. I'm not judging this it on any of the  faults of the original such as the weaker story, because really the game was about overcoming a lot of technical problems that plagued the previous game. *I liked a majority of the new elements the 3D space does have some added depth that adds a tiny bit more strategy to encounters, but after a few hours in that newness doesn't last very long. One of the things it added I really disliked is random platforming jumps later in the game to get some of the chests   and items. This isn't a huge part of the game but it is one of those things where it just pops in a few spots (on ice of coarse), so it's not something you have been doing. I would have rather had a lot more of it or simply none at all. *There's a lot of emptiness in the game, which was in the 2d game as well, but here it somehow feels even more so just because of the detail of it. There's very few things to interact with and I think that was a wasted opportunity for “something”. Collectibles, hidden goodies, maybe a random rare monster, mini game, really anything would have been nice. I can't fault it that much though.*I think it would be beating a dead horse to say the game is way too easy and the AI is all over the place, but I'll just mention a few major things. They will stand in whatever random death spell that is cast at them- actually they will likely change direction and run full force into it. Left to their on devices they will cast the most powerful and mana draining spells on a single target while running into a clump of heavily armored with a normal attack. I tend to just let them die, which slightly increases the difficulty. They auto res after the fight ends and there's plenty of golden statues around to refill their resources. You are limited to 9 of each item while in combat but you can carry more than you'll ever need so those stay topped off if you want to res them and micro mange for a bit for max damage. *The changes to spells and abilities was an interesting idea, but to me some of it seemed misplaced. They seemed to have tried to balance out all the classes giving some of them buff in the damage department so you can do okay melee damage with a caster /support class. The thing I am on the fence about is learning spells and skills to equip requires a heavy investment in a stat I'd rather not have. Choosing to put a chunk of points in strength to use the fire spell just seemed off and felt like a forced way to enforce some sort of balance but really just ends up making them better at smashing monsters. There doesn't seem to be be a lot of spells for the various elementals for the investment. Yes I know the original game didn't have tons of spells, but I also didn't need to put tons points in to use them. *I think a lot of the equipped skills are really situational and they are all passive effects, so you see stuff go off like a heal or bonus buff. I suppose they help a little, but the game isn't very hard. I tended to just stack things that regen health/mp/cs meter because they are mostly percentage based so they scale well, but again it felt just like set it and forget it till you dump 12 or so more points in something. *I think they missed an opportunity for some arena style pvp mode. would have been cool to fight five other people or as teams. The again the system isn't really robust enough for something like that on any competitive level. A boss battle endurance mode would have added some replay value outside the three major (similar) plots. Maybe some unlockable created character mode or some costumes tied to one of those things. These are just random thoughts though and I am just rambling now.Overall it seems like I am hard on the game, but it is very enjoyable and most of these things just boil down to nit picking. Expectations were very high going in and for the most part I was satisfied. Catch it on sale and it's a no brainier if you liked the original or action rpgs in general.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been loving the game.It oozes with 80s fantasy / fairy tales charm, visuals are vibrant and colorful, the music is incredible, the characters are pretty cute and cool, the world is pretty vast, and the gameplay systems have been a blast.Bullet points to keep it short :- Combat system is fun, starts fairly basic and opens up thanks to the stat trees and classes upgrades- The customization of each character's gameplay is an absolute blast- The story adapts itself to the characters in your party, it's a long adventure - While not technically super impressive, the simplistic artstyle looks gorgeous most of the time- The cutscenes are mediocre, in the literal sense, not helped by subpar English voice acting. Those voices do grow on you but if you can't stand them, you have the option to pick Japanese voices.- Once you have access to the world map, there is an emphasis on exploration that is extremely pleasant- PC performance has been extremely solid, no frame drops, fast load times, makes the game very responsiveAll in all, I do think the biggest disappointment is the removal of multiplayer, the action focus means it would have had to be online coop and I guess it was too much work to implement. It's a much better remake than Secret of Mana remake. You can tell that, while having a limited budget to work with, they cared about the original and wanted to make a game that is really fun to play, and I think they succeeded.They said if this does okay Square will allow them to make an original Mana game (Seiken Densetsu 5), so do you part !Tips : Use the repel attacks to create staggers on enemies, and if you start on Hard difficulty, know that the beginning of the game is extremely easy, difficulty kicks in little by little and it will become challenging !

_childDocuments_.review: One of the "solid" JRPG of all time. Seiken Densetsu 3 was good but Square decided not to port into US back in the day. _childDocuments_.review: A fun romp! I cleared all the way through the postgame, finished around level 70 with no superbosses or NG+Main game is a walk in the park even on Hard mode, the difficulty peaks fairly early and then the rest of the game is mostly trivial with maybe 1 or 2 tricky bosses. It is much, much easier than the original SD3.  Postgame is not really much harder. There is a superboss for those who want a steeper challenge.Despite the difficulty, building up your party and customizing their skills is still pretty fun, although the customization starts to feel a little lacking in meaning in the late game when you can kill pretty much everything with ease. Strongly recommend playing Kevin just because playing as a werewolf is great and all of his skills are really strong + look cool. (his postgame bonus fight is also one of the coolest)English VA is pretty subpar, the Japanese VA is quite a bit better, so the JP voices are definitely recommended if you can deal with subtitles. The game looks nice overall but there are a few angles in cutscenes and some boss arenas that look fairly flat and uninteresting. Nothing immersion-breaking though. The characters and environments all look great and are very faithful to the original game overall. The option to play with Kikuta's original SD3 soundtrack is also wonderful and I strongly recommend giving it a try.Got it on sale for around $15 and I would recommend waiting for a similar price, I got about ~17 hours of a single playthrough and I was playing pretty quickly and did not finish every single thing in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Positives first:It looks beautiful other than some curiously high skirts leading to near-permanent panty shots with Riesz and Angela.The remake devs heard us about missing the characters fly up and fall down when using cannons and they only updated the music rather than make really odd remixes of it like in SoMThe story does still feel like a SNES game that has been elevated with "more" character dialogue and extra features, but I didn't play the original as a translated port, so can't be sureThe negative:OK, I'm at just under 17 hours here and just did the Bil & Ben fight in the desert. This is the 4th "boss fight" in which I was better off letting my companions die and soloing the boss. Other fights just had them being stupid and walking into attacks, this one caused them to actively hinder me because you need to take Bil and Ben out within a certain amount of time of each other and the AI decided to target the weaker of the two over and over without me being able to change their behavior.I never played this game on the SNES, but it is nothing like Secret of Mana was. The remake changes combat so that it feels VERY generic with a bad camera behind you, causing you to pretty much lose sight of any enemy you are not actively targeting. The game makes you attack the enemy it wants you to unless you're casting a spell, leading to, again, in the Bil & Ben fight, the weaker of them to run up to me during a power attack and redirecting it from the one I wanted to hit.The English dubbing of this game is, like the remake of Secret of Mana, mostly terrible. I'm playing as Riesz with Angela and Hawkeye. So far Hawkeye, Belladonna, and The Hero King act decently well. Angela isn't bad, but not a standout. Riesz and the fairie are just bad. Riesz is hindered by a stilted, overly formal, speech pattern, but she also gives really odd inflections. They need to fire the vocal director for these remakes, the person accepts way too many bad takes and I do not understand why not a single person in a game that says "mana" repeatedly cannot pronounce the word correctly.Edit: for reference, I usually prefer English dubs in anime and games for a variety of reasons and this is cheap, early 80's anime dub bad for the most part.I also didn't care much for the new experience bonuses based on speed of completing fights or finishing moves, etc.; being trapped in fight "arenas" when travelling when I could just run past stuff in SoM; or the Item Wheel being the only way to access non-combat items like permanent buff items or the vehicle summoning item when I prefer to keep only combat items in it. And hiding the "return to title screen" in the pause menu the way they did it is very inconvenient.

_childDocuments_.review: + Runs smoothly+ Different goal for each character+ Choose your party from start+ Satisfying combos+ Music- A.I will often be a bit stupid and slow attacking in some battlesI never played the original but liked the style of the remake and tend to like games such as this with RPG elements and different party members.I loved the enemy designs and didn't get bored of battles even when having to re-run an area or two for missing collectables. Being able to switch to your other two party members even if not the main character chosen is nice to mix it up if you are bored of said-characters play-style and want to play as something else from your party.They dodge well and attack/heal often depending how you set them up in the menu (which you can switch anytime outside battle) though late-game I noticed a party member using a powerful MP move when no enemies were clearly never near her, wasting the move which was a bit frustrating.The remake music I did enjoy but you can choose the original which I stuck with around half way through as it just seems to fit better but nice they gave us the choice.You get a nice amount of play-time for your money even if you are not after all achievements.So far I find this the most fun and best looking out of the Mana remake series.My only nitpick is the hardest difficulty you can choose at the start is a total joke, only boss I had an issue with was a flying one due to the hitbox. You can get two harder difficulties on NG+ but that is a good 15-20 hours in and for those wanting a challenge from the very start it is abit of a let down for the starting hardest difficulty to seem more like normal difficulty.Overall, get the game if you are an RPG fan even if you never played the originals, the mana series never seems to disappoint on game-play and look forward to other games they will hopefully be remaking (please give us Children of Mana I want my frail-main back)
