_childDocuments_.review: After so many years, we are finally able to play Seiken Densetsu 3 in the best way possible. This is one of the best "remakes" I have played in a while, the story and characters are very faithful to the original version and the music has also been adapted in a brilliant way. Even if the story is rather simplistic for the modern era JRPG, the voice cast and new, more refined translation does a great job on filling the game with charm.However, the dialogue can feel a bit dated sometimes but it's kind of expected from an old timey, classic JRPG. Also, even if the combat is great, AI teammates can be extremelly frustrating in the higher difficulties as they tend to run around and get hit by every single attack and I can see how some people can find combat a bit repetitive after a while, but luckily with the class system and huge replay value this game brings, experimenting with different characters and classes can help keeping  things fresh.Overall, if you are looking for a Nostalgia trip or you are more curious about JRPGs from a different era, this is definitely a game you should play.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a full remake of Seiken Densetsu 3 from the Super Nintendo (originally released in 1995).I say this here not because I love pointless redundancy, but to establish where this game came from, as it will be relevant throughout my review. Yes, that means I played the original, way, way back in 2001 and have beaten the SNES game well over a dozen times prior to playing Trials of Mana.So, do I recommend Trials of Mana? Depends.I wouldn't recommend it to modern audiences unless they were very interested in the Mana Series OR if they were buying these games for a child as their first JRPG. (FYI, the Mana Series of games has always been intended as introductory RPGs for kids, love it or hate it)But as a remake of the original SNES game, it is an immense improvement over the original in nearly every way.++WHAT TRIALS OF MANA DOES RIGHT++COMBAT: For context, the single biggest problem I had with the original Seikden Densetsu 3 was actually the combat. It was MINDLESSLY simple. 95% of the gameplay was Attack-x4 -> Tech Attack -> Repeat, heal as needed...and even compared to its predecessor (SD2, aka 'Secret of Mana') it was made even simpler.The only thing that broke up the ad-nauseum were spells...assuming your party members had them. Depending on your party composition, your first spells could become available as early as the first boss of the game, or as late as 10 hours in.Since the bulk of the game revolves around clobbering small groups of monsters this was something of an issue for the first third of the game. It gets much better once most characters undergo their first class-change and start getting actual spells/abilities but...man was the original combat a dull slog.Trials of Mana overhauls the whole thing: Every character has their own move set for attacks, which vary based on when the player begins or continues their attack. Best of all, this includes the caster characters too, which works wonders in making them viable for anything but spell spamming into the late game.Simply put: This fixes the single biggest complaint I had with SD3.The other issue Trials addresses is magic and special/tech attacks. For context, magic in the SNES Mana games were fancy eye-candy attacks typical of SNES JRPGs. However, unlike most of their contemporary JRPGs, the Mana Series aren't turn-based but real-time action and the SNES simply wasn't powerful enough to render these effects AND keep the regular action going at all times, so combat came to an abrupt halt every time it rendered magic/tech effects.Since we're FAR beyond such technical limitations today how did Trials of Mana handle this? Well, you get a rudimentary warning zone on the ground when an enemy begins casting a spell or other such attack. Don't be there when it goes off. Simple, but effective enough. Player magic is auto-aimed, undodgeable and will work 99% of the time.Furthermore, some bosses have had their entire routine changed to account for this, including periods where you are bluntly intended to go purely evasive against their magical nukes, or use magic of your own to counter-barrage them.There were very few bosses like this in the original SD3, so I'm glad to see the mix-up.All of these changes does have one drawback: The combat is much less attrition-based. Consequently, it makes the game a bit too easy for most players and there isn't a simple solution to this available since it's a matter of pacing and just jacking up the numbers or frequency of enemy magic attacks would drag the game to a crawl.Overall though, the combat is still a vast improvement over the original.PRESENTATION: GRAPHICS AND SOUNDI will be blunt here: This was clearly a low-budget title intended to cash in on nostalgia.That cynical take aside, this is definitely one of the best modern Remakes Squeenix has produced.The graphics are trying to remain true to the style of the classic 2D spritework and watercolor aesthetic the Mana Series is reknowned for. Because of this, the models are kept 'cartoony' and simple, and the colors vibrant. I'm not much of a fan of the 3D renditions myself because 2D pixel art captures a part of the imagination that 3D rarely does, but I digress.The same can be said of the environments: These were superb-looking back in 1995 on the SNES and paragons of the 2D art-form at the time...but as 3D environments, they're very lacking especially by modern standards. (We've been so spoiled by games like Breath of the Wild, I swear)Sound is a very mixed blessing. The excellent soundtrack is another hallmark of the Mana Series and SD3 was no exception, possessing one of the best sound-tracks of the era (right up there with Mega Man X, Super Metroid and Chrono Trigger as far as I'm concerned).Thankfully, MERCIFULLY, unlike the Secret of Mana Remake's 'modernied' soundtrack (that was just full of bizarre/awful instrumentation) Trials of Mana's remixed modern renditions are mostly excellent and remain true to the tone of the original tracks. I'd say they got 95% of the tracks right, plus, the full original SD3 soundtack is available as an option if you don't like them or want to hear the originals.On the BAD side of things...the Voice Acting. SD3 didn't have any for what I hope are obvious reasons.Frankly...the new VAs are nearly universally awful. Mercifully, you can turn them off or swap to another language. Sadly, I know exactly why the VAs fail so badly and why they were done that way. (it wasn't just a decision due to cheapness either, though it's clear they were cutting corners there too)But I digress...PACING, STORY, ETCI will be brief here; this is a standard SNES story typical of a game made from that era. You have to understand, SD3 came out only 2 years before Metal Gear Solid 1 and Final Fantasy 7 revolutionized the industry by validating that gaming audiences wanted much larger and detailed stories in their games. Large 'epic' stories did exist prior to SD3, but they were the outlier exception, not the norm.Elementary, simple (or by today's standards, 'cliche'...keeping in mind every cliche has an origin before it becomes such a thing) stories were NORMAL and EXPECTED back then.I say all that to say this: Trials of Mana's story (and characters) is shackled to the original, and thus, inherits all the flaws, and poorly aged tropes therein. My biggest disappointment perhaps, is that Squeenix did not attempt to expand upon the lore, context, or characterization (something even the Secret of Mana Remake attempted) of the original.This is a missed opportunity, because for those who don't know, Trials of Mana was intended to be a PREQUEL to Secret of Mana, and establish what happened in the distant past so as to inform events in the future. In practice...well...SD3's story could have happened at any time really, because it has no hard connection to the other games by continuity. So...the story is weak and didn't get a proper update as I had hoped. Oh well.Beyond that, the pacing is the same. You go to the original areas, which are of comparable length to the originals, and do the same story beats. Not much to say here. There is more treasure looting and such, but it doesn't really matter due to equipment having flat, boring, linear progression with no real deviation or strategy. You just upgrade to bump up your numbers, as in the original. Again, another missed opportunity, likely constrained by the relatively small budget.Still, the game is perfectly playable, and doesn't contain any particularly cruel or backwards design decisions (unlike, say, Final Fantasy 2) that whack you in the face out of nowhere.CONCLUSION:Get Trials of Mana on sale if you're curious or nostalgic. It's a good remake, but not really a great modern RPG.Pick up Elden Ring or Breath of the Wild if you want something meatier in that camp from AAA. (at the very least, it wasn't Tales of Arise. Holy crap was that game's story BAD.)

_childDocuments_.review: Let's start with the TLDR: Get this game if you are a fan of 90's style hack and slash RPGs featuring a lot of variety and some beautiful art and music. It's short. It's fun. It's casual. Those looking for a deep, moving story, or interesting character arcs will be disappointed. It's very basic and straightforward. If you're a fan of this kind of gameplay, you'll love it; but if you're not... there's not much for you here.Now I'll elaborate. Trials of Mana is a great 90's style Saturday morning RPG.While it doesn't have the same depth or storytelling as a Dragon Quest, Ys, or Tales game; it does have a lot of charm and appeal.I 100% this game and that's something I seldom do. I kept coming back for more even after my second playthrough. The art direction in this game is beautiful. The animations, fluid combat, and beautiful soundtrack combine for a very satisfying and addicting combat loop of exploration, combat, leveling up, and character growth.The replay value is great because not only are the stories different with each character; but you carry over levels and abilities (such as 300% xp)  to assist you on your next playthrough. This makes the game even funner with each run. It's also really fun to experiment with the class system and party combinations. (however the three members you pick at the start of the game will be the only three you can play as for each playthrough)Sadly, the story is still just as uninteresting regardless of which character you pick. In addition to that; the English VO is atrocious. Some of the characters are downright obnoxious and offensive in the delivery of their lines. Fortunately, the game gives you the option to set the language to Japanese with English subtitles. (highly recommend it)Overall I loved this game and I would recommend it to any fan of action RPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: Square Enix fails again. An epic tale of cash grabbery. This is a minimum effort attempt to recapture the mana fanbase and it's a wholly disappointment. I can't believe they have the nerve the charge 50 dollars, I'm not even sure if it's worth 30. The voice acting is horrendous, and not in a fun bad way, it's just bad. The combat is a joke, they put zero effort into balancing it, they give you a god roll from the beginning that basically nullifies any attack (oh you can do it in the air too!) and there is no cool down either. The only challenge in the game is keeping your idiot AI partners alive who seem to go out of their way to run in front of enemy attacks and die constantly. There were many battles that I simply left them dead because it was simply easier to just god roll my way to victory. On top of it all, they removed the best feature of the original, co-op play! I'm not even asking for online co-op, local would be fine, but they deemed it too time consuming (expensive) to implement this feature. Why would they, as their loyal zombie fans will just buy it anyway (me included) and then it fattens their bottom line. Square Enix is a horrible horrible company, and has been ever since its inception after the merger. Nothing good has come from them, what a mess.I know there are plenty of you out there that want to latch on and like this, but no, please fight back against Square Enix and their awful attempts to sell you a bunk product slathered in nostalgia. They are playing us all for fools and we're lapping it up. If I could return this joke of a product, I would, but I guess the real joke is on me.And yes, on top of it all, it has Denuvo. I am not necessarily bothered by it, but I find it strange. This is a niche little product and sales are going to be much smaller than their other titles (considering this is also very obvious a budget title from them). Seems like a waste, the people who want this I really believe are just going to buy it, they are all old school fans who are now fully adults with jobs, this isn't something that is going to appeal to the masses. Just seems odd to spend that money to protect it from piracy (which it will only do for a few weeks at best anyway).The soundtrack at visuals are at least pretty good, but that's about the only good I can say about this lack luster affair that Square Enix is peddling.

It's a bit limited, and sometimes they just make terrible choices (buffing at the end of a fight, doing AoE attacks in places it won't hit anything, etc.)If you're accustomed to action/RPG, the game will be too easy to really appreciate most of the fights' mechanics. _childDocuments_.review: Hello! This is my first ever review that I had ever posted on Steam and out of all the games I've chose to review, I decided to review this childhood game of mine. It deserves it and boy oh boy, I have a lot of explaining to do.First off, Trials of Mana was originally called Seiken Densetsu 3 and it was the third Mana series game to be released....only it wasn't released in North America as promised by Nintendo and SquareSoft (Square Enix). Instead it was only released in Japan due to some complications and as a result of this, Secret of Evermore took it's place while Trials of Mana went into the dark.Compared to the original, the remake provides a lot more content and some changes that improve this game more. Square Enix decided to add the Lil' Cactus mini game, which provides the player a ton of benefits should they find the little guy from across the world. There is also a post game available too. The post game has access to some side quests that will let the 6 playable characters go into the brand new 4th class with a brand new boss and area to explore too. With the Quality of Life and improved graphics....it is no doubt that this is the version you want to play if you want to compare it to the original Trials of Mana. Did I also mention that the new difficulties Expert and No Future provide quite a challenge too should you play this in New Game Plus ?I guess I should also mention about the story too. When you first play Trials of Mana, the game usually asks you who your three playable characters are. The first character you pick is your Main character and that character is the one that affects the main story. Duran/Angela will have to deal with the Crimson Wizard's antics, Kevin/Charlotte will have Gormund.....who is also quite the madman and Hawkeye/Riesz will have to put up with Isabella. I won't explain much further than that.The last greatest thing that Trials of Mana provides is it's party formation. The 6 playable characters have 6 classes to choose from in the main story (I'm excluding the 4th classes and the Starting class.) and I will say this. Each class is unique. Some classes provide buffs, debuffs and a lot more customization depending on what you do.While I do praise this game quite a lot, there are some downsides too.  I think the biggest con is that the main story can become very repetitive as you play thru each character's story. It can be draining too if you are trying to grab all the achievements. The second biggest con would have to be Class item seeds (??? Seed). These particular item seeds that you get during the late game is rather difficult and you would have to do a TON of farming/grinding to get the particular Class Item Seed you want. The third and final Con that I have for this game is that sometimes the voice lines are a little cringey at times. It might be annoying for some players but other than that, I see no other problems.Do I recommend this remake ? Of course I do....especially that now everyone can play it and get their hands on this game quite easily compared to the SNES days. Well done Square Enix....well done.

_childDocuments_.review: Very linear.  Sort of an "intro to RPGs" type of game play.  The battle system is a lot of fun and there is a lot of progression.  Kevin (the beastman) is probably the most annoying character of this whole game, which is a shame because his abilities and fight styles is a blast!  But if I hear him talk in English that sounds like someone just ran 400 miles but is trying to tell you something while catching their breath "Many...People...Attack...Village...Not...Good" and whine about his stupid dog Karl again....I think I'll throw the controller across the room.  "NO ONE CARES ABOUT YOUR STUPID DOG KEVIN!"  *bashes head on wall*Aside from Kevin having the absolute lamest back story and an incredibly annoying voice and speech pattern, he's actually quite fun to play and everyone else have a MUCH better story. _childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a game that's relatively true to the original, and has been mostly improved upon - this is a solid pick up.  It took me about twenty hours to clear the game up to the new game plus point.  Now, because I'm a hater, despite recommending the game, I do have a few gripes(mostly gaming trends in general).It's far too easy, and it suffers from what many ARPG's of this format do, it's almost impossible to fail.  At your best, you never need items, and at your worst - you can infinitely spam them to overcome any fight.  Outside of Zhenova(which was actually pretty mechanically challenging), everything else was very simplistic, and I was capable of ignoring most all mechanics due to insignificant damage(this was on hard).  Not including multiplayer in this iteration of the game - with a combat system that would have been far more suited to having multiple people because it doesn't lock up other characters when you use your skills/moves, that's a negative.  Having dodge roll also trivializes whatever threat most of the game poses. Everything I've read about new game plus makes the game significantly easier than it already is, so I'm not looking forward to playing that.  I imagine I'm the minority when it comes to opinion.  Over all, was worth buying, and playing through.

_childDocuments_.review: Rather than give you generic details about what this game does right, (visuals, music, combat, exploration,) and what this game does wrong, (voice acting, story scenes, explaining things, VOICE ACTING,) I'm going to talk a bit about why I like the Mana series, and why this is a must play entry.When I think about Mana games, I think about nature. The games' stories are obviously about the magical power of nature and how it can be used for good or evil, but I'm talking about the simple joys of being in and observing the natural world. Even back on the SNES, these games were made up of lush forests and rocky spires. The artists pay special attention to these things, making them more prevalent than other games. Enter a village and you may see a person standing on a deck, watching a river. You'll see hanging herbs and spices, drying in the sun. Maybe you'll find a person standing in a field of flowers. You may even see some twinkling lights on a snowy tree. These little touches make the game special, and the accompanying soundtrack helps to bolster this feeling.Another thing that the Mana series does well is night. Many games have a day/night cycle, but how many games have not one, but three entire areas dedicated to the night? The night is such a multifaceted setting for games, and again, I feel that the Mana developers know this and use it well. You've got spooky, eerie night. You've got loud and boisterous festival night. You've got magical, mystical glowing night. This game does night so well that I found myself staying at inns just to advance to dusk.Finally, let's talk about remakes because this is one of those. I saw an importer's ad for "Secret of Mana 2" in the back of an old EGM magazine when I was a young lad, and then finally played the original Neill Corlett translation in the early 2000s. I remember thinking that I had to be dreaming, getting to play a game that I never thought I'd see. Flash forward 20 years, and now not only is the original available in the US, but a whole remake. Life can be fun sometimes, eh? This is a very competent remake, and I'm enjoying it very much. It makes me want to go and play the original once I finish. Maybe I can convince my wife to play it with me on the Switch...

_childDocuments_.review: So, I've finally gotten around to playing the game a day late, and now after playing it for just shy of 2 hours, I feel that I've gotten a pretty good feel for the game at a basic level, enough to write a review!DISCLAIMER: I have not played Seiken Densetsu 3, nor its official re-release on the Switch, more than just a few minutes because I didn't like the Menu and Combat System when I tried it on SNES. This review is coming from someone who never played the original game.Graphics: 8/10: It has a nice visual art style true to the Mana games, the models seem well-done, and well-animated, good water effects. I can't really say that I would have asked for much more; the Mana series has always been about bright colorful art styles, and I'm glad they kept true to that here. I wouldn't want it to look any more realistic; such would have ruined the theme and style compared to the rest of the franchise.Sound: 9/10: The sound effects are spot on, and the re-use of older games' sound effects for things like menus and such was a huge nostalgia trip and a touch of genius, all the sounds that you loved to hear in Secret of Mana, are back. The music I've heard thus far is spot-on, I can't say I've had any complaints about any of it. Tingles of Joy ran over my head, ASMR triggered by hearing what sounded like a remix of the Final Boss Theme from SoM in certain high action/danger scenes.Difficulty: 9/10: The game has a selectable difficulty level, always very nice to see. And from what I read on the settings screen, you can even adjust it during a playthrough which is nice, and even moreso, is the fact that difficulty has zero bearing on the story. Normal seems fair, perhaps slightly easy but then I started with one of the game's melee-oriented characters (Reisz). Early-game might be more challenging for one of the magic-users instead, perhaps? Either way, Normal seemed fine, and there's two settings easier, and two settings harder, so I'm sure there's plenty here to like for just about anybody.Voice Acting: 7/10: Solid, though perhaps not perfect. Some characters (Charlotte) seem like they might get annoying if they talk Too much. Angela (the other group member I chose) is just a tad bit grating, but then I think that's the whole point they were going for. I can't say I have any complaints here, and at least the mouth movement seems to have been adjusted for English voices, I didn't notice anybody's lips moving longer than the audio was playing.Gameplay: 8/10: I have only a couple little itty-bitty issues with the gameplay in this game. First, which does not seem to be fixable, is the camera. You will want a controller (an xbox360 controller works perfectly out of the box) for this as constant movement of the camera is absolutely necessary as the camera does not move with you. I wish they would have given us an option to give us a follow camera, where the camera stays behind the character as you turn and move. This does not appear to be an option, sadly. The other little nitpick I have, is the default button arrangement felt awkward, but I think this can be changed. I will likely be trying to change that. On the 360 controller, by default, A is jump which is well and good, but for some weird reason, X is dodge, B is light attack and Y is heavy attack which just seems really weird. You have 8 customizable quick-slots (RB/LB+ABXY); 4 for items, 4 for moves/spells which is really awesome. You can also swap your playable character at will, and the group AI seems to be competent but not perfect at dodging things (which is good, if it were perfect then one might be tempted to just stand back and let the AI kill everything).On the matter of dodging things, enemies use AoE markers similar to some MMOs, especially FFXIV and indeed the first boss uses mechanics I've seen in bosses from FFXIV, so you can tell that this is an SE-made game, which was a very nice touch!Other Comments:Biggest two nitpicks I have outside of what was mentioned above is A). Denuvo and B). Resolution settings. On the first, Denuvo didn't give me any problems. I did not notice any framerate drops except for perhaps during cutscenes, but battle was butter-smooth (I am running it at 1080p, windowed with a Ryzen5 1500X and a GTX 1050ti), with a stable internet connection.As to the other nitpick... I like to play games in windowed or borderless window mode, filling the entire screen except the taskbar. The game does allow you to choose windowed at a smaller resolution and the maximize button is indeed click-able, and it does work perfectly but for some reason when I was done with my session, and I exited to title screen.... the window shrank back down to the resolution I had specified. Also, it was hard to actually click the maximize button and took some fiddling around with the window's border before I could get it to actually click the button, and the game does not appear to remember that you want it maximized for whatever reason. Hopefully they can fix this with a patch, seems like something that should be easy to fix.Overall: 9/10Definitely recommend this game. Easily. No question about it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd only recommend this to someone who loved the original, just cause they'd appreciate things more+ Bug free+ Runs very well without requiring a supercomputer+ Gorgeous+ Voice acting+ Family Friendly+ Boss Fights are fun+ Nostalgia/ outside of combat it seems like a very faithful remake- Too expensive. Generally not a prob but when u run into a tough boss RIP to all your healing items.- Unless you are speedrunning there isn't much actual strategy necessary- Combat is boring and doesn't improve for like 6 hours. When it finally improves it's minor.I imagine a few other improvements but it's all too little too late.- It's tagged as a hack n slash but it's nowhere close. You only have 2 combos for the first 6 hours.You will poke enemies, dodge, repeat and mainly use abilities out of boredom rather than necessity- I coped myself into playing this remake of a"classic" for 9 hours and I finally reached a turning point where things improved but these were all marginal and it simply makes no sense for me to keep wasting my time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty fun.I will preface this by saying I'm not a huge fan of action RPGs in general.  I don't care about Kingdom Hearts or the new direction that the Final Fantasy franchise has been heading in for quite a while now.  In general, I like my JRPG combat to feel more like you are playing a table top/board game then a beat em up.  However, growing up I always had a soft spot for Secret of Mana.  I think this was mainly due to the fact that you could play with up to 2 other players, which pre-internet play, nothing made sleeping over at a buddies houses more fun than having a good game to play multiplayer.  I had previously attempted to play the translated ROM of this game at least 3 times in the past.  I gave up on it all 3 times.  It wasn't sucking me in.  Fast forward to now and with all the new fanciful paint and audio thrown in to this remake and I'm glad to have finally finished this one.Graphics?  Beautiful, very colorful.  Reminds me of Dragon Quest 11.  I don't think one can ask for much more visually outside of those demanding photo-realistic visuals on everything.Sound?  Charming.  The music was good.  The voice work however, could have used a bit more work.  The character Charlotte could get a bit grating on the ears, because she talked like a small child with a speech impediment.  The beast man Kevin should have got a deeper, more feral sounding voice to me, but that is just personal opinion.  All the vendors in every town have the same voice and you could really feel like some of the voice actors were reading from a script and didn't really know how to deliver the lines, but it wasn't that distracting.Also, you eventually get to ride a certain creature like a boat.  The sound he makes when you summon him is slightly higher than everything else audio-wise in the game and it will probably startle you every time you summon him.Story?  Well, heh... just remember that this game was originally a super nintendo game.  The story is... not that deep.  Which is a shame because there is some really good setup for an interesting world full of different kingdoms and groups of people, they just don't do much with it.  Every character you can choose from gets a very basic story of setting off to save someone or avenge someone or bettering themselves.  This game also handholds in all aspects in terms of what to do and the exact passageway that leads to the next spot you have to go.  This to me was actually kind of relaxing in that I could play this game while watching stuff on my second monitor and not worry too much about missing something or getting lost.  If you enjoy action RPGs to mostly see your party grow in terms of levels and skills and whatnot, then this game certainly shines in that area.  There are no real decisions to be made outside of what 3 characters out of the 6 you ultimately want in your party and how the storyline slightly changes based on this as well as how you want to shape your party through the various class changes your party undertakes during their journey.There is post game content in this version as well as all sorts of abilities and items that carry over in a new game+ mode (not to mention an ability that increases your exp gain by 300%) and you will have to play through the game at least 3 different times to get all of the achievements if that is your thing.  Overall I enjoyed the game and if you want a fairly stress free 30+ hours of beating up a bunch of adorable baddies while trying to figure out which classes you want to upgrade to next and which abilities to focus on, then this game might just scratch that itch.This game was worth the price I paid for it.

_childDocuments_.review: This remake is amazing, the level of detail that went into this game is jaw dropping. I love how fluid the combat system is, and how engaging each class feels. You can use a variety of builds with each character, and there are a bunch of different play styles you can experience. However, in my honest opinion, the game is far too easy for anyone to able to experience the full depth of the combat system. You can freely switch between characters at any point, which allows for some really dynamic ways of playing, however you really don't have to. Thankfully, there is a balance mod that exists (Google is your friend) which alleviates this a bit. Pros:- Fantastic OST, with the option to switch between classic and remake tracks- Great combat system, extremely fluid, engaging and fun- Fantastic visuals, fun costumes, and replay-ability - Pretty good post main story contentCons:- Game feels a bit like its holding your hand, even on the hardest difficulty (takes away from the great combat IMO)- God awful English voice acting...
_childDocuments_.name: Trials of Mana

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to play an RPG that was different from other RPGs I have played before. The fact that I can choose who my main character is, choose my party members, and the story changes based on my choice is really cool.I feel like this remake is so AAA 2020 modern that I am being spoon-fed gold. I like the graphic style. It's pretty and the characters and world are a bit whimsical. My friend complained that Japan was not producing interesting new jRPGs anymore and that they are just doing remakes. If the remakes are this good and superior, then I don't really feel it's a problem since there are already more games in existence than I could play in my lifetime. If they just choose amazing old games and improve them to this degree, then I will be blessed with more than I could ask for. The only thing is that I'm not a cool person who plays old game versions and I don't profit from nostalgia like this.The combat system is action-based and not turn-based. It's freaking cool. I love how I can customize characters by choosing their class progressions, abilities, and stat allocations. I also really appreciate that there is a respec feature for the stats and that classes choices can also be changed if I make a mistake (although it's much harder to change class and can only be done a limited number of times apparently due to needing items).The music is better than many games. It's better than Dragon Quest XI for sure (my opinion). There are some really cool tracks.The story is a bit wonky at times. Sometimes it's so corny or removed from logic that it breaks my suspension of disbelief but it has its moments. I wasn't looking for anything hardcore. I just wanted casual fun.Some people might complain that the game is too easy in terms of combat and story. Well, I do not mind that there are markers that tell me exactly where to go at all times. I often forget if I haven't played in a while. Sometimes I don't pay attention enough to RPG dialogue and miss what I'm supposed to do. I feel fine being treated like an idiot. _childDocuments_.review: An incredible remake of the original Seiken Densetsu 3 for SNES. The main thing about the original that kept me coming back and replaying it over and over were the various class paths and combinations, and the remake keeps that magic alive and amplifies it.The towns and wilderness areas are nearly identical in layout to the original, except that the designers have taken advantage of having three dimensions (and beautiful graphics) and have allowed those original maps to reach their full potential. As far as plot and flow of the game, it is almost shot-for-shot identical, even in the timing of the cutscenes and nearly all the dialog. As far as classes, they have kept the same light/dark class tree scheme and made it deeper and more nuanced by adding in ability trees and shared party abilities. The additions and liberties they've taken in no way take away from the original feel of the game. You can spend hours researching all the characters and finding the perfect combination of classes that amplify eachother. There is great freedom in designing your characters and your party. The 6 stats each grant their own progression of abilities allow for different play styles. The same exact class combination could be designed in a few different ways.The combat is great. The original game, unlike many other RPG's of its time, was live-action and not turn-based. Again Trials of Mana fully fleshes out this strength of the original in full 3D, with new combos and moves that make combat engaging and fun while not straying too far from the spirit of the original. The special abilities of enemies and bosses make movement very important; some boss fights are absolute chaos!And finally, this is just a... Well. Made. Game. It is simply well-crafted, well-designed, and solid. I mean that there are no bugs or glitches in sight, the controls are very responsive and everything flows very well. Entering and exiting combat is seamless. There are no weird clipping issues. Things just work. They always work as they should.And one negative point here: the voice acting is just... bad. At first it was jarring, but almost immediately I got caught up in simply playing the game and forgot all about it. There is too much good about this game for the voice acting to really matter!So obviously, I whole-heartedly recommend this to anyone who loved the original Seiken Densetsu 3. Looks like I've played 82 hours so far... oops.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall this remake is very satisfying to play. It expands and enhances the key gameplay elements from the original SNES release, but falls short in some areas. These shortcomings are not a dealbreaker by any means.Combat: This area was definitely the strongest suit of the original and it remains that way in the remake. The team at Square Enix has seamlessly brought the original ARPG style combat from the original and has enhanced it along the way. Each battle is exciting and feels well balanced. A lot of the annoyances (ex: undodgeable enemy moves, the treasure sequence at the end of some battles) have been done away with making it a much more fluid and satisfying experience. The AI system has been changed enough, however in some battles later in the game, I noticed my companions not doing too much, but often times this wasn't much of an issue. A lot of time in this game is spent in combat, so I'm glad they nailed this element. A+Story: Nothing really has changed here. 6 heroes are available for you to play. You form a party of 3 and the story develops depending on who you choose. While there are 6 characters, there are 3 story arcs. Pairs of characters will be involved in the same story arc. Duran and Angela, Kevin and Charlotte, and Riesz and Hawkeye. Exactly the type of story you would expect from a mid-90's video game. Peace is interrupted by someone's evil plot to take over the world and it is your duty to go thwart them and save the world. A new post-game story was added into the remake. This is the portion where it falls a bit short, but is by no means 'bad'. The content added is satisfying and expands a little on the backstory of each character, but the main antagonist doesn't seem very fleshed out. A.Sound Design: The remake music is incredible. I really think they did an excellent job bringing the original into a new age. Overall the sound is much cleaner, but it still retains all the charm of the original. Of course the option of using the original score is available. A win-win. A+Sound effects remain largely unchanged. Level-up sounds, item acquisitions, Vuscav's flute and Flammie's drum are both nearly identical to the original. The largest change here would have to be the battle sounds and enemy sounds. Those have been updated to fit the 2020 gaming scene quite nicely, aside from some potentially annoying sounds from particular enemies, but that doesn't happen too often. A+The voice acting...oh the voice acting. Atrocious. I have heard and read reviews that have said "It's not that bad", but I disagree wholeheartedly. The lines are delivered painstakingly awkwardly 99% of the time. It often sounds like a high schooler's final project more than a professional production. While the main cast is *bearable* at best, it's the side characters (shopkeepers, story NPCs) who are the main offenders. I often found myself imagining something completely different for a character. And then there's CHARLOTTE. Oh good lord Charlotte. She's supposed to be a cute and innocent kid. However, when I played the original, never did I think "Oh yea, she has an awful speech impediment. That'll make her cuter". Seriously. She doesn't sound like an endearing kid. She sounds like a 40 year-old woman who never got over her impediment nor did she seek help for it. God awful and I hate it. F.Graphics: Par for the course in terms of their recent remakes. Character models and enemy models are the stars here. They did a great job translating sprites into fully fleshed out 3D character models. All the charm of the cute (albeit sometimes deadly) enemies has been retained, and I think they look excellent. While the world retains the same feel, I do wish they were a bit more detailed. The transition to 3D is excellent, and it is very satisfying to revisit these familiar places in 3D and have them feel as you'd expect them to. The biggest shortcoming here are bland textures and bland interiors. While the SNES version wasn't exactly the most vibrant ever, I expected a bit more. Sometimes I found myself wanting the world to feel a bit more lived-in. Castle courtyards were often devoid of anything. Throne rooms were curiously bare. If more care was taken to detail the world, I think it could be really excellent. B+Mechanics: The item storage system has been done away with in favor of a single inventory, which is nice. Taking things out of storage felt like an unnecessary step to me in the original. The item cap is still 99 in your inventory. You are able to assign particular items to a ring menu which is available to you in-game. In battle you are still limited to 9 of any particular item per battle, so that hasn't changed. It feels largely the same as the original, with a few minor tweaks. The seed system has seen a few changes, mostly for the better. New seed variants have been added, which adds some new diversity. You are able to obtain item seeds, plant them in a pot at any inn, and it will reward you with a random item. Naturally, higher level seeds will yield better items, as well as a higher level pot. What I'm glad to see here though are the changes to ??? seeds. It used to be that ??? seeds would give you items to grant access to Class 3, but it would give you any item for all 6 characters. Now, the ??? seeds will give you only a narrower selection of class change items. For instance, if you picked the Light class 2, then the items you will get for that character from ??? seeds will only be items allowing you to change to Light-Light or Light-Dark. This makes hunting these items much more bearable. A very welcome change. A.Class System: This is the most unique system of this RPG, and in my opinion, it is the system that sets this game apart from all the rest. Each character has classes they can progress through and become stronger, gaining new attacks and abilities. From your base class, you can choose a Light class or a Dark class. From your Light class, you can then progress to a Light-Light class or a Light-Dark class. From your Dark class you can progress into a Dark-Dark or Dark-Light class. I somehow remember the class change system being more satisfying in the original. Perhaps it was because the experience in the original was scaled such that you were still a few levels under the requirement by the time you reached the first mana stone, which gave you the choice of grinding or not to get that class change before the upcoming boss. However, that isn't to say it isn't satisfying here. Not only does it net you a more powerful character, but it a new outfit as well, and who doesn't like cosmetics?? In the remake a new 4th class has been added and is only offered as Light or Dark (depending on which path you chose for Class 2). Another system that has been quite untouched and only enhanced. A+Overall: A. This game is very enjoyable and I am definitely not disappointed in what I got. I have finished my first playthrough and plan on going for 100% completion and beyond. As much as I hate the voice acting, it is still something I could soldier through because of all the other excellent qualities of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: A great remake for a great game, although not flawless. I compiled the items I wanted to highlight on bullets below for better clarity. Do bear in mind I'm halway through the game at the time of writing.-Overall comparison to the original: If you're one of those people feeling trauma over FFVIIR, rest assured that this game is extremely loyal to the original, at least up to what what current social standards allow (lookign at you, Sorceress class attack), the exception being the battle sytem, but we can all agree that the original's attack-retreat-weapon charged-attack cycle with screen freezing magic wouldn't fly beyond the SNES.In fact, one could argue that the game is loyal to a fault, as the weak points of the original, like the repeated instances of Golden Road walking and Heaven's Path climbing, or the fact they still didn't acknowledge your character broke a protective barrier and told no one about it. If there was a weak part in the story or pacing in the original, it'll still be there.- Graphics/presentation: If you're familiar with Atelier series, you'll find them oddly familiar. When you consider SquEnix's technical capabilities and resources, this is pretty much a budget title, which a price tag a bit above the budget title point, which is sure to have a lot of people on edge. The game, that considered, looks really nice, and is a beautiful reinterpretation of the original in a 3D environment, which included exploration and exploration bonuses to the mix. I saw a lot of people complain about "muted color palette", but I have no idea what they're talking about. The main issue you'll see is that sometimes textures will bump during cutscenes, suddenly loading into existence a few seconds after the cutscene starts. Not too much of an issue, but it's annoying on how eyecatching it is. Speaking of cutscenes, they all mostly work for their intended purpose, but don't expect anything too flashy or action packed. They also have this strange habit of trying to show the horizon, only to show up the total draw distance. Also, for reasons I can't figure out, while the compat does not look nor feel floaty, the class change cutscenes do...- Combat: Is much more improved than in the original, but still simple for the modern day standards. You knock down what can be CC'd and for the rest mash attack button until you need to dodge. I believe that the development team went for a way to make the original combat more dynamic, in which the prior game's "miss" message is now replaced by attacks actually failing to hit, and the much, MUCH needed removal of time freezing during spell effects. Additionally, the possibility to include certain spells on a quick menu is a huge QoL improvement when playing a caster class, making them more fluid.Unfortunately, as it is now, the game gives too many advantages to the player during combat. Characters are no longer slowed down while in battle, which coupled with 3D combat with a dodge mechanic, makes it possible for an experienced player to find themselves easily walking away from all damage. This is further emphatized by enemy skills, which take too long to cast/take effect, while also showing a very eye-catching orange indicator of the danger zone, like FFXIV. The game compensates this by dealing more damage to the player when caught, but still doesn't feel like it's enough for a hard mode. Bosses also have this "minigame" attack that deals large amounts of unavoidable damage if certain conditions are not met, but it basically revolves around a simple stat check to see if you're able to deal enough damage to something before something else triggers.- Classes/progression/customization: The game also allows much more character customization in battle, as the stats picked, which previously only served for marginal power increases and unlocking the new class spells, now provide additional bonuses you can equip to your characters, allowing to actually have a build. These boosts allow for more/better character combos than seen before, like adding Riesz's critical bonus to Kevin, or having Duran attract all enemy attention away from Angela. It also adds something to do with non casters before first class change, and imbues with personality to certain classes (Delvar, for example, can now go full lich mode and drain her own HP to empower spells, but also can get life from defeated enemies). Of course, some characters will be getting more than others with these changes. Angela, for example, has her spells spread across all stats, so despide you wanting to build INT for spell damage, you first need 2 points in WIS to even have the first spell, then 4 points in VIT if you want to use the second, then 6 points in LUK (of all things) if you want to use the third. That's 12 Job points to even have the basics at that point, so if you want to be up to date on things you can cast by class change, your actual free points to build outside the path are like 6. Another case is Riesz, who gets equipable passives to deal debuffs on crits on both her dark and light second classes, which is a great boon to complement light, and very redundant on dark. - Sound: The remixed themes are mostly improvements over the originals, with a few duds (sadly for me, one of those duds was High Tension Wire), but the sounds can be set between original and remaster at any point through the menu screen. Also the voice acting can be set between English and Japanese at meny screen, which is extremely important to have if you play certain characters. Simply put: Trials of Mana's English voice acting is now very good. There's some good cases, as Duran's rather solid, and Hawkeye's aimed hard to give him personality through a (somewhat forced) sarcastic tone; but then you find nightmares like Charlotte's really, REAAAALLY forcing her way through that baby speak, and Riesz's sounds like someone gave her the script with no context and said "just read it quick, so we can end the record early and go to lunch" (which is made even more hilarious by the contrast with Isabella's, who milked the evil performance for all it's worth). Switching to Japanese when not understanding the language is a hindrance, as there's a couple quotes like victory comments or item purchases which are not subtitled and will fly past you, but still recommended as the voice quality is overall better (or still bad, but the fact you can understand the difference makes it seem better, which is ultimately the same thing), and is likely the only way Charlotte will ever be tolerable.All things considered, the game is very enjoyable. It's accessible to new players with it's modern day amenities, but will still let the nostalgia kick in for veteran players of the original. The only parties to whom I wouldn't recomment the game are experienced ARPG players who are only looking for a challenge, as the battle system is too lenient even on hard.

_childDocuments_.review: I finished my first playthrough of the game, notably not going to be my last (on Hard, did entire postgame and Black Rabite), and I just want to say that for old-school fans of the game this remake delivers in a lot of ways.  Several issues from the base game are fixed including: actual viability for the "bad" classes because of passive abilities unique to each class, generally improved combat flow and AI since many animations are faster or don't pause the entire game anymore, elimination of most problematic glitches and useless abilities/stats, and removal of bosses effectively cheating and spamming their abilities in response to yours.  This game is good, but it's far from perfect.Upon closer examination you can tell they didn't put their S team or even their A team on this: most of the graphics are mediocre to poor, some of the remixed music falls very flat, the Japanese VAs are mostly good but the English VAs are roundly D-tier terrible, a lot of aspects of the combat are weak and unpolished (especially the lock-on camera's behavior and the lack of real hitpause on strong attacks), and very little was actually added to the game in terms of sidequests or gameplay variety.  It's obvious Squeenix puts all their money into FF and DQ, and didn't invest even 1/10th of that budget into this game.  It would be awesome if we actually got a big budget sequel in the future, but I don't think Square will give us that even if this game sells very well.If you've never played Seiken Densetsu 3, I don't actually know if you will like this game.  In all mana games (and several other ARPGs) the core combat never really changes.  If you hate the combat when your characters only have one spell, you aren't going to magically like it after they have 8 spells.  I'd play at least to the re-taking of Laurent before you make any real judgments on the game though, as that includes good examples of some of the best bosses in the game and is where you really start using abilities from your first class promotion.  I like the game in spite of its shortcomings.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a loaded review, because the original was one of the first games I ever played myself and beat (downloaded Neill Corlett and Lina's OG v1.0 romhack as a nine year old and hammered it out on snes9x...). So lots of fond memories, but I can still recommend it to anyone who wants a taste of how the best games of the 90s felt.The story is standard JRPG fare but executed well, and it's hard to say 'standard' when the original game pioneered many of the tropes. There are three main stories and six characters, and they're given a lot more characterization in this remake than they had in the original. The voices add a lot, but the script is still mostly that of the original game, so the cutscenes take a while. While there are mature elements, the story is still that of a child's journey of growth, and clear care was taken to retell this child's story without adding tongue in cheek nonsense or attempting to 'age up' or go 'hardcore'.The graphics  One obvious design decision made was to try to recreate the look and feel of SNES era RPGs and retain the color palette, so everything is bright and cheerful and rendered in a stylized low-poly way. This looks pretty good most of the time but the seams show when there are long range shots or horizons in view. To a modern gamer, a lot of the graphics will seem sort of artificially retro-faux, but I can say it hits the feel of the original game. Problem is, the original game had some of the best pixel spritework ever made, and the 3d here is only 'good'. A lot of the scenes do incorporate a lot of 2d artwork, which is excellent - Hiro Isono is homaged in much of the art, including the launch menu. The combat system is excellent, and a definite improvement over the original. The skill system creates a lot more room for customization and growth than the old system, and the stats actually work (in the original game, several stats and abilities were completely broken and didn't work at all, ex. 'evasion'). The combat system is definitely improved over 'hit 4 times and cast your level 1 special'.The music is absolutely outstanding. Hiroki Kikuta was brought back to oversee the remixes and most are as good if not better than the originals. Modern gamers will ding the soundtracks for being repetitive (most songs are on ~1 minute loops, playing the same pattern twice followed by a segue), but Kikuta made the most of the limited space he had to work with on the SNES cart and the remixes are overall excellent renditions. A strong recommendation. The only thing this is missing is local co-op multiplayer, but I really hope that comes in an update or mod going forward.

_childDocuments_.review: (X-posted to my wordpress blog, Gunlord500) Very good remake of the old Secret of Mana/Seiken Densetsu 3 game I loved as a kid playing on my best friend's emulator. It's a pretty simple ARPG with just normal attacks and power attacks, which you can change into combos as you unlock better classes. There are 6 different characters each with 6 different class changes, plus 2 endgame super classes, and since you can only choose 3 characters for your party there's a looooot of replay value. They added in a lot of nice stuff Seiken Densetsu 3 didn't have, even aside from turning it 3d, like the aforementioned endgame super classes (which SD3 didn't have), which themselves are part of a post-game extra epilogue that's brand new and references some of the other Mana games.The plot is essentially unchanged from the original SD3, again aside from the added epilogue, and it's not really that great. Also, the English voice acting is a little bad, especially Charlotte, one of the main characters XD The game is also pretty easy overall, even on the hardest difficulty, though there's another postgame super difficulty that's much harder. It's still no Sekiro though, haha. That's good, actually, because this is definitely a game for young people: There's no blood, graphic death, or sexual content aside from the late-game classes for female characters having bikini armor lol. The plot is also simple, not grim or political like Tactics Ogre, just a standard "save the world with the power of friendship!" story. So in that sense it's really good not just as a remake but as an intro to ARPGs for youngsters! It's still fun for adults too, ofc; I enjoyed it a lot again because of the class choices and also the excellent soundtrack. I recommend this with no reservations!

_childDocuments_.review: If you ever played Seiken Densetsu 3, you need to play this. Its probably the most perfect and faithful remake of a game I have played. All of the dialogue from the original is nearly recreated with a bunch of new stuff added for the paired combo heroes (Angela/Duran Hawkeye/Rieze Kevin/Charlotte) and the dialogue is not as cut and pasted as the original, your hero choice really feels unique in the story. The voice acting is a little corny at times, but the dialogue has always been corny. Its great for everyone of any age to play.The difficulty is a bit easy, so I suggest playing strictly on Hard. I did chose a bit of a gamey team though (My first ever team in the original was Angela main with Duran second and Hawkeye third member so I recreated that here). Angela has been insanely ramped up in strength from the original, which i'm happy with since she has always been my favorite character. I did Magus/Leige/Nightblade and focused on a magic damage team with incredible healing from Duran. I will be playing again very soon with Kevin/Charlotte/Rieze next time :D

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: I don't recommend the game. The devs did a great job remaking this classic with modern advances, but that creates a problem of combat challenge and balancing as most of that in the old game derived from the archaic technology of the SNES, which is not present & makes the combat dull.So a lot of people were pretty hyped over this game, the remake of Seiken Densetsu 3. I finally bought it during the sale & I wish I hadn't. Don't buy 30 Euro games often & this was basically money down the drain. But it happens. I thought I'd lay out my problems with it to inform you lot. First off, while there are a few legitimate problems with this that they introduced new problems, I don't actually blame the developers for the end state too much, because honestly most of these problems are related to the original game. This remake is a faithful remake to the original as far as is possible, but updated. In order to fix a version with far more artistic liberties needed to be taken. That said, let's get to it. Starting out everything feels amazing, the combat is sharp and responsive, the character moves well, everything feels like a remake needs to be. As you continue on though problems in the gameplay starts appearing, mostly how the combat is way too easy. Even if you take up the difficulty, it doesn't change much. Initially this applies to both regular enemies and bosses. Eventually though the bosses do become quite difficult, a bit more on that later, but it leads to a very lopsided situation where you slice through most regular enemies (including some damn difficult ones in the original) like butter & struggling like hell with the bosses that the original enemies in no way have prepared you to fight. That said, I can't point to anything being done wrong. The enemies all act like they did in the original, every move fits with what they did then. Some of them even hit hard. The problem is that most of the difficulty of the original (I went back and replayed a bit just to check) arose from the archaic controls of the SNES. It had a bunch of difficulties, but essentially they could not create as fluid of a system as they obviously wanted. This has been done in the remake, but that removes the main difficulty issue. More in a bit.A few problems introduced. The class-change or more importantly skill gain system has been revamped. Now instead of every character and class having different caps for all different stats (as makes sense with the classes) every class caps out at the same stat ceiling, but means a bit different to all characters. The healer for me was no problem, she capped out I'd increase her to not be useless when she isn't casting magic, but my pure physical fighter (dark Kevin) & Magic-user (Angela) caused problems to me. They removed agility as a stat and now you are yourself responsible for dodging. The issue with this is once you cap out strength & stamina (again he has no increased ceiling) there isn't anything to do with extra points. The game (like the old one) never really explains what does what, but all that remains (outside of intelligence which obviously not) is spirit & luck. Luck is always a dump stat, but I checked some of the old guides and they said it applies to opening chest, but even if it applies a bit to things like criticals it isn't an essential stat. Spirit the same, it has a few nice abilities, but as a stat he lacked any ability to actually use it with. The Magic-user has the opposite problem. In the old game, you unlocked all spells by finding the spirits & getting the class-changes. That is still true now, but you also need to have the right stats, which is not just related to the magic stats (intelligence & spirit), the sorceress needs to (nearly) max out EVERY STAT & there are not enough points to do so without hitting the limit for class gain, which often leads to fights where in the original you would have spells that well have a nice weakness against the opponent - now you might not, I don't think I ever did. They also removed the wind elemental's spell "scan" which told you not just HP (which is represented here), but also what elements they were weak against, which is very needed because until the late game where you fight the God Beasts (they renamed it to something I can't remember) most bosses do not have obvious weaknesses. And since they are also spongy, you get a problem of trying to kill them with a rusty spoon.So that's a pretty crap new system, but honestly it's managable. The basic problem is that the combat feels too easy & is actually pretty annoying because you can't go more than a few meters without having to fight so you can't really avoid it. But again, it's not like the combat system isn't what the old one made with more advanced technology would look like, the issue is simply that the old difficulty was based a lot in the old SNES controls & updating it would need to take some artistic liberties. As for quality of life improvements, they added 1, more should have been added, especially having to treck back to the beach while gathering the spirits every time without anything you can use to take it back, but the one they added is pretty cool, if you make it that far. It's an item chest that will level up and increase both drop rate & value of seeds. Now, this is minor, except for your second class change you need to get ??? seeds that drop in one area really rarely & has a random chance of getting the specific item you need for the specific charactrer to level up to the specific class you have in mind, so that's cool. The story & characters feels pretty good actually. I think some rewriting (there are a few touches, but not much) could have benefitted it, but it is the old one. Whether that holds up again is another issue, but it does the job. So in summation, I do not recommend the game, despite (with only my gripe with the stat & skill-gain system) them having done a fantastic job of updating the old game with modern advances, because that removes much of the challenge & engagement with the combat system & it needed more.

_childDocuments_.review: Been a fan of the original Seiken Densetsu for SNES since I played the fan translation rom when I was a little kid, this game is a remake of the then only japan released entry in the series, and manages to be an excellent remake.The game is an Action RPG, you choose 3 characters to make your team, the first one being your lead in the story you chose, with the possibility of your second one being your co protagonist depending if you selected a character who shares the same villain as your protagonist, this in itself adds replayability as there is 3 different possible final bosses.The battle system has been completaly reworked from the original, which although was excellent for it's time on the SNES it was held back by the limitations of the system, this game manages to reinvent the combat and make something exciting and dynamic, you start with a couple of basic combos, but as you recruit the other 2 characters in your team and get magic abilities the game develops into something much more intricate, you can also upgrade your class and get a new combos by each class upgrade the fighting is very addicting and satisfying, it's the game's strongest asset.The story of the game is pretty much 1:1 to the original game, only difference being the presentation, so if you know the story of the original SNES version, you will be happy to know that nothing has changed.The OST has been remastered from the original, but instead of going into a different direction, like the Secret of Mana Remake, it goes for simply remaking the tracks with newer intruments, keeping the original feeling of the songs untouched,   the work put into the remastered music is amazing and you can tell they cared and respected the original music, if you're still not happy with the remastered music, there is an in-game option to listen to the original SNES tracks, hurray for options!Graphics are very pretty, for a budget game, they managed to capture the original artstyle of SNES game into 3D, keeping even color palettes for enviroments and enemy designs transitioning seamlessly to 3D.The only downside I can name is that the english voice acting is a big mixed bag, you might like it or not, you can tell this is where the budget suffered the most, but there is a couple of characters that manage to do a pretty decent job with the little direction they were probably given, there is the japanese dub voice option if you'd rather listen to that.Character animation in the cutscenes might be a bit stiff and unexpressive, however they do enough to tell the story, this was clearly another hit from the low budget nature of the game.The developers had stated that first and foremost they focused on making an enjoyable single player experience and they nailed it in the end, even with it's shortcomings, this manages to be one of the best remakes, in my opinion, of all time.If you're a fan of the original SNES game, or an action RPG fan, this is definitely a big recommendation from me, hopefully you will enjoy this game as much as I did.

_childDocuments_.review: 100%'d the game and my opinion of the game didn't improve.Let's start with what i think a few of the problems with this remake are coming from: The original...Clearly basking in the success of Seiken Densetsu 2 (What we know as Secret of Mana) the devs were prolly like: let's make a sequel and let's make it bigger! The devs decided they should up the playable character count from 3 to 6.And although i want to commend this choice, i cannot.Mainly because with all the things the game tries to do with these characters, the game suffers from this choice quite a bit.And since the remake uses the same concept, you get a small butterfly effect.Since EACH character has their own story, the game ends up trying to tell a story that is too big for it's own size and due to this the 6 individual stories feel like they are shoehorned together to make a whole, which in the end does not pan out nicely because the goals of the 6 characters do not properly meet up at the end of the game.What seems to not help the story either is that the game seems to suffer from a less then perfect translation, this could be me but i've noticed a few things off about both the english text and voices.The text and English voiceovers match eachother word for word, but i'm going to leave that out of this mention for a bit longer because it doesn't matter with what i'm about to say first.I've had several conversations where the next "objective" is mentioned, not just once, but up to 3 or more times in the timespan of a few lines of dialogue and to me this feels as if the devs/translators are worried we as players would lose track or they think we are stupid or something.What doesn't help either in this regard is that you cannot go for 3 fights without either Faerie or one of your characters making some kind of comment on what your current objective is, over and over and over again to the point where you want to completely turn off the voices altogether.That brings my rant to the English Voiceovers, which are downright horrible in a multitude of places.Certain conversations sound and progress so ackwardly you'd think the voice actors were given ZERO background information on what the scenario of their conversations are about, this leads to ackward tone changes, weird pauses and horrendous punctuation.If it was just that, it wouldn't be so bad, but it gets a tad worse:There is a small cutscene where a couple of faeries are flying away from the mana tree near the start of the game.The Faeries are supposed to sound tired and exhausted, but the sounds i heard would have been more at place behind a closed bedroom door.And no it wasn't just me hearing this, My wife was reading a book and reacted to them as well and said that if she didn't know any better she'd think i was playing an Adult game.The Characters themselves are bit of a mixed bag, i picked Duran as my main character for my first playthrough and it took him less then an hour to piss me offHe want's to get stronger so he can defeat a certain enemy, but he doesn't want to put ANY effort into it whatsoever.Then i met Charlotte, my 2nd character, the game claims her to be 15 years old, but talks as if she's still in kindergarten, heck my 4 Year old son has better pronounciation then she does... (i know it's a personality, but i would have done it differently)And last but not least: Angela, owh BOY...Angela is pure fan-service, skimpy clothing and an attitude to match, Multiple mentions on how "sexy" she is in dialogue and what's the first thing she does when i meet her? Abuse her looks to help the party out of a tight spot...Then we get to the following cutscene and here stuff goes wrong some more, where Angela tells her story of how she got there etc (The game even tells you she told EVERY DETAIL) only for Duran to completely IGNORE almost everything of what she's told to berate her for coming from the same kingdom as the Jerk he's chasing, having to have Angela YET AGAIN tell Duran why she's not in her own kingdom anymore...I am not sure if this is the translation, the devs trying to be funny or just a plain plothole that was overlooked, but it wasn't charming.I've got not much to say about the graphics in the game. They fit the style of the game nicely, but i did notice a few tiny clipping issues and sometimes the textures take too long to stream which makes stuff looks blurry and this even happens with the game on an M.2 SSD which is just plain bad... The Combat is a mixed bag too, where in the original (and in Secret of mana) you had to "time" your attacks to maximize damage, Trials of Mana throws that out of the window and lets you spam attack your enemies to death without any penalty whatsoever.The first few bosses were facerolled by pure buttonmashing, didn't even need to do much aside from a dodgeroll here or there.Then in other instances, mobs become damage sponges and it takes way too long to kill them even with magic and summons.Speaking of which, your combat options at the start are quite limited and just plain leveling your characters doesn't help this much.The game hints at you every time that you obtain an elemental that you can use them for a variety of spells, providing you put points into the respective skill.What the game fails to explain is that you have to progress further into the game before you can actually do this. Last but not least is the sound and music, which is a trip down nostalgia alley.I can't really fault the devs for doing the same thing the devs of the original did in the past: Reuse the same music for 2 games, but in this day and age it just feels lazy...Don't get me wrong, i TRIED REALLY HARD to love this game, but in the end i wasn't able to love it as much as i wanted and hoped for, i hope Square does better with Visions of Mana because this game just struck too many nerves...

_childDocuments_.review: If you've ever played this on a SNES emulator, you need to play the remake. +Is a faithful remake to the original+Power fantasy for each class is demonstrated through a deep skills/perks system+Discovering chain abilities and lil cactus spots provide meaningful rewards for exploration and engagement with the world+Critical hits work+It's like a Candy Land RPG-The story looks even worse in 2020-It would have been cool to see more RPG mechanics introduced to differentiate repeat playthroughs (if thief could pick locks, fighter could break stuff to create a path, mages could make use of magic things throughout the world.. etc)-Some of the English voice acting is a crime against nature-New Game+ could have been done better

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the original game's availability on the SNES in the U.S., I swear I tried this game or something similar when I was younger. Either way, this remake is the fun action-adventure detour I needed right now.It has a few quirks, and its adaptation from being a classic SNES game really shows--things that would have been normal and convincing on that platform versus in a fully 3D title with modern-day graphics feel awkward and simplistic, but that's exactly what they were going for here, as these were intentional choices for a respectable remake, and I would probably hope for the same treatment if something like A Link to the Past was remade like this.I'm having fun with it, and if you need a small-medium-sized action RPG to fill in the gaps between other larger titles this year, I recommend trying the Demo and buying it if you like it!

_childDocuments_.review: *DIsclaimer* I have never played or seen the original Trials of Mana.So this game is pretty average all things considered but I found myself enjoying the game the entire way through. The Music is phenomenal for one and from what I've heard from listening to the original BGM it stays true to it's source material while creating a great modern take on the original score. The Graphics are beautiful, not on the same level of Final Fantasy VII Remake but still good in their own right. The gameplay during combat is similar to Dynasty Warriors, while during exploration it's a combo of Ys VIII and Dragon Quest XI. The story is okay but is marred by It needing to cater to 6 different characters with a different combination of the 6 being in a party of 3 with 1 being considered the "Main Character". This can be extended to the voice acting as well with many lines being delivered very generic and flat to accommodate for this gameplay decision leading the dramatic parts of the story to having very little impact. At $50 there is a lot of game here but buyer beware I would check out the demo to see if you can stick through the repetitive combat system and the bad VO the game has. Not speaking critically I love this game personally, the skills are flashy and there is a lot of ways to build your characters with many different classes for each to pick from. These 2 features alone give me great replay value so I will definitely be picking this game up from time to time.

Barry-from-Resident-Evil-1 levels of bad. The story is your most basic fantasy experience. Nobody is interesting enough to even slightly become invested in.There is just nothing to do outside of the main story. You can hunt down a little cactus man but I don't really see why. He gave me bonuses like 10% cheaper merchants, then 20% cheaper merchants but money was always extremely abundant. These discounts just weren't necessary or beneficial to me.I'm in the last few hours of the game now, around level 60 and its just laughably easy. I recommend playing on Hard just to get more out of it. I played on Normal. I never applied buffs or used any offense/defense items. I just haven't needed to. No deaths so far.I'd recommend this game on sale for maybe $10. There just isn't a lot to the game to justify the $40 I spent. Dungeons are laughably small. Puzzles are non-existent. _childDocuments_.review: The story is fairly uninteresting.The graphics are nice.The gameplay isn't that exciting or deep.I really like class change giving new costumes. I like some of the RPG elements, but they're not super in-depth. I like some the voice acting. And a few jokes landed decently.Overall. If you don't have nostalgia, I don't think this is a game you need to play.
