_childDocuments_.review: I will break this review in 3 parts, one for the people who never played or maybe never heard about this game to give it some context, then what I thought exclusively of this one as a stand alone, and then comparisons to the original (light spoilers ahead).1. About Seiken Densetsu 3 / Trials of Mana.This game was already on the works even before Sword of Mana, the original game in the Seiken Densetsu series was ported over to the west with the name Final Fantasy Adventure, for the Gameboy. Secret of Mana came later for the SNES, and somewhere along that timeframe while working on Secret of Mana, this game was being conceived slowly. This game came out originally for the SNES in 1995, and it never made it to the west (as a stand alone) due to arriving so late into the SNES lifespan it was not considered a wise move. This game would not be officially localized until 2019 with Collection of Mana. Fan translations and emulators were how non japanese speakers experienced this game. It... has a lot of flaws, which I will point out on part 3, at least to compare what the game needed improving and what did improve with this game. This game was originally designed to be a CD-ROM game, but when the Nintendo and Sony collaboration for a disk console didn't really work out, this game had to be hurriedly fit into a cartridge or probably would be scrapped for good. There were a lot of systems on the game that felt really barebones, and I do not doubt software limitations were a huge part on why. That is the context for the original, this game, came out of nowhere, 2019 we get hit with a double whammy, not only the game is being localized and released officially, it's also being remade. The game, as a stand alone, is solid. But you should not expect very deep action combat, complex combos or anything of the sort. It's a simple game, and you should come with the expectations for one, overall I found it very enjoyable, it did feel like a completely new experience even from the perspective of a veteran player. My advice if you're in the fence is simply play the demo, you can play a part of the game, test out every character if you feel like (although, not a lot, you can only play so much) and after the demo ends you actually keep the progress if you do buy the game. It's a fantastic demo model and there's no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, you just get to play a bit of the game, see if you like what you see and get out before wasting your time if you do not. If you play the demo be advised that if you expect the combat to really get a lot more complex than what you get, it does but not by a large amount, for the gameplay you get what you see.2. About this product itselfThis remake takes the top down rpg and turns it into a fully 3D action game that feels fast and satisfying. The tutorials lie a bit to you however, as they promise you can pick your companions moves and other stuff, the options you have are very very basic, and while the AI is no doubt a better partner on this than the original, their ability to do more can sometimes get on your way, but I'll get to that more on part 3. Aside from the fact that I wished I could better control the AI behaviour, the game (I have only beaten the main story, there is actually bonus content original to this game) was fairly easy. Because of some changes some bosses that were hard on the original were pathetically easy on this, and some that were pushovers on the original were very annoying in this. The main issue comes from enemies that spam AoE moves that can hit your entire party, dodging is very very easy, however getting hit can combo you to death when aoe overlaps, and the AI is very very bad at dealing with that as well, at some fights I found myself not keeping them alive and just beating the boss myself. If you're a very good player, switching characters is near instant and you can micro each one, but I doubt that unless you're a speedrunner of sorts you'll get this deep into the combat, as it is simply not necessary to beat the game. (I played on hard)If you want a challenge, try skipping most fights you really just don't need to fight once you got the things leveled you want. The game is already not that hard, if you overgrind it'll be easier. But again, this is an RPG and you're free to play it as you like, it is just a suggestion to those that want some more adrenaline.3. Compared to the originalIt's very very good. There are some complains like the AI, for instance Charlotte always learns offensive magic on class 2, and if you set her on anything but pure healer mode she'll want to cast spells if you have her to use MP, and you can't tell her to just use MP for healing, which is a bit odd, but again in the original you didn't tell her anything, the npcs walked around and hit stuff, you had to make them do everything else manually. Also on the original, most spells and actions froze the game action, played an animation and you just got hit, this game nearly everything can be dodged, there are a few things you have to break with DPS, but the dodge button is very powerful, there are lots of I-frames and since range indicators show up it's hard to get hit unless you simply don't care. Of course to balance this, healing items are overall more expensive (poto oils were OP anyway, so I will 100% agree) but they're also overall stronger because the HP pool has increased significantly. (I beat the game last month with near 600 HP on the original, this one my characters were all near 1000). You will however, if you get hit, more easily die than in the original, in the original you could very effectively tank and spank, because honestly what would you do? You couldn't dodge spells, so you had to. In here you have much much more control of the battle. Also, not everything that breathes will counter player spells anymore with undodgable screen wide attacks. Thank god, Angela is actually more fun to play (didn't beat the story with her but I did play a bit of her story.)Another very large change on this remake is the level curve. I never stopped to grind anywhere either on the original or here, I at best fought whatever was on my way as I explore and advance, but going back and forth, I didn't do that. In the original, once you reach the first Mana Stone, you're about level 11-13. In this game you can actually change your class on the first stone (level 18). That's crazy, but needed. On the original you get to your final class so late that basically all the traits like being able to cast elemental weapons on your party are useless and the only things that matter are how good the skills you will learn will be against the final set of bosses. So that's a really big positive. Overall, some things they changed might leave a sour taste in your mouth if you really liked them in the original, but I found myself enjoying pretty much everything they changed, and what they kept was just made better. The abilities are a very very cool concept, albeit simple. This game is definitely worth the purchase if you enjoyed the original. The game ran very well on my low spec laptop (with some popping issues here and there, some freezes sometimes, but only in some cutscenes and loading screens, the game itself ran without any slowdown or anything) and I can't say I regret the purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: Where do I even begin?Somewhere in the world, on a late Sunday afternoon during the early 2010s, you're scouring the internet for obscure Japanese RPGs that had yet to touch western soil. Having been already baptized by the much of the premiere JRPGs offerings that were available in North America at the time, such as Dragon Quest VIII and Persona 4, you yearn for more. You dive into Let's Plays of 90s SNES RPGs on YouTube that were highly revered on the other side of the pacific. Titles such as Terranigma, Treasure of the Rudras, and Shin Megami Tensei II start to occupy your headspace with intrigue and excitement. But all of a sudden, you come across a game, but not just any game, a successor to one of the most beloved RPGs of the SNES era, and it's called Seiken Densetsu 3 (now known as Trials of Mana)You look into the game's offerings, and you discover a robust class system stuffed with elemental class skills, power ups, special attacks, summons, and more. You discover a bright, colorful world crafted from scratch with beastmen, humans, faeries, gnomes, and other races that occupy the land. And the soundtrack! Some of these tracks would suddenly pop up in your head for years! You could listen to  Left-Handed Wolf and Swivel for ages without ever getting bored. You get the game. You never actually finish it: because you're so fascinated with the class and party system, which makes you play the first half of the game over and over again, seeing the overarching story  through multiple perspectives. Angela's hotheadedness, Hawkeye's silver tongue, the innocence of Charlotte.. you're fascinated by how they each interact with the world in their own unique way. The years pass on, and you begin to wonder why Square Enix hadn't revisited this game. A game filled with so much color, character, customization, personality, and a surprising amount of responsiveness for an SNES era action game.But then one day, Square Enix announces Collection of Mana, with Seiken Densetsu 3 (again, Trials of Mana..) being included...Afterwards, Secret of Mana Remake, it's predecessor, is released.You begin to wonder: there's no way they could...But then they did.When this game was announced, Trials of Mana, I almost couldn't believe what I was seeing. A lost gem of the Square Enix archives, finally getting the true appreciation that it deserves. The original score kept intact, with a brand new remade soundtrack that's fitting for a fresh face lift. A new 3D perspective, with a refined take on abilities, skills, and magic. Smoother action, verticality, brand new cutscenes, new special post-game classes. They took the original game, and expanded it in such a way that made it more accessible, more beautiful, and most important of all, more fun.This is about as campy as it gets for JRPGs, and it's a perfect entry point for anyone that's new to the genre. There's just so much customization and replayability with the narrative and the class system; a single play through won't be enough to satiate your cravings for sure. The story might not be the most philosophical or the most striking, but it merely serves as a vehicle to add context to the world that they had crafted. One of Square Enix's best offerings from the past decade. If you're on the fence, don't wait any longer, because this game is even worth it at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: *** Spoiler Free Review ***TLDR : Trials of Mana is a enjoyable game and a fun time overall. However It is not worth 50$, nor the 90%+ rating it got (at the time this review was written) . It's a great AA game worth 25$ and a 80-90% rating rather.// OVERALL //Secret of Mana was one of my favortie rpg (and the one that started my rpg journey twenty years ago), so it has a special place in my heart. Unfortunately, I couldn't play Secret of Mana 2 at the time since it was a japanese release only, so it was great Square Enix did a remake and I bought the game in a heartbeat.The game itself has "two games" in it : the original story/rpg it's based off (first playthrough basically), and  the new game plus mode, which makes it less a rpg and more a beat'em up/hack'n slash type of title (where you'll skip the story only to focus on beating bosses, unlocking new abilities/items and learning boss mechanics/tactics).Depending on how you want to play the game, it's a middle to long game. I don't want to spoil the length of the game by giving the hours it takes to beat, but let's say it's somewhere in the 15 to 25 hour range for the first playthrough. If you want to tackle harder difficulties and unlock additional endings however, it will bring you easily in the 50+ hours range, so the game has ood length and replayability.First playthrough, the game is a bit easy, even on hard mode. The real challenge is in new game+ with the new difficulties mode and that's where the game starts to be really interesting combat wise. Bascially the hard mode in normal game is just a normal difficulty. // COMBAT AND TEAM BUILDING //The combat remake is pretty nice overall : it's smooth, action based but also involves some tactics on harder difficulties.It is in between a beat'em up and tactical/rpg, depending on how you want to play it and the difficulty level or your main character. I liked it overall and there's plenty of replayability because of all the various classes and synergies to create between members.The combat mechanics are rather basic, it's there and impactful but not too deep neither. Same goes for boss mechanics, they're well designed but sometimes feel a bit like a drag and the precision of signaling and other mechanics is not high level per say. It's there but it's not an esport neither...The classes and the team building is great too, lots of strategies to play around with, for those who enjoy theory crafting, it's pretty good. There are 4 classes per character, and 6 characters to choose from to build your team of 3.// STORY //The story is basic/dull and very linear, but still enjoyable overall. Although the english voice acting definitely butchers the title...Eventhough I'm not into japanese voice and so on while playing my games, I had to switch it on at some point. It is really bad and immersion breaking and one is game's big CON. The japanese voices (from what I can tell, I don't speak japanese) had overall a better feel. The emotions seem to better fit the dialog subtitles. The experience was way better after switching to japanese, and I wish I had done it earlier, the experience would have been much better.// GRAPHICS and ENVIRONMENT //Graphics/character designs and animations are a strong point. The way the party progress visually, moves around and look just feels good and smooth.The world is beautiful/charming and well designed. It's instanced/non open world, but it doesn't feel limiting/claustrophobic.The game is performance friendly, you'll hit 50+ fps even on low/medium computers no problem (had 60+ fps with a GTX760).// MUSIC //Close to the orginal, it's awesome and typcial jrpg iconic SNES music.// FINAL WORDS //Trials of Mana is a good time, whether for nostalgia or as a newcomer, Square Enix did a good job and brought something new as well with the new combat system and game modes/challenges. I definitely recommend it at 25$ or less to any rpg fans, especially jrpg and action/rpg enthusiasts.

_childDocuments_.review: WARNING! Game time does not represent my total play time, I completed the game on Playstation 4 before grabbing the Steam version as well.                                                                               A blast from the pastIn September 1995 a little game called Seiken Densetsu 3 was released in Japan,it was another entry in the Mana series. A series composed of only 2 other games,Final Fantasy Adventure and Secret of Mana. During the months leading up to Trials of Mana's release,we were teased via video game magasines its release,it promised advanced visuals(for the time),branching story paths and a lot of incredible things that seemed impossible at the time. Sadly,it remained locked to Japan,until fans decided to taker matters into their own hands and release a fan translation. It is only 22 years later that we finally got it through the Collection of Mana on Nintendo Switch. Featuring an official translation for the very first time and with the added bonus of portability. And at the same time,we were also promised Trials of Mana's remake,which is the topic of this review. So let's get to it!Trials of Mana is an action oriented RPG featuring 6 characters each with their unique abilities and gameplay styles,. Each character has its own backstory and its own unique abilities,the main story is divided in three different paths that will change depending on who was chosen as the main character of your team. Each team consist of 3 characters and is highly customizable thanks to the class system. The class system has you changing classes as soon as the player meets certain requirements. Once at level 18(with no other requirements than the required level),the players can chose the light or dark path,both offering different classes with advantages and disadvantages. At level 38 and only after players have aquired certain items,they can chose  between two new classes. And finally,a final and ultimate class can be unlocked via the new exclusive content added in the remake.Speaking of content,this is an excellent moment to segway into this particular topic. In terms of content this game is very loyal to the source material,the same amount of dungeons,bosses and vistas to visit. What changed,however,is that the developpers added a whole new epilogue section,it isn't extremely long so it doesn't overstay its welcome and can be quite enjoyable if you enjoyed the base game,but to be quite frank,they could have made this so much more than it is. However the game feels complete as it is with its 00+ hours of gameplay separated in three different playthroughs resulting in different endings. Keep in mind that this is definitely a product of its time,this game coming straight from the 90's.Speaking of coming from the 90's,they have remade this game with a lot of care and it shows,everything is recognizable from the world itself to the music and gameplay style. Each and every towns have been rendered in full 3D and feature the exact same geographical locations to them,if on the Super Nintendo version a shop was on a little elevation,it will also be in the exact same position on the 3D map. This makes it so people who have played the original will have no problems at all getting their bearings around. Every single location in the game has been beautifully remade in 3D and with care and love rarely seen with remakes. The same can be said about the music in this game,every single song in the OST  has been beautifully arranged and feature added melodies or instruments making the song even more beautiful than in the original version. You can tell that a soundtrack is classic when 20 years later its as good as it originally was.I guess that the last thing that should be talked about is the gameplay itself,now this is where the biggest changes were made for sure. In the original game,characters were moved in a 2d environement from a top down view quite akin to The Legend of Zelda,the system was a weird mix between action and turn based because every characters had their turn all while moving around in real time. You had no dodge options and spells stopped the action so they could be performed with no way of avoiding the damage.In the remake,they added a dodge option,made it so light and heavy attacks could be done,added combos and made the special attacks far more impressive than they used to be. This all works incredibly well in the context of a remade 3D game and manages to retain the feel of the original.All in all this is an exceptional remake and one that should set the standard for what a remake should be.

_childDocuments_.review: JRPGs are something I want to like, but which are very hit-or-miss for me. The stories and/or characters in JRPGs often don't resonate well with me, the gameplay has some very peculiar design choices even when those choices change something arguably for the worse even if what was changed had worked well in past entries in series, they're too grindy, and the games just feel like they take too long to finish for the amount of story and gameplay variety involved. I am pleased to say that very few of these things were an issue for me with Trials of Mana.In Trials of Mana, you select a team of three characters from a pool of six, and can have any one of them be your main/starting character. You can switch between them with the press of a button once you've obtained the other characters, and it's very smoothly done. On that note, all the controls were quite slick and I have no complaints at all about them. Once you've picked your characters, you start in the role of the main character you chose, and he or she has his/her own starting area and scenes. Whomever you picked to start the game as, you will rather quickly find yourself at the same starting town as anyone else you would have picked, and from there, the game and story is largely identical.The only narrative differences in regard to who your party consists of, are generally who speaks and says what in the cutscenes, and which baddies are your endgame villains. Yes, the "big bad" of the main storyline changes depending on who you play as (a different big bad is predefined for each set of two player characters). Now, before you go getting excited about these promises of individual starting sections and three different villain sets, let me clarify one thing: in my opinion, this game's story is trash. It's not quite as rubbish as Secret of Mana's story (the game which comes before it in the series), but I did not find the characters to be very deep, nor the dialogue to be very gripping, nor the story beats to be interesting at all. Things happen, and after my first playthrough, I often skipped through cutscenes. Do NOT buy this game for the sake of story and well-written characters, as you will likely be thoroughly disappointed.For just a moment, I'd like to mention the game's music and sound. I've played through the original Seiken Densetsu 3 (the game this is a remake of), and the music is a pretty great recreation of it in better sound quality without being chiptunes (not that there's anything wrong with that, necessarily). The voices are pretty decent, but not great, in my opinion. Some of it is the actors' and/or director's fault, while other times, it's the writing's fault (Kevin's and Charlotte's writing has the former speaks in Tarzan/caveman speech at times, while the latter replaces her "R"s and "L"s with "W"s, such as saying "Wook ovew thewe!" instead of "Look over there!" which can get pretty annoying...but I *do* love how the actress says "I'm a natural" in that silly speech because she totally leans into it and nails her lines like a champ...even if it's horrid writing). Sound effects all seemed pretty great, though if you manually turn down all sounds in the game, torches outside a cavern you have to enter early on, a summoned sea creature, and a combat scene in some woods mid-game all have forced sound effects that play even if you muted all music, voices, and sounds in-game.Graphically, I found the game thoroughly enjoyable. Everything is lovely, and the enemies look just like they did in the original game...if someone made them look awesome and 3D. I am not one who goes for nostalgia, so when I praise this game concerning anything pertaining to the original, it is because this is indeed a remake, and as such, it stands to reason that there should be sufficient similarities to call it a remake, as opposed to a "reimagining," etc. Trials of Mana had a great art style to base its own characters and enemies off of, because the original game went for those nice 2D sprite animations in a cartoony fashion, as opposed to the often horrendous early Playstation 1 polygon characters (Final Fantasy VII, oof).As I mentioned earlier, I did do more than one playthrough. In fact, I did *three* playthroughs. That's part of the beauty of this game: it's not terrible long. The average player will probably finish it in two or three dozen hours, and that's great for me. At the beginning, I stated my qualms with many JRPGs: story/characters, gameplay, grind, and length. Although the story and characters in Trials of Mana - in my opinion - are pretty lame in terms of depth and being interesting, everything else in the game was pleasing to me. Just when the gameplay starts to get a little bit old, it'll be about the time you get a class change, which opens up new abilities and spots to allocate attribute points when you level up, not to mention adding an extra attack to your attack chains (very simple, no big combos here), and when that starts to get old, another class change, and I was very happy to have each one. The class changes add such nice bonuses that they gave me a really nice feeling of empowerment to my characters when I needed it.Additionally, the grind isn't bad here. As long as you have your item wheel stocked up with curatives, there is little to no need to grind in Trials of Mana, and that's coming from a guy who isn't very good at games in general. Unlike the original Seiken Densetsu 3, which had a really brutal difficulty and little direct player control in combat, Trials of Mana's difficulty is much fairer. I don't know how much fiddling they did between the original game's and the remake's stats of characters and the bosses, but the biggest difference in my opinion is the ability to avoid attacks yourself. Although there might be some exceptions, almost all boss attacks in Trials of Mana are shown as red cones, circles, lines, etc. on the ground, showing where the physical or magical attack will strike. In the original game, time stood still, the spell was cast, you couldn't do anything, and your party would just get wiped out if you hadn't been grinding enough or didn't have a kinda-obscure early-game item to boost your elemental defenses enough to survive one hit from max HP. In the remake, though, you can start running or rolling like mad to get out of the way of the attack, and can almost always succeed. The party A.I. is kinda idiotic and will often get hit, even on the really defensive A.I. settings, but if you are leveled enough, even they will manage to survive a hit or two so that you can use a healing item or spell. There are also a few moments when you will stun a boss (silly cartoon stars circle over it and it won't move for a few seconds), during which time you do a lot more damage and can unleash a resource-reliant special attack to deal great damage. Oh, and one of the biggest changes between this and a traditional JRPG/action JRPG: if a party member is KO'd during the boss fight and you win the battle, *everyone still gets the XP*!!! With dumb A.I., this is really important to me.Back on track, though, I finished this game three times. I normally don't finish a game at all, or finish a game once, then never play it again. Hey, even the games I do finish, I usually wait a few months or even years to play them again. However, with this one, I've completed it three times and it has only been a couple of months or so since I bought it, I think. It'll probably be a while before I play through it again because there are other games I've put off playing too much to continue giving Trials of Mana a go, but I think it speaks volumes of my enjoyment of this game that I finished it, then went "Man, I wanna do that again," then after finished it again, I still really wanted to do it again, so I did. And I didn't even touch the New Game + where you can go through the game again with previously earned levels/gear, as well as a bonus that lets you earn 300% more XP...

_childDocuments_.review: : This is what all remakes should aim to be. Games that build off the systems of the original while addressing the flaws the original had. Despite a few small issues, it's definitely a keeper.: As someone who played the Super Famicom version of this game but was not too fond of it, I was surprised to see this remake not only remain true to the original game, but also adjust things that I considered flaws in the original.Combat is not as slow as molasses, with the combo system being a nice addition to the hack-and-slash feel of other Mana games (Secret of Mana, Legend of Mana). The ability to jump makes sense given the game's transition into 3D, since you don't have 2D sprites for flying enemies that are on the same axis as the player character. The dodge option does seem to be more for movement rather than negating damage (the dodge as far as I can tell has no i-frames), but is still pretty useful. It was also nice to see that the game kept the ability to pause combat to summon the ring menu (a staple of the Mana games), and the quick access menus for items and class strikes adds a bit of convenience, too.The leveling system is also a huge improvement over what it was in the original, since stat investment is not something you do blindly when you level up, but instead you have incremental gains dependent on stat investment. I wondered if there was a way to respec, and eventually found out the game does have a way to not only respec stat investment, but also class changes.The story is your run-of-the-mill RPG story of protagonists saving the world. It's a straightforward plot, which can be a positive or negative depending on what one looks for in an RPG story.Camera is a bit janky, though the only time this was a problem was during a boss fight that had adds and was in an enclosed room.Overall I'm pleased with how this game was put together, and hope that anyone looking into game remakes takes notes on how this game respected the source material and built on it (instead of throw everything out the window).

_childDocuments_.review: A good remake of a great game. It remains faithful to its roots while adding a new spin to the overall experience, throwing in some extra endgame content the original SD3 didn't have for good measure. The overall gameplay loop is simple yet engaging, and remains fun regardless of which character you're in control of. The biggest gripes with the game I could find are that it's a bit easier than the original, which you can fix with a difficulty mod if you so wanted, and the voice acting at times. The voice work is serviceable for the most part, but there are certainly.. moments. The story is very reminiscent of a 90s RPG in that many of the NPC characters don't exist to be more than one-dimensional props to help advance the story, but that isn't necessarily a bad thing. It's just set against the backdrop of the modern-day RPG where it's more common for NPCs to have even a cursory backstory, the otherwise insignificant nature of some story NPCs can come off as something of a surprise. Regardless of or despite this, the game remains a solid experience that has yet to be anything short of fun.The greatest change the remake does in the game's favor though is to Angela and those . And her Magus model.. this girl ain't got no business being that damn thicc. 10/10, based deity of your choice bless that magnificent soul who worked on her 3D models.TL;DR: Great remake, faithful to the original. _childDocuments_.review: Very Generic. Pros:-Fun Fighting - Hack and Slash style -Traditional RPG Elements - Lvling up, Attack Combos/Spells/Artes, -Class Upgrades - Branching path to customize your own character development to a degree.-End Game Content - Additional stuff to do after game's main story has concluded and a lot of it.Cons:-Poor Story Telling - Made to centralize story around 3 picked characters out of the 6 with 1 main and 2 sub ultimately leads to no true cohesion of plot. -Lack of Power Spike - Game feels like your character is not getting all that much stronger. Enemies always die in 2-3 combos if leveling "properly" excluding bosses.-Poor Attribute System - Enemies have elements that they are weak against but changes game very little. No thinking required.-Easy Game - Even on hard the game is trivial.-Simple Animations - Character actions at times don't match with what they are conveying. Most recent example for me, villain takes something from you and leaves, main character yells stop but the animation is looking at ground and he is clutching his fist. No cut scene or animation of them remotely trying to stop them.-Short - Game was made to be replayed for other characters stories and small changes but doesn't give compelling reason to want too.-Horrid Day Cycle - Game cycles times of day by making the screen black with only your characters showing and unable to move. Only shows a clock changing between morning, evening, and night. Stops flow of game due to pure abruptness.Overall the game is fine. Very generic in every way. If you've played an RPG before you can guess everything that will happen. Good if you want to scratch that RPG itch and have nothing better back logged. Wouldn't recommend for full price. _childDocuments_.review: The GoodThis game is rather timeless, an aged contender for the JRPGs of old. I did not have the opportunity to play it back on the SNES so a comparison as far as a remake is not something I can accurately give. Despite this, long time fan of the Mana series of games, and this title holds up the standard of the series. Graphics are clean, characters are represented well, voice-acting is pretty good, and the combat is simple in and out.The BadMy criticisms with ToM stem from previous experience with SoM's remake, despite the fact they were developed by seperate teams it does change my experience. Primarily, my issue is with the music. Classic and Remake soundtracks are available and you can change whenever you want. However, with SoM's remake, the remake songs were also reimagined and they were beautifully done so. ToM's remake soundtrack is very faithful to a fault. Swapping from Original to Remake, the music may have just been titled 'SNES' or 'Not SNES' because the songs are very similar otherwise.In addition, difficulty is a downside, because IMO the game is too easy. I scaled it up to Hard after the third boss and it's still too easy for me. Not necessarily a bad thing, I guess. It does make for a easy-playing game, but I found myself pretty bored at certain parts. Mid-game it just picks up on you, though, but it's a sudden spike that doesnt stay around.The UglyI dont really have anything too terrible to say about this game. It's rather well-made, though I have heard about some gnarly bugs and crashes I have not experienced them myself, with the exception of a weird issue with the core files for Unreal engine that was fixed by running another Unreal engine game. Very strange, only happened once. Other than my complaints about the lackluster remake soundtrack I'd rec this game to anyone looking for a relaxing time with an RPG, a clean system, and a decent story.

_childDocuments_.review: Never played Seiken Densetsu 3 before this remake was released but still really enjoyed the game. The plot for this game depends on the character you choose which adds to other factors that make the replayability of this game good. For instance, there's 3 different endings and there are some cutscenes you will only see with certain pairs of characters. The writing in this game can be bad and apparently the English voice acting is bad  but I do not doubt the writing was OK or maybe even good when it originally released in 1995. Truth be told the writing did not keep me playing this game but instead was the combat and the classic RPG feel to this game. Don't get me wrong it's not horrible writing but there are points where you can see it has aged. Being the chosen one seems like an over used idea (because it is) but you have to remember this game was also made quite some time ago. Though, what Trials of Mana sets out to do is create a faithful yet enhanced version of Seiken Densetsu 3 and I think it did a wonderful job coming from someone who never played the original. There are dorky moments in this JRPG from the plot pacing or the writing but nonetheless it did not fail at immersing me in it's world.If you haven't played any classic RPGs or you've never played an ARPG I would recommend getting this game on sale. $50 may not seem worth it to some people who have only played the newest, most modern AAA titles on the market and nothing else. I say this because Seiken Densetsu 3 is a linear and quite frankly simple game. Though, the modern real-time combat they added to this remake makes it feel pretty good for a game that was created in 1995.TLDR: If you like classic RPGs pick this one up - it's a great remake. If you're new to this genre of game I'd recommend thinking about buying it on sale after reading this review and some others.

_childDocuments_.review: This is honestly the best of the Mana series now. Although I liked the Secret of Mana remake (or remastering) I was really surprised at the remake of Seiken Densetsu 3. It is one of the best remakes of a game I have ever seen.As for the style and look, unlike the Secret of Mana remake this one held to HACCAN's art style more faithfully, which is what they should do from now on. He should also be the premier main style of the Mana games from here on out, he is the modern Arthur Rackham and Edmund Dulac, truly he is. One of the greatest illustrators of our time.  As far as gameplay, THIS is what an action RPG should be. I'm so glad they ditched the isometric camera and went with 3rd person. If you have played the FF7 Remake, Witcher 3, or Darksiders you will like the combat of this game. While stylistically different those games are similar in their action combat. You no longer have to wait for a meter to attack like the original, plus you can jump and dodge now which actually greatly effects combat. Character progression is really good in this game with arching paths based on light and dark to prestige into at certain levels. And raising ability scores are more than just improving that stat and actually add skills and abilities that your character can preform, actively and passively. It also gives you an upgraded look based on the theme of your "prestige" or class change as it's called. And they're all great looking. The only criticism I have for the game is Charlotte's English voice  and maybe the story arc. Pwease...ahem...please don't let the English voice define her for you, she is a GREAT character, very endearing and fun to play. I solved this by just choosing the Japanese voice instead and she was no longer annoying. However, the subtitles are still done in her voice style replacing all the "Rs" with "Ws". This is annoying to read and hope they give an option for her subtitles to be normal. The story is basic and straight forward, but other than that there is noting to criticize as "bad" story. But, to be fair, they were staying faithful to the original Super Famicon game, and it's the same. I also wish there was more places to go and more story arcs like Legend of Mana, but LoM came after ToM so I understand. FINALLY! To simplify and make it easier on you I'll say this; If you were a fan of the original game and/or the Mana games in general then get this game. It was made for YOU.

_childDocuments_.review: A remake of the classic Seiken Densetsu 3, which (at the time of this writing) I have never played, but which was the sequel to Secret of Mana, which I believe to be one of the greatest SNES RPGs out there (and probably among the top JRPGs of ANY system).The music for the remake appears to be fairly similar to the "classic" music, which the remake purports to let you select on the options screen. The visuals are vibrant and generally quite nice (I greatly enjoyed seeing all the familiar enemies from Secret of Mana in 3D), however there is quite a bit of bad clipping on the various character models. Additionally, the devs spend WAY too much time lingering on the posterior regions of the underage female protagonists, especially Angela, to the point where I felt I had to address it in my stream as each successive class change caused her outfit to withdraw further into the crevices of her body. Similar attention was paid to Belladonna, and a good number of other female characters as well...I'm a guy, I get it, but this game takes it to a point where it seems cringey.Story was...okay. The fact that there are so many possible party arrangements means that the story could only be SO complex without becoming burdensome, however there were several instances of Deus Ex Machina, rapid "flythroughs" of what should have been important story points,  fact a great deal of the story feels rushed, as though the devs were more interested in getting you through the story than they were building up a strong, coherent narrative.Overall, the gameplay was fun, but the balancing on the boss fights was quite poor, with some boss fights boiling down to simply slugging it out for 20-30 minutes against an enemy with way too many hit points, while later bosses felt trivial...I never spent any significant time grinding, and while I BARELY survived a fight against two nameless thieves in the desert (and a magic wall, before that), my battle against the Dragon God Emperor to beat the main storyline was over in about 90 seconds, no sweat. Overall, the game was enjoyable enough (and has decent replay value due to New Game+ and the multiple antagonists / endings), however unless you are a fan of the genre or have some sort of nostalgia towards the original, I don't consider it a "must play" title.
_childDocuments_.name: Trials of Mana

_childDocuments_.review: I have played the original a long time ago and it was a lot of fun and I felt was better than even Secret of Mana on SNES.  Why?  It allowed you to pick 3 characters from the 6 possible ones and there was a class system for the characters with their own powers and upgrades.  It was limited to 3 tiers of classes but it was all good stuff.  More importantly, the story will change somewhat based on the people you brought with you to a degree and interactions with each other.  Now that we have the remake, it's a refreshing experience as everything is overhauled and for the better except 1 thing, the difficulty.The difficulty so far will leave you wondering if hard difficulty is actually supposed to be easy difficulty because you will just walk over everything like they are nothing, least at the beginning.  I understand the beginning is supposed to be trivial since it is supposed to slowly introduce the player to the contents of the game, but it's not much of an excuse when you pick the setting titled "Hard".  Anyways, the combat feels great and the animations are really well done.  Graphics are way over the top and makes other mana title games that were remade left in the dirt as this one is S tier in comparison.  The music is BEAUTIFUL and it seems to have lot of respect for the original soundtrack.  I am overall impressed by the audio of this game and wouldn't want to change it in any way.The voice acting is not that bad.  I mean, you going to not like certain voices but it's far from the worst and it doesn't annoy me.  Riesz so far is my favorite out of all the characters I have heard.  There is also option to switch to Japanese voices if that bothers you so don't worry about it.I have only played for a short period of time, but I still highly recommend the game.  I have high hopes that the later parts of the early game and mid/late game will provide a decent challenge.  Until then, this is all I have to say until I have played it entirely.My first run will be with Riesz, Duran, and Kevin in that order.Overall Score 8/10.  It loses points due to the lack of difficulty that I have experienced thus far.  It is scored highly because everything else is well done.

_childDocuments_.review: Trials of Mana does hearken back to the old SNES days. However, nostalgia shouldn't blind one to the quality of the product especially when a $50.00 price tag (as of this review) is on it.Graphics:Graphics were something I did expect going into this game somewhat. After all this is a Mana title so that means you will have bright colors and cartoonishly design enemies. Well by cartoonish more anime style. After all the Mana games are the light heart sibling to Final Fantasy. As expected that is what I saw in the design. From characters to monsters there is a very faithful recreation into the 3D space. However, that is when I noticed one major issue. For a 2020 game, the graphics look PS2 quality. Seriously, in looking at all the graphics taken into account, the first thing that came to mind was an old PS2 title Dawn of Mana. Sure Trials of Mana is more polished but that is about it. Other issues with the graphics I have noticed is with the animations during cutsceens. Several of the characters were glitching almost looking spastic. And I can vouch it isn’t a hardware issue for in the same cutsceens other characters would be playing out their animations just fine. A patch update should be able to fix this but one has yet to be released.One other interesting choice of the graphics is regarding the small and brief cutsceens when executing your character’s super attacks. More of this in the game play section but in short you are provided a very brief cutsceen where said character “powers up” to do their special attack. For anyone that has played any Dynasty Warriors title it is 99% like when you use you Musou abilities in that game.AudioFor the most part the audio in Trials of Mana are the reused sound bits from the old Seiken Densetsu 3 title that have been polished. The game however does give the option to listen to original game tracks and also includes new updated remixes. In all there was nothing I could really complain on this and audio was pulled off well in that respect.Voice acting is another matter especially for the English actors. Its bad. Just plain bad. However, you can switch to the Japanese voices which are excellently done. So that is one saving grace.CombatCombat is very simplistic and anyone that has never played a Mana title should understand this. You aren’t going to have some in-depth and complex controls period. With that Square did make some interesting choices. You essentially have a light attack, strong attack, dodge and jump. Jumping is the newest edition and needed to get to areal enemies. Attacks are mixed in a combo fashion that combine light and strong attacks or allow you to charge up for a power attack. One thing I was glad that did get revised were the different attack speeds of the characters. For instance, the character Kevin hits multiple times and fast where as the character Reiz is slower but hits in a wider area on some of her attacks. So it does require you to pay attention to what each character brings to the character.My chief complaint however in combat was sluggish in its inputs and strangely timed. For example, in dashing towards an enemy I was already able to enter the third attack in a combo even before the first one was shown animated. Additionally, after finish a light combo (three hits of light attacks) there was a stall in registering the dodge button. So combat is not fluid and clunky at best.RPG ElementsA mix bag at best. Narrative wise, the story and dialogue is a word for word rehash of the original game. Some word choices may be changed due to localization but in all it is the same story and dialogues used from the original game. For a remake it is to be expected but I was hoping for more content in this regard to be added, whether new ideas or those that didn’t make the final cut of the original game. Still for the writing you aren’t going to get a masterpiece. It is functional and gets the job done. However do keep in mind the characters were design to play heavily on the anime troupes.Mechanics wise, Trials of Mana does implement a new leveling system. When you level up you gain what are essentially skill points that can be spent on attributes. Each attribute is as what you would expect. Strength helps deal more damage, Intelligence increases magic potential, etc. Additionally for a set number of points you invest into a stat you unlock special abilities that can be equip to give additional effects such as extra damage, increase MP, etc. However, mixed into this are also the magical abilities that remain locked until you have invested enough points invested into the stat to unlock it. For magical characters like Angelia, this system is essentially going to force a player to pick and choose only certain powers while leaving others by the wayside. I was confused why this system was implemented to basically put a handicap on a character. There is options to reset the points you invest but again you are limiting what abilities your character has. And this is a game where elemental types do play a factor. Also as with the original you will get to a point where you can gain new classes in the classic light and dark paths that unlock new abilities and new special moves. Unlocking new classes also unlock new slots to equip these abilities. ConclusionI am going to recommend this game. Despite the above short comings I did enjoy myself not for the nostalgia factor but the game itself is enjoyable. Further it is a well design enough game to introduce new players to the Mana series whom have never played before.What I will advise all is the game with bugs and short comings is not worth the $50.00 price tag. At best this is a $30.00 product. Wait for this to go on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I've heard a lot about the Mana series and always wanted to try out one of the games. With Visions of Mana looking incredible from all the gameplay teasers, I knew I had to complete at least one game before its August release, just so I could get an idea of how it plays. I bought both Trials and Secret and decided to play this one.The moment you open the game, you can tell you are playing a remake. However, the remake itself already looks very dated, from the character designs down to the music and very simplistic story. The character designs I can tolerate, but the music isn't very good and the story is as surface level "go save the world, hero" as it gets.Prologue til Chapter II was really annoying because the game throws you back and forth between a few locations nonstop. At chapter III, the map opens up a lot more and there's more varied biomes to explore.I played with Angela as the MC and Kevin and Charlotte as my companions.Charlotte's AI makes Donald look like a world class healer. I could be on my knees in front of her, begging for my life, and she wouldn't heal me unless I set her AI to exclusively sit in a corner and heal me. And that's exactly what I did.Anyway I had some fun playing this game but everything from story to music is really mid. I still want to play Secret of Mana and the new Visions of Mana tho.

_childDocuments_.review: I think I'll start off by saying that, given Square-enix's treatment of the story in FFVII Remake, I harbor doubts regarding whether this game's story has been left unchanged. I haven't finished the current story yet (and to avoid spoilers I cannot look it up), so I can't verify it in this review if you share this concern. (Also note that this game contains Denuvo, the child nobody wanted.)That said, this game is incredible, beautiful, and fun as hell. Towns feel lively and populated, like they should be. The environments are vibrant and their musical scores/themes are like a lap-pillow for the ears. The voice-acting (JP, specifically) is impressive and high-quality, although there is the one guy...if you've played Angela's story, you know who I'm talking about... His voice is the audio equivalent of AIDS and it has led me to hate him despite there being nothing wrong or otherwise off-putting/unlikable about his character. Combat is fast-paced and fun but can get pretty difficult if you don't level adequately—I didn't over-level as I tend to in RPGs, but my party was half-past level 17 by the time we found the first mana crystal and 24 by the time I stopped playing. Bosses are pretty easy early on, but get pretty nutty (mechanically and attack pattern wise) as you progress. Enemy variety is impressive and (at least as far in as I've gotten) doesn't consist of recolored higher-health and attack enemies you've seen before—that's a rather big deal in this genre.Exploration actually feels rewarding even though most of what you pick up is Cups of Wishes, candy, and Lucre (money). These things add up and allow you feel like you can get a bit reckless without having to worry too much about getting wiped.With all this going for it, the game does have at least one issue: your companions' AI. They're as dumb as absolute f*ck completely oblivious of it. It isn't all that annoying against trash mobs you encounter as you travel, but during a boss fight your numbers advantage becomes detrimental. For example, during a particularly tricky boss in Angela's story, I had to spend 8 Cups of Wishes over the course of the fight to prevent myself from getting wiped because, every time I looked up from dps'ing the boss, one of the idiots was dead and the other close behind. Apparently, they had significant difficulty avoiding the boss's knock-back and spent their time dancing through the spike traps littered throughout the room while I wasn't looking.As I said earlier, this boss wasn't difficult, it was just tricky; my companions made it difficult. Regardless, the fight was so damn engaging and satisfying. Your experience may vary, but do keep it mind and plan accordingly. If this review hasn't told you what you need to know in order to make your decision or you're still on the fence about getting this game, consider taking a few minutes to watch the livestream:

_childDocuments_.review: The First half or maybe three quarters of the game are fun! Story is a little cut-and-dry, but the characters and gameplay itself aren't badUntil you get to the late game. From my experience, playing with Riesz, Duran and Charlotte, in the late game the enemies are just sponges. They have lots of big aoe moves or just downright annoying attacks that knock you back a lot. For example, the chess piece enemies - cool design but constantly using their "ambush" move so they cant be hit, and will knock back in a (small) aoe. Fighting multiple of these, alongside annoying wizards with big aoe spells, is just down right boring.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played through a few times now with different characters, and this might be my favorite RPG ever.Good:Fun combat, soft target lock system works perfectly every timeInteresting classes/character customizationGood storyGood length (~25 hours on first, thorough playthrough, down to less than 15 if I rush)Likable charactersCompletely customizable controlsCriticisms:Could be more difficult on hard, or provide a harder difficulty levelItemization is boring, no special weapons with properties, weapons with elemental damage or status effectsEnglish voice acting is pretty bad, turned it on Japanese and didn't look backAI is pretty dumb: will stand in fire or traps and die; characters set to heal will just not heal; characters with big damage spells will either use them at the very end of a fight after all enemies are basically defeated, or use them on single enemies; the heal spell has an infinite range, yet healer characters (when they heal) feel the need to move next to their target to heal, and will not heal when outside of some arbitrary range.AI behavior/strategy section is very limited, but perhaps I am spoiled by the Gambit system of FF12Lots of backtracking. You go through one area 5 times early in the game, another 3 times, another 2 times, and yet another you make 4 treks through. The early game is just backtracking through different areas over and over again. It gets better later on though.Though I have a lot of criticisms, they honestly don't get in the way of enjoying the game for me. Some of the harder boss fights are really only hard because the AI characters are very dumb and I'm basically playing solo. This can be frustrating. But that's really the only time I was not purely enjoying the game, even after three playthroughs. This is a great game and I hope that either they give this team more SE remakes, or give them their own game series to create. Excellent game!

_childDocuments_.review: When the world was shrouded in darkness, the Goddess of Mana drew forth the Sword of Mana to smite the eight Benevodons, monsters of destruction. name: The Uncertain: Light At The End
detailed_description: You are afraid. You are forced to hide. Those who served you till recently have suddenly turned against you. Now they hunt you. They’ve kidnapped your friends and family. You have no idea where they are or what’s become of them. There is nothing you can do about it. Your only option is to hide, surviving with no hope, not understanding what’s going on around you. You are an outcast, an outlaw because you are human. Humankind has disappeared. Robots rule the Earth now. In The Uncertain: Last Quiet Day, we saw an inventor robot named RT join a small group of like-minded machines trying to help the few surviving humans. The protagonist of Light At The End is one of these survivors—a girl named Emily. Together with Emily, one of the outcasts, you will have to survive in a world ruled by robots, searching for clues about the human disappearance. Was it an AI gone rogue or something else altogether? Game features: Jump on a third-person sci-fi adventure in a world dominated by robots. Learn about the past and present world by interacting with it. Solve unique puzzles Make plot-driving decisions Enjoy beautiful locations and mood-setting music

short_description: The Uncertain is a story-driven adventure game set in a post-apocalyptic world. Humanity disappeared from the face of the Earth and has been replaced by robots. Together with Emily, one of the survivors, you will have to witness how people try to live in a world ruled by robots.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the first game in the series and I was following the development updates for Light At The End, looking forward to its release. After playing this sequel though I'm left disappointed, and with very little hope for the series' future.Just to list some of the stuff that awaits you:It's obvious that the game was released in an unpolished, unfinished and untested state, so it feels like the devs might have found themselves in a bad financial position and had to release whatever they had as quickly as possible, without properly disclosing this as an Early Access or beta release.While they seem willing to look into fixing at least the most glaring bugs - the softlocks might be fixed by the time I write this - I think it's inexcusable that they released the game in such a state. no amount of bug fixing will fix the one-dimensional characters, poorly paced story and general lack of content. To achieve that they'd probably need to fully remake this game, but I seriously doubt that's gonna happen.It remains to be seen if the series will be abandoned after this game or if they'll try to complete the trilogy, but as I mentioned in the intro I don't really have any hope for it either way.

_childDocuments_.review: (TU:LATE) is a third-person narrative adventure set in a post-apocalyptic world, where machines reign supreme after the fall of human civilization. Survivors are hunted and deported to unknown locations - or outright killed. Players impersonate Emily, that along with a small group of other humans, tries to get by and evade the watchful eye of the Robot Police. Facing daily struggles such as dangerous supply runs and being on the move in hostile territory, the survivor group's hardships have only just begun.🟩 🟥 🎮 Gameplay is divided into Exploration, Dialogues, Action Sequences and Minigames.Is performed on foot, across various environments ranging from disheveled shops, ruined buildings to sewer conducts and metro stations. Generally speaking, each location has a good amount of interactive objects that Emily can activate, examine or combine with other previously acquired items. Finding and using the right items to open up new areas is actually one of the most common forms of "puzzle" found across the game, other than actual enigmas with their own mechanics. Interacting with some special objects may trigger hidden minigames or unlock lore entries.Are initiated with other characters, usually when back at the group's hideout or more rarely during outside runs. Most chats with other survivors will be about additional information on the current events, their opinions on them, or their past stories. Less common are dialogue choices supporting or otherwise obstructing someone's ideas, which influence Emily's reputation with the group, of course. Having a certain item for the right character can trigger unique interactions.Come in the form of quick-time events and stealth sections. The first ones are about pressing the right key at the appropriate time, to perform quick actions like shooting, dodging or escaping. Failing them may have lasting consequence or trigger a restart from the last checkpoint - depending on the case. Stealth sequences are on-rail, fixed path tracks where players need to move from cover to cover at the right times to avoid detection. Some of these latter sections may prove quite inaccurate and frustrating, but generally it's not the case.Are stored in Emily's smartwatch, and usually are closed of iconic classic games like Snake, to name one. They do not give any impact on the story but have some achievements behind them. A specific minigame is instead a VR shooter with enemies, dodging and upgrades - and is one of the most consistent ones in the adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: The last half is literally one boring cut scene after another with only seconds of game play inbetween. _childDocuments_.review: : Played through the game again, cutscenes and dialogues are still not skippable. 30th October was last patch day, nothing much was fixed, at least not anything noticeable. Lip syncing is off, the colors are burned out in some areas, visuals are overly sharp and the rest from the review still stands. Puzzles are now skippable. 2 achievements are bugged and currently cannot be unlocked.I played this a week before release and was very uncertain what the developers thought when they released that broken shell to reviewers. I couldn't continue my save with the patched release version, so I had to start a new game. Turns out, some more time in the factory removed a lot of uncertainty and fixed a lot of visual and technical glitches and bugs. It didn't really fix the game though. That went off the production line as a shiny new robot design, got run over by a forklift as it stepped out the door and then quickly got put back together for the public reveal.A short, dystopian adventure game about a group of survivors living on Earth where the robots seem to have concluded that the only way to save it is to wipe out humanity. That sounds like a solid idea for a sci-fi story, right? And it would have been, if you could get to it under all the mediocre gameplay, awful english translation and sentence structure, poorly explained puzzles, uninspired characters and writing, disjointed story, unskippable dialogues and cutscenes (developers promised to fix this in a future patch) and more wooden, blank staring faces than you can shake a stick at.It plays out like a modern light adventure game with interactible points in the environment, QTE's, dialogue wheel choices, some puzzles, very few items you can pick up and not much guessing where you need to use them. There are a few stealth segments which are done very shoddily and clearly put the poor animations on display. There's quite a few collectibles that slightly enhance the lore and a ton of references to other games. The main character gets a smart watch at one point, which is a nice touch, where you can check notes, audio logs, take photos and play mini games that get added as you find small toy robots in-game. The environments are well done, but some things and items look much more detailed than others and it gets kind of jarring. If you're inclined to look for all the references and toys and love playing games within games within games, gameception style, the fun jumps exponentially. For a short while at least.A lot of bugs other reviews are mentioning got fixed, including lip syncing, most weird animations, clipping issues, sound overlays, repeated voice lines and black screens. But the character animations remain stilted, faces are still wooden and deeply uncanny valley, voices are uneven, cringe worthy and sometimes have a weird echo, characters are forgettable and worst of all, the story scenes seem to jump around like they were cut with scissors, start and end abruptly like there's something missing between them. The game also drags along in some places at a drunk snail's pace. I thought the main character would outrun it, she's just slightly faster, and break the 4th wall. And the ending is just baffling.Developers do respond quickly and seem to be willing to fix the glaring issues and bugs and I do hope they fix all of them. But the game is still a badly edited, incomprehensible hot mess with dull characters and the underlying gameplay and mechanics can't be fixed without remaking it completely. We'll see what the future patches bring. And for what it offers, it's not really cheap. If you're at all interested, look for it on sale. P.S. I haven't played the first episode, , so I can't compare them, but based on this I doubt I'd recommend it. Take a peek inside the  if you like to walk off the beaten path and only sometimes return to the main roads. You might find something worth exploring. And if you do, thank you for the visit.

_childDocuments_.review: You Feel Cheated:  The game itself is OK. It is basically just a bunch of 'cut scenes' sewn together by your choices. There are puzzles here and there that are fair (except the collector drainage puzzle needs improvement).The graphics and sound were fine and I had No Problems with any glitches or hiccups.I can't say that I loved or hated the game.<<<It did keep me engaged for 5 to 8 hours but my MAIN GRIP was, if you can call it that, the ending...:   You are chugging along just fine and then, all of a sudden, the game just ends! No Credits, No Ending, Just goes to a black screen? It's as if you are Right In The Middle Of Your Quest when the main character says: "This is not the end"....And then the screen just goes black.It's basically just TELLING YOU THAT THERE IS A SEQUEL COMING! _childDocuments_.review: The Uncertain: Light At The End is a third-person adventure game serving as a direct sequel to The Uncertain: Last Quiet Day. These games see a post-apocalyptic version of Earth where robots roam and control the planet, with humans being hunted down and eradicated wherever possible. If you are familiar with the first game, you may know that the ending was abrupt to say the least, with the story stated to continue. You would think that Light At The End would do that then, right? That's what I thought. Colour me surprised when I found out that not only does the overall story barely continue at all, it follows a completely different group of characters whose connection to the first game is only apparent in the final moments of this one.I might've been more okay with this if these characters were actually likeable, but alas they're really not. They're more caricatures than genuine people, and even then, their personalities are all over the place. Their struggle for survival does make for a compelling narrative, but when it's this hard to take them seriously, it does break the immersion.What I will say is that visually it is much better than its predecessor. Environments look great, and for the most part, there is a greater attention to detail. Some of the levels in the third act are a bit lacklustre in terms of what you can find, but generally they are great to wander through.Likewise the gameplay is smoother here, and that's mainly thanks to the switching up of the camera. Now you can move it to your heart's content. Unfortunately, as far as puzzles are concerned, these are much more tedious, and in some cases completely absurd. They even let you skip them, which does say something about them.All in all, I really struggle to recommend this game, unless you've played the first game and are really curious about this one. Regardless, buy it on discount since it gets really cheap. If you would like to see a more detailed version of this review, be sure to check out my video review for the game here:

_childDocuments_.review: Not the best, although the price and length do encourage a playthrough. A very sci-fi setting.  This game has a great amount of voice acting, from what I remember. Not the best, but still much appreciated! The story is a mishmash of many popular stories, not very original but one that we can't have enough of. And finally I remember that the story has some drastic player choices. All in all I feel that the game received a lot of love from the creators. It's not a great game, but the length and price do make a playthrough enjoyable. 68/100

_childDocuments_.review: You know, I bought it at less than 4 bucks and for that it's kinda ok.I don't know the makers of the game and for a hobbyist or very small studio without solid financial backing, it is probably a very decent achievement ... unfortunately, it never really gets interesting.The characters are very wooden, both personality-wise and animation-wise. With Uncertain: The Last Quiet Day that didn't matter much, because the protagonists were robots. Now the protagonists are humans and they feel just like robots, anyway. Also, while it sounds promising to switch perspective in this game (which with other visual novel type games would just have been the second episode of one game) Light At the End doesn't really add anything to the story. There is one minor reveal about what's going on.So, 4 bucks for 5 hrs of gameplay. That's less than a pay-per-view movie rental, but I would possibly have had my finger on the fast-forward button during that movie, too, waiting for the plot-twist that never comes. Will I play a sequel? Well, maybe just to see how the story evolves, when the sequel is on sale, too.

_childDocuments_.review: The long-awaited continuation of the "The Uncertain" series. Help Emily meet RT-217NP while rescuing a group of survivors in a post-apocalyptic world overrun by robots!Like many players, I expected the continuation of the story of RT-217NP and the survivors - but our hopes were not destined to come true. This story will run parallel to the first game, introducing us to a group of survivors - who are trying not to die in the world of robots.Admittedly, it's all rather boring. The characters are quite cardboard, although they have a history - if Emily pester them with questions.The plot is much weaker than the first game. There are a million plot holes.The only plus is the Easter eggs. Looking for them is quite interesting.In the game, in addition to the slow narrative of the plot, which is also stretched by slow animations of the characters, there are logical puzzles. Some of them are quite excellent, so I recommend trying them on your own, and not skipping them for the sake of a quick end to the game.As the game progresses, we often encounter the possibility of choosing an outcome - which affects the relationship in the group of survivors and leads to certain achievements. But to the greatest disappointment - all your choices in no way affect the ending of the story.I also want to note the multiple bugs in which the camera can go beyond the map, passes through walls and objects. Heroes can disappear right during the cut-scene, interrupt the dialogue - but leaving subtitles, or even vice versa: the possibility of disappearing subtitles, but with the continuation of the dialogue. What's funny is that the subtitles are different from what the characters are saying. Why this was done is not known.If you often hold down the "scroll" button during cutscenes, then this effect may remain during the main game, interfering with the gameplay.Some items have a point of interest - but cannot be activated to inspect or receive a comment from the hero.I would like to highlight optimization as a separate item. It is not in the game, because it was made on Unity. So get ready for unstable frames, long loading times, lags and constant switching of graphics quality and restarting the game - to pass some places.I would really like to recommend this game for purchase - but unfortunately. can't do it.A game in which only Easter eggs can be distinguished is not worth it to spend the amount indicated by the developers for retail.If you still decide to buy it for your collection - try to buy it during sales, when the discount is more than 80%.

_childDocuments_.review: After 'The Last Quiet Day', 'The Uncertain' now comes with the second chapter 'Light At The End'.In total there would be three chapters that show an extensive story in its entirety where the earth is no longer dominated by humans but by robots.After you experienced part of the story yourself as a helpful and friendly robot in chapter one,now in chapter two you are part of a group of human survivors in the current 'robot-guarded world'You will experience the other side of life in this apocalyptic world as 'Emily'whose family has disappeared along with most of the people on the planet.Are they still alive? where are they? What eventually happened? and why?Emily is determined to find out what she can find out, but this does not come without confusion or danger.Very advanced robotics are lurking everywhere, ready to find the people who are hiding.During your journey you will also have to deal with a number of puzzles that will often place your math skills and memory on the test.Regardless of the scenario in which 'The Uncertain' is located, the game is also very relaxing to experience from an exploration perspective.
