_childDocuments_.review: The continuation of the adventure game "The Uncertain: Last Quiet Day", released in 2016, was hotly expected by me, because that game quite competently revealed the theme of the conflict between man and artificial intelligence. And, she also did it through the artificial eyes of that very rebellious intellect. The sequel, which received the cheerful title "Light At The End", turns out not to be a direct sequel, but rather a parallel story to the first game, in which people play the main role. A girl named Emily is hiding from the robots along with her group of survivors, trying to figure out the causes of the Incident, and at the same time not to get caught by the predatory creatures scurrying around everywhere. In my subjective opinion, the plot of the first game was more interesting, because we have already seen stories about groups of survivors quite often, but nevertheless, the writers managed to squeeze the maximum out of it. It is very interesting to follow the story, the characters are often ambiguous, the creators even prepared a certain kind of non-linearity of the game process. Our actions affect relations with people in the group, we can generally lose many of them on missions, many tasks can be performed in various ways, which allows us to diversify the gameplay. Thanks to this system, the game's replayability increases, which is also a positive factor.The technical side is not yet so perfect, I ran into non-critical bugs several times (the appearance of subtitles from future dialogues in conversations, ghost characters in front of the metro station, suddenly appearing near your orphaned group, the disappearance of facial animations), but it is clear that work is underway to fix it. The puzzles here are very difficult, although there are some that can be completed in a couple of minutes. They are located creatively, and it is clear that their creation was treated with attention. There are a lot of collectibles, and it is very strange that I was not able to find everything, although I searched the locations with great care. And what I really didn’t like was that the story again ends with a cliffhanger, as it was in the last game, which means that in order to answer questions, I’ll have to wait for the next game (I would have waited for it anyway, guys, why torture that) ... In general, the impression was quite positive, it remains only to polish the technical part. Enjoyable adventure from talented developers, good luck in the future!
_childDocuments_.name: The Uncertain: Light At The End

_childDocuments_.review: It’s been four years since the very first episode of The Uncertain was released, portraying a world long lost to the robots. After changes in the development, the studio is now called , and this new episode is published by  (who also released the popular game ). is the long awaited second episode where this time around Emily and a group of survivors try to survive the best they can. We finally have an overview of how the remaining humans survive, by scavenging for the remaining food cans and leftover electronics.Although it’s well established that you can play any of the games regardless of order, I must emphasize how that’s not entirely true. Both games are directly connected in a time frame, you’ll miss a large chunk of events by missing the first game, which is really good and recommended.As the story goes, it portrays all the necessary sequences for a classic contemporary post-apocalyptic scenario: The recently born child who needs medical care, the old couple who still remembers the old days, and the poor and sick elderly who share their wisdom, the strong “Action-Man'' of the group delivering a strong and independent image, and lastly, our protagonist, a young woman trying to survive with hopes for a change.It takes time, but you can actually feel the group coming together, and they’ll grow on you, one way or another. Character placement is very predictable, but still enjoyable. The story is still heavily scripted as you’d expect, but there are some changes based on your decisions. The biggest change is perhaps the positive fact that you can now explore all text dialogue options, which didn’t happen in the first episode.Another improvement is the gameplay, where controlling Emily feels much better, and the controls are fluid and very smooth. It’s a complete contrast to the previous episode. Players can still check objects, collect them and interact with characters to progress in the main story, as well as complete simple side-quests.Either traversing the empty yet under surveillance roads, or escaping, there’s a new mechanic included, which works as stealth sections to avoid being caught. I personally like when games, add little extensions to their normal gameplay without making it overly complex. It works and suits well the game’s overall behavior.As expected, puzzles are back with some being easier and others almost getting into that medium-difficulty level. I personally feel there was a huge climb in difficulty from the first game to the second, which doesn’t mean it’s an issue or a negative annotation, just something I consider worth mentioning. The puzzles still have parts that are very original and they remained feeling fresh throughout the game.Unfortunately we cannot avoid talking about the bugs that are still present within the game. I feel that when it comes to , gameplay and optimization are connected. The game feels and plays out really well, but please take in consideration that it’s an indie game. Despite its fluidity, the gameplay can still feel like it could be polished a little. However, I’m not going to be picky about it, when the developers clearly worked very hard to deliver what they had in mind.What we cannot let slide are some of the other unfinished parts that I personally believe will be patched throughout the year. This goes to voice sync, animations, and overall performance. The latest patch already fixed many of these issues, but some animations could be improved as well.The visual presentation follows the same line as the previous episode, as far as quality goes. There’s better lighting and effects that we can call “new” and they sure add value to the overall quality. The characters are well designed but lacking in proper animation, which is clearly the weakest link in the game. Coming from a robot design that looks simply amazing, humans don’t really look as good. They are much harder to create after all, and attaching emotions to them, is even harder.Overall the presentation is decent, and remember, not every indie developer studio has the ability to create such an experience with a low budget. Many of the said issues are connected with the Unity engine. The performance is on par as expected, with my RX 580 4GB model I manage to reach 60fps on high settings, but with some dips to the 50’s in some areas. Medium settings stables at the 60’s meter easily, with practically the same quality.The soundtrack is once again a high point of development, with a strong post-apocalyptic theme, which if you played the first episode, should be quickly familiar with. The audio dialogues are also quite good, unfortunately I noticed an uncommon bug that makes some dialogue lines fast-forward.All in all,  is the culmination of a strong development team who is passionate about this series, with the inevitable issues of a rushed product which could take a couple of extra months of development. I personally enjoy this episode, and I firmly believe it’s a fantastic step in the right direction. I have no doubt more updates are on their way, and when they do, it’s going to be a Mostly Positive game on Steam.All the requirements are already present: A good narrative, a solid gameplay, and a brilliant atmospheric presence. Time will be a good healer for this second episode, of that I am sure. If anything, this game reflects what Indie games need, a push towards the horizon, where aiming for more is not a problem.Thank you , for keeping developing an amazing franchise!

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't call this game a sequel, unless you count the last 1 minute cutscene at the end, instead you get to experience the story from a human perspective. it doesn't feel too much different from the first game, both gameplay and graphics wise. Another great feature is that you can skip the puzzles, I can't remember if the option was present in the first entry though so maybe it's nothing new.For those who liked the first game, it's a no brainer, definitely worth giving it a try. I expected a little more, especially the ending felt somewhat unsatisfying. What also sucks is you need to replay the game at least once for all the achievements and honestly, I don't think the story was that good for me to sit through another 3 hours for a couple of different outcomes.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the second part of a trilogy, so discussing it is going to require some spoilers for part one. If you haven't yet played the first part 'last quiet day': it is a fully 3d take on point & click / puzzling, with a fairly engaging story that takes place after mankind is believed to have destroyed itself, and their robots now rule the earth. SPOILERS FOR PART ONE:In the first game you played as a robot that discovered evidence humanity might still be alive, and for some reason this existence is being covered up by abducting the people and executing any robot witnesses. It finished with the robot finally seeing humans for the first time, as it encountered a group trying to escape from some police androids.Part two tells the story of this group, and fills in some of the details from the human perspective. Chronologically then, it takes place before the events of 'last quiet day' and uses this non-linear approach to add new information that builds up this conspiracy behind faking humanities "disappearance"Unfortunately, if you like getting any resolution to conundrums, you won't find them here. The "how" of why humanity "disappeared" is addressed, but the "why" is not. This second part doesn't end with a cliffhanger, or anything like that, it just raises further questions for the final part to answer.Reviewing it is a bit problematic, as I have no clue if the story is ultimately worth investing in, since it's unfinished and is with-holding any revelations. You end part two none the wiser than you did finishing part one. It's not a super intriguing plot in and of itself. Part one managed to get by thanks to its robot lead being a charming and amusing character, and the same is true here. Decent voice acting, reasonable writing and enjoyable puzzles are more compelling than the narrative, which is deliberately left stewing for a final reveal in part three. I can't help but think some people will be saying to themselves "huh! might as well wait for part three to be finished then, to play them all at once" and I can't really think of much about this to persuade them otherwise.I played part one and enjoyed it, I played part two and enjoyed it. But both being reasonably cheap and not overly long has a bearing on that, given it is somewhat unsatisfying to still have no clue of where it's going. A tv show with a weeks wait between episodes could get away with this "suspenseful" kind of storytelling, but when it's a game that might take years to develop....I don't think it's the right approach for anyone but super patient people, as I can't easily sum up why YOU might buy these games, and I've played them to completion..... Further to this lack of substantial reveals is the jankiness. It looks okay for an indie title, but has some rough self shadowing on characters and bog standard facial animation. Sometimes the lip syncing fails, or it has other glitches such as absent characters briefly appearing in cutscenes before vanishing for the next camera cut. The controls can be wonky, and there's a few points where playing on a controller won't work so I had to switch over to my mouse.All in all it's a hard sell for a game that isn't actually awful, so I'm not that keen to recommend it or totally write it off. There's nothing game breaking, and it does have some elements that work, such as the writing which is passable.Having it all hinge on a reveal that never comes though....I can't imagine that will make many people happy when there's games out there that are complete and better produced. For sure they might be more expensive, like Heavy Rain or Man Of Medan (narrative driven titles, albeit thematically miles apart), but they deliver a complete story.For all three parts it could easily end up being in the vicinity of £35 to £40, and I won't know until part 3 is released whether you'd be better off saving your money for something else. Personally I'd give it a 6 out of 10, and that's still a recommended in my book, just not a particularly enthusiastic one.If you found this review to be helpful then why not check out my curator page here:

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very VERY rough around the edges. If you are easily bothered by bugs, crashes (the game autosaves often, so that doesn't mean loss of progress), stuck or weird animations (there's even one that's reminiscent of the exorcist xD), missing audio, and other stuff like that, then you should stay out of this game for now. I presume (and hope) a lot of this is going to get fixed in future updates, because as it is, it doesn't seem worth full price, because it doesn't look like a finished product that much. However, I came here after playing the first game, which I generally liked, especially the story, and this one seems like a good follow-up. I didn't love it, I think the first game was better than this one, but still, it was engaging enough. In the end, I was able to overlook all the other problems and enjoy it. Soundtrack and voice acting are still good (mostly), and there are no game breaking bugs or anything of the sort. You can skip animations, mini-games, and reload saves from any part of the game, so it does have some things implemented to help impatient people get through it. It is still heavily story-based, but it has some fun and nice puzzles. It also rewards exploration of the environment; there are a lot of easter eggs, some of which are relevant to get achievements, and others that aren't (much like the first game). It also ends open ended, but this one makes you feel a lot more closure than the first one, which is greatly appreciated. Achievements are mostly fine, some of them require you to follow specific dialog choices though, and that can be a pain, because if you play it without a walkthrough, and then want to get the achievements, you'll almost certainly need three playthroughs to get all of them. I'll probably play it only one more time now and then leave the last playthrough for just before the next installment is released (whenever that is). In any case, it's tough to review, and mixed seems about right for the state this game is in, but it is likely to be improved if and when more updates are released, and I enjoyed it enough to recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Having been a big fan of the first game I eventually picked this one up, I was especially curious to see what happened to the main character from the first uncertain, but I couldn’t even make it through the whole game. The developers threw away two golden opportunities. First of all you don’t play as a Robot, or really interact with them. Which besides being extremely unique also meant that voice acting and animation didn’t need to be life-like, because well they’re  All the characters are super stiff and Janky and the voice acting isn’t very good. It comes together some of the time, but you just wish you were still playing as the bots.They also forwent the traditional point and click gameplay for a more modern third person style for really no reason. You still can only interact with only a few things in the environment, all it seems to really do is complicate development because now all the areas have to be fully traversable. I’m also assuming this is why the visuals have had such an extreme downgrade, as well as exhibiting a litany of bugs.I could probably deal with this stuff, because I was still digging the melancholy vibe (although the first game was also vastly superior in this regard) but when I was looking something up about a puzzle I came to find out this game ALSO ends on a cliffhanger and the developers have flat out stated there not going to continue this series.Yeah that did it for me. I skimmed the rest of the game on youtube and I can confirm that it clearly is meant to be a part of a larger story and without the rest it's just not worth getting invested in. It’s been stated by the developer/publisher that they aren’t continuing due to low sales, but I can’t really blame anyone for not being interested in this due to the fact that it's a downgrade in every conceivable way.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a cautious recommendation.At the time of writing, 16 December 2020, the game still has a number of bugs. These are mostly relating to dialogue (subtitles missing, subtitles not matching audio, subtitles being in the wrong place, audio not playing, no lip syncing), visual issues (Vera disappearing, Matthew lying on a different bed to the hotspot) and hotspots being inaccessible - so blocking off achievements (first robot outside hideout is inaccessible though I saw it, oil inside hideout is inaccessible). I gather a lot of the most serious bugs have been fixed now, but these still remain, and I hope they'll be another update.Nevertheless, the setting is compelling. The story is engaging. The voice acting is largely very good. The soundtrack is wonderful. The look and feel is great, and I wasn't bothered by any texture issues others mentioned. The puzzles are a bit hit and miss, with one especially randomly tricky one in the first outing with Matthew. I enjoyed it. I absolutely loved the first game, and while I still think the first was overall better - because the main character (a robot, that time around) was somehow more compelling in his curiosity - I like where this is going. It started to have a bit of a Walking Dead sort of feel, which worked well in this setting. While the ultimate feel is "unfinished", that certainly does not mean "unenjoyable". Just perhaps it's not something for the people used to polished AAA-style games. In terms of narrative games being an art form that allow the creators to tell engaging and new stories, The Uncertain: Light At The End fills its promise. I'd give it a 6.5/10 for now - though it'd be a solid 8/10 if they could fix those bugs.

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: An excellent eurojank adventure title with some oblique choice and consequence elements with an interesting setting.Long version: You probably won't get stuck on what to do next very often, and a lot of the most difficult puzzles are presented with a "pass" button, meaning you are in charge of the level of frustration you want to put up with.  I really appreciated this approach, because I was playing the game for the story, not the Towers of Hanoi puzzles.  Besides a bit of an annoying auto-save system and some very unwelcome QTE sequences that feel like they were designed for a tablet game, I can only say positive things about this The Uncertain: Light at the End.The game is written very simply, and I feel like the script was maybe passed through a translation program, where some phrasing in dialogue and in-game menus comes off a little awkward.  It does get a little B-movie in places, but that also gives the game a level of charm.  These types of choice and consequence adventure titles are a niche genre, and Light at the End fits in with the best of them.  There are a lot of pop culture references jammed into the game that actually incentivize and reward attention to detail.  I'll be walking through a certain level and in the span of 90 seconds, see Rick's portal gun hidden in a cabinet, or find a powered down Clank slumped against a wall, and a bunch of 40k Marines ready for sale.  It's cute and endearing, and trying to find that type of stuff actually leads you to where you need to be to advance the plot.I had no idea that this was a sequel, but jumping in to the story from the second game didn't leave me at all confused on what was going on.  I'm going to start playing The Uncertain: Last Quiet Day after I get finished with Light at the End, although I have probably spoiled the first game's major plot twist for myself by going through them in this order.  I don't mind, though, I just want to spend much more time in this interesting and well built world, and I'm going to miss it when I complete both games.Really well done.

_childDocuments_.review: The game lasts about 4 hours with an open door for a second playthrough, should you wish to see if different choices make a significant difference. For what it is, the game doesn't offer much to be impressed by. An additional few hours of gameplay would make for a perfect indie adventure.Let's dive into the gameplay, a brilliant blend inspired by the Life is Strange and Telltale series. It offers a unique exploration and interaction experience with standard dialogue sequences, quick-time events, mini-games, and decision-making. Despite some delivery issues, the interactive and explanatory aspects echo the appeal of Life is Strange. Cutscenes, initially unskippable, are now fast-forwardable post-update. However, the vagueness in the outcomes of choices poses a challenge, as similar options lead to slightly altered, inconsistent results.A simple icon indicating the 'kind' of outcome for each choice would improve clarity, especially since choices lack distinguishable markers, impacting relationships within the group. The game, designed for multiple playthroughs, lacks a comprehensive journal for understanding its choices. On a positive note, the collectibles provide depth to the world, revealing its functioning and events. Yet, a log displaying the percentage or number of collectibles is absent. Although earlier issues with missing interactive dialogue have mostly been resolved, the save game system remains notably problematic.The texture resolution impressively contributes to, considering the development budget, visually stunning environments, and objects. However, minor glitches, such as occasional issues around the eyes of certain human characters and examples of objects disappearing from the scene, are present. While not game-breaking, they are noteworthy. The sound design, on the other hand, is weird. Specific sound cues lack naturalism; for instance, footsteps on concrete don't accurately replicate the sound of concrete, and the same applies to walking on metal surfaces. Notably, there were significant problems with dialogue cut-offs at the game's launch, where conversations would abruptly end mid-sentence, leaving players hanging. While some issues persist, the developers have addressed and resolved a substantial portion. The animation quality is subpar, with 97% of the dialogue scenes featuring characters who appear lifeless, lacking meaningful hand gestures or body movements.The expressions are so static that it's challenging to discern their emotional states. Moreover, robots and humans share identical animations, resulting in a lack of distinction between the two; robots move like humans, and vice versa. This unnatural feel takes away from the visual experience. The portrayal of stairs is glitchy, resembling a portal to another dimension. While ascending seems normal, descending leads to supernatural occurrences, such as my character floating or teleporting to floors above or below. Despite these visual issues, the controls are precise, a crucial aspect of a game of this nature. However, the absence of a sprint function and occasional limitations on camera movement during specific sequences detract from the overall gameplay experience.The game unfolds in a distant future where robots have forcibly seized the world. While the narrative has potential, it falls short of being a proficient storytelling experience. Nevertheless, the execution and overall structure are commendable, and I found genuine enjoyment. The voice acting is acceptable, and the characters boast detailed backgrounds, developing a connection with the player. The abundance of elements available for exploration adds depth to the experience. Although not on the scale of an open-world game, nearly every corner within a specific area is accessible.As a sci-fi enthusiast, I enjoyed the overall experience despite all the shortcomings and issues with the narrative. It is a worthwhile addition to any video game collection, particularly for fans of titles like Life is Strange and Telltale games. While the replayability factor may not be outstanding, there are alternative choices that lead to different outcomes, providing some incentive for multiple playthroughs. Although the impact of these choices is not revolutionary, they offer a modest yet enticing reason to revisit the game for a second or potentially third time.This game presents quite a challenge, even for the higher-end portion of PC hardware, as it doesn't deliver visuals that justify the demand-to-quality ratio. While the game updates improved average FPS, the game still falls short of fully leveraging the hardware capabilities. The loading times are fast, and the gameplay remains free of stutters. However, occasional frame drops do occur. Despite its indie origin, the PC hardware demand can't be justified, as games that look a lot better play at much higher framerates.The Uncertain: Light At The End is an enjoyable sci-fi indie release. Despite its issues, it offers a gameplay experience worthy of a chance. I've thoroughly explored all the aspects, providing a comprehensive understanding of what to expect from this title.

_childDocuments_.review: Whelp, once again the world has been overtaken by robots and Humanity is barely able to survive. The Uncertain: Light At The End is an adventure puzzle game, by developer New Game Order and publisher META Publishing, where you play out the game’s story by progressing through chapters and solving puzzles as you do so. While there is some success with the game, there is a lot of opportunities for improvement that could be made with future patches and updates. While the story and puzzle minigames can be engaging and challenging, it’s hard to stay invested in either due to the design quality and voice acting. Is this second installment worth your time? Let’s find out. Story - The Uncertain: Light At The End is the second installment to The Uncertain series and throws us into a world controlled by autonomous robots. After a frightening event where the once subservient machines drugged and kidnapped most of Humanity, the remaining survivors huddle together in small pockets scavenging and fighting for survival. Traversing through the cities is incredibly dangerous due to roaming police bots, and has become increasingly challenging due to more domestic robots also reporting any Human they see. In this iteration, you follow Emily as she and her group attempt to eke out a living in these treacherous conditions. Early on, you get a sense of who the characters are; their goals, personalities, and ambitions. Throughout the game, you will be able to make decisions that… don’t affect much of anything. Maybe some voice lines will change depending on your actions, but the story will quickly railroad itself back on its predesigned track, so don’t worry too much about making the right choices. You’ll be fine either way. While the concept itself is interesting, it isn’t anything we haven’t seen before. A group of survivors, trying to survive, run into extreme adversity, and through loss, sacrifice, and a little luck, a few of them manage to find new reasons to push forward. What makes this story unique is its cast, but again, we run into familiar tropes among them also. Developer New Game Order tells… a story. One we’ve seen. One we’re familiar with. One we understand. Certain parts do seem rushed. Others seemed forced in order to conform to the narrative, but it is still a fun and interesting concept regardless of a few missed opportunities to make it stand out. Gameplay & Mechanics - The Uncertain: Light At The End has two main gameplay loops: Scavenger Hunt, and Puzzles. Scavenger Hunt is where you spend your time looking for clues scattered throughout the level in order to advance to the next Puzzle. The Uncertain: Light At The End hits the basics with easy-to-see popups when you’re close to interactables, button prompts to give you an idea of what it is you’re interacting with, but nothing noteworthy. Moving through the levels can be painfully slow with clunky animations weighing down the tense atmosphere. An example is in the first level: Once you restore power to the refrigerator, you have to press a button to rotate the shelves and check off the items on your scavenger hunt. However, if you attempt to press the button while you’re character is not directly in front of the fridge, you’re treated to the most excruciatingly slow animation of Emily trying to remember how to move her body two inches to the right in order to hit a button. And please, please don’t accidentally check the shelf to see if you can grab the items yet, only to find out that you can’t and have to get back into position to press the button again. The puzzles in the game are what offer it some redemption. They are varied, challenging, and best of all, completely optional! Developer New Game Order has built-in a much-appreciated skip button, allowing you to automatically solve the puzzle in front of you and get on with the game. Math puzzles are definitely not my thing and, with the first puzzle in the game being one, I knew I was going to have a bad time with this title. Fortunately, after spending 10 minutes with the thing, I found the skip button and was on my way. Most of the other puzzles were more than doable and even fun. These were truly the strongest area of The Uncertain: Light At The End. Aside from that, there are a few quick time events scattered through the story, but not enough to warrant its own section. Aesthetics & Sound - Aesthetically, the art quality is mixed. While most of the backgrounds, cityscapes, and levels are oozing high res goodness, the character models look just as rough as an indy project from 2010. I know we’re supposed to be afraid of the robots, but these some of the creepiest, dead-eyed, unblinking character models I’ve seen in a while. The voice acting, at first, seemed lacking. Something was missing that I couldn’t quite put my finger on. That is, until I messed around in the options and found there is a Russian voice setting as well. Believing that I’d found the original voice audio, I quickly switched to that and… I still wasn’t impressed. I don’t speak Russian, and I don’t pretend to know how authentic Russian is supposed to sound, but the voice acting was still extremely lacking in my opinion. Summary The Uncertain: Light At The End is a game. That’s really all it’s got going for it. For everything it did well, it only did so by sticking to the bare basics without taking too many risks on improving or innovating. Its opportunity areas, however, are ever-present and in need of improvement. Bugs and technical glitches run abound from start to finish and while I have yet to encounter anything game-breaking, the immersion is long gone before it even has a chance to establish itself. I hope Developer New Game Order takes the time to at least iron out the rougher technical parts of the game. There is some true potential here. But for now, I wouldn’t give this title a high recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: ‘The Uncertain: Light at the End’ is the second game in the ‘The Uncertain’ series about a post-apocalyptic society ruled by robots, following on from ‘The Uncertain: The Last Quiet Day’, or more accurately, happening in parallel to it.Although the first game in the series had us taking a role of a robot citizen of the new society ruled by robots, this time round we’re playing from the point of view of Emily, a young teenage girl, who, along with a few other human survivors, is trying to get by, scavenge for supplies, and avoid being discovered by robot police. I personally found the first game's story to be more engaging because we were right in the middle of the robot society and seeing it from the point of view of one of the robots in it. In addition, it had a mystery hook introduced quite early on. By contrast, in this part we just follow a very ordinary group of humans who are trying to survive in a post-apocalyptic society - the kind of plotline we've seen a lot of times already.The gameplay is the same as in the first part. It involves us exploring the 3D environments and interacting with various parts of it in order to make progress, and at times solving puzzles and mini-games too, akin to standard point and click gameplay. Most puzzles are well-designed and get you thinking. All of them can be skipped though, so this fits a casual experience more than anything challenging. There are also a few simple stealth sections, dialogues with NPCs, and collectibles.Visuals are pretty decent and atmospheric, though character animations are a bit stiff and unnatural. Musically there's very little happening and could certainly use improvement. For some reason, climatic scenes still continued having ambient music playing, even though it would've been better to have something intense playing during them.Most bugs must've been fixed since release, though a few minor ones still remain. Generally, I didn't come across anything game-breaking.Not a bad 4-hour game, but felt too lukewarm. The first game is better in terms of plot and originality, in my opinion, so I'd recommend you to try that one instead. And if you care about the plot enough after playing that one, then get this one too when it's on a big discount.For a more in-depth review, check here:

_childDocuments_.review: This is the second part and continuation of the dystopian story of . It’s a second part, since it develops the plot as a parallel story from the human side. And a continuation due to the reuse of previously established gameplay elements. Although it has some technical details, I focused on its narrative and gameplay.The story commences with Emily and Park's search for medicine. When they finally obtain them, a police robot come in the store. They run away and get to their refuge. But they comprehend that baby Vera is unwell. It’s a matter of time before the supplies run out or survivors be found by the machines. So with a lack of determination and decision, they’re coerced to abandon their shelter.If there’s something I liked about the preceding game, it was its context: a world where machines «believe» the myth of human extinction. Its plot expressed a mysterious atmosphere about humans, as tacit things are mentioned and considered at all times. There’s no elucidation, but only progress with the course of story (the machine society).In this second episode, the game tries to clarify certain happenings in the plot with an aspiration to become immersed contextually from the humans and get a dissimilar perspective. It isn’t a sequel, but a narrative extension as a parallelism. If we play the previous game it’s about robot, in this case, the story offers importance to humans.The game desires to attain a plot twist through an incident on the human side. I’m not entirely persuaded, as I said, of this exertion to clarify the mystery of extinction. The idea for this episode to present a context is to designate what really happened to humanity. The proposal of how it initiated through nanotechnology in water and about the creation of the myth of human extinction through a firmware update to robots, it was a great indication through which it manages to expose a typical rebellion of machines against humans.The first game succeeded to develop a new and almost original story. But in this second it takes up many things as a recycling of the machine-themed stories. I’d have loved its sci-fi thriller, but turning it off with an attempt to explain by searching for answers disenchanted me. At the end of the plot, Emily along with RT will both investigate for answers to what happened: humanity wasn’t extinct due to prolonged wars, but for an unknown reason they’re kidnapped.The game isn’t bad at all. It wants to relate me its story as an FMV. The voice acting is respectable, each character is irreplaceable and discernible. They achieve to convey affections of sympathy or refusal with some. It performs human feelings as well as their behaviours. As part of the gameplay involves interaction with the characters, I have the selection of responses that affect the decisions and relationships with each of them. It seems that game with possible endings is being attempted.The script is decent, I liked the Russian voices. The interaction is well arranged, subsequently I can feel that I’m talking to a human character. However, sometimes I just heard blah-blah without affecting me any greater attention in the dramatic development. Although it has a variety of lines of dialogue, it gave me an impression of being an FMV. In other words, some moments have several conversations that promote a continuous narrative as an interactive film. A good proposal due to the fair-minded designs of the 3D characters, a script can be immersive and the cutscene performed in real time within the game.If the narrative is to be a continuous plot, pacing the game through gameplay is important. To see it one way, there are conversations, exploration, interaction with objects, solving puzzles, and quick time events. This way the game doesn’t become monotonous. But if the narrative was considered, I didn’t see the prominence of adding other elements that fracture or interrupt the continuity of the experience. An example of displeasure was skipping puzzles.As for the riddles, either solve them or skip them, and that’s due to its obstacle. They’re logical-mathematical puzzles of patterns, sequences or successions. Let's say they’re resolved quickly to remain attentive to the plot. But in other cases, such as quick time events, it can give a different scenario with an alternative possibility of proceeding in the plot. In the  to get the story items, either use the employee's credentials or delete the inventory information; all of that in turn, do it before the alarm goes off or do it after.All of this has the appearance of a preparation, which is suitable to distinguish a gameplay adjusts to the narrative. Something I didn't like was the Easter eggs forced to implement in locations. On the other hand, having inventory was worthy, although it’s important to consider whether this will be necessary for its constant use. For example, a way to distract oneself as an interruption are some mini-games (found in toys that are later added to the inventory). Inquisitive implementation, but it entails meaningful how to ponder them in moments of free time or time out within the game, when there aren’t quests something to do.I assumed the game as an experimental test of a possible plot. It has many components that require to be well crafted, especially optimization, the soundtrack, the quality of the cutscene and the plot. Its rhythm is also important to be worked on. I also didn't like the hyperbolic dramatization for Emily through forced themes of our generation. But the story of this second episode bonds, although hastily, with the previous game.I could have given a negative review, but I have good expectations about the continuation of the story. I want to know what truth Emily and RT will unravel. The game has an interesting start, although it’s important to work on the gameplay as it’s the path of how the story will be told through interaction, experience and intention. I recommend the first game more; and this one, take it as a series of narrative practices for its continuation and part.

_childDocuments_.review: Want a simple paragraph with which I can sum up this game?"The Jank must flow. This is a Janky Frankenstein's monster loosely stitched together from half baked Gameplay ideas, absolutely terrifying human models, and the most bog standard apocalyptic story. And it won't take long for you to see just how quickly this miniature homonculus comes apart right before your eyes."The graphics are serviceable, with environments even looking somewhat decent (Kudos to the artists), but by god the humans look like lifeless puppets animated by shoestrings and copper pipes. Their lifeless eyes, the lips that flutter ever so slightly when speaking, the permanent thousand yard stares...why they ditched the robot protagonists of the original Uncertain is beyond me. Not only did this move introduce absolute uncanny valley-level humans, but it also arguably robbed us of the only interesting narrative thread on this otherwise completely bog-bloody-standard story. I, Robot (2004) much? You could substitute the mechanical menace in the story with a whole bucket list of apocalyptic baddies and almost nothing would change. The characters are shallow as puddles. There is no intrigue, nuance, no unique take on post apocalypse of this specific flavor, and the first hour of the story has writing stuck in such campy waters, I thought they called in the lads who made Resident Bloody evil 1. The voice over also seemed rough in the first hour, with the actors completely missing their emotional target, but it gradually picked up the pace and was mostly serviceable. I think the gameplay is trying its damnedest to be a mixture of last of us + telltale games, coupled with an incredibly slow pace of our heroine, which no doubt were intended to pad its length. The Entire 4 or so hours of the game has only like 4 quick time events, a half baked 3rd person shooter minigame for some reason that overstays its welcome. Apart from that it also runs as smooth as a colonoscopy performed with a cactus, with frequent audio glitches, control bugs, animation errors...like how could they coitus up a Story and Exploration focused game is beyond me...The puzzles were nice though. Most of them were not too hard, but not moronically easy. Two puzzles though were confusing, a fact that could be attributed to the language barrier and poor translaiton.  All of this combined with the fact that there will be no third game culminating the story means you will be left off with a clifhanger that has no resolution.In the end, even if you have a high tolerance for Janky games there is a much, MUCH better use for the 4 hours of your life than...this.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm reviewing the prequel of this game here + a bit of this game because Steam did not record my 11h on the prequel because I played offline...I really wanted to recommend these games because they have a good story and beautiful graphics:- it's a story about what would happen if AI/robots were allowed to evolve freely- the graphics are not AAA alright but they are really beautiful and the world feel very alive. It's a work of art.Unfortunately this game felt short on almost every aspects.1. The gameplay itself is a point and click. In the second game they added QTE. It should be hard to get that part wrong but in the first game you move the slowest character ever. Fortunately the fixed camera (like old Resident Evil) make it easy to find and click on object. In the second game, your character is faster thanks but the 3D camera combined with pointing objects makes it hard to click and find objects. Pick your devil.2. The premise of the story is excellent but the first game has too few narrative and details on the universe. I haven't play enough of the second game to tell if it's any better unfortunately, but it looks like it has improved a bit because there are a lot more human characters.So let's talk about characters now because I think it's a major flaw of the first game. In the first game you control an apathetic robot. There are a few fun lines here and there but he is mostly very boring and since they don't develop any details on the main protagonist, it's hard to feel attached to the character. In the second game however you play and interact with humans and it does feel better. Unfortunately the settings feel more like The Last of Us which makes the overall game less original.I don't know why the first game feels that wrong... At some point you meet other robots and some of them have more personality in their voice. There is even a feminine robot. Maybe the voice of the main protagonist is too monotonic (probably on purpose, it's supposed to be a robot after all) or maybe they did not developed the story of that character enough (we only know it works as a freelancer/repair guy or something). I think it's a bit of both and it makes it really hard to connect with it.The closest game I can compare the first game with is Primordia. But Primordia is a masterpiece because it's way deeper than this.I wish I could give more review on the second game because it does look better than the first but its running poorly on the Steam Deck. The shadows are not rendering properly and it's blinking. Also there is a white outline on the characters at times. The first game works normally though. But both suffer from very poor performance. From what I read on the discussions, even with a PC on Windows the performance are terrible.

_childDocuments_.review: so i bought this game in spite of "Mixed Reviews".    it was on sale and looked interesting.PROS:gameplay was really comfortable, with the mouse doing almost everything: looking, touching, taking. the only keys that i remember were movement, WASD, plus tab for inventory.  so it was simple to play with a very easy learning curve. it also had a SKIP option when puzzles got too difficult or just annoying. and it SAVED when i wanted, something sorely lacking in many games. the game had a fun plot, humans hiding from robots who took over the world.CONS:it had bugs in the sewer area of the game. i could repeat them at will. try to travel back across the discharge water by moving sideways on the ledge results in the screen going black and staying black. i was able to get out of it by pressing TAB and using the camera, then walking towards my compatriot. problem then became me seeing him in duplicate for awhile. so the important thing is that the few bugs didn't prevent game play from continuing if you figured out how to get out of being in a black screen like this. so i liked the game. it was short, just under 6 hours for me, but i only paid $8.74, so i thought it was a bargain, really. the ending was disappointing. i guess i was hoping for a happier ending, after having to walk through sewers .:Dbut, i did like it anyway! i'd give the game 4 stars out of 5, mainly cause i just had fun with it's playability, save feature, simple learning curve. but i can see how someone might think it was too easy or something.  not too easy for me though.i thought the Devs really gave their public some good features that i mentioned. i appreciated the easy learning curve, i like the simple game control play, the lack of keys to learn, the save feature too, the lack of action puzzles -i remember only 1 that stumped me but i got through it anyway (the pharmacy storage area with the security lasers after me).so i gave it a really high score cause it was fun, entertaining, with a good plot, and easy to play, plus a save feature!

_childDocuments_.review: How much you enjoy The Uncertain: Light At The End will depend a lot on your tolerance for janky sci-fi adventures. Fortunately, that's one of my favorite genres.Light At The End continues the story from Last Quiet Day, showing you small fragments of a future where humanity and robots lived side-by-side until some kind of event happened that led to the robots rounding up and disappearing the humans. For why? We will never know, because it seems the developers have abandoned the series. But the mystery is compelling.The game is quiet and subdued. You aren't some epic hero at the center of everything or some impossibly cool wisecracking hipster, you're just an ordinary person trying to survive. Everybody feels down-to-Earth. There is the usual set of adventure game logic puzzles used to gate advancement through the scenes, but for the most part this is a narrative adventure/walking sim where you just walk around and talk to people and experience the world. The continuity is sometimes a bit off, the script isn't always great, but overall it's a peaceful, relaxing game punctuated with the odd QTE. Something cozy for the weekend, if you are a sci-fi fan who can look past the jank and unfinished story.

_childDocuments_.review: , while the game is mostly coherent, it’s plagued with small things that chip away at immersion which jeopardizes the enjoyment of this story-driven game. With a handful of plot inconsistencies, weird and questionable gameplay segments, and an incredibly broken sound design (mostly in the last 25% of the game), the game needs some love and care before I could consider recommending it for play.The Uncertain: Light at the End is a lightweight adventure game that features puzzle-solving, decision-making, quick-time events, and some light appearances of stealth walking. You take the role as Emily, who is a survivor of a robot uprising that’s referred to as . During , humans were rounded up and taken , with the remaining hiding and scavenging to survive. I was able to complete this game in four hours, so that’s the amount of gameplay you could probably expect since I typically operate slower for the review process.The story is primarily driven by the groups’ changing needs to survive in the world they’re no longer welcome in. Emily in specific serves a small hideout of survivors as one of the capable scavengers. The survivors feature a diverse cast of iconic tropes that typically provide the most interesting dynamic in the environment. During your time in the hideout or out with a cohabitant, you’ll learn more about them, yourself, and the world around them through use of artifacts such as newspaper articles, advertisements, and audio recordings.If you’re still reading on, let’s move onto what I do like about this game.My favorite part about this game easily was the puzzle diversity. There’s a good dozen or so in this game, and I’d say this was fulfilled as a promise in the above  list. Some of the puzzles are much easier to solve than others, and there are a couple of puzzles I’d consider hard, but none of them took over six-ish minutes to solve each. I would say that the  was one of the harder ones, which took me about four minutes to solve, and was probably a poor choice to put as the  puzzle in the game. There is one puzzle  where I just pressed Q on it almost immediately after it opened and it completed the puzzle without me really understanding the prompt… not sure if it’s bugged, or if my arrangement was just lucky.Another thing I liked is the voice acting*, just note I did tack on an asterisk at the end. The voice acting for a $15.00 game in English is surprisingly good, with most of the lines being delivered well. There are  shortcomings in the overall voice-acting, but I can overlook those because the rest of the cast seems to really knock it out of the park.Lastly, I do think the overall art direction of the world is nice. It’s not mind-blowing or innovative, but it’s subtle and I think they captured the sci-fi feeling in a somewhat-dystopian future pretty accurately. I wish there was a little more variety in robot design, but they’re . In terms of facial expression, they’re definitely not amazing, but the lip syncing is pretty accurate… when it works, since there are a small handful of lines that are delivered without the models moving their mouth.Now that we’ve covered the good, I do need to talk about what I didn’t like.One of the smaller things that I didn’t like is that there are some plot inconsistencies in the story. Nothing  major where it becomes a huge plot hole, but it’s just things that might have been overlooked in scripting. For example, there’s a point where Matt cuts his hand, says he can’t do anything with it, and rests. Later that night, he opens a sewer door that takes some significant amount of effort -- now if you think it just healed, probably about half a day later, Matt says he can’t open another door because his hand is still hurt. Another one for the books is that Brian fixes Emily’s smartwatch but tells her he disabled the navigation and antenna features so that she can’t be tracked.  later on, Emily references using her map on her smart watch, which should have been disabled with the navigation module.Another thing I didn’t like was just some questionable gameplay experiences -- the robots seem blind and deaf for the most part. The game either makes it convenient that they cannot see you  indicates with great confidence that  the time to make your move. However, Emily can clip into some of these guards which have no impact, and in a particular mission Brian stays pretty far away from cover in the open as he follows Emily, which just kind of breaks the immersion. There’s also an electrified puddle of water that kills a robot, but Emily’s able to walk into it without a second thought and takes no damage. These are just  of the examples where the gameplay disconnects threats for either convenience or an accidental oversight.Lastly, the sound design is my biggest gripe with the game, and it’s time to talk about that asterisk. There're  of moments where the lines aren’t properly equalized, have strange fades applied to them, or sound like they’re speaking through a radio when they’re in-person. Some lines are even spoken with great speed, which changes the pitch of the voice actor. In the last quarter of the game, there are several examples where lines aren’t actually delivered at all, where if I didn’t have subtitles turned on I may have missed a gameplay hint from Emily that could have stopped my progress. But that’s not all I have to say for the sound design.Some additionals against the sound design is that sound effects seem to be missing. There are several other events that  have caused a sound (pipe dropping, rustling of boxes, operation of electronics) that just come up dead silent. I’m not sure if this is unintentional or if the developer just didn’t have the means to reproduce a sound for it, but it is very abstracting. Finally, the game does say that the game contains mood-fitting music, but I just had to disagree. The game has a small catalogue of features, but the music has been mostly forgettable and I don’t consider that feature fulfilled.Well, that’s about all the character-count I got for this. Ultimately, this game could be cured with some fixes, hopefully with some focus on the sound design implementation because I could largely forgive the others if the audible experience wasn’t such a disconnect. I also didn’t realize this game was a continuation of  until I read other reviews; I feel like the game nor the developers made any indication of that. It’s unfortunate because that game seems to be doing  well, but this sophomore release just seemed to be a miss.I could see myself re-reviewing the game depending on how the patch notes in the future rollout.

_childDocuments_.review: Honesty, I don't know what to say about this game. Yes, it is short and bugged. I'm pretty sure the devs will fix the bugs - judging by the original title. Yes, the "we will release it as one story divided into short chapters" approach is annoying as hell taking into consideration the price and time (how long will it take to be completed?). On the other hand I really dig the vibe, the world, the robots, the scenery etc. I feel like the first part was done much better and "Light at the end" isn't as good as the original... but this might be the case of me wanting a 1:1 continuation, with the same main character (come on, RT was so awesome!). So yes, it is disappointing.And yet I still enjoyed it a lot. All in all... I'd say - if you're into this kind of games, wait for a sale and try it out. I don't regret playing it at all. It's just a pity that the studio didn't work on it more... and didn't drop the 'story in chapters' approach.

_childDocuments_.review: Although this game is not as short as the previous one it is still short. In 5 hours I finished it. It may have been faster had I not overlooked some stuff starting out but really it's a little over 4 hours. The characters are ok. Even when talking to all of them you don't really feel much attachment to them minus the guy you start out with in the very beginning of the game. The voice acting from the main character was probably the most believable of the whole lot. The end of the game is annoying if you played the first one. I won't spoil it for you but the reason I played this was to find out what happened after the first game. The walking mechanics felt a little better here than the first one but still needs a little improving. Maybe give an option to run? IDK it still feels clunky but not as bad. Since this game left off on the literal same note as the previous one I don't recommend buying the first game if that matters to you. You know about what you need to know from that game in the second in conversation. I'm not sure if I even want to buy the third one (assuming they're making one) since two games left off at the same point. I don't feel like I made any progression. Also I'd really like for the characters to be likeable - have more dialogue options based on choices you'd made. Having choices matter too - like what if someone suggests we go on a supply run and I didn't sleep? If I volunteer to go I may pass out or something or need caffeine to stay awake IDK just have a decision matter.  If the game turned into a choices matter kind of deal then I think you'd feel more attached to the characters because everything you do has more weight. And simple decisions will make you wonder if what you said made a character do or not do what you asked or what someone else asked. This game is better than the first one and the first one can be skipped if you don't want to deal with clunkier controls. Character development needed work and the game desperately needed to be longer. The puzzles are ok but it takes me out of the game that is supposed to make me feel scared and on the run. I don't feel scared and I don't feel like I am running away from anything.I recommend this game because I like supporting indie devs but if you don't like people talking or an ok storytelling experience then look elsewhere. I am a sucker for stories and this one could be better but it's interesting enough to get a thumbs up from me.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I start, I'd like to say that anyone who wants to try this game out should play "The Uncertain: Last Quiet Day" first otherwise you'll miss out on a good chunk of the story. Anyway, much like it's predecessor it uses the Unity Engine but the developers have managed take things to next level by making it look like it is something created with the Unreal 3 Engine instead. They also managed to preserve the art style one would see in the original game while also polishing up the graphics a little. That being said there are a couple of things I'd like to nitpick about, mainly how limited the facial expressions of the human characters are, even though the developers made up for it with the excellent job they did with Motion Capturing. Gameplay-wise, things are a little different. Rather than having a camera shift positions on where the character is like a point-and-click game, you control the character and the camera over the main character's should much like a third-person shooter. Another change is the addition of quick-time events that can and will affect the storyline of the game if you fail to use them as well as the addition of dialogue choices or actions that could possibly affect other characters in the game. The inventory system of the previous game which was fairly limited has been supplemented by the main character's smart watch which also contains her own diary entries, a few mini-games, as well as an archive of audio logs and notes that you can collect. There are some bugs and issues that are present in the game at the moment, some of which will need fixes and patches in the future but considering how much work the developers put in, one can hope that the quality will improve over time. Among the issues I ran into were a few glitched cutscenes as a result of loading previous saves with one level in particular having the worst issues but other then that I've managed to get through it without any other issues.Story-wise, rather than taking place from a robot's point-of-view you play as one of the human survivors instead (Once again, I recommend playing The Uncertain: Last Quiet Day for context) and her quest(s) to gather supplies for her fellow survivors and eventually leave your shelter for a new safe haven. That being said however, your actions and dialogue choices will affect the views and relationships between the main character and the other survivors which may have consequences later on in-game. A nice addition to this episodic series of games albeit one that could also use a bit of polishing and post-release updates/patches.7.5/10One last thing of note: Much like with the previous game if you look around you can see various easter eggs and references to other video games and media if you do a bit of perusing around certain areas or levels.

_childDocuments_.review: The follow up to Uncertain: Last Quiet Day. Not nearly as good as the first game, but adds to the story and does contain more emotional depth, as this time you are playing as humans rather than robots.As with the first game, the graphics aren't exactly anything spectacular, perhaps on par with PS3 / Xbox 360, buit they get the job done well enough. It's a good game, but it has it's issues. A fair few if I'm honest. I encountered many MANY bugs, two game breaking, I got locked out of one puzzle after backing out of it, and another time my screen went totally black unless I paused the game. But the others were small issues that popped up like animations not working or multiples of one character appearing on screen and some dialogue options not working, forcing you to chose a different option. (For clarification, I encountered no bugs of any kind in the first game.)Most of the puzzles are very good except for one, which is easily the most infuriating thing I have ever come across in a game of late, made all the worse by a severe lack of instructions or explanation of what you're actually supposed to do to solve it. The only instruction given was so hideously vague that after 20 minutes I just gave up and skipped it (an option that I am incredibly grateful for)The controls at times could also be a bit frustrating. I played using a controller and at some points of the game I had to switch to using a mouse just to get the precision and accuracy I needed to proceed.

_childDocuments_.review: Just like the first game, The Uncertain: Light At The End sets up some interesting story beats only for them to never go anywhere. It essentially connects with the first game's ending, but not until the last few minutes, and since the third game will never happen, it all goes nowhere. Unlike the first game, TU:LATE features actual humans trying to survive in a world ruled by robots. Judging by the facial animations and movements, those humans also seem to be robots in disguise - at the very least, they have a hard time showing any emotions or more than rigid movements.As a result, the story isn't really all that convincing and the characters range from annoying to bearable, but they all have one-tone personalities that, obviously, do not get any time to develop in a game that is only four hours long. As for the gameplay, it mostly consists of finding objects in the environment and solving some simple, if heavily misplaced, puzzles. A lock doesn't need a puzzle that a fifth-grader can solve; that won't keep anyone out, especially after you already found a key anyway.Honestly, though, this all sounds unnecessarily harsh, but I am upset that this supposed trilogy never got a third game to shine. There are good ideas here; just like in the first game, the desolate, (mostly) human-less environment builds up atmosphere, the soundtrack is very well done and the general ideas in the story make sense, even though they aren't executed in the most convincing way. There are even some mini games you can play and a very simple morality system. The puzzles can all be skipped if you just want to focus on the story, though I would recommend doing them. It's a game hamstrung by it's budget and/or lack of experience, but you can tell there's a seed here that never got a chance to fully blossom.Overall, I will give it a thumbs up because the gameplay part itself is mostly inoffensive and it stands as a good introduction to a universe that never really evolved in the way it should've. If you can look past some clunky animations and the simple gameplay, The Uncertain: Light At The End and the first game, Last Quiet Day, are interesting games to check out, at least under the pretext of getting a glimpse into something that never came to be.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing the first game in this series (Uncertain: Last Quiet Day) I absolutely fell in love with the universe and plot that New Game Order built. Especially after the ending, I HAD to know more, what happened next. So I checked out this sequel.I have to say, the plot and writing in my opinion is really interesting and made me genuinely more invested than ever in these characters and this world's story. There *were* some buggy parts of the game, such as a few pieces of dialogue not being spoken even when they appeared on-screen, occasional moments of the dialogue being spoken not matching the subtitles, and little object errors (ex. teabag clipping through mug in one cutscene every time without fail, or baby disappearing from mother's arms, with her continuing to rock an empty space of air.)Taking a moment to ignore those, it's an absolute fabulous game that i recommend 100%, although you should definitely play the first game to better understand what's going on (and it's a great game as well). After all, with the story being solid, and my only CONS being technical bugs, it can only go up from here as occasional bug fixes are released :)

_childDocuments_.review: The Uncertain: Light At The End is the second entry of the franchise. I can just barely recommend the game and here's why:In the first game it's much more about the mystery of where did the humans disappear to, what happened to them, why are the robots taking over, meeting the outlawed (malfunctioning) robots etc., whereas the second game shows you the other side of this story. So you'll be taking control of Emily and you'll interact with the most painful group of the survivors ever. While the second entry has larger rooms to explore, much more pop references to find (Halo, SW, Portal among many others) and more puzzles that will cater to just about any level, the human aspect makes it annoying though, since they're all so ungrateful that game  will soon  put you in the mood of abandoning them or calling the cops on 'em (none of which you can sadly do). I suppose devs tried to show the pure cold logic of following the programming in 1st part VS the human feelings in 2nd part. There's one nice  nightmare segment part that looks like something out of Silent Hill and it makes you think that this game will really be amazing and much more intense after that but no- it just continues to decline after that. I also had some glitches/bugs towards the end in form of: My language was changed to Russian (in game), subs were going too fast or showed too early in cutscenes, main menu music was playing during the game constantly, sometimes cut scenes were totally silent. Overall game still felt short - I got it finished in 6 hrs with all the puzzles done. I did skip some of the dialogue though. Take it while it's heavily discounted.✅ Puzzles that caters to all skill levels✅ Visually okay-ish✅ Mini games✅ Skippable cutscenes and puzzles✅ Bigger rooms to explore✅ Even more pop references in this instalment❌ Some characters are annoying and/or ungrateful❌ Got a few glitches/bugs❌ Still too short★★★☆☆ It leaves me UNCERTAIN how the third instalment will be. Positives do outweigh the negatives, but it's still a lukewarm experience. Better call the (robo)cops on their sorry asses.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR good setting/concept, abysmal implementation. Very disappointedI got this game when it popped up in the Steam Store, thinking it looked similar in concept to games I really enjoyed, like Detroit: Become Human, many games by Telltale. I was pretty excited to get into a new story driven game featuring interesting characters who make important decisions. I played through maybe an hour, and I was disappointed. The concept was there, but the implementation was so poorly done, I couldn't bring myself to subject myself to more of the game. The voice acting doesn't make it clear whether a character is having dialogue or talking to themselves, the characters' mouths barely move at all, let alone resemble the words the characters are supposed to be saying. The game did little to nothing in terms of getting me to care about the characters, and besides the clearly Telltale-inspired gameplay of puzzle-solving by finding the necessary items, there were puzzle minigames that didn't fit at all, and a quicktime event that was both too easy to mess up without any indication, and made it impossible to skip the intro cutscene. By the time I got to the first choice of the game, I was so frustrated, and the choice really felt like a no-brainer. Despite the situation being objectively dangerous for the characters, I felt as if there were 0 stakes after all the aimless wandering and the explicit (told, not shown) setting exposition.Overall, I really like the concept and the setting, but so many things about the game need redoing for me to even be willing to play it again, let alone enjoy it

_childDocuments_.review: At least I got my money's worth.  You get what you pay for I suppose.  However, I would gladly pay more than $1.75 for a completed game.  This game doesn't even end at a cliffhanger, it ends after the the intro.  Otherwise, the concept is nice, music is appealing, and the graphics are pretty nice.  The gameplay is more story/dialogue driven, and the voice acting is believable.  The game is fairly buggy for a linear story game.  Certain sequences seemed to load when they felt like it.  Also, the 2 tutorials are completely broken, causing you to Alt+f4, then re-launch.  Luckily, re-launching causes you to start where you stopped.  However, some bugs will cause you to repeat several tedious steps to get past.  Something else to note.  The puzzles are creative and challenging, while still being achievable.  Overall, I like this game for the beginning of the story, story potential, and puzzles.  Where this game falls short is by passing off the first act of a story as a complete game, coupled with all the bugs that are easy to spot, just by playing the thing.  I'm not sure what happened in development here, I just see a lot of wasted potential in this would-be great title. 2 of 10

_childDocuments_.review: This game by itself is not very well executed, but for the overall story and in hope of a 3rd chapter, I recommend the overall Uncertain experience (Chapter 1 and this one).The story and environment as a whole is unique and really interesting.The atmosphere is cool, and character/robot design overall memorable.In isolation, good voice acting (when you ignore higher level/sensical context).In case you cannot look past them, here are game's shortcomings (IMO):1) Buggy. Things disappear sometimes, loading from certain saves causes weird states, I even once had 2 instances of the same character hanging around.2) Lifeless facial animations.3) Very ambitiously dynamic dialogue and story tree, but with some hard-to-swallow issues where thing being said are just not appropriate to others - sudden dialogue hostility for no reason at all, dialogues that are not believable in context to multi-character conversation, sudden anime-like outbursts of positivity even in completely tragic overall situations, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: After the mess it was the controls in the previous game, I thought I wouldn't want to play this, but it was equivalent to less than $1 in my currency so I gave it a shot. This is an improvement, but it's still rough around the edges. I can't count how many times I got my character stuck near a wall. There is no running mechanic, so it can get really boring to move around sometimes. I appreciate the new camera angle though. I hate games with the fixed camera angle that was present in the first game. The puzzles in this one are honestly well thought out, but most take a bit too long to solve, The design is there, but the execution could be improved. Thanks for adding a skip button to the puzzles. I'm curious to see the next game in the series if it's going to have all the improvements I would like to see. With this ending, I have to assume there will be a third game. On another note, when the story is completed, I would like to see a complete remake of the whole series as one single game with new, improved mechanics.So, here is the thing with my recommendation: I only recommend this to people who played the first game. But I definitely do not recommend playing the first game in the first place.

_childDocuments_.review: I have never written a review before, but here I just feel I have to... For the start, I really wanted to like this game - I loved the first chapter (Last Quiet Day). Sadly, the bugs prevented me from having a good experience and got worse the longer the game went on. In the end I was just getting frustrated all the time and wanted to quit this game several times. Missing voice lines, missing sound in the last part of the game, weird character movements, the game not saving, not letting me pick up things or open doors. I am surprised I could even finish it as I had to restart the last save spot several times. The pacing was also off and most of the time you just take control of the character for 2 minutes until a very long cutscene plays again and you are left to just watch people argue with each other.The good things were the puzzles and I really liked the main character, she was cute. The end is also promising and the world building was again very nice. If a third chapter ever comes out, I would still play it cause I like the story, but hope that the devs are working to improve the gaming experience as this just ended up being a buggy mess.

_childDocuments_.review: I must admit I mostly enjoyed the game and I am interested to see how the story continues but there was a lot of problems with the game. Firstly there was text where it seemed like people would talk and then the voice line never played. The chats between the people are too rushed and out of place, moments where something is said without there being a proper cue for it. Example is when Claire, sounding partially frustrated, telling him to rest too and yet Alex never said anything before indicating he didn't want to rest. There are also moments with glitches, like with monitors where if your far away the screen glitches uncontrollably, and characters when in a chat dialog and their model is still moving causing them to turn their head too far. The story also ended abruptly, with Olga losing her daughter and then suddenly all the cops arrive and we don't learn what happened to Em's friends. I wouldn't say its a bad game it is good in its own way but there are parts where it is choppy, as if the developers cut corners when making it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is refreshing to play, it feels reminiscent of early Telltale Games as far as how scenes play out, how you interact with the environment around you and even some fun quicktime events thrown in for good measure. The 'look' of the game, the backdrops, world building and characters have a real charm to them, I got the sense pretty early on that this has been made with care and attention. It has some evidence of being an Indie studio game with one or two things that i feel needed a polish, the characters, although animated well and look great, suffer with a case of the dead eyes. Also there were one of two scenes where dialogue was contradictory to what actually happened in the events prior. Lastly...the ending kinda happens at an unusual spot. It kinda feels like maybe a dead line was reached so the game kinda just .. stops. To summarise the game starts off very strong and ends a little weak,  but if you can ignore this issue, and I do hope that you will, you'l find something really special here. I look forward to carrying on.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has an intriguing storyline. The premise is equally interesting. I like how some choices affect the gameplay, but this is all overshadowed by the many bugs and raised questions with no answers. Some puzzles are challenging, but they gave a ''skip'' option. Some parts felt a little repetitive - fetch this, go there. Furthermore, the credit scene doesn't even pop up! Devs have been aware of this problem for years, but have abandoned the game. Do not get this game. If you're interested in the storyline, check out some vods on YouTube.

_childDocuments_.review: If you were hoping that the next chapter would be an improvement from the previous, disappointment would like to introduce itself. Instead of a group of emotionless robots, we now have a group of emotionless humans. Progress! No adjective can adequately convey how boring the story is, it's fascinating in a deeply perverted sense.
