_childDocuments_.review: Another review, another tactical RPG. I’ve been paying attention to Broken Lines for quite a while now and through its development, it’s only continued to improve. Now that it’s finally had to put its money where its mouth is, I’m even more impressed with its innovation and soul than I thought I would be. Strong writing and an emphasis on tactical combat make this title stand triumphantly over much of its competition in the genre.The setting of Broken Lines is somehow both what you would expect and something altogether different. Your squad is made up of eight soldiers from the United Kingdom of varying backgrounds who end up being on board a plane that crash lands deep in territory that they had believed to be neutral. Their equipment checks out for the World War II setting, but the alternate history begins as soon they realize that their enemy is something entirely different, and perhaps even more sinister than what they had expected.The story starts off a bit slow after the plane goes down but after the first few missions are completed and you’ve reunited your party, it takes off in a big way. The gas mask-wearing “faceless” (or ‘ginks’ if you prefer) are engaging in some rather nefarious activities in the area and your squad will be deciding along the way on how exactly they’re going to deal with it. The amount of dialogue here seems to hit a sweet spot for me, it creates a tense story of survival, budding friendships, and deepening rivalries with particularly exceptional character development. Each choice will make you think, whether it is simply choosing which soldier has the best idea for how to hunt the local wildlife, whether to blow up an enemy radio tower or try to repurpose it, or even which mission you’ll take advantage of while losing the opportunities provided by the others. More often than not, your options frame the idealism of your recruits and the raw pragmatism of your veterans in a way that will keep you on your toes. You’re spoiled for choice and I look forward to a second playthrough and beyond, not only for these choices but for the handful of endings that are available based on them.By far the best part of Broken Lines is its cast of characters. From the burly and tough King to the grizzled former sergeant Morgan to the smart-talking recruit Wood, I found myself fully invested in the squad of eight’s survival throughout the story. Camp, in particular, leads to a significant amount of character development as your squad discusses the issue at hand as well as having side conversations between them that can deepen their bonds with one another or put them increasingly at each other’s throats. These side stories not only alter how well characters work together on missions but also unlock powerful abilities that can be very useful or detrimental to that character’s performance.Each soldier begins with a single unique ability of their own but can learn others as the game progresses. New capabilities are acquired both from the dialogue of camp and side stories as well as completing missions, the latter of which tends to offer generic abilities that can be permanently equipped to any member of your party. These soldiers will also be packing some heat in the form of submachine guns, shotguns, rifles, and utility items, all of which can be upgraded by new purchases from a merchant ally that you meet early on. Submachine guns are dangerous at medium range and can suppress enemies, forcing them to panic instead of posing a threat to your squad for a time. This often opens up the opportunity to slide one of your shotgun-wielding soldiers in to clean them up at short range, freely blasting them off their feet so that you can lay even more punishment on them before they can pose a serious threat. Rifles, on the other hand, are best at longer ranges and can be aimed to boost their accuracy at the cost of their firing rate to pick off dangerous targets before they can close the distance. Utility items come in many categories including healing items like bandages and additional heavy firepower like bazookas.It’s important to note that Broken Lines isn’t turn-based in the strictest sense of what we’ve come to expect from the term; it’s more of a Frozen Synapse than an XCOM. When you issue your orders, you do so to each squad member while time is stopped and once you hit play, several seconds will go by as they carry them out, rinse and repeat. I really enjoyed seeing this type of combat show itself again, although I certainly love classic turn-based games, I’d like to see solid games with these kinds of mechanics hitting the digital store shelves as well.The overall presentation of the title doesn’t fall behind in the genre, but I would say that it’s not particularly impressive. Character models look fine from a distance, though they’re rather unpleasant to look at up close, especially around the campfire. The audio isn’t anything that stands out, it does its part without getting in the way but it isn’t particularly exceptional or memorable. Fortunately for this title, I found that its superb gameplay and writing made me not at all concerned with either of those elements being less of a focus.If you’re a fan of tactical gaming, pick Broken Lines up. It has enough of a unique feel to it that it will most likely not be competing with many other titles in your library; the story itself is enough for me to push that statement even further. The variety of mission choices each day as well as the varied equipment and abilities add to the replay value and I can absolutely see me picking this one up again in the future to try out some of the other options. PortaPlay has now caught my eye as a developer who may have a bright future ahead of them if they can continue to put games of this quality out, just don’t go into it expecting a lesson in history.

_childDocuments_.review: Broken Lines:~~~~~~~~~~   Two military airplanes carrying 11 British paratroopers each are flying in neutral territory over Eastern Europe on their way to a highly classified and dangerous mission, when the unexpected happens! The instruments start to malfunction and soon after, break down. But the worst of it is when all engines are shut down, and both planes are descending rapidly towards the ground. Within a short period of time, both have crashed into the earth, killing all except 8 soldiers. Scattered around both crash sites, the survivors must regroup and find their way back home.  What are they going to encounter in this unknown territory? You’ll found out, in Broken Lines!Broken Lines is a turn-based strategy game developed by PortaPlay and published by Super(dot)com on the 25th of February 2020 on the Steam platform.What a really interesting and fun game Broken Lines is! As you might know, I am a very big fan of turn-based strategy games, especially those that have a close connection with World War II. Despite being set in an alternative World War II history, the British Army's uniform and most weapons of WWII are well reproduced in Broken Lines.  What really struck me from the start is that instead of having a certain number of movements/action points per character in each turn, you have to plan each of your soldier’s orders; when you are ready, you can see them being executed over a period of 8 seconds. I must say that I was a bit confused early on, but I quickly figured it out. Your goal per mission is to reach the white flag icon (which is generally on the opposite side of the map) as fast as you can, and of course to make sure you are not losing any of your soldiers.Your first mission will start close by the plane crash site, and you’ll be controlling only one character for a short time until you find a couple of other survivors. This mission is more or less a tutorial which you can switch on and off at your leisure, but I would recommend going through it. From then on, you’ll be introduced to the campfire screen which will appear at the end of each mission, or at the end of each day and before starting a new mission the next day. In this section of the game, some of the characters will interact with each other; the story will unfold and you’ll be asked to choose who you prefer to follow within the discussion. Your choice will impact the relationship between the two characters either positively or negatively, as well as the composure of the entire group. However, when the next day starts, you’ll see a map on the bottom left corner of the campfire screen. By clicking on that map, you’ll be able to choose your next mission from between two or three available to you. You can also choose to visit Izkor shop, buy new weapons and activate random events. These random events can be good, and you might receive additional supplies you need to feed your group of eight soldiers every day, but you might also get one of your soldiers severely injured in the process. In terms of the shop, you need salvage points to purchase new weapons or utilities (grenades, bandages, etc.). You’ll earn salvage points at the end of each mission, depending on whether you managed to finish the mission under the time limit, how many enemy soldiers you’ve killed, and a couple of other things.So far, I’ve managed to survive 8 days, and more than half of my soldiers are on the brink of death! Each day is more challenging than the previous one, and that is playing on the medium level of four difficulties: easy, medium, hard and custom.Regarding your soldiers, there are only three types:  the soldiers with a shotgun (who are extremely deadly at short range), the rifleman/woman (who inflicts powerful damage from a distance) and the machine gunner (who can shoot several rounds of bullets into medium-range enemies, suppress them, and inflict serious damage). Each soldier will have a primary weapon, two utility slots for other items, and can add up to 3 abilities and traits! You can change all of these options at the campfire screen.Most levels I played were very well-designed, and in most of them, you can follow a couple of paths, which is good.  The combination of open spaces, buildings and places to hide is well balanced and offers the gamer several options on how to lay out your strategy and orders. As I mentioned previously, I really like the 8-second execution phases, or progressive gameplay. As you start each of the missions, the first 2 or 3 execution phases will usually not produce an encounter with enemies. Still, if one of your soldiers sights for the first time an enemy within the 8 seconds frame of the execution phase, the time will stop. You can re-evaluate each of your soldier’s orders, and you can change them for the remaining execution phase if you need to. Also, make sure to spot the rectangle wooden crates within each level, as they will provide you with additional supplies when opened! The comic book style graphics are fabulous! The story is well-written and entertaining. I also like the feel of the unknown atmosphere that Broken Lines portrays. The game runs well, and it has been translated into 7 languages. On top of that, PortaPlay released a free DLC “The Dead and the Drunk” before Xmas 2020! Positives:~~~~~~~ +	Fabulous graphics+	Great storyline, narration and atmosphere+	Good tutorial+	Well-designed levels+	3 levels of difficulty and the possibility to customise your own level as well+	Fun and addictive gameplay+	Good replayability+	AchievementsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	No trading cards as yetBroken Lines: Plan and give your soldiers orders and see them being executed in an 8-second frame at a time! With a few choice matters elements and a fabulous storyline, this game is a must have! 9/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really wanted to thumbs up this game. The base game is OK enough. Not great, but definitely satisfying at times, and different enough that I want to support developers trying new gameplay styles like this. It's about 10 hours long and is probably barely worth playing if you want some tactical WW2 action with some story choices and very light RPG elements.The actual gameplay loop of issuing commands to your troops in 8-second intervals and then watching the battle play out is kind of janky and definitely can be weird and annoying at times, but is similarly satisfying when something executes perfectly for you.One of the biggest problems of this game is that it's always in Iron Man mode (i.e., you cannot manually save, you cannot manually reload prior saves, it is perma 'rogue-like'). _childDocuments_.review: It is an "ok" game if you have no better alternatives. The reason I gave a thumb down is because of so many super positive reviews with which I disagree and think they distort the picture here.TACTICS / GAMEPLAY -> 3/5The challenge curve is rather flat, mostly without any complex or demanding situations. Maps are all very similar in terms of combat challenges (very similar setups of obstacles, terrain, challenges etc).One of the top reviewers here complained about pulling extra pods in Xcom due to bad mechanics - IT IS THE SAME HERE! Once you spot 1 enemy then the time does not stop when you discover more enemies. So you end up pulling more and more enemies and your soldiers once told to go somewhere, will never abort the order even if going straight into the enemy guns.Flanking or direct assault in this game bring exactly the same results as in Xcom - you end up fighting more enemies that you planned to.TO BE CLEAR: you discover 1 enemy soldier and then the game is paused and you have to give orders to all members of your team for the next 8 secs. So if during these 8 s you discover 6 more enemies, it doesnt matter. You end up executing all orders regardless of what you have just discovered. And in 8 seconds a lot can happen.Explosives are useless: they dont really destroy much or hurt enemies (50% dmg of a snipers 1 shot) , especially that enemy is almost always moving, so good luck hitting them with that 8 sec bazooka. I wasnt even able to hit big targets with it, like tank. Besides, by simply using suppression / covering fire I can achieve much more - hold enemy in place and kill them behind any obstacle. Yes, suppression fire is one of the main killers in this game, regardless of covers... So, you end up playing always the same thing, some machine guns with range rifles and toss in a short range shotgun for extra fun and challenge.UNSATISFYING COMBAT - 2/5Basically the whole experience comes down to planning all the moves and possible interactions (your soldiers have no brain of their own and they will be shooting friendlies in the back repeatedly) and then comes 8 seconds during which you try to see what is going on with everybody on the whole map. So, you spend 99% of your time planing and then 1% "enjoying" those few seconds of action. When you hit "play" button all orders are executed in 8 secs period, including enemy movements. However, there is no replay or show me again or slow down options. So, soldiers are running on your screen and when you focus on 1 soldier/spot you miss the things that are happening outside your view. Often I had split team and was not able to see how my other team was doing. It is only possible to see a log after it all finish but its rather dull. I would like to be able to see again what just happened or/and slow down the speed of it. Otherwise you cant fully even enjoy the show that you planned so well.STORY - 0/5SPOILERNo matter what you do, which decisions you make, you will never know the answers, nor consequences of your choices. The story is irrelevant as the "random story" system implemented seems to be too random to create any value. The narrator is very irritating in the long run and brings nothing to the table.It is possible to believe that perhaps next version of this game will be much better if they learn on their mistakes.

_childDocuments_.review: This would have been a neutral rating if Steam had such a feature.Broken Lines is a unique attempt at making a story-driven phase-based alternate-history WW2 game. It's a genuine attempt at building something special, but it doesn't quite all come together. The story is interesting but leaves a bit too much to the imagination, the visuals are okay at best, and the customization of your squad lacks depth overall. The phase-based combat is quite decent, but has some quirks. One of the more annoying aspects is that the game recommends you flank enemies, but trying to outmaneuver them often leads you into revealing extra units that then get pulled into the fight, which often then creates more chaos. Overall, a decent game but not great. If you interested in playing a game with phase-based combat, you might want to check this one out when it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: After completing the campaign I feel like it's time to say a few words about this game.I picked it up on release day after finding out about its existence the day before. Something in the concept, the idea was very appealing (the alternate history, the WW2 weapons), exciting although I'm not a massive fan of turn-based games. My interest was fueled by the vague similarities with other games of the genre (which, of course, is pretty much expected) yet the execution seemed different.And it is. What you'll get is  turn-based combat, where the active phase lasts only for 8 seconds ; you plan, you issue orders, hit Space and, boom, 8 seconds of glory, marvelling at your tactical genius or your soldiers start panicking and run to certain doom. There's also some RPG elements, like various endings, shop with increasingly better gear, abilities, traits and some other stuff. Nothing groundbreaking but the way it's done works and works well.There's also replayability since you can't do all missions in one go. Random events that may or may not help your cause. Decent graphics, good audio and sountrack with some heavy dark ambient vibes. What's not to like.Two pleasant surprises: firstly, it's nice to see that this game is partly funded by Creative Europe. I remember going through the application documents out of curiosity a few years ago and thinking what kind of games are going to be done with the help of this programme. Glad to finally experience and play one. Secondly, every thread I checked in the forums had a dev answer and in most of them the devs were first to reply.  That to me is one of the signs of passion and investment. Keep up the good work!

_childDocuments_.review: Let me just say, I love the base mechanics of this game that pull a twist on the turn based format. I am a turn based game junkie but sometimes traditional turn taking can get stale. I very much appreciate the system in Broken Lines where you set up what your troops will do for the next eight seconds, then hit play! The great part of this is that your enemy is going to be reacting, moving, and shooting during those next eight seconds too, leading to some unexpected results. I also like the inclusion of elements like friendly fire, different cover types, stress levels, and height advantage.My only real gripe with this one is some of the style and writing choices. I'm completely cool with the alternate history take. That's groovy. But NONE of these characters talk like WW2 British squaddies. Not only are there some terribly anachronistic modern terms and military phrases that stick out like a sore thumb in the 1940s but the dialogue was clearly written by someone with no idea how people from the British isles speak. It really robs the game of a lot of the classic behind enemy lines spirit it's trying to instill. The same oddness goes for a lot of the graphical design choices which feel clunky or the choice of level music which feels incredibly out of place for the setting. A lot of the general sound effects and voices are also a bit suspect.So is it a superb game? No, but it's pretty good and it's something fresh. I really think this game has potential as something to build on and would love to see a more fully developed sequel or remake using the plan and go mechanics. Especially if they get better writers and voice acting to flesh it out. As it is, this is a lovely if flawed little diversion to try out if you need a break from X-Com and its peers. Get it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10 - Fantastic TBT indie for all fans of the genre+ Fantastic gameplay full of novel ideas and challenges+ Engaging difficulty curve that ramps up mostly to the end+ Great use of time to provide a sense of urgency to achieve gold+ Game could have been pause based but instead runs in 10 second intervals with pause separating each one+ Great deal of weapon/utilities to mix up strategies+ Phenomenal art direction both in engine and artwork with inspiring setting+ Dark mature story & dialog fleshes out the world+ Great fireplace chats and banter between characters+ Variety of enemies provide require different approaches for the majority of levels+ Very focused game with branching paths allowing for a different replay experience+ Mistakes are severely punished but game provides plenty opportunities for recovery+ Lack of manual saves provides a tense thrilling 'iron-man' ride+ Small indie team of a few dozen created such a gorgeous, polished experience - many kudos~ Most of character optional interactions are negative and cause loss (not entire sure if random)~ Shotguns weak; endgame weapons tear through enemies like butter - re-balancing could improve experience- Enemy AI a bit dumb and exploitable through lures and hugging level edges- Walk/Run/Crawl mechanics poorly explained - couldn't figure out how to use themWonderful experience highly recommended

_childDocuments_.review: A good tactical strategy game. The only problem I have is with the stress mechanic that cannot be turned off in the custom difficulty settings. The one thing I absolutely cannot stand in these kinds of games is soldiers disobeying orders and getting themselves killed because they didn't execute my plan, It really annoys me. I get that this is one of the themes of the game, as it's a bit of a Spec Ops The Line in strategy form. But you let me tweak difficulty to my liking in other areas, why not this?The gameplay is a solid compromise between real-time and turn-based. A the start of each turn you get to plan your actions. Each turn lasts 8 seconds. During that process there's nothing you can do, as the decisions have been set in stone, meaning you gotta think well before committing to ending the turn. The enemies move in real time during those 8 seconds. So a grenade that you threw at their position might not actually get them because they have moved on by then. If you ever had the chance to play Frozen Synapse you'll feel right at home here. I like this style of this gameplay a lot personally. A full on tactical pause is great, but it makes for a different game. Broken Lines is all about positioning, flanking, using special abilities and anticipating the enemy actions. It's good.The story seems very mysterious at first, especially if you keep picking wrong missions. However all you gotta do is to listen to your recruits instead of the veterans, and do more investigative work to understand what's going on. It's not that complicated once the cards have been laid out on the table. The atmosphere really shines through though. The enemies you face are intriguing, as nothing is as straightforward as it seems at first. I got in my opinion the best ending out of the five available ones, which really could just have been cut down to three. There's three extraction endings that differ little from one another, and make little sense with certain choices preceding them.The narrator as almost always in other media is freakin' annoying and should have been cut from the game completely. All she does is take away from the game. I kept skipping all of her word salad nonsense right before the final cutscene.I'd say it's worth picking it up on sale, but your mileage may vary on this. It's supposed to be played several times in order to understand the story... unless you luck out like I did, After that there's little point in staying. I'm yet to try the complementary DLC. But even now I'd say it's worth it picking up on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Bullets are flying past you and the air is thick with smoke and the smell of gunpowder. Another bullet grazes the box of crates you’ve hastily chosen to hide behind and small splinters of wood stick to your sweaty cheek. To stay still is to die, but to move out to get into a better position might mean death as well. Where should you go? What can you do to see the light of another dawn? These are the choices you will have to make in the tactical RPG, Broken Lines. Developed by PortaPlay and published by Super, Broken Lines will have you nose-diving into the horrors and hardships of war. This is no cakewalk in the park as the story begins with a bang and a crash. After narrowly avoiding death, you discover that your struggles have only just begun as you must find your surviving soldiers in a foreign land. You must never let your guard down as enemies can be hidden in the tall grass or the empty-looking houses. Similar to a game of chess, carefully plan each of your moves to anticipate how your opponent will counter. Unlike the average tactics game, there is no flat board-like arena to move your characters. Instead, there is an entire terrain to roam, explore and use to your advantage. Decide between choosing the strategic high grounds of hills and cliffs, or the safety of ducking behind sandbags and boulders. Just don’t forget that you are in enemy territory and they know their home turf better than you. Your enemies also do not stay in place as you move and will actively try to gun down your soldiers. One false move can spell disaster for your party. 	Not all NPCs are going to be enemies as an unfortunate side-effect of war are the innocent civilians involved. Throughout your journey, your characters must decide, defend, and or take from the noncombatant citizens to survive. The choices and the hardships the soldiers must endure eventually takes a toll on their psyche as the breaks between chapters will begin to reveal the thoughts plaguing their minds. Every decision is not made lightly, and the consequences of their actions will affect the squad’s bond and camaraderie with one another. This can be seen through the soldier’s dialogues as the further you progress with the storyline; the more is revealed with each of the characters.Broken Lines is challenging, thrilling, and will have you reaching for your eye drops after prolonged, focused stares. Much planning is involved and is certainly not a game for those who are looking for something more carefree or light-hearted. It is highly recommended for new players unfamiliar to tactical games to start with the tutorial and work up to higher difficulty settings. Once the gameplay has been well understood, your bold moves and astute strategies will be your only other allies. Will you be able to keep you soldiers sane and alive to the very end? Or will your rash and harsh choices lead to your downfall?   PROS: Very mentally stimulating, captivating storyline, great graphics/artwork.CONS: High learning curve, can be stress-inducing.SCORE: 7/10
_childDocuments_.name: Broken Lines

_childDocuments_.review: Story-wise, Broken Lines feels more like a ghost story than a realistic WWII game. However, as far as war ghost stories go it's a dang good one. Gave me Band of Brothers-meets-CoD Zombies-vibes. Weird combo, but I liked it. The characters are very likeable too; I ended up genuinely caring about them and doing my best to keep them all alive and sane throughout the campaign. The fact that your choices matter (really, they do) is also really neat.Gameplay-wise, Broken Lines sadly leaves some things to be desired. The combat system is pretty easy to learn, which is good. The bad however, is that proper strategy doesn't really work in this game: For example, you as the player are taught to always flank enemies whenever you can, which would normally be very sound strategy in any other wargame. In this game however, 9 out of 10 times there are even more enemies guarding these flanking routes than you would originally have fought if you tried to push through the dumb, straight-forward Rush B-way. I get that in a real combat situation no plan survives contact with the enemy, but it is pretty annoying that there is no real way to adapt and work around it in this game.tl;dr: I really enjoyed the story, but the actual gameplay felt a bit meh to me. Still, it's definitely worth playing through for the story alone if you don't mind some weird infected/zombie-like stuff and artistic license in your WWII game.

_childDocuments_.review: I randomly stumbled across the dev-stream for the release of the free Expansion: The Dead and the Drunk.I did not know, what I really should expect from this game but I was looking for some "fresh air" pretty desperately so I thought to myself that this would be a suitable christmas present to myself, as a joke.Oh boy, I was so wrong.Let me be a "Negative Nancy" first:The graphics between missions are not great. Some of the weapons don't "fit" in the hands of the soldiers or hang somewhere in the air.I've encountered one bug in my 3 completed (I lost count of the incomplete ones) campaigns: One of my guys went full "Come at me, bro!"-mode and charged the enemy on my comand - but T-posing.Well, I can't say anything worse than that. I really tried.The "fresh air" I wanted so badly was delivered by the games "WeGo" Mechanic- it's turnbased, but you have to predict for a full 8 sec round of action. while this might seem a little too unpredictable for some players, I think it's by far more manageable as a whole than other tacticgames approach of percentage-hitchances but you basically must kill everything on sight, or it'll turn bad pretty fast. (Yeah, I'm looking at you X-com2!)As a player, who likes to be challenged on a tactical level, I started the game and went on to play hardmode right from the start.I found, what I've been looking for. Again: The game does not feel as punishing as Xcom does to me, yet it's mechanics allow for important descisions - they WILL impact your game. They MAY make it harder. Nevertheless I was able to handle a run where I would go "maximum overkill", not careing about the well-being of anyone as well as another, where I tried to "just stay alive" the latter was my first one.Despite my 20h experience with the game and it's expansion, my last, havoc-wrecking run was the hardest, for the sole reason of my descisions between missions.Once on the battlefield the graphics are fine. I wouldn't wish for more. It's detailed, scary, beautiful and sometimes gruesome but it does not reach detaillevels that would seem overkill. The Artwork in general seems easy, repetetive and might bore some people.Yet, these simple cards are played to a perfect fit with the well-written storyline(s) behind it. Everyone of your little guys gets some personality over time and with that, their portraits might fit even better!But! Every Playthrough seems to randomize a little who will get a little more or a little less character and that leads me to the biggest reason for my review:The replayability. Some may complain, that this game is pretty shot. Well, it is. Once combat feels somewhat like "home" (or on a lesser diff. setting) you'll be able to finish a run in (far) under 10 hours.But the game engages you to replay it with:-A hand full of different endings-antilinear characterdevelopment-random encounters, which really are random and seem to have quite the pool of encounters on the backend.-The expansion unlocks different starting squads for itself after playing with a specific oneSo you see, I am really surprised by this game. I thought it was an xcom with another combat system and bought it. What I found is a loveable piece of nieche art that will give anyone who emphasizes tactics in their strategy games a great experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I get into the review itself, I'd like to mention that I received a copy of the game for free by the developer for review purposes. I also completed the roughly 15 minute long tutorial which was recommended to do before getting into the campaign mode and would encourage you to do the same to get familiar with the combat system and some game mechanics if you didn't play a tactical turn based game before or just want to be really well prepared. Additionally I only played the game on the medium difficulty setting. There is an easy mode for absolute beginners who just want to lean back and enjoy the story and also a hard mode for fans of the genre who want to face a little challenge. Broken Lines is about a group of soliders which get lost in enemy territory after surviving a plane crash. Look for survivors, any kind of hints on your location, ways to rescue your remaining squad members and deal with enemies which can approach you any time when you don't except them during your operations.The game is split in a linear path of missions that advance the story and it also features various choices that the player has to pick in many situations which will impact the outcome of the campaign and offer a nice replay incentive (the game has 3 save files). It is also filled with humorous dialogues which make the story pretty entertaining aswell and help to develop some kind of interest in individual characters which helps the player to get engaged into the game.Gameplay wise it really offers some well executed content. Every character can have a different weapon type (shotguns, rifles and so on) and also different skills like healing abilities, grenades or other supportive moves.It functions like a normal turn-based tactics game but whenever new enemies get revealed, the game gets paused so the player can react, adapt and cancel/edit actions of his soliders if needed.Aside from that the game has cool visuals and a good narrative voice wish tells the story and really helps with a good atmosphere in general. Voice acting and character lines and well done too.Overall I struggle to find negatives of this game aside from a mentionable 24.99€ price tag but then again I need to admit that I barely had any other experience with turn-based tactics games. What I can definitely say is that this game gave me a good firstimpression of this genre and I will finish this game after writing the review because the story got me hooked + I wonder if the late game levels will make me struggle. If you are looking for a turn-based tactics game that offers difficulty settings, a tutorial and a cool story for beginners but also a hard more for veterans of this genre and you like the fictional World War II setting then this game is definitely worth looking into!If you are a game developer and would like to get your game reviewed, feel free to email contact@dnbmedia.co

And, each campaign is about 10-12 hours of game play. I only played one campaign.  So, working through all the decision trees should take maybe 40 hours? _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: It's like XCOM mixed with BAC, without the good parts of either one.The art style of the cut scenes and characters is interesting. It's a mix between gritty and cartoony. But the 3D models look creepy and stiff but not in a stylized way. The story seems interesting from the 4 Missions I played.  I would really like to get deeper into the story but the gameplay is terrible.Its a turn based "breach and clear" style game where everything is broken into 8 second intervals but the game is not fast paced enough to do that. Unlike BAC it doesn't show you where your 'limit' is for the actions in that turn and to do any decent tactics you have to do addition in your head. You also only control the characters movement and special abilities and nothing else. They shoot at seemingly random enemies even if it's not the smartest move and you can't really stop them from shooting, causing them to reload at random times. It's way too random to do any meaningful tactics. Many times I would flank an enemy but my unit would refuse to shoot and the enemy would move of my unit would die. Also units refuse to shoot if anyone is in their line of sight. An XCOM style of play would've been better.Also some kind of replay or play back function is needed. Unless you keep your units tight together it's impossible to see everything going on. Many times my units would die for seemingly no reason and i'd have no idea why.There's no variety of weapons that is really meaningful and the characters have "combat styles" but it doesn't seem to have an effect on the actual gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: The impressions of this game reminded me very much of the situation with the other tactical game “Sword Legacy: Omen”, which arose in my head right after the final credits. If you take a scalpel and begin to disassemble each element of both of these games separately: graphics, plot, tactics, character elaboration, general atmosphere, then there seems to be nothing extraordinary in them. But when they connect together, they form a Voltron, that is, an excellent result, and I could not tear myself away from the game, it fascinated me so much. This is some very strange feeling, once again reminding that sometimes you just need to enjoy the games, and not try to criticize each of their elements.«Broken Lines» is a tactical game that takes place during World War II, somewhere in Eastern Europe. In the center of some inexplicable madness is a detachment of soldiers, which we will control, periodically choosing different soldiers on a mission. And the first thing I want to note is the nonlinearity of story. I approximately counted three completely different options for passing (and different endings, respectively), and far from the fact that there are no more. The player is constantly faced with a choice between two or even three parallel missions, each of which will lead the player in a different direction. In addition to all this, completely random events occur between missions, which also greatly affect the composition of your team. The game is filled with black humor; the fighters do not hesitate to fight each other, to say nothing of your poor enemies. It’s very fun to follow the plot, it is noticeable that very serious attention was paid to it.The tactical element of the game resurrected in my head the memories of my favorite «Brothers in Arms» series of games, where the principle of “suppress - bypasses from the flank - win” often brought the desired result. It is unlikely that any new heights of tactical art can be conquered here, but the game itself is not stupid, so don’t think that everything is primitive here. At the toughest level of difficulty, you will suffer, of course, but at the average level, finding your ideal squad formula and tactics, you will defeat enemies quite easily. At the same time, I repeat, this does not interfere with enjoying the game at all. This is a really interesting and original project, in which the creative potential of the creators who did such an interesting thing is noticeable. I definitely liked it, fans of tactical games would definitely recommend

_childDocuments_.review: This is kinda game you either love or hate. I personally find it weird. I can appreciate bold creativity with mixing lot of ideas and genres, but downside of "reinventing the wheel" is - it not always work. My issue is a general feeling that all is bit accidental, random, not precise, uncertain. Unit placement seems completely free (grid is fake) in diverse terrain and there is often no telling if your position actually provides you cover (or partial cover or can be shoot through - unless you clearly hide behind huge rock or in high grass). So... this is actually turn-based game (distance limit, time limit, actions limit) or this is (planning) start-stop game? You tell me. In planning phase, you have 3 possible move tempos, everybody moves mostly in straight lines but in 360 degrees and each activity takes different duration. So unless you are a math champion, you have no idea how your plan will exactly execute. Ok, that might be partially the idea - but if you compare this to ex. Doorkickers planning, you can see how this management is half-baked. The main idea should be I'm able to come with an actual tactic and see whether it worked or not, right? It's just... some action happens, but it's mostly more or less accidental shootout.  WW2 theme is barely holding, I feel like playing Walking Dead sort of clone (really, zombies again?). The game would benefit greatly if authors would keep real WW2 setup and all of the available choices could really shine then, even in this cartoon form. "Fairy tale" narrative voice is another weird addition to already mixed style. Jazzy looking Z's are also somewhat ridiculous. Levels on the other hand are good looking, they are polished, despite the fact you have to often zoom and rotate camera to get terrain right (as mentioned). If you look for a good tactical game in a cartoon style - Hard West or Invisible Inc. are definitely waaaaay better.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game. Really, I do. But the clunky controls are making it difficult. _childDocuments_.review: I would recommend Broken Lines for those seeking a simpler, yet more raw/ intense tactics gaming experience than XCom. If you're just a fan of third person tactic games and want to try something with a neat tactical twist, Broken Lines is a great purchase. Differences from your average squad based tactics game: - Biggest difference is the 8 second command increments. You provide your soldiers a series of orders to execute in sequence, then let time flow and see how they worked out. - Set characters means being able to bake in things like how your soldiers work together or interact based on your back story.- Your soldiers grow as you play, but generally not through going on missions but rather on inter-mission decisions you make. - Strategic choices you make have definite consequences. Do you try to accomplish your original mission? Do you try to flee back to your home despite what's going on in the world around you? The missions you pick will determine your success on whichever path you elect. Pros: By far, the 8 second command system is my favourite part of this. Tell everyone what they should do right down to the second which they execute the order and you can create a masterful symphony or a chaotic mess. I like this mechanic so much in fact, that I'd have loved to see it developed further right down to orders only being adjustable every 10-15 seconds, or maybe even only from the ranking soldier, etc... Contact with the enemy is messy, and I really enjoy the idea of starting with a clean plan, and then having to improvise once the bullets start flying. While simple, the rock-paper-scissors mechanics of automatic weapon-rifle-shotgun rewards a combined arms approach which feels great when it works well. Sure you could all just sit behind a sandbag wall and shoot till one side emerges the winner, but suppressing a line of soldiers while rifles pick off key targets so your shotgun can rush in behind their lines is great.The characters and their interactions may be shallow, but they all definitely have their backstories which reflect in both their individual abilities and story beats. As the game progresses, you'll find yourself having to adjust squad compositions because you have people who dislike working around each other, or because soldiers are starting to lose composure.Cons:It feels like some parts of the game documentation isn't completely fleshed out. It's not inherently clear that there isn't a natural way to re-raise composure (a key stat in keeping your soldiers happy and fighting), and that there's no way to salvage old equipment (yet there is a way to delete gear for no benefit to yourself). You'll be told about your soldiers being able to chat at night, and yet this won't happen until mission 4 (the first three missions are prologue/ tutorial missions). One super frustrating thing I found on missions was how the 'end condition' might jump out at you when you don't want it to. For instance, something you can do is scour a map for supplies to keep your troops fed as you push from mission to mission. If your mission is 'kill all the dudes in the village', and there are supplies in that village; you need to recover those supplies mid-firefight which the game does not warn you about. If you, like me, try to first deal with the hostiles before picking up the boxes of supplies, the mission ends the moment the last goon dies and everyone just goes 'welp, guess we'll head home and leave behind all those boxes'. Other missions may go 'here's a warehouse full of supplies, and in one of the boxes is the thing you're looking for'; at which point you actually hope you don't find what you're looking for right away because it might mean you don't get to grab all the supplies that are right in front of you, etc... For a game that relies on coordination, one frustration was that you can't tell soldiers to take one another's positions. If soldier A is behind some form of small cover (a block of concrete for instance) and I tell them to move up, I can't actually tell soldier B to take their place until soldier A has physically moved out of the spot because soldier A's silhouette is still there.As much as I loved the 8 second tactical planner, I did find it a little annoying at times where it wasn't needed. After the firefight is over, it'd be nice if I could just say 'advance towards this next point' without having to check back in every 8 seconds.I'm not sure if I should add it as a con, but choices feel a little too heavy which is only forgivable because it's a fairly short game which you're expected to play a few times over. Small decisions like 'should this soldier talk about her past trauma', or 'should I let that soldier keep the harmonica' can have major impacts on how soldiers play. In one instance, my star rifleman made a seemingly minor decision and became a pacifist (reducing her dps substantially) which felt like an odd thing to suddenly have dropped at my feet after investing so many abilities into her. In another instance, a soldier of mine needed to be held down as we operated on them despite their protests, and the reward for picking one of the choices was amazingly good but completely unexplained which again; felt very heavy despite something that felt like a flip of the coin.And perhaps it's intentional, but the endings feel like a very particular riddle that you need to have heard before in order to answer correctly. Did you grab fuel, but not go on the mission to secure an escape vehicle? Well then grabbing fuel was pointless. Why does my whole squad talk about blowing up the final objective, and only realise that they don't have any explosives after we get to the spot to plant them? Again, perhaps this is more forgivable because it's a short game and you're meant to play it repeatedly, but it does feel like you need to have decided what you want to do before you're asked the questions in order to get to the endings you want. (In my first play through, I tried to be investigative and helpful, and find out as much as I could about what was happening to the locals, and that information never really made a difference to my story line).Conclusion: Broken Lines is great. I'd love to see further use of the 8 second tactics mechanic, and the game play itself is solid. A little more refinement with tutorials and mission/ map creation; and this game would be a slam dunk. As it is, it's a great game to pass the time if you'd like a change from your xcom campaign.

_childDocuments_.review: I decided to play this on the hardest setting. I almost never do that with games. Too old and slow! :DThis was very enjoyable! Played Commandos and Hidden & Dangerous way way back when I had more hair, and loved them. This feels like a combination of them both, with a really clever and intuitive pause & play mechanic. But it's got so much more. Read on for more info (no story spoilers but mechanics spoilers follow - I call them spoilers, because they are introduced in such a way that the game reveals itself so much more - which is great).Even the camp screen is not just a place for equipping and sorting your team, this is also place for interaction and story development, so it all feels integral to the game, but unlike UFO Enemy Unknown, this really focuses on story at character interaction at that point as opposed to resource building, and equipping your interchangeable soldiers. That is one thing that is really great, aside from the threat of permadeath, and that is that characters get on or they don't, like in dragon age, and this impacts their effectiveness. Something that was never a factor of the mannequins from UFO, or earlier games. So, character relationships, and their state of mind, coupled with polarizing choices makes for interesting squad dynamics.The map has alternate approaches, which add to the replayability, there are mission choices that without a doubt you'll want to try on your next run-through.Great atmosphere and the graphics are very easy on the eye for an indie game of this type, great stuff.And always remember supressing fire is your friend! With Avery or Fry dug in and pinning the enemy down, you can really control things.

_childDocuments_.review: Get this game if you like: - turn-based games like XCOM- dark and atmospheric games like Darkest Dungeon- rogue-like games with permadeath- to do moral decisions that have impact- WW2 themeHowever I must also mention that this is not purely turn-based game, it is some sort of a mix of turn-based and real-time game. You assign commands to your squad, hit the go button and the commands are executed in real-time for next 8 seconds. After that, the time stops and you get to assign your commands again. I was surprised by this, as I expected standard turn-based game, but I must say, I really like this approach!!Combat feels nice and challenging (playing on hard difficulty).

_childDocuments_.review: Game comes recommended as it is fun, the story is engaging and it allows you to make choices within the story that affect the whole without feeling as if there are no actual choices (Doesn't make you believe there are massively different endings and not deliver). Fun and engaging story line, supply/salvage system, a lot to learn but simple to do so (learn once and done, not complicated rules). The system for having your troops wait after pressing E and drawing your mouse  farther away from the dial' center was not immediately intuitive. It did not help that the dial appears directly on the character who may be off screen or at the edge of the screen. Also several times because the dial is sectioned into pie slices my mouse went too high/low on accident so I clicked out of waiting instead of telling a character to wait, this led to people not being healed or running into grenades on occasion which is frustrating.Troops running into each other instead of going around is a bit frustrating as they jostle out of position. Friendly fire system is frustrating, all too many times my troops are shot by each other while moving and reacting to enemies (not during a planned attack), I can understand if I run someone through suppressing fire/explosives, but it's frustrating to lose half the health on 2 plus soldiers because the enemy appeared at the front of a line and they all shot at him when they clearly will have to shoot through friendlies.Make the dial glow/flash slowly on the options after pressing E and have a visible line between the dial center and cursor when an option is selected. Possibly add a text number for the time told to wait instead of just the blueish number on the dial which I did not notice for a while.Somehow I have zero achievements after beating the campaign once on Hard which took 8 plus hours, maybe this was because I wasn't connected to the internet?

_childDocuments_.review: Broken Lines is a turn-based strategy game with in an imaginary WWII setting. You command a unit of soldiers through a land strife with tragedy and conflict. The choices you make and the missions you take will have an impact on the morale and functioning on your team as well how you will interact with the locals and how the story will progress.I found the game very enjoyable to play. The combat system was easy to grip and interesting to use. The storyline was deep, well-written and properly acted out by characters. It had kind of silly retro feel to it from time to time - something I personally can enjoy. It has a couple of playthroughs in it, so you can experiment with the game a bit. All in all I recommend Broken Lines to anyone who's interested in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game for its fresh feal to a game mechanic but wouldn't recommend it for its staying power and replayability.I think they laid a great base for combining their system with other CRPG style games.  I could imagine playing DOS 2 in this style or POE.What I don't like is how harsh the learning curve can be and for me, it makes it less fun. Having to restart the whole mission on a first playthrough while you are learning the game is a bit much IMO.  I think that setting is great but for a game with progression of the squad maybe add that feature as an ironman feature, not a base game feature.I like difficult games but I would like to learn the game first rather than just get wrecked for a small mistake and then having to restart a 30-minute mission to figure out what went wrong.I finished my first campaign on hard and it went okay nothing crazy lost 3 soldiers mind you.I tried the first mission on the zombie campaign and ...well I lost 5 3 soldiers.I think having zombies spawning on top of your units is a bit much since the AI can react faster than your soldiers at times.Also wish there was a way to engage enemies better. Setting a trigger to open up on command rather than letting the units attack as soon as they see something insight. A lot of times I was able to spot the enemies without being spotted but couldn't set up a good ambush properly unless I timed it all perfectly for each individual soldier.Good concept mediocre execution. was good enough to check them out for a future game through.

_childDocuments_.review: + tactical game play with action planning+ roguelite principle without save / load+ the possibility of modifying the soldiers and their equipment+ part of the ability and perks are formed according to the decision in the course- lower variability of enemies- short campaign- The mechanics of the game do not have significant depth- monotonous musicBroken Lines is a tactical game where the player manages a group of paratroopers in World War II on an unspecified mission in an unknown state. With the help of event planning within 8 sec rounds, it goes through a short campaign, which is built on replayability, as it is not possible to complete all missions and explore all the choices within a single campaign.Each soldier has his own equipment and the main weapon, which determines his focus in combat, he can have special equipment in the form of smoke, blind, assault grenades, or equipment for healing. He also has various abilities that can be assigned to him within the campaign and traits, which he acquires on the basis of various decisions within the campaign and interaction with other members of the unit. Everyone has their own personality and relationships with other team members.In the mission itself, it is important to keep the unit together, to use every possibility of cover, a combination of tactics of cover fire and flank, differences in the range of the weapons.The mission is attended by 4-5 members, the tasks are simple, usually it is just about arriving at a designated place. At the end of the mission, there is an evaluation according to expectations and progress and gaining supplies.On the medium difficulty, that the authors recommend, the game is simple, one campaign is fast but the game offers replayability in the form of selecting other missions, decisions and leads to different endings.Overall, the game is quite a fun game with good ideas, but really short, so I recommend buying for a discounted price.

_childDocuments_.review: I finished it in roughly 6 hours which doesnt mean it is short on content.It is more like a "choose your own adventure" book where you get random events and choices that affect the whole game. I am looking forward to trying different paths in the future. And I will most certainly kill Fry every run.It was a deep, engaging experience. Choices were never truely good or bad, in the end, I went from doing the morally right, or at least trying to do that exact thing, to raiding a booze facility just to keep morale going because my people have seen so much traumatic and depressing ♥♥♥♥ it felt needed. Even poured myself some vodka.It truely is wonderful, engaging and has the right amount of holes in its story to "kind of" have enough to piece it together, but to know for certain you need to try different paths, different interactions and go with different characters.THIS is Story and Character Development DONE RIGHT and they DESERVE every cent they ask for. If you like gritty games, morally dubious choices, characters doing random ♥♥♥♥ just to not go crazy and a struggle between just staying alive, escaping and rescuing innocent people that may or may not want to be rescued. This is your game. Gameplay is fun and you can do a lot of stuff. My Favorites were Hailey and Connor and I don't know why but Irish Women always are my favorite companions like Cait in Fallout 4.Seriously Fry is garbage.. Attacks everyone, has stupid plans, constantly hurts the team both physically and mentally, he sucks at combat because his only "good" trait is being a bloody coward while his other one turned out to be that he is bloody great at bleading. Seriously Fry. Stop.Original:So far its brilliant. Difficult, but brilliantYou need to think, you need to evaluate, you need to listen to your team.Everyone besides Fry has something useful to say, their own skills, talents, quirks and thoughts.Everyone besides Fry is useful and fits a different role, sometimes you need to switch out their gun types to figure it out. Random events happen, choices are needed to be made to progress. Do we go into the village, to the mysterious gas machine, or the cliffs? There is no obvious right or wrong, the only certain thing is that fry will and I repeat HE WILL wound 4 of your characters in one single event because he wanted to punch King, the big, tough black guy of the group.That being said, the crew has feelings towards one another, thoughts about each other, they shape how they fight together, how they behave and what permanent stat buffs or debuffs they get. _childDocuments_.review: Judging by the way the game is made, you can feel the devs have done all this work with passion and love.The game has quite interesting story line, although in my opinion the things this story wants to tell us should have been explained better. The game has multiple endings, which are depending on the decisions you make along the road to your main objective. The dialogues are interesting, sometimes funny and they definitely are not dull, but there is close to none voice acting. Only one strange woman, reading a few lines by the loading screen who, again, could have been explained who is she. The encounters for sure deserve a plus, because depending on how you wish to solve some cases, can reward you immensely, or punish you very hard. The relationship mechanic could use some tweaking, as there is close to none possibility to change it. Only by encounters, and i think there was some way to do it better. The combat is pretty fun, and I always like how the game forces you to change the plan sometimes, or to try using a different tactics for each encounter. The variety of weapons which each has its own pros and cons. The graphics are... not the best to be honest, but I bought it for gameplay purposes only, so if you can just accept this fact, then you will get used to it. The theme here is little scary but it gives this feeling of being on enemy's territory. The AI is decent, and it truly gets better if you select high difficulty. Then they use different tactics and equipment, and you can even tweak the gameplay's options, for instance the variety of enemies, or how hard they hit. It is also worth to notice, that the game received a free dlc, which lets you to play agains the zombies. So that deserves some recognition. But I have to rant about the game' lenght. You can beat it in only about 8 hours. That is not what I was expecting to be honest...In overall, I really enjoyed  the game, and I honestly recommend it to anyone who likes tactical or turn-based games. I look forward to seeing how the developers get from this point, and what the next game might be.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved this game. Great mix of turn-based combat with real-time action. You set up the next 8 seconds of battle and then watch it play out. _childDocuments_.review: Hello Im Skill Incarnate and Welcome to My Games Review Series.My reviews cover indie games that i have bought, had gifted to me and have been provided by developers for review.In This Episode I cover a new title by  Games called Broken Lines.Broken Lines is a Strategic Turn Based Strategy Games set during an alternate history version of World War 2. The player controls a squad of soldiers on a secret mission who have been trapped behind behind enemy lines. Your forcesall have their own personaties and agendas with some of them wanting to complete their mission and others trying to escape the war. You have complete freedom in how to complete your mission and can opt for a quiet stealthy approach, avoiding combat or opt to battle your foes head on. Just remember that every decision has consequences for your group.This is a fantastic implementation of Turn Based Strategy in a more real world setting rather than the Sci Fi Turn basedgames such as X-Com that ive enjoyed in the past and will appeal to strategy gaming enthusiasts.Disclaimer: While this title was provided by a prospective sponsor I was not paid by the Developer for this video.Game was provided for review purposes.================================================Broken Lines First ImpressionsSkill Incarnates Gaming ChannelSkill Incarnates Gaming Channel on BitchuteSkill Incarnates Gaming Channel on ParlerTwitter:Facebook:Email EnquiriesBroken Lines on Steam================================================

_childDocuments_.review: *Reviewed by Aiori on On Broken Lines’ main campaign, you play as a lost military squadron in an enemy country, after a plane accident. First, you will look for the other members. Then, you will investigate if there are other survivors or orders, and, without knowledge of the current situation, you will encounter stranger enemies. Also, you will meet some allies too.On the second campaign, the most recent, The Dead and the Drunk, you play as your squadron in the same enemy country, but things start and develop differently. One of your local allies, Izkor, informs you that the dead comes to life as undead, and they are spreading along all the country. You decide to investigate it, with surprising and funny results.Both campaigns are independent, and they have some unique mechanics, making them enjoyable to play. Static images and dialogues narrate the stories, with characters designed with comic style, and a good load of jokes, making their development enjoyable....Broken Lines is a turn-based and time-based strategy game with a few RPG components, a cartoonish style and an important sense of humour, resulting in a solid and enjoyable experience. _childDocuments_.review: Broken lines is a.... Have you ever played 7.62 high caliber? Its a really underground russian made indie game with an unique gameplay, where the game is an RTS that pauses every time one of the character completes an action, which takes X amount of seconds or hundredths of a second to complete, like changing stance, running, reloading, and so on.This game isn't QUITE like that (which was dubbed smart pause system) but its similar. The game is actually a turn based game in which turns are 8 second sections, although if you suddenly come into contact with an enemy the previous turn and actions stops and you get the chance to cancel the previous orders and make new ones to not sprint into an ambush.The only complain i have with this system is really that maybe you wanna execute a new order after telling, say, a medic to heal the entire squad, and while that takes 2 seconds, you still have to wait 6 more before you can issue new orders.Other than that, the game is, from a gameplay perspective, fun, interesting, and well executed.The issues i've got with the game, however, are technical and balance-wise.The game runs like ♥♥♥♥. Now, i've got a 3400G APU with 16gb of DDR4 3200mhz, not exactly a supercomputer, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, between max settings and all minimum the game runs exactly the same. Sometimes i SWEAR the FPS is capped at 16 while other times the game runs up to 60 just fine. The game also needs a full loading cycle when getting INTO a mission or tutorial and ANOTHER ONE to return to the main menu. Getting through the short tutorials was almost a chore in this regard.One of the game mechanics is a darkest-dungeon-like morale meter for the squad. The more you restart a mission or return to a checkpoint the more drain the composure/morale will happen. Which would be fine if not because i've had the game glitch out and freeze the 3d image in a certain spot while the HUD elements moved freely, and reloading the checkpoints did nothing, forcing me to restart the mission... twice, all the while my save file taking the penalty from doing so.I cant tell if my UI and orders issue happened BECAUSE of my reduced framerate or independantly from it, but they both happened, so be aware that the game can be quite finicky about where you click and sometimes fails to register clicks.The game also tries to make you feel guilty about killing civilians, except that it does so terribly so. I've had a between-mission speech event between soldiers discussing the guilt of killing civilians and how many they had taken... Except that the map clearly says "0 civilians killed". The only time i killed civilians was 2 near the end of the game, and that's because their AI is incredibly dumb and will both walk into the fire and stand still while the enemies uses them as meat shields in true palestinian tactics.The game has a vendor that works as a resupply and store shop between missions, where he sells a few very interesting upgrade weapons and items, except that no matter what you buy, you cant sell whatever you previously had? Even if you delete it, you wont get anything for it, you wont get extra salvage (currency) for it or anything, all you can do is buy items. Very strange gameplay choice, considering you are unlikely to stick to any starter weapons.In the average difficulty you will have a few "what is this ♥♥♥♥?" moments where your shotgunner will take over 5 shots at point blank range to kill an enemy that is panicking and unable to fight back, although compared to other strategy games, this is nowhere near the amount of bullshittery x-com (new or old) or xenonauts players are used to. Thankfuly the AI shoots by themselves, and while not very accurate, put them in a firing line and even if they dont hit, they will suppress the enemies very accurately.The story sadly is not only... I dont want to say pretentious, but i want to say ominous while at the same time leading to absolutely jack ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥, but its also quite short. There are just a few missions, fun, of course, but the game can be completed in one afternoon if you know what you are doing. And while you get multiple endings, some requiring you to have done things rather early on in the campaign, they are just different ending screens to the end of the final mision, all of them bittersweet or just bad endings.Then there's the dead and the drunk, which is an expansion that adds a new campaign (which, i have not completed, but didn't seem very fun) and a... Minor new mechanic that could have been added into the main game and would have probably worked better universally. Other than that there's nothing. No workshop support, no mod support that i know of (but maybe the game playerbase is too small for that), no multiplayer, skirmish, extra challenges or mission editor. You play both campaigns and that's it.Im recommending this game more in a way to help support the devs which seem to be very friendly and into the community and they obviously have some neat ideas, but the game doesn't seem to be getting much more support now and its still borderline a technical mess. You dont even get to use all 8 characters at the same time. Honestly if you want something similar but maybe more refined you should play Partisans 1941.

_childDocuments_.review: Like classic rock done right or purist jazz done with technique and abandon, Broken Lines attacks the overdone genre as though it’s being done for the very first time. Attention to detail, clean mechanics, and an enthralling story make this game a rarity among WWII strategy dimes a dozen. My favorite element of the game is the conspiratorial/fantastical element to it which is executed with enough nuance as to leave the patient player on the edge of their seat as though they were reading an especially entrancing Stephen King novel. Company of heroes fans: pick it up. It’ll revive your dying love for the genre. PC gamers: pick it up. It’s a play that’s casual enough to enjoy but challenging enough to get you hooked. Lots of respect for the team behind this fully fledged strategy classic. Cheers!

_childDocuments_.review: Bought the game day of release and have mixed feelings, here's why.Starting off the story behind the game makes very little sense. In one plane there was no Command and about 40 soldiers knew nothing of the mission and had no map.Spoiler alert, both planes crash, with no explanation why, and no one knows what the mission is. That is a pretty shaky start to a story. One that the whole campaign relies upon, since you will be discovering your mission along the way.The gameplay is superb, tactics are on point and you are rewarded for fast and very aggressive maneuvers.On the other hand every mission is almost identical. Essentially making choices is a zero sum game. Some times you will lose something some other times you will gain something. Overall dialogue options do not really affect the game in any way in the long run.Overall, it is a great game to pick up at a discount. 25 euros was not worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is based just on the main campaign, as I have not played the second campaign yet. The game itself is an interesting title. It operates like a wego system, you issue orders and then hit play and watch the results play out over 'real time.' There are a lot of similarities with other turn based tactical games like Xcom, Jagged Alliance, and Warhammer: Chaos Gate. Players attempt to utilize cover and stealth to setup attacks, which include 'skills' based on either the characteristics of the soldiers personalities or their equipped weapons. The combat itself is really the core of the game and is both engaging and entertaining; however, the combat is not without its issues.For example, the only way for the player to keep his soldiers from firing their weapons at sighted enemies within range is to order them crouch while moving and to set rather clumsy pause timers at the end of movement orders. Combined with the fact that players cannot pause gameplay during the "pause" version of each turn, this made even attempting to use stealth or to setup finally coordinated attacks more trouble than it is worth. Between each mission soldiers are given downtime at camp, where some basic interactions between the characters is possible through scripted chat bubbles. Players can also use that time to use their salvage to get new weapons, do scripted "random encounters" that are only chat based scenes, and usually get to pick between 2 to 3 options for the next mission. While new missions need to be picked carefully as they impact the story and passed over missions cannot be returned to later, most of the non-combat mission portions of the game are pretty bare bones. Finally the game seems very short--it took me about 8 hours to complete the campaign--but there is some replay potential in starting a new campaign and selecting missions you passed over in previous playthroughs. I certainly had fun playing the game, and I can cautiously recommend it; however, I purchased the game when it was 80%. I do think I probably would have been much more disappointed with my purchase had I payed full price ($24.99 at the time of the writing of this review).

_childDocuments_.review: No time for a review so I give this game a rank B.Good game - if you have time give it a chance!See my profile for more details about my reviews.Additional notes: I am very surprised and impressed by this game! I thought it would be a cheap, casual, mediocre to average game, but it is much more than that, it just does not show it! Don't get me wrong though, it is far from being an amazing game, and it will be forgotten sadly. But for a Danish game (pretty rare, that's cool!) that presents itself a bit like a casual, almost tablet based game, I just think they got the wrong marketing/audience. Imagine a mix of XCom, Warhammer-like table+figurines war games, Commandos (series from 1990s), some comics/casual based tablet games and a bit of RTS-lite/War-lite games that you can find on Steam... so, lots of influence, a very interesting mix, but most of all a remarkable effort in the details. This game is packed of genuine and heartful details where I was like "wow! why would they put SO MUCH in a casual game? most players won't notice!", so, bravo to them for that ungrateful effort (ungrateful because I sadly believe the game never really took off). Between the heroes personal history, their RPG stats, their inventory, their skills, the warhammer/table combats with all the stats, the guns stats... This is a game that went casual on the looks but super nerdy on the inside, and that's such a shame!Now beware, there are a few downsides: the narration/pace is quite slow, I don't adhere with the voiceover, the game was developed by a studio which I believe lacks a bit of experience so it still "feels" casual on many aspects of the gameplay, sometimes the game mechanisms do not behave super oily like in a AAA game, people even report bugs in the reviews (none for me though *shrug*), and finally the difficulty is not super balanced (I doubt I will ever finish it with my preciously few free time: you may RUN through some missions because it is so EASY, but then you may restart ONE mission MANY times because it is so HARD...). So if you can forgive these (minor) flaws, for the crazy price (5 bucks at -80%! AND with a FREE dlc! how laudable from the guys), you will get one very authentic, personal, worthy of trying game! I look forward to seeing this studio's next games.

_childDocuments_.review: Broken Lines are a tactical RPG with an interesting real-time turn based combat system. The combat consists of approximately 3 seconds turns. You issue commands for your squad and sync their actions based on the time estimates. Once you end the turn, all the actions play out simultaneously with the movement and actions of enemy units. It's original, it's frustrating at time, but deeply satisfying once you grasp the concept. The story is played out in-between the missions, where your group of marooned soldiers (4 fresh recruits and 4 veterans) discuss their plans and develop their relationships in short dialogues. The personalities of your squad are interesting and likable, but the dialogues are mostly linear, sometimes with a binary choice, so even in my second campaign, I just skipped most of them. There is some basic inventory and resource management, but it's all pretty barebones. The campaign is about 6-7 hours long (12 missions of approximately 20-30 min, plus some campsite downtime) and it's clearly meant to be replayed at least once, since in most stages, you get to choose between two or three missions to progress your story. The game also has a number (4? 6?) of possible endings. It's quite obvious that it was developed by a small team with little previous experience, but I haven't encountered any game-breaking bugs. If you like tactical strategies or RPGs, but want a break from all the XCOM clones, you should give Broken Lines at least a try.

_childDocuments_.review: This game does a few things very well. One of the best mouse cam controls I have seen in this type of game. No jankiness. With one hand you can pan full 360 and adjust a 0 pitch angle while zooming in all at the same time. Its WEGO! Yay more games should either have a wego or a plan and go system. The map art is nice, well constructed objects and terrain, with depth of field. I found the vibrance a little heavy at times, and longed for the odd map with mid tones. Scripting is good for the AI enemy. Maps have limited avenues of approach, often requiring you to stick to paths, some branching terrain. Cut scenes with comic art adds to atmosphere for sure.What's missing. There is not enough tactical immersion in this game. It just made me want to go back and play JABIA (Back in Action). You can move soldiers and have them crouch for a cover bonus, but you can't fire crouched. In fact there is no stance control for firing, so no bonus accuracy for supported fire versus hip fire versus prone fire. No time penalty for precision aiming. Soldiers cannot be ordered to crawl. No bullet conserving, just unlimited ammunition with mag changing. The game boasts suppression fire can be used. But the caveat in realistic terms would be expending unnecessary ammunition, but ammo is unlimited. No tactical choices to make. You cannot even override a target selection. Your soldiers automatically select a target based on proximity, which is good standard feature, but we should have an option to select a higher priority target if required. This all makes things seem very arcadic. The overall strategy is limited to acquiring longer range rapid firing weapons, and positioning your soldiers to their best automated effect. - Which is certainly valid, but that's it, that's all.
