_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to give a positive review for this game, but I can't. I hope some of the developers read this, because I will list a lot of issues this (in general great) game has. In advance: I am very alone with my opinion, that AoE III is the best part of the AoE series. The graphics (even in the old version) were great, the physics (escpecially in combat) are awesome for an RTS, music and sound was elevated, and I loved the evolved gameplay with the home town setting and card deck technique. That makes the strategy deeper and more interesting to me, BUT:1. The game crashes all the time. I couldn't finish a specific mission, when I get to close to the enemy's headquater which I head to destroy (I had to destroy it from the distance to proceed in the campaign). Now I am playing the Asian Dynasties addon. It always craches in mission 1, when I get to close to the castle of Osaka. Cannot finish the mission/campaign/game. Makes me very angry.2. The translation is a catastrophe. I play the German version. The main game is fine, but the addon "the warchiefs" is hell on earth. As some of you know, the were new translations (voice/text) added, to make the historic aspect more accurate (espescially on native american's point of view). I am fine to that in general, but in the sequences shown between the missions, the main character you play talks German (new translated text, subtitle correspondents), but the person he talks to, answers still in English (old untranslated text, subtitle is German, but old version of text, too). Nothing fits together. Not a single discussion makes sense. So even if you play in English only, the text passages do not fit together either. How could this pass QA? Very bad job, because easy to find out.Additionally the main character and some other units respond still in English (in German version), if you select them within the missions (some are translated). No big deal, but strange as well.3. AI: I cannot tell about the multiplayer-AI so far, because I haven't tested it, but in the campaigns the AI is horrible (I read somewhere else that this is the same in multiplayer matches). I play on hard mode and in most (not all) missions, the AI does not attack properly and act very strange. Sometimes it is very easy to defeat, in other mission the enemy just produces a huge amount of units, but does not attack, so if you attack them, you will face a huge army in their base, which is sometimes to hard to defeat. Sometimes the enemy army get stuck, too and cannot leave the enemy base.4. Bugs, bugs, bugs. I work as a developer myself and I know, that not all bugs can be found until a final release, but there are so many minor bugs, that I am really wondering why nobody took care of them. 4.1: If you get new trading-cards and want to put them in your deck. You cannot do this immediately, because the new cards are marked as "already selected" (but do not appear inside the deck). You have to uncheck the new card and select it again, to add it to the deck. Otherwise you cannot use it in the next mission.4.2: A couple of times some units in the missions get stuck. Mine and enemies' units, too. In one mission my main character was stuck in a buildling after establishing an outpost nearby. Had to restart the mission. In another mssion, where you have to protect 20 railwayworkers (by sending them to a specific area in your base), 3 workers were not assigned to my party after sending them to the mentioned area. So I did not win, because I only safed 19 until then.In another mission, only a couple of the rescued allies were assigned to my party afterwards.4.3: As mentioned above, the game crashes (at least on my win10, intel i7, gtx 970, 64 gb ram) often.Summary: I love AoE3 and love that they made an even better looking definitive edition. I really wanted to recommend it to other people until I played the main campaign. After playing the warchief campaign I was struggling, because so many obvious bugs and problems cannot be ignored, but nothing was a huge game changer until then. But when I started the Asian Dynasties campaign and problems won't stop. The campaign cannot be finished because crashes are continuing, I cannot recommend this (in general awesome) game, to anyone else. If you love AoE as I do, you should wait until some major pathches are out or play something else instead. The (by many people) hated EA company did an aweseme job on the C&C remaster collection. I can really recommend it! That is how remastered version should be done.Dear developers: Bad job so far. Shame on you to release such an unfinished bugversion. Do you want to lose your reputation as Blizzard Entertainment did with "Warcraft III Reforged"? You almost did. If you do not want to lose your fanbase, I wish you would fix this soon. I, myself, will not buy any of your products again (the same I did with blizzard games) until this version works as good as AoE I & II DE. Poor times we are living in, when even EA does better remasters than Blizzard and Microsoft/EssembledStudios.Update No. I (10/24/2020): Essembled Studios released Update 3352 a few days ago which just should have fixed some problems including many causes for crashing. I would recommend the game if this patch solved the major problems, but it did not. The game still crashes in Asian Dynasties misson 1 all the time. Additionaly it crashed in some "historic missions". In the russian historic mission all enemy units were stuck in a small outpost, so when I attacked this outpost, dozens of enemy units attacked me. And more minor bugs like:Some of my units also get stucked a lot. I could not get some sheep from a farm, because only 1 of 4 did not stuck at the fence. I could not use three units of my own, because the were placed under my fort. I could not use a worker, because he was stuck between a tree and a building. a.m.m.As long as the major craches and some pathfinding improvements weren't patched, I keep up with my negative review. Update No. I (10/29/2020): Essembled Studios released a Hotfix (second patch in such a short time), which should solve a lot of crashing issues many players from the coomunity have reported. There seem to be a lot of gamers with problems similar to mine. Would love to tell you, I could change my review, but I can't. Asian Dynasty Mission 1 still crashes the game.Update No. II (11/05/2020): After a hotfix and a second update by Essembled Studios within a short period, I am far less angry about the game. I sent an official bugreport via aoe-website and after a couple of days my biggest issue (that I could not finish the game, because the mission "Siege of Osaka" crached all the time) was fixed.Now, after I could finish the game finally, I can recommend it to others, because as mentioned above the game in general is great. BUT: There are still some crashes (I had to restart the game sometimes, but then it worked). And there are still a lot of minor bugs, especially for pathfinding of units that get stuck sometimes.I do not know, if the transalations issues mentioned above are still in the game, because I haven't replayed those mission, but in the end, I can recommend this game with at least 4/5 stars. Hope that the final bugs will be fixed soon (major update was released today).Nevertheless it is sad, that gamers had to deal with such buggy games on release date. But this is the same for almost every game nowadays. No good job here by the developers, but thank to them for fixing all bugs very soon!

_childDocuments_.review: Solid entry or re-entry to the RTS market.  I've played all of them from back in the 90s to this one before it was turned into a DE.  I love the original and the 2nd one to death but not needing resource drop off points was one of the biggest improvements to this series.  More focus on tactics and battle and less on economy.  This isn't to say you can ignore economy, build orders and resources are definitely important but less so than previously.I think they did a fantastic job at the remaster and adding in new civs.  That being said, some of the new civs are way to gimicky and complex.  I play to relax as the older I get the slower I get.  For me, the USA and other civs have too much RNG for what you may get and the build orders are so strict that it isn't fun, at least for me.  If that's your thing, then this is right up your alley.  Overall, RTS these days are often drowned out due to the Gen Z desire for the next Call of Duty 800,000 or Battlefield 9,000,000.  It's refreshing to see a company target their older gamers a well as new ones trying to get into the RTS field.  This is about as modern as it gets for a classic game.  Give it a shot, you won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: I played Age of Empires 3 for the first time in 2005. My machine at the time was not powerful enough to handle this game, so I went back to AOE II. 17 years later, I picked up this game on Steam.I paid $5.99 for the definitive edition, which includes Warchiefs and Asian Dynasties. I also purchased the United States Civilization for $2.49. I am yet to play any skirmish matches with United States Civilization. I played all the story missions including the expansions. I am by no means a strategy games expert. I do not play PvP. I wanted to play all the campaign missions, and because the game was on sale, I decided to take a chance. I am glad I did because I thoroughly enjoyed my time with the game. The main campaign missions are quite well done. The story begins during the early settlement of the new world, and goes all the way to the founding of America. There are some very interesting missions here. The expansions are also quite well done for the most part. The highlight of the expansions for me were the Japanese missions.There is something aesthetically pleasing about the Japanese setting. I liked the Chinese missions the least. There is nothing particularly wrong with them, I just did not find them very interesting. The Indian missions are quite good too, but the story is rather comical. They made The East India Company the cartoon villain and whether there is any truth to this, I am not sure. It did not stop me from having a decent time with the missions. Graphics in the game are excellent. The snow covered landscape of New England, desert canyons of the south west, tropical jungles of South America, the visuals are very striking. I do not know if this is because of HD textures that were added in the modern edition or if they always looked this good. Explosions, water effects, and physics in game are all very well done. In addition to excellent graphics it also works great at ultra wide resolution. I played this game at 3440x1440 resolution, and it ran perfectly fine. I also occasionally played it at 1080p in windowed mode. I was very pleased with the graphics and gameplay options. I wish all PC games implemented options like this. Gameplay is much the same as the previous versions. There are certain choices that focus on efficiency, which may not be well liked by veterans. I am ambivalent to this change. Logging camps and mining camps are no longer needed to collect resources.In fact resource gathering is far more rudimentary now than it was in AOE II. There are only 3 resources to gather - food, wood and gold. Other than wood, there are infinite options for both food and gold. In Asian Dynasties, rice paddy can be used to farm food and gold. It's rather bizarre, but it's not game breaking or anything. There are some odd choices made with unit production. Indian villagers require wood instead of food. Seems rather arbitrary. Naval combat in this game is very underwhelming. The scale of the map does not allow for large- scale naval battles. AOE II did this a lot better. The map scale is smaller than AOE II. Certain AOE II maps are absolutely massive such as Bukhara and Dos Pilas. No such maps exist in AOE III. It's not a deal breaker, but the advance in technology did not bring us bigger, better maps. It took well over 60 hours for me to get through the entire campaign (including the expansions). I totally got my money’s worth. In hindsight, I should not have purchased the DLC for it. I don't see myself going back to playing skirmish matches. I am currently playing AOE2 Definitive Edition. I think overall, I enjoy AOE2 more than AOE3, but you can't go wrong for the price. I look forward to playing AOE I and AOE IV some day. For the price I paid for it, I recommend this game. + Visuals+ Graphics & gameplay options+ Interesting main campaign+ Expansions- Smaller scale maps- Naval combat- Arbitrary choices for resource requirement

_childDocuments_.review: 50 Minute Presentation review: This  game is an apology to the original AOE III - because it had historical inaccuracies. I loved the original, but I love this one EVEN MORE :) because it's really crisp, for 2020. Strategy has been re-lit , like an Olympic torch. AOE IV< is probably going to be gob-smacking.While each definitive edition tries to improve on the old, also by including all DLC's in the packages, sometimes the redefining of the old engine can only go so far, but it just continues to get better.Strategy in 2005 was either this, Warcraft 3, or Lord of the Rings Battle for Middle Earth, with 2 and DLC, following in the next 2 years. It was great, and then MOBA's took the lead. Anyway, this has city-deck building, RTS, tonnes of cinematics, historical accuracy, and precision, with LOTS< and lots of funny auto-dialogues, when you click around,Looks gorgeous - SSA by default - GTX 1070 regarded as 'very good' CPU - i5 10400 - regarded as medium - lol Streamed it while playing. Flawless.Strategy is highly required in mapping your armies, if you assign ONE slow unit to your legion, your entire army will die in slow motion - path finding - NOT AN ERROR _ You must not mix artillery, and foot soldiers, or melee heroes with cavalry. You will definitely need to be using the CTRL + 1 , 2, 3 , 4, Etc. Mappings to get your people in check. This can negatively impact your multiplayer gaming, the single player, skirmishes, etc.Firstly, this game is jam-packed with content. Historical content. Love. Lots and lots of incredible love. We start off as pirates needing to fight middle-easterns with bow and arrows, vs. their rifles. Feels very reminiscent of BF1, except, we're stuck in the past. Your strategy will require economic management, resource gathering, at a constant Pace.Shift + giving new commands in a row, or holding it to deploy buildings is where this game excels. Another cool feature was letting any other civilian join the build queue you create for one, as it's visible on the terrain.You can zoom in incredibly close.The image that stuck with me in the beginning was the cannon balls from my Ottoman bombardier rolling down the terrain after it based a collection of soldiers. The accuracy of animations of the cannonball interacting with the buildings. _childDocuments_.review: The first thing the game greets you with on launch is a little pop up explaining they've spent time consulting with representatives of the native American cultures and adjusted a few things 'for historical accuracy'. Which appears to represent one third of the work that went in to this remaster. The other two thirds would be some shiny new graphics which scale up well to modern resolutions (though unfortunately the same can't be said of any of the new UI's) and two new factions. All of the issues in the original, beyond presumably the offense apparently being caused by the bits they renamed, make a return. Unstable multiplayer code, missing features for factions that weren't in the original game and the AI's inability to comprehend how oceans work are present and malfunctioning just as well as they were in the original AoE III. That's not to say this is a bare bones, minimum effort remaster though. It's quite clear a lot of effort went in to introducing new problems and breaking existing features. The AI is a prime example. In the original, Settlers tasked with collecting a resource such as gold would shift to a nearby resource if one was present once their current resource was exhausted. In this version, sometimes they do, sometimes they won't, and instead simply stand around despite having another viable resource source nearby. The same affects building; try queuing buildings or building a wall for example and they'll sometimes complete it, sometimes they'll do half the blueprint and just stop. The AI opponents equally suffer such stunning displays of stupidity - sometimes it's troops will start attacking your settlement, other times they'll come to a halt at the settlement walls and simply stand there in awe of your masterful stonework. It also has a tendency to try and send it's settlers to harvest resources right next to your town centre, ignoring multiple copies of the same resource it has to pass on the way that quite notably aren't surrounded by angry men with guns, and to keep doing so despite you gunning down every settler they send. Then there's the stuff that's missing. One of the stand out features of the original was the pseudo-physics based destruction of structures and ships. Whenever a building or ship transitioned to a different damaged model it spawned debris which went rag dolling away from the structure. That's gone, instead they simply transition through their damage models until they fall down. While not the most vital gameplay component, it was a cool feature and sorely missed. However, it doesn't stop there; another big selling point of the original game was it's concept of the Home City - a persistent base you could have for each faction which would level up as you play, unlocking bonuses you could build into a deck for future games. In the original it was a neat idea which gave a little incentive to play both multiplayer and single player skirmishes, included in part due to the shorter campaign. In this 'definitive edition' it's gone, in favour of giving you access to all of the cards from the off, although the shortened campaign remains. At least you can still get some sense of progression via the cosmetic unlocks which are still available. For the original factions, the expansion factions and the two new ones are still missing them. Throw in additionally reported performance issues and occasional crashes to desktop to boot. So in summary, if you're looking for the definitive edition of Age of Empires III with expansions there's probably a bundle available here on Steam or your e-tailer of choice. If on the other hand you want a version with higher resolution support, modern graphics, half the functionality and twice the bugs this version won't fail to disappoint.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok i'll give everyone a tip which will help people worrying about frame drops. I have a beast of a rig and unless you limit the frames you naturally will get frame drops, pauses etc.Once you open the game go straight to graphics and set super sampling straight to 200%. ( If it lags a little bit, drop it to 150%) The game looks horrible in standard 1080p so this is a must. Then after limiting your fps to 60, put everything else on high. If you have a spud of a pc then just set everything else to low/off except super sampling and try leaving textures on high. If not drop it to med/low.The game runs flawless for me after limiting it. _childDocuments_.review: I feel truly saddened by giving this review, since I´m a big fan of the AOE series and AOE3 in particular especially the Napoleonic Era (NE) and the Wars of Liberty (WOL) mods. so let me explain why I cannot recommend this game and what reasonable expectations were:Expectations: Obviously this is the Definite Edition to a game produced a long time ago, so improved graphics, sounds and AI is what I´d call a bare minimum. Additionally it would be reasonable that with the many fun and good mods available for the original some more civs, maps and units would have been presented. And of course as a fan I was hoping that there would be some new improvements to gameplay from the previous mods.General feedback:Based on these expectations I can honestly say that the devs did do a good job with the bare minimums, so that the graphics, sounds (mostly) is improved and there are 2 new civs, and added historic battles and art of war tutorial. So this would be good news right!? and yes it would if the devs had stayed at that but no which I´ll list in Pros & Cons.Pros: 1. The possibilities for customization are great regarding the exterior parts such as graphics, colors, zooming, game display (However, TRUE original look is not possible).2. A very smooth and player friendly way to navigate in the home menu, great for finding mods etc and the home cities are pleasant to look at when looking for cards to send.3. Richer and co-created information on native americans and first nations Cons:1. While I was positive for the richer and co-created information for the 3 native civs there were modifications gameplay such as no mining for historical correctness and others more for PC such as renaming ages and units connected to colonialism (combined with the introductory statement) that felt more like activism than wanting to make a better and more authentic game since others civs did not get the same inclusiveness and consideration in the DE. There are still British Longbowmen in Imperial Age,  Ronins in NA Saloons, Mughals are just Indians, Qing just Chinese, now North and East Europeans have dark/black settlers, no mention of slavery or slaves (Plantations renamed to Estates etc). So while the original could be easily forgiven this one seems worse than than the original due to the massive amount of good authentic and fun units created in mods since the first vanilla version was launched and was omitted here. 2. The homecity card deck and leveling ruined. I know this is one that divides the crowd, since for those who play online there were large issues but for us who LEARNED to love the card deck and finds joy in  playing skirmishes just to try out new combinations it was THE ESSENCE of this game since it allowed for tuning strategies and tactics depending on map and foe. Removing the possibility to level just destroyed the game for us. a better solution would have been to have an option for online or offline mode so that we who enjoy leveling can have that. without leveling and all it does I can just play AOE2 DE instead. also the new technology tree is a mess compared to vanilla. with so much customization available why not have this as an option.3. Finally, while there has been a lot of improvements with the exterior the game seems to have lost a bit of its charm. this can obviously be an effect of hype and too critical community, but I think that AOE2 DE and C&C and Red Alert actually managed to keep the feeling of the game making it fun for both new players and old farts like me. Conclusion:While the game is not necessarily bad I still think that the original AOE3 or the AOE2 DE is better, so unless graphics is VERY important for you or you just want to spend extra cash for a good game you already got there is no need to buy this one. Sorry.

_childDocuments_.review: I understand that I'm in the minority here, but 95% of my time in the classic version of AOE3 (Physical and then purchased Digitally) was leveling the Home Cities and feeling more powerful as I played. I never played against other players, only AI. And if I played 'with' other players, it was always against the AI. (I also feel that City Leveling for Cards SHOULD be taken out of Ranked Matches, just kept in non-ranked. Halo Wars 2 does something similar, in the proper way.)A lot of my enjoyment was derived from unlocking things and trying to get more experience to see what new addition I could make to my cards. _childDocuments_.review: Update: Review returned to original after the critical bug fixed.Update 2: Readability upgrade. (I still have the same sentiment after years have passed.)This game is reworked edition of Age of Empires III plus its two expansion packs; The Warchiefs, The Asian Dynasties. It tries to improve graphics, multiplayer experience; adds 2 new civs; Incas and Swedes.Overall AOE3 DE doesn't feel as polished and complete as AOE3 or its expansions did when they launched. Worsened parts of the game surpass improved parts. Therefore I cannot say that this game deserves an upvote even though this upsets me as an AOE3 player.Graphics seem worse. Polygon count and texture quality of units and buildings are improved. But shaders, lightning and color palette choice are bad. It causes players to not distinguish units. Default zoomed-out camera also play a minuscule role here as it zooms out further than the original game. Even if you zoom in to classic levels, you can see details but still have difficulties identifying units.Wonders, common buildings, ships, home cities lack detail and look bleached. New added foliage is distracting and low resolution. (Note: This foliage is only seen when 'Foliage Quality' is set to HIGH in the settings. You may return to original looking terrain by setting it to MEDIUM.)Sound design and score of AOE3 and its expansions were brilliant. While they kept the score, sound design is changed. Artillery and gunshots are new. Gunshots seems to differ greatly between units, causing confusion for the player. This is an issue for a switching player (from original game to DE) and be nullified by time yet I didn't like some of these new gunshots. So I would prefer if the original sounds were kept.Physics like sound design suffers from intended improvements. In reality they are just a cheap knock-out, like an inexperienced individual tried to imitate AOE III's physics for its own game. AOE III used Havok physics engine and it looked so satisfying, and it still is today. Buildings and ships gave the impression that they have an actual weight to their breaking off parts, be it bricks, roofs, flagpole, ship mast. AOE3 DE doesn't give the same satisfaction as buildings collapse on themselves. Ships also collapse on themselves in DE. AOE III's implementation was better as they were breaking apart from their midship section into two parts and slowly sink into the sea. Physics of cannonballs stay the same. Burning effect of buildings looks better in DE.AI is absolutely worse than the original game but there is room for improvement as DE just came out. AI players tend to exclusively defend their base and fort; and it seems they don't have any intention to destroy your base and achieve victory which is sad because in the original game AI players would actually attack and destroy you even though their strategies to do it had it's loopholes.AOE 3 DE tries to be welcoming to all players. It's UI looks similar to AOE 3's yet is different. It is more similar to AOE 2 DE's as in placement of elements. There are three options for UI (Default, Definitive, Classic). Default UI is similar to AOE 2 DE's; Definitive UI is closer to original game's minimized UI but mini-map location is inverted; and lastly Classic UI is similar to original game's UI but not the same in any way.Reading units' attack bonuses is harder because of size, spacing, shading and font of the text. Speaking of UI game has a different pointing system which reaches to very big numbers. I see this change as unnecessary. There are customization options for player colors under Accessibility Settings which is a good improvement. Post-game screen is also changed visually, looking more wide and open. Text size is very small in comparison to size of text-field they have. Developers seem to throw some changes without making fine adjustments.Players don't need to level up to unlock new cards for their homecities. All homecity cards come unlocked. Yet there still is leveling up. These help you to customize your homecities as in the original game and also tell you that how a player is experienced to play a civilization. Civilizations come with a tech tree similar to AOE 2. Tech trees have some wrong info, incorrect placement of technologies and incorrect tags to them. These are bugs and I hope they will be fixed. Making decks is much harder because we are not given a tech tree. All cards are randomly shown on a rectangle window so it is really hard to tell which card does what, and which one is an improvement to another. Game also does not tell you why you should make your own decks, what the cards are and what can you achieve with them. It does all these changes to be welcoming while also expecting the player to be very experienced with the original AOE 3.There are changes to cards, units but they are not worth mentioning for a review. What worth mentioning is new options to Age-Up for civilizations. European civilizations are given some new politicians to choose. These options are detailed have potential to change how a match is going to be played and how a civilization works as The Logistician (II) for The British changes Manor Houses ability to grant a free settler to a free longbowman. There are also a lot of revolution options (16 in total. One option is United States which is almost as same as the original revolution option. Revolt into Hungary has 3 variant for 3 civilization bringing total variation to 18). These changes seem good, fun and welcomed. They need time to be explored if any of them can be exploited. What I'm holding my reservation is that we now have a lot of variation for a civilization can turn into. Multiplayer is revamped but not improved at all fronts. Players are now have ELOs compared to military ranks of ESO (Multiplayer system of AOE 3). There are competitive games and unranked games which can be joined from a game browser as it was in ESO. But players do not see how good a player in a game lobby. This was not the case in AOE 3. Also once you joined a game lobby, you are not able to browse the game list. This was also the opposite in AOE 3. Inviting a friend and finding a game is buggy. Invitations does not work at all times and invite button disappears forever after one try. Some games also don't appear on the game list. Inviting through Steam overlay (Opens by pressing SHIFT + TAB; invite a friend by selecting him/her on your Steam friends list then invite) is the only way works at launch. Players online started to report infamous "Out of Sync" error message appearing, as this was the biggest headache of playing AOE 3 online before DE. Developers said that this and other multiplayer problems will be fixed when DE is launched but this does not seem to be the case.All and all developers of Age of Empires III DE (and its publisher Microsoft) does give the impression that they didn't have a overall design direction in front of them. It also seems to me that different teams worked seperately and put their output later together. They tried to improve what they seem appropriate better or worse. They didn't have any art direction as the graphics are really not that improved. Physics are changed for a worse version, another unnecessary change. They did unnecessary changes to age names, civilization names, building names. I disagree with all those changes.Age of Empires III Definitive Edition could be much better product than what it is at it's launch since it carries a fan base older than a decade and already polished product. There were small adjustments to be done and continue in the direction of Ensemble Studio (Developer of AOE 3). New developers failed miserably, What we have right now is mediocre at best and this is a shame.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick advice: for starters, the game needs at least 16GB of RAM and a SSD drive. Close your game completely after a treaty match (especially a long one), or keep monitoring your RAM usage, people with not enough RAM get tired of the HEAVY lags and resigns prematurely. Also keep an eye on GPU usage, the lags are also caused by the GPU dropping to 0% use.Update III: Even though they tried to address the torps "aura" not being visible on certain terrains the bug is still present, in some maps the aura is not visible at all.Matchmaking takes a long time to find players and the service fails when it does.Update: Age of Disaster Part II.They fixed the cav box, and the BASIC shift+click on banner to select all unoccupied settlers however they ruined all legacy hotkeys, WHAT A MESS.They added "Ranks" on custom games (kinda), however it shows stats from Ranked games, if you have never played ranked your stats are 0.And now the disconnection problems seem to be more frequent. This is really an early access game.Age of Disaster Part I:Quick Resume: AOE 3 Definitive Edition is worse than many early access indie games on steam.Please note that my review is focused on Treaty game mode of the game.I will be listing first the "improvements" over the legacy AOE 3.+Updated graphics+Ranked matchmaking for treaty.and... that's it.Now let's start with the extensive list of bugs, design flaws and how Microsoft can ruin an old game that only cheaters made look bad.-How the system makes the teams in ranked matches is awful. I have seen the Top 20 players in the same team and 2 totally new players in the other with awful decks, basically you are condemned to 40 minutes of waiting to a painful 2-3 minutes defeat.To make the issue even worse, you can invite a partner before looking for a game, the bad part is when the TOP 10 players invite each other and are in the same team. No chance of winning or having fun. It is just NOOB-BASHING.The game should force Split players based on winning % and rank, and allow them to play 2v2, 3v3 or 4v4 only with other premade teams of similar rank. Using legacy aoe 3 ranks as template, right now the game is letting 2 brigadiers noob bash 2 corporals.-You can't check other players deck before starting a game, making worse the point above.-In some maps you can build walls over the water/rivers.-The game is a bug fest. One team gets to make natives and upgrades while the other not. One team gets to make docks and go fishing/whales and the other team doesn't. Which is a HUGE game changer, especially for Portuguese civ.-There should be a healthy limit on fishing boats, unlimited fishing boats when only a team can make docks is just unintelligent. A civ shouldn’t surpass 80/99/120 population either with fishing boats or settlers.-Warships going on land due to bugs-Legacy AOE3 had a bug were settlers got stuck on mills/plantations. now the bugs are even worse. The Hero/Explorer gets stuck in native trade posts, ARMY get stuck INSIDE mills/plantations, army in general gets stuck in walls (there are gates in front of them and they just stand still), settlers get stuck in trade routes while making walls/trade posts etc.-Memory leaks all over the place. After each match RAM usage gets incremented by 2GB, until it starts to show heavy stutters until you end up in the "AOE3DE.EXE" is not responding screen. After the last patch, the game uses up to 8GB of ram itself after loading the map.-Out of sync errors, and teammates getting kicked out 15-20 minutes in-game, sometimes even after loading the map.And that’s it, we can say the game is pretty much a disaster. UPD for Badge :P

_childDocuments_.review: Of all AoE games, the third was my favorite. I really liked the timeframe this game covers and the mechanics the original brought in.As the DE was announced, I was of course overjoyed about the news. Finally my favorite AoE would get a remaster.While the game has some improvements, unfortunatly for me as a long time original AoE player the deteriorations overweight the actual improvents.Pro:- The general graphics were improved, although there were also bad changes (More on that later)- The new Civs appear to be a nice addition.- The new options for european nations for changing ages is very nice. - The same goes for the addition of the revolution options.- You can use one home city for both standart and deathmatch. This is a nice change.Neg:- The new destroyed animations are just bad. While in a game from 2007 the buildings actually collapsed, in this "DE" they slip into the ground, like the old games from before 2000- The AI of the settlers is now worse. They often fail to get to the next ressource on their own, sometimes even stand infront of a tree.- The AI in general is also weird. They're very passiv. If they attack, their units often just stop and let themselve get slaughtered.- The pathfinding is still horrible. Select to many units in combat and giving them a new target still causes them to reform their formation before finally attacking the target again.- Also units can get stuck in the settlements. You cannot get them out of there again.- The UI is bad. Thankfully the option for the classic exists.- The main menu is not good either. The old version was very nice, since you could get from the home port interface directly in a skirmish. After finishing the skirmish, you could immediatly adjust stuff in you port. Now you have to switch back to the main menu, get in to the ports, change what you want there , then return to the main menu before get into a skirmish again.- The removal of the card tech tree in the home city is the biggest disappointment for me. 1 The new card UI is just horrible. It's all just thrown together without any real option to view it (You can order it either per building of per age, not both at the same time)2 You get all the cards right from the start. For PvP this makes sense, since you don't want new players to have more disadvantages then they already have. For the PvE players however, you nothing really to grind for. While the decorations for the old ports still remain (Native Americans, Asians and the new Civs don't get the options), this is nothing to get excited about.- While I respect the changes done to the natives, changes like the renaming of an age just because it has the word  "colonization" are just plain stupid.I hope this game will get some changes down it's road. Unfortunatly, this DE gives me little reason to play it over the original.Which is kinda sad, concerning how the other two DEs are.

_childDocuments_.review: In its current state, I do not recommend. (Edit, somewhat improved from when this review was originally written.)Graphics: Looks good up close, but blurry and unclear from a distance. In some cases the lower resolution textures of the old game look better from a distance, since all the detail doesn't turn into a blurry mess. However, the performance hit from all of this is borderline unacceptable. The game doesn't look good enough to require the graphics processing this demands.Game UI: The new stuff is 1 step forward and 2 steps back. The DE version moves the resources to where I want them at the top of the screen, but it also makes it so that you can't see what units are in your selection unless you click a little arrow every game. It adds grid hotkeys, but there is a fourth command line, for orders like attack-move, garrison, and DELETE UNIT. Since there are only 3 rows of keys, it maps it all the way on the right side of the keyboard. Oops, I meant attack move, not delete yourself.  Apparently it's too much to ask for grid hotkeys and consistent UI location. I guess I have to stick with legacy hotkeys, because having attack-move be "K" half the time, unless it isn't, is dumb. Commands need to be separated and unique from the grid.Home City: Well, they give you the cards from the start, which is how it should be. But I do not like the new way the cards are organized. Not a huge deal. It has pretty much the same customizations available from what I can tell.Bugs: Crashes aplenty. Literally cannot finish the campaign because it always crashes during the Russian Heavy Cannon mission. Also the same fun collision issues I ran into in the AoM:EE release. Your units will spontaneously enter impassable terrain only to remember it's impassable and then never leave.Overall, it's a botched release. This should still be called the beta, because the game is absolutely not done. Hopefully they don't leave it as terrible as Age of Mythology, but it's pretty much on that same course. I am disappoint.Edit: They have worked on some of these issues. Mostly the UI has seen some improvement, and improved customizability of hotkeys. I've seen fewer units get trapped in terrain, though the pathfinding is questionable at best. The home city card setup is still pretty garbage compared to what it used to be. The graphics are more customizable (you can disable the bad anti-aliasing that blurs everything) but still pretty questionable. God forbid a Gatling Gun fires, since it will kill your frames much more than anything else.

Unfortunately this game is a disaster . For starters the balance is completely unbalanced, Things like Aztec war rafts. destroying a European  monitor in 4 shots, mortars that have insane range ,mercenaries that are way too powerful for their tiny cost, forts that are far too plentiful.  Ships that move around like ice skaters and now you can't tell what they are transporting , walls that don't go where you want units that get stuck inside trading post with no way to force them out cannons that can shoot through cliffs, music that is incredibly stuttery and painful to listen to with new music not matching the style of the original , and a new UI that is messy and confusing to navigate. with things like unit history being crammed into a single text line box that you have to scroll through to read  Speaking of changes to graphics, the new units and updated art are very inconsistent in style  with some looking like they are meant to be realistic and others looking like a cartoon which makes me feel like this project was poorly managed, or rushed. The single player campaign has lots of missing dialogue,or dialogue that doesn't match the original witch causes chunks of the story to disappear. Odd, overly stern sims like characters that don't match the look of the rest of the units. I have  finished all of the campaigns in the original at lest 6-7 times , and the expansions 3-4 times so I remember them well and unfortunately this definitive edition does not play nearly as well and feels as rushed and messed up as the rest of this game. with broken home cities. crashy scenarios  AI that is to relaxed in some missions and so there's no challenge at all ,  secondary mission objectives that don't give you XP. The multiplayer is also a mistake , and while the original lobby was not amazing by any stretch this new one does little to improve on it with few options for customization, lack of a reason for new things like friends (no direct chat or invite to match options with friends) and filters that don't actually do anything when searching for a match .Finally, while I can appreciate the Devs' decision to update the native American, Indian and Asian Civilisations to be more politically correct , these changes don't seem to expand on or add much to the gameplay or even to the single player story witch adds confusing new things like the tribal marketplace for coin, instead of just tasking villages to mine  (witch dispite the information i found in and  interview with Anthony brave still shows Villages mining, making the whole point of the change redundant)If you are looking to get into age of empires 3 I urge you to avoid this mess and stick to the original version witch still functions properly .

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Age of Empires III gameplay, you'll like this. Fair warning, you are basically paying for a slightly better looking AoE3 with two new civs. Now mind you, if this was any other game you'd probably be ok paying $15 for two new factions, or rather you wouldn't be ok with it but you would do it anyway. Consider that, and consider that you also get a discount on this if you own Age III.A note on Historical Revisionism:As someone with a BA in History, and who understands the current political climate, I understand and support why you changed the names of the Sioux and Iroquois to their preferred name. That doesn't bother me in the slightest, and it really has only positives for people of those backgrounds and cultures to support their representation. However, I find it problematic that you are attempting to erase the word Colony/Colonial from a game that is about the whole colonial system. You guys felt the need to apologize for creating this game in a climate that generally had no issue with these words, and you changed them to appeal to changing political climates. What you fail to understand, is that at least your campaign does a good job of explaining the brutal and unjust nature of imperialism and colonialism. The whole India campaign is an amazing scorch of British imperialism, as the Warchief section is a scathing and honest representation of US imperialism.By changing terms and pretending this game is something it's not, all you're doing is attempting to conceal history. Terminology matters when discussing history, changing terms makes no sense. In the academic community, we don't alter colonialism from our terminology, rather, we acknowledge it for what it is/was and write or study it. Also, be mindful this game greatly exaggerates all societies and communities, and while some portrayals can be considered unsavory in our 2020 world, just note that the European communities represented are also stereotypes. Why is this important? Because it's a VIDEO GAME!

_childDocuments_.review: Age of Empires 3: Definitive Edition is split into two parts basically. The Free to Play part which gives you access to some campaings and missions ("a first look at the 'Blood' Story Mode campaign, the Algiers Historical Battle, along with the tutorial and The Art of War challenge missions" according to the store page) as for civilizations themselves, the countries you can play they rotate every month so each month you can play with some different civilization. Just like the store page says the Free to Play version is pretty much just a demo, a trial. To get the full experience you know more civs, being able to play them whenever etc you need to buy the Base Game DLC. Steam lists it as a DLC but from the explanation I made before its not really a DLC, you get the point. As for the game itself...+Its a classic game. Gather resources, build your city, build units, gather more resources, grow bigger and stronger and try to win. Gameplay is enjoyable.+UI is easy to use.+You have different ages these don't do that much, they do the classic stuff you'd expect with each new age you get new units, buildings etc. Simple, easy to understand, easy to use.+I really like the deck system. You have a bunch of cards, each does or gives something different to you and for some cards to both you and your allies in a match. There's tons of cool cards and creating decks is honestly one of my favorite parts of the entire game.+If I'm not wrong this system is specific to some nations but you can do a "Revolution" and become a different civilization in a single match. For example you can play as Russia, go through the different ages and after a while you can do a "Revolution" and become another nation like Finland. I'm not sure how many of these different nations exist, I don't know if this system is specific to some nations or if every civilization has this option but its there and its cool.+/- Of course the limitations on the free edition are not good but it is free so thats up to you to decide if its a good thing or not.-The rock-paper-scissor mentality is something I don't like. Maybe its just me but in this game I feel like its a bit too... Exaggerated I guess? It feels like if you don't have the counter to some unit you'll fail even if you have more units then your enemy does.-I don't like the native nations, tribes, civilizations. They all feel and look so similar, building decks for them isn't fun like when I look at the stuff they have, the cards they can use I immediately lose all interest nothing looks cool or fun. They all feel like they were copied and pasted. A few cards look interesting but it doesn't feel enough. I feel like they could have done cooler stuff with them.The free edition is, well, free. The gameplay loop is enjoyable enough, its a classic game anyways so not much to say. I'll recommend it because its free I'm gonna do a similar but seperate review for the Base Game DLC, edition whatever you wanna name it.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Age of Empires 3. It was one of my first PC games ever, and even though I was mostly playing PS2 and Xbox games, I still spent a really long time watching Mortars blow bits off of Forts in slow motion on my crap as hell Computer because it was good damn fun.But I cannot say that I can put up with slow motion mortars NOT blowing bits off of forts on my embarrassingly expensive PC in modern day in a 'definitive' remastered game.Bad frame rate, Boom beach art-style with a healthy dose of petroleum jelly smeared over the in game camera, pointless homecity levels, busted campaign, russian roulette multiplayer connection, annoying UI and glitchy unit commands, Main menu that sometimes looks like the MissingNo. Pokemon, Arse AI(And still unplayable on water maps too), Dog fart SFX(the new ones anyway), No Dynamic Building destruction or Ship destruction, Hilarious balancing, and even immortal farm animals(rare to be fair).This isn't even mentioning the cultural changes to Native American Civs, which by the way are all my favourite civs in the original. Most of these I don't care about, like changing the names of the Native Units(actually I liked that change) and replacing the dance pit, but some of them are just dumb. Like I'm sure you've seen people talk about the fur trading post that you need to make gold which is fine, but then why does it need to be made next to gold mines and why does it just destroy itself when the gold runs out. Makes no sense in theme and stinks of trying to fit it's lop-sided ideals into a game without trying to think of a seamless or clever way of implementing it. I don't mind changing the exonyms for various civs either, but they only did it to the Sioux and Iroquois and even then they renamed the Sioux to one of the tribes that made up the Sioux people instead of the name that represented all of them. Nothing in this paragraph was a deal-breaker though that's important to mention. There's a few people who are spinning the negative attention on this game to make it seem like the people with issues are just morons who hate the 'SJW agenda' and how removing the word colonial is 'PC gone mad' or some ♥♥♥♥ and how people have their feelings hurt by all the historical revisionism. I don't like it, but if the game itself was all in good order, I wouldn't care overall. I just wish they had poured their time and energy into other areas of the game is all. Like there's the above issues, and then there's some changes that feel a little pointless. Was there a reason to rename light infantry to shock infantry? Or is it to add an extra bulletpoint in a list of changes like a last minute school assignment?  I am extremely disappointed by this release. Age 3 is and will always be my fav AoE game in this(for now) trilogy, and because of how unique it is compared to the others I was beyond excited to hear it was getting remade and waited eagerly for it. AoE 1 DE didn't break my hope. AoE 2 DE was Mmmm oh so good and added so much quality to the point I can't play the OG version. Age of Empires III Definitive edition? Well, it doesn't feel very definitive when you constantly ALT+F4 out of frozen loading screens

_childDocuments_.review: This review is more or less  people have given this game. As mentioned by some people, the card system has changed (all cards are unlocked for everyone). Although I'm not necessarily a fan of this change, I don't find it a deal-breaker. Some people didn't like the old system and I respect that the developers tried to change it a bit. The 'historical' changes that have been made is also a big point for some. While some of these changes are unnecessary, I don't find it game-breaking or a reason to refrain from buying this game. Other people rightfully reported the extreme optimization issues. For me, there were no extreme optimization issues at all, and after the update, most optimization problems were solved (for people I know at least). In my opinion, the connection/playability problems regarding multiplayer are also a bit overstated, as me and my friends have no experience with major problems whatsoever. However, I have experienced some problems, which I will summarize below:- Hotkeys don't work or can't be changed- Pathfinding is a bit weird sometimes- The AI on water maps are absolutely retarded - Sometimes it is hard to find units/settlers - Gates along railroads seem to bug out and mess with the frames in late game from time to time- The multiplayer menus are a bit overwhelming - To my knowledge you can't join friends from the in-game friendlist, making that list kinda uselessIn my opinion, these problems are not infuriating to the point of having regrets that I bought the game. As others pointed out, there are a lot of positive aspects this definitive edition brings too. The game feels like the old AoE3, and I am sure that people who loved the original AoE3 will not regret buying this game. Especially because the most prominent problems are easy to patch. . Personally, I don't get or have experienced some of the negative points mentioned in the other reviews but I can guarentee you that's not the case for everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: if you're new to AOE, then by all means pick up this game (or better yet, the whole bundle it comes with.) $20-40 for a crappy port of some bona fide classics is pretty good. If you already own AOE3 or any of the other games in this bundle, then just don't bother unless you want to have some easy multiplayer fun with your friends. If you're on the fence, then read on and have a look at some of the other excellent reviews here.While some other fellas here have commented on the historical revisionism (which I frankly don't really care about as long as the game is faithful to the original in terms of gameplay), I'd like to bring up some very specific complaints:1. If you're used to the original, then the graphics will look like you either took off your glasses or just had some eye surgery. Everything is unnecessarily blurry and for whatever reason they seemed to have taken half the fun out of that classic mid '00s havok physics (ie. if you're expecting chunks to blow off of everything or enemies to ragdoll everywhere on every artillery shot, you'll be sorely disappointed)2. The AI is frankly too easy. If you're new to AOE 3, then ignore this. Otherwise keep in mind that "normal" difficulty is a few steps down from the original. I won't claim to be great at the game, but I recall the normal AI providing a reasonably stiff challenge (not hard, but it can keep you on your toes if you don't know what you're doing), especially for new players to git gud. 3. City management is somehow marginally more confusing than the original. Not a real beef, but pay attention to the terrible UI and you'll be fine. The default land deck doesn't provide you with any food (very useful if you want to spam villagers to get that sweet, sweet economic victory), but it has the factory in the industrial age, which is a nice touch. 4. By default, the keybinds make absolutely no sense if you're already used to any AOE game. Fortunately, you can change this very easily. 5. The godawful 200 unit cap is still in place.7. They have the balls to call this the definitive edition of the game.On the positive side (since I'm not a total curmudgeon):1. With the right configuration, you can set the keybinds to whatever you're used to (ie. if you're used to mashing "e" to build houses from playing every old AOE game, you'll be right at home)2. It looks kind of good in youtube gameplay videos, I guess.3. On a very fundamental level, the games are unchanged from the originals. They play just about the same, barring the complaints above, so if you're a new player, you'll be prepared for the original copies of whatever games you play here. 4. Given Microsoft's recent history of releasing kinda bad games, then patching them to perfection (all of you lads with the MCC from 2013 will know what I'm talking about), this collection will likely improve a LOT in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: After Microsoft created an absolute megahit with Age of Empires 2 20 years ago and recently re-released it with a Definitive Edition, part 3 of the series has now been released in a version improved for modern computers - the Age of Empires 3: Definitive Edition.The Definitive Edition includes the main game and its two extensions "The War Chiefs" and "The Asian Dynasties", like the "Complete Collection", which is available on DVD or on Steam or in the Microsoft Store. However, the Definitive Edition is a remaster, the graphics and music have been reworked, a few things (historical battles, two new nations) have been added and many details have been improved and modernized.Age of Empires 3 was released in 2005, when the golden age of real-time strategy games was slowly coming to an end. Compared to its medieval predecessor, it tried to redesign a lot of things and not just turn the clock back a few centuries. Age of Empires 3 Definitive Edition is set in the age of colonialism, with muskets and cannons now regularly available alongside classic weapons such as swords and spears. The result is quite a good game, although not as brilliant as its predecessor. Age of Empires 3 Definitive Edition is set in the "New World" (America) and combines a fictional story about Knights Templar and the hunt for the Fountain of Youth with historical events in Canada in the north to Patagonia at the southern tip of the continent. Eight European powers fight for influence in America, while the Native Americans can usually only watch the important decisions being made and are rarely really relevant. As a player you can ally with the Indians to gain advantages. To do this, you slaughter the tribal warriors and then set up a trading post in the Indian settlement. Only in the expansion "The War Chiefs" will the Native Americans play a more important role.The game principle corresponds to the real-time strategy standard. The goal is to create as many and powerful units as possible as quickly as possible in order to destroy the enemy. To do this, raw materials must be collected or produced, which are divided into food, wood and coins. You use the raw materials to build buildings, produce units or improve your civilization. In addition to building up your own economy and military power, it is also necessary for a victory to quickly explore the initially hidden map in order to discover locations of natural resources, treasures and your opponents. The game principle rewards aggressive, speedy action. It is important to use your resources in a targeted manner and not to waste them on pointless attacks, but a purely passive strategy is hardly likely to win a game (or campaign mission).The expansions change the game sometimes very massively. In The War Chiefs, three powerful Indian tribes are added as further playable races. The Aztecs, the Iroquois and the Sioux, each with their own buildings, skills and units. Each tribe has its own strengths and weaknesses - the Aztecs have powerful armies, the Iroquois also use European inventions and the Sioux are fantastic horsemen. Instead of a hometown they have a tribal council, instead of an explorer they have a warchief. For the powers from the "Old World" there is a fifth age - the revolution - in addition to a few units already available in earlier ages (spy, elmeti, ninja and others). Finally you can use a Gatling Gun and decimate the ranks of your enemies. The new Ironclad is also a powerful weapon to incinerate buildings on land in the shortest possible time. In the campaign, natives fight among themselves as well as against the colonial powers (Especially cool: The Battle of Little Big Horn against General Custer or the Aztec's fight against the Spanish conquistadors), but many missions are also battles between Europeans (inspired by the American War of Independence, Simon Bolivar's fight for freedom, The Alamo) or against brutal Wild West bandits transferred directly out of an western movie. In the second expansion, "The Asian Dynasties", three Asian cultures are added to the game - the Japanese, Chinese and Indians, all with their own units and buildings again. Each of the cultures also has its own campaign, from the Indians' struggle for independence against the British to the unification of Japan under a single ruler, the Shogun. The Chinese have been given a completely fictional story, with a huge Chinese fleet with a megalomaniacal leader landing in America to conquer it. Pretty interesting to play. Some game mechanics are changed a little bit again. The hometowns will be replaced by consulates for the new cultures, which will allow trade with the European powers. In order to advance into the next age, monuments have to be erected that will bring permanent advantages.In addition to the single player campaigns and newly added historical battles, you can also play a skirmish against the computer at any time on a map of your choice and with peoples of your choice. You can also use the races from the expansions and the Swedes and Incas, newly added for the Definitive Edition. The skirmish mode is probably the best way to prepare for demanding multiplayer games. Multiplayer includes leaderboards, own multiplayer servers and automatic matchmaking. Besides the standard game mode (Dominance) there will also be a game variant that starts with many resources (Deathmatch) and a variant in which no attacks are possible for a certain time (Contract). You can also set up King of the Hill games.A good improvement of the 2005-2007 released originals that is still a lot of fun and contains an enormous amount of playable content for both single player and multiplayer. In addition to the reworked user interface, even more content, a smarter AI and graphical and sound improvements, additional resolutions and zoom levels as well as multi-core processors are now supported. However, Age of Empires 3 does not quite come close to the borderline genius of Age of Empires 2, even in the Definitive Edition.I did not experience frame drops or other serious bugs, as some other users reported.If you already own the original Age of Empires 3, you certainly don't need to buy the Definitive Edition for the single player mode. But if you like historical real-time strategy games and don't know it yet, I can only recommend this game. In order to play the multiplayer mode, it is of course necessary to own the new version, no matter if it is from Steam or the Microsoft Store.

_childDocuments_.review: Age of Empires 3: Definitive Edition Age of Empires 3 was something of a different beast for Microsoft when it released in 2005. It wasn’t ever as revered as AoE2: Age of Kings and there seems to be this feeling that perhaps in attempting to keep it fresh, Ensemble created an unbalanced game. Despite that though, it was still a fantastic RTS experience in its own right and one that dared to shake up the established formula. Fast forward to 2020 and that daring approach may just mean that this title holds up in modern times better than than the other entries in the franchise.For me, AoE3 was actually the game in the franchise I played the most. This was primarily due to the fantastic campaigns that featured in both the main game and two hefty expansions. At this time, telling a good story in an RTS was still something of a novelty, Blizzard had some success with Starcraft and Warcraft 3, but otherwise, everything was cheesy and hamfisted (I am looking at you Command and Conquer.) This still holds true today and these rollicking tales of discovery and destruction are just as entertaining. What immediately impressed me however is the fact that as I booted up the game I was greeted with a screen explaining that the developers had gone back over the story, with help from indigenous peoples, and changed offensive depictions, improving accurate representation and overall making the game more historically accurate.  In my mind this is something truly wonderful, it would have been easy for the developers to simply shrug their shoulders and brush it off as a product of its time, so this extra effort should be congratulated.For those that never played AoE3 the gameplay, while very similar to the previous entries, has had some interesting tweaks that you will either love or hate. The first is the addition of an extra resource, experience. This experience can be used to purchase shipments from a custom made list at your home base. These shipments may be something simple like crates of food, a new cannon or a couple of villagers, but it could also be something like improving mining speed or increasing food production. This addition can throw out the flow of some matches though as often a match can be won based on the shipments sent, without the need to build up any sort of army in a traditional RTS manner. I feel like, while I adore the metagame of unlocking and creating the perfect list of shipments to help me in my conquest, others may find it a little tedious or unbalanced. The second major addition to gameplay is trading posts and trade routes. Trading posts can be built on set locations on the map and will give the player access to a native people’s units or allow players to collect resources from a trade route. This is a nice addition and creates some interesting tactics in the race to claim these prized locations.Graphically the game has had a nice bump. Sure there is no confusing it for a modern title, but the higher resolutions (up to 4K if your rig can handle it) and the addition of advanced anti-aliasing have given the game a much-needed facelift. There is nothing here that stands out as ugly or hard on the eyes at all despite the game’s age. If I could have asked for one thing, it would have been the ability to zoom out further. I felt a little restricted with my view and after all, monitors have gotten a lot bigger since this game came out so it would have been nice to be able you use that space a bit better. I am guessing that was just too far out of scope for this sort of re-release.Content-wise, everything you expect is here. The main game and both expansions are present along with a rock-solid skirmish/multiplayer mode and a brand new Historical Battles mode which recreates great battles from the past and finally the “Art of War” mode which present players with short battles that come with a set of pre-defined conditions designed to test player’s skill. Under the hood, the game has also received numerous tweaks, like a spectator mode for multiplayer, a massively improved UI and advanced AI (which is immediately noticeable to someone who has played the original release.) In all, it is a nice collection of quality of life updates and gameplay tweaks that make the title extremely playable in the year 2020.AoE3 has always been a little bit of a black sheep in the franchise and that still holds true. Some of the additions to the gameplay split opinion upon its original release, but I feel it is those very additions are the things that make this game hold up so well. I adore the metagame, the addition of trading and, of course, the traditional Age of Empires gameplay and can see myself getting addicted all over again. AoE 3 will never be remembered as the all-time classic that AoE 2 is, but it still deserves to be remembered as an upper-tier RTS title that dared to try something new. With the release of this definitive edition, AoE 3 may just reach the classic status that I think it deserves, but even if it doesn’t, I am glad to have it back.

_childDocuments_.review: I won't deny that this game is fantastic and I love it. There are many varieties of civilisations to play, and countless cards and strategies allow for a combination of play styles. It's why I have a total of over 2,000 hours of game time (including the legacy version of the game). And what makes me excited are the countless updates that happen from time to time, which adds to its sandbox gameplay. In fact, my best childhood memories were just casually playing AOE3 when I was 5-7 years old back in the late-2000s. Note: I'm only commenting on the game's team-base community. Not 1v1. However, the community of this definitive edition (DE) is not the same as the legacy edition (LE). Before DE was released, I used to be active in the LE's multiplayer community from 2014 to 2020. People were friendly, always willing to help others, and would often engage in conversations. This would happen even when both the lobby and the quick match had rank on. I remember the community being so nonchalant, even during its peak player count during the weekends. This was also the time when players could review other people's decks in the lobby, which resulted in two things happening. Players with poor decks were either removed or consulted on making a better deck. It's not the same with DE. Players have to rely on the amount of games they played, their ELO, and civilisation experience. But that can only go so far until someone on your team checks your deck after 10 minutes of the game starting, complains, throws a tantrum, and leaves. As a result, the entire game disbands. This really wasn't much of an issue back in LE, but it's one of these frustrations that causes players to become aggressive. Another issue that DE has compared to LE is removing the "ranking" system from LE. Almost every lobby was ranked back in LE, which caused players to either try to balance the lobby by low/high players "break even" into opposing teams. For example, two lower players are not placed on the same team but on opposite teams to balance out the game. The other was gatekeeping the lobby to similar skill levels. Sounds bad, but in practice, it develops a community of familiar/known players; LE players tend to be more polite and tolerant of each other because why make enemies with your regular friends? There were many times where engage in small talk. Often asking each other where they're from, what they do, how's everyone's night. This was when Europeans, Latin Americans and some Japanese players dominated the servers in LE. Now, in DE, most lobbies have someone worried about another player or their entire teaming being "noobs" or "idiots." How can you develop a community when players are accusing each other of being noobs? This only reinforces hostility between players. Additionally, the introduction of other regions brought players with a bad mouth who enjoy taunting players. I'm calling out South East Asians and sometimes Chinese players. I've never seen tantrums as stronger than them. When they don't like something they throw a fit, and leave the game to reinforce their point, which ruins the game for everyone. I spent 4 years, since the release of DE trying to be nice to them. Have a conversation, and mediate issues between players and myself sometimes. They just won't have it. I get that they want to play the game but don't go ruining it for everyone. It's one of the reasons why I left Company of Heros 2 after 800 hours of playing its multiplayer. The community there was so toxic. In COH2, you can try muting your teammates until they start team-killing you. In this game, you can try muting these players only to lose out on possible teamwork, future lobbies, or someone rage quitting. My last issue with his game is teamwork. It's dead compared to LE. Back in LE, players used to write in chat about their plans. Sometimes, it turns into a short military council. We would say, "fb (forward base) here", "fb mid", "this player is weak [with explanations]", "they might rush look at their decks", etc... Now, it's just silent. Chinese players normally keep to themselves and rarely communicate in English. It's cool as long as they understand what's going on or have a grip on the flow of the game. But it's truly disappointing to watch a team-based game become so quiet. Communication is usually left to asking their team to help them with/on raids. I guess, LE set the standards high in communications back then. In my opinion, the community is dead. My childhood game, my favourite RTS game is dead. You have a rise of angry players who distrust their team, new groups of players who are starting to make the game toxic, and poor communication. If you're going to play multiplayer then just play 1v1 or with a group of people you know.  Otherwise,  don't bother with randoms. I'm really tired of watching games fall apart, genuine aggressive players spawn and a lack of/poor communication with my team. I loved this game...once.

_childDocuments_.review: As a newcomer to the world of real-time strategy (RTS) games, Age of Empires III was my first foray into this captivating genre. With its rich historical setting, engaging game play mechanics, and stunning visuals, this game provided an immersive and enjoyable experience for a beginner like me.One of the first things that caught my attention was the game's historical backdrop. The setting spans the early modern period, allowing players to take control of one of several European civilizations as they embark on a journey of exploration, colonization, and empire-building. Each civilization comes with its unique strengths and units, adding depth and diversity to the gameplay.The initial learning curve was a bit steep for me, but thankfully, the game offers an extensive tutorial that guides newcomers step-by-step through the basics. Learning how to manage resources, construct buildings, and assemble armies took some time, but the rewarding feeling of progress kept me motivated.The graphics and visuals in Age of Empires III are simply breathtaking. The attention to detail in the environments, structures, and units enhanced my overall experience. Whether I was exploring uncharted territories, building bustling cities, or leading my troops into battle, the game never failed to impress me with its aesthetics.The single-player campaign provided an enjoyable way to hone my skills and experience various historical events. It was both entertaining and educational, showcasing the richness of the time period and the significance of different civilizations' contributions.However, as a beginner, I sometimes found the pace of game play to be quite fast and overwhelming. Managing multiple tasks simultaneously and coordinating my units during intense battles was a challenge. I would have appreciated a more gradual difficulty curve in the campaign or additional guidance in managing my empire more efficiently.Despite the occasional challenges, I found myself hooked on the multiplayer mode. Teaming up with friends or competing against other players from around the world added a whole new dimension of excitement to the game. The thrill of facing off against real opponents was both nerve-wracking and exhilarating.In conclusion, Age of Empires III is an outstanding game for beginners eager to explore the RTS genre. _childDocuments_.review: First of all I only played the original game for 3 hours a few weeks before the release of Age 3 DE, so I am not very familiar with the original game. So I will mainly review this as a brand-new game.The only thing I will say what this one does new/different:you get two new civs (Incas and Swedes), 10 Art of War Challenges (similar to Age 2 DE), but no new campaign, just 4 historical battles which are basically single campaign missions. So, that's not that much. Of course you also get better graphics and some little improvements. Compare that to Age 2 DE which added 4 new civs, the Art of War challenges, 3 new campaigns, ...Talking about the campaigns: that is the main thing I play. In Age 3 DE all 3 campaigns took me about 40 hours to beat them. (And I was very slow.) With getting all gold medals in Art of War, the historial battles and getting the remaining achievements you can add 10 more hours. That's not a lot compared to Age 2 DE which has tons of campaigns which take about 200 hours. Another benefit Age 2 DE has: you are already playing (most) of the different civs in the campaigns, so you know them at least a little bit. In Age 3 DE you are mostly playing custom civs in the campaigns (except the third campaign where you play every asian civ.) So, after the campaigns you have no clue what the different civs are about, especially with the new civs. Such a wasted opportunity I think.Now I will talk about the bad reviews this version gets on steam:-Yes, the AI is bad, it's too passive, rarely attacks and often sends vills right through your military or base; THIS NEEDS TO BE FIXED, but is not a reason for me to rate this negative-I haven't encountered a single crash in 50h, even though people report that they get crashes-I also rarely get frame rate issues, usually it's very stable; I mean sometimes you can get like 20-30 fps, but come on, this is a strategy game, it's very playable even with just 20 fps-it seems a lot of people are mad about the changes for the native american civs, I don't get that-and which most people don't even mention: some campaign cutscenes are broken: some are just stuck at the beginning and you have to press ESC to start the mission, and in some (in german language) the voice lines are totally different to the subtitles or suddenly some voice lines are in english, instead of german; that's not a huge thing but still annoyingNow talking about the game itself: Age 3 is a way more simplified game than Age 2, why:-vills don't need to drop of ressources-there are far less technologies to research and the one existing are just a few eco techs and military techs that just give your corresponding unit more hp and more attack. That's it. Compare that to Age 2. Loom, Wheelbarrow, Handcart, + the "regular" eco techs, blacksmith upgrades which are SUPER important (some civs in Age 3 have also a blacksmith called arsenal, but theese barely do anything and like I said most civs don't even have that), whoole monastery thing which is mostly missing in Age 3, all university techs like balistics which is so important for any archer unit, or chemistry, then you have husbandry, bloodlines for your cav, thumb ring for your archers and parthian tactics for your cav archers-you can build mills which are bascially 10 farms with infinite ressources and you can build estates which is basically the same thing for gold; of course theese gather ressources slower but in late game that's the way to goSome other stuff I am not the biggest fan of:-it's sometimes unintuitive or at least not obvious at all which units counters which one-the whole shipment and deck thing-you can train units in groups of 5So, overall I do think Age 3 (DE) is a good RTS, but definitly not as good as Age 2 (DE). Age 3 DE still needs some work, especially with the AI, but it's definitly recommendable for me.
