It took time, but it gave purpose and incentive to play the game. Some people are probably happy with this change but I am not one of them. As a huge fan of this series I am going to recommend this game, but only for one reason. After falling flat on their face with AOEO, Microsoft did an outstanding job with AOE II DE. The game had a bumpy start but has been updated and patched until it was up to par. In it's current state AOE III DE has game breaking bugs, specifically the crashing game. Of my 22 hours of play, 12 or so of it is probably lost to the crashes. This HAS TO BE FIXED. I will give the devs one month to fix the crashing bug before my rating changes to "Will not recommend." Around the holidays I always play AOE III, but all my friends are sick of spending hours building up and fighting to have it erased for no reason. If you ruin my Christmas I will never forgive you. _childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this by saying I love Age 3 and I think this is a good remaster. As a history major and lover of especially war history, I can appreciate some historical accuracy, and changing the Native American nations was something I was perfectly happy with. However, at the same time, the team behind the remaster has chosen to rename the Colonial Age to the Commerce Age and the Plantation building to the Estate. These changes were completely unnecessary and do more to take away from historical accuracy than add to it. Multiple mechanics revolve around the very real colonial period in world history. Chattel Slavery and the Plantation economy were evil, but they were also a driving force behind colonial efforts and the Plantation's purpose as a cash producing farm is a perfect adaptation. Colonialism and its long reaching effects are a hot topic in our current political landscape, but to change these very real concepts while celebrating historical accuracy is dare I say, hypocritical.Update: 7/19/22 After playing many more hours of the game and enjoying the new content for it, I have decided to change my review to a positive one. On reflection my nitpicks with changes were just that, nitpicks. I have enjoyed this remaster for many hours and will continue to put hours into it as the devs release new content. I am leaving up my original review for transparency but the game is absolutely worth getting.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who grew up on AoE2, and then later got interested in competitive RTS play, I feel that AoE3 is not really an eSports-viable title and the civs are probably a little too unbalanced (lookin' at you, America) to be a great competitive game...But AoE3 is REALLY freaking fun.I love the card system, which effectively allows you to customize your playstyle and build to the kinds of things you enjoy in a game. I especially enjoy that you can have different decks that specialize you in different ways. So if for example you're playing a team game in the pocket, you can build KILLER econ. If you're on an edge defending, you can build for a turtle style, or hyperfocus one of your military units.I love that each civilization feels unique with multiple unique units, and different core mechanics for basic things like villager construction or age advancement. This is a major draw for me, actually, over AoE2, where most of the civs have a sort of subtractive design (there's the big tech tree that everyone shares and each civ is restricted to only certain parts of it; their flavor is defined entirely by civ bonuses and their single unique unit/tech). The only sameyness I felt in AoE3 was between the different European civs.I love the experience system and how controlling trade routes is really important. It gives an important objective and a reason to keep moving out on the map to expand and defend.I love that there's only three primary resources instead of four. Stone always felt a bit extraneous in AoE2.I love the DE's options to change up the UI, and the other quality-of-life features.TL;DR: AoE3 is a ton of fun as a casual customizable RTS, and it plays best in that spirit, I think!

_childDocuments_.review: Where to even begin...I have hundreds of hours into this title, here are some comparisons from the original to the definitive edition.They have sacrificed core mechanics of the game in favor of historical accuracy despite never being a historically accurate game in the first place. The native civs can no longer tame animals, which was one of their coolest features, and the North American natives can no longer mine and are required to construct an additional building to be able to acquire coin. Changing things in the game to be more accurate and considerate towards people who were presented in the game in a way that was ignorant or even disrespectful is fine, great even, such as changing the names of the civs to what they actually call themselves, but changing core mechanics and lazily introducing them is not. This is an absurd and unnecessary change that is an insult to veteran players.A major pet peeve of mine is the change from colonial era to commerce era. Are you trying to tell me that a game, that is built around the theme of colonialism, around the era of colonialism and who's entire game play is based around building a colony can't have the colonial era in it because it is too offensive? Was colonization an awful thing for many people, YES, absolutely, but it happened and its what the game is based around, the game isn't making it out to be some glorious thing. This change of course does nothing to the actual game play so I'm not going to give up on the game just because of that but it is extremely idiotic and useless.Home city progression has been almost completely removed. You can still level up your home city, however, it only unlocks the customization options for the visual appearance of your home city and no longer unlocks shipment cards, as you now start with all of them. While this works great for multiplayer as you no longer have to grind of out matches to get the cards you need to stay competitive, it is awful for single player. There is no more sense of progress or goals to work towards and the main replayability of single player is simply gone. This is the change that makes me just not want to play the game, I used to love unlocking and experimenting with different makeshift shipment decks as I worked my way up to the more powerful ones, but that is no more.The UI is a complete and utter joke. The visual design of it looks as though someone made a bunch of text boxes in Microsoft Word and copied and pasted them onto the edges of the screen. The original AoE III had a UI design that was full of character and had amazing satisfying sounds to match. The definitive edition UI is completely soulless and had ear-piercing horrendous sounds mixed in with some rehashed sounds from the original version that somehow sound worse. To add on to this, the deck editing menu is nigh unusable, its essentially just a massive blob of the possible shipments you can use with very little sorting options. The original deck editor showed you what building the card type, what era you could get the shipments in and the progression trees all at the same time, allowing for easy location and identification of each card. In the definitive deck editor you can sort by age or by card type that's it, enjoy, and the cards are in a seemingly random order with no visual separation making it a long unsorted messy list of shipments that fit said categories.I've heard many other people mention how poorly optimized the game is, but I have had no issues with performance as of yet, so be cautious in checking if your computer can actually run the game. One last thing I'll mention about the censorship of history because that is what really makes me nearly down vote this game is that every time one tries to censor what happened in the past to protect the present, what you end up doing is denying the victims their right to have it known that trauma happened to them. There's that old quote that everyone knows, the one that goes "Those who forget their history are doomed to repeat it." Well...

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR If you're like me and loved AOE3 and quite honestly just wanted to play with two new factions in a game you have too much nostalgia for, you'll find yourself wondering if you can bear with it long enough to do so.I have a self rule where I will never preorder a game, I believe it is a bad Idea to buy a product you know nothing about other than promotional material that is designed to get you to buy the game, and many of the games I preordered were sequels to titles I found amazing, or made by developers that had a good history, and even if it would eventually be fixed later post-launch, its still disheartening to get excited for, pay money for, and ultimately be disappointed when you finally get to play it. Wait for the reviews, it will always pay off in the end.I broke that rule for AOE3: DE, because I felt like I would've acquired it anyway regardless, just to try out the new factions, regardless of how bad it may have ended up being. AOE3 was the first game I ever played online, I have played countless hours of it, online treaty matches particularly, and was always amazed that you could get into matches that lasted so long, like 5+hours, that the win would end up being a result of whoever didn't have to eventually go to sleep. It was a test of will as much as skill in some aspects. Although for the most part its just people playing absurd headbutting matches on choke point maps like Orinco because I guess just ♥♥♥♥ actually trying to think in a strategy game. This purchase reminded why I don't preorder games.Granted I don't have most of the performance problems I see a lot of others post in their reviews, with the exception of a few sound bugs, like seriously what in the hell is the noise the game makes when you click the fort towers in the the 1st Campaign mission.This is subjective as hell, but if you have a similar nostalgic view for the game itself, this issues I did have in my limited playtime may bother you as well, and I wanted to list them.The Graphics:As much as people like to spout out 4K ULTRA HD as a selling point, it is honestly meaningless in remasters that do the equivalent of bumping the graphics of a PS1 to a PS2 in the era of the PS4, are they better, arguably, are the close to a current industry standard? No. The lighting, shadows, water, etc, all the fancy effects that drain the hell out of a GPU are all definitely improved, and the framerate and resolution can now be much higher, but that actual models, the things that you are going to be looking at the most, are not that much better, they are just smoother. The screenshots do not show the problem several have pointed out in that all the colors seem to blend into one another. Funnily enough if you zoom in, the textures actually look nicer, because there is almost a layer of fog or distortion when looking at objects from max zoom out range, which is ideally where you want to be, you know, to see the map. I find the blend of colors with the smooth models actually makes it difficult to tell what is what from max distance if you are used to the original game's look. I mean hell I didn't even know the berry bush was a berry bush, If I wasn't playing on Deccan which everyone who played treaty has PTSD from at this point, I would have thought it was a tree. If you are having trouble figuring out what something is at a glance in a remaster of a game you have hundreds of hours in, I think there is a problem.The UI and Menus:In a game that is supposed to bring people back to a game they loved, why in the hell would you move everything they are used to. While they do have a legacy option for both the UI and keybindings, even with it "in the right place" things are still very different, stats are now always displayed instead of being a second panel, the unit card/healthbar is no longer in the center of the screen even with legacy, the game now shows you more of the map by condensing the UI, which you can argue as an improvement, but I personally never found it an issue before and now find it more of an issue that all of the information I want to look at is either moved or smaller, on top of the distraction of now having moving objects underneath the UI.The Progression:Completely removed, there is no reason to level a home city now, as all decks now have 25 slots, and all cards are available at the start, with the exception of customizing the home city, home city levels are meaningless. I know a lot of people may have had issues with that when playing online, but to those who did, you could always level online home cities without playing against other people, and you only had to do it once, the second one home city got to level 50, every home city you made after that started at level 50. As someone who actually liked the progression, getting stronger cards and improving your play style with a nation over time (offline), this is sad to see.Sounds:Similar to the graphics have massive improvements in some aspects while much less done in others, the sounds are a mixture of classic sounds and newer sounds, the two most notable ones for me are the cannon's firing and the sound of a building being destroyed. The cannon sound is different, I don't think its better or worse, just different. The building destruction on the other hand I have a problem with, its very loud, noticeable, and since its different you aren't actually sure what it means right away. It does not trigger the same "something just blew up" thought since every building had the same destruction noise in the original. Also in the original, the volume of the building being destroyed or cannons firing is dependent on how close the building or unit is to your current camera view, It felt like they increased either the volume of the noises at a distance, or increased the range you can hear it from, so now its quieter further away then it was. Because it hits peak volume in a much wider radius, it will sound like its happening right in front of you when its not even on the screen.All in all I think a mixed review score is pretty accurate, it seems like they were trying to build the game to appeal to newer players as well as those who have played it endlessly, and failed at both. There was no reason I can see for a lot of the changes from the original in which the only goal it achieved is confusing people who were already use to an existing layout and design, and then failing to offer a true "legacy" style design for them to use. Playing this version quite honestly just makes me want to play the original version instead.

_childDocuments_.review: The final remaster for the franchise,  (AoE3:DE), is an overhaul of the original 2007 edition, and comes with two brand new factions - the Swedes and the Inca - as well as adding a Historical Battles (HB) game mode (where you play through real-life battles), and the 'Art of War' tutoring battles.The campaign mode offers three - sadly fictional - different sets of campaigns to play through. Most of the campaigns were pretty 'meh', and I couldn't develop any personal connection to them, as I could in AoE2. So I'd say that having a fictional story is a real drawback for what could have been a key game feature.But all is not lost! The new HB maps were really well done, and I actually . Granted with a big opportunity, it is sad to say that the developers did not go all in, as there are currently only six of these HB scenarios. If more are released in future updates, I would be a very happy man. offers limitless amounts of time battling through single-player skirmish, or competing with and against others in multiplayer. This is a key feature of any RTS game, but admittedly  never really 'had me hooked'. I guess I just never liked certain game-play aspects, such as 100% accurate shooting 100% of the time and unrealistic damage multipliers.Another update in the Definitive Edition are the so-called 'politically correct' changes. These include the renaming of the Iroquois and Sioux civs, renaming the first two ages, renaming the plantation, as well as creating a whole new gold gathering mechanic for Sioux and Iroquois (they are now required to build a 'tribal marketplace' near mines and need to gather gold from that). I find these changes utterly pointless, confusing, and unfair - why make two civs more 'historically accurate', while doing nothing to the blatant inaccuracies of other civs?  caters to all your multiplayer needs, but not exactly in the best way. Multiplayer has been split into 'ranked' and 'unranked' games, much to community anger. This opens the way for massive imbalance when playing ranked, as you cannot even out civ choices or teams before the match. Differing even more from the original,  completely removes the need to grind multiplayer games to level up your home city and thus unlock cards. Honestly, this change was more a negative than a positive, and really reduces any feelings of accomplishment as well as lowering the game's replay value. Players now have the option to have four different sets of teams, creating a more fun and challenging game. You are also now able to fine tune your colors in accessibility menu.One of the most important goals of any remaster is to improve graphical detail and make a game more visually appealing.  has met this expectation to the most part. Buildings and artillery particularly, are now very detailed; however, other units are still not very tasteful to look at, and should have been given more effort. Ah, beloved zoom. Adding the ability to zoom in on anything has made the overall details of things stand out. It also gives a little more to do while waiting for that wood to be gathered, or advancing to the next age. Unfortunately, zoom has a single drawback. While zooming in with 'foliage' on high, the game lagged incredibly. Switching to medium removed an unnoticeable amount of foliage but made the game run very smoothly - still looking spectacular.Building destruction scenes have also been updated, and now are more realistic. Gone are the days of huge flying chunks of fort! I especially like the new flame animation, it makes destroying things even more attractive!I never really enjoyed the in-game music, and I have not noticed any of the supposed changes to it in the Definitive Edition. Overall it's just pretty mediocre, and could've been much better if the effort was put forth.I do, however, really like the new battle sounds. Guns and cannons in particular sound a lot 'sharper' than they used to, adding to the game's realism.  is suitable for anyone with a passion for history and RTS. The game is mildly violent, and there are no bodies being blown to pieces or blood pools to be seen (although there is a minute bit of blood that a trained eye can see when a unit is shot while zoomed in).I ran the game with all graphics settings on high except for foliage (this option caused severe fps drop in my game, so I selected medium for it). CPU: Ryzen 3 3300X GPU: Galax 1650 Super 4GBRAM: 16GB DDR4 @2666MhzOther: 500GB SSD Although minor, the game may sometimes have a quick fps drop at key moments - such as advancing age, destroying big buildings/ships, etc. - but is still perfectly stable at all other times. has new graphics, sounds, and civs; but has done little in terms of adding replay value or making single-player more enjoyable (no new campaigns (or real life ones), not enough HBs). I have mixed feelings on the multiplayer home city level grind change, but I think I need to agree unlocking all cards from the start has made the game less exciting and gives the player no sense of achievement. Honestly, AoE3 has been the worst addition of the franchise since it was released, and this remaster did naught but 'put lipstick on the pig'. I still recommend buying it for the many hours of possible enjoyment, but do not expect a long and challenging single-player experience. For US$20, it is satisfactory for a game of its content.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the HD version of AoE III, complete with campaigns, some new stuff, and graphical upgrades. We'll start with the positives first because I'm a positive lady, sometimes. The positives: two new civilizations, Sweden and the Inca, a welcome addition to the game. I like the graphical upgrades, though the new style for the characters is rather cartoonish, it's a nice semi-realism that I can live with.Some of the technical issues include audio glitches where there's no spoken speech even though a character in a campaign is clearly speaking. In addition to speech cutting out, I've also had game sound going out when it comes to building or unit sounds (e.g., clicking on a ship and having it make no sound). Other than the audio weirdness, which was in the 2007 version from Steam too, it's a welcome upgrade. I think Microsoft will fix most of that.Apart from that, I'm fine with them changing the names of the indigenous nations with the guidance of actual members of those nations. I'm also okay with the renaming "plantations" to "estates" and changing the "colonial age" to the "commerce age." I think the change to commerce age was because, for most indigenous nations, this period wouldn't have been "colonial" because they wouldn't have been out building empires (generally). As for plantations, I think Microsoft didn't want to go down the rabbit hole of slavery. I get both sides of the argument, but I'm choosing to just accept it as is. No one expects a strict history lesson from a video game, so it's fine. This is historical fiction, so based on truth with a heavy grain of salt applied. If this bothers you, though, maybe this version of the game isn't for you. I recommend it for fans, though, since the upgrades graphically make it worth it for me and Microsoft is working on fixing things (like the audio glitches, hopefully).

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT APRIL 2022: My initial review was negative. The game had issues at launch, but I can happily say that the developers have worked incredibly hard to fix all the major gameplay issues. Performance is good, AI is good, gameplay itself is fun and engaging, and we are getting constant updates. AoE III. My childhood. I was so excited when the Definitive Edition was announced. But in the current state of the game, it's inferior to the original.I don't understand the change of Native American civilizations. The Iroquois were supposed to represent the Iroquois confederation, and I see nothing offensive in using a name people can *actually* somewhat pronounce. You put so much effort into making native civilizations historically accurate, despite the fact that NONE of the European civilizations are historically accurate. You have Napoleon fighting Ivan the Terrible for crying out loud. But it doesn't matter now does it, since Europeans aren't minorities. Now to actual gameplay. I've only played a couple of games I must admit, but I can only pinpoint a few negatives. The AI: It's acting very... weirdly. In Age II it was building houses very close to my town center for no apparent reason, also sending settlers to resources very close to my base. It didn't built any trading posts and it didn't seem to build up as much. Multiple smaller raids, all easy to kill off, something very different from what I'm used with classic AoE. It's armies also seem to protect their villagers a lot more, which is good I guess?The UI: Oh God. It's a mess. I appreciate trying to simplify it somewhat, but the classic UI is a nightmare to use. all sort of extra buttons, the health bar is WAY too small, and other frustrating tiny things. I appreciate the further zoom though. Gameplay and balancing: I've only played European civs, and everything mostly feels the same. One thing I am greatly saddened by is the elimination of the home city XP system. It was a very fun thing to grind in SP, bit unfair in the MP but I hope they'll adjust this soon. One bug I experienced is that after advancing to Age IV, my town center disappeared. I have no clue why, it didn't get deleted, still showed on the minimap, and received shipments there, but I could not select it.Graphics: They're better. Can't complain. Except Lizzie. What have you done to my poor Lizzie, she looks like some crappy devianart character.Overall I am disappointed. I hope the devs will listen to the community and fix some critical issues.

_childDocuments_.review: Its back, in the best way.Ill address how buggy a botch it was at launch. Now its not. Its one of the few instances where the developer (Tantalus) came though and fixed the mess. They should have spent some more time polishing it before releasing, but the spitshines on now and boy does it look good. Watch hundreds of Strelets go flying everywhere, as their pathetic bayonet charge on a cluster of your concealed Swedish porta cannons goes exactly as expected. Laugh as platoons of your elite french cavalry crash into a pile of pikemen and just crush them beneath the weight of horseflesh. _childDocuments_.review: As of right now, AOE3 (2007) is the better version of this game.  They need to bring back the leveling system, even if it's optional, and optimize the game to play as well as the old versions did (Which was still bad, but not this bad).  As far s this version goes, there's nothing here of value really besides playing the new civs, other than that it feels like a stripped down version of AOE3.In my opinion, AOE3 is a good game but AOE2 does most of what it does better, with the exception of the progression system built into older versions AOE3.  It made games feel more meaningful to gain XP that has real gameplay changes attached to it. You play a game, get out, get some new cards, switch up your deck, and you're excited to play the next one because something has changed.  There's not very many RTS games that can claim that, and the only other one I can think of is Warlord's Battlecry 3, where you level up a main hero in an RPG fashion between games and get equipment in those games that you carry between them. That's what made AOE3 special in my opinion.All that is gone in this edition -- you have all cards from the start and there's nothing to look forward to, so I don't really see a reason to play it over AOE2, which has the better combat, strategy, graphics, balance and general gameplay.  Even if you want to play AOE3 because you like the gameplay in it better, I don't see any reason to buy this one over the older 2007 version that still has the leveling system built into it and was properly playtested before release.  All in all, I'd buy this game again because I love the franchise enough to try it despite it's flaws, but I wouldn't recommend it to anyone but the most hardcore fans, and only if you understand the flaws and still want to check it out anyways.  If the leveling system returns and the game starts to run better than the older version, I'd change this rating, but until then, just buy AOE3 (2007).Oh, and the PC changes aren't a problem you racist morons, if you can't handle someone changing the name of the Colonial Age then you're desperate to feel outraged over nothing.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR The only real improvements are the 2 new factions.  Most changes are strictly for the worse.Pros:  -Caroleans  -O.P. invisible Incan shenanigans that make the other native civs jealous  -Excellent remixes to some of the music  -All cards are unlocked from the start  -Caroleans.Neutral:  -UI updates are more practical, but the "classic" option isn't really classic.  -Can't select villagers alongside military units by default.  Obvious pros and cons to this.  -New textures are rather cartoony.  -New sounds are new.  Someone else commented on their lack of bass, and I must agree.Cons:  -Game crashes periodically and is significantly heavier to run.  -"Political correctness" updates change the names of many units without cause.  Some name updates were made for the sake of historical accuracy, but most changes became less accurate in order to be P.C.  (Ex. Plantations are now called Estates?  Really?)    -A.I. pathing for melee fighters is either the same (buggy) or worse than in the original.  -Many, many hotkeys have been straight up removed from the game.  (Ex. Want to hit Town Bell hotkey to save a low HP villager?  Too bad, you have to use the mouse to click on it, while that villager takes one more hit.)  -Rebalancing/changes to cards and a several different civs.  This wouldn't be so bad at face value if they hadn't  This makes learning the gameplay changes that much more time consuming, as you wade through the myriad of cosmetic name changes.

_childDocuments_.review: After 100 hours of playing, it is time...I read some reviews at launch and I immediately thought that some players were too harsh on the game or just plain childish. However, I experienced what they were going through: crashes, glitches, stuttering, lag, weird AI behavior, etc. They were right and on point. My apologies for misjudging you. We were bound to get it anyhow but I insisted that we wait. Of course he didn't listen to me and bought it for both of us at launch. The reason I continue playing Age of Empires III Definitive Edition is the inevitable improvements. After all the hotfixes and updates so far, AOE 3 DE is getting better and better. It's still NOT perfect. I understand completely as to why people would refund this game; due to its incomplete and unpolished status (which is still the case unfortunately) and I can't ask people to do the same as I did (continue playing it and hope for quick updates even though this is not how it is supposed to be!) I agree with the fact that this is unacceptable from the developers & publishers' side; to release a game of such hype and let it easily die from hungry bugs simply because they didn't hire a good pest control company (haha).I find it extremely frustrating to get & have AOE 3 DE in this state. _childDocuments_.review: Age of Empires 3: Definitive Edition is a game that has disappointed many fans of the franchise. Despite being marketed as an improved version of the original game, the optimization is poor, and the graphics are even worse. The game struggles to run smoothly, and the visual upgrades do little to enhance the overall experience.One of the major problems with the Definitive Edition is the lack of improvement to the gameplay. The new AI is a far cry from the old one, and often freezes or fails to react appropriately. This can be frustrating for players who are used to the smooth and seamless gameplay of the original game.Another issue with the game is its pay-to-win mechanics. The introduction of new factions and the ability to purchase upgrades has changed the game's dynamic, making it less enjoyable for those who prefer a more balanced experience.Additionally, the timeline in the game is broken, and the inclusion of the USA in the timeline makes little sense. The Ottoman Empire, in particular, is stuck in the 16th century, and requires a new age with new types of units. The current system of cards is not enough to sustain late-game play, and the lack of a proper rework for both the German and Ottoman factions is disappointing.In conclusion, AOE III: Definitive Edition is a disappointing cash grab that fails to live up to its name. The optimization and graphics are poor, the new AI is frustrating, and the pay-to-win mechanics are a major drawback. The broken timeline and lack of proper rework for the factions make it a game that is best avoided by fans of the franchise and strategy games in general.

_childDocuments_.review: (also called the Age of Discovery) began in the 1400s and continued through the 1600s. It was a period of time when the European nations began exploring the world. They discovered new routes to India, much of the Far East, and the Americas. The Age of Exploration took place at the same time as the Renaissance. Outfitting an expedition could be expensive and risky. Many ships never returned. So why did the Europeans want to explore? The simple answer is money. Although, some individual explorers wanted to gain fame or experience adventure, the main purpose of an expedition was to make money.Expeditions made money primarily by discovering new trade routes for their nations. When the Ottoman Empire captured Constantinople in 1453, many existing trade routes to India and China were shut down. These trade routes were very valuable as they brought in expensive products such as spices and silk. New expeditions tried to discover oceangoing routes to India and the Far East. Some expeditions became rich by discovering gold and silver, such as the expeditions of the Spanish to the Americas. They also found new land where colonies could be established and crops such as sugar, cotton, and tobacco could be grown.  The Age of Exploration began in the nation of Portugal under the leadership of Henry the Navigator. Henry sent out ships to map and explore the west coast of Africa. They went further south than any previous European expedition and mapped much of western Africa for the Portuguese. In ♥♥♥♥, Portuguese explorer Bartolomeu Dias was the first European to sail around the southern tip of Africa and into the Indian Ocean.Soon the Spanish wanted to find a trade route to the Far East. Explorer Christopher Columbus thought that he could sail west, across the Atlantic Ocean, to China. He could not get the Portuguese to fund his expedition, so he went to the Spanish. Spanish monarchs Isabella and Ferdinand agreed to pay for Columbus' trip. In 1492 Columbus discovered the New World of the Americas.Portugal and Spain became the early leaders in the Age of Exploration. Through the Treaty of Tordesillas the two countries agreed to divide up the New World. Spain got most of the Americas while Portugal got Brazil, India, and Asia.  Spain sent over conquistadors to explore the Americas and to conquer the peoples there. Hernan Cortes conquered the Aztec Empire in Mexico and Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca Empire in Peru. They made Spain rich with the gold and silver they found in the Americas.Portugal sent out Vasco da Gama who found a trade route around the southern tip of Africa and to India. They also explored much of the Far East and were the first Europeans to establish a trading colony in China at Macau.Other countries such as Great Britain and the Netherlands established colonies in the New World. Eventually Great Britain would surpass all of the European nations in terms of the size of their world wide empire including the thirteen colonies in the Americas that later became the United States.The Age of Exploration was one of the most important times in the history of world geography. A significant portion of the unknown world was mapped during this short period. Also, many advances were made in navigation and mapping which helped future explorers and travelers.....and this is just the first of many ages depicted in this masterpiece of a game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a lazy and probably rushed remaster. I asked for a refund.They delivered on the graphics upgrade. It is satisfying even if it could be better in certain spots such as the canon textures. This is pretty much the only pro of this remaster.The optimization is just not there, performance is really bad even on top-of-the-line hardware.RTS veterans will not be satisfied with the hotkeys and even less by how configurable they are. Hotkeys are not standard by default (A-click is K by default for example, and is located just next to J, which is "Delete unit"). Keys are grid-based and not context-aware, meaning that you can't use separate hotkeys for buildings, settlers and military units.Units and AI are so dumb you spend more time fighting your own units so they march forward instead of getting stuck between themselves. They take a significant delay before responding to orders, an A-click move can take up to 3 seconds before units start firing, and sometimes units ignore enemies entirely and march through them to their demise.Technical limitations of the times haven't been removed and no quality of life improvements have been made: for example you can still only select 50 units at once, not more. There are no markers for chained actions (with shift), villagers don't gather cows automatically, and many more inconvenience like this.Don't buy it, you'll be disappointed, and the nostalgia feeling fades away very, very quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite "AOEIII" having always been my personal favorite of the series, for some reason, I remained skeptical of this "improved" version for very a long time. But now, that I have finally had the chance to delve into it, I am happy to see that it has got a similar kind of "Definitive Edition" care to that of its older brother "AOEII", including various graphical and QoL improvements, extended multiplayer support as well as new DLC updates. Unfortunately, the singleplayer campaigns are still far from great. To be fair, none of the "AOE" games tried extremely hard to be historically accurate, but I always found the fantasy-adjacent stories and soap opera-level dialogue of the campaigns in this one to be quite abysmal. The newly added "Historical Battles", on the other hand, are simply amazing and even on par with the mastery of "AOEII" scenario and map design. If the devs can keep up the support at close to current levels, then this game still has a very bright future ahead.

I think this game took a lot of risks in altering that classic AoE2 formula and honestly, it worked for me. It took the good bits and added new interesting bits. I like the addition of buildings that provide unlimited resources, they allow me to make a nice tidy base... and that feels good. 8)The nations are actually different this time around and play differently too. Units are a lot more diverse and you actually feel like you're playing your faction rather than some copy and paste faction with one or two unique units as was the case in AoE2.The campaign had a decent amount of content and at the time of writing this review, I've completed all 3 main campaigns and all their acts on the middle difficulty, so it's definitely not as long as AoE2's campaigns (of which I'm STILL working on).That being said, don't expect a lot of depth and history in the campaigns–they've taken a fictional AoM route set in historical periods around real events.Weird part, as usual, is that projectiles fire straight through walls as if they don't exist haha. _childDocuments_.review: As opposed to what most people have been saying about this, I'd like to say that the hard work put in by the developers can be seen the moment you step into a game. Besides the new content, I like the presentation, the UI and the sound. There are some things which they could have kept from the original, for example I still prefer watching the ships sink than blowing up but these small inconveniences aside, I'm glad that they delivered what they promised in the trailer.The textures look so much better compared to the original. I never liked that excessive bloom which plagued the original and I am really glad that they got rid of it here. It looks neat, and the textures pop out when you zoom in on the units and terrain. The sounds are nice, artillery definitely packs a punch with it's overhauled sound effects. Multiplayer feels nice. Haven't had any issues so far. The servers have been running just as they would in Age 2 DE. I like the fact that multiplayer feels more leveled this time around, no need to grind for the cards. However, there are a few things which I want the developers to address. First one being the population limit, remind me again why is it capped at 200 ? I mean sure, it would break the game but give us an option to increase it to 300 or 400 or something in the single player atleast. Another issue being the performance, it is alright but it isn't that ideal either. It needs some patchwork and I am sure with time, the developers will improve the performance as we go. UPDATE: Patch 1, released on 23rd of October, 2020 seemed to have addressed some major issues. Now you have the option to turn off the AA. The AI seems a little more aggressive this time around but could use some more work. Performance feels better than it did before. Everything feels more much smoother. UPDATE 2: After a series of patches, the performance is much smoother now, I'm hitting 55-60 FPS without any stutters. I can run it as I should given the specifications that I have, at medium preset in 1080p. Crashes were non-existent for me but after this patch, I've heard the reports that most of the crashes and bugs were ironed out.

_childDocuments_.review: I played AOE3 a fair bit as a kid and was excited to return to it when I heard they had released a definitive edition. After giving it a good run I decided it needs my review, because the game is severely underappreciated right now. CONS- - The Game has some bugs. I can't say if they'll still be around by the time you're reading this, but the main bugs I've run into involve 2 home city shipments that don't deliver properly. While not game-breaking, this can be highly frustrating, especially if you forget which ones are bugged. - The community is small. This isn't a particularly big deal for me, as I'm happy as long as there are enough players for me to find games, but for more community oriented player this could be a significant downside. - The voice acting of new civilizations is fine at best (Sweden) to atrocious at worst (Hausa, Ethiopia, and revoices for non-Aztec native civs). I've heard there are mods to fix this, I haven't used any. - Presently, the African civilizations are grossly overpowered. This is widely expected to be toned down in the upcoming patch, but it generally imparts the impression to me that the developers feel pressure to power creep in order to sell expansions. I personally don't feel they need to do that as long as the content is interesting (it is). - Units only have one type of armor. Units, with very few exceptions, either have ranged armor or melee armor. While this is great for simplifying the game system and making the units easier to learn, it means that most units completely lack resistance to one type of damage, and a lot of potential design space is lost. Also because ranged damage is a lot more common than melee damage, units with melee armor can feel a bit shafted by this system. PROS- - Major improvements over AOE2. I realize that this is the minority opinion, since AOE2 has a much larger fanbase. But I also bought Age of Empires 2: Definitive Edition at the same time and tried to play them side by side. If you don't have a decade's worth of familiarity with Age 2 the differences in playability are massive. Economic busywork has been removed (no more reseeding farms, YUCK), villagers train more slowly and cost more so that much less of your game is spent constantly babysitting your town center. Animations are more sophisticated and the game has a physics engine rather than a series of precanned death / combat animations. This is especially satisfying when it comes to Age 3's artillery. Civilizations actually feel different and highly unique rather than all basically having the same 2-3 strategies. - Less punishing gameplay compared to Age II. The existence of the minutemen system and the ability to garrison far more villagers in your TC means that taking one bad fight or getting rushed don't automatically end your game- there is room for recovery and counterplay. Home city shipments have the same effect- battles don't snowball as hard because you can turn the tide with well timed reinforcements and mastering the home city system is a skill of its own. Some may prefer the tough-as-nails gameplay of yesteryear, but I prefer a nimble back and forth between the players. - Massive unit roster. There are so many fun and different units in this game that even at almost 500 hours invested I still haven't tried them all. Whereas in games like Civ or Age of Empires 2 a civilization might have 1 or two unique units, in Age 3, its common for European civs to have 3 or more, and nonwestern civilizations like the Aztecs to have entire rosters of unique units. -Native Civilizations. To me this adds a huge variety to the game by giving flavor to the different maps and adding some spice to your army compositions. For example, my main (the United States) has serious problems in their unit roster countering cavalry because they historically never used pikes and their Dragoon unit is complete trash. On maps with Zen natives, however, USA can ally with the Sohei Naginata to open up a powerful rush and anti-cavalry option. Unique technologies for natives also add a lot of variance for gameplay, with cool combos like Germany and Akan. -Home city system gives you more customization over your favorites civilizations. This opens up lots of different ways to play each different civ, and for me having more unique features per civ is a major advantage, adding depth to the game. -Clean and easily understandable unit counter system. Some like Spirit of the Law have said that that they find Napoleonic units harder to read at a glance, but Age III makes it a lot easier to understand what counters what if you understand their basic unit catagory. Light infantry loses to cannons and heavy cavalry, heavy cavalry loses to heavy infantry and light cavalry, heavy infantry loses to light infantry, and so does light cavalry. As long as you can figure out what quadrant a unit you're up against belongs to, you can counter it. By contrast, how do you counter a Woad Raider or a Cataphract? The answer is a lot more complicated. -The new civilizations are generally VERY unique, and often among the most interesting. This is certainly true for the USA, Inca, and Sweden, although I haven't had a chance to try the hated African civs yet. -The theme for Age 3 is very strong and immersive. Some of this is just personal preference, since the early modern period (IE renaissance and industrial) are much more fascinating and dynamic for me than the much more overexposed middle ages or modern periods. You're experiencing a huge and unprecedented Colombian Exchange, mixing new and old cultures, and irrevocably altering the world and seeing the dawn of liberalism, new philosophical movements and truly global empires.

_childDocuments_.review: AOE3 has always been a divisive game and this version is no different. The original AOE3 brought many new gameplay mechanics that were simply too out there for players who wanted something along of the lines of the wildly successful AOE2. 15 years later and AOE3 remains a unique experience not found anywhere else in RTS games. This update addresses a few of the problems that stopped the original from taking off completely but at its core, it is still the same game.Pros- All shipments unlocked from the get go. Makes it much easier to jump right in- The servers are significantly less laggy than the old AOE3 server (at least for me, also I have had no drop issues)- The new civs (Sweden and Inca) are interesting and fun to play. I assume that they will receive some small balance touch ups but otherwise they are good additions.- The graphics changes are overall good imo with some exceptions I discuss below. Some feel it is overly cartoony but I like the added color, especially on maps with lower amounts of brightness.- The balance seems good with my limited experience. Some of the weak/unplayable civs from the previous version are now much stronger and there is a lot of civ diversity in the games I am playingCons- Fairly buggy although the problems do seem to be getting fixed so I have hope this won't be an issue going forward- The game still runs poorly on water maps for many CPU set ups- The graphics feel slightly washed at times (download the anti aliasing mod in the tools section to fix this). Some of the added battle animations are a little overboard and I wish there were more options to customize the exact level of graphics you want to display.- The multiplayer UI feels like a step back for me, removing many of the features the old version had. Overall I am really enjoying it and would recommend to anyone that liked playing the original game. Most of the problems it has are extremely fixable and I look forward to a more optimized version in the coming months.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the more complex RTS games, with tons of room for varied strategies and play, a ton of factions and quite possibly the deepest counter system of any RTS game. The early game has been made more interesting with the need to herd huntable animals and go treasure hunting with your explorer.At the same time one can tell that a lot of thought has been put into the game's systems and a ton of things have been streamlined and improved over AoE2, no longer needing drop off points for your villagers (Although they're still as vulnurable to raids as ever), units being trained in batches (Usually of 5) and reducing the number of resource types to 3 (Food, wood and stone).Building things, destroying things or taking over the trade routes on the maps give you experience points which let you send shipments from a deck you create before the game for your faction, allowing for a lot more varied strategies and builds than most(any other?) RTS game, and more swingy gameplay where a well timed shipment of units or a buff to your army can turn the tide, making each game quite exciting.The Definitive Edition has made a ton improvements in all areas (including balance), most importantly that you now get access to all decks immedietly and do not need to "level up" each faction like the original (which in my opinion is, along with the learning curve, the reason why AoE3 is regrettably one of the least popular Age of- games).All in all, lovely game, still with a strong player base for 1vs1 multiplayer (Albeit not as strong as AoE2 or AoE 4, more of a forgotten middle child). Probably my favourite RTS of all time when it comes to 1vs1 multiplayer.

_childDocuments_.review: Other reviews have covered the mess of bugs, atrocious UI, audio errors, graphical errors and so forth, so I might as well cover another point of contention: the changes made to make things more 'historically accurate'. You know that when you're greeted with a paragraph talking about how they have removed 'problematic' elements (the dev's word, not mine) to make the game more accurate, you're in for a ride. The changes themselves are relatively minor; some are as simple as recasting fifteen year old lines, others are as game-changing as removing the ability of the Iroquois and Sioux (who I will refer to as such) to mine coin and instead forcing them to trade for it through buildings. Some of the changes for the sake of historical accuracy actually *do* make things more accurate - mainly the name changes to some native units. Others are just a blatant grab at brownie points; such as the removal of all instances of the word 'colonial'. Yes, a game focused on the period of history that saw the growth of great colonial empires no longer has the word colonial within it - the Colonial age was renamed to the Commerce Age, Colonial Militia were renamed to Revolutionary Militia. Plantations were renamed to Estates, the Discovery Age was renamed to the Exploration age, and - most puzzling of all - Light Infantry was renamed to *Shock* Infantry. Meanwhile, the Sioux and Iroquois have been renamed to use the terms they referred to themselves as (or, rather, the Iroquois have - the Sioux were just renamed to the Lakota, who are not the only Siouan people to exist). This was done in the name of inclusivity. The old names did not prevent these empires from being added in the first expansion a decade ago, nor did it prevent anyone from getting into the game; I also reject the idea that the new names make the game more historically accurate. Not just because there is nothing inherently inaccurate about an exonym, but because of how selective the application of these changes were. The Japanese, who do not call themselves Japanese, are still Japanese and led by the isolationist Tokugawa in a global empire building game. The Indians and Chinese are still led by the Mughal and Qing dynasties, despite the fact that neither of these dynasties called themselves Indian or Chinese (both those words also being European in origin) or even viewed themselves as being representative of Indian and Chinese nationhood. The Aztecs are still called the Aztecs despite the Mexica being the actual tribe that represented them, if we want to go by the renaming convention for the Sioux. The Ottomans - who were a dynasty - are still called the Ottomans rather than the Turks. I probably shouldn't have to mention that the Germans don't actually call themselves German either. It is not only wildly inconsistent, it is entertainingly inconsistent: in their effort to promote the terms that natives used to refer to themselves, they'd leave the Manchu Qing, who went out of their way to impose Manchu culture on the Han, representing China, or still pretend that India is a uniform civilization best represented under a Turko-Persian Islamic dynasty.In their quest to make things more historically accurate for two native civs, they've left things virtually unchanged for the Europeans (and Asians). Prince Henry the Navigator, who was never a head of state, still represents the Portuguese despite all other leaders being actual rulers. Napoleon, who gave up France's colonial empire to pursue European hegemony, leads the French in a game that doesn't have European maps, and for some reason still flies the *medieval* Capetian coat of arms. The British, despite their name, still have nothing representing the Scots unique to their roster, and the Germans are just Prussians, with the only thing representing something else in the HRE still being Czech War Wagons of all things. Moreover, while the Iroquois and Sioux are restricted to trade posts for gathering coin in the name of historical accuracy, Europeans - despite the fact that the overwhelming majority of European settlers never set foot anywhere near a gold or silver mine - still get most of their coin through mining rather than growing tobacco, making rum or trading furs like they actually did. The implication of this, of course, is that the devs might think the Iroquois and Sioux simply wouldn't know how to mine precious metal deposits if they were presented with them - given that their removal of all terms referring to colonization also implies that the natives were Noble Savages who didn't engage in empire building or colonization of their own and that the Europeans didn't even colonize the New World, I can believe that the devs are actually that based and paternalistic. Of course, the actual reason is more likely that the devs just wanted to virtue signal, and went about it in some of the most thoughtless and wasteful ways imaginable. And I do mean wasteful. They spent time, money and effort in consulting native tribes and recasting fifteen year old voice lines because someone might have found them problematic, rather than doing something actually inclusive like allowing all empires to customize their home city (a feature still restricted to the original eight European empires) or otherwise actually applying more polish to their remaster. I would not call this a remaster either. The graphical updates are nice - when they work - and the Swedes and Inca are a plus, but aside from that and having access to the entirety of your card deck from the start there are no further improvements, and the mechanical changes made to the native empires were to their gameplay detriment. This is not a remaster, this is an expansion pack with a graphics update - and the only saving grace is that it is at least priced like an expansion pack and not a whole game.

_childDocuments_.review: This review reflects 86 hours on DE and many hundreds of hours playing the original.Graphics: 5/5Maps: 5/5AI: 3/5Strategic Gameplay: 4/5Single Player Content: 5/5Multiplayer/Competitive: -/5 (I don't play it)Developer Support: 5/5Historical Accuracy: 2/5*Age 3 DE is an excellent addition to the Age of Empires line of RTS games and is absolutely worth the low asking price.Updated from the 2007 original release, the DE version brings the game's graphics up to par with what modern graphics cards can display. Unit models have been updated, and while still somewhat blocky are subtantially improved over the original while still being faithful to it. Maps are procedurally rendered and beautiful to look at. There is tremendous diversity available reflecting regions from all over the world from New England to California, the Pampas to Siberia. There is an ample map pool for both naval maps and land-only maps.The AI still has significant flaws that carry over from the original game. It struggles to build and maintain a late game economy, relying on cards for early pressure and difficulty-based free resources in the late game. It routinely commits "villie suicide" by not adequately protecting its economy. Pathing can be difficult at times as well. It is sufficient to provide an entertaining experience to the single player, but not quite adequate to provide the challenge of proper multiplayer.A key feature for me is the concept of easy to learn and difficult to master. I find that Age 3 strikes a generally good balance of introducing the basic rock-paper-scissors unit dynamics core to the RTS experience. Unit formations add a layer of complexity. And there are significant enough differences in the playable civilizations to make their individual experiences feel like their own style to master. My only hesitation is that with each initial expansion, they added new layers of complexity such that some civilizations require tremendous effort to really figure out their quirks and play optimally. It's almost too much.The 3 campaigns from the 2007 version are remastered in the DE version, with updated in-game rendered cinematics. The stories are interesting, with a good mix of missions that make them engaging and fun to play through, even if they're a bit far-fetched at times. The game also includes historical battles that can be refought which have been faithfully designed to reflect how the real battles unfolded historically. The careful eye to detail and accuracy makes these a great addition to the game. And of course, you can skirmish vs the AI.I simply cannot comment here, since I don't play it.Many developers create a game, then dump it and move on. Microsoft has thankfully done the opposite, continuing to invest in regular hotfixes and balance patches. In addition, new content continues to be added to the game, which makes it feel engaging and new. This is critical to maintaining an active player base for multiplayer, and for maintaining the long-term viability of the game. The original game, like all Age of Empires games, is rooted in history - in this case, the history of the colonial period. It's civilizations, units, upgrades, and cards all reflect the unique history of each civilization as it progressed through that period with a keen eye towards accuracy. The 2007 version would receive a 5/5.The DE version, however, is woke. They removed the word "colonial" for example, among many other subtle but critical revisions to history in order to reshape how the history is perceived. It is particularly insidious since so much of the game is deeply rooted in fact, that it gives a false impression to people who may be learning for the first time from the game itself rather than classic academic study. Woke revision of history is a cancer on society at large and in this game as well, and tarnishes an otherwise excellent game.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR – Age of Empires III Definitive Edition is worth a buy if you haven’t played the original or are willing to spend $€Ł15/20 for updated graphics and a few new extras. Age of Empires III: Definitive Edition is, as the title suggests, an updated re-release of 2005’s Age of Empires III and its two expansion packs.Like other Age of Empires games, this one is a base-building RTS, this time set in the age of prolonged wars in Europe and blooming colonial empires in the rest of the world.A short intro for completely new players: you start with a Town Center and a few settlers/villagers and have to collect resources, build buildings, progress through 4 (and a half) ages, train an army and eliminate your opponents while defending your positions from counterattacks. You win either by destroying the enemy’s town center and villagers or by forming a trade monopoly, controlling the vast majority of trading posts on the map and defending them for a given time.The game is set in various settings around the world, mainly in America, but, due to the inclusion of the Asian Dynasties expansion, also in some African, Asian and Pacific regions.It has several new concepts from the first two Age of Empires games, such as home cities, from which you can request shipments (of units, buildings, resources or upgrades) when you gain a new level, the native villages which provide whoever builds a trading post in it with unique units and technologies, trade routes (on most but not all maps) which generate free resources periodically, treasures (caches of resources defended by guardians scattered around the map) or the concept that settlers/villagers don’t need to return to collection building with their resources, generating a constant stream of income instead.This edition has vastly improved graphics, a remastered soundtrack, new Art of War (introduction to the game’s systems) and Historical Battles scenarios and two new civilizations.*The graphics – this is the biggest difference, it scales up to higher resolutions really nicely and units and buildings are considerably more detailed than in the original game. Overall, they did some very nice work with it. (A note: I read in some reviews that the game struggles even on high-end machines. My PC is certainly not high-end and it still runs smoothly and looks nice, so it’s certainly not a universal issue.)*Art of war – these are nice learn-by-doing tutorials focusing on various aspects of the game, helping new (or after long time returning) players learn the ropes.*Historical battles – these are also nice to have, providing a more guided experience.*The two new factions look interesting, but I haven’t tried any of them yet, so can’t really pass judgement on them.*Allegedly, the dev team fixed some of the “liberties” takes in regards to native cultures, which is a nice thing to do. I’m no expert of this field and can’t really say what was corrected, so I’ll have to take their word for it.*The gameplay is still fun.*The AI. After seeing what these devs did with the Age 2 AI, I could not wait to see the work done on this one’s, but this is, unfortunately, a disappointment. From what I have seen so far, there is at most little improvement compared to the original (AI players still don’t know you are supposed to build a navy on water, their units are still marching in uniform blocks…). Still, there  improvement on the higher difficulties.An odd thing is that the jump between Moderate and Hard is huge. On Moderate and below, the AI may as well be brain dead, doing mostly nothing, very rarely sending a small force to attack. On Hard, the next difficulty level, it already attacks with impunity and exploits weaknesses. A more gradual improvement from level to level would be better.*Home city improvements – Unlike in the original, you don’t need to level up your home city to get access to ever more useful shipments, everything is unlocked from the start, gaining levels only means you can unlock new customization options (and even that is only for European cities). Your mileage will vary on this, but I find this a step back as it removes the feeling of progression from game to game.*In general, I get the feeling this game got less attention than Age 2 DE, which was a substantial improvement over the original. While this may be due to the fact that this game was more polished, gameplay-wise, to begin with, this does feel more like a graphics update than a real remaster.It’s times like this when I wish there was a third option besides Recommended and Not Recommended.On the one hand, all in all, it  a nice upgrade for a good game, on the other, I can’t fully endorse getting it if someone already has the original Age 3, as I don’t feel like it got as much of an improvement as the first two definitive editions.Still, $€Ł20 is a good price for those who are new to the game, and if one already owns Age 3 on Steam, they can get this one for $€Ł15, which is not a  price. It’s just that one doesn’t lose that much by sticking to the original.

_childDocuments_.review: Buyer beware, developers were more concerned with social justice than game play and it shows. TL;DR version: The prevailing theme of their changes is "lets make unnecessary changes to make us feel better about ourselves and act like we are helping brown people". In the process they axed several features that were fun. But it wouldn't be gamer gate bait without social justice. And it wouldn't be social justice if it wasn't bowing to a demand to change things nearly everyone is fine with.You are met immediately with some virtue signaling about how they changed the name of the Iroquois and Sioux, replaced the fire pit and hired real brown voice actors this time. Meanwhile the Asian civs used to get mocked for their bad voice acting and nothing was changed there. Bravo on the thinly veiled concern about something nobody asked for.This is relevant to game play as well. In order to prevent you from just renaming your home cities to "Sioux" or "Iroquois" you know only have one home city per civilization. But don't worry about picking cards for game modes. Because you unlock them as your HC level increases, all of them. This makes the HC choices seem even more detached. And discourages players from really learning how their HC works. It also removes any long term strategy.They also removed "nature friendship" ability replacing it with one that only works on humans. As well as the fire pit, both for being cliché. No complaint on the fire pit and I like the replacement. But nature friendship was fun, using animals to scout the enemy base was easier. People ignored them. And they could have replaced it with "adopt into tribe" or something like that, still letting you tame animals. Or hell give all explorers the ability to tame animals.Also their culture consultants were ignorant to history. For the Sioux and Iroquios, they can no longer mine gold. Instead the build a market next to gold mines for no real reason. The reason given is that mining is insulting to mother earth. Which is about the most cliché thing I have heard of, but I digress. One of the oldest mines in the USA was a copper mine at lake superior. This ended up being Iroqois territory, but the mine predates them by several thousand years. Although, to be fair it was the only known metal extraction mine. Native Americans did mine other materials as well, and even metal as Europeans arrived and were willing to hire them. Reminder, 1492 and 1876 AD is roughly the date range for the game, through most of this mining would be reasonable to expect. This is just some BS their consultants came up with. Now, they could have made mining unavailable until the fortress age. And maybe given the tribes essentially a discount plantation (called "estate" now) in the first age.Many of the changes made sense. Renaming Sioux to Lakota did. Renaming Iroquois to Haud... uhh.. whatever they call it doesn't. The game is targeted an audience that would know them name Iroquois. The reasoning given is "those are the names the settlers gave them" which is more of just a statement not a reason. That would be like saying Germany needs to be renamed to Heiliges Römisches Reich, or Deutschland. The plantation renaming is somewhat historically accurate as cotton wasn't a good money crop until nearly the end of the date range the game takes place in.Overall, its still age of empires. It's not quite aoe 3 though. It's a good game still. Not great. Needs work and shows promise. And most importantly it needs people who actually play and love the age of series of games working on it. Most of these decisions were made with the same reasoning that made gamer gate such a scandal. Gamers want to be entertained not lectured. The devs need to rethink everything, and start with a mindset of "is this feature fun?". If it isn't, toss it. Find some other way to satisfy your craving for feigned moral superiority.

_childDocuments_.review: If there was an option for a mixed review on Steam I'd pick that to be honest.Age of Empires III is like its predecessor a game about leading an empire in real time. There are 16 playable civs  from all around the world ranging from Aztecs, French to Chinese which all play very differently compared to its predecessor.They've added two new civs, the Incas and Sweden, though not completely. What do you mean by not completely? Well, there are still a lot of the translations in German and French which are missing. But not only that. The base game civs sometimes also talk in English. There are mods out there like Wars of Liberty which feature more civs of higher quality for free, where you can kinda accept that the leader dialogue isn't localized but that from professional devs is kinda inexcusable.The graphics are hit and miss to be honest. Yes, they've been considerably visually improved but for some reason the game looks way more blurry than what is shown in the screenshots. The textures need also very long to load which makes the game look even worse for a view secondsFrom a gameplay point of view, there have been quite some renamings like Colonial Age to Commerce Age or Plantation to Estate. Also you're not abandoning your colony anymore but your town. Overall, considering that those changes don't affect gameplay, I don't really care about those name changes but some people might. Colonialism is horrible and being colonized too but I think that's not the way to handle the whole problematic.While we're at renamings, the Iroquois and Sioux have been renamed to Haudenosaunee and Lakota which I personally find a great change. It would be nice if every civ would be using their endonyms as faction names.Some changes for them I find rather not fleshed out though. The community plaza which replaces the fire pit doesn't tell you as well as its predecessor how many people are on it considering some of the animations of it are pretty much idle animations. The dancing in circle told you more about how many people were on it than what we have now. Also the change with fur trading purely from a gameplay point of view seems rather unnecessary (villagers need to build a very cheap Fur market next to a mine to start trading fur aka getting gold) but I respect the choice they made. It's just an awkward game mechanic though. I really respect the decision though trying to be more accurate when it comes to the representation of civs ingame.The UI changes don't seem me really to be a plus, sometimes you don't even see that you have a shipment at disposable due to the fact that the number is on a transparent and not black background anymore like in the original game.There are new historic battles and Art of War scenarios which is really nice. They also feature some battles in Africa, a region I'd love to see covered in the future by AOE3:DEI really like AOE3, otherwise I wouldn't have bought it, but the state of the game right now is not really satisfying. I'm hoping they're going to fix most of the issues and especially make the animations on the community plaza clearer so that my opinion of this game improves a bit because right now I'm not sure if I'm simply going to switch to Wars of Liberty. The only thing which saves it is that it's pretty cheap but that's about it.TL:DR: Wait for a few patches if you can't wait to try out the new civs and new scenarios/historical battles. If you really want to play tons of new civs, try out Wars of Liberty:.EDIT: Actually, the recent patch improved the graphics a lot. Now, they don't take as long to load. Kudos to the devs.

No, The campaigns have numerous bugs including but not limited to: No sound during cut-scenes, crashing between missions (to desktop) and the home city is almost always bugged making you unable to grab new cards or edit your deck. These problems ONLY affect the campaigns however so it isn't really that much of a bother since the majority of the fun is in skirmishes and online play. Is the game fun? Yes, I have sank over 100 hours playing two of my favourite civs extensively and I plan to play a few others hard as well. As previously stated, The bugs I experienced only affected the campaign so I have had well over 100 hours of fun already without having any issues whatsoever. I fully expect the campaigns bugs to be fixed in time, I can be patient. I made it through the vanilla campaign so far.This is not my most favourite RTS title as I don't really care for all the colonial era style warfare. I always preferred swords and bows. That being said, through the home city/deck system you can upgrade archaic units to be more on par with musketeers which takes the sting out of it for me, making it more than enjoyable experience. I would recommend this game simply to anyone that enjoys the PvP and single player skirmish RTS style 100%. The campaigns bugs need to be fixed, though.

_childDocuments_.review: It's great to see the game get a DE remake, but it doesn’t feel like it was done with the care that AoE2:DE had. Naturally, the graphics and soundtrack are great and the new civs are exciting, however there are glaring issues that let it down in a big way. When a game launches, it's expected that there'll be a bug or two that'll get ironed out in a few days, but based on the number of bugs, and how obvious some of them are, it feels like the game was hugely rushed and not tested. Some of the bugs I found when it shipped are:livestock - Livestock run from settlers and takes about five right clicks before they start gatheringcutscenes - Some campaign cutscenes are broken (eg "reunion" from the John Black campaign, where the characters just stare at each other and don't talk)The whole cards/deck system - Selecting cards puts them in the deck but they don't show up, removing cards from the deck removes incorrect ones. It just is quite clunky overall. Also the system feels counter-intuitive compared to the original, but that might just be my personal preference.Teleporting units - I don't know how it happened, but I found a few of my units on top of inaccessible plateaus, unable to get down.I'll leave it there, but I think you get the point.Following that, there's just a few changes that are either unnecessary or poorly implemented.One that bugs me is that unit waypoints no longer show up as flags so you can't see what they're going to do next. Sounds such as the "home city level up" now play when buildings are repaired. While I like the idea that anyone can make a fully levelled deck for multiplayer, I liked the progression for single player. I haven't played the edited campaigns yet, so I can't comment on that, but I didn't see anything hugely wrong with the original.While this is quite a negative review, the game does still look promising. Just maybe wait a month or two for the bugs and issues to get ironed out.Edit 29/11: After a month and a half, the game is getting more stable and most of the previously mentioned bugs have been fixed, although not all of them yet. It's improving, but not all that quickly.
