_childDocuments_.review: I really want to love this game but it's just so rough and unpolished that I really regret the $36 (even 10% discounted) I spent on the game. If the devs are listening, please...I know you put a lot of hard work into this but you really let your players down when you charge premium prices for such a clear unfinished game. Please fix this and deliver the product that I paid for.On the one hand, the visuals are beautiful and the story has the potential to be wonderfully heart-wrenching. The player character is great and identifiable. The concept of controlling the seasons and the puzzles that come out of that are great. The combat is simple but fun. There is so much potential here...But there is so much wrong with this game that I feel a bit robbed. I have to agree with many of the reviews here. The collisions are rough, the objectives are sometime unclear, the mini-map is weirdly out of place (pixel gfx in pixar style animation, please no) and deficient at guiding the player to way-points. The options, menus and resolutions are totally unfinished and buggy. Also there is barely any voice acting in the game with almost every interaction beginning with a grunt and then lots of text, which is fine for an rpg on gameboy in 1990 but this is not what I would shell out 40 bucks for.I hope whatever money they pulled in with this rushed and buggy release will be used to truly fix the game and update it for the players and fans that supported a game that could be great but is at the moment a disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, so it's definitely still rough around the edges. I encountered most of the bugs the developer mentions in the launch day update, as well as a few of my own. None of them actually broke the game completely though, with one exception. The game can get stuck trying to autosave, which means that it's NOT actually autosaving. I lost my progress through an entire dungeon this way. Now, that being said, it didn't prevent me from completing the game, I just had to do the dungeon over again.The story is very sweet, although the end was a little bit out of nowhere. The main character is memorable and cute and very enjoyable to play, and they did a great job with outfits and weapons. The combat is fun too, and the game can be VERY hard on the harder settings. The platforming was good too.Basically, I took about 13 hours to get to the ending and at no point did I feel like I was wasting my time. As a result, I don't feel any qualms about recommending it. Try to get it on sale, at least until the rest of the bugs are fixed, but the developer seems to be working hard to iron all of them out.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought Ary on sale for half price... and my advice is to wait until it is even lower than that, if you buy it at all. Just go play A Hat in Time instead if you want decent combat and excellent platforming in a game with linear level design and delightful characters. At first the charm of Ary overcame my little gripes about the jankiness of it; I wanted an open world adventure in a colorful world setting where I used a variety of tools to solve puzzles and explore. I was willing to overlook a lot of what I thought were superficial problems to have that experience. Ultimately that isn't really what Ary is about Ary is an extremely frustrating experience to actually play. Initially I felt like the game did a ton of railroading and hand holding. Behind every new development I thought they'd finally set me free to go explore their world and engage with the various puzzles hidden throughout... if there is such an inflection point I still haven't reached it. Instead there are a series of quests which you have to follow exactly and in only one order, a series of repeated hallways to traverse with different scenery, some side-quests, and the same four shops. There are times where you get new tools to interact with the world, but only in the one specific way in which the developers intended you to use them. Many of the 'puzzles' feel extremely narrow in their solutions; I'd often think of three or four ways to solve a scenario that the devs only considered one for. Sometimes I'd get lucky and be able to solve a puzzle my own way, usually that wasn't the case. The whole design feels restrictive in that way. Example:  The WHOLE GAME is riddled with arbitrary, nonsensical solutions that feels like playing DnD with an incredibly inflexible DM. Other concerns involve EXTREMELY janky platforming where every single jump has a space just the right size for Ary to fall through, extremely jarring death/respawn scenes, very janky and unexplained combat mechanics, a really garbage assortment of items to buy that seemingly do nothing for you, powers that feel basically useless, extremely predictable plot elements.... ugh.... Another example of how inflexible the devs were when designing their game can be seen in how NPCs and quests work.... A quest early on tells you to leave a town. An NPC stops you and gives you stock dialog for that scene. Fine. If you go back toward the town and go to pass the NPC again, HE STOPS YOU AND REPEATS THE SAME DIALOG. That's how linear the game is. The devs didn't think you'd ever go back up.... or if this was reported to them in playtesting, they never fixed it. In another instance you're supposed to collect and item for an NPC. This involves a possible solution to a side-quest.  Surely that wasn't what was intended... but it works. Clearly I'm upset... but I'm going to keep playing because my girlfriend thinks the game is cute.... and it is .... and I like Ary as a protagonist even though she and most people she allies with are dumber than several bags of hammers. I'm upset because I see all the promise this game had and just how terrible it turned out to be. Of exploration, puzzle solving, combat, and world building it really doesn't excel at any of them. If you want a linear, frustrating, often very campy game that tries to be cute in its terrible game play, then maybe this is for you. If you like video games that feel good to play, it probably isn't.

_childDocuments_.review: Since a lot of people seemed to have bug issues with this game, I decided to hold off on reviewing it until I got pretty far into the game.  Honestly, aside from one time I noclipped into the space underneath a town trying to double-jump onto edifices instead of using the stairs, or cutscenes where Ary's scar appears and disappears, I haven't had issues. _childDocuments_.review: Ary and the Secret of Seasons’ story revolves around Ary, the daughter of the winter’s guardian. After some crystals fall from the sky, changing the seasons, Ary’s father is summoned to a meeting with the other guardians. Unluckily, he is unable to go due to his state, grieving after Ary’s disappeared brother. This prompts Ary to decide to go in his stead, changing her appearance to look like her brother Flynn and taking his dad’s winter crystal. Once she arrives at the meeting, Ary finds out the other guardians have been knocked out and their crystals stolen. Luckily, Dagdann, the guardian of summer, reveals he left his at home, where Ary must go to retrieve it.This is where the preview left off, cutting the story shot. The full release continues forward and promptly gives players a main draw to keep playing, but at the cost of completely sacking what appears to be the villain initially. Instead, another villain, who had been previously foreshadowed, comes to be. While this big bad evil does actually entail stakes, the reason for his appearance is poorly written to say the least.The game’s graphics are not its high point either, despite what one may have expected. It is true buildings and cities are impressive and beautiful, and that the characters are well animated and expressive. Sadly, some other things are mediocre at best; characters clip through textures, the shine in certain materials is unnatural and the environment textures are repetitive. This last one is especially true for winter areas, which have the same “white with random blue patches” look everywhere.When clipping through textures was mentioned it was also for a reason; there is nothing that breaks suspense of disbelief more than seeing a character’s fingers go through the static texture of a soup. This also applies to when Ary’s hair in the prologue goes crazy and filters to her face or when certain walls are see-through.Luckily, after so much dark and grime there is some good left. Ary and the Secret of Seasons does a stellar job with its sound direction, from the great soundtrack to the amazing voice acting. The first covers a variety of high quality tracks which accompany the player everywhere, while the second occurs only in cutscenes. This voice acting has been clearly made by a passionate team who knew what they were doing. The line delivery is great and fleshes out the characters without ever sounding out of place. That said, the previously mentioned limitation to cutscenes is a shame, every other dialogue only entails a few gibberish-like sounds.Ary and the Secret of Seasons is both a 3d platformer and a puzzle game, these second being mostly limited to dungeons à la Zelda. In the game the player roams around controlling Ary and employing the powers of the season crystals to unlock new areas. Along the way secondary quests, chests and other things can be found, though they are mostly irrelevant for reasons that will be covered later.The game’s dungeons are well designed, wearing the influence from the Zelda series on their sleeves. Each dungeon has one gimmick item that must be obtained in order to further progress, be it double jump, a magnet, etc. Most puzzles are quite simple; definitely not the kinds that would break any heads or require much effort. They are often little more than moving an object to a trigger or beating a few enemies, mostly relying on the platforming to work.As mentioned in the preview, gameplay is a quite weak spot for the game. Both the combat and exploration mechanics are limited and clunky. The first is little more than whacking enemies and parrying or dodging (the second being often more reliable). It is true there are also special seasonal attacks, but these are little more than an afterthought, seeing as they deal virtually no damage. Attempting to fight clusters of enemies often becomes a complete pain, being unable to hit all of them at once while they can all attack with different timing. The reason for why the exploration is so limited is how the world is comprised of a “fake” open-world. The player can roam anywhere they want, but there is no fast travelling system and nothing to see. At most, some chests can be found while exploring around, but these only contain a few coins, limited in use to a few upgrades and cosmetics. There is little to no incentive in exploring, everything feels samey and repetitive, with chests containing as little as 8 gold coins becoming complete wastes of time.This time wasting issue also applies to side quests in the game, which, besides a few exceptions, are all fetch quests. A character will ask Ary to go somewhere and obtain something and bring it back. This, due to the lack of movement options, becomes very old very quick. Similarly to exploration and chests, these side-quests also offer completely irrelevant, to not say worse, rewards. At best a new cosmetic items will be obtained, and at worst a measly amount of gold.Ary and the Secret of Seasons offers very little value for the player’s time, sending them around for no reason to obtain nothing. This also applies to the main story quest, which soon becomes the tired cliché of obtaining items to defeat the evil guy, aka a whole new fetch quest. The issues with the game don’t end here though, seeing as it currently (as of September 9th 2020) is riddled with bugs. These include but are not limited to: cutscenes without audio, environmental clipping, bosses retaining damage dealt after player defeat, bosses becoming softlocked, etc. It is very clear the game is still very unpolished and rough around the edges, not to talk about the woeful UI with no keyboard mapping.Ary and the Secret of Seasons is an alright-at-best game with a load of bugs and issues. For the incredibly high price tag of £34.99/$39,99/€ it is definitely not worthy of purchase or even consideration, at least in its current state. It is a shame since the game showed some potential, but a lot of issues from the preview remained without being even slightly retouched.

_childDocuments_.review: A 3d-zelda style Action-Adventure, which though it has excelent assets, good plot and competent dungeon, puzzle and platforming design; fails to quite stick the landing.The story is good but somewhat clumsily excecuted. With a janky pacing that manages to both front load too much and not enough.The gameplay is great, but rough. The combat is unpolished, but fun enough, though I found melee to not be overly worthwhile after finding the projectile weapon easily oneshots most enemies, and two-shots the rest.The dungeon and puzzle design is really competent. And what platforming there is also has a solid design. If the gameplay design was fully realized, the game would have been near-flawless.As is, the game's riddled with minor bugs and janky interactions. And a lot of relatively basic stuff feels unfinished.If this was a late beta version it would be a lot easier to forgive the bugs and jank, but for a full release there's too much going on.The ending feels quite a bit like sequel bait. And I'm looking forward to see what comes next from the dev.tl;dr: a 3d-zelda style Action-Adventure with great design, and a good story. Held back by bugs and jank making it feel unfinished.

_childDocuments_.review: This review may contain spoilers.At the time of writing this review the full price of this game was $56.95 AUD. I would not recommend buying this game at that price on Steam and would recommend buying it only at a heavy discount or in a cheap bundle.The game is OK, a bit buggy at times, and is pretty much a Zelda clone. The game is very linear. I played through the game twice, once on hard and once on very hard. The difficulty setting did not make much of a difference. I played through with mouse and keyboardSome things I liked about the game:-I liked the mechanic of casting the season spheres and solving puzzles this way. The puzzles were fairly easy though.-Has some replay value if you want to do a speedrun, no side-quests run, no deaths run.-The fast travel system is OK, though there is no point in returning to an area once it has been clearedSome issues I had with the game:-Combat with the sword is a bit clunky and sometimes countering the enemy's attack didn't work properly and I would get hit. This led to mainly using the slingshot to 1-hit enemies from a distance or just running past them altogether. The slingshot is the best weapon.-Sometimes when I loaded a save I would get a black screen-Buying different clothing, hats or weapons from the vendors is pointless as they are only a cosmetic change.-The upgrades you can buy e.g. increased attack damage, increased agility in combat etc, don't appear to do much, regeneration might be the only useful upgrade. Due to this and the above point money in the game is pretty much worthless.-I only used the solstice powers in the first boss fight. Never had a reason to use them again in combat, they are pointless.-Some cutscenes were unskippable.-Limited to 5 heart containers only for the first half of the game.-Escaping the collapsing mine area. This was the most frustrating experience in this game. Any minor collision with an obstacle and you get sent back to the start of the escape run. Sometimes the ram chasing me would grab me, causing a restart, and I could not see a reason why-Some collectables quests completed before I had collected all the items.-I found the humour lame, but I doubt that I am the target audience.-The platforming could be a bit iffy at times, especially with latching on to edges-The world is a bit bland, most NPCs look the same and just stand in one spot. There are many houses with doors, but you can't enter the house.-No limited invulnerability when hit by an enemy or trap, meaning multiple enemies can damage you at once and kill you instantly if they all attack at the same time.-The Yule elevator is very slow and should just be a teleport mechanic instead

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not worth forty bucks. It's barely worth fifteen. While it has good ideas and a decent soundtrack, it desperately needed more beta testers because it can be really buggy. For example, enemies hit boxes wont go away after defeating them, you sometimes end up either in the sky or under the map, one enemy somehow climbed up a wall, mushrooms will fly around as if in a tornado, and some cut scenes will repeat for no reason. Even without the bugs, it can get pretty dull. Two of the guardians you don't even get to fight. Sometimes there's just the temple to go to. The story really needed some work, I feel like it loses sight of itself and allows things that make no sense happen.Honestly, I feel like this game could be great if it were in the proper hands.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is still technically stuck in a beta or early access state, unfortunetally.Difficulty ★★★☆☆☆☆☆☆☆ * cute artstyle* some cosmetic items* level design and story was ok* basic game idea was good* nice puzzle ideas with the season spheres (though devs missed a lot of good chances to make use of the mechanics, especially summer and autumn sphere felt mostly pointless)* movement and clipping is overall aweful* climbing is so tedious and slow (it really needs fixing)* game uses unnatural invisible walls instead of proper level boundaries* areas or cities do not feel really alive and are too empty* unless some few story and intro cutscenes, the rest of the game only has textboxes* insta-death enemy attacks on higher difficulties* insta-reset if you touch thorns (why?)* not footsprints or even particle effects while walking through sand or snow (common, it is 2023)* fight system needs a lot of rework (actually a lot of things need some polishing)* no ingame helps to find collectibles (marker, area pointers, etc.), can be annoying to find some of them you missed* NPC often don't react on permanent season changes (eg. peons do field works on frozen firelds or kids bathing in a frozen lake)* bug: you can bethesda around a lot (typical Unity engine issue with double jumps)* bug: enemies sometimes do not move or stand around like dead (loot already dropped)* bug: autumn sphere does play a rain sound but you will not see the rain inside the sphere* bug: I had to constantly re-equipe my head cosmetics after every cutscene, even my weapon after each destroyed crystal cutscene* bug: boss fight bugged out - he just levitated into the sky (wtf?)I wanted to like the game, and my overall opinion is mostly neutral. But at the current state I cannot really recommend this game because it needs a lot of polishing and is buggy. I will change my mind as soon as the game comes out of the beta state it is currently in. But it does not feel like a full release atm, so don't pay full price. If you get it on a sale, it is still entertaining enough though.

_childDocuments_.review: There were many bugs that stopped me from Immersively playing. The world, while not detailed, seemed to have a lot of exploration and adventure. However, the more i played, the emptier it looked despite the seemingly expansive maps.NPCs felt one-dimensional, either just to mock Ary or repeating the same dialogues even if it didn't make sense anymore. The quests were predominantly fetch quests, which is okay, but it doesn't help that most NPCs were uninteresting. That said, i really liked one NPC and that's the Minotaur, he was cute, gentle and goofy.The puzzles were okay, especially those that integrated with the seasonal mechanics. Some of course were frustrating, like the ones that required moving the ball.The bugs were what stopped me from playing. From quest markers resetting on reloading saves to dungeon mechanisms failing to function properly. The main questline had poor pacing and confusing progression, things happened prematurely, like getting all the elemental crystals even though i haven't explored all the 4 regions, or the glove that's needed for the golem dungeons was only pointed out during the 3rd dungeon.I think this could have been a great game that could have been fun too, and it has potential, but the negatives and shortcomings of the game outweighs the positives. I don't think it's worth the asking price in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Buy when on sale, ok game but still needs to be polished and fixed of some bugs~Positive~The game looks nice and feels ok to control (least with a controller). The lands you visit are nicely packed with people even though almost all are just for decoration and sometimes the land will have wide open space with nothing there but an invisible wall.I did however enjoy exploring for side quests or treasures to get some coins for costumes or even upgrades to my stats.The puzzles are ok, not hard but some can be on the super easy side, only challenge I got was from the stork towers.The flipping of seasons and using them to solve puzzles I think could of been done better, most times it takes 1 season to do the puzzle and rarely takes a 2nd season in-play to be needed. This includes the bosses. Pretty much all bosses can be taken down with one season with only a 2nd one needed to do 1 thing which is a let down. Most bosses can be done within 1 minute and even the final boss was a 2 minute joke  with one season needed.~Negative~75% through and the game decides it no longer wanted to run forcing me to restart many times in a room due to my frames just died for no reason and Ary just refused to move on some vines making it impossible to continue until the 5th actual restart of the game.This game is still buggy, parts of the environment are floating in the air, Ary often won't climb certain areas she is meant to and reloading the game from some save points can actually soft lock you causing you to restart the game from scratch. Not fun at all when you are half way through.Bosses are a joke but that is when you know what to do, pretty much you are never told nor hinted what you need to do to defeat a boss often causing not only myself but many others to legit look up a video to even get an idea on how to damage the bosses. This only happened on first boss but some indication would of been nice.As mentioned above, the final boss is a 2 minute joke, no real challenge which is a shame and doesn't even feel like a final boss.Chests and certain quest items don't show on the map even though they are on the map in other areas which makes me confused to why some appear and others do not. Also a pain to check the map, you have a mini-map but to bring up the map itself you need to pause and go to the inventory menu to get to it, no quick button mapping for some reason.Overall, I did have fun until the game decided it no longer wanted to work for a certain amount of time and I was lucky to not soft lock myself even on a no-death run but there are parts of this game that still needs to be polished and fixed which seems to be not happening anytime soon.I would only buy this when it is on sale because even not knowing what to do it only took me 7 hours to 100% on a blind run.

_childDocuments_.review: I greatly enjoyed this game. There were some lingering bugs, but they did not affect my game progress or my ability to have fun (they were all quite minor). I'm sure they will be patched soon. The dungeons are where this game shines the best; they are very well-designed. Unfortunately, you have to play for a few hours before you reach the first full "proper" dungeon. Even so, it's worth the time investment. You are given access to all 4 seasons before the first dungeon, and that means you have mostly free reign to explore the world with a lot of options from very early on. There are essentially 4 different versions of the same world to explore - as the seasons can be activated anywhere in the entire game. You can have all 4 seasons represented in the same room.The whole game feels like a passion project. You can tell that a lot of care was put into the animations and character designs. The story is neat - not groundbreaking or anything, but it was enjoyable. The combat was a bit easy (on normal mode). Sometimes it felt like the game tried to do too many things, and that means that some of them just don't feel as important or fleshed out as others. I think it's clear that the story/cut-scene, characters, town, and dungeon designs got the most attention. But the game also has a bunch of optional cosmetics, skill upgrades, and sidequests to go through. Despite its flaws, I love this game for the dungeons alone. If you like games like The Legend of Zelda series, I highly recommend Ary and the Secret of Seasons.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know if I am of a simpler mind than other players, but I really enjoyed the game. There are undoubtedly flaws as many of the other reviews stated, but personally I did not encounter any game breaking ones (at least none that I didn't provoke myself by climbing to places you're obviously not supposed to be) in my playthrough.I was intrigued by the season mechanics the moment I saw the game at Gamescom and seeing it applied in the final product, it feels like the first time you understand the mechanics of Portal. It felt amazing to cheese my way through one of the temples using the season spheres, skipping most of the puzzles, only to then find out I had to go through most of it again with severely reduced season powers, so this time I had to play them properly! The developers stated in one press interview that a bunch of puzzles got cut after play testing revealed that some players would get stuck on them, but I'd like to see them added back in!The story is cute, but a bit too compressed. Everything happens rather quickly. There is optional content, some of which with a lot of word building and background info on the main characters. Speaking of which, the main cast is a bunch of likeable characters, helped along by some brilliant voice acting during the cutscenes. At first you're belittled by most people you meet, but over the course of the story this prejudice against Ary is turned around.The boss fights are a mixed bag, but overall fun. Most of them follow the established pattern of figuring out the mechanic and repeating that mechanic a couple of times, very much like any Zelda boss. The final fight in the game is pretty underwhelming, however. It really felt like a stage one of some larger battle. It's a shame, because overall the fights where creative, using your season abilities to find the enemy's weak spot.Overall, would I recommend it? Yeah, give it a try! Again, I had quite some fun exploring the world and its story, from which the flaws did not distract me.

_childDocuments_.review: Normally I wouldn't start a review with technical descriptions, but in the case of Ary, it's really necessary. The unfinished state also caused frustration when playing from the beginning - especially on the consoles (as it seems judged by internet reviews). On the PC, there was a more classic and eye-pleasing action-adventure flair. The story about an evil mage, hyenas invading the land and missing children like Ary's brother doesn't exactly win any originality awards, especially since its characters also seem relatively interchangeable. This impression is also created in the many dull fetch-and-carry side quests. In an over-frozen summer idyll, for example, the population standing around in bathing suits must be warmed up, as they are too comfortable to get warmer clothes for themselves. Since mysterious crystals fell from the sky, everything has changed in the realm of Valdi, because the eternal seasons of the four regions have been thrown into disarray.Ary and her helpers basically come across as likeable, but this is undermined by the deliberately comical humour. This is revealed, for example, in the excessive boogie dancing of the oldest member of the Seasonal Council. Or in the heroine telling thousands of opponents that they stink. In general, the undemanding battles do not exactly convey the feeling of being a chosen warrior on a mission around which ancient legends are entwined in the land. I could easily jog past the majority of the unmotivated standard warriors without breaking a sweat. In the long run, the battles become more varied - thanks to small combos, energy upgrades, alternative weapons from the merchant or a slingshot. But despite the focus on a young target group, I would have expected more excitement when I raided camps full of sheep guards, healing mages or fireball flowers. Above all, the easy-to-execute counter-attack is clearly too powerful!During the eleven-hour adventure, only the eponymous seasonal puzzles provided a nice sense of discovery. Aryelle (that's her full name) "slipped" into gaps in dungeons from time to time. But once I got the feeling for the different seasons, it was quite motivating to experiment with the abilities, some of which are cleverly combined. Large masses of water froze into a bridge in the blink of an eye or melted secret grotto entrances. Or I dived to the bottom of a pond to install a giant air bell next to a magic stone and tinker with ancient contraptions.Here, spiked traps are frozen, stone balls are balanced on connected switches with a flashing beam or gate traps are outwitted with a sprint. Water spheres invite you to swim upwards or abruptly stop a huge rolling spider goblin. However, the hectic camera also made the multi-level boss fights a bit bumpy.Ary and the Secret of Seasons has everything an amazing adventure game needs: a good story, great characters, no repetitive puzzles and an innovative game idea ... BUT it has to fight with a certain number of bugs and a "wonky camera". Without the bugs, the game would have been a lot better. Most of the bugs can easily be ignored and the game is fully functional / playable. If you're expecting a neat 8-11 hour adventure, then you're good to go because the biggest bugs seem to be fixed from what I've played. I didn't encounter a single gamebreaking bug whatsoever.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a mix of good and bad. The story and puzzle dungeons are the good but the combat and side quests are the bad. I couldn't make it through the whole game. With all the forced combat and overall lack of polish it was too much.Anyway, the puzzle dungeons are the best part of the game. They're large with tons of opportunities to use your powers. They're fairly open so you can figure them out in your own way. Where you want to place the season's bubble. There are power amplification towers too which make the season bubble much larger. The dungeons get even more exciting later on when you start to collect season powers.Where the game falls apart is the combat. It's all a bit amateur with little feedback given to the player. It ends up being button mashing and not the good kind like in a warriors game. Also, there's nothing to gain by fighting. Sometimes a chest but it gives you money to upgrade powers. Not needed if I'm going to be trying to skip as much combat as possible. But you will run into a few required bosses so there are places the game forces you. Unfortunately it all feels forced. If you're making a game it has to have combat right? I wonder if playing on easy makes it any better.The side quests are not much better. Boring running between two points. They do add flavor to the game world and help introduce you to the regular citizens of the world. But having to go fetch someone's hot chocolate for some gold isn't exciting. Especially in these giant areas that feel incredibly empty. These too feel forced into the game for little reason.Overall, Ary and the Secrets of the Seasons is OK. While the season mechanics are interesting the lack of polish is substantial. As I mentioned playing the game on easy might make it better to focus on the story. It is a cute game with a lot of voice acting. Now, I don't normally comment on the price of the game but $40 is a shocker. The developer has every right to charge whatever they want. I would skip it for now since you could pick up a couple games with the funds instead.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll update this review after I have played more. This game has a lot of charm in a lot of places, but there are places where the charm is absent. it feels as though this was a very ambitious game, but turned out to be just a little bit too much. there is lovely world building, such as describing a place as a centre for spiritual learning, but there being a relative absence of any signs of spiritual learning such as monks meditating, etc. there's a funny bit with a guy trying to fish, but the water is iced over... it's funny until you remeber the place is eternal winter, so why would he even think to try fishing? some areas of the town have no access routes, no steps or paths, which just seems il thought out. some NPC's display no animation when you talk to them. these are just small reasons as to why this game fails in places, but it still has charm in many ways, the main character is cute and likeable. the controls feel good, there is good exploration and nice music. it feels compelling with a world that makes me want to see more. then of course there is the price. I recommend this game, on the proviso that you find it at more than 50% off. there is just such a lack of polish that it doesn't warrant the high price tag and it just feels bad. there are many things in the game that just feel unfinished that makes me feel, asking such a high price is almost an insult. I do like it so far though, so I provisionally recommend this.

_childDocuments_.review: Reviewing at 50% of the way through the game.I get how this has mixed reviews, there are definitely aspects that could be better (if you play a Zelda-like for the combat this game will certainly disappoint, as the combat is uninteresting, but mercifully quick). I mostly don't give a crap about the combat in this genre, and it does pretty well at the other aspects.The story is a bit trite but works fine. The collectibles are maybe a bit annoying in that you go past them unable to reach them so to get them all is presumably a two playthrough thing, which is not for me; luckily I don't care too much about collectibles either. The puzzles are decently done so far; they feel a bit surprisingly unforgiving to me, but I think that's mostly my struggling to navigate in 3D games when there's no minimap - I occasionally spend a while looking for the puzzle, more than it being difficult to *solve* the puzzle. (The game has a minimap but not inside the temples.)I wouldn't recommend it at full price, as it's certainly not the quality of a real Zelda game, but at a reasonable indie game price point it's a fine deal for a game that's pretty relaxing and fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, it's definitly a good one... just not a great one, unfortunately.For starters, the game feels a bit incomplete at times. Like there are 4 seasons, but only two of them actually "do" something, and winter certainly does "the most".I did not encounter crashes, but I got into an endless loop with an NPC not getting out of its dialogue, repeating the same box over and over and over again. Some enemies like to leave a hitbox with their gold drop inside, making it unreachable, and the game occasionally makes enemy corpses fly away, or has you clip through the ground. "Used" things on the map aren't always grayed out, and there's probably a lot of other minor-ish bugs.In general, it feels like it could use some bugfixing.And, of course, there are various annoyances. In particualar, part of the story is found through collectibles -- and the imprecise/unpredictable controls makes it a pain to collect anything (so, I didn't 100% it). There's no way to know which area still has stuff to find.I'm not sure whether shop items actually do something. It appears that items have no stats/properties, so I only spent my money on upgrades because those actually do something (or so I hope...).Bosses have been surprising okay...-ish. As always, the game doesn't tell you anything, but I actually liked some of the bosses to some extent. And that's probably means something, considering I generally hate bosses in games.Abd whule many games have incomplete voice acting, this one uses the "stupid noises" scheme for dialogue without voice acting: characters will just give you annoying noises or fragments that are supposed to somewhat match the tone of what they are saying; I'd very much prefer if they would just not get any voice if they didn't record the proper lines.All in all, the game felt like it has potential. It plays decent enough if you're not trying to get collectibles that require better controls, it looks good, it sounds good, and the I liked the main characters. It just feels like there could be more.

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of weird clipping issues (ie. nonexistent hitboxes, hitboxes too large, hitboxes too small). Not well optimized, very poor performance. Many bugs beyond just clipping. As examples, you can end up double buying items, enemies may become invincible for no apparent reason, and enemies AIs might just randomly freeze. If you save in the hub area, you might end up seeing a cutscene multiple times because the game doesn't seem to properly check whether the cutscene should apply after a load.A lot of weird resultant bugs too, such as rooms locking when they should be unlocked or things breaking when they shouldn't because of weird hitboxes. Enemies also have fairly short respawns now where if you go past a certain distance, they respawn. This is great for farming, but not so great for exploring.Due to weird clipping and physics, the platforming portions can be more difficult than they should be. For example, if you touch a highly slanted object (over 45 degree slant) during a jump, you might start sliding or if you touch a wall, you might end up floating. This can make platforming more difficult, especially if a key platform decides to count as a highly slanted object - in which case you sometimes have to exit and reenter the area or reload a previous save.Also, beware of minor sequence breaks. For example, if you go to open a chest in the summer area that requires you to go underwater by waiting for the tide to change to push you underwater, you may end up trapped inside as the clipping inside causes you to walk into the air instead of diving back under. Instead, the game expects you to open the chest later on when you can freely dive. Worst is if you accidentally save while trapped.Also, be aware of changing windows as the game still takes input while out of focus. Not an issue for most players, but can be annoying for players in certain situations, like if you are trying to look up whether something is a known bug with a solution or not.Save in a NEW slot often in case something goes wrong, so you only lose 5-60 minutes of work. From what I've played so far, the speedrun achievement is mostly luck - how badly will bugs slow down your run matters more than your actual skill.Also, for the impaired, be aware that there is white text on white/near white backgrounds.

_childDocuments_.review: Ary and the Secret of Seasons is a 3D, open world, puzzle platformer. Ary has a wholesome story line which is very kid friendly. The puzzles found in Ary aren't really difficult. If you can't seem to solve something, it probably means you don't currently have the tools to deal with it at that time so come back to it later.My main critique with it is that it needs more polish. The game has numerous collision detection issues which can be annoying in some spots; however, it's not really that big of a deal in most places. If you can look past these, you should have a good deal of fun with the game.Not sure if I'd pay full price for it, though. I bought the game when it was on sale and I'm happy with my purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: I was surprised this game has so many negative reviews so I decided to give it a try myself and now I can see why. In the first cutscene, the game looks really good, even voice acting is alright, and you can clearly tell some effort went into the game. Once the cutscene ends, you get the taste of how the movement works and I have to say it's quite mediocre to say the least. Then you leave the house and start seeing what the gameplay is actually all about, it's nothing short of disappointing. Besides the numerous bugs you encounter just, the combat is boring and so is the whole premise. However, I like how you have the power to change 4 seasons (which is cool I guess but I never got far enough to test out anything else other than winter). Another good thing is there are various vendors where you can buy new cosmetics, weapons and skills, it's a nice addition for sure but it's not a gamechanger.I don't understand, though, why only 1 side quest shows up at a time (not to mention the way how those quests are displayed feels extremely cheap) and arrow pointing at where supposed to go on the mini map is kinda useless too. All of those things would be bearable to an extend, what really made me uninstall the game is I managed to soft lock myself. I even tried reloading the last auto-save but nothing happened. I was supposed to grab a gear inside a windmill but I never got prompted to pick it up, even if I mashed the right button.This game definitely had potential but failed to ultimately deliver. Other than the steep price tag (though you can get it on fanatical for about 50 cents), it's just a buggy mess that's more pain to play than fun.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is still a bit rough around the edges. I encountered most of the bugs the developer mentioned in the launch day update, along with a few additional ones of my own. None of these completely broke the game, except for one issue: the autosave system can get stuck, meaning it doesn’t actually save. This caused me to lose all progress through an entire dungeon. That said, it didn’t stop me from finishing the game—I just had to replay the dungeon.  The story is charming and sweet, although the ending felt a bit abrupt. The main character is adorable, memorable, and genuinely fun to play. The developers did a great job designing the outfits and weapons. The combat is enjoyable and can be surprisingly challenging on higher difficulty settings. The platforming sections were also well done.  It took me around 13 hours the first time to reach the end, and I never felt like my time was wasted. That being said, I’d recommend picking it up on sale until the remaining bugs are resolved. The good news is that the developer seems dedicated to ironing out the issues.

_childDocuments_.review: Good concept, but very buggy.I liked most of the game, though some of the segments are frustratingGood:-Fun game mechanics-Amazing world building-Great graphicsBad:-parkour and puzzles in the temples get more frustrating as you progress, it often feels like I am using some speedrun mechanics skip mechanics to get to other areas-extremely buggy->lots of wall/floor glitches->whenever you destroy a crystal, it equips the mechanical sword; sure, it's acquired later on and likely the default sword you should use, but if I equip a different sword, it should stay equipped->"saving" doesn't save your current progress; you get sent back to some automatic save spot and need to repeat a lot when you load "your" save file->(this lead to me dropping the game) the winter temple entrance can't be reached because the ice platforms I see in other videos do not exist whether I use winter magic or notI would overlook most of these bugs, but if the game becomes only beatable with speedrunning tactics, I cannot recommend this game if it's not sold with that premise being the focus of the game.I do think the developer can make good games, but they should test the game and fix bugs like this before releasing it.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, buy this game on sale as it's buggy. If you save the game manually often, you should be fine. Now that's aside, I really did enjoy this game! _childDocuments_.review: I hesitated for a long time to get "Ary and the Secret of Seasons" because of the mixed Steam reviews. But bought it and couldn't put it down. (Played on PC with mouse and keyboard.)First my subjective opinion. Ary is a great puzzle platformer game. I love the mechanics and every new puzzle required thinking. The world isn't big, but exploring off the beaten track has always been worthwhile.But I would also like to give you my objective comments for your purchase decision. I did my first 100% run in 18 hours and I'll probably do another speed run for the last archivments. There's no denying that the game could have used a little more polish, but none of the minor glitches, texture glitches, or camera glitches really diminished my enjoyment of the game. I didn't have any crashes, the graphics were okay and I didn't have to load a desperate save game either.@eXiin: I was really excited about your game. I hope you have more time for your next game, I felt that you still had a lot of things with Ary that you couldn't bring in anymore. But I could feel your passion and love for the idea of the game and also the freedom/creativity you allow the players. I would definitely love a sequel to Ary. Keep up the good work.

_childDocuments_.review: I really loved this game, but it is hard to recommend to anyone but the most dedicated players. It is the kind of game that has a big heart, and a low budget, and some players will find it to be a hidden gem. IF they can tolerate bugs almost all the way through the journey.PRO:- lovely world and characters- mix between Zelda and Fenyx Rising- season bubbles are a really fun mechanic, and the puzzles are mostly well implemented for itCON:- some puzzles are not too well presented, they miss the "professional touch" to guide you, or some are just outright janky mechanically- BUGS: this is the big negative unfortunately. I'm not sure I ever seen so much bugs. There are some smaller bugs at platforming, but the big ones are related to fighting. Sometimes enemies just die, more often you will die when nothing even tounched you (even from max health), enemies will hit you from afar. An other area where bugs will happen is after reloading when you've died. Sometimes enemies you've killed are dead already, sometimes they are alive, sometimes they teleport around, and sometimes you die right after reloading :D.- fight system is bad. Its not fun to use, and you can be stunlocked after hit. Upgrades are there to spend money, but except the damage ones they are not needed (some I don't even know what they do)- some new abilities are not prompted when received, or the message just bugs out and don't appear. Once I got 2 season powers and the game didn't even mention it to me. It doesn't tell you either what exactly seasons do. Winter and Spring has clear uses, but I'm not even sure if Summer and Autumn have any unique mechanics that needs to be used.All in all if you can tolerate one of the buggiest game, you can have a great time with Ary and the secret of seasons. Maybe just imagine you are a tester :). Oh, and definately wait for a sale or a patch (but honestly I don't think they will be able to patch all the problems).

_childDocuments_.review: Ary and the Secret of Seasons is a Zelda-like in which you control seasons. These seasonal differences come in to play in puzzles as well as combat. There are environmental differences based on the season you've used and it's really cool to see all the details they included. The characters, voice acting, and writing all seem really good so far; not too silly, not too serious. The combat against basic enemies is a bit too easy with upgrades, so I would recommend a higher difficulty than normal for seasoned gamers. (Seasoned gamers! Get it? The story is pretty good, but not fully explained. The seasons end up out of balance and you have to restore that balance, by visiting different regions experiencing different seasons, going through dungeons (mostly puzzles), and fighting golems. The story finished off with a pretty satisfying twist, and I'd say is pretty open for a sequel.There's an absolute pile of bugs which may impact your enjoyment of the game, but so far the devs have been good about patching things up, and I'd argue that the game is still enjoyable enough to pick up.The game is such a fun concept that I hope they make a sequel. This is definitely worth checking out if you're in the market for a new Zelda-like!

_childDocuments_.review: Journey across the magnificent world of Valdi! Ary and the Secret of Seasons is an award-winning adventure game following a young girl named Aryelle, or Ary, as she journeys across the great world of Valdi. By becoming the Guardian of Winter, Ary gains the ability to manipulate the seasons around her. Ary will learn to control the seasons and use them to defeat enemies, overcome obstacles, and solve complex puzzles on her adventure across Valdi. Long ago, the world of Valdi was threatened by an evil mage. After a great struggle, he was defeated by the Legendary Warrior and sealed inside the Vault, imprisoned for all eternity. To ensure the mage's imprisonment, four great sages swore to keep watch and protect the Vault. They formed the original Guardians of Seasons, a secretive organization now steeped in history and legend. After a mysterious force throws the seasons of Valdi into disarray, Ary decides to assist the Guardians of Seasons and sets out to find the source of the mayhem. Using her wits and courage, Ary will have to overcome monstrous enemies, secret plots, and stuffy traditions to save Valdi and bring balance to the world once more.

detailed_description: Deluxe Edition The Life is Strange: True Colors Deluxe edition contains: Life is Strange: True Colors: the complete game. Exclusive Bonus Story: ‘Wavelengths’: play as Steph in the year before Alex came to Haven Springs, in a standalone story set in the iconic Rocky Mountain Record Traders store and KRCT radio station. Exclusive Life is Strange Hero Outfit Pack: change up Alex's look with 4 new outfits inspired by past protagonists. The pack includes clothing inspired by Chloe’s Misfit Skull, Sean’s Wolf Squad, Daniel’s Space Mission, and Max’s Jane Doe outfits, with one outfit available for Alex to wear in each chapter of the main game. Ultimate Edition The Life is Strange: True Colors Ultimate edition contains: Life is Strange: True Colors Exclusive Bonus Story: ‘Wavelengths’ Exclusive Life is Strange Hero Outfit Pack Life is Strange Remastered Life is Strange: Before the Storm Remastered Reviews & Accolades “Fantastic game that offers a great story.” IGN – 9/10 “Beautiful and brilliant.” Eurogamer – Recommended “An incredible new addition to the series.” TheSixthAxis – 9/10 “Truly something special.” TheGamer – 5/5 “At its heart, True Colors is a story about community and what it means to not be alone.” Gayming Magazine – 5/5 “Shows off what the next-generation of the series can deliver.” GamesRadar+ - 9/10 “It’s been a long time since a narrative resonated with us the way True Colors did.” CBR “Made me laugh, made me cry, and made me fall in love with its characters.” CGMagazine “Incredible piece of art.” Escapist “As beautiful as it is heart-wrenching.” NME - 4/5 “My game of the year so far.” Kinda Funny Games “Highly refreshing.” Metro - 8/10 “Players will be heartbroken to leave the imperfectly perfect town of Haven Springs.” GameRant “The most intimate game of the last decade.” Inverse “Best game I’ve played in 2021.” UPROXX “In a world that’s so vastly divided by difference, True Colors is a pertinent and urgent story.” Pink News - 4/5 “True Colors is the peak of the Life is Strange series to date.” Shacknews “Life is Strange: True Colors is one of those rare follow-ups to a classic that not only outshines the original but also reinvents itself from the ground up without losing what made the series great.” TechRaptor “A big-budget experience from beginning to end.” Tom’s Guide “A beautiful story of empathy and new beginnings.” Noisey Pixel “Emotionally resonant.” ComicBook . com – 4.5/5 “An artistic achievement.” Common Sense Media – 5/5 “Deck Nine has taken the franchise to the next level.” PC Invasion – 9/10 “A hit.” MP1st – 9/10 “An absolute gem.” App Trigger – 10/10 “Near perfect.” GamerHeadquarters – 9.5/10 About the Game A bold new era of the award-winning Life is Strange begins, with an all-new playable lead character and a thrilling mystery to solve! Alex Chen has long suppressed her 'curse': the supernatural ability to experience, absorb and manipulate the strong emotions of others, which she sees as blazing, colored auras. When her brother dies in a so-called accident, Alex must embrace her volatile power to find the truth – and uncover the dark secrets buried by a small town. THE TRUTH WILL HURT Discover the shocking secrets behind your brother’s death in an emotional roller-coaster of an adventure. FEEL EVERYTHING Change fate and change lives with the psychic power of Empathy. FORGE DEEP RELATIONSHIPS Build trust with the townsfolk – and embrace friendship or romance with Ryan and Steph. A TRULY PERSONAL STORY Make tough decisions and choose your own future. Freely roam the streets, stores, and hidden spaces of Haven Springs and meet unforgettable characters. FIND YOUR VOICE And decide Alex's style, with up to 24 outfits in your wardrobe. EXCLUSIVE SOUNDTRACK Original score by Angus & Julia Stone, new tracks by mxmtoon and Novo Amor, and extensive licensed songs including Radiohead, Phoebe Bridgers, Gabrielle Aplin, and more.

_childDocuments_.review: This one's gonna be a bit personal, by necessity.Saying money is a premium for me would be an understatement, so I try to put a lot of thought into my purchases. But everything about this has made it... at least currently, my favorite game full stop. Granted ymmv. Some of the things that made it so impactful for me is that, Alex's backstory is, while not fully accurate to my own, very familiar. And I'm currently (and have been for a while), in the same emotional space Alex occupies at the start of the story. It helped me realize a lot about myself, and what I want for my life.So ye gods, if you had a traumatic childhood and are neurodivergent, I can't stress enough how much of a must-buy this likely is. Beyond it being a great story, in which even some of the unnamed background characters have some emotional depth and the main cast brought me to tears more than once. It's one of the rare cases where I ended up referring to alex as "I" a couple times, in the far more personal way that video games can sometimes touch us than any other form of media, in my experience.On another note, the accessibility settings are above-and-beyond that which most games offer. Relevant to myself in particular, it has a "loud sound warning" that you can use to open the settings menu and adjust volume levels before louder scenes. But I didn't even end up needing it, because the mixing is done so well that it never managed to ♥♥♥♥ with my sensory integration.Can't recommend it enough, 11/10, personal game of the decade easily unless something else comes along that blows my socks off and thirteen feet into the ground. I'd say "You did it again". But it's more accurate to say "You managed to do it better than I ever could have hoped for".Bravo, encore. Idk what to even say for this. I've always loved the Life is Strange series, but Deck Nine managed to make something really special into something unbelievably so.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece in so many ways, and I have a lot to say about it. To make your reading experience easier, I’ll divide this review into sections so you can easily navigate it.This game handles emotions incredibly well. It centers around Alex Chen, a young woman with the interesting ability to see and absorb emotions from other people. As the player, you are given the option to help people who are going through difficult situations by understanding why they are hurting.Some of these situations really pulled on my heartstrings. For instance, there is an elderly woman with Alzheimer’s whom I personally related to, as I have a grandfather with the same disease. Her segment of the game was done extremely well, with so much care put into it. It felt so real.The small town of Haven Springs is possibly one of the best open worlds I have ever explored. Every small corner and back alley is littered with details and secrets to discover. It felt like a real, living world, with all of its inhabitants whose lives you can affect by doing small “side quests” for them.Chapter 2 is especially awesome since it gives you full freedom to explore the town and interact with its citizens. Each one was interesting and fun to learn about!This game’s story was fantastic from beginning to end. Without spoiling anything, it has by far the best story of a Life Is Strange game. Unlike previous entries in the series where you would have to wait months between episodes, this game released with all five chapters ready to play. They all feel connected and tied together nicely, which is something I cannot say for its predecessors.Overall, this is a very well-made game with a beautiful open world and a great story. I highly recommend playing it!

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the first four chapters (out of five) in Life is Strange: True Colors a lot. It's clear that the developers wanted to capture some of the cozy atmosphere from the first game, and they succeeded at least partially. The characters are charming and their acting is on point. The facial animation and motion capture is marvellous. You become intimately familiar with the town and its residents over the course of these four chapters.The game completely falls apart in the fifth chapter, though. I've heard some people call it rushed, but that's not the case at all. The issue is that the writers suddenly turn to the most clichéd tropes imaginable in a story like this, and it doesn't even serve a point. Half the chapter is spent on a pointless and unrealistic dream sequence (seriously, nobody dreams this way) that is supposed to add personal stakes to a story that... already has more than enough personal stakes. It doesn't help that the attempt is extremely clumsy, heavy-handed, and poorly conceived. Without going into spoiler territory, it all resolves in a very bizarre way that isn't supported by the narrative up to this point, and major characters begin to act very out of character to add drama (again, for stakes that aren't needed). Still, I do recommend this game. It's very much a Life is Strange game that has more in common with the much-loved first entry than the second (which is still a great game). Does it stick the landing? No, not at all. But to be fair, the original game fell into some of the same pitfalls in its final chapter too, though for different reasons. LiS1's final chapter was rushed. LiS:TC's final chapter is poorly written.Go into this with the proper expectations and you'll have a great time.

_childDocuments_.review: Difficulty: Emotional DamageStory (Spoiler alert abviously):Okay, jokes aside, well made, story is told interesting and makes you wanna binge the chapters (except chapter 3, that was skippable).As per usual in a interactive movie like game, you are participating in a linear main story ark, but you can change some dialog options to achieve different outcomes of conversations.In LiS2, your choices didn't matter, this time, there acually are some different outcomes in the "non final" chapters. The choices still don't have as much impact as they had in the first one (commiting suicide or not, getting thrown out of school or not, appearing in the final chapter or not), but there are still some choices to change some scenes. For example, there is a romance again, like in the first one, and the prequal. As usual, there is a straight, gay and platonical option to choose, nothing really new. I didn't even want the romance, but got one with Ryan anyways, even though I didn't kiss him and also didn't give him a rose, there should have really been a non romantic ending for me trying to friendzone him so hard ;P.In the final chapter, all the "major" choices just boil down to "does XY stand up for you". This means the big choices don't really change anything (signing the affidavit or publishing the evidence seemed like such an important choice, but in the end, it doesn't even matter).Graphics:The Game looks okay, and you sure need a good setup to run this (12th gen i9, rtx 3070 gave me about 30-60 FPS on a 4k TV on very high, since cinematic had stutters). Sadly there are black bars if you play on anything else than a 16:9 screen (played on a 16:10 TV), but luckily there is UUU3021)Voice Acting;Other than graphics: Voice acting is great, there is lots of stuff to read and discover outside of the main story line which is nice.Level Design:Still lots to discover, memories to find, zen moments to have, backstory to read etc.Length:I had about 9.5 hours for my first playthrough, but didn't get the collectables. After using repaly mode to get the 100% I was at 10.7h. Thats about half the playtime I normally have. (In LiS1, Before the Storm and LiS2 I had about 20h at least in everey game.Bugs:Never encountered a single one (Well except Ethan hovering over the floor a bit)Replayability:I'd really like to replay it, but without a skip cutscene button on a second playthrough, it feels like a drag. To quote u/Chabb:"Basically, the game has a "replay" feature for collectibles and achievements. This mode allows you to fast forward through cutscenes, dialogs and actions within a section of a chapter you've already played. Which is by itself super fine and extremely useful to experience different things and jump straight to the point. But if you finish a section through that mode, instead of progressing onto the next one, it just brings you back to the main menu. That means there is no way to explore different outcomes from potential new choices that happen in later sections/chapters outside a full official restart... In which there is no fast forward feature, forcing you to sit through cutscenes conversations again you've already witnessed."In the end, because of that I chose to not replay it. Lots of wasted potential.Tldr: your choices don't matter (as usual in LiS), but its still a nice adventure, if you want a game where your choices have an impact, play detroit become human I guess^^

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I can't remember if I payed the full 60 euro/dollar price for this game or got a slight discount, but either way I just don't think it was worth it. TL;DR it just doesn't scratch the itch that LiS 1 did. Long version: The game felt pretty short and the setting didn't feel like it took me to many places. The story itself dissappointed me for a couple reasons. First, it did not do a great job of creating suspense, adventure and intrigue after the first chapter. True colors has some very simplistic, vanilla romance options and lacks the slow-burn, memorable sexual tension of the first game. Second, where LiS 1 forged a satisfying deep connection between the two main characters and then intelligently played the interactions with the other minor characters off of that, True colors  just didn't: you meet alot of people and have occassionally interesting interactions with them, but there is no core to it, nobody with which the main character has any consistant intimacy or drama. For such a friendly-faced atmosphere, on a meta level it's a profoundly lonely game. Third, I would also say the small-town dynamic of the game is literally too small, like it just feels like a collection of slice-of-life moments with neighbors who all live on the same street and are almost all friends. There's no attempt to create a realistic divide between the protagonist's immediate social circle and the community as a whole. You never feel at home or out in the world, everything is blended toegther in an alienating way, and I don't think would resonates with many people's actual experiences of life in the USA, small town or not. This rural colorado town of layed back hipster residents with no deep poltical, cultural, class or generational conflicts amongst eachother also just feels like a broken fantasy version of America. Fifth and finally, there are some sad moments that might make you tear up if they trigger your own memories of loss, but overall, the protagonist's trauma is only explored in a shallow, overly abstracted way that isn't that memorable, and as stated, broader social problems are mostly ignored. I won't say this game is straight up bad. It's entertaining while you play it, sort of, but when it ends you realized it was super underwhelming compared to the compeling highs, lows, and striking cultural insight of the first one. It just doesn't feel like "an experience,' if you know what I mean. Final verdict: perhaps worth buying when the price comes down.

_childDocuments_.review: I finished living is odd 3 and it’s a 7/10 but closer to a 6SPOILERS FOR THE GAMEI did end up caring for most of the people in the game. Especially Riley and Nana (I related a lot to Riley in the sense she wanted to pursue her own dreams and leave the small town but would drop it all to take care of her grandma) which she ended up not doing it in my play through cuz I hid Nana’s sickness from herDuckie got 3 scenes total but his final scene is probably one of my favorites in the game.There’s still some characters that just aren’t intriguing at all. And you could tell this game would've rather be a slice of life since we spent a whole chapter doing a larp session. And all the good parts I mentioned beforehand don’t even relate to the murder mystery and if you ask somebody their favorite parts of the game- you might just not guess there's even a murder mystery involved. _childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: My recommendation is to buy Deluxe Edition on sale for 35€. I'm not recommending dropping 60€ on a 14 hour game. That being said,I love the original Life is Strange. It's one of my favourite pieces of art across all media. My fealings towards it's prequel, Before the Storm (Deck 9's first game) were mixed. It had a few great moments but it felt fan-servicey and lacked the depth of it predecessor. However it's biggest "flaw", IMO was that it was inviting comparison to LiS and those shoes were just too big for it to fill.True Colors, meanwhile, is almost completely unrelated to the previous LiS games, except for magical realism and the inclusion of one character from Before the Storm; and the game is much better for it because it allowed authors the freedom to do their own thing. The result is excellent. The story is heart-felt but in a completely new way (although the starting setup is similar to DONTNOD's excellent Tell Me Why). Exploring feels more free then in any of the previous LiS titles . Also, to my eye at least, there is a greater richness and nuance of those little choices that enable the player to make the story their own. The new power is really interesting and using it is a lot of fun. I'm tempted as hell to say more about it but I feel like anything more would be venturing into spoiler territory. Alex is an awesome character, right up there in the PriceField tier of awesomeness. The supporting characters are all pretty engaging, well worth your time to get to know them. There is one possible "one note" exception but overall, they're a fun bunch.Finally the length: the game feels short. However, this is not due to the lack of content - it's because the story progresses at a steady pace and time does fly when you're having fun. Fourteen hours I finished it in over a weekend flew by, but during it, I was never bored, not even when I replayed one whole scene just to alter one ill-considered dialogue choice (Max Caufield's power would make life so much easier :) ). I'm pretty sure that I'll replay it at least once, maybe as early as next weekend. Verdict: Nothing compares to LiS Season 1, but True Colors is very good in it's own way. If you want to play a character you want to root for through a story with miles of heart then this is a game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Life is Strange True Colors really surprised me as a standalone new entry into the series with its own story and characters and not being a sequel to any other one. My experience with the series are that I played the first LiS before and I found out to be quite fun game with good plot twist and rememberable characters with good story choices. And same goes for this one. The story takes place in Haven Springs which is a small town in the mountains of Colorado and it's beautifully detailed. You play as Alex Chen which is the main protagonist. She has some sort of superpowers to feel others emotions and experience them. I won't write more about the story you must go through it by yourself but I can at least say that it is really emotional and breathtaking to me. But let's talk about other things like gameplay. Don't expect much from this part because it feels more like interactive movie than a game and I'm okay with this tbh who would expect something else. Most of your time you'll just walk and explore the beauty of Heaven Springs for yourself by interacting with objects and persons in it. There are almost everytime a certain dialogue options and important decisions in cutscenes which will shape your story and Alex's behaviour but not as much as you would thought. Don't think of this like another Detroit Become Human thing. Of course the graphics has been pushed on a next level since LiS predecessors. The game just looks gorgeous and well optimized. The level of detail the game has. Characters are good written, rememberable, interesting and well played by their actors. You can also have romance with two of them, Ryan or Steph. The length of this game is approximately 14 hours but I bet you can finish it even faster. I was really exploring every corner of the game and I advise you to do the same because if you don't then you may not find some things related to the story.

_childDocuments_.review: The Life is Strange I once knew and loved is back. I walked into this with all the doubt in the world that the series could ever comeback after Life is Strange 2 and Tell Me Why. They weren't *bad* games - but the story simply didn't grip me at all. Shortly after started playing True Colors, I realized just how much I was audibly commenting about the characters as I play. "She's such a dork," I said many times throughout the game. It reminded me of Life is Strange 1 and Before the Storm. The characters were likable, and there was a well balance between the much needed humor that Life is Strange 2 was simply lacking. I genuinely felt attached to the story and its characters. Well done, Deck Nine. You've outdone yourself again.

_childDocuments_.review: Life is Strange: True Colors does a lot of things right. The graphics and environments are stunning (Haven Springs is perhaps the most vividly beatiful location in any of the games), the acting and character writing feels solid, and the gameplay mechanics surrounding Alex's powers are, at their best, nicely integrated into the plot in a way we haven't seen since the first Life is Strange. In its best moments, TC even manages to bring about some genuinely harrowing and emotionally raw scenes of a quality that you rarely see in these kind of games. However, there is someting just... lacking from TC as well. Despite its great production values and overall solid story from a character point of view, TC never really grabs hold of me the way LiS, LiS2 and even Before the Storm did in it's places. Despite a well-written and fleshed out backstory for Alex, I can't escape the feeling that more could have been done with the moral and emotional implications of Alex's power, similar to how the original framed Max's time powers. When we finally see her use it to actively change someone, it's quite far into the game, and ends up feeling desperately underused, despite the consequences it has for the story.It also feels very much like DeckNine wanted to "go back to the roots" of the original games small town mystery, but in a much more down to earth fashion. The mystery here is more grounded in real life and relatable human character flaws, which is admirable, but sadly also makes the mystery parts of the story a bit predictable and... well, linear. The investigative parts of the game are enjoyable, but regrettably few, and as soon as the plot starts to thicken, the game is almost over. Charming and cute as it was, I couldn't help but think that the game could have shortened the extensive and quite time consuming LARP portion of the game in favor of some more detective gameplay that made use of Alex's powers even further. Overall, TC:s strength lies in the small details, the slices of ordinary life in Haven Springs: running around and "listening in" on the emotions of the townfolks, exploring the hidden memories scattered throughout the game, doing small good deeds to help a random stranger on the street, playing silly minigames with the npc:s. All of these things work (and work excellently) in a game that at its core is about the concept of "home" and how to belong somewhere. In the end, TC is an extremely well made and beautiful addition to the LiS canon that is enjoyable, fun and at its best really well written and impactful, but sadly lacks the cringey charm, powerful sense of mystery and gut-punch emotional scenes that made both LiS 1 and LiS 2 so very special and unique. Not bad, just a bit underwhelming. Also felt weirdly short, despite finishing it in about as many hours as the previous games. Personally, my least favourite in the series so far, but would still recommend for fans of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: While the game is better than Life is Strange 2, it is definitely worse than the first game. The power to absorb and feel other people’s emotions doesn’t have the same universal appeal that time travel had in the original Life is Strange. The power is just straight up boring and you will forget to use it outside of the hard scripted events.The side effect of such an ability also makes the main character come off as weak and confused anytime there’s even the slightest bit of social tension, which doesn’t make her as interesting as Max from the first game, as she doesn’t really seem to be in control of anything at all.The storytelling sticks to the Life is Strange formula with dramatic events that kicks things off, setting the tone for the rest of the episodes, and the final episode is supposed to deliver a big payoff. The issue, though, is that I guessed who the bad guy was right after the first episode, so from there, the game just felt predictable. I was basically waiting for it to end, which made it drag. I know this doesn’t apply to everyone, but the bad guy is painfully obvious and I think the majority of players will solve this “mystery” within the first few episodes.One thing I did like though, is the environment. The small mountain town looks and feels super cozy, like a place I’d love to visit or maybe even live in. The atmosphere is one of the best parts of the game, no question. Credit to the level designers.The awkward smiles… All the characters in this game have some of the most awkward smiles I’ve ever seen. They all look like “Hide the Pain Harold” and it’s honestly really distracting., while the setting is great, the game itself just doesn’t live up to the original.After I just completed the last episode, I was like, alright it wasn’t terrible. But then after having chewed on it for a bit and compared it to LiS 1 and other similar games, I actually do think this game is terrible. It just isnt worth the time or money. It’s just too boring and the story, characters and  events just doesn’t hit you or stick with you.

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot believe that this game has received such positive reviews. It must be because people have a fandom for "Life is Strange". The absurdity that this game cost $60 is genuinely shocking to me. I have now played every LiS game because I'm a fan of the format -- I even presented an academic paper at Oxford on The Walking Dead a decade ago. This game is a travesty. We've gone forward this far in game development, we choose a premise such as "empathy", and we can't give the player more control, variance, experiences than this? Even in its predecessor, the game where you're dealing with a telekenetic weapon like some sort of Magneto, you feel so much more choice and variance/impact than in this game. The only way in which this game presents you with even the ILLUSION of choice, is that your character might lash out a maximum of two times out of your control. They literally present 4 distinct emotions, and you only get to take "extreme" (medium) action with TWO of them. This game is a denigration of the episodic storytelling format.The literal only positive note about this game was how cute and fun the "LARP" section was. Everything else was absolutely atrocious. It honestly even grossed me out how much they "shoehorned" the LGBTQ protagonist and their options of the "hot drummer chick" or the "hunky park ranger guy" and the entire romantic buildup is "do you hug this one, or do you tell this one they're hot?". There's a grand total of one emotional interaction between each possible partner, and absolutely makes no sense that they would result in the kind of crazy "heartsick romantic acts" that this game presents. It's just ludicrous. What an absolute disaster of a game, and a huge embarrassment to the history of the franchise. If I could refund this after a full play-through, I would.
