_childDocuments_.review: Really intresing idea! and the co-op (while not the main focus, and kinda unbalanced)  is a ton of fun.But there are some real issues here in terms of resource management, they  have a wide slection of dogs, but not enough reason to use most of them.Youre avalible slots dont upgrade fast enough, and passive and active buffs share the same slots, so sometimes youll unlock a new dog that gives faster movment speed, but that just pales in comparison to an attacking dog with special abilities, multiple teirs of upgrades, and that takes up space to block foes.Overall the game is very charming in both story and visuals, but the dog  options just feel very odd, and a little to restrictive despite the varaity.And because of this the game can get failry repeitive. Especially with thr lack of variaity in the events in levelsFor people looking for a few hours of an intresting new experince, id say check it out!I feel like i got well more than $15 of fun when playing in co-op, but dont really feel the need to complete it. And may have played less without the co-op.(Only player 1 can actually build, player 2 has limited support options.)Its a pretty fun plants vs zombies inspired beat-em-up, Id love to see a refind version of these ideas in a sequel!Hopfully with more intresting dog/resource managament, more inegrated co-op, and more intresting levels to play though.I wish the devs (and their dogs) all the best in thrir future projects

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to recommend this game, but this feels like a bad console port. The controls are awful on keyboard and you can't rebind the keys. Using a controller is definitely recommended, but it still feels like I'm doing mid-tier fighting game combos just to place towers.Really hurts to leave the game a negative review since all the towers are good boys and they didn't do anything wrong.However, there is a bug that prevents waves from coming so you just can't win some levels. I highly doubt this issue is going to get addressed since the game has been out for a long while now, something game breaking like this should've been caught and corrected by now. If the dev is reading, it probably has something to do with using level 3 Barbet really early and occurred sometime shortly after reaching second granny.I want to love this game, but all the small problems built up, and having 100% of my progress halted was the last straw on the camel's back for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Tower Defence? Beat 'em Up? Gigachad Protagonist? ... Doggos? . This is important enough to mention on it's own. Imagine PvZ, but Crazy Dave is now an average  and proceeds to piledrive the zombies back into the grave himself. Let's be real here, you get to play a grid-based tower defence game, where the towers are actually turrets piloted by dogs, and you get to play as an absolute chad on his quest to protect all the doggos in the world by applying  against  who would do otherwise. Game takes about  without skipping anything and getting all the dogs, stars and side-quests. Game is responsive, has plenty of different towers and passive skills for different builds, and varied gameplay segments to break up the constant Tower Defence levels along with a simple story to follow. , but it doesn't need to be; I'm a vet when it comes to TDF games, but I can see even someone new to TDF can cruse through the game no sweat. Expanding on that, , and I can understand why. You can basically solo the game regardless of your towers because you can kill most of the ads before they even reach your walls; when you add in special moves, like the shoryuken, and the fact you can stunlock enemies with well-times combos even the """""" ads go down in seconds. I stuck with the first few towers I unlocked and never once had to change my classic PvZ layout; if I'm being honest I only did that out of habit, and the  satisfaction I get out of having a clean looking layout, rather out of necessity. You could honestly just do anything and probably breeze through no-sweat. I, personally, have no beef with this; not every game needs to be ball-crushingly difficult out of a misunderstood interpretation of Dark Souls' design, it's kosher if a game wants to just be a vibe with a great looking stylised art style and slamming beats; the issue is that it means all of the towers are nearly interchangeable and really provide no real benefit over another, along with the fact the ads will already be a read smear on the pavement before they get to the defences.It just feels like its wasted potential on what could be a great mix on both of the genres this game juggles where you have to prioritise the right ads, maybe some could be resistant to the Alpha's attacks such as flying enemies, etc., and you'd have to make sure you had the right towers or elements to deal with them, and some need intervention from the Alpha to make them take more vulnerable to your towers, of which these are already present in the game in the form of shielded ads and tanks. Regardless, it's pretty pointless speculating what a game  rather than discussing , the game is a beat-em-up  and a TDF , hell maybe even , that doesn't mean it isn't enjoyable, just don't expect any big-brain strategy moments. need to discuss this, you can see from the screenshots and videos on the store page that the game looks great with a crisp visual style and I can confirm that the soundtrack  beginning to end, .The game is fun, looks great, sounds great, is reasonably priced along with having bundle options, and  has a ton of good puppers, give it a go!

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game.Tower defense in the style of Plants vs Zombies, but you also control a character capable of fighting enemies directly.There are a good variety of towers, as well as companions that increase your character's stats or combat abilities. There are also several different ultimate abilities.Every tower and companion can be upgraded, as well as your RV (which you are defending in most missions).Main thoughts...1. Lots of variety is good, but most of the missions are too easy. I would routinely find myself with an unbeatable defense and hundreds or thousands of extra scrap that I had no use for. You'd have to try pretty hard to make a setup that can't beat most missions.2. That being said, you can't save any builds and it's a bit annoying since you have to frequently change between tower defense missions and no tower missions.3. There are some boss fights (with no towers) that aren't really that fun and can be a pretty big difficulty spike.4. The doggos are cute, there is a corgi you can unlock early. Major bonus points.5. Animation style is nice.Overall, a good game to relax to. Would be nice to see a NG+ with harder missions requiring more skills, but this is a fun game that tower defense fans should check out.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Friend

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little tower defense game with some beat 'em up action courtesy of the main character. I'm not much of a dog person, so that aspect doesn't really do it for me, but the art and variety of species on display is pretty solid. It runs out of steam a bit towards the end, and even though it tries to add some mission variety every now and then, nothing really stands out as exceptional. The hit feedback on your basic combo attacks doesn't feel great, but the dog-enhanced special attacks kind of make up for it. I think this game is a good example of needing to keep its scope in check and work on enhancing the features that are already there rather than trying to do too many extra things half-heartedly.7/10, if you can get it on sale, go for it. It's a nice way to kill an afternoon.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Friend

_childDocuments_.review: Great and fun indie game. It was a genius idea to mix up the tower defense and beat'em up genres. The art style and the OST are really good. It's cool to unlock new dogs and see what powers they have so you can make the build you want for the character. I went for a parry build and worked wonders. Some aspects of the game I didn't like are that the combat gets kind of repetitive by the end of the game and the sound mixing is weird with some turrets (the one that fires rockets, for example, is much louder than the other ones) but those downsides do not come close to the huge number of pros that the game has.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked this game a lot. It has many doggos. :3 They are v good. Considering its pretty solid quality compared to a number of games with way more reviews/downloads it seems and it has a good theme to it I'm surprised it isnt more popular/known. The only issues I had were that sometimes it would hop to excessive lanes, hits were sometime missed even though I was pretty sure they were correct, the game alt tabbed out by itself seeming later in the game and then a few of the shields wouldnt be upgradable in a battle even though they were only level 1 or 2. _childDocuments_.review: I found this game very fun. The ridiculous humor with the references and digs at certain groups of people were very fun, if leaning rather hard on the zeitgeist of "Twitter Toddlers", jokes about smartphone workaholics, and the more mentally unstable and questionable "preppers and patriots" of the world. The main gameplay loop was also rather well made, with a variety of options for being a turret master in the backlines or rushing in to break the enemy ranks while the turrets mop up after you.Also, dogs. Lot of dogs. I found a Rottweiler and named them after my long-deceased Cheddar, and I used her for several rounds and was happy because she fit with my turret master style. She was a good girl, as is this digital Cheddar.However, I have issues with the game.The Star System is very bland. All 3 goals just add up to "Perfect Run", "Almost Perfect Run", and "Clear the Level". There was so much opportunity for creative goals that encourage you to experiment, like "End this level with X amount of Y tower at level 2/3." so you can figure out which dogs you may want to try, aside from your favorites and the old staples like good old T. Juan and his simple, but very effective single/triple lane direct damage.There's rather too much variety but only so many options I found myself using. The developers evidently worked very hard to provide plentiful options for both a Brawler and a Turret Master playstyle. There are also levels that specifically emphasize using one or the other, along with the Sidequests giving you a specific loadout for a special challenge. I liked those ones especially.However, because there's so many options, levels get so chaotic, and later levels heavily encourage you to start upgrading your puppers because LV1 turrets just won't cut it against this amount of firepower anymore, I found myself gravitating to one single team and the usual abilities, upgrading those, and never finding out how much better certain dogs could be if I decided to invest in them.The game isn't stingy about rewards. Dog treats, especially with the RV upgrade, start raining, which is useful considering how many different doggos you need to give delicious treats to help them grow stronger (and a bit chubbier).However, I feel like I wasn't given much reason to experiment outside of the sidequests and again, the lack of creative star mechanics.I really like the art style. The personality of the game is incredible and fun, my favorite part is the monastery of clean-living New Age Hippies that borrow Tibetan monk aesthetics, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ do I laugh at the Cross-Fit Runners that power up with their super food juices and kick me in the face using splits. There is, aside from the ridiculousness of it all, also a great amount of variety and coherence with the level designs, the jokes, and the dangers that each enemy will show you, though overall in difficulty, only the Patriots in the 2nd to last level got me restarting.I like all the dogs. There's such a large variety of them in fascinating designs and seeing them in their little turrets gradually getting more and more like doggy war crime committers is hilarious.The gameplay loop sustained me up until I finished the main campaign with all stars on each level.There's a decent variety of missions that test your brawler, your tower defense, and other skills.However, I don't see myself playing this again, afterward. There simply is no incentive or clear goals for me to experiment, and after some of the hectic fights that I beat, I don't particularly feel like trying out an experimental new tactic "just for kicks". My psychology has not been suitably manipulated for that and the core gameplay loop is fun, but not that fun.Still, I recommend it. It's cute, it's creative, it's funny, it's got so many good boys and girls. It's also on the cheap side, and I'd love to see more like this, smaller games that do silly things well.

_childDocuments_.review: Seamlessly blending both the arcade action of games like Streets of Rage with the strategical thinking of titles like Plants vs. Zombies, The Last Friend quickly becomes a battle of man and canine standing stalwart against the end of the world. The Last Friend brings in a horde of super-powered dogs to help players drive back the violent mutants and gangs of the apocalypse in a fun, fast-paced hybrid of Brawler and Tower Defense. You’ll work your way across a vast dystopian, wasteland rescuing doggos who will in turn help you save the world in your roving battle station of conversion van that would make Harry from Dumb and Dumber incredibly jealous.

name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles
detailed_description: Discover our new typing game Become a Fox Rider Join a community of players from Epistory and Nanotale who decided to take part in the adventure, and help us to create another memorable experience. About the Game Nanotale - Typing Chronicles is an atmospheric typing adventure RPG set in a colorful vibrant world. Follow Rosalind, a novice Archivist, as she journeys out to explore a distant world. On her quest to gather knowledge, she collects samples of mystic natural beauties. Everything is peaceful. War is a thing of the distant past. In the shadows, a tale of dissonant magic is spreading, instilling corruption into broken hearts. Play with magic Combine powerful spells, change their shapes, and enhance them to defeat enemies. Use your magic on the environment and make it resonate with your creativity. Knowledge is power As a member of the order, your role as an archivist is to gather knowledge. The more you learn about the world, the stronger you become. Explore a rich world Embark on a journey to the Ancestral Forest, discover the Blue Desert and try not to get lost in the Sunken Caves. Meet the inhabitants of these new lands, be amazed by the beauty of the flora blooming in these diverse biomes, be intrigued by the critters roaming on your path but be careful not to cross paths with the dangerous creatures looming over. Reveal secrets Step in a fascinating story with multiple faces that have left their mark on these lands. Meet people, listen to their tales, and catalog mysterious occurrences, in an attempt to unravel the secrets behind dissonant magic. Your mightiest weapon, your keyboard In Nanotale, everything is played with your keyboard. From puzzles to dialogues, combats to menus the entire game can be played solely with your favorite keyboard. All keys are re-bindable, supporting all kinds of layouts (Qwerty, Azerty, Qwertz, Dvorak, Colemak, BÉPO,...). Enjoy the game in 11 different languages and create your own Nanotale experience. You can choose to have the tutorial and story in one language and select another one for gameplay and typable elements.

short_description: Something is wrong with the heart of magic. Play a young archivist venturing out into a dying world, cataloging its mysteries and its wonders to unearth the truth. Nanotale is the new adventure from the Typing Chronicles franchise and the spiritual successor to the acclaimed Epistory.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun game that you might be able to count as school credit, Nonotale is a good time for those who want to show off their typing skills--or, perhaps, just practice them in a more entertaining matter. A stronger narrative, quests, and cataloging build on the foundation set by the first Typing Chronicles, Epistory, though story and questing have plenty of room for improvement. However, the game suffers from many bugs and perhaps should have spent a bit longer in the oven. Not bad enough for a "no": none I encountered were game-breaking, just irksome, and the developer is still working on updates and fixes as of this review. Therefore, unless you have a massive hankering for typed combat (get it), hold off on buying this for another month or three after release while bugs get ironed out. ^H^H^H^H^H^H^H^H^H^H I loved the first Typing Chronicles, Epistory. The basic gameplay remains the same in Nanotale: Type words to attack enemies and cast spells. Nanotale expands on this by introducing modifiers and having much stronger puzzle-solving mechanics. All of these are environmental--no sliding puzzles here!--and while most require a specific spell the solution still has flexibility. Unfortunately, mechanics and world interaction need better explanation, many situations require trial-and-error. A spell learned in the first act takes on a new use in the third act, and my first encounter gave the wrong information of how it needed to be used.Just like Epistory, Nanotale has a modular difficulty system: The better you are at typing, the more complex words the game serves. The default English dictionary feels a tad limited, as many enemies had only a handful of words associated with them. (Though this creates a very subtle-but-interesting adjustment in the final fight.) While I did not give it a try, the dictionary can also be modified to include names/places/terms as you like, or for a language without official support. Touch-typing is a must-have, along with memorizing the spell terms (which is easy, as they're short): "arenas" require you to watch massive waves of enemies, and having to hunt-and-peck or review your spell list means death. Basic attacks are "free", but you'll need mana-consuming spells for large groups; unfortunately, you have to look at the very bottom of the screen to see if you have sufficient mana to cast. You also can't prep a cast while mana is regenerating.  I found the music and visuals of Epistory to be just as strong as the typing gameplay: As you explored the papercraft-stylized world, pieces of it would literally unfold in an origami-manner with  tracks to everything. Nanotale keeps the great music, but the world takes a more typical fantasy setting. Gone are the fun animations and world style, but the world still looks great and now includes cataloging (not just a bestiary, but also flora and archaeology). Ditching the paper-craft aesthetic does allow for a more complex world, with lots of levels and some nice camera work in certain sequences. It also creates more than a few bugs as your character, Rosalind, gets stuck on ledges or in barriers that can be turned on/off. This becomes more annoying when environment modification comes into play, creating bridges, and knowing where to actually walk requires trial-and-error. Some sloped terrain has non-intuitive "walls" along the lower edges that--as they are not frequent--will trip you up in arenas. The devs are aware of this, though, and you can respawn at a checkpoint from the menu to get unstuck (without losing progress, as far as I could tell from the few times I had to use it.) Epistory  have a story, but it was more vague/ambient until the absolute end and could have been removed without hurting the game.  For Nanotale, the story is... a story. It's stronger and works, but twists are generic and very easy to forget. The narration is great, even better than the first game; unfortunately, the animations of the character narrating doesn't match the energy and emotion in the voice. The first villain sounds enigmatic but their character model will look like it's doing some basic stretches. The in-game critter friends (one per biome) have the most interesting animation; I wouldn't mind a Steam sticker or something of each.  The quests could have been neat, but it felt like I wasn't assigned any of them until I did the first part without realizing it. There are side-quests where I was more aware of "accepting" them (which only requires talking to a certain NPC) but I often completed them without realizing I was about to do so. And, as side-quests didn't seem to have any impact, there just wasn't a point to them at all. I stopped talking to NPCs after the first act unless I couldn't figure out what to do, which was fine because they all look incredibly alike. The second and third act had 2-3 "important" NPCs but it's impossible for me to recall any of their names or pick them out of a line-up. (It didn't help that many seemed to transport between areas, adding to confusion.)  Nanotale suffers from a number of technical issues: It's a massive memory hog (even at the low quality setting), cutscenes can fail or be jittery, and basic barriers/paths will reset on game load or area re-entry.  The game also uses an auto-save system; the checkpoints are plentiful, but the only indicator of a save is a tiny icon in the lower-right corner that flashes far too quickly. There's no way to manually save, and no indicator to tell you how long ago the last save was; I had minor worry when quitting that I was going to lose progress. My experience may be worse than average, though, as I don't meet their minimum requirements: Win7, a graphics card from five years ago, barely meet RAM requirement. But, again, their specs seem incredibly high for a game like this which probably needs a few efficiency passes.The developer is active in the game's Discussions, though, and I expect they'll put out updates and patches for at least the largest of issues. But even if the game's current state turns out to be the game's final state, I didn't find the bugs horrible enough to recommend against the game (though I would change my recommendation to "buy on steep discount" in that case.) While Nanotale suffers from bugs, a ho-hum story, and an almost-pointless side-quest system, the gameplay, music, and world lore collection are strong enough to make those quibbles instead of show-stoppers. If you want to put those Mario Teaches Typing results to good use in a 7-9 hour jaunt, Nanotale is right up your alley. But maybe wait a few months for kinks to get ironed out, and/or a sale that drops it at least 25%. All tale-ed, it's a good follow-up to Epistory; I look forward to a future third entry with vast improvements to the story, quest system, and engine efficiency. And if you think this review is long... it's a typing game. Why wouldn't I type words for the review, too, maxing out Steam's character li

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved Epistory, but I cannot recommend Nanotale in good conscience. This game often does not look finished, as it is riddled with all kinds of bugs, wether they be mechanical (getting stuck somewhere, attacks not registering, enemies clipping through walls), video (sometimes the hitbox and camera moves along with the player's commands, but the character model doesn't follow) or audio (music just straight up stopping). There are weird and badly edited transition (the most jarring has to be at the complete end of the game, when the credits kind of unexpectedly pop and end without any sense of timing with the music that accompanies it).The gameplay is fun. In fact, it's almost exactly the same as Epistory's... but on a map I kept getting lost on and wishing for some options for fast travel, and with interactions with NPC I couldn't skip quickly enough. At least, I got the good old typing gameplay I was looking for, but once the game is beaten, there is no arena mode akin to that of Epistory, so I can't just go crazy typing. It's just a few hours, and then it's really over, and the convoluted map really makes it so I have no intention at all to go back and try to get all the archives.It reaaaally pains me to say this, but this is very big letdown. Maybe the mistake was letting it out of early access so soon.

_childDocuments_.review: If you played Epistory and enjoyed it... get this game. Right now the thing that makes me the most angry is that I listened to the bad reviews and spent so long not playing this game.At the time of writing this I'm about 4.5 hours in and have completed the entire first area (including getting all the lore from plants and such) and have moved onto the second area.Let's get this out of the way first. If you like typing games this is a fantastic typing game. You'll like it. Get it. Art is lovely. Voice acting is.... eh? So far the story isn't blowing me away, but it's not a bad story. End of day if you like typing games, it's a good one. Get it.Now for the rest of you. The people here because you played Epistory. I wanna make some things clear out the gate.There is A LOT this game has in common with Epistory with some key differences. So I'm not going to go over the similar things because frankly for me that is a much longer list than the things that aren't similar.-The absolute biggest difference is boss fight areas. Unlike in Epistory you are allowed to move around in the areas. This was something I read in the reviews before and decided it turned me off the game cause it sounded clunky. It's not. Also movement is NOT WASD it's EDSF. Trust me it sounds weird but don't change it. It helps the game flow a lot better when you are switching between moving around and attacking. The movement helps a lot with strategy as another difference is that you can use enemies to effect the environment around you and to do damage to other enemies.For instance there is an enemy that explodes into flames. Position yourself right and attack that, make it explode, and it will burn near by enemies. Between the movement in locked in an arena fights and the addition of enemies that have different effects and abilities makes it so the game is not going to get boring and samey like some of the gameplay in Epistory did. Instead of a bigger and bigger enemy meaning you are just typing bigger or more complex words. They can ram you, move faster, explode, etc. It adds a lot of flavor to the formula that was Epistory.-The next big difference is your abilities. Where as you had a few set abilities in Epistory. In Nanotale you have a lot more to work with because you can change the way an ability acts. For instance. Just like you had Fire in Epistory you also have it in Nanotale. However. When you cast Fire on a certain point or enemy you can also had a combination of other words to deal extra damage or make it have a wider range. You can type Fire, Long, and Ray to fire a long ray of fire or just type fire to get a small circular area of effect or type large fire and you will get a bigger circular area of effect.So far I have mostly used these abilities outside of battle to do things like move around sheep that are blocking my path or to get to new places in an area. If you use them in battle though it takes a lot of thinking on your feet as you are evading enemies and typing and throwing attacks their way. Again though I find it to be a very fluid system that I have gotten the hang of very quickly.-Another possibly off putting part of the game that is different is the art. It has a very similar feel and look as Epistory with the main difference being that we don't have the folded paper origami look of Epistory. It's still beautiful design though.-Last thing is that this game does have collecting. You will find various plants and creatures that you need to get close enough to to type out their words and "collect" them to get additional story, to level up, and unlock new abilities.In summary all of the biggest differences so far in the game have also been the ones I've seen people ♥♥♥♥♥ about the most. Seen people say it's an inferior game to Epistory. Saying it's clunky movement and so on. However I will absolutely argue that the games mechanics and controls are no where near clunky and have been very fluid for me. I'm having a blast. Is it better or worse than Epistory? No. I do think it is on par with it though and that neither is better than the other. They are similar games but they are a very different experience so far for me.There are a couple negatives though that I do find incredibly frustrating about the game and I do want to point them out.-It took me till I was at the big boss fight at the end of the first area to realize that I can target ANYTHING with my abilities. There are crystals placed in strategic ways around the map. At first these are explained as basically a focus point for you to use your abilities. You can't just cast an ability where ever you want. You have to have a point from which you cast it. Fair enough. However the game makes it seem like you can ONLY use those crystals. Which is not the case. You can cast your abilities on ANYTHING that requires a word to type. I really wish the game had explained this better as it would have saved me the few areas of frustration I was having and from having to look up how to get to the boss fight because I couldn't physically get to it without targeting something other than a crystal. PLEASE! Devs make it more clear in the game that you can target anything.-Saves are another thing. Another thing I had to google. The game doesn't ever state that it auto saves and there is no save button. However when I looked into it I found a steam discussion where the dev says that the game as LOADS of save points. They also say that the save icon appears in the lower right hand corner. Which is cool. I've had no issues with saves picking up where I left off so far. Even though I've only started playing tonight I did have to close the game several times while playing to do other things. It doesn't change that I wish the game at least had a pop up that TOLD YOU these things. I shouldn't have to google it Fishing Cactus. You need a pop up in game that tells players how the save works so that people don't have to look it up or just risk their save not happening. Heck even if your game has auto saves and loads of save points. Actually having a save button would be nice and is something that exists in a lot of games with auto saves for the reason of allowing players peace of mind that their game saved before closing it.-This next one is maybe me being dumb, but for the life of me I can't find quest details in the pause menu. My map also zoomed in really far and I can't figure out how to unzoom it. So a bit of a better navigation situation on the pause menu would be nice. Being able to actually interact with the map by clicking on icons would also be nice. Looking at the map I can tell what is a main quest and what is a side quest but from what I can tell I can't tell what each quest is without walking to it.All in all. It's a great game and if you liked Epistory I recommend picking it up. I got it on Fanatical in a bundle currently going on for $3 but I would have paid around $15 for the game. So wait for a little bit of a sale and pick up the game if you like Epistory or enjoy typing games. This game frankly gets more hate than it deserves and is underrated from what I've seen of it so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game, but not a really good one, and I'm saying that while ignoring the bugs (like immediately teleporting back while moving between areas, map toggle inverting or the player getting stuck literally everywhere).Most people buying it probably do it after playing the wonderful game, Epistory. No what is different here? In short, everything... and for the worse.Everything better in Epistory:- The latter had style this one lacks. Visuals are generic 3D look both in presentation and in quality, and the really few cutscenes just look awful. Compared to the hand drawings and origami style of Epistory, a definite downgrade.- NPC interactions are awful with initially no indication for the player on what input is needed to continue and wether choices of words matter, and sidequest are just there for nothing, pointless and weightless.- Enemy variety dropped significantly, and combat is dull. In Epistory, roaming enemies were the filler and static typing combat was the core gameplay. This is now the other way around, the player spends most of the time battling enemies scattered around the map. A boring and tedious activity that's anything but challenging. - Even in the few arenas, things work differently. It's expected from the player to move around, instead of just focusing at tactical typing. Getting hit isn't really punishing, the player can take several hits and even gets a heal.- The whole move to the conventional RPG character properties just hurt the game. Healthbar, mana, damage modifiers, etc. Health is lenient and allows the player to be reckless, and the developer to create less though-out scenarios. Mana is needlessly restricting. And the inceased damage with character progression just makes an easy game even easier.- As damage is now  a different property, words only serve as ability aims at enemies. No longer are enemies defined by word cound and length, they just get a thematically fitting snippet of letters to guide the attack. The greatest downgrade of the combat really. They take (or not) some damage, then offer a new word. Trash mob enemies and large hulks get the same words, sometimes 4 letters, sometimes 12, no difference. They literally managed to ruin the single greatest thing Epistory had going for it.- New spell modifier system is tedious, and mostly pointless. Never got to learn what "Sharp" really does, except for making the spell smaller, as I could not see any increase in damage. Never got to use Water and Poison modifiers, as they are aquired right at the end of the game, and there is no reason to use them anywhere. The Push and Pull modifiers I guess were meant for puzzling, but that never got into the game, I have literally never used Pull, and only used Push in early game where there was no other option, and at the end to open like 3-4 gates. And the Fox decoy ability is laughably useless, except for crashing the game by locking up controls permanenty. The mana cost for these modifiers is a joke as well, outside of arenas, the player can spam literally everything, while inside the arenas regeneration is so small, I rather typed everything out for basic attacks. And the monster possession is only useful for getting enemies near points of interest to cast spells off of them. It really shows, that most of these systems were meant for content, that never got made.- The plot is all over the place. I mean, there is one, but I wished there wasn't. There are three separate areas with non-obvious connections at first, due to the lack of proper storytelling (swapping names when entering different areas and pretending that the player is already aware of the connection), that's still so trivially simple my only thought was wether the game just failed to play a custscene to tie the two parts together. And when at the end everything comes together, it's a resounding nothing. Lame, pointless and unexplained (preceded by the most anticlimactic bossfight of the game).Improvements compared to Epistory:- The player always knows where to go next and areas can't be skipped accidentally, the only problem I had with Epistory. At least they managed to fix this one, but at what cost...In the end, Nanotale is a neat looking game, that manages to fail at every step its predecessor succeeded. It's boring, tedious and unimaginative. Fails to deliver any challenge (except of course challengin one's patience).Neat in presentation, tolerable in mechanics, but no fun in any regards.

_childDocuments_.review: (Long review incoming -- apologies!  tl;dr: I like Epistory more, but this is well worth checking out regardless.  Note that my playtime here is quite artificially inflated.  I'd accidentally left the game running more than once, so this is  the time required to finish the game.) It would have been easy for Fishing Cactus to rest on their laurels and put out a game that was effectively Epistory 2, but instead they took a gamble and struck off in some new directions for Nanotale.  It's a bold move, especially in a market where typing games are infrequent at best.  The result is a game which, despite sharing a  of DNA with Epistory, ends up feeling quite a bit different.  For me, the changes are a mixed bag (and I have to admit I prefer Epistory), but I'd definitely recommend the game regardless. One of the major changes in Nanotale is the spellcasting system.  Just typing a target name will always do a "basic" attack, but you can prefix it with "FIRE" or "ICE" (or a variety of other spell types) to cast special attacks.  Also, instead of just typing "FIRE" to set up a fire spell, you can add modifiers, such as "FIRE RAY LONG," which will send a long beam of fire towards your target (potentially hitting other targets on the way), which burns for a longer than usual time.  It adds for a lot of flexibility in combat, and is also integral to the sometimes-tricky puzzles in the game.Complicating the spellcasting is the addition of a mana bar, which will get used up as you cast your spells in combat.  When the mana bar dips below a certain point, all you have available is your "basic" attack, meaning you don't have access to fire/ice/etc.  Unlike in Epistory, where you'd "lock" in your attack type, every attack has to be prefixed with your spell type, if you want more than the basic attack, so you'll find yourself using just the basic attack pretty often. As a result, Nanotale places a much higher emphasis on  during combat.  In Epistory's wave-based arenas, your character's position would be fixed and it was a matter of raw typing speed combined with strategic use of your elemental type locks.  In Nanotale, you're free to move around, and you'll find yourself lining up "RAY" shots, zipping around between teleporters, and making use of environmental cover while your mana bar recharges, so that you can unleash some more elemental AOE attacks on groups of enemies.   It's got the curious effect where often Nanotale doesn't even  like a typing game, really -- it's more akin to some kind of mage-based "action-adventure" RPG, where instead of mouse clicks or hotkeys, you're using the keyboard to manage your attacks.I do miss Epistory's tighter characterization of words to use when attacking enemies.  Nanotale's creatures  each have their own unique set of dictionary words which characterize them pretty well, but I miss having the variety of little fast-flying single-letter enemies, slower-moving slugs which required long strings of three-letter words, hidden safes which required numerical combinations, etc.  The enemies in Nanotale end up feeling a bit "samey," even though they have different attack patterns and behaviors, because there's little typographical difference between them.In regards to the spellcasting system once more, Nanotale does let you do your own exploration and discovery with the various spell combinations, and very rarely holds your hand through any of that.  I appreciate when a game does this, though it does mean that you're prone to sometimes missing very obvious things.  I went through basically the entire game without realizing that you can dispel fog using your PUSH/PULL spells, for instance, and got stuck at the end for quite some time because I didn't realize something was possible.  I was embarrassingly far into the game before I realized that I could be using "ICE" on enemies, just because having to prefix every spell with that modifier made me never even think to change up my "FIRE" muscle memory.  Still, that dedication to letting the player figure out the mechanics themselves feels like an intentional choice and it's difficult to fault them for sticking to their guns.In the end, though, my primary complaint really is just that it didn't  like a typing game, on account of the more complicated spellcasting system and emphasis on movement (I realize that's a weird complaint to levy at a typing game).  There were only a couple of arena-like fights (such as the end battle) which really felt like an exercise in raw typing ability.  I think the new spellcasting system was an admirable attempt at doing something new, but I don't think it entirely paid off in the end.  Still, fans of Epistory should find much to enjoy in here regardless, and fans of typing games in general aren't especially spoiled for choice, so do check it out anyway.  :)I do feel I need to mention that as of just a few days after 1.0 release, the game  still a bit janky, having just come out of Early Access.  There's a number of fiddly little bugs and annoyances still in there, but I'm confident that Fishing Cactus will get them sorted soon.  There's already been two bugfix releases in the few days since release, and the devs have been extremely responsive on the bugreport forums on here.Okay, sheesh, this is by far the longest review I've ever put up on Steam.  I can't imagine anyone's still reading by this point.  If anyone : hi.

_childDocuments_.review: Trust me, I really really wanted to love this game, but it is worse than its predecessor Epistory - Typing Chronicles in every single possible way except that you can now move during "boss" battles:- the typing mechanic is worse,- there is no workshop support anymore,- story is worse,- upgrades and leveling up system is worse,- this one is personal preference but I liked Epistory art style much better,- the adaptive difficulty doesn't seem to work as well or at all. In Epistory it actually made the game decently challenging, this one just felt really easy all the way through.It is also packed full of bugs. Just a few from the top of my head:- keybinds reset every time you restart the game. No, I don't wanna use esdf for movement game...- at some point the ground literally swallowed me up and killed me while I was standing still,- maybe I was just doing something wrong, but it felt like it was swallowing input a lot,- there is multiple locations where I managed to get myself into places I wasn't really supposed to go to,- playing arena screws up your progress in the main game,- some sound effects ignore the audio settings,- starting and ending cutscenes were just black with audio,- typos... in a typing game...I am sure I am probably forgetting more, but I think already this lists gives you a good idea how bad it is.Basically skip this game and go play Epistory instead because unlike this game Epistory is absolutely amazing.Other than all the issues already listed there is no additional problems with the Linux version of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely lovely concept and art for a typing RPG. Main and side missions aplenty. You easily get stuck or lost during exploring though, as some objectives are unclear and characters all look the same so remembering who tf "Arvid" was out of a bunch or clones scattered across a desert landscape is quite frustrating. Especially since the world is in layers, meaning you might be going for someone on level one and standing above them on level two, not being able to reach down. Completely infested with bugs too, as well as some really clunky controls, repetitive words and music, and alot of getting stuck in scenery and invisible walls (obstacles you need to clear can be invisible too if you return to areas you've sorted out before, so the visual and factual scenery doesn't always match up). Lots of music cutting off and crashes to desktop. If the majority of bugs are cleared out and the map would add names of characters you've met, I would give it a thumbs up because there's alot of love for and in this.

_childDocuments_.review: If you don't have patience to explore a rough draft of the game please wait for it to be released. That being said, if you enjoy working through restarts and being part of the process then snap this game up! The developers are super involved, responsive and quickly ironing out a lot of the bugs that are being uncovered.There's about 90 minutes of gameplay now and it is set in a gorgeous creative world, with unique  mechanics and a peek into the deep lore that's being established.

_childDocuments_.review: Big disappointment after Epistory. The fact that this game is out of early access is a joke.Visuals are very nice, and world lore bits are interesting, but the rest of it is a disaster.Bugs everywhere - during the gameplay experienced couple crashes, multiple instances of having character stuck, had to quit in the middle of a boss fight because the fight gets stuck etc.Combat is just not implemented properly - skills are not balanced, animations aren't synced up properly (can't really tell that enemies hit you), and it's just dull. Story is very mediocre at best, and the game lacks exploration aspect of Epistory - most of the game is very linear.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Worse than Epistory on all fronts except scope and graphics (and the latter is debatable). The low production values on the narration of Epistory strongly complimented the idea that it is an intimate story being shared with you, so I assumed it was intentional. Turns out that isn't the case, Fishing Cactus are just a thoroughly amateur production who do not understand their own limitations. Nanotale is plagued by low quality voice-acting which is exacerbated by poor direction (if there was any). In a game based on typing and vocabulary, there are frequent grammatical errors in dialogue, and the dialogue is painfully modern for something set in a fantasy world. Finally, I encountered a very easily repeatable geometry glitch which completely trapped my character, and apparently this is a common issue because the devs put a respawn-at-checkpoint button on the pause menu specifically to help you get out of bugs... instead of, y'know, fixing them?
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? No, it is still in Early Access, but it is already a fine game. It is an action RPG, but one where you don't have to be fast with your mouse, but only with your keyboard, because the main requirement to get through the game is... typing words as they appear on screen. Similar to Typing of The Dead or the older Epistory.Play 18-year old Rosalind, a young witch, as she explores the Ancestral Forest, full of plants, animals and magic. She examines stuff by... typing words. She casts spells by... typing words. She writes down notes by... typing words. She interacts with the environement by... typing words. She talks with creatures by... typing words. She fights monsters by... typing words fast. Type too slow and you get hit. Mistype a letter, and you have to restart. No stress.Young Rosalind enters the forest together with her teacher, but of course she is alone very soon. After riding on the spirit of a fox, she is far deeper into the forest than she was supposed to be. Now it is up to her to unearth the secrets of the forest and defeat the evil within. Ok, she is not completely alone, the spirit of the fox stays in her head and talks to her... Explore the maze-like map, learn new abilities, upgrade your stats, solve puzzles by manipulating plants and enemies, meet the mysterious White Queen. Just like in a real action RPG.Nice art style and music, ultrawidescreen is not supported.Cute explorative action RPG that teaches you to type. Actually, the action is TYPING.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Nanotale is a pretty okay game, but all of the changes since Epistory end up making Nanotale's combat feel like an action game with a bit of a typing gimmick, more than anything else. Likewise, past the second of three areas, it feels like they ran out of puzzle ideas for the most part, while Epistory was interesting all the way up to the end. It's also a bit shorter, about 6 hours instead of 8 for me, but this might have been because Nanotale requires less backtracking and makes it easier to find things for 100% completion, in comparison.On the bright side, I still enjoyed it, and the story and ending didn't make me nearly as annoyed as Epistory's did. Recommended somewhat weakly, since I don't feel like it really lived up to being a typing game in any sense, but as far as puzzle games with action-based combat go, it's not bad.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this one SO much since I am a big fan of Epistory, this one's predecessor, but...alas I cannot in good faith. Let's get through the positives first. Clearly the lore of the game is done with a lot of heart and love for the product so that was fun to see. It also retains the unique gameplay element of typing to fight and interact with the environment. But now come the negatives and what is even worse is that they are almost entirely technical, so could have been entirely prevented. So, the game really plays like a beta demo, years after it's release. The optimization is horrendous. Particle effects can grind even my relatively powerful machine to a stutter and considering the graphics levels this is entirely unjustified. The quests are buggy and honestly kind of bland to begin with. You get them if you randomly do part of the quest with very little explanation. Some achievements are tied to typing a certain amount of words or reaching a certain character level, but there is no word counter anywhere or a way to check your level other than seeing an xp bar briefly flash when you discover lore, making it incredibly difficult to track. While on that note, levels are rather useless as they show some bars going up but honestly I felt no power/endurance difference at all. You get a new skill per level up but after the initial few levels you are usually given the "choice" of...one skill that generously you get to click on. And then there are the movement bugs. Oh my lord, the movement bugs! The movement itself is a bit floaty which would be fine if you didnt get stuck on every little corner. I am sure the devs knew this was bad because on the very options menu there's a big option to "respawn". Still, having to respawn so often, especially in a game which relies heavily on creating platforms and walkable areas in order to progress this can be beyond frustrating and quickly takes you out of the immersion. I have no idea how to justify the insane drop of quality between Epistory and Nanotale, but it is indisputably present. It is not impossible to enjoy, but it is an exercise of frustration more so than the fun little lore experience packed in unique gameplay that it was meant to be. A very sad thumbs down to this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: It is October 2022. The game has been out for, what, a year or so? The developers are no longer patching it. I play the game for the first time after letting it sit in my installed games for months. The initial cutscene does not display. It PLAYS--you can hear it--but it's supposed to be shown on top of the world screen where your character is standing, and it doesn't, so you wonder why you can't move until the cutscene finishes. The third time you restart the game you figure out what the heck is going on.Then, when you get past that, the game crashes. Still running, but shows nothing, and has to be force-quit. The third time, you can proceed, to the point where you can finally move your character around, but by now your confidence is shot and you go to find some other game instead.I liked Epistory a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sorry but ths game doesn't do justice to Epistory, here the story feels weirder, environmental boundaries are forced, the combat mechanics aren't implemented in a way that's as satisfying as in the first title and an enumeration of bugs. Almost every element appears like in the first title except somewhat less enjoyable. Anticipated it for quite some time and I do value the direction the team went with these two projects, but this is not what it could have been.

_childDocuments_.review: The first typing game that Fishing Cactus did was much, much better than this game. I remember playing Epistory when I was 14-15 years old when I was just barely getting a quicker typing speed. I have an average typing speed of around 96-100 words per minute nowadays, so when I saw this game in my inventory, I was excited to play it. Some of the words that you type in this game are ones that I've never heard before, which I appreciate, but I wish there were more words to use to damage enemies. I've probably typed the word "gun" and "err" 20 times each and I didn't finish the game. After a while of this it gets very repetitive.This game is also pretty buggy. Within the game you can make ice bridges to cross tiny streams, but it seems like half of the time that I do, I'll get stuck in one spot for a moment. There's a quest where you have to find a bunch of flowers for a  cave creature, but even though I found all the flowers and went back to talk to the cave creature (I can't remember it's name, sorry) it seemed to never finish the quest. I googled my problem and it seems like other people have had the same problem in the past. I wouldn't recommend this game. If you haven't already played Epistory, I would very very much recommend that one.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: I remember playing Epistory a few years ago and liking it, even though it had some flaws, but Nanotale is somehow worse in so many ways that it hurts my heart. The aesthetics of the game serve their purpose, though they are nowhere near as charming as the origami look of Epistory, and the soundtrack, story and voice acting are just there, but not terrible. What's terrible, however, is how incredibly glitchy and bugged the game is. The menu literally has a Respawn button in case you get stuck - that should set off alarm bells immediately.And getting stuck you will - among many other things. I got stuck in the scenery or on obstacles just walking around dozens of times. Some of the quests bugged out for me, making them impossible to complete, with many bug reports in the forums stating the same thing. Typing has randomly reset for me a few times, rarely key inputs are being swallowed. Getting attacked during cutscenes happened to me as well - sometimes you can attack back by typing, sometimes it didn't work, so I am not sure if that was even intended. Options randomly reset, including control bindings if you choose to change them. If you have an HDR monitor, the game will look extremely washed out, with graphical elements in the menu being way too bright. The only way to fix it is to turn off HDR before starting the game, then turning it back on after it loads. The list goes on and on.The map is extremely bugged as well, with the minimap bordering on completely useless as it zooms in when you enter an area of interest, but it zooms in even when you are at the very edge of it, making navigation much more frustrating than it needs to be, compounded with getting stuck. Why not just have it center on the player instead so you always know where you are? The bigger map in the ESC menu has it's own problems, randomly changing size, making you constantly have to zoom in and out as it just can't seem to ever retain it's zoom level. The quest markers are a mixed bag too - not a bug, I think, but they don't go away even when you finish a part of a quest in an area, which can lead to confusion.The gameplay itself is fine, you travel around, type words to archive plants, creatures and fight monsters. You learn words to augment what you type as you go, such as creating a fiery explosion when you type "Fire" first, and making it larger by typing "Fire" and "Large". Those spells cost mana, which you can replenish with flowers in the area or waiting around. It's pretty much the same as Epistory, which makes how unpolished the game is stand out even more. I remember Epistory being just fine (though I played it in 2017, so I may misremember).If the bugs would have been fixed over time, the game would have been just fine, if a little too easy and repetitive if you are a fast typer. But even after several patches the game has apparently received after release, the game is still a buggy mess and has been left to forever be in this state. If you want to play a fun typing game, I would look elsewhere - it's not a total miss, but the glitches and bugs make it extremely unenjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely gorgeous, and I really like the new combat style update from the first game. I found it a bit easier overall than the first, a bit less stressful and more tactical, which I liked a lot. My only complaints are a couple of bugs (mainly quest markers misbehaving), the map navigation is a bit clunky, and it's easy to get stuck on things like ice and brambles. But the plot was lovely, and overall it was a beautiful story and piece of art!
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Disapointing.I absolutely loved Epistory, so I was very exciting for this. Nanotale is not a bad game though, but it just doesnt feel finished.  Its not even close of being a polished game.The movement is soooo clunky. It has SO MANY bugs and glitches. You're constantly bumping into invisible walls, your character disapearing, and the level design doesnt help at all, especially at the desert area where you can find yourself being softlock requiring to respawn or going back to the main menu to fix it. The ending was so lackluster and felt rushed. Throughout the game every Boss encounter had some unique gameplay mechaninc attached to it. The final boss was just, kill all the enemies on the screen and that's it, boring and repetitive. There is no replayablity in this one, they could at least add some arcade mode like the first game where you fight waves of enemies or something, but there is nothing.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: A step up from the predecessor of this game Epistory, Nanotale has more gameplay elements. Main quests and side quests, cutscenes and more voiced characters.Gameplay loop of Epistory felt tighter however Nanotale opens up the possibility for different strategies due to being able to move while in combat. Nanotale is more focused on puzzles.Overall this is a good game, I give extra credit since the game is actually making typing into an engaging experience.Still I have to mention issues I ran into while playing.Having to rebind keys every startup.Long initial loading screen when entering the campaign.Random stutters.Buggy pathing, stuck on objects.Falling through the ground.I believe the devs are aware of the occurrence of bugs as there is an button specific to respawn if stuck.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Bugged as hell, botched beginning, limp narration with zero drive or direction, laughably rushed ending, annoying cumbersome gameplay (element + spell tweaking system that requires you to type qualifiers over and over again before each action, extremely limited vocabulary, a mana system that punishes you for typing too fast, etc), weird collisions with the environment all over the place, no quest tracking, no fast travel, buggy map, numerous mostly uninteresting lore tidbits and hollow npc interactions but somehow zero explanations on what a new spell does, navigation and guidance in general is severely lacking.This game's clearly not finished and it's shameful that it's officially out of early access. Play Epistory instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Worth the try, just don't expect a full and bug free game. This is still in development so please be mindful of that! It is definitely a unique play experience that I look forward to continuing in the future. I started this because I played Epistory and LOVED the game immensely. This is not a sequel, but it shares very similar elements. If you're looking to have the same kind of play but without repeating the old story, this is absolutely for you! Keep an open mind, though, because there are a lot of different elements to this one. My main take-aways: - New story line, new characters, and new world. I feel this story is more hashed out for you as the player character than Epistory was  - New powers that work a bit differently depending on how you utilize and combine commands, providing playstyle versatility - New learning experience, keeping me engaged - This is a bit more difficult than Epistory from the get-go as it is using words I wouldn't normally type that are longer and more complex
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Will put a caveat where I WOULD RECOMMEND this game purely on the grounds of gameplay.The game has a lot of charm to it and the world that was built is fantastic. Looking at the bigger picture, this is a game that I would really wanted to love. However, there's way too many instances of which the game felt very unpolished to a point where I often find myself frustrated.The straw that broke the camel's back for me from recommending this game is the main story - as much as the core story outline has a lot of potential - the execution of how events progressed felt very forced, trite and overly convenient. There are a lot of really good NPCs, mini stories and ideas but almost all of them are too short and doesn't have enough room for me to feel emotionally invested in them.Also important to note that on the technical front, the game felt unoptimized and the performance sluggish. There'll be some points of frustrations of terrain that you would believe could move into but being blocked due to bugs or that in later stages where Rosalind would get stuck in random edge geometries. That being said, the developer are actively tracking and patching the game, so would expect this to improve as the game gets patched.In summary, really wanted to love the game but the flaws in the main story are too big and immersion breaking to ignore. But if you are content w/ good gameplay and a casual collect-a-thon experience (with fun worldbuilding) - I think you'd enjoy this.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: I used this and Epistory to learn Colemak dh, and epistory was much better. Not just for typing practice, but also for engagement. Sure, the story was better than in Epistory, but that doesn't count for much when the game isn't fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend to buy the game in it's current state for the price asked. Pros:- Typing is satisfying.- Art is pretty.- There might be about half an hour of enjoyable exploration without figuring out what the game wants from you.Cons:- Quite a few game-breaking bugs that require restarting the game to progress. - About 2 hours of gameplay and no way of backtracking after finishing the early access.- No way of knowing if I missed some quests or areas before finishing the game. No clear depiction of what areas are accessible in the early access from the map view. - Unfinished UI, no quest log, no ability overview.- No way of pausing the game.That being said, I loved Epistory and I hope Nanotale gets to its level some day, but I get a feeling it would require at least another year of work and I could get more satisfaction in the meantime playing a more polished game rather than a raw Nanotale prototype.

_childDocuments_.review: Just a littany of issues.  I played Epistory two years ago and loved it.  The animations in this don't feel as smooth, the world feels less vibrant than the old one, oddly enough, despite the forest, characters, and new enemies (kind of).  The visuals are nice, but it lost the lovely "paper" feeling Epistory had, and what made it unique.  The story elements were interesting, but not driven.  I loved Epistory's.....story, as it felt different from every other game I've played.  It was like living a child's story book.  This just felt like every other game I've played, and while I haven't finished the game, I played an hour and feel I know where the story is headed as it's somewhat laid out in the beginning.  The voice acting felt mediocre as well.  I am running this on a fairly modern system but was still receiving graphical hitches occasionally.  I was able to put up with this until I wanted a break.Upon starting the game again I noticed all of my progress was completely gone, whereas the old game seemed to either save very often or just wherever I left off.  I quit the game correctly too, exiting to menu then exiting to desktop, not force quitting.  This was the straw that broke me and I am deciding to return the game after a little over an hour of playtime.  I'm sorry, I'll look forward to the next iteration. _childDocuments_.review: Nothing spectacular, but it's decent. This is not really a typing game, though, it's more of a light metoroidvania that happens to use typing controls.Brilliant level design, pretty art style, and fantastic spell combination mechanic, but weak story, abysmal voice acting (much worse than the previous game by the same studio!) and LOTS of annoying bugs.Generally, this game lacks polish in a way that is typical for most small indie studios. Character animations don't stick, framerates are very unstable, it's too easy to accidentally leave game area, the final boss battle glitched for me in 8 different ways preventing progress, until I eventually gave up.And it's a shame, because while it's a short game (took me 7 hours to 100% it), level design is outstanding, and puzzles designed to motivate you explore available spell combinations are very satisfying. Typing them feels very natural. For instance, to cast a big, ray-shaped ball of fire towards an enemy labeled "divergent", you keep your hands on your keyboard and just type "large ray fire divergent". I find that incredibly intuitive, just think of an action combining your spells, your fingers type it automatically, and you see your character doing what you think. It takes some training, but once you get fluent, it's amazing, and I wish for more games utilizing this type of controls where you type what you think.Of course, that satisfactory feeling can only be experienced by players who are experienced typists. And unlike other game in this series, I don't think this one can teach you to type faster or look at your keyboard less. The game does not motivate you to type quickly. There are just a few battles where timing matters at all, and if you think and strategize well with your spell combos, you don't need to be fast even on the hardest difficulty levels. Which is ... completely fine, but it means typing is no longer a gameplay mechanism, it's just a control scheme. You don't need to type well to progress through the game.So while it's very rough round the edges, I still liked this game due to its unique controls and well-thought levels.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun typing game! If you liked Epistory, you'll like this!The story is less personal, more "epic", than in Epistory. There's lot more world building/lore though, and it's pretty fun to gather.It's been less of a challenge for me than Epistory, but still wasn't just waltzing through. No fights here could be compared in difficulty to late game Nests!The only downside of the game is that as of 11 Oct 2021 it still has some game breaking bugs. For me, it was a bug near the end of the game, that completely blocked my progress. Other folks seem to have been stuck at some other quests. However, the devs were able to help and edit the save I had to fix the problem. I would really wish they fixed those bugs, so that new players could have a smooth experience.The game took me 8 hours to finish, getting all but one achievement (not sure if some secret or just bugged), had all the lore, etc. So it's on a short side, but IMO, well worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles has a simple gameplay idea: explore the land to find animals, plants and other noticeable things, learn new magic elements by that and type the words on the screen to use your magic or interact with those. It's understandable and well paced throughout the game. Also, it has some puzzles parts, where you have to use the correct element to move forward or to take on certain enemies. The story is interesting, but I find the ending a bit rushed. Graphics is pretty good, but at some point if there are lot of effects on the screen, the game can stutter. Soundtrack is relaxing.Although Nanotale is a simple and likable game, it has some detection issues, especially when you try to cross two different surface next to each other, and also there are places where you can get stuck. Writing words can be difficult too, as you try to type a word, but the game doesn't register it, but this one happens rarely. Last but not least, the first area is pretty straight forward, however the last one gets really tricky to get all of the collectibles or even find your way forward.If you want to get better at typing, meanwhile you want to relax and explore a bit, Nanotale - Typing Chronicles is for you and I can definitely recommend it. I think 20€ is a bit much for it, but 10-15 is all right.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a huge step down from Epistory. I read that none of the current devs worked on Epistory - I'm not sure if that means that no Epistory devs worked on Nanotale at any point of its development, but it wouldn't surprise me. It just feels like a poor imitation of the game it's "spiritually succeeding".The game is a buggy mess - the fact that there's a dedicated respawn button in the menu specifically designed for when you get stuck in walls or similar glitches tells you all you need to know.The quest design was bizarre - I'm pretty sure I accidentally triggered a main quest towards the end of the game sooner than I was meant to, skipping a chunk of the game. There is no quest log, meaning that you'll often complete side quests without even realising what you did to complete it.Gameplay is what you'd expect from a typing game, but not any improvement on Epistory. Some of the level design in Nanotale requires precise placement of platforms using various skills you pick up throughout the game, and this often results in frustration where you just can't walk across platforms for some reason (often resulting in the glitches mentioned above).The 3 or 4 main bosses throughout the game force you to use skills you've recently picked up (such as freezing water to create platforms) but the final boss is just a long string of normal fights with dialogue in between - this might've worked better if the story was more interesting, but it was an odd way to end the game either way.As you can probably guess, I would recommend passing on Nanotale and just grab Epistory instead if you don't already own it.

_childDocuments_.review: The short version: buy Epistory instead.The long version: I was really excited when I saw the makers of Epistory were producing another typing game: so excited, in fact, that I bought Nanotale in Early Access because I was so keen to start playing. However, after having to restart many times due to game-breaking bugs, and not even getting through the first realm, I decided to leave it until the game was fully released before I tried again.Now, I've come back to it, there's a lot that's improved. The narration and cut-scenes (although a bit juddery on my pc) make the whole thing feel much more coherent than it was in early access. The map/objectives are also much clearer than when I last played. However (and I feel really bad saying this, as clearly a lot of love has gone into the game) it's just not my cup of tea.I understand that it can't be 'the same' as Epistory, but I was really hoping that it would have the same emotional tug as that first game, and it just doesn't for me. Take the opening as an example. After the initial tutorial, you're whisked away into the forest, and yet Rosalind doesn't seem the slightest bit scared. There's no sense that she wants to reunite with her professor, or that she's worried for her own safety; she just happily carries on collecting plant samples. Maybe this is something that gets fleshed out later, but at the moment it just doesn't feel real to me, and so I struggle to care about the objectives/progress of the game. With Epistory, I was desperate to play on. I wanted to reclaim the fragments of this girl's life, find out more about her, and explore more of the beautiful, paper world. I felt like I was *living* the game, and it made my own struggles and fears seem less daunting.So, that's the main reason why I'm disappointed by this game. As a small aside, I also find the new magic mechanics frustrating (having to line up really carefully, and then type Ray and Large and Pull, before you can cast your spell to move something seems a bit torturous). Similarly, the fact that you can move in the battles makes them feel less threatening, and I prefer the element system from Epistory.All that being said, the world is still beautiful, and there's clearly been a lot of thought and attention put into the plant lore, which is really nice. I'm sure that most people who are just looking for a typing game will enjoy this one, and I'm sorry I couldn't enjoy it more. I just hope that, if they make another one of the series, it's more like Epistory - visiting past memories and emerging triumphant was such a beautiful process to include in a game. I've played it over and over again, and it never fails to delight and move me.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: I was simply ecstatic when I first heard The Typing Chronicles was getting another entry. Epistory remains one of my favourite indiegames to date: A brilliant combination of typing gameplay, exploring in true Legend of Zelda fashion and a wonderful origami artstyle.If there is one thing that returning Fox-Riders will immediately notice though, it’s the different art-style. The papercraft world of Epistory has made way for a vivid watercolour aesthetic. I have to admit I was sceptical about this change at first, as the unfolding world was one of the greatest strengths of the original, but I quickly grew fond of this new style as well.The early access is still a bit rough around the edges though. While the game shows promise to be another indie-hit there were a few bugs still hindering my progress: The camera would sometimes zoom out so far that higher platforms blocked my view and the bridges you activate would become impossible to cross. Rest assured: these issues are being reported to the developers on Steam and in their Discord so they should be fixed in no time.I have no doubt Nanotale will be a must-play title at some point, but it still needs a few hours in the oven and lots of player feedback. So don’t dawdle and check out the Early Access so you can help contribute!FULL PREVIEW:

_childDocuments_.review: Story and gameplay not as good as the studio's earlier game Epistory. I thought the story was rather childish and the protagonist has no story of her own and is only a vessel through which you explore the three areas of the world and get the story about the fox and antagonist. _childDocuments_.review: I got this game with my split keyboard to help practice typing on it.It was a great experience playing through it 😄 The story is fun, the visuals are great, the animals and animations are super cute.
