_childDocuments_.review: Still No.I like Epistory, though I find some quirky and gave it a thumb down. However, I find Epistory gives me decent amount of satisfactions.However, Nanotale gives me only frustrations.- Locks due to poor level design. Like in the first biome when you just finish the first encounter and obtain the first shard. There are no more path ahead so you have to track back to the city and find another path. But there are no indicator for which way to go next and make you lost for too long. And it's annoying to see that the progression path require you to pop up a fire bomb, but the bomb is somewhat visually hidden... Why this design? This is not a metroidvania!- No PROPER quest tracker. There are in game quest marks, but it show only quests for the current biome. So if you miss some side-quests from other biomes, then there is no way to know what you miss unless you travel there, which brings to ...- No fast travel within the biome, nor between biomes. Which might still be forgivable if there are some kind of shortcut route that you can navigate real quick, or at least navigate pleasantly. However, those paths that connect between important places often feature annoying enemies that block your way.- Navigate map doesn't feel right. I can feel a lack & no snap when trying to move cursor around. This is super critical since, see the first point, you have no quest listing, and the way to show quest detail is to place your cursor over quest marker on map.- Map is useless, since you'll later have a skill to teleport onto beacons. But there are no beacon markers on map, so I can hardly tell if I can go off this cliff or not.- And the map also draw path that's just don't exists! (A passage way to an open plateau directly to the south of the town in the cave. An arch in the forest that hint you to build a bridge to go over, but cut off due to limited budget.)- Too many interactable NPCs. But almost all of them just deliver one line and have no other purpose in game anymore. Also they look practically the same! So good luck receiving some side-quest that you have to find some other NPCs, or have to go back to deliver quest completion.- Voice over is some kind of poor quality. The most irritating one is in the final boss fight sequence when two character talks. The dialogue on the screen state whose currently saying, and the voice actor deliver the line. Then the dialogue update (still same character), but the voice change like there are different voice actor reading this line.- The story is somewhat boring and confusing from the start, ending with the anti-climax that makes you wonder "is this all it had to offer?".- 3D platform puzzle is annoying. Later in game you can freeze water to make ice and step on it. It's sound good, but execute so badly that you'll have a hard time walk onto the icy-platform that you made.- Vocabulary list is super-duper small, you'll encounter same vocabulary over and over very fast and very often. There're also come in small variety, most of them just are only about fighting and staying alive. No fun variant categories like sport, food, literature, science, etc. - No difficulty setting, nor auto difficulty adjustment according to player's proficiency. I'm just around 50-60 wpm on average, and I basically breeze through the typing part without any challenge at all. I thought when I finish the game I would somewhat feel like I'm better at typewriting. But no, the game failed this part unforgivably.---Update: reply to developerFor the secret quests: I understand that those 3 quests are meant to be secret. However, it is just in-game secret, but not Steam's achievement. I'm confused if it wanna be secret or not? 🤔I think the secret aspect is fine to kept. But there should be some hint telling the player that's there are secrets out there begging to be discovered. Imagine that if it the game has quest tracker, then it might show complete quest count, like "[complete]/[all quests]". So if there are, says, 20 quests in total, when you start a new game, it is "0/20"; when you finish the game without discovering any secret quests, it shows "17/20". Something like that would be enough.But once a secret quest been revealed. It should be show up on a map, so player can go back and read quest summary. Because now it feel super weird to unlock "Only They Know" by accidentally stumble upon that place and quest complete message pop up out of no where.For the bugged lore: yes, it is the last flower after healing the boss in the cave.For the difficulty: I've try turn off adaptive difficulty and find that +20 wpm difficulty is about right. Since it require me to run around avoiding foe attack occasionally. And also makes me trying to type faster. This is much more exciting than standing aground typing at ease knowing they can't touch me.By the way, I never select "Options" on the main menu, and I assume that the in-game "Options" will be the same (like other games). Maybe if the game want to make them different then use different keywords, such as, on the main menu it says "Setting"; while in-game it says "Options". Something like that would tell the player that they are indeed different.---Update: fixed issues move here- Also some quests don't show up as quest markers on map AT ALL (Only They Know, Jasper, and Mushrooms).- Lore marker on map also haven't update correctly, sometime I've already interact with an that lore already, and I can't interact with them more. But it still shown on map.- Also if you finish the main quest of the biome, you can't complete some side-quests anymore (mushrooms). Since the NPC that you have to interact with will congratulate you on the main quest, getting rid of any other interactions.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite it's bugs, Nanotale is still a good game that encourages building a great skill set (typing) under pressure. I wish certain parts were a bit clearer and the zoom on the map was more intuitive. Beautiful art and music, though, and it keeps you wanting to continue playing the game despite those challenges. There is some accessibility but it is a typing game which will require dexterity to some degree. The difficulty is adjusted to your current typing speed so you will be improving no matter the level you're at! Brilliant design elements.Edit:I absolutely need to update this review. The devs are SO DEDICATED TO MAKING THEIR PLAYER BASE HAPPY. I was about 2/3 of the way through the game when a Steam Cloud error deleted my save file. We ALL know how bad this feels. I had posted earlier about a point I got stuck on, and within minutes the devs offered to help me out with a file that dropped me back exactly where I was when the Steam Cloud error happened. This wasn't even their bug; it was very clearly a Steam issue, and they still reached out and fixed it. I get to keep playing (instead of waiting a couple months to replay the first couple sections because I'm frustrattttted) and I am SO THANKFUL this dev team is working on this project the way they are. There are bugs still, but the love and dedication they have to sorting things out is well beyond what I've seen elsewhere. The game itself is of course still solid to play through and I cannot recommend this game enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome graphics, nice game mechanics. Also, if you like to improve your typing skill, you can't do anything wrong with this game!I also recommend playing its predecessor Epistory, if you haven't already.If you have, I'll note some differences for you:Differences:- No more Origami graphics. While I liked the origami graphic from Epistory a lot, the Nanotale graphics are a lot different, but still awesome. You need some more GPU power though, when compared to Epistory (but still nothing compared to AAA titles ofc)- More spells and interactions: The spells interact more with the environment, not just on specific places. This adds more to the puzzle aspect of the game- A health bar. Ever found yourself in a tough battle, and as soon as an enemy touched you, you died? Not anymore. Also, you can move during arena battles, which makes a huge difference. However, I found it generally easier in my playthroughs, because you can evade.- Nanotale has still some rough edges. Now and then it just doesn't feel as natural as Epistory did. This is caused by the more complex interactions, and I do know that Fishing Cactus is fixing them (have a look at their discord to get in touch)The general game concept is still the same. There are substantial mechanical differences, but it feels like a successor of Epistory, while still providing interesting new things to discover.If you dislike games that lack PvP, Controller Support or long-term-playability, this game is not for you (I estimate 1 playthrough around 10h, at least when you are doing some discovery beside the main quest). Also, if you don't like games that have some rough edges here and there, better wait some weeks until it is polished (although I found a lot of AAA titles more buggy and annoying than nanotale!). In any other case, I recommend you give it a shot!

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game as soon as I came out, because I loved Epistory and this promised to be another game of similar quality and genre. _childDocuments_.review: Nanotale isn't as good as its predecessor Epistory in my opinion - so why still give it a positive review?There's nothing wrong with the game and I quite enjoyed my time with it. I'll recommend it to anyone who enjoys typing games and except for some frustration navigating the puzzles in the third area of the game, which might've been on me, it was a smooth ride with some enjoyable visuals.I want to give it a positive review because I applaud the developers effort to change up the formula. There are changes to the art style and combat system that make it feels distinct enough from Epistory to give Nanotale its own character and not appear like a formulaic cash grab.At the same time, I'm not a fan of those changes.1. The ability to move around and use AoE spells has made combat more tactical, but also significantly easier. I'm not sure it's what a community that is prone to brag about their wpm at times is looking for. 2. Epistory had a very unique art style with a world appearing entirely made out of paper that slowly unfolds as the writer-protagonist progresses their story. Nanotales art style is more detailed and polished, but also generic, just like its world is a generic fantasy world with a weak story. By all means. If you've enjoyed the first game, get this one. You'll probably still enjoy it. If you only intend to play one though, I'd say stick to the predecessor.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this after playing Epistory from the Humble Trove and I have to say both games are awesome. Never thought I'd say 'wow I love playing a typing game' but I think the key here is that this is just a really well done, fun game that happens to be about typing. It goes to show that it's the skill and creativity of the developers involved that makes the quality of a game and not the genre it's defined in.I thought it'd be incredible as an educational tool for typing as I know I would've loved it back in middle school, and even high school so it's good to see that it is available for teachers. I read a review where the guy basically said the exploration/adventure built around the typing is fun, but it'd eventually grow wearisome. That guys a ♥♥♥♥, FYI. I've never heard a kid say 'oh yeah I loved the typing part but this adventure thing got old pretty fast' because that makes sense. I hold the opposite belief - the adventure and mystery you've built around the typing and exploration adds a depth that children would find hard to pry themselves away from. You've thoroughly captured my attention as an adult, let alone a child. The adaptive difficulty isn't just great for all levels of players - it's amazing to create a consistent and gratifying curve of progression as you become better with your typing.Moving away from the tangent, this game is still in early access so I can't give a clear judgement yet but I've had a lot of fun so far. The main thing is always the lack of polish as it's still being built. More complex systems have been built into the game that gives it a type of simple complexity that is great to learn and hard to master. For constructive criticism, here's a few things:- the levelling system feels worse then the first (the first one was alright but not interesting). I find the problem twofold: the first is that basic mechanics are included in the levelling which I can't enjoy (a level should give the player some 'oomph' but when you're unlocking the ability to sprint faster, it feels very lackluster and you lose that spark of interest towards the next level). Levels can be slower, and fewer, but hopefully more interesting. Being excited to get that next level goes away quickly when any choice is a boring one.The second problem with levelling is that you've chosen a three-choice system that has no choices. When you pick one of the three options, the next option replaces the one you picked. It's an illusion of choice, you're really following a linear levelling system that happens to give you the chance to pick an option early. If you want to give players a choice, there must be a consequence (i.e they lose access to the other two choices or a smaller, but still consequential outcome). Otherwise it'd be better to stick with a similar levelling system to the one you had in Epistory.- the reading is a bit too long-winded. How you told the story in the first one was beautiful. I'm not going to say the text is bad, it really isn't. It just isn't incredible. It doesn't have that spark the first one did. A unique way to show and develop the story and its characters would really enliven the world.- Quests are confusing. The one where I have to save her sheep. Which ones? There are a lot. Where to? is it the flower patch in front of her? A visual system for the quests could be helpful in this regard (say an icon displayed above the area the sheep go to, and then a number showing how many are needed and how many have been placed). The character being more involved in the quest could be another way (her pointing or showing the character where to go, she could call out from far away when you're near one of her sheep etc.).- the moment you receive the spirit wolf/it dies? needs to be much clearer as well. The player should also get a moment with the beast, it feels too rushed. I don't get that minute to really appreciate the moment/my new companion.Great game, looking forward to seeing its future progress. I hope you keep making amazing games like this :)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing.  Pushes your limits of typing and problem solving. + Graphics are superb+Story is pretty decent - its not overly complicated or anything+Leveling is cool - abilities you unlock are fun and make the gameplay interesting. + RE-Spawn on escape menu is great if you glitch out. But sometimes the quest markers are complete and I'm looking for a way to the next challenge and get lost.  At the beginning of the game there is a fairy that guides you, it would be nice if there was something like that in the other areas if you get stuck/lost e.g. make it another spell perhaps so you use one of the crystals/plants/creatures and have it use mana or whatever just like a regular spell. "Fairy spell" or something.-I have kids so it would be nice if there were different modes to adjust typing speed/difficulty. Or even an auto-balance - so difficulty ramps up as you are beating the creatures until they ultimately plateau.-The cave/serpent quests are hard to figure out all around. it would be cool if there were some clues along the way to help you.  This isn't 100% necessary but maybe under a difficulty setting - have guided quest this may solve for the "guiding fairy spell" suggested above. _childDocuments_.review: I think it's important to review an Early Access game as a work-in-progress. The developer's previous game, Epistory, is another adventure played by typing, and it was a beautifully crafted game with a 95% positive rating. Nanotale is shaping up to be everything Epistory was, but more. The art is even more beautiful, the story is good, and the gameplay takes everything great about Epistory, and adds more.In it's current state (Oct. 27, as of the date of this review), Nanotale has some bugs and incomplete or rough features. But given the developers track record with Epistory, I have every confidence that these will be completed and addressed, and we'll get a game even better than the amazing Epistory. Some of these bugs can be game-breaking, but Fishing Cactus is working hard to address them quickly. Again, this is Early Access, which, by it's very definition, means it's an incomplete work-in-progress. The whole point is an iterative process where players provide feedback (report bugs, say what they like/don't like), the developers incorporate that into new builds, and the loop repeats.I recommend checking out Epistory (there's a free demo, so you can try it out). If you like what you see there, you can come on in and join the gang giving feedback on Nanotale (it's a very nice community!), or you can wait a bit if you'd rather wait until Nanotale is fully complete. Either way, you'll get the full game when it's complete, and you can bet that this labor of love by a passionate, small development team will be a beautiful experience.

_childDocuments_.review: A promising game marred by far too many bugs. There are many things to like in this game. I used it to teach myself to touch type with a new keyboard and layout, and it was very helpful for that. The adaptive difficulty works well, the lore snippets are fun. the gameplay is surprisingly complex for a typing game, the graphics look nice. The story is nothing special, but serviceable. All in all, it was a successful way to turn learning to touch type into something fun.But it's been a long time since I encountered a game this buggy. I just had to restart the final boss battle halfway through because it glitched - the dialog tree got confused and went back to a previous part of the conversation and then the terrain moved and trapped my character in place. This did not surprise me much. The devs have put a 'respawn' button in place to save you from such situations, albeit losing some progress, but there should not be so many of them. I've played their previous game, Epistory, which is much less ambitious in gameplay but way more stable and polished. The number of incredibly easy to replicate bugs that have just been left... If they give you a phrase to type in a conversation and you type the space, the highlighted letters will be one off for the rest of the word. You can change keybindings for movement etc, which was very useful on a non-qwerty layout, but when you enter the new keybinding it still fires whatever event it might be bound to. I've also had multiple times when the keybindings have been reset to default when I reload my save. Starting it up on steam deck the performance definitely suffers, and until it had had time to cache a bit it was pretty unplayable. Just lots of little bugs that aren't game breaking but are frustrating and immersion breaking and far too frequent.Much as I enjoy all the quality of life improvements compared to Epistory and the wider variety of puzzles and magic systems, I'd still have to recommend Epistory over this.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: It's impossible to review this game without comparing it to its predecessor, Epistory.Good points:- The new skills and puzzle system lead to some interesting mechanics. This game does provide some fun figuring out how to combine abilities in order to unlock multiple parts of the map.- The art and music looks gorgeous.- Cataloging the environment is reasonably fun.Bad points:- Different skills don't seem to make that much of a difference in battle.- The leveling system doesn't seem to make any difference in the character's strength or endurance. There is basically no visibility into your level progression.- There are MANY movement bugs. They happen frequently and usually at the worst moments, completely destroying any immersion you can achieve in the game. The sheer fact that the game offers a "respawn" command and suggests using it if you get stuck is an immediate red flag.- The story is kinda meh. Most of the NPCs have no personality and look uninteresting.- The map doesn't seem to update in real time. It's not always untuitive to understand where the main character is.- Some skills are very narrowly explored throughout the game. Would be nice to see them getting reused more closer to the end.At the end of the day, giving this a thumbs down because of the movement bugs making it seem like an early release game. If at least that got fixed, it would be worth more of a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is specially made for those who like to get all the achievements. Minor spoilers ahead. Nanotale - Typing Chronicles is an adventure fantasy RPG game with typing mechanics: you have to type words to advance in conversations, collect lore and attack enemies. Collecting lore and finishing quests give you XP, that will unlock upgrades and increase your total life and mana and this will make the game easier, but you still need to type particularly fast on the combat challenges. The story might be a little cliché and what you usually find in fantasy games but it was still enjoyable for me. It’s well written, the character motivations are logical and so the story overall is believable. The worldbuilding in particular has received a lot of attention from the developers: each plant and animal has several notes describing what they are and what they are used for, and all cultural aspects associated with them.The world is visually stunning. The 3D models are stylized and a little cartoon-ish but the scenarios and characters are well designed and look original, while I still think that it took some inspiration from games like Legend of Zelda. The spell effects are also great to look at, especially the fire spells that can burn away large parts of the world and the enemies inside them.The music, narration and sound effects were also good in my opinion. Some other reviewers mentioned that they are worse than Epistory but I haven’t played that game yet to compare them.Regarding the gameplay, I think most of the negative reviews come from the fact that the game isn’t friendly to casual players. You need to type fast. I decided to pick english despite not being my native language, because I think it has the shortest words and no typing accents, but even in english, you need to type sentences to use strongest spells. Getting spell shards isn’t easy either, there are lots of obstacles you need to overcome by using specific kinds of spells but the game doesn’t hold your hand nor explains to you what to do. This can frustrate some players in the beginning of the game.Despite all this, I think the spell's mechanics are fun to use and the system itself allows some freedom when dealing with enemies, even if you have to type a lot.Some people also complained about the bugs, and it’s true that I found some, mostly near the edges of the maps, with some path finding issues and also some quests/story sequences not advancing, but it happened just a few times in the total eight hours I played, so I think it’s insignificant, and reloading a checkpoint and restarting the game fixed them.   34 Achievements. Around 8,5 hours to complete everything, using a guide only for a few last side quests I didn’t complete. Medium, it requires some typing speed and some thinking and planning to overcome the puzzles/obstacles. Medium, there are a few achievements that require a little extra effort. You can finish the story without spoilers and come back to do the rest you missed afterwards. By the end of the game you will probably be missing a few side quest related achievements (guides are available), the player level and lore collecting achievements (these are related, collecting all entries with get you these) and the total words typed achievements (I got all but the last one in a normal playthrough). For these, there is a script available but I have a keyboard with macros, so I just programmed two keys to type 4 or 5 words at a time and alternated between them to get the last few hundred I was missing.      Nanotale is a good adventure fantasy RPG game that is challenging in the beginning and requires fast typing, but has fun mechanics and a great, beautiful world to explore. I got a few bugs too but nothing major.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is genuinely fun, and excellent typing practice. The graphics are very pretty, the soundtrack is nice, and the voice acting is really fun, if occasionally a bit inconsistent. _childDocuments_.review: I played Epistory and have been eagerly awaiting this next game. And it does not disappoint so far. It built on Epistory's mechanics quite well and has become quite challenging in some regards, but not impossibly so. If you like to puzzle through things and use the environment as your weapon, you'll really love this game. When I was a kid, I wasn't allowed video or computer games so the closest I got was Mavis Beacon... trying to consistently become a faster and faster typer. It all paid off for this series. :P But, I love the story and the art as well. It runs smoothly and has a great start of a story and lore. Looking forward to more, for sure!

_childDocuments_.review: If you've played Epistory before, this is basically more Epistory with a better focus on the combat. You can move your character freely now in the arenas outside of sandbox areas and you have a real time spell "crafting" option. The story is less emotional and more fantasy oriented this time around. It looks prettier and offers more of the sameIf you /haven't/ played Epistory, Nanotale is probably as good of a starting point if you're interested in the genre. The difficulty is scalable, you don't need to be a typing god, and has an adaptive scaling option. For 80WPM as tracked ingame it worked out pretty well for me. The story is a bit on the light side, most of the gameplay is about positioning and of course, typing, though rarely will you be forced into arenas where you need to be really good. A lot of it happens in the sandbox and the experience is pretty lightweight. All in all, if you're a fan of, or want to try out a game that just works off of typing words and the like of Textorcist or Typing of the Dead don't do anything for you, give Nanotale's charm a go.

_childDocuments_.review: An overall good game from a small team of dev. The gameplay rely on typing keyword to use magic, such as thunder, fire, ice, etc... _childDocuments_.review: Nanotale is a successor of Epistory, and it shows. Staying true to the typing style game, Nanotale have successfully made an SRPG-like game, where you have to strategize where and what you type. The elements are back with added powers that you can do. Aside from the elements affecting the enemies, you also need these different powers to manipulate the environment. Example: life to erase poison, ice to freeze water and make harder surface to walk on. You'll encounter puzzling places where you need to apply your typing powers in order to continue the story OR to complete your journal since you are an Archivist. There are definitely more world building and lore that are introduced in Nanotale, with places that represents the beautiful things you see. Certain plants have names and use, even the enemies have a name and descriptions. All of this allows you to explore with excitement.There are still minor bugs (that are being improved constantly by the super hands-on developers), but in my own playthrough it doesn't detach me from the game itself. It's a short game, that is always replayable if you like. Challenge yourself by not using any powerful abilities when the horde attacks. Or limit yourself with only fighting with a certain power. Explore. Have fun. Immerse yourself with the world of Nanotale.

_childDocuments_.review: : A great typing game with a charming aesthetic and RPG elements.: One of the things that I really appreciate about this game that is better than its predecessor, Epistory, is that there are no achievements or mechanics that require attaining a certain typing speed, nor is a level of typing accuracy a requisite. You are never blocked from continuing the game because you can't  hit a target number...Where  is a quasi-adventure game,  is a quasi-RPG. As you explore the world and interact with it, you gain experience, and each time you gain a level of experience, you get a new spell that you can type in combat to achieve some kind of special effect. This leads, in a small way, to a Metroidvania-like mechanic where you revisit areas you've already completed and are able to access things that you couldn't reach previously. As cool as that is, there is very little of that backtracking, and you don't  to do any backtracking to complete the story.There are two ways to unlock abilities, both involving exploration: first, the story advances only when you complete environmental puzzles wherein you must find and step on pressure plates. These pressure plates are linked to magical founts that heal an area of the dark magic that has drained life (and, visibly, color) from an area. You have to do these to advance the game, and each fount that you restore gives you a new spell. The other method is optional: as you wander the lands, you can take naturalist notes on different flora and fauna that you encounter. If you complete all the entries for a particular species, you get a new spell. These are completely optional; you can complete the story without engaging with this naturalist aspect of the game at all. But, being a completionist, I took notes on everything I could find. I amassed so many abilities by the end of the game that I had a LOT of different choices for how to defeat the waves of enemies that assaulted me. More spells = more tactics for achieving your goals. I had so many abilities by the end of the game, that there were some that I still haven't tried!
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game. I really do. But the bugs are a bit of a problem. Only way I've found to get it to stop is to completely restart the game. There are a few other bugs, but that one is the most problematic for me currently. If not for that, I would have no qualms over recommending this game. I recommend it anyway, but I'd feel better about it if some of these bugs were fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from Epistory, I'd like to say Nanotale is equally great, if not even better. Graphics are great. The music and sound effects are immersive. And more importantly, the plot is simple but well-written.Now for the actual typing. There are more spells here than in Epistory. The vocabulary is plenty but not plenty enough for repetitions to go unnoticed. Battles are intense. You have to keep making decisions between typing to attack the monsters, crafting spells to crowd control, healing yourself, or moving away from the horde! However, this game doesn't penalize you too much when you're dead. You simply go back to the last point before the battle, which makes this game pretty relaxing.Occasionally, there are small non game-breaking bugs here and there. Your character might get stuck. But rest assured, for the developers have prepared a "RESPAWN" feature for this.Aside from the main storyline, there are plenty to discover and will unlock your achievements, as well as more optional (fun) spells. This discovery adventure might double your playtime or more, but it's well worth it.I tried this game when it was in beta. So I know they improved A LOT since then.Their Discord server is pretty well-maintained. You can also talk to the developers there.Back then I was stuck somewhere in the map due to a bug. I asked for help in their Discord server and promptly received a response. They went out of their way to fix my save data so that I could continue playing. Yes, the "RESPAWN" feature wasn't working well back then, but I assure you it is working well now!Kudos to the developers for their unrelenting work, especially during the pandemic.Final thoughts: Definitely try this game out if you are a typing enthusiast!

_childDocuments_.review: Played both Epistory and Nanotale through in one sitting.Epistory is superior not just because it's a finished game, but it's just a purer and better game.As in Epistory, Nanotale mixes up the typing mechanic by having word modifiers.  Epistory was limited to elemental modifiers (Spark, Fire, Ice, Wind), and Nanotale expands on this idea by adding modifiers that change the shape of the spell (Ray, Large, Sharp) and add directionality - e.g. you can lay a trail of fire by shooting a ray at a distant target, hitting everything in between, much like the Wind spell in Epistory.By doing this, Nanotale adds a puzzle mechanic that allows spells to be directionally fired to change the environment in ways that are not obvious.  e.g. in Epistory, it is very obvious you have to use an Ice spell to freeze a section of river clearly marked for freezing. In Nanotale, you can shape the Ice spell to freeze portions of a river or pond and figure out where you should cross, or even creating your own bridges if there are handy monsters around that happen to be water carriers (which as a mechanic, is confusing, since a water carrier doesn't do anything besides drop water, unlike poison and fire carriers which are actually dangerous).All well and good on paper, but unfortunately a lot of the game is confusing camera angles and pointless busy work during exploration (a bit like Epistory) but where it falls down is the combat.  It's just incredibly slow and dull, and doesn't have the polish and split second tactical decision making that Epistory has.Also, the aesthetic of Epistory (folded paper worlds coming alive) was more uniquely attractive and made sense given its a typing game and made a low budget look very good.  Unfortunately, Nanotale looks like a very cheap Torchlight knock off.In conclusion, as far as gameplay is concerned it's a step backwards from its predecessor in terms of fun.  Lots of nice ideas but they just don't excite in execution.
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: I am reviewing this as of May 8, 2020; the game is still in Early Access and is not complete!Coming directly from Epistory, the movement controls are very different than what I had become accustomed to in Epistory. The great news is that you can customize your controls to suit your needs, which I promptly did. I don't have the list on hand at the moment but if you would like the Epistory control key mapping, let me know and I'll pull it up! The story itself is engaging and the initial tutorial stage lets you learn quickly without too much info-dumping. I will say that all the lore tidbits in Nanotale are very interesting and flesh out the world well. However, currently you cannot see your current quests in a neat list anywhere—you have to find them on the map, which is frustrating to say the least, particularly because this map is a "paper" map, and thus lacks colors and features that you can see in-game to orient yourself. I'm hoping that the development team is planning to change this, as it led me to run around in circles for a while. This was also because some quests are not where their markers are—in fact, I skipped a step for a side quest completely and was unable to complete it. The lore view on the map is also buggy; some markers will disappear once you've collected the lore, while others remain, again leading to me running around in circles, since I'm a bit of a completionist. The Caves in particular were pretty annoying in this aspect, because wanting to go certain places meant I ended up running around the entire map to get to the one entryway. It could be that I'm not good at finding the correct entrance, but the map doesn't always accurately portray clear paths. Sometimes you think a path is blocked, and it's not; sometimes you think a path is clear, and it's blocked by structures.Overall this was fun and quite relaxing, and I'm excited for more updates! I talked a lot about the current issues I encountered, but that's because it's in EA and I figured the more feedback on what is and isn't working would be helpful!

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, that was a bad opening to the story. We start without any real introduction as to why the main character is interesting; instead, we get her narrating every five steps with some completely inane detail in her log book, things we as the players absolutely do not need to read. She's been excited her whole life to go to this ancestral forest, but we as the players have only known her for... a minute? So we can't possibly share that excitement. Even a bit of buildup as for what came prior would've really helped set up why this is exciting and why we, as the players, should be excited.Then, we get a very rushed point of no return, which is explained to us in the moment through exposition. Again, any kind of setup would've made this work better. It would've made us aware that something like this could happen, as well as why it's exciting (again).I think we could've gotten a tutorial after the opening was done rather than during the opening. Have a few button prompts on the screen to help people get out of the opening and then do a tutorial right when the game really begins. Because I definitely felt a lack of focus in what was also a really rushed opening. _childDocuments_.review: Nanotale is another entry in the not nearly big enough pool of typing games that aren't just "type words as they appear on screen". Long awaited by myself after playing through the first entry in the saga, Epistory, I was excited to play through this one. The developers certainly tried a lot of new things in this one, which was a welcome change. A few of them sadly fell a bit flat, but nothing actively detracted from the experience.In short: I very much enjoyed it. It felt somewhat different from Epistory, a lot less fighting waves, and more puzzles and wondering how to reach another area with a plant I wanted to catalogue. The spells you unlock give you a lot of flexibility and ways to manipulate both enemies and yourself/your environment. Positioning yourself just right for that angle you need to freeze the water you zapped out of an enemy a second ago, so the charging enemy can't hit you in the face in a few seconds, is very satisfying.The artstyle is as gorgeous to look at as I expected, and some of the areas I would love to set as my desktop background. The story is okay, gets the point across and gives you a bit of a reference as to why you're doing what you're doing. The start was a bit rocky but it felt more like a medium to carry the experience forward. The (somewhat intermittent) voice acting also sounded solid.Navigation and "quest" management are a bit weird to get used to, but work well enough and didn't cause me any problems. The map shows enough to give you a good idea of where to go, and with some minor effort on your own side to memorize the layout of the land a bit, combined with the numerous shortcuts, you can get around quickly through areas you've already been through.Sometimes I got a bit confused on where to go next, but double checking older areas generally presented a new path forward, and I never really got stuck (well, if you don't count that one time I trapped myself between two energy barriers).Some minor bugs were experienced, but the devs responded quickly after reporting them and I hope the fixes for them come soon. No gamebreaking bugs, and whenever something didn't quite work right, using the built-in respawn function and doing it slightly differently helped to solve the issues.Final judgement: A very solid game in a very niche genre, with some minor flaws that for me personally did not hinder the experience to a point where it seriously affected my fun. Audiovisual presentation really stands out. If you like pretty typing games that aren't exclusively focused on typing words as fast as possible, but instead bring a bit of story, exploration and puzzle solving with them, definitely get this. If you just want to type words, maybe check out some gameplay first before you buy it, but still consider it!
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: I'm excited this Early Access release is only about 35% of Nanotale! I'm a completionist and I wasn't able to hit 100% because there's just more content than I could figure out how to access. It's one of those games where, though the concept and gameplay are simple enough, Fishing Cactus is fitting in those  bits that are so enjoyable to the completionist. Little side quests for certain NPCs, hopefully roping in a little companion animal, etc.The music, visual, and light design each have blown me completely away. Words cannot get there.  Because this game is  wholesome, it's a breath of fresh air to sit down and lose myself in the beauty and story here. The gameplay is really neat; you're a female character that possesses the capacity for True Magic, essentially "crafting" spells by typing words that pertain to what and  you want to cast your spell. AOE? Long distance? Specific enemy? Ice? Fire? Push? It's neat, guys. It's neat. It's really beautiful. It sounds surreal and is so creative. Hopefully they're still working on it, because I am stoked to play the rest. Maybe they're coming up with even more content to occupy our days during quarantine.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this developer's previous game, Epistory, so I caved in and got this even though it's still unfinished. Nanotale has a different aesthetic to Epistory's papercraft/origami aesthetic, but it's still incredibly beautiful. This game has you exploring the wilderness with many various organic forms, but it's still easy to read the pathways and make your way through them. The zones feel sprawling and expansive, which sometimes leads me to just running around to explore instead of Getting Stuff Done -- this is not a complaint, btw lol, Some people have reported that they've gotten stuck in places (there's a respawn option available if you do), but I managed to get through the currently available content without any problems. A few bugs(?): I have to change to my preferred keyboard configuration because it reverts each time I re-open the game; I can view the plants in my field journal just fine, but I can't view any fauna; when . Finally, I feel like my typo/error rate is so much higher in this game compared to other typing games I've played. I think a big part of it has to do with a certain amount of indecision involved when enhancing attacks on enemies on top of trying to figure out which mobs to hit in what order. I do like the freedom of being able to run around  within an arena, and the variety of attacks you have access to (kinetic options in addition to elemental) means a whole lot more complexity to battles than Nanotale set me up to expecting. I guess it's something I have to get used to... My all-time favorite Typing of the Dead (the original) had you on rails and even indicated the proximity of its mobs, but it's not like I can expect every typing game to be like that. I might start to feel really discouraged when accuracy achievements get implemented and I have exact figures staring me in the face. orz Anyway, despite my issues, I'm really looking forward to further developments and the full release of this game! Also curious to see how many more zones I'll get to explore and if we learn more about Rosalind's character and whether she starts to personally connect to anyone else (the spirit fox? her mentor?).
_childDocuments_.name: Nanotale - Typing Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Love this game & its predecessor Epistory! Very beautiful and atmospheric scenery, typing controls are intuitive and rewarding. The quests and objectives are simple in nature as you explore a Dark Forest and learn about the corruption affecting the tree-beings that live there, guiding you through a passionately crafted world. There are different enemies that take different tools and strategies to defeat, and experimentation to figure out the best methods. Some clever use of the environment is required in order to access all of the flowers & other things you can research for experience, using an innovative spell-modifier mechanic that the game introduces via a quest and then leaves open for the player to figure out how to apply its full usage.The dev team is very responsive to any bugs and suggestions, especially on discord. I've played through it three times and saw clear improvement each time. Can't wait to see what more is in store for nanotale!

_childDocuments_.review: I really loved Epistory and really wanted to enjoy Nanotale, but honestly couldn't.I first attempted to play when this was early access, and got stuck due to a bug that completely locked up the game. I understood it was early access and waited a while to play it again. When I did try again with a new game, I ran into bugs with visuals and audio during NPC interactions and cut scenes. There were a few cases where I had issues with the quick / mini map that caused me to have to quit and re-open. For example, after beating one of the guardians, I opened the quick map to find the next one and somehow got it where the quick map was always on screen. I had to hold Tab to keep it closed.Overall, the gameplay felt annoying more than fun. The challenge didn't scale well so I found myself running through an area to wipe the enemies out and then going through again to figure out the puzzles. Also, I may be misremembering, but I believe in Epistory the word length lined up with the enemy level. So easy enemies were very short (three letter) words, and the harder the enemy was the longer the word. I was surprised at how many times I had to type "malfeasance" for a one hit kill enemy.The power ups were pretty useless. I never used the ghost fox or possession. I accidentally triggered the ghost fox a few times but never in a battle. I legitimately could not tell you how possession works. The controls said to hold space bar, and when I did there were no words to type for enemies. The sharp and long modifiers didn't seem to do anything? I kept trying the long modifier when using fire on the turtle-like enemy and it seemed to fade as quickly as it did without it. All of these I may have been using wrong, but I was able to get through the game easily without any of them.The story could have been interesting, but as is it was boring. I like the idea of the competing magic forces, but the only place I felt like I actually saw a difference was in the caves. In the caves, people were actually hurt / dying due to the dissonant magic. And the poison that it was causing was something my character could clean up. The characters there were different enough that I could tell them apart and remember who was who. That was definitely the strongest area story-wise. The other areas had some visual effects to show the magic was "hurting" it, but the people generally were unaffected by the magic. If I talked to 0 NPCs in those areas, I wouldn't have felt I missed anything. Plus, the fact that no one was really bothered by the roaming enemies and vice versa. Someone in the desert explicitly called out that I was killing the enemies and was just like "eh, they don't bother us". Also in the desert, one of the NPCs (maybe Arvid?) was just standing in an area surrounded by enemies. When I got down to him, I figured he would be knocked out and I'd have to clear the area to help him. But no, I could just walk over and talk to him and leave the enemies around. It just feels disconnected. Like, there are these cool zones to explore, people to meet with some quests, and plants / animals to discover. Separately there is an evil magic killing the world that you need to stop. And the two barely intertwine besides in 1 of the 3 zones.I was also really thrown off by the end. I had just gotten the self spell and I hadn't even gotten the water spell yet. I killed the 5 guardians so I went to the gate figuring it would lead to the next zone. And then wham, final boss battle which was weirdly easy and mostly exposition between father and son. I never once had to use any of my special abilities in the final battle, or even hit the boss. I thought maybe I'd have to hit him with my life spell to heal the evil in him. But no.Overall, it doesn't live up to Epistory in story or gameplay. It's a bit buggy but not the worst I've ever played. Sometimes the typing was fun but most of the time it was tedious. It's not a bad game but also not one I would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Another game in the typing chronicles franchise, I wouldn't necessarily call it a sequel as this game doesn't have much in common, all I can tell is they both have foxes and the same typing mechanics. The game as a whole takes a different open world approach, if that's a good or bad thing I'll leave it up to you. However, where the previous game shines, this one is kinda meh. As I already mentioned above, this game tries to be less linear and tries to give the player more options to move freely and even complete side-quests. Also this time you have more magical powers which you can now combine, for example you can make fire, you can shoot fire rays and/or shoot long fire rays etc.What you need to keep in mind, though, before playing this game is its flaws and there are a lot of them. Let me start off with the story and quests, it's nice this game has 3 cutscenes but other than that, the story/quests are mainly text-based and quite honestly the most boring stuff I ever heard/read. Not to mention, some of the quests appear to be missable with the way how buggy and glitchy the game is you can always come back to them and just type in the keyword you might've missed. This brings me to the overall quality, the game feels rushed and unfinished. You constantly keep on getting stuck somewhere and the developers know it very well that's why they added a respawn button in the pause menu. Matter of fact, there is a place which I could only get into by glitching through the invisible wall as I couldn't figure how on earth am I supposed to get to a lower level with spells only.Then there is the open-world and collectibles. In comparison to the previous game, there is a lot less diversity and the 3 biomes you can explore aren't that terribly made actually, they have a lot of things crammed together. Well, the collectibles are basically just mob, relic or plant inspects accompanied by a short voiced boring monologue. There is a good amount of mob diversity but the novelty wears out really quickly because of how repetitive the gameplay is (it needs to be pointed out the gameplay is supposed to be repetitive due to the nature of how this game works, still it could've been much better considering the approach the devs took).It's clear to me, the game is far from being finished. And even though the previous game released more than 5 years ago, you'd expect some kind of improvement, yet here we are with a barebones game that barely does what it's supposed to. It's a big let down and if you played the first game you'll be on the same page as me. Still, despite all its shortcomings, it's not the worst game you can play but giving it a positive review doesn't feel right.
