_childDocuments_.review: Little turn-based strategy featuring satirical humor and graphics that kind of resemble maps of old.The only available game mode covers 13 campaigns, each consisting of 3-4 missions while each mission is one battle where your ship(s) fight enemy ships or monsters. It will probably take you around 10h to get through, give it or take it. Battles are short, so I would suggest playing 2-3 campaigns a day at the beginning and later 1 a day for an experience where you don't get bored and have a constant daily progress.The story is a satire of how Columbus discovered America featuring beliefs of that period as well as throwing pop culture references into a tasty stew. Humor is ok, not hilarious but far from forced or misdelivered either. Music fits nicely in the background and sound effects are satisfying.It's a very tactical game and quite challenging. The missions are made in a way to constantly force you to adjust your approach instead of developing a single tactic to grind through the entire game. Your ships' stats can progress between missions of a single campaign but don't transfer to next one. It's actually logical, as you are leading various characters in different campaigns.There are stats and actions available for you and the other side and what will be used is decided by allocating dice at the begging of each turn. RNG is a factor, but it seems to me it's done right, as it has helped and hindered me in pretty much equal amount. There are also bottles that are kind of like "fate points" that you collect each turn or when you defeat one enemy and can be used for various actions meant to help you turn things to your favor.Even though it can be labeled as a modern indie game, it has that "just right" feeling that games from the golden period of gaming had. I, for one, would really like to play a bigger/better/longer Here Be Dragons 2 in the future. So, fingers crossed the devs have such plans.Bought it at -70% and I'm super happy with the value I got. Since the base price is not high, I would argue that for tactical gamers and those who prefer indie games, this one is a good buy even at full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Here Be Dragons

_childDocuments_.review: GRADE: F+. It feels like a super long tutorial. and what little strategy there is is completely destroyed by the RNG elements. In fact the best strategy is to restart until you get a starting Dice roll that lets you take your turn, and hurts the enemy and stops them from taking their turn. "Here There Be Dragons" lures you in with adorable dragons and pixelated charm, but prepare for a quick journey that only leads to disappointment. Where strategy takes a backseat to pure luck. Each battle feels like the same repetitive dance. Even at a discounted price, the lack of depth and reliance on RNG make this a Hard Pass. You're better off steering clear of this underwhelming adventure. Spend your money and your time elsewhere,
_childDocuments_.name: Here Be Dragons

_childDocuments_.review: It's really boring. It's mostly lacking customization. You always have 2 ships and the ships abilities and starting hp is determined by the "campaign" you are currently playing (it's just 3-4 levels in a row each). And after each level you can increase stats of the ships but those don't carry over to other campaigns. If you had a load out you could change each play through then it might actually be more interesting. The actual gameplay also lacks in depth. You roll dice, asign the dice to your ships skills and that's it. There are some minor stuff like lower dice give you initiative and collecting ink bottles but nothing that takes good strategy or planning. Just hope that the dice are useable by you and not by the enemy and that's the game. The Asthetic is cool and why I bought the game, but the story is really bad. It makes attempts at humor that fall flat and rely on every character being too stupid to live. If anything it would probably be a good phone game in how mindless it is. But they sell it here on steam so that's their problem.
_childDocuments_.name: Here Be Dragons

_childDocuments_.review: So, know upfront that this isn't a lot of gameplay. Replayability, for me, is completely absent. That being said, I got my money's worth.What's good: While the game is very mechanically simple it's got the crunchiness of a medium weight strategic board game. In your haste to execute what appears to be a good plan, you'll wipe and realize you should have actually taken a sub-optimal line instead. The enemies, while not particularly varied, mostly feel unique. (my most challenging fight was the snakes that heal to the highest health of snakes at the end of each round) Difficulty feels...okay. With additional refinement it could be both more difficult while also being increasingly fair.The audio is sharp, sound effects please, voice overs good (but the game would certainly feel more alive if each text box were accompanied by a voice with a personality. The humor left something to be desired.What's bad: Well, I've already touched on all of it. The game walks a fine line for me, I _almost_ regret the purchase. Why? I feel like a $20 game should have a bit more content. The bones are here, it's got the makings of something great. I'm certain it was difficult to balance but it needs more. More ships and options, for example would be a great start. There is a small portion of the game where you pilot three ships but the addition of the third simply showcases it can be done with respect to balance. I'm not a dice fan, I'm a avid board gamer and while this system gives you the ability to manipulate dice...it's just so RNG. (See: F your plans)Super easy to recommend on sale. Did I get my return on investment? Sure. It's COVID-19 day..again..and I got 9 hours of entertainment for $20.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended for fans of casual turn-based battles and a light history-meets-mythology atmosphere.+Art style, wackiness+Turn-based ship battles+Unique shared dice mechanics for stats/abilities+Ship upgrade choices+Good number of missions/content+Enemy and ability variety-No voiced dialogue-Barebones options, even more limited at start-Awkward UI at times-No story cohesion-Upgrades only last a couple battles-Repetitive-Missed opportunity to weave in some actual history

_childDocuments_.review: is a tactical turn-based strategy game that could also have been a board game. The game is currently in Early Access so things can change. During my time playing, I encountered no bugs whatsoever, and it does not feel like an Early Access title at all.Starting up you will get a good interactive tutorial. It does not overwhelm you and you will learn as you play. As it is turn-based, the tutorial is set up so that you learn one new move each turn. I enjoy the pace that the information is introduced.The story shows an alternative satirical history of the discovery of America by Christopher Columbus. You can read a little more about it on the store page. The story unfolds in between battles.The game is a tactical turn-based game that also makes use of dice, which are used to upgrade attacks or boost defenses, among other things.The game is broken up in levels and you need to win one in order to move onto the next.In each level you have one more more ships to control and various enemies to encounter.The player who has the most initiative chooses the dice that they wish to use and attacks first. Initiative can be regained each turn. Aside from your own attacks you will need to keep a close eye on enemy attacks, because sometimes the winning strategy isn't necessarily to attack.The game starts off fairly easily, but it gets harder with each level. You can redo any level and there is no punishment for failing.The artwork is just awesome. The style resembles ink/calligraphy drawings. It's just a pleasure to look at.There is not a lot of music but the parts that do have it are very good. No complaints from me.The sound effects in-game are quite nice too. can be fully played with a mouse.There are currently 6 campaigns that will last around 5 hours. At a base price of $14.99/€12.49, this is worth noting. For me, the content is definitely worth the price. For people looking to get at least one hour per dollar/euro spent, the ratio does not quite meet that standard. Though the plan is to add another "6-8 campaigns (18-24 scenarios) containing new enemies, story characters, player skills and challenges."It is sometimes unfair for everyone to use the money/time ratio to judge the worth of a game. So if you think it's priced too high, you should still definitely check it out when it's on sale at a price more reasonable for you. is what I would call a true gem. It isn't a big release but it's so much fun. If you enjoy tactical turn-based combat, then be sure to check it out. If you enjoy board-game style games, you might also want to give it a chance. Don't forget it's in Early Access currently, so I do anticipate it getting even better. I do think that lack of achievements is a glaring omission at this time. Hopefully they will be added so the game can garner some more attention.The price might be a point of hesitation for some; however, whether you pick it at the base price or on sale another time, I think it's worth it.For me, it's an absolute recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: Here Be Dragons

_childDocuments_.review: I love the art style, the old drawn map style is very fitting to the theme.The game look a few hours to finish, hoping to see more content released soon.The dice based combat isn't too random. The balance between doing high damage (high value dice) and getting lead in initiative (low value dice) is nicely done. The tutorial was too slow for me, they could introduce the combat mechanic in half the fights.There is absolutely no customisation so there is no replay value, hoping they can change this with the future updates.I do recommend this game, seeing that it is very cheap, a few hours of enjoyable gameplay is well worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't think I was going to like this game once I learned that you have very little choice in how your characters are built. In fact, the game is very linear and chooses exactly what ships and abilities you will get, as well as what baddies and abilities are on the other side.Every single fight is different in *some* way. Be that a new type of bad guy, a stronger version of a bad guy, or some other effect on the board that changes the way you can fight.The game starts of relatively easy (I played on the "challenge" difficulty). I think I might have got through the first 7 or 8 chapters of the game without losing a single battle. At some point the game gets quite a bit harder, but as previously discussed, the developer has pre-determined both sides of the battlefield. Given that there are plenty of people who have beat the whole game (15% according to the achievement stats) you can be sure that while the battlefield may look stacked against you -- there is certainly a path to victory. The thing I liked most about being put into canned scenarios is that you're forced to use different tactics depending on the fight. It's actually an improvement over most games like this in my opinion where you can just build a really good deck and stomp the CPU via your preferred method. Overall 8/10. The game is a little too long imo and also there's SO much dialogue that's basically pop culture references shrouded in pirate jokes it's a lot to read.
_childDocuments_.name: Here Be Dragons

_childDocuments_.review: Tactical game with a board game feel. Just right difficulty level, not too hard but not too easy. Superb graphics in style of "Don't Starve", very clean and well thought interface. Unfortunatelly I didn't had occasion to play longer (my 2 and 3 year old kids insisted on change). I have a feeling choices of special attacks and ship upgrades form a complex system which makes game better as gameplay progresses.
_childDocuments_.name: Here Be Dragons

_childDocuments_.review: "Here be dragons" is unique in many ways, being everything, but not what I expected. And if you're open-minded, that is very positively. The artworks are aesthetically - I like the way everything looks like an old map. When I first saw the scenes with the governor and the walking on the city maps, I expected some kind of management or adventure game, which it isn't. These are - as far as I can see - only fixed sequences to drive the plot. In a humorous way. The gameplay itself is not a roguelike or open-world, but 'campaign'-driven, with campaign meaning some battles in a row, between which I can temporarily upgrade my ships, meaning to add a point for defense for example. The battles itself are the main part of the game, difficult even on 'fun'-difficulty, and being puzzle-like and outcome heavily influencd by dice. And this random dice throwing adds hell of thrill to the game, and every dice-placement has to be well thinked over. You can place dice into abilities, upgrading the ships hull or cannons, and use bottles to change the results to trap enemies. This way, it becomes a puzzle-battler, something I didn't xpect, and highly like!
_childDocuments_.name: Here Be Dragons

_childDocuments_.review: Combat is core and . Even though it's dice-based I didn't find randomness game-breaking. Each time I did lose a battle it was due to me not foreseeing the consequences of my decisions or not being fully aware of the situation on the field. There were of course more or less lucky turns but generally, they didn't decide whether I lose or not.Though simple at the core - it requires thinking due to new mechanics being introduced every now and then: getting to know both skills of enemies and yours, calculating ahead of time to minimize/maximize damage, being aware of environmental hazards or extra rules for the fight, deciding whether it's actually good to start round first, etc. . In case of difficulties - there's also a system to make encounters easier.Each sea expedition is preceded by a small bit of story which I found intriguing due to the characters being... well, different to say the least. As confusing as it may seem at times, it's nice to have some background behind the events. Together with really fitting artwork both create a fun world to be a part of.Do not expect grand adventure with sailing, pillaging, managing your crew, and so on.  is a fun combat-oriented puzzle game that is great to be picked up on the go. Fights are short, fun, tense, and even with some randomness in play - feels fair.

_childDocuments_.review: Set in a satirical, alternate 15th century,  is a pseudo-historical, turn-based strategy game. Players take on the role of the ‘real’ explorers, fools and lunatics forcibly sailing across a living map under royal order, battling pirates and sea creatures with a combination of tactics and luck. Here be Dragons will provide multiple hours of gameplay featuring a range of combat and enemies, a touch of humour and some pleasing visuals. It is a satisfying tactical experience with replayability afforded to it by the random nature of the dice mechanic and I’d happily recommend it to anyone looking for a turn-based strategy game with a more casual feel.My full, detailed review of this game is available at

Funny characters and writing.Until I got to the Neptune stage and then got caught in a vicious cycle of stalemate with a whale - the game ground to a halt and the fun got sucked out of the room. _childDocuments_.review: Utter Crap!  First up, the game is pretty. It's very smooth with nice animations and imagery and the style is tolerable although very unoriginal. But it's nothing a first year programmer couldn't do in an afternoon. Secondly: Gameplay. Very very stupid slow confusing and boring, not to mention ridiculously hard and impossible. Usually with a game like this there's some way to upgrade your ships to make them handle this sort of thing but I didn't see anything like that here. Maybe there is further along but the game got very annoying way before this point. Any game that relies so heavily on random dice generation is instantly a BAD idea. Having to choose where to assign the dice and how it effects initiative is also badly done and annoying and drags the game down. It's hard to explain how bad this combat system is and that's the entirety of the game by the way, stupid combat scenarios. You really have to play it yourself which I don't recommend even trying. _childDocuments_.review: Has its appeal. It is a strong game with clear vision, mechanics, but limited. It has potential, and I'm sad to see it is leaving early access so soon. Although I did not encounter any bugs or glitches, I think a lot more can be done with the concept. A few things have kept me from finding it enjoyable enough to return to:No character creation or customization. Sure, the game clearly markets as a strategy game, not an RPG or simulator, but I would have loved to be able to at least name my captain, if not choose their appearance, and the specific attributes they bring to battle. Instead, the game cycles you through different "pre-made" captains in order to tell a story that I wasn't that interested in. You have no choice over when to play with the captains, what their special skills are, etc.The level design is too guided, linear. Like I mentioned, the game doesn't let you choose when to play with what character. They also don't let you choose which level to play and when. The specific levels seem to be designed for a specific captain, allowing for no discovery, no synergy, and frankly no challenge. It would have been so much more fun to discover which captains work best for each levels, or which skills work best against specific enemies. There is no re-playability. The humour is a highlight in this game, but it is a bit insensitive at some points. Theres a particularly troublesome joke in the early game when you are battling an island inhabited by "tropical natives". It is implied that the island is festering with sexually transmitted infections, and the characters even hint that they've been infected after the encounter. I believe this is a good game! The actual strategy / combat mechanics are solid, and are only foiled by the lack of player agency. It is not worth the asking price, however.

_childDocuments_.review: There were two good things in this game that made me complete the game: battle mechanics and solid visual style during battles. But other elements of the game must be rewritten from the scratch:- dialogs - thay are boooring; guys, please don't try to do all the pieces of the game by yourselves, find good writer. Alternatively make an option "skip dialogs" to save time- technically I don't understand why 2D game had been made using Unity. It's huge overkill, there're many crossplatform libraries and frameworks for 2D games that can be run anywhere. Because of your poor decision the game doesn't run on Linux- sound - I turned it off to stop listen to monotonic and invasive battle sounds. If you like to understand why sounds must be redone close your eyes and ask someone to play the game- visual style during  cut scenes - not only it looked cheap but also it didn't match visual style of battles- AI - it was somewhat stupid; the game has quite strict and limited actions, it's not like chess, go or athello, so with appropriate classical AI algorithms you could calculate several turns ahead. But here it seemed like you just applied simple rules for each enemy in a predictable way for player to win.- please make the possibility to skip the credits after the game had been complete. I know, you put a lot of efforts to make this scene, but.. are you sure it's fun to force your users to see the credits after all the issues?I do understand that making a game into production is titanic work and also this's early access, so you've got some time to fix the issues. You found an interesting and original game mechanics, but failed (so far) to wrap it into good scenario.

_childDocuments_.review: Ultimately I think this game is mostly fine, but nothing good about it stands out, and playing it is a little annoying. For me, this is worse than being a bad game with a few good elements,but everyone engages with games differently, so you might not feel the same.Here Be Dragons' core concept is that it's a dice placement board game simulating naval battles. Placing higher dice has more aggressive effects, but placing a high sum of dice causes you to act second in the initiative order. If you don't place dice, you take damage.This creates kind of a neat push-and-pull in theory, where you're going for slow high damage on some turns and fast defenses on others, but the balance on the game isn't loose enough to let you play around. It's built more like a puzzle game, but a puzzle game where you routinely need to get certain combinations of dice. Which means one of the strongest moves you can make is just to restart a level and get a different initial roll.There are some *very* light rpg elements, where you can upgrade your ships between maps, but only during certain short strings of levels. After the string is done, the upgrades reset. Moreover, you switch between characters and abilities after every string, and a lot of the characters don't feel great to use.It's not *too* hard, but sometimes the rng just hands you a garbage starting roll, or it serves the enemy exactly the dice they need on a round where they have the initiative and they instantly focus down one of your ships, and there's no incentive not to immediately restart the level.The art is solid, and the creatures look fun and detailed and menacing, but the writing did not land with me. It's a picaresque about bad people plundering and murdering and starting wars with the ocean, but it uses this setup to... quote Monty Python jokes.Hey, man. Do you remember the Knights Who Say Ni? Yeah, that's SO funny. I'm gonna randomly say Ni and you're gonna laugh and we're all gonna laugh. Over and over and over again.It feels stale and uninspired in a way that the rest of the game isn't.I think as a board game, where you're physically interacting with the dice and paging through the rulebook and maybe there's pvp, this would be fun.As-is, it felt more frustrating than enjoyable.If you like dice placement games and puzzle games and want to turn your brain off a bit, it's probably not a bad pick on sale. But if you were hoping for a more robust strategy rpg like I was, this ain't that.
_childDocuments_.name: Here Be Dragons

_childDocuments_.review: You won't find dragons nor the Americas, but a ton of dice and bad translations are waiting for you!This is a strategy game where you place dice to cast your ships' (fighters by another name) skills, or to improve their stats for the fight. The whole combat is rather interesting, what with a initiative system that favors using lower rolls (which often but not always can only be used on weaker or more defensive abilities), sharing the pool of dice with your enemies, having special modifiers for some fights, and ink, a special mana-like resource that can be used for roll tweaks, healing, free skills and ultimately reviving your ships.It's all well and good that Here be dragons can stand on the premise of its combat system, because everything else ranges from mediocre to plain bad. Randomness is a major factor, to the point that by the end of the game I would routinely restart a mission if the starting roll wasn't good -- the luck of the draw is somewhat manageable after a couple of rounds, but it is not at the beginning of the scuffle. The AI is bad at playing the game (which is just as well, because it serves to mitigate the effects of randomness) and there are bugs (which is just as well, because it serves to mitigate the effects of randomness). The missions are structured around episodes of (mostly) three battles, with some minor stat improvement between missions -- with no information that would do for proper strategizing, though. There is zero build-up between episodes and you begin each new expedition with a new set of ships (which is kinda nice, as you have to adapt your strategies, but making do with the new set for the episode sometimes feels like a pain). Despite having a wide variety of enemies and the nonexistence of persistent upgrades between episodes, the game cannot escape the power creep, both on your fresh new ships for each episode and on the enemies. Expect to see some of the earlier enemies in at least three different power levels, differentiated only by the size of the sprite.The story (something barely comprehensible about an alchemist with a strong liking for explosives manipulating the chancellor of a fictional court of Europe (Europe as a country, apparently) to eliminate the many mythological menaces of the Atlantic and then the beast slayers themselves so that ) is poor and very poorly translated, with very bad humor that translates poorly from Polish and/or to the written word (plenty of references to popular songs, apparently; I was only able to recognize one). You start caring little for each character and by the end you will care even less, as the poor dialogues and narrative texts give zero development, and as you will meet most of them in only one or two episodes. During the tutorial there is some "comedy" done at the expense of tribal natives (nothing particularly racist, mind you) that won't appear again, which I ended up missing for some drama or whatever.The graphics are nice, with bold lines that are used both to enhance the game's comic feel and to evoke the maps and drawings of the past. The sound is alright but completely forgettable. The interface is serviceable but a bit wonky when selecting skills and targets. Expect very few options in the settings panel, mostly geared to skip the most annoying stuff like having to roll the die by "blowing" a cherub, and activating "easy" mode (which doesn't seem so different, as apparently only doubles your ink/mana available). The achievements are mostly unlocked by playing the campaign, except for two that you will accidentally unlock just by normal play anyway. There's zero replayability.All in all, a pretty poor game saved by the fresh combat system.Verdict: C

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, this was a fun, short dice strategy game with some interesting ideas. The story is funny and the scenarios are challenging. My main gripes were being railroaded into specific strategies to solve a scenario (if you take each scenario as a puzzle to solve then I think the game is more enjoyable) and the dice glitches/bugs. Several times I would be one or two hit points away from winning and the game would crash or glitch out and I'd have to start again. This was especially annoying on the long battles where I was whittling down many monsters. In another instance, I ended up in a case where there were no dice that the AI could assign so got stuck without being able to move on or forfeit the turn -- a case that wasn't coded in as a possible scenario so I had to start the scenario again. Luckily, this game is quite short and absorbing enough to make it to the end without feeling like a grind.

_childDocuments_.review: Although not perfect, this game is wonderful! However, it may not be what you expect. This is not the ( true!) story of how Christopher Columbus reached the New World, but the (indeed  true!) telling of the events which led to his protagonism. While the former make us think this is a traditional RPG, with exploration, battles and a progression system consisting of evolving one or few characters until the end, the latter gives room to what it really is: a combat-only game with many characters, each of which protagonist in their own short campaigns, and where character progression starts after the first battle of the campaign and ends just before the last. What really progresses throughout all the game is combat complexity and the greater scheme which ties all campaigns together. So let's dive deeper into both aspects.The Spanish Crown has the ambition to  seek out new lands, new civilizations, boldly going where no one has ever been. It must, however, deal first with the terrible monsters roaming the seas. It is both the Chancelor's, the King's right hand, and the Royal Alchemist's job to get rid of them and they hire many  brave men, eager to write their names in the annals of history.Throught the game we follow the stories of these captains, many of them recurring characters, and the jokes they bring with them. One is a robot captain called RoboCap, whose abilities' names looks more like the result of the developer's incompetence than the names the designers intended (imagine healing your units with "Dice..Heal.dll" instead of "Heal companion"). Another is a green (newbie) knight called Sir Green, so assertive that he is the only character with an ability that damages a random opponent. There is still a woman disguised as man, constantly talking about her "masculine intuition" or that she will "beat those bastards or tear apart my totally real beard". There are others, still, each with their unique jokes. My favorite was definitely Captain Fish! Just wait for it!Many of the jokes, even the story itself, are not completely original, but I've found them good enough. Most of them amusing, and a few really worth some good laughs. All in all, this is a well written story with well placed jokes that can entertain, I believe, anyone who just want some fun.This is the meat of Here Be Dragons. Its core. Its heart! Its... well... the only thing you can do in the game. Fortunately, the folks at Zero Red Games nailed it! Its basics are simple. It is turn based and each turn is divided into three phases: preparation, salvos and actions. Whomever gets the initiative, acts first in each phase.When the turn begins, one dice is rolled for each character alive, both player's an AI's, and they are stored in a common pool. On the preparation phase, the side with the initiative assigns some of those dices, one for each of theirs characters, on stats (Basic Attack and Basic Defense) and special abilities, called Actions. Then, on the salvos phase, both sides choose their targets and attack, confronting their Basic Attacks with the targets Basic Defense. On the actions phase, each character uses their activated Actions to damage, heal or apply status effects. Some actions can even allow one side to remove assigned dice from the other, potentially negating an Action that would be activated otherwise.The real complexity, though, comes from the assignment mechanic and how it relates to abilities and the initiative order. All Actions and stats can only be charged by dices with certain values: some, for example, can be charged by any dice with values from 1 to 3, while others accepts only a 6. Generally, higher values are reserved for offense while lower values are for defense and healing. Meanwhile, whichever side gets the lowest sum on all charged actions or stats gets the initiative. This means that, if you want to go all in, you may be forced to forgo the initiative, confronting you with a constant trade-off between dealing heavy damage and dealing damage, healing and even choose your dice first. You can always choose to not assign a dice to help you go first, but this causes all of your units to receive 1 damage for each unassigned dice. The same happens with the AI.If you think all of this is overwhelming, don't worry too much, they introduce these mechanics in a very good pace. After the tutorial, the game progresses by presenting you increasingly complex abilities and, for me, the entire game is a big exploration of everything these mechanics have to offer. I really liked being forced to look at the same problem and its different variations at very different angles, making each battle a new puzzle to solve. One may complain that the combat is too dependent on the dice rolls, making your victories or losses almost random, but I don't think it is true. Even if I felt they had more impact then I'd wish, the game gives you many ways to control the outcomes by making the AI acting quite predictably and giving you Erratas, a mechanic made mostly to modify dice rolls. With these in hand and paying attention to the AI's behaviour, you can predict very accurately the consequences of your choices. Therefore, randomness is not decisive, even if a little more influential than it should.With a few failures and lots of successes Here Be Dragons presents the players with engaging and increasingly difficult battles and many ways of using the same mechanics, all spiced with amusing humour, making battling sea monsters a journey worth taking and, why not, at full price for those who like the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I can`t recommend this game.This is my fault to a point. I expected some kind of funny roguelike that has you use your skill to get the right dice and deny the opponent.What I got is a seemingly unending "campaign" with Monty Python references in lieu of actual humor.  Might be a different experience for you.The campaigns is divided in chapters and you don`t keep any progress. The game is also slow. Even in fast mode, turns take long.Last but not least, there is not that much skill involved. You take dice for yourself to power your number based abilites or upgrade your defense/ attack and the enemies take the rest and power theirs (and the lower your number the better your intiative). In practice this means you often can use every thing besides the 3 and the enemy everything besides the 1. (There is a refillable ability to change the dice value as well.)So you have quite a choice what to do and what to deny the enemy. But in practice the numbers are so wide spread, that the enemy will get his numbers most of the time (and you will get yours as well). The problem than comes with the abilites At a point your 2 ships will fight 3 enemies at once, which will buff themselves up every turn, because of the wide spread. Each of them takes time to kill and around turn 3 they will sink your first ship, because you just can`t keep up.  So you have a choice. Restart the fight until you just roll 1`s a few times, so you can pull ahead oder roll your eyes, quit after 5 tries and write this review.tl;dr This might be your jam, but maybe watch a lets play first, that covers at least the first 7 chapters You won`t miss out on story here. Just inform yourself beforehand. I wish, I did. Maybe I will get my refund with 2 hours in.

_childDocuments_.review: The graphics are neat, the story is sorta interesting. However the game falls flat, after the first 2 missions. It just becomes repetitive. After you complete the missions for one captain, you take control of another captain and each one has their own unique abilities which cool. The annoying part is, that upgrades applied to previous ships don't carry over and its just the same thing over and over. I would like to see more dice manipulation abilities, as your pretty much leaving it to chance if the dice roll in your favor. I wouldn't recommend purchasing this game, unless you really like doing the same thing over and over.

_childDocuments_.review: An awesome blend of boardgaming and a strategy video game, this game delivers on many fronts. Great visuals on "a living map" make this game stand out from the crowd as well as a great sense of humour that reminds me greatly of the greatest Lucas Arts gaming era.Interesting world setup, where before americas were discovered someone had to get rid us of all the sea monsters on the way. Cool mechanics that involve dice throwing but counter-balance the dice throwing randomness with interesting dice assignment mechanics make it an enjoyable experience. Game is very well polished and long enough to make it a non-early access title already, so go ahead and grab it. If the authors dish out more content in the future it will be even more worth of your $$$$.
_childDocuments_.name: Here Be Dragons

_childDocuments_.review: I'm loving this game so far. Cool art, really interesting combat mechanics, dialogue is hilarious. The combat system is really great. It's completely novel as far as I know, but it's very interesting tactically (lots of moves seem promising, but there are ways to optimize), and every fight you have to make a tough strategic call of when to go aggressive and finish off your enemies and when to play defensively and control the board position. The variety of enemies was pretty amazing for an early access game. Some of them you have to burn down ASAP but others you have to control the board until the very last turn or they will turn the tables on you. Also the AI adapts to you healing ships or building armor. It focuses fire on the weaker ships and doesn't waste dice by charging up abilities on units that are about to die.I found all the fights were winnable even with "bad luck" (great for a dice game). Also losses aren't punishing at all. You just restart the battle. Early on when I didn't understand the strategies I got stuck on a couple of fights and replayed them until I got lucky rolls, but the game keeps you on a steady learning curve and challenges you with different enemies until you realize you have to change strategies. When I replayed those early fights, they were actually really easy.Game is very polished for early access, but there's less than 3 hours of content in the game. I'm hoping for more of the same content when the game gets finished as well as more difficulty and more.Pros: * Art style* Hilarious* Very interesting combat system* Huge variety of enemies* AI is goodCons (mostly early access criticisms)* Some QoL like undo and controls can feel a little clunky* Not much content yet, only about 2-3 hours of content* Sounds are simplistic and repetitive* Game is on a great learning curve, but I don't think they're done with any endgame content, because it still feels quite easy by the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Here Be Dragons

_childDocuments_.review: I had a lot of fun with this game. It took me about three hours to get through and I worry that the game will be a little short even when it is completed. However, for a light game with a reasonable challenge I would recommend it.The writing is fun and has many pop culture Easter Eggs mixed in. I like the art style; it really suits the game and helps set the mood. Will it be worth the full asking price on completion? I think that is up for debate but what is here right now is solid.I would appreciate it if, later down the line, the developers gave us incentive to return after the campaign is done, maybe an endless or survival mode or even just make your own skirmishes battles. This would also help with the asking price.As for the stability of the early access? I only saw a few T pose during the start of the tavern cutscenes beyond that it runs smoothly.
_childDocuments_.name: Here Be Dragons

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice tactical, turn-based game. It's hard to stop playing (played 3h straight).Pros:- Doesn't look like early access. It's stable and 100% playable- Very nice graphic. The design reminds me of board games- It definitely has this "one-more-battle" vibe- It works well if you only have like 10 minutes and also if you want to play longer. Nintendo Switch port please? ;)- Humor! I laughed out loud often- Has a huge potentialCons:- No "undo" button. - Some tweaks to difficulty (balance) would be great- No ultra-wide monitor support, but I guess it's very easy to fixIn overall, I really like it and will continue playing.Needs multiplayer, maybe some random scenarios and it would be great!Nice job!

name: Buildings Have Feelings Too!
detailed_description: Old Pete, “The Dock Yard”, is being demolished. He’s the first of his group of friends to go. It was unexpected and everyone is a bit worried. Being made of bricks and mortar doesn’t mean you don’t have your own things to worry about. This ragtag group of friends were there, right from the start, when it really became a city. With them they brought the titans of the industry, hundreds of jobs and hundreds more houses. But the Linen Mill’s not been getting many textile orders come through this year, the Warehouse lost another contract from the neighbouring city and the Old Bank’s having money troubles. Something’s not quite right. Change is coming. What if they’re next? Fortunately, you, The Halfway Hotel, are at hand to step in and reassure everyone that things will be ok. But what starts off as small odd-jobs ends up unravelling into more problems, as history moves faster than you can keep up with. Buildings Have Feelings Too! is an exciting new city-management/puzzle game about buildings and the city they inhabit. Imagine a city where buildings can walk and talk to one another. Each one has its own aspirations, hopes and fears. Most of the time they are just trying to get along with each other and make it through the day. Grow your city into a bustling metropolitan centre with an array of shops, offices, entertainment facilities and amenities, to help your buildings thrive; or risk them being demolished forever. Discover and equip a wide range of businesses from the Victorian era right through to the modern day. Befriend a range of Buildings, each with their own aspirations, hopes and fears, as they come to grips with the changing world around them. Customise and rearrange your city’s layout by moving buildings and find the perfect combination for your city to grow. Expand across multiple neighbourhoods of your city, discovering new landmark characters and districts.

_childDocuments_.review: These buildings might have feelings easily swayed and broken like humans do, but they certainly also have some serious control and UI issues, tend to overcomplicate things, are prone to sudden outbursts of poorly worded explanations and get lost in their thoughts often.On the surface, it's a quaint, charming 2D city builder with anthropomorphic buildings and a rundown, old hotel as the main protagonist. But, take a shovel to it and it turns into a somewhat obtuse and fiddly puzzle game of micromanaging buildings and trying to satisfy their wants and needs in the form of upgrade requirements and appeal increases. A city builder in the traditional sense this really ain't.The visuals are swanky. Stately even. Buildings look like detailed cardboard cutouts with stick arms and legs. They're beautifully animated and each one has quips and different conversations when talking to other buildings in their neighbourhood, depending what business occupies them. Backgrounds and foregrounds blend into the cutouts superbly and you can decorate the foreground where the stick people walk with different items, from park benches to bright red mailboxes. The soundtrack is a bit less chic, consisting of a monotone track that quickly loses its charm.Form over function is, unfortunately, where Buildings excels. Puzzle game in a very light city builder seems like a novel idea at first and it would probably function well, if only the game explained its mechanics and gameplay better. Tutorial is kind of okish, but it's very easy to get lost and confused in menus and icons. There's no real overview of your neighbourhoods, building productions and appeals. You need to walk with your avatar so the buildings you want to check on are visible on screen. And even then, the information you get is kind of like a dilapidated building, neglected, boarded with badly organized planks and confusing to passersby.Poor controls, even after 2 hotfixes, really don't help much. Placing or moving buildings is done by selecting a spot and that's occasionally harder than it looks because the selector flies all over. Good thing that you can click on any spot and then scroll. But only as far as you can see. Clicking around the Business Index that lists different buildings you've unlocked seems a bit unresponsive when using mouse and keyboard. Keybinds are not rebindable and seem slow and clunky in general, compared to a controller. Walking everywhere with your hotel also gets a bit tedious in the long run.The gameplay loop consists of upgrading your buildings and satisfying their requests for cool neighbours. It gets complicated later as new buildings and new requirements are introduced. And those can get very confusing when you start balancing out more and more buildings with different requirements. Building and upgrading a bank requires tailors, mad hatters and gourmet restaurants which in turn requires posh coffee shops, accountant offices and whiskey distilleries which require sloppy pubs, greengrocers and unruly mobs that you can't get without family housing or dirt cheap rented rooms. Only slightly exaggerated, but you get the idea. There's also a mechanic with different bonus infrastructure cards that buildings can acquire, but that's really poorly explained as well.Make a few mistakes in that balancing and swapping of neighbours and the buildings quickly start deteriorating and with fiddly controls, you'll have a hard time doing things quick enough so your businesses don't close and you're forced to remove them and build from scratch. Couple that with bricks earned from doing tasks and upgrading buildings as your only income and you can find yourself in a bricked up situation with no way out but restarting your game. No saves for you. Only a single quicksave.I might not be the target audience here as I was drawn to this game by it's visuals and had expectations of a whimsical, no rush, eccentric light city builder with sassy buildings. I wasn't expecting a somewhat cold-hearted, methodical puzzle game with clunky controls, confusing menus and overly needy daisy chain buildings. Perhaps a few more fixes will improve the controls more, making all the other gameplay problems slightly more tolerable. But, these neighbourhoods are not something I'd really like to revisit. Unless my achievement hunting brain tricks me.
_childDocuments_.name: Buildings Have Feelings Too!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty fun, but the controls are a bit awkward, and it's easy to get stuck in the Tutorial.   It's a unique idea, and I've played enough games that I love unique ideas.  So I would recommend this game, if you want something unique and interesting.  But understand that a big part of the "game" is fighting the controls.A big part of the problem stems from the fact that you can't go straight left-right when selecting a spot to build.  If you go past the spot you are trying to select and turn around, you jump to the other side of your avatar, which is 4-5 building spots over.  So selecting the right spot is tricky.Then there is the fact that sometimes left mouse click can sub for space, an other times it can't.  Which is confusing.  And the first time they throw you into the tab menu in the tutorial (to look up 'Construction' and figure out how to construct a building) they haven't yet explained to you that 'Q' is the way to go back, so I got stuck there pressing escape and button mashing.  HINT:  If you are stuck in the tutorial try pressing "Q" not "ESCAPE".Put all this together and it feels like a big part of the game right now is fighting the UI, and not solving the puzzles.  Another big one -- when I want to move a building just let me click drag a building, and not do that whole lead it somewhere thing, when selecting the place you want to put it is so hard (see above).   Add to that that the buildings will move over if you accidentally place a new building in the wrong spot.   The puzzle should be figuring out where to put the buildings not struggling to select the right spot to put teach one multiple times.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw Buildings Have Feelings Too (BHF) as a possible game to review, and although I thought it looked kind of cute, it wasn't something I was actively looking for. However, out of the blue, someone associated with BHF sent me an email with a review key, before I even responded to show my potential interest. I'm not one to snub an offer like that, so I gave it try, but didn't love the experience. These buildings have feelings though, so I'll try to be tactful. The goal of BHF is to check with the buildings of the neighborhood, find out what their desires are, and try to satisfy them. This usually revolves around getting enough buildings of a particular type and star level in place. Some of your effort will be spent on upgrading what's already in place, though you'll also have to establish a few buildings from scratch. The resource available for buying items is bricks, which you earn from completing specific requests and upgrading buildings. It doesn't take long to build up a decent stack, but if you aren't efficient and have to keep recycling structures to put in a new business, you can wind up in a downward spiral. A simple problem I encountered was not knowing where to find the next item necessary for upgrading the building, such as whiskey barrels, which comes from distilleries. Until you unlock and level-up a building with that resource, it won't be displayed on the building that requires it, which isn't very useful for someone new to the game. One concern I'd have about BHF is how complicated it'd get with such requirements, considering that early on, it was already balancing the appeal of buildings on grounds such as being close to a pub, away from a factory, and near a distillery that has whiskey barrels. I'd hate having to do something like build a school, requiring paper, civil servants, and young people, which would need me to create a paper mill, offices, and new housing. All of which would have their own requirements, with the school being used to make something else, none of which could be near a pub, except the housing that would require it.  Although it's possible to play BHF with the mouse and keyboard, this seems to be even less ideal than playing with the controller. The main issue is how troublesome interacting with the game's UI, menus, and the buildings themselves is, no matter which control scheme you choose. Trying to navigate all of the possible areas of information, such as the ones that pop up when holding down the shoulder buttons, or when talking to a building directly, is cumbersome and unintuitive. Another simple issue is that buildings are moved around often, but moving them requires precise selection of a small icon. You'll inadvertently walk past the one you want and have to double-back to try again repeatedly. Things open up on a grim note, as the building you control observes an old, derelict building at the docks being demolished for not keeping up with its own repairs. It transitions away from this quite suddenly, as you're now in a different area, and in spite of being the newcomer, are going to be helping the current residents deal with their issues. For the little I played, the introduction didn't connect with what followed, since this part of town had nothing to do with the docks.Without question, this is the area that will draw people's attention in the first place, with anthropomorphized buildings walking around. Although there's a certain charm to this, the downside is that these buildings aren't as human or detailed as they could be. Meaning that when you build the same buildings throughout the game, they'll always look the same. There's some distinguishing aspects that help you tell the nature of a building just from a glance, primarily the banner, but more could have been done to make them distinct. I tried looking for a soundtrack of BHF, but wasn't able to find anything on YouTube. When I intentionally listened to the music, I didn't notice more than one song playing on loop, so if there is more music, I'm not aware of it. It's a decent enough track, with a mellow tone to it, which seems suitable enough for a game like this. Without more variety though, it wouldn't be something to leave on in the background, as it'd wear out its welcome. There's a few sound effects, such as when constructing buildings or acquiring bricks, and they were good enough for the job. 🌟 The game's design is a great icebreaker, because it looks quite cute and charming. Plus, the buildings conversing with each other is also surprisingly sweet, to an extent.❌ Having gotten past the tutorial, I wasn't sure of the mechanics I was working with in the area immediately afterwards. At one point, a series of buildings couldn't be moved whatsoever. Then suddenly the smaller ones could be moved around, though I didn't know why. However, the largest building was still immovable.❌ What you can build inside the structures doesn't always fit the design well and makes it look like you're making a mistake or being inefficient. For instance, the small factory with an overly large chimney, or a tall, skinny office building with a pub or restaurant inside it.❌ The game would function much better if you didn't have an avatar, and simply scrolled back and forth across the screen the way most city management games do.❌ Nobody seems to like the controls.🔍 Try learning the UI and how it works early on, because you'll be utilizing it repeatedly. Having the system down pat would be essential for making progress long-term. Unfortunately, BHF is a great example of why you should never design something on the basis of form over function, as the up-close perspective is a large detriment to the functionality of the gameplay. Even if it did work much better, the gameplay isn't that satisfying for this sort of resource/city management game. Since you can move buildings around, it's built around this mechanic, so you'll establish a few buildings and improve upon them, just to shuffle things around to advance another group of buildings, before reorganizing them for the most appeal possible.Instead of having more space and freedom to organize things as you see fit and establish city areas for the long-term, you're playing a shell game to exploit what the buildings want before dumping them in the corner. If this is a game I had purchased directly through Steam, I'd have refunded it shortly after getting past the tutorial section, as it's that unenjoyable and clunky. Unless there's a pretty major overhaul, spare these buildings their feelings, and don't play the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Cute and charming puzzle game with just absolutely terrible controls and hampered by a poorly designed tutorial.The controls are keyboard focused, it's VERY fiddly to use WASD to move correctly and select specific objects or spaces, and the keys used in menus change from panel to panel. It's not intuitive or friendly at all. Just as an example: when you open up the game, there's a button next to "New Game" labelled "A". If you push the "A" key, because that's what you do when a button is on a menu and labelled with "A", the icon suddenly changes to a space bar, and that's what you actually have to press to start.The tutorial didn't start for me until I'd begun testing keys to see what moved me around, and frequently the bread crumb trail was missing or hidden - it would often wait until I had opened a menu before popping up, but never indicated to open that menu, or would be indicated by a talk icon slightly larger than the normal talk icon. If you're willing to slog along with it, or if hotfix for some level of mouse support they just dropped is any good, it seems like it's a good set of puzzles with very adorable buildings nattering on in the background. I'm not sure that I am.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a lovely puzzle.  It plays very similarly to Reus.  You place can place different buildings along a limited number of horizontal spaces.  Each kind of building can hold different kinds of businesses like apartments, cafes, and the like.  Each building provides benefits (and sometimes costs) to their neighbors which when stacked properly allows you to upgrade them.  Fully upgrading a building unlocks more advanced buildings as well.  Unlike Reus, the missions are not timed, and a core mechanic is that you can pick up and shuffle building locations with a cute jogging animation.  So, the game is much more forgiving in that sense. This game also has a very easy UI, and I find it easy to gather necessary information.  I can quickly see what each building gives to its neighbors and wants from them.  If a building needs something (like vegetables), I can quickly see what possible neighbors could fill that need.  The menu also has an easy to use encyclopedia of buildings unlocked and the next rung available to unlock.  By comparison, I had to make a notebook full of combinations and upgrade paths when I play Reus. I have played the first half dozen missions, and I quite like the game.  The art, dialogue, and music is charming.  The puzzle is engaging though not overly difficult.  The only real challenge in a game is that you must keep buildings happy or they fall into disrepair and shut down.  If you upgrade a building, it comes to expect certain benefits from its neighbors. So, swapping out that grocery store may cause the whole neighborhood to slowly collapse.  This is easy enough to avoid with some foresight or a quick reshuffling.  My only complaint about this mechanic is that there is no undo button.  If I miscalculate and swap an fully upgraded building for something else, I may not be able to recreate that fully upgraded building fast enough to save the neighborhood.  I haven't had the same frustration with controls that other people have.  I prefer to use the xbox controller over the keyboard, but both seem fine. It did take me a few missions to realize that I could shift buildings down rather than stress about placing them exactly where I wanted them - perhaps this is what frustrated other reviewers?  The game seems bug-free.I am not sure there is as much depth as Reus, but I also haven't gotten to the highest levels yet.  It is also unclear if there is a sandbox mode.  Perhaps there will be once I beat the game? If you enjoy combo puzzles like Reus or Islanders, you'll enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: To be frank,  is definitely one of the weirder city-builders that I've reviewed. It gives the game a unique feel but unfortunately, the game is marred by several crucial gameplay issues that turned it from a on-the-fence Thumbs-up to a Thumbs-down.The highlight of the game is that the buildings in this game has "feelings". The game does its best to personify the different buildings and some of the stuff the buildings talk about, such as the hardships of being abandoned after economy shifts and industries crumble, is actually pretty interesting... and not just mere smack talk. From just playing the game, you can see the impact of the economy not only on the people (and jobs) but also on buildings in the affected section of the city - how they are changed... have to change... to be relevant to the new opportunities that may arise or to simply wallow in oblivion. All of this is interesting but I'm still not convinced... let's take a look at the gameplay.----------------------------------------------------------------------Now, the gameplay is fairly puzzly IMHO. The goal is to construct and arrange the buildings in such a way that the objectives you're given are fulfilled and the game doesn't really give you a whole lot of leeway to do so, limiting the number of buildings you can build as well as the "slots" you can build them on. This is why I feel like I'm playing a puzzle game rather than the usual sandbox-oriented city-builder.Buildings have synergies in this game and by putting them within close distance of each other, they will provide nearby buildings with "appeals" a.k.a. criteria. By fulfilling all the criteria, you can then upgrade a building to the next star level, right up to 3 stars max. Every star level achieved will grant you bricks, which you'll then need to build new buildings or repair damaged ones. Maxing out star levels for your buildings will also unlock new building types via the Business Index (or what I'd call "building progression").There are also planning restrictions where certain "building slots" are reserved for certain types of buildings, but personally, I don't find that these restrictions matter much at least at the start of the game. Perhaps it'll pose more of a challenge in later levels though.Once you're done with the objectives for a location, you can then move on to the next one. There are plenty of well-varied locations you can visit around the (unnamed) city and you'll also "get to know" the various buildings that inhabit these areas, from the cocky white-collar buildings on the High Streets and the mournful factories in the "slums".As interesting as the game may be, like I said, it has several (IMHO) major downsides that turned me off the game. Firstly, the objective (and/or tutorial) isn't clear enough. Within less than first hour of my gameplay, I've already hit a wall, and am at a complete loss as to what to do. I really dislike how the game just give you no info whatsoever where or how you can get a certain criteria fulfilled, especially if the building related to said criteria isn't unlocked yet. The hint/details that is supposed to help just comes up empty. There are also special building types that you couldn't build or unlock that the game has neglected to point out. There's an objective where you are required to convert a Work House into a 2-star Lawyers. Initially, I thought I haven't unlocked the so-called Work House yet and I tried to guess how I can unlock this Work House via the Business Index. Gave up, ended my stream, and head to Steam to check the discussions... this is where I found the additional FAQ stating that Work House is a building type that cannot be unlocked through the usual means. This FAQ would have been helpful had it been added to the game.This flailing around in the dark while the game withheld crucial gameplay-related information is something that I'm not a fan of tbh. In fact, I think the Business Index should reveal all the building types available just so the player can at least try to "guess" which building might produce the item a criterion requires.Personally, I also feel like the building character that you control seems rather redundant and that the entire game could play out in its 2D format minus the character that seems to just be in the way of the buildings behind it. You can control an invisible floating hand that can swap around buildings (god-mode-style) and the game would work just fine. It's not like you get to interact with the other buildings via the dialogues anyway. Most of the time, you just say "..." just to move the conversation forward. That said, this is merely my first impression of the game and perhaps the importance of the building character you play will become more pronounced later on.+ A unique look at the impact of economic changes of a city on the buildings rather than just the people and jobs.+ Gorgeous artwork. Love the building designs.+ Interesting puzzle-based challenges that involve "building synergies"- Gameplay leaves much to be desired. Withholding important gameplay info from the player is a no-no. - Personally, I think the building-based character that I play in this game seems redundant.- Unlike a typical city-builder, you don't have much freedom in setting up your buildings. Even if you have the bricks to do so, expect lots of limitations when it comes to building stuff. - Personally as well, I think the music started off okay but ended up sounding rather annoying. Maybe it's just me though.I think that Buildings Have Feelings Too! has the potential to be a fun and relaxing city-building-based puzzle game, but it is unfortunately marred by several major (again, IMHO) downsides that turned the game experience from mildly enjoyable to frustrating. The extra FAQ on Steam should definitely be added into the game - in the quest text, in the hints section, in the details or even in an extra bit of tutorial. However, do take note that this is merely a first impression review so take it as you will. Since I know how to get through the part where I got stuck, thanks to the FAQ, I'll see if I can put in a bit more time into the game later and flesh this review out a bit more, but for now, I would not recommend the game at its full-price... Maybe to people who enjoy niche puzzle games at a discount. But of course, if you find the game not to your taste, you could always ask for a refund.

_childDocuments_.review: Video Review:      I Like the charm of the game it has personality and that’s why I really want to give this game full run through to find the best in this game. But I can’t finish it the game-play loop is so tiring and tedious. The graphics and the dialogue you have with each building are nice and oddly strange that you start to sympathies with a high rise. I don’t want to say this game is terrible I'm sure a group of people will love this game, but I feel like it’s a small group. With all its issues most will only play about 2 hours of the game and be bored, but look at the game-play and take my words with a grain of salt if it seems like something you might have fun with and 15.99 is the price right now seems good to you then don’t be shy and pick it up.  Buildings have feelings too! From the developers at Blackstaff games is a city builder/management/ puzzle game where you start the game off seeing your friend the dock yard being straight murdered by a wrecking ball and all the other buildings are in fear this will soon be there fate as well, playing as the halfway hotel you will revamp the areas you travel to, by building new friends and renovating the old to conform to the new era.  Straight off the bat the visuals are what drew me to this game, the cute style with a surprising amount of detail given to each style of building and whatever jobs you select for them.  The mechanics of buildings have feelings are not what you would call simplistic despite the visuals. Each building can acquire specific jobs indicted by the tabs under each building. These jobs range from housing, shops, business, and entertainment, each selection can be upgraded up to 3 stars as long as you have met the buildings requirements to do so, like a family house that gives you friendly locals, also needs friendly locals to be upgraded so you need at least 2 in the vicinity of each other to upgrade, and this is where the game can get complicated and downright difficult. In later stages and later buildings, they require 3-star buildings to level up to 2 stars so you need to perform an upgrading bonanza with a string of buildings and trying to fit them all together like a strange game of Tetris just so you can upgrade one building. Adding to the difficulty and the frustration when you preform the upgrade sometimes the requirements to keep the vanity up, change and can cause the structure to begin to decay and will fail after the gauge fills up, forcing you to make quick changes or try to move the building to save all your progress. This can then lead to a chain effect of other buildings failing because you have move one of their needed resources.  Making this game on occasions annoying and frustrating to play. With this you have the currency bricks, Bricks are what you use to build your friends, in the same aspect if you need to change the job you need to pay bricks to close it, since you demolished the job, this will also encore damage that can be repaired costing bricks. You can earn bricks by completing task and upgrading the buildings, but from what I have heard some people have ran out of bricks, Luckily I did not, but with no restart level system if you are out of bricks you will need to restart the entire game making this essential a rogue like as well. I won’t knock this though just because I find it very difficult to do this and I can only see this happening in the first section of the game where you are limited on what you have, so don’t screw it up on the first stage.     Then some of my biggest issues with this game, one being the controls, keyboard and mouse don’t even try it its clunky and difficult to navigate anything, menus moving buildings, anything. Controller seems to be the intended way that the developers want you to play, but at the same time the menu and, moving buildings still seems a clunky. There are finer controls you can use but none are ever indicated to you or told to you in the beginning, actually a fair amount of the mechanics in this game are absent in the help menu leaving you lost at times and needing to run through trial and error.  Then you have the unlocking system, to unlock new job types you need to max upgrade a specific job, and with all the previous requirements need to do this leads to the chain effect again, that is honestly tedious, boring, and is not a very fun game-play loop, and you need to do this in some areas just so you can get the required building job for a task, making this loop inevitable.

_childDocuments_.review: Here's the thing:  I have no issue with city builders or sim management titles.  Especially if they put an interesting twist to separate themselves from the pack.  That's exactly the case for Buildings Have Feelings Too!  It's quirky approach to buildings creating buildings to coexist with OTHER buildings is certainly a fresh idea.  Unfortunately, confiding it to a 2D plane whale constantly retracing your steps in order to maintain a set of conditions is mentally taxing.  I understand what they were going for here, and I very much applaud it, but I couldn't keep up with want it wanted me to do.  One small move of a building to another part of town or developing a new building between other buildings would sometimes create chaos that would demolish everything I was working toward.  This led to more frustration than fun on my end.  Sim and management buffs need only apply, as the casual appearance will be a bit misleading to any newcomers in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: The controls aren't bad a lot of people I think don't realize you can use the dpad to fine tune placement and selection.  However the premise of building the city from a building you move around is not a great idea.  Imagine playing City Skylines but instead of just being the omnipresent camera you were a civilian and could only see and build in your immediate vicinity.  The game would be better if I was just a camera rather than a character.Having played thirty minutes I can say this isn't a satisfying puzzle game.  The solutions are checklists and because of the control method mentioned above it is time consuming to get to the solution which isn't satisfying to solve as its just a checklist.  Puzzle games live and die by their snappy journey to the solution.  The puzzle should be as quick to solve as finding the solution and no slower.  In this game it is slower and that's a grave sin in the puzzle genre.To elaborate on the checklist the buildings demand X icons around them to be satisfied and each building provides icons.  Its not fundamentally different from a game like Factorio where you put coal in the smelter.  Ultimately the only new ideas presented here are that the buildings are people but that is only in flavor not in practice.  The dialogue is cute but the game mechanics are a slog as described above and don't offer anything new to alleviate the slog.Other games that have the same ideas: Shepherds Crossing.

_childDocuments_.review: and now onto the short review//intro//Hello comrades and thank you for tuning into another less than 10 mins review, today I take a look at Buildings Have Feelings Too! A city management/puzzle game hybrid where you play as a building that goes around managing the neighborhoods to make sure buildings have a fufilling life. But is Buildings Have Feelings Too a game that will make you appreciate older buildings or will this game be no longer be fit for human habitation? Let's find out!//Graphics, Sound & Artstyle//I want to start off by saying that holy hell is this game charming. The opening scene with the old building being demolished, the style of art gives it a very Pixar meets Dreamworks- personifying a random object, in this case being buildings. Sound is good, overall a visually pleasing game.//Gameplay//Gameplay in Buildings have feelings too has a steep learning curve that on the surface seems easy but a lot more complex than it leads on. All buildings cost a certain amount of resouce called brick, and with each star level up on a building you get more of it. You can also acquire some via objectives, in the objectives you will be tasked with creating the best possible arrangement for a specific building or rise certain buildings in an area. All buildings have specific areas of effect, for example the grocers reach only a certain amount so to level it up, the buildings need to be in it's parameter for it to receive and give off its effects. Complicated enough for you? Well repositioning is essential and you will need to change the type of business the building upholds and make repairs using bricks to interchange. Buildings will deteriorate over time and this is where problems arise as you will not be able to start over in the same neighborhood but start the game all over as the amount of bricks received and charged are glitched.   //Price//19,99 USD//How many hours estimated//I hate to say it but until the game is fixed of its glitches, I don't really have an alotted time//Final Thoughts//I wanted to like this game a lot, but i found myself more frustrated than anything. I couldn't go past the second level because I needed my Lawyer building to get to two stars but couldnt because I didn't have enough brick to fix the mold so when I tried to acquire more brick through leveling up more buildings- as you can see here I gained 6 but it didn't reflect that on the counter. The rot mechanic truly is rotten. Buildings rot when their Appeal Goals aren't met- so whenever you level a building up your appeal goals wont be immediately met and will start rotting. Juggling this with the limited space is more frustrating than anythingHopefully I am in the minority and others aren't experiencing this, as I was enjoying a stream of BHFT in the dock area. But as of today release date 4/22/21 Personally, I am not recommending this game.  The game feels too broken if you go into it blind as I went into it and as I'm sure more casual players will go into it as well.Whether these are indeed bugs or I just suck at the game is to be seen, personally I will be checking out other reviews to see if anyone else encountered these bugs as well & will either keep or change my review accordingly- I'm saying do not buy, and perhaps once it gets patched up- a Wait for Sale....

_childDocuments_.review: Overall the writing, even if it uses some tiresome clichès such as the “advanced, forgotten civilization” one and the “you’re the chosen one” type of thing, still manages to involve the player enough between fairly-unique characters, their backstories, and events that aren’t always as plain as one might expect. While the choices you’ll make won’t always have the same impact, it’s good to have a say in the event, instead of a streamlined linear story, which wouldn’t do justice to a RPG after all. Don’t expect a heavy roleplay component dependent on skill-checks and such, though, as you won’t find it here.The worldbuilding is adequate for its setting, however an excessive repetition of biomes, locations and structures can be noticed between dungeons and story areas. While there are some lore pieces in the form of notes or examinable environment objects, this game isn’t lore-heavy at all and doesn’t require a lot of reading - for the better or worse. Some more elaboration on the Ancient civilization would have been interesting and welcome, same for the various sub-cultures and factions encountered.Each location on the world map, revealed in a linear way after specific events came to pass, is a self-contained area in the form of a dungeon filled with enemies, traps, secondary areas, and usually one or more objectives. Your party can explore dungeons freely, and even evade enemy encounters using a rudimentary stealth system – I wouldn’t recommend it, though, as you’ll need as much XP as you can get. Other than the main path, dungeons usually will have secondary areas with color-coded chests, with matching randomized loot and resources. There won’t be any breathtaking secrets or Easter eggs in any dungeon; at most, you’ll find optional puzzles and relatively secluded areas containing extra resources or equipment, but overall everything is laid-out on the global map pretty easily, with a wide exploration radius. The level of interaction with the environment is minimal, with at most you having to find some keys to open locked doors. Still, the ‘unknown factor’ is strong enough to promote exploration without knowing what’s behind the next corner.Combat plays out in real-time, with the option to either slow it down or completely stop it, to better issue orders to your party members. On its own, the flow of battles is rather fast-paced, however it doesn’t really matter given the pause-anytime system. Fights can and will become chaotic soon, especially when involving a dozen or more enemies - you’ll have to frequently micro-manage your party’s positions, skill casts, active abilities and such, because even if there’s an “autonomous” AI mode that can do so for you, it just isn’t good enough.With six active skills and four passives to choose for each hero depending on their class, and the possibility to respec anytime, there’s a lot of flexibility to adjust your party’s focus based on the fight ahead. Facing a boss soon? Swap to more single target abilities for that specific fight. Speaking of bosses, they’re very inconsistent, ranging from extreme difficulty spikes far overpowered for their level, to pushovers you won’t have a problem with even on the hardest setting. While they’re all unique and have multiple, evolving phases, they don’t all feel equally epic.At each Xp-based level up, your characters will gain 3 attribute points (also respec-able at any time) and two abilities and, when unlocked, two specialization points. You can freely invest them to unlock new skills, or more powerful versions of existing ones. Each character can further choose a specialization from level 7, and an additional one later on - but these can’t be respec, so choose carefully. You’ll get the most XP from quests, and a little also from slain enemies, so it’s worth doing all side-missions and companion assignments. All characters are very much gear-dependent, as in DE, that will bestow massive attribute and stat bonuses depending on the type of armor or trinket, and is also further enchantable with passives  for a cost in resources.Speaking of crafting, you’ll be able to acquire blueprints from merchants and loot chests, that you’ll then forge using the materials at your disposal - the better the material quality and rarity levels, the better the stats of the crafted item. To unlock most enchants and crafting options, you’ll have to research them, using points found in dungeons or bought - at a high price and limited quantity - from traders. Merchants can also source powerful items without you having to dungeon raid for them, some may even be Unique in rarity, but they will cost a fortune.
