_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game. I seriously did - since Event Horizon showed that they could do interesting combat scenarios with Tower of Time, but this... it just falls apart after the first hour or so. Between the bland level design, unbalanced combat, uninteresting story and bugginess of the game, it's disappointing.First, the level design - gone are the interesting levels from Tower of Time that have lots of nooks and crannies to explore. They're replaced with square-ish rooms connected by long hallways. Outside of two levels in the game, there aren't any puzzles to solve, no interesting side content, no real reason to explore the full breadth of an area outside of gathering more materials. It also doesn't help that the areas are littered with traps and other hazards (such as explosive barrels) that aren't really positioned in a way that they can be utilized in combat (as most are situated outside of combat arenas). They end up being more of a nuisance more than anything else, as your characters have a very bad tendency to wander into them, despite having an option to prevent such a thing from happening (more on that later). Every area is just wandering from one room to the next to get into yet another combat scenario where you can witness how unbalanced classes are.In Dark Envoy, not all DPS classes are made equal - far, far from it. I had one of the two main characters set up as a Blademaster, which absolutely outpaced every single other DPS character I had by . This was only compounded by the fact that it was  easy to get said character up to 100% critical hit rate and an attack speed that was hilarious in comparison to what other classes could do. It got to the point where I was resolving most combat scenarios in record time - and this included the final boss, who I took out in roughly 30 seconds despite their huge health pool. I did like the fact that you could only bring 5 skills into combat for each character and that you can pretty much respec your point distribution at any time. However, once you really get an idea for what you want each character to do, there really wasn't any incentive to put points into anything else, so for the last handful of levels, I was just randomly distributing them. Stats also felt like they were contributing very little to my party's combat prowess after a while, considering how strong gear can get.The equipment you find in this game is rather boring - granted, I did like how the different types (Elven vs. Imperial, etc.) affected the stats, but the differences tended to be rather minute, so I mainly stuck with Elven gear for its mana regen. The real power came from the additional effects that could roll during item crafting - and the enchantment system. These proved to be the breaking point, since it was easy to craft gear that was far more powerful than you could find, making exploration nigh useless after you get enough materials for a tier to freely craft whatever you need. For instance, it was easier to craft gear that pushed your skill power to ridiculous levels, which made the Elementalist specialty far more powerful than any other mage specialization. Which brings me to my next point... the hazards.Many of the magic spells in this game leave a DoT damage field on the ground after the initial effect - which is normally all fine and dandy. But the major exception to this is if you have the "avoid hazards" pathfinding option on - which doesn't work outside of combat, but becomes a major crutch in combat scenarios. You see, even if it's a damage field that ultimately doesn't hurt your party members (as it's one that's cast by your own party member), your characters will find the longest path around to avoid them, sometimes traveling the entire circumference of an arena to do so. So most of the time, you're having to wrangle your party members into more advantageous positions, except the autonomous setups (that aren't really configurable, by the way) you can set will override your decision almost immediately and they'll be back on their leisurely 5 mile jog while your weaker party members get pummeled. I wouldn't have much problem with all this if it was in service of a better story.You see, this game has a really, really bad habit of making your party the errand boy for the vast majority of the game. Instead of finding interesting ways to piecemeal out plot information, your party, more often than not just goes "Well, let's go see what other errands we can run for these two groups that absolutely hate our guts." I literally screamed after a certain point when, after a major plot point was revealed, instead of going "we should follow up on that", Malakai was all "let's see what other errands we can run!" It's frustrating, since the story did not feel like it was in service of a game as long as this one. It felt more like they sat down and said, "Okay, we're making a 30 hour RPG" first and foremost without thinking of a plot that could fill in that time. Plus the amount of times the game teases you with a plot twist only to go "sorry, but I can't tell you about that right now" is . Gah! The story lets you make a lot of potential choices throughout, but they all carry very little weight, as only a handful have any impact on the plot and who your last party member is. Plus . Now, even with a weak story and weak gameplay, I can still sometimes wrangle some enjoyment out of a game, but the instability of this game brought it low.It became a common occurrence for me to run this with the task manager on my second monitor, as the game had a real bad habit of hard locking and refusing to go underneath any other program I had open. There was no real rhyme or reason to when these hard locks occurred, but they happened frequently enough that I dreaded playing more than 1-2 hours at a time. It also doesn't help that this game takes a couple minutes to initially load, even off of a higher end SSD. Plus it had a bad habit of not properly rendering the skin on characters with full-faced helmets on in scenes where their helmets aren't displayed (like the party selection screen), leaving them to be a solid grey husk. There was also an issue with a character showing up in cutscenes with glowing swords glued to their hands.For this verison being a "Director's Cut", it certainly could have used a bit more time in the oven. I hope that if Event Horizon makes a third RPG, they can take some lessons from this and Tower of Time and make something more in line with ToT than this.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? I would have loved to say that it is, but unfortunately the game is ok and a clear recommendation for fans of the genre, but not great. And I am not talking about the online mode, which I did not try.The first thing is to edit your heroes, Malakai and Kaela. They are brother and sister. Choose how they look like, choose their class - Warrior, Engineer, Adept, Ranger, all with different hitpoints and special skills. Then you can edit their five attributes a bit (power, speed, endurance,...) and select their starting equipment by selecting one of four pre-defined sets. After selecting one of five difficulty settings the main game begins. The game takes place in a fantasy world full of magic. There are elves, humans and two other races, and they are at war. The human Empire, not really good at using magic but having developed some advanced technology, against the other three races, united in the League. Our two heroes are humans, but they do not take part in the war. They are relic hunters, searching for old stuff buried below the earth, or at least hidden in long abandoned places. They start at an old temple on the edge of a desert, far away from the main population centers of the planet.Our characters move in real time. As soon as an enemy spots us, time is slowed down to tactical mode. Time now passes in slow-motion, and we can select an enemy to attack or use our skills and equipment. If we want, we can pause the combat completely (or switch to real-time). Taking cover helps to reduce ranged damage, using the environment (like gun turrets to hack, plants or barrels that explode when you shoot them or quicksand that slows everyone crossing it down) may provide positive effects. As soon as everyone (but us) is dead, you will probably switch to real-time again and collect the loot before moving on. You can only see what is directly around you, and the rest of the (already discovered) map is consumed by a fog of war where you do not see enemies anymore. Works a bit like in an old real-time strategy game. The game was made by the devs responsible for Tower of Time. I was not happy with the way combat was handled in Tower of Time. Here it works better. Just let your heroes fight alone in real-time, or pause and think about the situation and then give commands during slow-otion. Once we are inside the temple, we find it is not really empty. Soldiers from the Empire and the League roam around, and ancient things seem to protect the temple. What will we find here and bring back to our town? There are moral choices during the story - use a violent way or maybe be a bit more diplomatically? I liked that. Find (or buy) enough ressources and you can craft stuff. Research new items or tactics, enchant stuff. Earn enough experience points to level up and learn new skills. Always use the best items you have found and sell the other things. Search the environments for hotspots, talk with everyone (that wants to talk to you). Your party has up to 4 characters, and you can just assign each of them a fighting style (defensive, aggressive, autonomous) and have them fight all by themself. You fly around with your airship and complete the main missions on the map. If you want, you can access random dungeons between the main missions to level up and find some rare loot. Its a classic RPG, although in light mode. Do not expect the complexity of a game like Baldur's Gate 3. Zooming in/out and turning the camera works really good, the environment looks great. You walk through the tunnel-like levels, and unlock waypoints as you find them. They allow you to teleport between them to move around a map fast. A map is drawn and shown on the top screen. The game saves automatically, and you can generate manual saves (nearly) any time (not during combat). Ultrawide works fine, gamepad is supported (but I played with the mouse). The keybindings can be changed.Fantasy steampunk RPG with slow-motion combat. Explore levels, kill enemies, collect loot, level up your heroes - all the usual stuff.

_childDocuments_.review: Dark Envoy is about 70% of a great game. This fantasy steampunk cRPG from second-time developer Event Horizon features buttery smooth real-time combat with a tactical pause option, a robust skill system that rewards experimentation, an engaging and heartfelt fully-voice acted story, and dozens of narrative decisions each with tangible consequences. Alas, Dark Envoy is also 30% of a terrible game, as its lip sync is among the worst I’ve ever encountered, its janky cutscenes consistently break player immersion, rebinding keys barely works if at all, and on multiple occasions the game’s broken reload save function sent me irreversibly back in time 30 minutes or more. And I don’t like that kind of thing. And yet, through this whirlwind of jank, I persisted, in part because I have truly nothing better to do, and in part because this game’s story intrigued me. You are relic hunting siblings Malakai and Kaela (M&K) from the sandy City of Bones (#foreshadowing). After designing your characters and grinding through a handful of early game dungeons, M&K return home to find their desert town a smoldering ruin that’s been caught in the middle of a world war between the steampunky human Empire and The League—a conglomeration of non-huminoid magical races. M&K spend the next ten or so hours working with and against both the Empire and League in order to find out who sacked their town and turned their lives upside down. Along the way, M&K learn that their intertwined destiny in this war and world is much bigger than they ever could’ve imagined. It’s an interesting plot that injects relatable human drama into large-scale geopolitical conflict, and it’s carried by two well-written, likeable leads that complement each other well. M&K’s supporting cast is made up of a nice variety of personalities, each with their own personal side quest, and while the dialogue is a bit stiff, there’s a lot of it and all at least decently voice acted, with some standout performances. Of course, the real reason you’re here is Dark Envoy’s excellent tactical real-time combat system that’s amplified by a nifty audio slowdown distortion effect. The game’s toggleable pause and slowdown feature allows you to take a beat and fully survey the battlefield before linking together devastating skill combos across your four available classes—warrior, ranger, engineer, and adept—each with three elite specializations. I had a great time playing around with each class, and the game lets you reset all skill points at any time, which is a nice touch that encourages experimentation. Too bad the enemies feel more or less identical, and all you'll really do in this game is kill your way through trash mob after trash mob each dungeon, as there’s a disappointing dearth of boss fights with what’s here mostly just amounting to souped-up standard enemies. This said, there is a stealth mechanic, and once unlocking the permacloack ranger skill you can actually just run past mobs, loot all the chests and mine all the nodes right under their noses, and then teleport the rest of your party to safety. Keep this gimmick in mind, as your party won’t regenerate health between fights until reaching one of the depletable healing towers scattered about each level. If you ever do get wiped and have to reload... well, good luck with that! A handful of familiar non-combat features round out the rest of Dark Envoy. There’s crafting, item enhancement and modification, and party-wide buffs you can research, though the per dungeon drops you’ll get are pretty generous to the point I never really felt obligated to craft anything. Finally, a few words on style. Dark Envoy’s visuals are a mixed bag of decent textures, solid particle effects, and super janky animations. The dungeons themselves have nice environmental variety to them, but their simple and straightforward level layouts tend to blur together. While the game’s half-orchestral, half-electric guitar-driven soundtrack works thematically by bridging the game’s fantasy and steampunk aesthetics, the actual music is rather repetitive. And, while I like the game’s tactical pause audio slowdown effect, a number of other sounds here stood out to me as rough or missing entirely. In the end, Dark Envoy is a janky yet endearing cRPG that’s makes up for most of its shortcomings with solid storytelling and satisfying combat. With a 20-hour runtime, I think Dark Envoy presents decent value at $30, so I’m giving it an aggregate MEGA score of 3.14/5 (full scoring breakdown available in video form). Thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so I'm not someone whose been super up to date with this game. But I am a big lover of Isometric RPG's. I've played a bunch of em if not all of em. Plus I've had this game in my sights for a very long time.Now is it what you'd normally get in an isometric RPG? No. So don't come into this expecting Baldur's Gate or Pillars of Eternity. It's more action oriented with less choices and free will. You're pretty much forced on a linear path with very few deviations. In smaller linear maps with very few opportunities for exploration.However, that's not to say it's a bad game. First off the writing is really well done, the plot and the lore is very engaging and interesting. The combat is different, it might not be for some as it's more focused on timing and brute force then strategy. It does have SOME choices in cutscenes but these are pretty much, bribe them or kill them. Destroy this or save this. They're sure to have some consequences later but for now it's an interesting premise.Plus the 30 dollar pricetag for all that's here is a great sign as well. The stability has some serious issues and the gameplay is an acquired taste, but everything else here is doing a really good job. So yes I recommend this game, just don't go into it expecting it to be like those other games. It's its own thing.If you'd like a more in-depth look then please check out the video on my YouTube Channel (link below).Otherwise thanks so much for reading and I hope I managed to help some of you out there spend your money wisely.

_childDocuments_.review: I played Dark Envoy when it released for about 12 hours and thought it was fun, but quite flawed. So I told myself : "I'm going to wait for somes patches to improve on the issues I found".Here we are like 6 months after release, I relaunched it, an it was an even worse mess than the first time. I played coop with a friend and it was 2 very long hours : crash, performance issues (including memory leak thats was supposed to be fixed with the arrival of 1.4), boooooooooooooooooooring cutscenes, tedious itemization and many problems directly related to coop mode, like the game redistributing characters randomly (I was the invited player, but after every last loading screen, the characters were redistributed, and I ended controlling the 2 characters, only one, but not mine, or even none of them), some abilities not working properly, like the turret that was impossible to summon if my character was moving, but draining my mana and cooldown anyway.It was a mess, and that is my message to indie devellopers : stop trying to turn yourselves in AA/AAA-ish studios by implementing cutscenes, coop and other trendy features that require a lot of work, money and time you don't have. You could have saved so much dev time proposing dialogue textboxes with beautifully drawn character portraits, yet you chose to spend your ressources into mediocre cutscenes.You want to know why it was possible in Baldur's Gate 3 ? Because Larian went all in : used an engine they've been develloping, refining and mastering for more than a decade, updated it to ensure that character and NPC models would be nice to look at up close, made animations from motion and performance capture to make them believable and recruited talented comedians for the interpretation. That's why it works.And not having all that expertise, or as much money as Larian is not an issue. You can make pretty amazing games if you know how many ressources you have to spend, and when you choose where to spend them so your game ends being a finished product.My advice to players  now : play Tower of Time.

_childDocuments_.review: Some pros;-Being able to stop and slowdown time during combat keeps things interesting and lets you do the kind of micro-managing typically reserved for turn-based combat. You can even adjust the slow-down percent in the settings.-Crafting and enchanting gear added an enjoyable and value-added layer to beefing up all my character's combat effectiveness. You can quantify how certain gear/skill builds affect your dps in the training room. My max dps was ~2400.-The steampunk vibe and world the developers built is cool-Took about 60 hours to beatSome cons;-After level 10 or so, the good skills get maxed out and leveling up just to put points into skills I knew I wouldnt use was lame-Crashes were frequent-Occasionally had to re-equip items to get the stat bonuses-Inventory would get messed up and hide rows of items, happens after selling loads of gear to a merchant-Some of the choices you are faced with don't appear to have any impact on how the game plays out-Voice acting was fine, but the dialogue is stale

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best isometric RPGs out there. It is really polished, even at this point. The quests so far are fairly straightforward, it reminds me of Dragon Age, but without all the walking. The combats are loads of fun, and require practically no reflexes, as you can pause or slow down to 12% normal time with a click. All of the keys can be remapped, so you can remap them to align with your favorite game.  It is a blend of CRPG and ARGP, and actually does it pretty well. It is heavy on fighting and has a compelling story. The game blends technology and magic elements, similar to Grim Dawn.The graphics are good and the game runs smoothly on my RTX 3070. The game is very stable - I've had one crash in 19 hours of play. The beginning story plays once when the game is first run but does not do so again afterword. Initial loading is less than 2 minutes, and after that new areas load in a matter of seconds (with a NVMe drive).There are four main classes - engineer, warrior, ranger, and mage - which have about 10 skills that you can put varying amounts of points in. Once you get to 7th level - which takes awhile - three paths become available to specialize your PC. All the ability points and skills can be reassigned so far, so you can concentrate on finding the right build for you.There is crafting, but not where you have to go around picking up multiple components. The system is straightforward and doesn't take hours to use, so you can get back to adventuring quickly.Different concepts, such as Research, Crafting, and Enchanting are introduced in successive missions. When hovering over an item description, the character sheet shows you its effect on your stats. It doesn't take into account effects that can randomly happen from your weapon abilities, I don't think - don't quote me on that. In any event the abilities are clear and well-defined. No more having to plot out 20 levels of development at level 1 - it concentrates more on tactical decisions and strategy.The builds, tactics, and equipment you choose all matter. Some battles are much easier with certain set-ups or weapons. I am playing on Normal and the game beat me on multiple occasions before I learned how to deal with the AI's tactics, which are pretty good. Skills have cooldowns and most cost mana, your resource for using them. The battles are themed for the area you are in, fun, and challenging and have a good variety - you are sometimes lulled into a false sense of security with a few easy battles, and then wham! Note that the highest difficulty fights are separated by a border on the map, so you have advance warning to bring your A-game. Another feature I like is once you go past the border, you have to complete the fight. You can still try to run around the enemy and snipe to your heart's content, but no going back and forth. That feature is welcome in my eyes.Of course, there are a few small issues, which I'd imagine stem from budget limitations. One is that your main two characters - a brother and sister - always have the same names and personalities. While you can customize them some, a robust character creation system is not there. You do get to make choices every once in a while, which I am already seeing the consequences of. But if you can't stand the characters, you are unfortunately stuck with them. I am sure having a smaller studio at this point limits what they are realistically able to do. I will say I found the characters both very likable and my son actually LoL'd at some of the dialogue while passing by. If these guys had an Owlcat budget, or were a division of EA, I think you'd be amazed at what they could do.All in all, I'd give this one a 4.5 at its regular price as an isometric dungeon crawler, maybe a 3.5 or 4 if you are trying it with no CRPG or ARPG experience. Of course, it is still being worked on, so you may want to wait for it to be finalized. It does have a lot of content now - I am not sure what parts of the game are being worked on. They have a Discord server and I have found their tech and media support to be very helpful.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Envoy

_childDocuments_.review: Finished it, enjoyed it, cant rate it highly though.Really cool mechanics like "bullet time pause" aka 12% game speed pause which you can toggle back and fourth to full pause. Freeform drawing skills are fantastic and something that really should be seen in more games. Improves on tower of times MOBAesque design. I enjoyed the crafting system, especially the ability to reroll items so you arent lumped with scores of useless items like other games crafting systems.However, the bad side of it is that the story feels like an absolute slog to get through and feels somewhat uninspired. Leveling feels mostly dead after level 12 and like your skill points arent going anywhere useful. Combat does become rather repetitive which was incredibly sad considering the first major boss fight gives you a good feeling of needing to move around with dynamic threats happening all around you, and then prettymuch every single boss fight afterwards felt like "just burn it down as fast as you can". Level design felt significantly weaker than tower of time and didnt really feel inspiring, especially when its often littered with traps that aren't more sophisticated than "lol, if you step on this flower by accident your warrior will go berserk and systematically one shot each member of your party"Glad I played it, again, mostly because I enjoyed tower of time, but you couldn't pay me to replay it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Envoy

_childDocuments_.review: I mainly bought this because I absolutely loved the developers' previous game "Tower of Time". This one here... not so much. It really feels like a step back in so many ways. Tower of Time was for me the perfect combination of exploration, fights and a riddle here and there. It was fun exploring the tower, a huge semi-3D environment, and engage in the fights that happened in separated arenas. Here in Dark Envoy, exploration is... just no fun. The levels feel monotonous and boring, no interesting details to look at, just flat and seemingly being shaped by the same cookie cutter tool. It's neither interesting nor rewarding, you cannot revisit any levels, and you probably would not even want to as there is not anything interesting to find there anyway. Technically the game may be fine, you have more choices regarding your classes, spells, and specializations, but more choices do not necessarily mean more fun, the fixed classes in ToT were completely fine. Having the fights happen in the maps themselves does not make it more interesting than in ToT, rather the opposite. In ToT the arenas were well crafted, and the whole fight felt like a puzzle to be solved (and could be solved with many different character combinations and approaches). Here, I just don't feel it. The fights just feel uninspired, almost no interesting bosses or mechanics - this being the spiritual successor of ToT, it's incomprehensible. Also, the final fight is just a joke and compared to the epicness that the final fight in ToT was just lackluster. Finally, the story. The storytelling in ToT was superb for my taste, I liked the graphical style of the cutscenes, the narration, everything. I don't have any feeling not even of greatness in Dark Envoy. It's just, disappointing. All in all, coming from the same developer, they must have taken a wrong turn somewhere, and it also shows in the sales numbers compared to ToT. I wish they would make a real successor of ToT, not whatever this game here is supposed to be. Makes me quite sad that it turned out that way, as I really had high hopes.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR in case you don't want to watch the video:1. Although there are options between a full pause, and a 'slow-mo' tactical mode, there isn't any true turn based mode (at least not yet).2. Fans of Baldur's Gate 2, the Pillars of Eternity games, and Tower of Time would be familiar with the gameplay here; although there is markedly less customizable options when it comes to party roles, compositions, order of opening spells and moves, and even party formations. There are 3 'stances' you can choose from, but I really wish there were more options besides those.3. Some boss fights felt lacklustre and 'arcade'-ish, with a heavy focus on pausing at the right time, and dodging boss abilities and spells. I wish there was more focus on overcoming strengths and exploiting weaknesses using tactics, strategy, and skill builds as opposed to simply burst damage and movement.4. That said, the map and level design is really great - this made some fights - in particular, defending against waves of mobs that attack you - fun and intense! 5. Graphics and sound design were top notch; it is fully voiced, and although there is some jank when it comes to character movement, it really can be overlooked by the great voice acting and character design.6. There is plenty of exploration to be had, but I wish there were more side quests! The character quests also felt pretty short and sometimes unfulfilling. The hubs were beautifully crafted, but felt empty with a lack of interactions with NPCs and side quests.7. Many dialogue choices are also limited to 'either / or' with no real impact on gameplay aside from losing some gold, or having a slightly different type of quest later on. I wish there was also some form of skill check, or multiple ways to resolve things aside from simply 'talk or fight'.At its core, it has so much potential to be a great game - and I was decently invested into the story to want to see this game become better. However, with its current flaws, it really is a big toss up on whether you should try it or not.Perhaps get it on a sale if you're a RTWP fan - but otherwise, just keep an eye on it for now whilst the devs work on ironing out the flaws, and hopefully, make this into the kind of game it deserves to be!

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of customizable and easy-to-learn RPG experiences, the fantasy steampunk Dark Envoy might be a game for you.Dark Envoy offers a combat system that's both accessible and rewarding. Controlling all four party members feels intuitive, and the ability to set stances allows them to act autonomously, which means you won't need to micromanage every action. They’ll handle basic attacks on their own, leaving you free to focus on strategy and special abilities.The game’s depth shines through in how you can combine various debuffs to amplify damage or create new status effects, adding a layer of complexity that keeps battles engaging. One unique feature of Dark Envoy is the possibility to draw how some spells should be deployed.You can choose to play battles in real-time, slow-motion, or even pause the combat entirely. Taking cover reduces ranged damage and using the environment to your advantage—like hacking gun turrets, shooting explosive barrels or plants, or slowing enemies down with quicksand—can give you an edge in the fight.Character customization is a good feature, with 4 classes and 12 specializations that allow for a wide range of character builds. You have a limited number of passive and active abilities to equip, but game’s flexible respec system lets you experiment freely until you find the perfect build.Your characters rely heavily on their gear, which can give huge boosts to their stats and attributes based on the type of armor or trinket they’re wearing. You can also enchant this gear with passive bonuses.The story might start off slow, but it really picks up as unexpected plot twists emerge, gradually revealing a rich and intriguing narrative. Each location on the world map unlocks in a set order after key events, and each one is like its own dungeon packed with enemies, traps, side areas, and usually one or more objectives to complete. You can explore these dungeons at your own pace, even sneaking past enemies with a basic stealth system. Besides the main path, you'll often find side areas with color-coded chests that contain random loot and resources.During the main campaign you have the option to make impactful story choices such as repair or destroy a powerful machine.This game checks all the boxes for a traditional RPG experience, offering everything from attribute allocation during level-ups to crafting, unique items, and upgradeable abilities. Plus, the quality-of-life features like free respecs, save-anywhere functionality, able to paus in battles and various difficulty options make it convenient to play.Whether you're a seasoned RPG enthusiast or new to the genre, the Guns N’ Sorcery world of Dark Envoy delivers a rich and engaging journey that’s well worth your time. It’s not Baldurs gate 3 perfection but it delivers on what is most important, it’s very fun to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Envoy

_childDocuments_.review: An indie tactical RPG with an original class system, powerbuilding and skillshots galore and different endings based on story choices.It's a fairly typical RPG hero's journey. Chosen ones running errands in a junk heap, hometown gets attacked, mentor figures die, goes to big city... eventually fights God.That said, the world-building is good and choices can lead to different endings. One major decision halfway through also decides between two branches of the main story that play very differently. It's written well and the game's art and environments help to flesh it out.At some points it sounds like the character voices might have been reading from a script but to me voices are a bonus. The replay value for making different choices is nice.The environments look good, whether it's a lush forest or sprawling industrial complex. I daresay the characters look good too from an art perspective. It's so refreshing to see long hair in a modern game.The sounds are functional. This genre can get very hectic because there's so much going on when it's 4 characters vs an army, so I wouldn't expect anything crazy impactful. What's in the game works.There is some jank. As of writing, turn off Screen Space Global Illumination because it causes strange dots to appear on characters. UI is a bit clunky, it's hard to compare gear in the shop screen but the devs are working on it. Character stats sometimes don't update when you increase their attributes, so you have to close and open the window. Also there's some conversation desyncs, occasional repeated lines and so on. Nothing major but don't expect AAA polish right now.I played this exclusively in single player and the Tactical RPG part is done well. There's a lot of room for customization. Different classes, skills, faction gear, enchantments, party composition and more leads to lot of ways to gear and play.Combat in Dark Envoy feels more like a Tower Defense or Survival Strategy game. When you trigger combat, enemies start pouring out from various reinforcement positions. Meanwhile, each class has different ways to control enemy movement, from setting up walls to floor hazards to skillshots. Bosses also create their fair share of hazards. There's a pause button so it puts a big focus on planning, both with character builds and tactics. There's a lot of ways to play, from making a traditional tank/healer/DPS party to a tower defense party to stacking specific enchantments to turn a character into a walking zone of death. Most enemies by themselves are one-note, but the variety comes from their composition and and terrain layout.The classes feel strong in their own way and the gear system encourages creativity. I wanted the Guardian companion to continuously cast protective abilities and use area of effects to draw attention, and I could put casting-focused gear with Mana and Mana Regen on him, as well as a magic staff that builds mana on critical hits to do exactly that. A Ranger can be built both as a passive auto attacker or an active AoE or boss killer ability spammer. The casters can go with either a weapon user build, a magic build, a summoning build, support, heals and more. And there's item crafting and enchantments to give a character that focus.At the time of writing, a patch broke quite a few abilities, but they will be fixed soon so I won't be deducting points for that.(Likely 7.5 or more after more issues are fixed)I have to say the negative reviews have a point. This game is a gem, but still needs a bit more polish. I personally think it should have launched in Early Access instead of full release, but if you can look past the issues it's a fun take on the Tactical RPG genre, and quite ambitious for an indie studio, given the voicing and cutscenes where many other indies use still images with no voices.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a lukewarm recommendation, at best.I purchased the game at a 40% sale when the 1.4 patch came out. I guess I got my money's worth, but I'm mostly frustrated - because the game has interesting systems and mechanics that basically stop mattering half way through the game. It also has stability issues - it locked my PC multiple times requiring a reboot.There are interesting classes and abilities, but since you are limited to how many passive/active abilities you can equip, once you've unlocked and leveled the skills you care about, there is nothing to do from then on. Roughly the last third of my character level ups I only leveled the raw stats (Attributes) and left the Skill points untouched.There is a diversity of gear - armor/weapons/amulets, which you can find, buy or craft. Once you have access to purple (legendary) rarity items, which have a slot for enchantments which enhance it, and got the minimum full kit, all lesser rarity gear becomes an auto-sell, so most of the stuff you find becomes meaningless. I think it was around late chapter 2 that I fully ignored all non-purple (or unique) gear and I probably didn't even equip/craft a single new purple or unique item on my team from mid chapter 3 until the end of the game.There's a research tree where you unlock tactical abilities, stat improvements, and ability to craft and enchant better gear. It was probably around early chapter 3 that I researched all I cared about and didn't look at the research tree from that point on. There are companions which have just a single side-story individual optional mission (for which you have to equip them and do the whole class build selection) which then goes nowhere and whether you did that or not is not even reflected in their ending after game completion. Companions are indistinguishable mechanically - the class/stats define their role, and there are no unique stat/abilities/mechanics to give them some character.In combat, pathfinding was a constant source of frustration. Characters (and the various summoned/constructed units) can not path one through another, the maps almost always have constrained pathways/bridges/chokepoints, and the various units take more space than is visually intuitive. So when playing with constructor/summoner classes, they spend much of combat blocking one another and running half around the map because the small summon you created apparently blocks the whole passage. And there's no way to define a formation - so when initiating combat your melee tank/taunt guy will be running last behind your squishy mage and gunslinger, blocked by them, unless you manually and carefully rearrange them every time.A lot of cool ideas and mechanics, that were interesting to learn and experiment with - and then there was the whole second half of the game. Difficulty was awkward - I had a character downed in combat only once, in the initial chapter where you have only 2 characters, on Normal difficulty. I changed to Hard on Chapter 2, and to Insane from Chapter 3 till the end, but once you have the full party and gear/skills set up, I didn't really notice the difference.

_childDocuments_.review: Updated review.In this game you play as a team of heroes as they vanquish enemies in dungeons using real time / pause / slow down time.This system is interesting, but it just gets boring very quickly becaue fights lack any tactical depth - smash them hard with skills untill they die.Game implements an indepth skill system for every class, allowing some limited dibs into other classes for a cool combos. There is a crafting system with item improvement that can help with finishing a build. There are defined roles - takes, melee damage, range damage, summoners etcThere even exist a working combo system - you place effects on enemies like confusion or weakness and other attacks gets extra benefits on enemies suffering correct statuses.Fights happen in real time and you can slow down time how much you want or use pause to issue commands.However with all that every fight looks almost the same. The only difference is that "patrols" do not get reinforcements. But any stationary group gets some kind of reinforcements.There are also some more challenging side objectives in dungeones to get extra loot.Enemy actions are also telegraphed in a good way, but to have any chance to avoid enemy attacks you need to play on slowdown 80-90%.--Is there a story in this game?Yes there is one. It is not a very interesting or good one, just get from one dungeon to next one.--Are there choices in this game?Yes, you are sometimes asked to make a choice and sometimes there are consequences to it, but nothing major.--Why I do not recommend this game:- bad story- combat is repetetive and boring, it needs to be more interesting that hitting enemeis with skills when they are off cooldown- some enemies are badly designed - the ones who don't die and get +100% damage for 10sec- I think this game should implement less different sub-systems, but connect the ones it has in a better, more compelling way

_childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly good.  The game goes from sort of tactical action RPG, to a Diablo top down ARPG, to a grind fest, and in the final few hours, an RTS.  Nobody likes grinding, but on lower difficulties (I played on normal), the AI control is good enough that if you've done the work of putting a good character together, the game can play itself very successfully.  I eventually only rarely had to step in and take direct control for boss fights, or if a character was stubbornly insisting on standing in an AOE effect.  They use their abilities extremely well, with the one exception being berserk, which causes your melee character to attack whatever is closest to them, which is almost always their allies when it is automatically used.Pretty good story, and I loved the ending I got.  There's about 20 hours of game here, I left it running while I was doing laundry or dishes, so my numbers got pumped up, but I feel like that's great for a budget game.  The character customization is amazing, I love that you get to make a male and female character.  The sister character was impossible to make unattractive, she's probably got the best model in the game, and that's doubly impressive that she's customizable.I don't like RNG loot, this game is very chest heavy.  Almost everything turns into hot garbage when you're able to craft, so unless you like the look of a particular orange (unique), the crafted purples are almost always superior by quite a lot.  Great weapon variety, although it was a little disappointing that there are so many melee weapons, but really only one melee class with three specializations.  I went through the game with a main party of one of each class, and felt like combat was really well balanced, especially since I specialized their damage types across ice, electricity, fire and chaos, but you can build your party how you like.  It doesn't really matter who you bring on quests, if someone has dialogue for a particular setting, they just show up, so it's okay to focus on gear for two party members and let everyone else wear the common/uncommon/rare trash you get from the RNG chests.I'm really impressed with Dark Envoy.  I hope there's more stories and games from this franchise in the future.  There's room for growth here, certainly, but I certainly recommend this game as is on its own.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Envoy

_childDocuments_.review: Dark Envoy is a tactical 4 character team-based RPG with a pause. Combat reminds you a bit of old Baldur's Gate 1-2 or Neverwinter Nights titles. Although it doesn't use any D&D systems, it feels qite similar: you enter combat, game pauses, and you decide what course of action your party will take.The story is simple journey of a brother and sister(both of which are customizable characters when you start your playthrough). While maybe story itself is not as unique as it could be, what makes it good is the setting - a scavenger's life in inhospitable world with every hardship it brings. Gladly our protagonists have family bonds to help them surviveWhile I haven't finised the story yet, I'm sure it will be very interesting to follow Kaela and Malakai on their path.Combat is the best part of the game, if you ever wanted to try a tactical party-based RPG, look no further. We have 4 classes to choose from, with 3 specializations for all of them. Gear is not locked between classes, so amount of builds is surpisingly big.Electrical melee mage? Sure. Armored warrior with a bow? Yep. Summoning robots and turrets? That's right! Stealth poison rogue? Sounds fun (until the enemy is immune to poison...)One of the best features is that you can swap skills and stat points on the fly. Found a unique aoe gauss cannon and not sure how your mage is supposed to use it? Swap his stats into crit and attack speed for free at any moment and watch him melting those pesky spiders with a cannon, completely forgetting he can use chain lightning as wellI can't say I'm not biased, I really love Tower of Time, their previous game, and just can't not recommend this one. But game has its flaws.Graphics are outdated. Even by my standards, I have quite old PC and I barely got Baldurs Gate 3 playing on lowest settings. But even I notice clunky animations or stiff facial animations. I don't really care about it, but I know a lot of people do.I wish devs decided to do more stylistic graphics, like, for example, Pathfinder did. Even though their animations and graphics are not good, a more cartoonish style makes game look much prettierWhile not many, but bugs are there. Team is working on fixing, but you can still notice problems from time to time. At the moment I'm writing this, most annoying bug for me is that one of the spells doesn't auto-cast as it should, but I know it's gonna be adressed in the next patch.UI has some issues, at least for me, I can notice some glitches here or there. For example, game keeps comparison screen for the ring I already removed, so it should not be there any more. I'm sure it will be fixed, but can't say it's not annoying._For me, as I sit here a big fan of the genre, it's a 8/10, and when they fix the bugs and glitches, it will be 8.5/10, removing a point for graphics and half of a point for not having a romancable party members.But I'm very biased. I look through the rose-tinted glasses and understand the game is far from perfect. But if you are looking for a tactical RPG with combat as your priority, you will not be disappointed
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Envoy

_childDocuments_.review: After years of games like Divinity, Baldur's Gate, X-Com, Pathfinder, Wasteland, etc., it's really nice to return to a "real-time with pause (or at least slow-mo)" combat system (like in BG1/2 or Neverwinter Nights), along with having party AI that can take care of basic character actions for you. The combat is refreshingly tactical (as opposed to mostly build and stats-based), with real-time positioning and repositioning playing a big role. They borrow some MMO mechanics like having boss attack indicators for you to dodge, and add some fun novelties like being able to "draw" your AoE spells along a path with your mouse, instead of being limited to just a simple radius or cone.I played with a warrior (tank/paladin) and engineer (pet class with turret), and it was a blast of a duo to start with, reminding me of old-school MMOs and the "holy triad". Some battles involved swarms of weak enemies that the AoE spells (and well-placed explosive barrels) easily took care of, while boss battles involved tactical positioning, keeping the support character out of harm's way and constantly taunting, etc.Overall, I really enjoyed the combat and wish I could see more of it. I'm the kind of player that mostly skips the story in these games, but even then, the overall pacing felt pretty slow. After a couple hours of play, I'm still only level 3 or 4, despite having gone through several quests and dungeons, and my character builds are barely developing. Most of the time I'm just waiting for cooldowns to refresh, when really I wish I could be juggling more characters or skills -- it's too much waiting around in the first few hours.After learning the basic game, I was excited to join a multiplayer game and experience more action. Sadly, there doesn't seem to be a matchmaking system or public lobbies, just a room code system to join :( For those of us without steady gaming friends, I guess that just means more soloing. Too bad.Still, it's a thumbs up for me just for bringing something refreshingly new to a pretty saturated genre. I'm excited to keep playing, but I do wish things moved a bit faster. The game is also slow outside of combat, with slow character walk speeds, many world transitions between zones (like a Fallout-style world map that doesn't really add anything but more loading screens), and unnecessary dialogue (that you can skip, but then you're presented with choices that have no context). Maybe that's just my preference for faster-paced ARPGs over traditional CRPGs coming out, but if this is attempting to be a hybrid game spanning genres, I hope the pacing can be sped up a bit -- maybe even a "skip tutorial"-like option that fast-tracks you into a later chapter, skipping the beginning parts and starting you out with a more developed character and skill points? Right now the leveling is too slow, your skill points are shared between active and passive abilities, and too many of the fun active abilities are gated behind skill spend requirements -- meaning you don't see much actual character development in these first few levels. Eventually the characters can specialize into advanced classes, but those seem so far away right now =/ I know I'm impatient, buuuut... there's a lot of RPGs out there right now, and the first few hours are when they make the biggest impression.Other than the pacing complaint, a minor gripe: The game could use more in-game tooltips when you hover over UI elements or character stats. It wasn't clear to me what the green and gray bars were (HP and armor, I think? How do you recharge armor? No idea.), or what the different kinds of status effects and resistances were  (What does "Vulnerable 12%" mean?). Mostly they were tiny icons and numbers without a clear enough explanation. I wish there was a way to "hold" a tooltip in place and get more details on particular keywords in there (in Baldur's Gate, this is where you hold down "T" to persist a tooltip and read more details for certain keywords in it).Still, for a small indie game, I love that they are experimenting with something different and fun!
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Envoy

_childDocuments_.review: It could have been a good game, but a lot of things are flawed and/or buggy:* Loot becomes meaningless in the last 30% of the game: I had crafted better equipment than you could find at the start of act 3, had no reason to loot anything anymore* Likewise for XP: You hit max level halfway through act3, but run out of skills to invest in somewhere in act2* Dialog/plot/characters are not consistently written: It often feels like I missed some crucial plot development since the last cutscene/dialog* Repetetive level design* Lots of buggy skills/enchants, e.g. Inner Void resets after every fight, instead of the end of the dungeon, some skills get worse when leveled up or stay the same, a few crashes, etcI wanted to like this game, but I had to force myself to finish it. It clearly needed about one more year of polish.I would advise to play Tower of Time instead, a game that is better than this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Envoy

_childDocuments_.review: If you are unsure about this game, go download the demo. The demo is surprisingly long. I ended up buying the game before finishing the demo.Story wise, well the story is there to move things along. It does give you decision points to determine your morality. Things like kill the bandits or talk them out of it. Other than that, there are no dialog choices. Cut scenes and conversations are just there for you to watch. You control siblings Malakai and Kaela in a world torn by war between two factions. You can customize their looks to an extent and pick their base class. You'll then recruit companions along the way as you uncover whatever conspiracy is behind the war.There are 4 base classes: warrior, ranger, adept, and engineer. Each class has 3 specializations. You pick one specialization at level 7 and another at lvl 14, which reminds me Dragon Age again since specializations unlock at 7 and 14 there as well. Leveling up gives you 2 skills points for your base class and 2 skill points for your specialization.  Which means you'll eventually learn way more skills than you can equip. You might think, "okay, equip different skills for different situations". But you can freely reallocate your skill points at any time. So all those extra skill points do is save you a few clicks from reallocating skill points.The warrior is the tank and melee dps class. Ranger is obviously the ranged dps class and it can either specialize in low speed high damage, or high speed low damage. Adept is a burst damage caster class with a healer specialization (but no heals outside of that specialization). Engineer is a mix between ranged dps and caster with lots of CC and utility skills.Combat reminds me of Dragon Age Origins. Managing mana and cool downs as you decide between bursting a high priority target or using CC skills. You also have to manage positioning as you avoid AoEs. Hiding behind boxes and stuff gives you cover. There are plenty of destructible exploding barrels and traps everywhere on the map. The annoying repetitive part is enemies spawn in waves similar to Dragon Age 2. At least spawn points are marked on the mini map so you can kinda plan for it.The game play loop can get repetitive. You have a town hub that you return to in between quests (missions). When you set off on a quest, you go to some map where you proceed to clear all the enemies and interact with whatever quest objective you have. Go back to town, rinse and repeat. Sometimes I'm in the mood to just kill stuff, so this loop is fine by me.The oddest thing is the design decision to have randomized loot and crafting with diablo style random equipment modifiers. It would have been fine if you could grind maps over and over again to farm crafting mats. But you can't. Your party's power level can wildly vary depending on gear RNG.Overall, for its price point, I'm not expecting for anything to be too in-depth. I've been looking for a party-based rpg with a class system and this fits the bill.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game when if first came out and I had high hopes for it. A core reason why I got it was the now-stripped co-op play. I bought 4 copies of this waste of data. But I will give you a full Pro/Con breakdown below and you can judge for yourself.PROS-The magitech setting is interesting and the thematic melding of magic and steampunk is clean and well-made.-The diametrically opposed sides with no clear good guys really does make the choices of the game carry weight no matter what you choose.-The reduced combat time function does make it a lot easier to manage the full party effectively.CONS-When the game had co-op it was a flaming hot mess that fostered only toxicity and animosity between me and my friends because only the host of the game could control things like character equipment.-The lists of abilities for each class and subclass were paltry. Only having a choice of nine abilities or so in total made me feel more than a little railroaded into certain choices.-The characters you interacted with or gained in your party all came across as flat and simplistic. Maybe its just that I'm an author who can spend hours refining a single character into someone with depth, but the entire caste came across as bland and boring with simple motives and only one or two emotional states.-ALL equipment I used in the game always seemed to have some form or hazardous drawback that threw the balancing way off course. Some weapons had a reasonable attack speed but dealt pitiful damage that could not be compensated for with enough hits. Other weapons could deal reasonable damage, but the windup seemed to take ages and made each attack with it feel like a gamble with no reasonable pay off.-BAD CONTROLS!!!! The key bindings CANT be changed and are tied to keys that make almost no sense. The controller layout is just as bad if not worse. And I find it to be a very wasteful choice to not have this game Steam Deck compatible. If it were playable on the portable and the bindings could be changed, then it might be at least partly redeemed.

It’s a typical euro jank RPG that surprises you with how the consequences of your choices hits you, at times harder than most triple A RPGs out there. I cannot help but give it a thumbs up at the lack of a neutral choice. It is one of those 6-6,5/10 games that is all about personal preferences rather than it being outright bad or good. _childDocuments_.name: Dark Envoy

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I really enjoyed this one. It ended up being longer than I expected and I am looking forward to their next game whenever that may be. The character art and environments are great. The combat was a lot of fun with great visuals and did a great job with the real-time with slowdown/pause. I will probably play through it again on a higher difficulty setting after some more updates. I did not encounter any crashes or blocking issues. For the size of the game, there were relatively few bugs/issues. I did report a handful of minor bugs to the developers on their discord and with the in-game reporting tool and they seemed very responsive and looking to continue making improvements to the game. I played through after the 1.4 patch and from what they have said will be in the 1.5 patch, it looks like the game is just going to keep getting better. I think the story was good overall. The level designs while visually great, many of them were just trash packs of enemies  spread around. Plenty for a good dungeon stomp but sometimes it felt like filler without a challenge instead of helpful to the story. I really enjoyed the levels that had more interactive elements, objectives and story points. I ended up skipping over side dungeons after about level 11 or so unless there was a specific unique reward inside that I wanted as they were just trash packs of enemies without any story. Maybe in the future they could add a selection of random mini-stories to the side missions and they would feel more enjoyable. Thanks for the great adventure!

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of writing this (April 24th, 2024) I'm writing to let you know this game DOES have multiplayer officially and this review will mostly be about it and my experiences. To start off, I want to say to take caution with it.Now it's nothing like a virus or anything serious, but be prepared because the game desyncs you and your co-op partner a lot. As the person who joined, I often times found my characters fighting but having their damage take effect later on - abilities I would cast would sometimes be eaten up (Go on cooldown & consume mana with no effect)According to my bud though, some of those did go through on his end so in the end it's disorientating whenever something will actually work or notNOW! The big thing, so pay attention: This game was not designed for multiplayer and I knew that. This game has worked extremely well solo play, but if you want a friend to join you on this, expect a good handful of problems for the "Player 2"

_childDocuments_.review: Dark Envoy is a tactical RPG game.Is a game that does everything right, all the rpgs should be like this one.The story is very interesting and compelling, I heard it has connection with the previous game of the developer (event horizon) called "tower of time" but for me isn't a issue at all; You start in a city where the main characters are 2 brothers which will be forced go outsite and discover the mysteries of the war between 2 factions while you taking hard choices which result in diferent paths on your journey. In my case, my plan is sabotage this war because nobody deserve to win, both factions are just malevolent XD The gameplay is solid with a lot of strategy and tactical moves and I love they took the time for create each item, when you equip 1 item it shows that item on the character, not a premade item that you see on all the run as happen with most of the last rpgs I saw.The game for me looks like a triple AAA rpg with the half of that price and getting more fun, so worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: a very solid tactical rpgas a baseline you gotta keep the pricing in mind, it's very cheapthere's a fully voiced presentation, but don't expect some the Witcher 3 like production qualitythe englisch VO is hit'n miss, it often feels awekward even when it comes to animation during the cutscenes (ingame engine), kinda like eurotrash (witch is not ment as an attack, i love Prihana Bytes and co.)the OST is pretty good and the soundeffects are also high qualitythe grafic however is subpar, it doesn't look "bad" per se, there's a distinct style to architecture and characters, but quality wise this ain't standout in any way shape or form, yet it needs ressources like there's no tomorrow. this game makes my rig work more than Lords of the Fallen (on high to ultra settings) does, yet looks 5 generations worse.it runs well enough, but there's no argument to be made for the "power" it needs.the rpg elements are actualy pretty good. there's kinda randomized gear, there's a lot of stats, skills and classes to tinker around with. it's not the most complex mechanics sandbox, but looking at the price: it's quite impressive.combat on it's face value is also quit enjoyable; it's realtime with pause (or slowmo, optional), which is already the right approach. rpg mechanics and actual tactical combat work very well together, you got positioning, active and passive skills, etc. . it's quite entertaining.but there are glaring issue:the map is mission based. you pick the next mission on an overworld map. there are randomized "side mission areas" (basicaly just ressource and combat encounters), but you are limited to 1 during each main plot mission. probably they didn't want you to grind out these mission, but frankly this just feels bad. ever since the rize of roguelikes and soulslike people forgot that some of the greatest rpgs never used these balance and scaling tactics. you had the choice. do i want to grind more to make the game easier or do i want more challange and grind less.it just feels very restrictive to have this side-area limitation in an already very onrails game. it would do a lot to make the game feel more open and sanboxish if they would just allow you to as many side-areas as you want.then there's simple things. while you can limit or increase the number of autosaves, the quick save for whatever reason always creates a new file. color me surpised when i wanted to do a hard save and saw 50 quicksaves. that's just sad. quick save and the F5 are stables of pc-gaming and normaly there's a quicksave just beeing overwritten (with 1 to 2 files at most).there's a lot of "fluff" missing. i get that this is a budget question. but there's also a very limited, very tiny designed, hub-structure and there's barely any live in em. you can't even have these pointless rpg-conversations with random npcs. you can barely even "click" something to get some sort of feedback...it's honestly hard to explain, but everything past the "dungeons" could just aswell be 1 simpel static screen.and one of the "worst" offenders is how encounters are designed. pretty much in every fight there's a reinforcement system (represented also by a bar in the U.I.), which means you start a fight and enemies just keep on coming from random directions. this system just feels weird. but again looking at the price it's a very solid, almost great, small little tactical rpg.what needs to be fixed is the way quicksaves work (1 file, just beeing overwritten) and i'd strongly recommend letting players do howmany ever side-areas/fights they want. this would not just help in making the game feel more "open", but also grant the game more content...with a rather simple measure mind you.

_childDocuments_.review: Dark Envoy is a captivating RPG-adventure that seamlessly blends elements of technology and magic in a conflict-torn world of Guns N’ Sorcery. The game presents a compelling narrative, tactical real-time combat, and an enticing online co-op mode that promises a immersive gaming experience.The game introduces you to a world where the forces of Technology and Magic collide, sparking a conflict that can only have one victor. You take on the role of a party of relic hunters, and your journey unfolds in a gripping tale of destiny. Dark Envoy's narrative is rich and engaging, and the conflict-torn world you explore is filled with depth and intrigue. The story is well-paced and keeps you invested in the characters and their struggles.Dark Envoy's gameplay is where it truly shines. The tactical real-time combat system is both challenging and rewarding. You have the freedom to approach battles in various ways, and the game continually presents fresh and exciting challenges, ensuring that combat never becomes monotonous or repetitive. The inclusion of five different difficulty options caters to a wide range of players, with the highest setting demanding true mastery of the combat system.One of Dark Envoy's standout features is its extensive roster of characters and classes. There are four core classes and an impressive twelve distinct specializations, each offering a unique playstyle. This diversity ensures that no two characters feel the same, making character progression and party composition a delight. The class and specialization system adds depth and strategy to the game.Dark Envoy offers meaningful choices that influence the story and its conclusion. Bugs.. There were many bugs on the build i was playing on. The team was very responsive when i reported these bugs and got to see all of them or most fixed after a day or two. I kinda had fun theory-crafting how can i overcome these bugs, but it still was pretty frustrating.Conclusion:Dark Envoy is a remarkable RPG-adventure that successfully combines technology and magic in a conflict-ridden world, offering engaging storytelling, deep gameplay, and the joy of cooperative play. It might not be a flawless masterpiece, but it's an experience well worth your time if you're a fan of the genre. With a captivating world and dynamic combat system, Dark Envoy stands as an excellent addition to the RPG-adventure genre.Check out my full game walkthrough!:

_childDocuments_.review: Dark Envoy is a pretty cool kind of game. It's narrative is rough to start with a whole lot of backstory just tossed at you, but I was willing to look past that.Originally I bought it at full price and refunded it due to this awful artifacting (apparently called 'dithering') created by shadows and hair, which you can view in these screenshots here:I picked it up again on sale because the premise seemed cool and the gameplay looked fun, and to its credit, it is! But in the last 2.5 hours,  I've had the game lock up and hard crash 3 times. That's more than once an hour; I'm not underspecced either, as i'm running a 4080 with 32 GB of RAM and a Ryzen 9 3950X. And to add icing on the cake, that dithering effect is all over the game, not just around the hair and the hair that you see in my screenshots above are about as good as it ever looks. I attempted using TAA to smooth it out, but that did nothing. I could overlook the ugly dithering effects if i'm honest, but crashing every other mission so hard that the game can't even let unity crash manager pop up in front of it is something I haven't experienced in an indie game in years and is the reason I can't recommend it. It isn't even crashing due to large numbers of effects on screen; I had it crash while opening an inventory once and twice when entering a side quest area.Edit: The graphical issue isn't just in character creation. It's visible elsewhere as well and in my experience it's worse there. I've had cutscenes where shadows artifact across Kaela's chest in a pixelated mess. This wouldnt be an issue if not for the zoomed in cutscenes, but again, this problem is nothing compared to the crashes. I had two more yesterday when I tried to play again, as I recall, both occurred as I approached an enemy sightline.

_childDocuments_.review: After Tower of Time, Dark Envoy is the second game of indie studio Event Horizon and for the most part - more on that later - it is improving on the formula of the action oriented cRPG with real time with pause (or slow motion) combat. The 2 stories are connected but can be played independently: the events take place in a universe mixing magic and technology, which somehow I find has some vibes of Arcanum: of steamworks and magick obscura.I'd recommend the game if you like RPGs and want to try something different and more dynamic than the usual turn by turn combat system. The story is quite good but I wouldn't recommend the game solely on that: I think the highlight is the combat system, the way you can experiment with the different classes and builds, min/max the attributes and tinker with the crafting system. There is no penalty or grind required for respec attributes or changing skills, so it is really encouraging experiments. Only the crafting requires materials which are in limited quantities that you can loot or buy.However,  you may want to wait for a few patches: the developers are listening to the feedback and already have fixed some bugs, but there are still some rough edges as of 2 weeks after launch. I didn't experience any game breaking bugs and I managed to finish the game and complete every side quests, but there are some annoyances and glitches here and there. So the game needs a bit more polish, and some rebalancing.Finally, I said the game improves for the most part on Tower of Time, but I have mixed feelings about 2 things that I don't see as an improvement:- in ToT there was a clear sense of progression by going further in the the tower levels, here the game feels scattered because of the side missions and the extra random dungeons. It feels more like running errands from cities to some random points on the map, back and forth and not really progressing towards the finale- the addition of voiceovers is welcome but the mocap and the animation sequences arerather awkward since they are out of sync with the voice. Obviously this kind of things cost a lot and require a big team, so I absolutely don't expect AAA studio level of animation and I actually would  have preferred something more static, like adventure games do. Overall the game is good and I'll most probably come back to it later to try some other builds and combinations, after a few patches have come through.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent game that improved in some areas over Tower of Time. You can still put points into specialization skills, but you really don't need to. Also, any gear you find will be on par with or worse than what you already have. Crafting doesn't help because the items you craft aren't as powerful as what you already have.Despite the drawbacks, I look forward to the next game from Event Horizon. Hopefully it will offer meaningful progression throughout the game, rather than just for the first half.

_childDocuments_.review: Dark Envoy is the second game made by the polish company Event Horizon; following in the footsteps of Tower of Time. I enjoyed Tower of Time and thought to give Dark Envoy a try. I write this review having finished the game solo recently at about 34 hours; though this time might be greatly extended if I was playing on a higher difficulty (foreshadowing). Overall, I think this could be a fun time sink for folks who enjoy RTS hero style gameplay similar, though clunkier, to what you might find in something like like League of Legends, Dawn of War 2, Heroes of the Storm, and etc. It might also be enjoyable if you like a healthy mix of magic and technology in your fiction and intriguing morale choices (sorta). The game is quite large considering the team that made it, well voice acted, and rarely fatally buggy. The respec system is wonderful and the only flaw is that you cannot respec your specializations that you unlock for each class at levels 7 and 14 from the menu mid dungeon. This game is quite good and fun for what it is. However, it is also exceedingly flawed; and so I wanted to get my praise and my general recommendation out of the way before I sunk my teeth into the problems.    I had an indepth analysis going but I hit the review character limit so I'll go over things quickly. The combat is clunky in comparison to most mobas so you can't kite enemies as a ranged attacker without using abilities, abilities have too high mana costs or cooldowns to use them consistently to kite anyway, the wounding system lasting the entire mission sucks and turns off specific styles of play, aggro management is the most important part of the entire game and once you've solved that there isn't a challenge anymore, the loot system has problems, the difficulty selector just makes enemies harder to kill and you easier to kill and if I'd kept it high I'd have gone insane from how slow I'd have needed to play, I'm pretty sure shops only refresh whenever you level up which is wild considering how little money the game gives you to even shop in the first place and how spending money on anything other than blueprints, enchantments, and tier 3 equipment/ore means you've made a mistake, you can't create formations for your team to use when walking so you'll just have to walk them directly into hazards unless you stop and pilot each of them individually around it, the autonomous AI isn't good at using its abilities on the correct target and sometimes forgets that its in a fight entirely or pathfinds your character to the other end of the map, the bosses are universally boring, the lack of speed selector means that you are either playing real time/realtime with pause/12% speed - it could have used a 50/75% speed option, the game has teleporters scattered around which is really nice because walking across these maps is incredibly tedious - but instead of making them smaller or more interesting they decided to give you these teleporters with zero animation to them, and lastly none of the morale choices are super impactful because the story is on some pretty hefty rails. I personally enjoyed thinking about the morale choices a lot more than actually making them and seeing the impact.This game is fine, its even fun. Despite my complaints I had a good time, heck its because I had a good time that I care enough to write my complaints out. There were many steps forward form Tower of Time, and a few steps back. This game tells a decent story, it lets you spend some time in a fantasy world controlling some heroes as they try to solve the mysteries about their world, and its story leads back to Tower of Time which is also a fun but flawed game. If you pick this up for 30 USD you'll get about a dollar per hour of entertainment, if you can pick it up cheaper then you're really doing well with your $$$.I honestly hope to see another game in this series. These aren't for everyone and they have some serious flaws, but I've enjoyed my time spent with both enough to hope to see a sequel in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Envoy

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game would have garnered a stronger reaction if it didn't launch in the same year as BGIII and Rogue Trader. I really enjoyed Tower of Time so I was willing to give the publisher the benefit of the doubt. This is a casually fun game. I'm not going to say it has a thrilling narrative or intense gameplay, but it's modestly entertaining. I'm making slow progress along the storyline. The optional dungeons feel WAY too optional, but the greedy loot-goblin in me can't pass them up. So they are 'filler' material for the most part. Tons of party flexibility, with four primary classes and three sub-classes per primary. The two protagonists and starting members are a brother and sister team, which I always find a refreshing choice in gameplay. Overall, reasonably entertaining game that i'm enjoying playing through. But, it doesn't have the gripping, 'oh crap how is it 4 AM' feel that the other big RPGs this year provoked in me.
_childDocuments_.name: Dark Envoy

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this, but with one big qualifier: compared to Tower of Time, while the combat and character build options are improved, Dark Envoy is worse in every other way. The music is similar, but not as memorable. The move from 2.5D to to full 3D was apparently not a worthwhile use of a small studio's assets. The environments are less grand and impressive that ToT's. The voice acting and writing are all over the place. And there are a lot of bugs and things that feel half-baked and rushed out.That said, I think Tower of Time punched way above its weight class. Dark Envoy doesn't, but it's still an enjoyable game.

Still a solid game that makes me want to try it again at some point and maybe try to impose some artificial difficulty by not using gunslingers with two guns.

_childDocuments_.review: Two things - combat is a bit floating. Movements should be changed based on position and two, more physics applied when certain abilities are used with obvious restrictions, but set on when certain abilities are used and maybe a posture gauge of some kind. This combat just feels way too "floaty." Make it less fast and more tactical. The movement is all over the place. Add more protection from shields when the pullets/spells/sword attacks are coming from that direction. Basic logic for more immersion.Tower of Time had the mystery carrying it and cool companions when combat would usually get stale. They took a fair amount of mystery our with the intro. DON'T DO THAT ♥♥♥♥!Overall, worth it on sale or if you're playing for the story, but I think a scaled down version of the world with "impactful" gameplay would've been better. Sounds, effects were also lacking that punch that gives the player that feeling of satisfaction.Also, less flat battlegrounds. Some "verticality" would be nice. Flanking damage needed to feel more immersive, as well. Less, but stronger foes would be better than swarms of foes that are spunges, but everyone is weak. It's not tactical. It's a slug fest at times.Pros: animations are mostly good to very good in some places. Graphics are above what I expected (not great). The character models are actually good. Maybe a little better. The real-time with pause/slow motion is great, the classes are fun, and the world is fun/unique. Worth a play through.I'll recommend, but on sale, only.
