_childDocuments_.review: I liked a lot Tower of Time, so I might be a little biased in favor of this game. I am playing solo (at normal difficulty), so this review completely ignores co-op. For people who don't know it: this is not a CRPG, even if it includes some RPG elements like character progression. It is a tactical combat game in a heroic-fantasy world.Pros:- Funny RTWP combat; this is the core of the game.- Good visuals- Ok story. Characters are likeable.- Optional (small) dungeons- Friendly devs, that obviously read forums and care for their users.Cons:- Very linear story- Bad pathfinding: characters often become stuck while there is an obvious path. I even had the case once where all fours characters became stuck while trying to go through  the same narrow path. They ended creating a nice circle arc, every character being stuck at the same distance from the bottleneck. I had to manually move them to unblock the situation. I strongly suggest to allow characters to at least partially overlap when moving.- Unpleasant loud noise when pausing/slowing down time during fights. I think it is a recent addition. This noise is directly and ONLY controlled my the master sound setting, which makes it difficult to get rid of or at least to attenuate it. Lowering the master sound setting while increasing all secondary ones somewhat mitigates the issue but is still not a satisfying solution.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh man, this is a good game.I was on the fence about buying this after it popped up in my Recommendations queue. I noticed that these folks were associated with Tower of Time and that sold me - and I'm so glad it did.The game system is real time with slowdown, not pause. This means that there's always pressure to keep moving and acting. You're never exactly "safe". I find this kind of aggressive pressure a lot of fun - I'm not just sitting back and watching my people do their thing, although that's always an option. If the combat doesn't grab you immediately, it likely won't be something you enjoy - it doesn't change appreciatively throughout the game. I will say this is a bit of a letdown; I would prefer twice the skills and more customization options. Hopefully this game will get some DLC or mod support for same.Yes, the graphics are a little dated and the voice acting is... uneven at best. It's still quite fun to play.Hello this is me from the future, admitting I was wrong. It's not good. The combat is the same every time and it is way too long for what it is. Your characters stay put like my mother-in-law at the buffet, refusing to move. So with four characters, you need to constantly micro-manage every inch of movement. Did you tell a character to move between two traps? No worries, she'll find a way to walk on one of them!The game could be excellent with some FF12-style basic "scripting". As is, it's... mediocre and boring. I'm sorry if anyone bought this based on a positive review I wrote.

_childDocuments_.review: After 30 years or so of CRPGs, I can tell this is easily among the more fun ones--Dark Envoy's combat is a near perfect realization of real-time strategic command. We've seen so many turned-based titles come out in the CRPG world over the last several years, it's refreshing to see a different combat system implemented so well.  Bonus: battles don't take 20 minutes! Instead it's moment to moment excitement clearing a "dungeon" in 20 minutes! I've played all the big CRPGs, including the more recent BG3, Pathfinder franchise, and Pillars of Eternity (all of which I love), and the combat system in Dark Envoy competes with or betters those heavy weights. There's a campy feel to the story and characters in Dark Envoy. It isn't the epic scope of Wrath of the Righteous or the dark tone of Baldur's Gate, but the camp is fun and engaging (say, a Batman the Brave and the Bold as against Nolan's Batman triology). I wanted to write this review after a few hours of play because I suspect this game will either be a sleeper hit in the CRPG community or a hidden gem. I've seen reference to some "jank", which annoys me. It doesn't take away from the overall experience. It's like the people who get excited when they find a typo in the New York Times. It certainly doesn't detract from the completed product--and more than that, misses the point entirely. Give Dark Envoy a go! In the ways it distinguishes itself from other CRPGs, it shines. And it's a fun ride to boot.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely a fun game overall. Suffers from some balance issues that can make the game on the easier side if you use the stronger builds. I will say Tower of Time story was something special, but this one has been good as well. I still have a long ways to go though and there's a lot about story branches etc. (I imagine other choices result in other stories) that I'm not certain about. There's also some jankiness to the UI but that's not a big deal in my opinion. Overall I'd give it a 7.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Dark Envoy is an isometric RPG or CRPG with a real time with pause/slow time combat system.Which is pretty good all things considered. It has a fairly standard RPG class system, with a few unique choices and a specialization system for your class once reaching a certain level. Making it a decently fleshed out system, for a double A release like this. The level up system also allows you at any point to completely reset your skills and attribute points for free. This makes experimenting with different builds and class pairs fairly easy and pretty fun to do. This also reduces the fear of choosing a skill that may not exactly work with the build you're attempting to achieve. If this problem arises, you can simply reset and choose a different option. I did not play on the higher difficulties as my play time is a little low. But, I would also surmise that this would allow you to tailor your builds to specific fights in the event that your standard build just wasn’t cutting it. I would say that the combat system is overall engaging and fun to play. Which is a good thing, because the big negative of this game is the jank animation.Which really hurts the overall tone that the story is trying to convey. The game has these odd in-engine cutscenes that just look down right bad. I would also say the two main characters and supporting cast during these cutscenes don’t have the best story or voice acting. Which is in direct contrast to the unanimated “slideshow” cutscenes you get in-between major events. The voice acting in those actually keeps me fairly engaged with the overarching plot. Which leads me to believe it’s not really that the story is bad, it’s simply the way it’s conveyed that brings it down. The mass majority of these story bits are in the in-engine animated cutscenes. I almost wish they had put in “less” effort and just did the black and white slideshow ones for each event. As I think that would have drastically helped with the overall tone. However, even with the jank animations I think the story is serviceable and I have heard that its predecessor,Tower of Time, also had a pretty decent story that this is a continuation of. So if you played the previous game and liked its story, you may find this one a little more enjoyable then I.  All in all, Dark Envoy is a perfect example of why steam needs more than a simple, yes or no option for their review system. As it is neither a solid yes or no. I honestly think for the price of the game if you are okay with a decently well done double A experience then it’s probably worth it. But, if you are looking for a more polished and refined game with a ton of intricate systems, then I’d say this isn’t for you. Overall it’s a solid 5 out of 10.

_childDocuments_.review: - I am having a lot of fun with the combat. And once I get more characters and classes unlocked, I can see the potential for a lot of replay value.- I started out on Normal and I have a character die here and there, but the so far the game isn't too difficult. I might play for a while longer before upping the difficulty.- The intro sequence doesn't feel like it would be too much of a slog to get through once you know the controls (even on my first time I was through it in about an hour), so new files wont feel like there is a bunch you  to get through before you get into the game.- Free respecs! You can reallocate all of your points. So you can experiment with all of the spells, passives, and stats. It's nice because it protects you from having a bad spec, but I can't help by feel like it lessens the impact of the choices.- Not sure if this is going to persist into other areas, but the first city has some quick-travel node that are placed in such a way that it would be faster to walk from one node to the other than it would to use the node and click on the small icon on the map (plus side: no load screen from any of the travel nodes because you have the whole area loaded into memory).The game has some issues that I'm sure will get ironed out soon enough-- though I think some are things that should have been caught immediately since that is when I found them.- I changed some of the controls to be more like BG3 and had to restart the game to even control my character- If there are tutorials on the screen still when you enter a cut scene and try to click them away, they advance the dialog as if you are trying to skip voiced lines.- The voice acting isn't terrible, but could definitely be better. The audio quality isn't great- After playing through BG3, I'm a little spoiled by mouth flaps that look like they are trying to match what is being said. In Dark Envoy, the mouths have a little bit of variation in their movement, but aren't much better than jaws that just move up and down.- There is one spot where you might be able to soft-lock yourself when you get to the first town. Make sure to follow the quest prompt after your parents give you some money before going too crazy. I had to sell some crafting mats to be able to afford crafting mats to progress the quest...- When you hit  to open the map, I don't think you can zoom in and out to get a better idea of where you are and orient yourself how you might like.

Malakai and Kaela are children of war refugees, living the day-to-day life of adventurers as they seek ancient relics and forgotten places. Soon they too will have to learn how to survive in the chaos of war, as blood and tragedy will mark the beginning of their true journey.

name: Axiom Verge 2
detailed_description: You may have played Axiom Verge, or heard it referenced as a benchmark for indie action-exploration games. This long awaited sequel expands on the universe with completely new characters, abilities, and gameplay. Indra, the billionaire behind the worldwide Globe 3 conglomerate, heads to Antarctica to investigate the disappearance of her daughter, but ultimately finds herself in an entirely different reality, infected by parasitic machines that both aid and confound her. Where is she? Who is the mysterious person goading her from the other end of the computer terminal? Explore an alternate Earth-like world, replete with the ruins of an ancient, high-tech civilization. Hack machines. Battle monsters. Use your remote drone to enter the Breach, a parallel but connected reality that is filled with its own dangers. You’ll want to search every inch for the hidden items and upgrades you need to survive.

_childDocuments_.review: It's OKIt is missing a lot of stuff I was expecting from Axiom Verge 1.- It's a prequel / side story so no answers on what happened to Athetos / Trace- No arsenal of guns, You've got a boomerang, melee weapon, and that's it. You can't go on a side quest to get a flamethrower or chain lightening- No real boss fights, there are big enemies around with a lot of health that drop items, but they aren't really boss fights.- The world doesn't really feel alien. Green grass, blue water, snow and pine trees. I don't feel like I'm in another universe.- You don't get your L1 ability until the very end of the game so an entire button on your controller goes unused until the last 10 minutes of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Real quick: this is not a continuation of Trace's story. Trace himself appears in logs, and the more attention you pay the more connections you'll see. But if anything, this game's a  rather than a sequel - although that depends on where you're looking... it's complicated. It also seems like the game's very hit-or-miss. "It's nothing like AV1" is a common complaint, but I'm not sure if I agree; it depends on what sort of comparison you're making. However, the achievement stats paint a completely different picture: 42% of players have beaten the final boss, which is a very high number - even higher than AV1's 30%.In a sense, it's one of the best Metroidvanias I've ever played. It just grabs you and keeps you in. To me, the main sensation of a Metroidvania is discovery, and I think there's a lot to discover here. Just like in AV1, many hard to reach places contain lore pieces instead of powerups, and almost every single one adds something to the ever-growing picture.The way your arsenal of traversal abilities grows is also fantastic. Can you believe that this game  If you're a Metroidvania veteran you're probably used to "predicting" what sort of powerups you'll be getting based on the level design; Well, here the game caught me completely off guard. Excellent game design.Because of this, the game has some very good pacing. Admittedly, I got lost twice (as in, didn't know where to go), but the map is always there for you, it even has an outline of the level so you can see walls and such. And even if you -do- get lost, you'll surely end up finding a lot of powerups/lore pieces you couldn't reach before, so even that is satisfying.An arguably controversial element of the game is combat. See, even though most enemies are robots with laser guns, you're mostly stuck with... a melee weapon. In other words, the world is more "metroid" but you are "vania". Peronally, I didn't have much of a problem with it, though - for one, the enemies go down in just a few hits, but also the game feels like you're  to engage in combat needlessly.Almost every single enemy has a visible field of view, and they will only start chasing you once they take a good look at you. So it's entirely possible to just sneak/run past many of them, espcially considered that you actually can sneak by walking while crouching. The game's hacking system also allows you to simply take over one of the enemies and have others focus on this one while you make yourself scarce. I mean, you're not a warrior, you're a CEO! It just makes sense.Oh, right. The protagonist. How many games have you played that star a 40+ woman of indian descent, who's also an evil CEO of a mega-corp? That's so incredibly refreshing, especially since, well, things  over the course of the game. Indra doesn't manage to be as interesting as Trace (or rather... you know), but let's just say that she's not just some random woman. That's all I'm going to say.Finally, I think the game's aesthetic is a huge improvement over the first one. The pixel art is incredibly varied and beautiful, the music is wonderful and hauting. Combined with the excellent writing and rich lore, this game's a feast in more ways than just something fun to play. But of course that's a subjective thing.I've praised the game a lot, but I have to say: all those excellent elements kind of fail to come together. The game is very fun to play, but I don't think it will remain in my mind as a timeless masterpiece, and I can't say why. Still: I think it's very fun, to me, it's a great follow-up to the awesome weirdness that AV1 was.(oh, and if, for some reason, you read the whole thing but haven't played Axiom Verge 1, get the bundle of both games together and play them back-to-back. It will make much more sense that way)
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like a lot of people are being emotional in judging this game. I will try to be as pragmatic as I can to give a clear view of what I experienced. I will also mention that I did finish the game as well as got 100% completion (items/map). I did not experience a single crash and I don't recall encountering any bugs at all in my 14 hours of play. The game world is rather big. As in it takes up a lot of space. There are two main "worlds" you traverse. The Overworld and The Breach. The Overworld is a huge natural landscape with different biomes. As such, a lot of screens could feel same-y because of the natural/ruin/abandoned nature of the world. It still is a lot of space and there's a lot to explore and there is a fair bit of variety. Both in level design and also gameplay of each biome. The Breach on the other hand feels like a more retro version of the world, both in design and gameplay. The screens are smaller. The map is not as big and expansive as the Overworld and I would say the main use of it is traversal during the main story. There really isn't much use to going to the Breach once you have most of the game explored other than for hunting secrets. I should also mention that the Breach is a lot more dangerous than the Overworld with more enemies and tight spaces. The main gameplay of the game is exploration. The abilities you find throughout the game are almost all used for traversal. There are two types of enemies in the game. Normal enemies you encounter all over the world, and stronger, unique enemies you may call "bosses". Combat in the game I would say does work but it is lackluster. Up until near the end of the game, almost all normal enemies are an annoyance mainly because of the melee combat. That being said combat is not your only option. There's also hacking that you can invest some skill points into and use against most enemies to ease the fight. But again it's a simple system and doesn't really make you feel smart or skilled for using it. The "bosses" I'm sad to say are all pushovers, every single one. There's no contact damage so you can just go into the boss' body and spam melee and there's a good chance you won't die. On top of that, spending some time upgrading your damage skills and finding good weapons makes combat trivial, and fast. I see so many reviews mentioning how the game is not as good as the first one. I personally don't agree with this sentiment. Reason being Axiom Verge 2 has evolved and built upon what Axiom Verge did best. The map is so much bigger. The unique abilities used for traversal and combat are still there and I would say they've become more integrated and fit together very well to enhance your experience. Another major complaint mentioned in other reviews is the overall theme and feel of the world not being alien. That is both true and false. It's true that the game does not at all feel like the first game but that's not a bad thing in itself. I think what has disappointed some is just the bland/abandoned feel the new world. It's just a different theme altogether, and I personally didn't mind it. That being said, the world is not all nature and landscapes. There are structures and environments that have the same alien feel the first game had, but again they are all mostly abandoned or in ruins, as is the theme of the world. Axiom Verge 2 does have its shortcomings, mainly in the lackluster combat and to an extent having a mostly bland world. It really is a completely different feeling from the first game. However, in my experience, as I explored about half of the game, due to the abilities and upgrades I had acquired, and the variety in biomes and so many different areas to explore, I did start to enjoy the game more and more and in the end I did really enjoy moving around and exploring the world to the point that I decided to find every item and explore the entire map. It's understandable that the game did not meet many players' expectations coming from the first game however the game itself is not a bad game.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: As a hardcore fan of all things metroidvania, including the original Metroid, Super Metroid and Castlevania: SotN, I was also a hardcore fan of the first game. I ended up scouring every inch of Axiom Verge 1, looking for everything and getting all the achievements.So, with my "credentials" out of the way, is Axiom Verge 2 worth your time? I was very hesitant to a start. The game sure takes it time to really kick into gear, but so did the first now that I think back to it. However, first some review info:Very reminiscent of the first game, but brighter and more "earthly". It's very clear that while Sudra is an alien place with weird creatures and strange flora, Kiengir is a more familiar place. Some might find this off-putting, but it did make for some absolutely gorgeous scenery. Graphics gets a big thumbs up for me.With the exception of a few sounds (charging weapon, I'm looking at you) sound design is just as great as the first. Sounds are clear and distinct and you quickly learn what means what.Music is a step up from the first game. It keeps its weird, otherwordly feel with odd vocals and choruses, but it adds to the alien feeling of the game. I also absolutely adored hearing motifs from the first soundtrack make returns in places that remind you of Sudra.This is by far the largest difference between the first and second games. AV2 forgoes ranged pewpew weapons and instead relies on melee weapons and a throwable. At first, I was very hesitant to this, especially since enemies were numerous and very dangerous. I tried approaching combat as in the first game, where enemies are largely fodder. But, turns out, this is more Dark Souls in terms of combat. Every enemy is a puzzle, requiring the right strategy, application of weapon, movement and hacking. This lead to combat never really getting stale, but I admit it took me several hours to get used to, and to enjoy, this new style of combat.True to form, mr Happ brings abilities that are mind blowing. While AV1 had its glitching through walls mechanic, this game allows you to manipulate the Breach as if you were a PatternMind almost. It gives you some absolutely brain-wrangling puzzles to solve when trying to figure out how to apply the skills you have. Bosses are weirdly enough not very "bossy", and in most cases not even required to defeat to win the game. They are really just larger scale enemies that drop very valuable rewards when defeated. If you come into this game expecting a linear experience with boss progression, this is not it. Some bosses were also straight up puzzles, requiring very unorthodox strategies to defeat.While the story of the first game wasn't anything truly special, the way it was told certainly was. This game really took its time getting the story off the ground. At first I had a much harder time connecting to Indra as the protagonist than I did Trace. Trace had a clear goal and a very relatable situation to be in. Indra felt more like an explorer. It wasn't clear if she was in any real danger and her attitude was more of annoyance than fear.In the end though I do feel like the story does pull together and wrap up most loose threads. The twists weren't so out of the blue that you couldn't figure them out beforehand, but I still feel they were decent.Something I did not expect in this game was all the Lore. The first game hinted a lot at events of the far past, events taking place on other worlds, on the other side of the Breach. This game just straight up drowns you in knowledge. It was a lot of fun delving through all the lore and trying to piece together what happened, and if anything is related to AV1 (aside from the very obvious).All in all, I did enjoy my time in Axiom Verge 2. It took a lot more thinking and experimentation than AV1 and I felt myself completely lost many more times in this than AV1. But that's kind of the Metroidvania experience, so not really a fault of the game in any way. If you like metroidvanias, but not straight up carbon copies of the old, this is a game you will enjoy. If you're a hardcore AV1 fan, you might enjoy it. I can't really say, because there's many reasons to love a game, and while I certainly loved this one, I can see why many wouldn't, with its vastly different combat.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Buy it. It's different from AV1 - less Meroid, more Castlevania. And it means mostly melee combat, more emphasis on exploration, you will never feel like you are OP and killing everything you see in one hit (And I actually couldn't notice effect of any damage upgrade). Plus focus here on many different exploration skills that you need to use to progress and find secrets.  But it have crazy setting, insane music, great visuals and big world to explore. What else do you need?  P.S. I actually found what else do I need - epic boss battles. AV2 is lacking in this area.In AV1 boss battles where interesting and part of the lore. In AV2 all bosses are optional and doesn't add to the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a completely different beast than the first one, however it's still good in it's own right.If you enjoyed the surreal world and trippy music from the first game, this sequel delivers in spades. The new environment is otherworldly, with ancient mysteries and lore throughout. Platforming is fun, and discovering more about it's fallen civilization was engaging to the end.Combat is much different than the first game however, which I think will be a disappointment for some. It's more melee focused this time around, with heavy emphasis on 'hacking' enemies during fights to swing the tide. Through exploration, resources can be found to upgrade your weapons and hacking abilities, which makes fighting less of a chore.The intricate boss battles from the first game are instead replaced by 'strong enemies' which kind of just exist in the overworld. They're distinct visually and look like bosses, however they're no longer a puzzle you have to figure out, and can easily be defeated spamming melee attacks once you find their blindspot. It's kind of repetitive, but they're interesting to run into nonetheless, if only for their unique visual designs.Even with the lackluster combat, I still recommend this game if your a fan of Axiom Verge, or Metroidvanias in general. The environments and enemy designs are fantastic, the platforming is fun and rewarding, and the story expands upon the original whilst adding it's own layers of depth.If you're a fan of the original, I recommend this game as a solid sequel. The combat takes a backseat, but the universe and worldbuilding holds the game up with ease.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: What a huge disappointment.The player character is slow, stiff, and clunky. Enemies get way too many unfair hits in, a lot of damage is just unavoidable. Combat is limited to a melee weapon and a boomerang, yet every enemy takes at least 3 hits to kill and never gives you back as much health as you lost. You end up needing to take cheap shots from a distance or you come off second best. This is especially a problem in the dark sections where you only get a weak torch, you don't even know something is there and you've instantly lost half your health. The only way to really play is to quickly run away from all enemies, which seems the opposite of what a metroidvania should be. To me this breaks the number 1 rule of game design - don't punish the player for exploring.I consider Axiom Verge 1 to be the best game of the last decade and I really wanted to love this or at least like it, but I can't. Sorry Tom, this is frustrating and not enjoyable, it just feels bad.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Usually I tend to appreciate the sequels that introduce entirely different atmosphere and themes from their predecessors. Sure, it takes a moment or two to get used to the changes but in the end they offer a familiar experience dressed up in an entirely new set of clothes. In the case of Axiom 2 the changes are glaring. The music that welcomes the player even before they can see the game's menu is milder than it used to be in the original, the game discards it's browns and bloody reds in favor of shades of blue and steers away from the glitched bio-punk towards the more metaphysical concepts.  Having said that, I don't believe that in the case of Axiom Verge such a transformation is a success. Too much of the original's appeal relied on its nature including its grungy, melty looks, it's raw, synthetic* music and the insane amount of effort put into making the game resemble Super Metroid without actually shamelessly copying it. The sequel discards almost all of that in favor of somewhat shallow metaphysical musings that additionally never get sufficiently developed. Being an owner of a global supercorporation, the game's protagonist, Indra, initially appeared to me a fascinating possibility. She seemed far more interesting than the first game's Trace who was basically a generic scientist. And while Axiom1 had managed to build Trace up and make his story sufficiently intricate, the sequel does exactly the opposite. The motivations driving the characters' actions, the history of the game's alternate dimensions, basically every element of the narrative  felt to me as if introduced not to create a congruent world, but a facade of gambits necessary to push the events forward. And it didn't help that almost every single of those plot tokens was instantly dropped and forgotten the moment they served their purpose.The characters Indra meets are shallow and uninteresting. Most of the encounters are only a few lines of dialogue long. And while there is one event that affects them later in the game, I've found it disappointing how the characters reacted in exactly the same fashion when Indra approached them as a drone as they did when she was a human. There is some worldbuilding done in the logs and tablets found throughout the game but, as mentioned before, the plot seemed to me rather forced and not particularly interesting.    The art is a mixed bag. Some of the bosses look monumental and are animated with quality I would never expect from a pixel art game. Backgrounds are usually somewhere between adequate and very good, and there’s a lot of effort put in creating a distinct art style for the alternate dimension of Breach that the protagonist visits. The human characters, on the other hand, look disappointing. I've found the music difficult to withstand. While the opening theme is pleasant to listen to and actually unexpectedly upbeat, somewhere around the half of the story the player is subjected to ceaseless chanting which I've found obnoxious.Mechanics are a mess. The basic platforming remain similar to the original game – basic but solid. I've also appreciated how the game switched the combat balance towards the melee. Still, almost none of the choices make sense when put together. For example, there is an enormous amount of collectible upgrades hidden throughout the world but there is no point in looking for them since any boss can be skipped with the exception of the final one, which turns out to be a puzzle fight. The enemies are often irritating until the player realizes that in most of the scenarios the drone can be used to scout and clear the areas without any punishment. Admittedly, some of the abilities are unique and interesting like the already mentioned drone transformation, climbing vertical surfaces which offers a welcome alternative to the usual wall jump mechanics or visiting the Breach. Hacking the enemies during the combat is also an extremely welcome option, although it seems – like the entirety of this game – more tamed than glitching them in and out of the reality in the first game.   **Axiom2 does a lot of things right, but in the long run I could not escape the feeling that it crumbles underneath the weight of its own ambition. The world(s) are expansive, but also unnecessarily complicated which makes exploring them tedious and irritating, the game lacks some balancing and polish and certain enemies are nothing more than a nuisance. The mechanics did not evolve much since the first game and at some points they even seem like a downgrade. Axiom2 made me realize the staggering difference that exists between a 6 out of 10 game and a 7. The first Axiom was a 7. 7+ even. It grew on me in time. It's world and ideas managed to convince me after a while. Axiom2 lacks in most of these areas. Perhaps, it is me who fails to appreciate or even understand the complexities of the world given***. Nonetheless, it is best to assume that Axiom Verge 2 will be mostly enjoyable to the fans of the original game while the new players should first try the prequel.   * I am perfectly aware that if you take a closer look at it, the words 'raw' and 'synthetic' are antonyms, and I believe this is exactly what made the soundtrack of the first game such an unique experience.** I’ve grown to absolutely love the original game’s Axiom1. Therefore I’ve tried to keep the titles of my paragraphs here in the same fashion and also resembling my attempts at understanding the game’s storyline. *** There is also a very distinct possibility that Axiom Verge 2 is setting the stage for yet another sequel. Not only, as mentioned above, some branches of the story get cut short before they are able to sufficiently grow. There are some events that notably change the lore or even contradict some of the story known from the previous game. These discrepancies are, in my opinion, too substantial to be a coincidence and I can think about at least several interesting possibilities in which they could affect the lore of Axiom Verge. Long story short, yes, I’m waiting for the third installment.

_childDocuments_.review: look, i'm gonna be real here. a metroidvania lives and dies by its map design, and this game has that. i loved the pacing of the game, not just in story, but the gameplay. however, the combat here is definitely worse than in the first game, as others have said here.however! this game is still a blast, and has plenty of meaty platforming challenges and some very cool worldbuilding. if you love metroidvanias, you should absolutely check this one out.

_childDocuments_.review: A sub-par metroidvania. Axiom Verge 2 disregards many strong points from Axiom Verge 1 and instead builds on those aspects of Axiom Verge 1 that weren't great to begin with. Minor spoilers ahead.- Combat is Zelda-esque melee with an additional (low-damage) bumerang now. This alone is not a problem, but many enemies have ranged weapons and an AI that deliberately exploits the limits of your attacks (e. g. by moving away when you jump into melee range). In the end, combat feels tedious and in many cases, it sadly is more fun to just run past (or through) the enemies than to fight them.- Fluid controls weren't a strong suit of AV1 and controls are even worse here: Normal movement is slow and stiff. You get near to no skills for faster, more fluid progression (e. g. double jump), and those skills you do get just feel bad. Climbing, for example, unintentionally sticks you to walls and has a pointless, limited range you need to cheese around by drone form.- There are many items and upgrades for your human form, but most of these see little to no use. You lose human form about half-way through the game and only regain it shortly before the end. And even then, you'll be keeping to drone form because it is so much easier to move around with.- The path through the game world is a random mess, even for a metroidvania. You just explore open ends until you find another progression upgrade at some unpredictable hiding spot. Upgrades are disdainfully waiting for you on the ground. There is not a single leading boss fight and in most cases, there is not even any kind of celebratory architecture (say, a shrine) around the upgrade.- Exploration is excessively tedious. This comes from the limited movement options (as above), but also from the irregularly distributed quicktravel spots and the annoyingly pointless choice of prohibiting quicktravel between both game worlds.- Dialogue is just as obtuse as in Axiom Verge 1, but there's two things worse now: First, dialogue boxes don't show pop-up heads anymore, so it is hard to follow who is talking. Second, the dialogues between humans sound weird, like unrelated monologues rather than communication (as if two people both had a stroke while talking).- I experienced several minor bugs and glitches: from 100% CPU load while the game is minimized to momentarily getting stuck in walls to items that said I could "take" them, but I couldn't (without any "nope" sound or anything).- The pixel art has improved over AV1. However, since the environment with its La-Mulanese touch isn't as technical and abstract as in AV1 anymore, the minor flaws in the pixel art become much more apparent. - I still like the lore and the setting, the new biomes are interesting and varied, and the soundtrack is awesome.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I have been withholding a review until finishing both this game and the first one, and I've got to say: if the first one was a phenomenal game, this one is on another level. Let me get this disclaimer out of the way first: if you loved axiom verge 1 and come to this game with the expectation of more of the same, you will be sorely disappointed. These two are very different games, which to me helps both establish their own identity and find their own strengths.I loved the exploration focus. Almost everything in the game is geared towards encouraging and helping exploration, and while it's easy to get lost when you're not paying attention, it is hard to stay lost once you start thinking about where you are and where you're going. I can only think of two occasions on which I was stumped during regular play, and I eventually figured them out on my own. The only occasion I needed guides was after finishing the game, for some of the more obscure collectibles (some of which are admittedly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥). I especially appreciate the save point teleportation; after 100%ing this game I went back to axiom verge to try and do the same, and it's not happening. The only complaint I have is how long it takes for your character to spawn when you teleport. I started playing mostly as the drone because it doesn't have a getting off the ground animation after the already pretty lengthy particle tornado spawn animation. An option to skip the animation and get right back into playing would not be amiss.I did encounter some minor bugs, but they're all menu stuff so it doesn't really affect the gameplay, which is quite polished. The enemy AI is quite smart and the flying ones can be particularly annoying due to the limited range of your attacks, and the limited angles of your only ranged attack, but the combat isn't really the focus of this game so I am more than happy to give it a pass, especially considering there are no mandatory fights in this game. The two boss fights I can think of that you can't just go around or escape literally have respawn stations inside the room you are doing the fighting in.The game is committed to not let anything get in the way of the story and the exploration. If you're here for combat action, it probably won't be for you, but if you're here for exploratory platforming in a gorgeously presented world, I can't recommend this game enough!
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: For as long as it lasted, I was completely absorbed in this game. One after another, perhaps in unintended order you unlock new systems and movement options. You have time to learn them, combine them and then mercilessly exploit them and reach places and upgrades that were supposed to be out of your reach.There is great emphasis on exploration and experimentation, so if that interests you then you should definitely try this one out. Just beware of possible softlocks if you have a strange brain (like I do)

_childDocuments_.review: I connected with the world of Axiom Verge 2 quite a bit more than Axiom Verge 1.  My favorite aspect of the metroidvania genre is exploration, and I just really love the vibe of this world.  The soundtrack perfectly fits the mood, as well, and elevates the experience of just moving around in this environment.With the addition of the breach world, a sort of low-res alternate universe that connects with the main world in certain points, I was favorably reminded of Knytt Underground, one of my favorite games of all time.For what its worth re: crashes, which some other reviews are mentioning, I bought this game at launch, and experienced frequent crashes for the first few hours after release, but a patch appears to have been quickly pushed through that same day which resolved all of the issues.  I find the  game to be perfectly stable since this patch, and it runs with no problems.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played a lot, but so far this seems like a downgrade from the first game. It is not bad, but way behind what came before. The characters are less interesting (especially the main character) and the atmosphere is nothing compared to the alien feel of the first one. If you like metroidvanias, you can definetly pick it up and have a good time. But it didn't manage to hook me in like the original.(I will probably pick it up again at some point, so my thoughts might change)
