_childDocuments_.review: Despite all the warnings and cautioning, I absolutely LOVED this game. Beat it a few minutes ago with 98% map and all weapons and all arms. In some ways I love it even more than the first one.The world is a lot more open ended where the first felt a bit constrained. I LOVE how the huge bosses are entirely optional which to me gives a lot more of a realistic vibe to it. Also, there was that huge worm thing in the water that I really felt bad putting down, it's just so cute.I didn't really like the protagonist though and the whole narrative seemed a bit jumbled, though it was interesting and seemed like  but no, no spoilers. The world building was impeccable and the overlay of Kiengir, the Breach and the Overworld and how they interact and how you explore all three was again genius.The visuals I really like, especially how varied the Breach is and how mind-bending the Overworld is.I also loved how combat was de-emphasized and how I managed to rely on the hacking mechanism a whole lot more. This made exploration so much more enjoyable to me with creative items that make the traversal really interesting rather than just another big gun whoopdy-f-doo. I didn't even mind that the little combat that remained was primarily made melee. I didn't use it all that much anyway.Finally, the music. The music is extremely amazing this time around as well and even better than the first game. Just take a listen to the track titled Monsoon with a good headset or sound system.All in all this is a very solid 9/10 for me and I highly recommend it to whoever like the first one.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: My playtime might seem low but I got it on the Switch day one. I've bought the Axiom Verge duology on Steam mostly just to show the dev some extra love but I will replay both soon.Personally I thought this sequel was better than the first game in each and every way (and I really enjoyed the first game). Prettier graphics, better flowing gameplay, and another interesting story set in the same universe.You don't need to have played the first to enjoy the second. I recommend both, but the first game is really a big love letter to Super Metroid and the second game is more its own thing.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is better than the first in some aspects in worse in others. Let's make a list:Pros:- Much less obtuse backtracking causing you to wander in circles against your will.- Difficulty never quite gets absurd.- Travelling around the map in general is a much more enjoyable experience.Cons:- Game secrets are not nearly as interesting or well hidden.- Combat options are way more streamlined, making combat less interesting.- Breach sections while much larger, have hard stops all over the place with little progress until you find key items.Overall, the game was a lot more playable in general and wasn't as hard of a recommend as the original, the difficulty spikes in game didn't make this one a "don't recommend unless they like hard metroidvania."
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I want to recommend this game because of how good the first one was. I really want to. But this just doesn't carry the same punch as a sequel. I knew going in that there wouldn't be guns. Sure, fine, whatever. The exploration is fun and kind of interesting. The fast travel was a welcome addition. The spritework is fantastic. The music is good.Maybe this game set itself up for failure by calling itself a sequel and then failing to deliver on that. It's in the same world, which is cool and all, though I'm not much of a lore guy in general, so it raised the expectation on the gameplay.This game is sooo close to earning a positive review from me, except that it suffers from a few critical flaws:- No bosses- or at least not any real ones that block your way. Just some big robots in certain rooms that don't respawn and drop some upgrades when they die.- I got totally stuck because I think the game spawned the wrong upgrade somewhere. Or at least that's what a guide I found seems to indicate.- Stick sensitivity. The up/down deadzone is far too sensitive, causing you to run up stairs when you least expect it and drop through platforms when you mean to jump. This is inexcusable for a game that has already been out for a year and leaves me even more baffled when noting that the character has a walking animation.This game just doesn't have the same oomph and wonder in it as the first game. The whole Epic store situation is irrelevant as far as I'm concerned and you should ignore all the review bombing related to it.It was a good effort from Thomas Happ, but it fell flat IMO. Maybe I'll finish it one day, but I think I'm ready to put it down without finishing it. I am thoroughly disappointed because I liked the first one enough to beat it twice (or maybe three times, IDK)
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Sideways thumb.It has some really nice music, varied environments and you find a lot of upgrades early on.  On top of regular metroidvania abilities, you acquire skillpoints that you can put into things like HP, weapon damage and perhaps most interestingly: Hacking.  You can hack enemies to take control of them or bosses to disable much of their weaponry.  Despite all these positive factors, i felt very take or leave it with the game (and am leaving it).  Kinda how I felt with games like MindSeize and Vision Soft Reset.  It's hard for me to pinpoint anything specific that leaves me feeling this way about it.  Navigation has the potential to get a little confusing and that is definitely one factor.. Perhaps i'm just not enraptured enough with its level design.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Seven years ago Axiom Verge got released and while I had a fair share of criticisms towards it, it really was a fantastic metroidvania. Without being too novel, it had several extremely clever additions to the formula of the genre and apart from that was a solid game with unforgettable soundtrack and cool visual style. A year ago Axiom Verge 2 got released on several platforms and had far less excited reviews overall, most emphasizing the change in focus of the game from action to exploration. Which excited me, because I love exploration in metroidvania games and the combat in the first title was my least favorite thing about it. Now that I’ve finally had a chance to play the sequel myself, I have to say that I love it even more than the original. Yet, I can see how it’s not going to be for everyone.What haven’t changed is how cool the visual style of the game is, with creepy biomechanical Giger-esque elements (though this time this is somewhat de-emphasized), and how incredible the soundtrack is. As with the first game – I urge you to check out the music even if you have not interest in the game, it’s great. Maybe less consistently awesome, but still fantastic. The metroidvania basics also remain, with a map that you gradually fill, while getting new abilities and finding optional upgrades. Though, this time there’s a simple skill tree added on top, that is unlocked via one of the types of optional items.But the way the game plays and feels is vastly different. Where Axiom Verge was mostly about tighter corridors, following the classic Metroid structure, and also heavily emphasized action, a crazy amount of different guns and many boss battles, Axiom Verge 2 is all about exploration. You still have combat, but it’s mainly in the melee range and isn’t really necessary, apart from clearing the way. There are boss enemies, but all apart from 2 boss encounters are entirely optional. And the world is extremely open at almost all times, giving you plenty of possibilities to explore and find cool stuff. There are clear goals, but you can often ignore them and try to explore as much as possible without going for the main story. Though, main goals is what often gives you upgrades that open up your possibilities.This world is what, I fear, may overwhelm a lot of people. There are only a couple of moments where it’s very unclear on how you should get to where you need to, but that could be enough for some to get frustrated. But there at the same time, when you accept that it’s all about exploring and looking for interesting discoveries and possibilities, the game is amazing. The idea of a parallel world here is very reminiscent of the Spectral Realm from Legacy of Kain titles, meaning that after a certain point you start thinking of the entire huge world map in parallel versions (which is helpfully visualized by the game) and a lot of navigation puzzles are solved in genuinely inventive and fun ways due to that.I guess that’s what Axiom Verge 2 is in the first place – inventive. Where apart from corruption and “save the progress of the map and items even when dying” the original title was a pretty conventional Super Metroid-like game, this sequel does everything to be something else. And apart from the La-Mulana titles, I think the last time I’ve played a metroidvania that was so wildly different and exciting was Toki Tori 2+ from 9 years ago. Another title that didn’t click with many.And I can see that coming from the action filled original to the sequel is going to be a shock. Especially since I also feel that the enemies can be get really obnoxious at the beginning as you will undoubtedly be taking damage and dying as part of the experience. But, once you accept that this is part of the game, that avoiding the combat where possible is a better choice, that it’s all about the exploration and the navigation, the game gets very enjoyable… if you’re into this sort of thing in the first place, of course.I loved Axiom Verge 2 and at one moment, when I realized how a new ability suddenly gave me so many crazy possibilities to explore, was unlike anything I’ve felt from games in a long time. Because more often than not metroidvanias are predictable, as great as they get despite this. But Axiom Verge 2 is anything but predictable. It’s a bit rough, it’s not for people who like action adventure platformers for the “action” part, not the “adventure platforming”. But it’s fresh, inventive and absolutely amazing if you love exploring these metroidvania worlds.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Ugh this game should not have been called Axiom Verge 2. It has almost nothing to do with the first one and is just an inferior game despite what people are saying.There is a clever main exploration mechanic that is really the reason this game can be played (despite not being the first game to use this mechanic). Other than that it's a mediocre metroidvania, especially given this is a supposed sequel and will be compared with the first game. The combat is bad, clunky, with weak weapons and doesn't really improve later on. It's hard to balance combat when you give the player such a large health bar and for there to be any risk you need to get cheap shots in by the enemies. It's kind of hilarious that the last enemies you fight . The hacking mechanic is so silly that I never used it even once other than the mandatory parts. Like if you are that close to an enemy and you have time to hack, you just smash it anyway.  The enemies are either super fast and cheese you or they are so slow and harmless you just ignore them.Many abilities are only used a handful of times throughout the game and feel like they were just thrown in there. The upgrades are very weak and add very little to the game.The last few hours are drawn outttttt and for no good reason, you just look for the next place you could possibly advance to and then you're forced to walk through many pointless rooms until you reach the end (well sounds like the first game) and the ending sequence is really bizarre and unfun.It does scratch an exploration and mystery itch. Obviously a lot of work has been put into this, and I actually thought I was going to give this a thumbs up for most of my playtime, but I just kept hoping for something really fun to come up and it never did.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I have the game on the other platform, it's a good metroidvania. I hope they will bring in the same options as in AV1. Speedrun and random.The environments are varied and the skills are delivered a bit differently than in previous version, It's non linear, though you tend to explore each area separately, until it happens. (vague on purpose)This game is for those who enjoy exploration and can be a bit hard at times. Yet, you should consider pushing through instead of lowering the difficulty.I feel obligated to write this: FIRST.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I was really looking forward to this, but it failed to hit all the right notes. I would have given it a neutral score if that was an option. It's still a mostly competent metroidvania. Cool art, good music. And then that's about it.Combat is disappointing. Some shared worldbuilding is done, but the story of this one barely holds together as an arc. Very little to do with the first game. Not sure how I even felt about exploration. At times it felt like I was stuck for way too long. At other times it felt like there's too much to revisit at once.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I will start by saying the choice to switch from gun-play from the first, to melee combat in this one, wasn't really fun at first and it really isn't until you get all the upgrades.  Just get the Bronze Axe  always charge your attacks, and prioritize your infection/hacking ability. Since hacking your enemies (especially if they're stronger) is typically safer and faster. Other than that, this is an incredible sequel! Exploration+mobility is very fun, and the overarching story, as well as it's telling is absolutely amazing. I can't wait to see what the next chapter holds.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Finally reached the end of Axiom Verge 2. I can see why people didn't like it as much as the first game:There's no wide array of weaponry to find and upgrade (there's like 6 weapons and 4 of them can be upgraded outside of the Skill Tree system). Edit: I guess there's more weapons than I ended up finding but still, it's way less diverse than the first game.Environments are more organic and less gamified, making things feel a bit blander. For example, takes place in a world that is very similar to ours rather than an entirely alien world which resulted in blander environments to explore.Exploration felt a lot less rewarding as a lot of your upgrades (not abilities, those you have to find) are unlocked via a Skill Menu. There's considerably fewer Health and Weapon Damage upgrades to find throughout the environments because there are Skill trees that buff this too. You do have to find Skill Points but finding those isn't quite the same feeling as finding a carefully placed health, damage, hacking etc. upgrade in the environment.I don't think there's any movement enhancing abilities to unlock, which makes the gameplay feel a lot slower than the first game since you move the same speed throughout the entire game.Enemies didn't have anywhere near as interesting Hacking effects as the first game and I think enemy variety was lessened. The first enemy you encounter is frequently re-used for example.I found the abilities to both move  made exploration a bit of a headache. My issue with exploration however may be because I kept overlooking what should've been an obvious route through an area of the game. The sky graphics along the path to the  looked like a wall so I never realized I could  a certain way to hit a switch until I started looking at a text walkthrough ( ).It's a competent experience... but not quite what you'd expect from a sequel. It's much more focused on telling a story than is focused on the gameplay and the world design kinda necessitated map markers telling you where the next big thing to find/do is located due to there being many big open areas to tread and re-tread as you get new abilities instead of tight corridors.Overall, I'd say it's worthy of your time but don't go in to it expecting a deeper gameplay experience than the first game.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I bought Axiom Verge 2 the day it came out on Steam. At the time it had mixed reviews. I was a little worried at the time, but I still bought it out of faith in the developer. And I'm happy to say that it exceeded my expectations.It's a wonderful expansion of the original, in terms of both mechanics and setting. The breach is like an awesome, scaled up version of Axiom Verge's hidden worlds. It's totally mind-blowing, and I don't want to spoil anything by explaining how it works. The Worldstream is also further explained and explored and it's gotta be one of the most compelling sci-fi settings that I've seen.I was very satisfied with Axiom Verge 2, but much like its predecessor, it's left me hungry for more. The mystery runs deep, and I can't wait to discover more in the next installment.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to thumbs down this but... This game is just Axiom Verge 1 with less fun weapons, a less interesting plot, less to do, and just... less. There's a lot of Epic Exclusivity hate, and I get that, but even without that, this game just isn't as good as Axiom Verge 1. If you're debating on picking up either or, just pick up the first one. If you want to get this one, be my guest, but i'm posting this review after I beat the game with ~ 80% content done. I could 100% this game in about 2 more hours. 20 bucks for 10 hours of content. You be the judge if that's worth your time.Sorry Thomas, but I think you just made a bad game. If you take some of the dangling threads and give us a free DLC for an after story, then maybe the game will be wroth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I was sceptical of this game given the changes from AV1 (no guns), but the change from a Metroid to Castlevania focus is welcome. Using a few short range weapons on enemies felt strange given AV1, but in a few minutes you get the hang of it. The droid is awesome!! This game builds off the first in every way (combat, music, game design, lore, and overall atmosphere). I am glad this game is different. A purely derivative game from AV1 would have sucked. Excited for Axiom Verge 3!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Axiom Verge 1 (bought the bundle with both games), thought it was pretty-good-but-not-great, and got enough out of my playthrough that I would recommend it but I'm probably not interested in playing through again.AV2, I didn't enjoy. I'm not a fan of the switch to (awkward) melee as the primary mechanic, and the "hacking" is novel but not enjoyable. It IS made necessary by the game though.I played AV2 for 2 hours and I'm ready to shelve it. Play the original but skip the sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game, but with a few problems. Level tree is a bit out of whack, since you spend a great deal of time as the little drone, which makes those upgrades more important. Combat feels very optional given how open the world is. The open world nature makes it sometimes unclear where to go next.This game is very experimental though - really turns the idea of a metroidvania on it's head. Being able to explore a large portion of the map right from the start with very few powerup gates was really interesting. I also prefer the more natural aesthetics of this game to the more alien of the original. I do recommend giving it a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Already played through it several times on the EGS version, but I bought it here to support Tom Happ. I love both AV1 and AV2, but they are undeniably different games - if you go into the sequel expecting more of the exact same gameplay as the first, you may be disappointed. However, if you enjoyed the first game at all, I strongly encourage you to give Axiom Verge 2 a try with an open mind - it iterates on the gameplay and world design in some fascinating ways. There is more focus on exploration and navigation instead of boss fights, which I personally prefer. Though, I do rather miss the large variety of weapons that Trace had at his disposal.In many ways, what captures my attention about Axiom Verge and its sequel the most is the story and worldbuilding. I've always felt that there's a qualitative difference between a story built on a comprehensive foundation and one with just the appearance of one. Even if the player never learns all or even most of it, the fact that the fictional world is built on a common truth, rather than a cool-looking empty box, makes things feel more real. When the game is throwing out fictional terms, references to places and events, they feel like more than just set dressing. They feel like glimpses at a larger world. Enough to tantalize and inspire the imagination without simply infodumping. Into The Breach and Dark Souls, for example, do an excellent job of this. So do both Axiom Verge games.Like the first game, the plot may seem rather bare-bones and straightforward if you don't pay much attention. However, diligence and attention to detail is rewarded - especially if the first game is fresh in your mind, the timeline of Kiengir and how it links to the plot of Axiom Verge will come into focus, and AV2 fleshes out the series universe in some new and fascinating ways. I love digging into game lore like this, and if you enjoy constructing fictional timelines and looking up Akkadian definitions, I think you will too. Personally, I'm crossing my fingers to see Axiom Verge 3 a few years down the line. Very few fictional worlds capture my imagination like Axiom Verge's does, and I can't wait to dive back in.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Axiom Verge 2 improves on the platforming mechanics from the first game in a lot of fun and interesting ways. This game is enormous and has a ton of stuff to discover, and in the same fashion as its predecessor, it only offers a small amount of guidance to get you to the next objective.I found Axiom Verge 2 to be significantly easier than the first game. The sequel has a much heavier focus on exploration puzzles and although enemies are present all over the map, they often feel like an afterthought and are easily avoided. With that said, I played through the game on normal difficulty, so perhaps that was a mistake.It felt like the soundtrack in this game leaned much more heavily on female vocals which I did not like as much. I recognized throwbacks to the first game's soundtrack when they appeared and appreciated those making it into the game. My favorite track is probably the title screen, they hit you with the best one first - this is cool because it's a great first impression but I don't think the rest of the OST lives up to that impression. None of this is to say the soundtrack is bad - it's quality content, it just didn't resonate with me as much as the first game did when it comes to music.Overall I really enjoyed this game. My first playthrough was a solid ten hours and I never really felt like I hit many significant snags or ever became too lost to progress. I think two fights were way easier than they should have been (this is probably dev overcompensation due to players not being able to kill certain bosses in the first game) and often found regular mook engagements with good positioning to be harder than boss and miniboss fights.Definitely worth picking up, but play the first one too.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Axiom Verge 2 feels more like an "open world" metroidvania.It is significantly different than the first game. As in the second game is more castlevania-like with melee attacks and limited range, whereas the first game is more metroid with gun.I started playing AV2 right after AV1, but I didn't quite enjoy it initially since I was expecting more of the same AV1 style of gameplay.Once I got my expectations of this game adjusted, I thought was a really good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: An actual masterpiece of metroidvania design imo. Very different from the first game and more open, with some pretty inventive mechanics and a few that feel like callbacks to classics of the genre. The movement and hacking are the focus here and they're very well-realized. Lots of powers and skill points to collect scattered around the nicely sized world, to the point where exploring every obscure corner of the map feels well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: It is really bad how much this game strays away from the first one - and makes everything worse. It tries to be more streamlined and accessible. But really it isn't. The gameplay is much more frustrating as the map is much harder to understand and navigate. The combat is extremely frustrating. The enemies are severely overpowered. The main combat switched to melee in this part - but the enemies more often than not still shoot at you! The art style is less intriguing. It is overall more boring, less engaging, more frustrating and the plot and story telling just can not hook you up from second one like the first one. I had to stop giving this game a chance about 100 minutes in, in order to be sure to have enough time left to still refund it. Too bad, as the first game was a master piece!
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: For starters, this is not a shooter like the previous game. The gameplay is melee based. Closer to Hollow Knight than Metroid.In the beginning I was skeptical, because this game is a lot different than the first one. New character, new themes and visuals, new gameplay style.But hear me out, it's a great game. If you enjoy metroidvanias, can't miss this one. It only keeps getting better as you progress and unlock new powers to traverse the map.The new powers are fun and creative. And the map design is really good.The game starts kinda slow, but it grows on you as you go on.The soundtrack is 10 out of 10.And why is the sound when you charge an attack so damn loud? I rarely use charged attacks because of this.Personally I think I like AV1 the most, but nonetheless, AV2 is definitely worth playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I can see why some people wouldn't like it due to it not having the same shooting style combat of the first, but for me it was thoroughly enjoyable and made me realize that my favorite part of Metroidvanias is the exploring and acquiring new skills that help you get around.  So while the combat in this sequel does feel kinda underwhelming, the exploring of the map was super enjoyable once you get the upgrades that really open everything up to exploration.  I'll take an Axiom Verge 3 for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like it but this "sequel" is not even close to AV1 in terms of gameplay.The biggest source of disappointment for me is the fighting and enemy placement.There are a lot of cheap shots at the player, ranging from hidden enemies in tiles that just bop out of them and track you down which are unavoidable, drones that shoot at you and mimic your vertical velocity, meaning if you move up so do they. You will be barely able to catch them with the forced melee approach this game has. Every other grounded enemy forces you to trade blows, you can not dodge, you cant block or even spot dodge, you have to trade the blow. Every other option is not viable because they are just so freaking fast. A lot of enemies will flail at you (spiders in a jungle) or shoot at you from off screen. The projectiles will even have an aoe area. The mines that track you down also have a big aoe which means if you attack them you will take a blow too and they take off a considerable amount of health. The fighting which happens in every room is just frustrating, its not even hard as most of the time you can just run past the enemies but I dont think that is what the developer wanted.The game also has unnecessary game mechanics. Why can the main character crouch-walk but not move into any vent unless he transforms into the drone? On top of that you will actually bug out and get out of bounds if you try to crouch into crevices that seem like you can get into but you can not. The deadzone for the crouch-walk is also too big. Most of the time you hold the stick to the left or right and only mildly up and down and you end up crouch-walking. Absolutely unnecessary.The Breach sections with the drone are also laggy probably due to the camera not updating properly. The tileset seems to lag behind, I do not know if this is what the developer wanted but it does not feel good if everything is jittering. Get your integer movement speeds right :pThe overall story is kinda neat but the protagonist is somewhat unlikeable.5/10, I waited a year to get disappointed
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Remember how great the first game is?  This is not.Imagine all the enemies and bosses from metroid, but samus doesn't have a gun.  That's this game.  An exercise in frustration.  The best strategy is to throw your endlessly respawning drone out and full clear the map from several rooms away before leaving your checkpoint.  Not at all like the first game, and not fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: After enjoying the first game a lot, I was excited to pick this game up. However, while the first was very heavily Metroid inspired, this one leans away from that much to my dissatisfaction.Having just finished it, I feel the story ended just as it was starting and didn't fully deliver on its ideas, unlike the first which felt complete.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: The short of it is: I felt let down by Axiom Verge 2.It is not a bad game. You can play Axiom Verge 2, without playing Axiom Verge 1.I do hope there is a third one.AV2 has great style and music, but I couldn't enjoy it fully.Maybe I expected more from it?I can't be more specific without spoilers, so this is your SPOILER WARNING.Spoilery review (complaints?) below...Keep going...Just a bit more...Ok.You were warned.I'll get to the drone part, but first things first.---I couldn't get into the story. And this has 3 levels for me. - Indra's story (the protagonist's story).She's just being led on the whole game. Go to Antarctica. Go to this coordinate, now go to this other coordinate. Why? Because. Now go. Get your body back. Now go kill the big bad. She doesn't really achieve anything in the game. Couldn't get back, couldn't find her daughter, didn't kill the big bad at the end (well, one Indra did). She was just the errand girl for Hammond, the big bad and Lamassu. And about the 2 Indras at the end... That just like, happened. Didn't really had a payoff for me. I'd rather have the drone arm get Indra back on his own than, oh, it's just a copy of her mind or something. At least, it would be some sort of accomplishment by one of them. Indra accomplished nothing as far as I am concerned.- The big picture story.That was just too convoluted for me. Sure, I like reading about it in the wiki, seeing all the things I missed, and I appreciate the mystery surrounding it. But it just flew over my head during my playthrough.Also, lots and lots of loose ends. Where was Hammond? Did Hammond die? Then who was Indra talking to? How was she talking to her? Where was Indra's daughter? The other people she met just mutated and died? Why was there even a mention of the kazzacks (cosssacks?)? jut died She goes to Antarctica to find Hammond and her daughter. She does not find her daughter. Did she find Hammond? I am not sure, She finds a body that's supposedly her, but then talks to her on the last ansible or something. Like I said, the story is not clear.So, while looking for Hammond she does errands for the bad Arm and then loses her body to it. - The comparison with Axiom Verge 1.There is a point to be made that the same thing happened to Trace in AV1. Everyone lied to him and he was just let on. But he did succeed in his task. And the twist had a huge payoff for me. Maybe it didn't make an impression on me because of the similarities.I could overlook the story, but other aspects of the game also felt like just things to do or get with no relevance. Sure, lots of things are needed to advance the story, but they didn't feel useful or fun to use.--- Now the main game mechanics.Where to start?- Weapons. Basically, and the for the most part, melee only. You get a boomerang early on, but I don't think anybody uses it. It's slow, does little damage. It sits mostly forgotten on the menu. I was willing to give it a chance when I found my second or third weapon and noticed different attack animations and thought they could have different uses or attack styles. But no, those weapons didn't matter because of:- The over-reliance on the drone. I thought it was just a section of the game that used the drone, but it's more like .... 70% (?). At least, it felt like that to me. I didn't like the drone at first, but it grew on me. I preferred it late game because of its mobility options. But no mistake, it is overused.There's a sub-world, called the Breach, only accessible to the drone. Ok.Then, you have to use the drone for some puzzle/exploration elements. Ok.Then, you don't have a human body, so the drone is all you have.This is when I noticed this was the primary game element of AV2. You do get a human(ish) body later, but by that time, the drone's mobility is better than the other body, so you don't want to switch back. What are the consequences of the overuse of the drone?- Useless skills, weapons, upgrades.Indra has a choice of several melee weapons. You don't need them. There is no reason to change the starting weapon.Indra gets 2, well 3, boomerangs. Couldn't find a use for the first 2. Maybe, occasionally to get the attention of an enemy or hit a switch. The 3rd. one does not count as a weapon. It's more of an item. It's a remote control boomerang that you need to use once (maybe twice) to hit an out of the way switch. Useless as a weapon.The skill points, skill tree and most of the exploration are rendered pointless for the following:     . There's zero need to upgrade the combat skill tree.     . Maybe upgrading health is useful, but you do find health upgrades on the map, so this is redundant.     . There's a ... let's call it mist cloud skill, and you can use points to move faster, but there is no need for it.     . Hacking skill upgrades... meh. Some are mandatory. Useless for the most part. It could have been fun, but it was not properly developed or used.     . Just do all the drone upgrades.Leave some points available for when hacking is necessary. Otherwise, go nuts with the drone.Random grievances: - The grab on the ledge skill. Really?- The see in the dark skill. You could've just put a switch to turn on the light in the area.- The flashlight as a separate item. Could've just left it as a default feature.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR I would say this game is really interesting mainly for platforming/metroidvania exploration. Just disappointing as a sequel. I personally can't recommend it because I think it misses a ton of potential for this reason. Have completed this game around two and a half times including other platforms but am distinctly mixed. Memorable more for its cool, unique art and music. If you hoped for "just Axiom Verge but improved and expanded upon" this is not that. With hope that the game would still turn out good because its predecessor left an amazing impression, it's a bittersweet experience to play this. There is really awesome stuff here. Melee weapon+ boomerang gameplay as well as hacking alongside it/ offering many interactions with different enemies is really, really promising, but much like the storytelling & plot, throughout the game does not seem to flesh itself out to a satisfactory amount before the game abruptly ends.Scenery & backgrounds are pretty & cool, but the colour palettes that take up most of the screentime can appear bland after a while, in contrast to AV1's vibrant alien setting. Personally I think a lot of the soundtrack is gorgeous, inspired, and even entrancing. Some really awesome work on the soundtrack in my opinion. Overall though, I find myself a lot more frustrated with the pace of the exploration, dying repeatedly to certain combinations of enemies & platforming but still somewhat being able to brute force through obstacles or ignoring threats altogether, etc. Hacking is really interesting but combat isn't very satisfying because of this. This may also hurt the exploration with feelings of early-game sluggishness and requiring a few hours before things get only sort of satisfying. Skill ceiling/minimal deaths certainly requires a different set of skills than AV1, but I do not find myself nearly as drawn to this game enough to get similar satisfaction out of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed Axiom Verge and was excited to find out there is a new one to play. Surprisingly, the game is very different from AV1 apparently due to being based off of Castlevania instead of Metroid. TBH I hated it at first, but decided to push on because I was curious if it was going to get better.Well it did. I'm not sure exactly what made it really endearing to me but around 3 hours in it just sort of clicked, and I really started to love it even more than the first one. There is a scene where you stand at the edge of the world near an ocean, and you can really see how bizarrely the world is structured. There is a song that plays in this area called "White Sand City." Hearing and seeing that at the same time hit home to me that this isn't just a sequel to AV1, its an evolution of that game's soul. Moments like that are special in gaming. If you know, you know.The music and art design work together fantastically to communicate an odd feeling that you can't really put into words but permeates both Axiom Verge games. The story is somehow even more strange than the first game and even more bold in the big-brain sci-fi ideas department. The beginning is difficult, but just like in AV1 you end up horrendously overpowered very quickly and the abilities are far more interesting and useful than in AV1. That is NOT a diss on AV1.Go into this one with an open mind and some patience and you will be rewarded.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great metroidvania.Stellar exploration.  Two overlaid fully fleshed out maps to jump back and forth between. Much, much, much better than the first game's obtuse level design. Sublime.Stellar music.  Hopping from zone to zone with quick travel and the music evolves abruptly and seamlessly.Combat exists is easy and is not a focus.  Frankly, I wish more modern  metroidvanias toned down the combat in favor of puzzles/exploration.Story/Lore: its a hot mess.  Main protagonist feels like she's a protagonist from an Ayn Rand novel,  some of the writing in the English version clearly wasn't edited by a native English speaker.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: People who criticize this title are really not fair with this game.They were hoping for a sequel being more like a copy paste of the first and if this what they'd got, they would have complained it was the same all over again.Anyway, the game is good, it's a well thought metroidvania, there is no real boss fight as in classic metroidvania but instead axed it on exploration and there is a new light "rpg element" where you can collect sort of skill points and increase stats like health, attack, ... how you see fit.I heard Thomas Happ wanted to do some kind fantasy metroidvania but stayed in a science-fiction world. As a result, the  game is mainly melee fighting, it works pretty well, it's different than guns but it isn't bad.Gameplay wise, it works, nothing to say, just like the first one, controls are responsive and exploring is pretty fun. You can set reminders on the map and mark the area where you should return to inspect something once you get the correct power and it's welcomed. I used that feature a bit late and I ended with 92% items collected as a result when I was hoping to 100% it. Length wise, As you can see, I took 18h to complete it but I explored a lot and turned in circle to find how to get to some places a bunch of times. The game isn't really long but this is correct for a metroidvania.I felt like you were getting new powers crazy fast which isn't a bad thing and I could appreciate having almost no boss.Graphics are pretty cool, same quality as the first game, at one point you also go back to 8 bit graphics instead of 16.The music is equivalent to the first game, it's pretty entertaining. Some tracks are really cool some other I don't like that much and I had the same feeling during the first game. Some people say the first game had better graphics and better soundtrack, I don't think so, the game very much succeeds at what it's trying to be.The story is somewhat linked to first game but you do not have to play it to understand what's happening. It's rather complex but easier to understand than in the first game.To sum it up without spoilers, you're a woman going after her daughter, you use a mysterious portal and you find yourself in a new world invaded by drones and machines. Doesn't sound great? Well, there's more to it and it's hard to talk about the details without spoiling it and ruining the pleasure to discover each and every events.And while the game, the story and the music can feel familiar and like you've seen/heard it somewhere already (especially if you played axiom verge 1), it always succeeds to add something new.But all in all, it's a really fun and great game. Highly recommend, especially if you liked the first.***Now, a bit of spoiler warning about powers***At one point, you will be able to turn yourself into a drone and that drone will get super useful skills to explore the landscape. As a result, I spent most of my time as a drone rather than a human. This can be a bit weird / disappointing but it's still enjoyable.You also get the power to hack enemies and occasionally some doors, it's not explained very well but you need to invest points in your skill tree to hack higher level doors (the skill, at the moment, only mention hacking enemies)This was a bit confusing. Also, I saw some people playing like crazy with hacking, for my part, I rarely used it because it did cost too much energy and was only temporary + it was faster to just attack them.There are some pretty cool stuff you can do with hacking though and you need to use it two or three times to access hidden objects.*** Spoiler Alert on secrets which you might not notice ***During the game, you will see some stones with an eye drawn on it. (mark a reminder on the map each time you see one)You should use your "sight" skill next to it which usually reveal hidden portals. The stone is always an indication there is a secret nearby but for some stones, in red, you will see 8 big arrows (4 top, 4 bottom) appearing.Just input the "code" near the stone (by reading the arrows left to right, top to bottom) and it will modify the landscape to allow you to reach a secret item. The game contains many secrets, they're fun to track and some are really hard to find. I had to google some of them (luckily the game has coordinates so it's not too hard to ask about which secrets you're looking for)
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Good Metroidvania but very annoying music and sounds, I played almost in mute!It's not a sequel of Axiom Verge 1 but it's hinted that is slightly connected through a couple of journal and machines you are going to see.Lots of coming and going like this genre is used to with nice secrets to discover, but the combat is quite clunky when facing this modular mini bosses that always tend to be a hair too far for your hits to connect, nevertheless there is nothing difficult regarding combat, only the positioning.I squeezed 13 hours of gameplay with 99% of the map and 92% of the items, so I was quite happy with the length of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Late game Update: The game comes together by the end. The cosmic body horror starts to come into play. And most importantly I finally figured out how the game actually functions and in that regard it is actually very well made: Also after even 10 hours of play I had not a single crash, which is probably since I still have Win 7 on my PC. So my guess is that Win 10 or 11 just f***ed something up in the recent updates or similar. Original Text: If you were to play Axiom Verge 2 before 1 you would be forgiven for thinking that AV2 was the first game developed by a single person and AV1 was the more refined 2nd game he made after. Its still an ok game, I do not regret purchasing... buuut The tonal shift is weird. AV1 had a very dark tone to it that fitted the eldrich horrors you face. I mean the line "I think I am beyond fear already" stuck with me for the longest time. Here the opening sequence is very clunky and feels very off beat. We casually drown and get revived. And it doesn't seem to faze the protagonist one bit. And all that normal green nature doesn't really give you the same feeling like the Metroid inspired tile set. Gameplay wise, you don't get a gun but only an awful boomerang (which doesn't mean that the enemies in the game aren't still best disposed of by ranged attacks with most being flying enemies) So there isn't actually a melee focused stealth gameplay here even though the vision cones and stealth bushes might suggest that this was the intention. And then there are the bugs. My screenshot folder can be renamed bug report at this point. My drone has 2 hacking abilities that block me from correctly assigning the abilities correctly as the bugged one cant be reassigned or removed. Restarting doesn't fix it and I already have overwritten my savefile. Once hacking glitched out and was stuck in an endless animation. Hacked enemies turned friendly will have their AI bug out. I personally didn't experience crashes but looking at the other reviews that might be just a matter of time. In the end its still an ok game to play. The exploration is still good and some of the new hacking interactions are interesting. But this is a far worse experience than AV1.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: The vibe this game creates is substantially different from AV1, in a way that is less to my taste personally. The game is fine on its own but I would place it a couple tiers down from the original. To me it didn't feel like the rewards for exploring were as meaningful as the first, Lack of weapon variety was definitely noticed. I also found myself playing most of the game as the drone, due to mobility reasons primarily, which is fine, but it means I basically didn't interact with any of the human form character systems after the first couple hours of the game, which doesn't feel like the intended experience. I also found the ending to be somewhat anticlimactic, I was a little surprised when it ended and was expecting another couple hours of story to happen (you can put together the pieces with the lore pages, but I was still expecting to do more before the credits), the default ending cutscene feels like its setting up the final act of the game rather than putting a bow on things, but I suppose the ending of AX1 was a little similar in that regard, just in a way that felt different to me.TLDR, buy the game if you need a metroidvania fix, but don't go in expecting AV1.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: (8/10)An interesting sequel to one of the most incredible indie metroidvania's ever made.  This time the action is more close in and a bit more SOTN like, with exploration and melee combat being the primary focus.  In some ways this comes as a shock as a sequel, as the original game leaned very heavily towards the Metroid style of weapon based ranged gameplay.  This has several ramifications across the play style as you need to be more defensive and cautious, staying on top of the enemy movement patterns and beefier health pools.  This is going to push you harder to find every little secret to get enough resources to upgrade your health/combat stats and be able to push into the deeper areas of the game.The music is still just as good as ever and a real highlight of playing and finding new areas as you explore, and the graphics are a bit more 16-bit styled vs the 8 bit styling of the original game.Overall its a good game, and standing alone I think it would be more favorably reviewed, but standing on the shoulders of a giant of a game (the original Axiom Verge) this game doesn't quite live up to the bombastic nature of the first one.  I enjoyed it and I think most Metroidvania fans will as well, but it is going to have a somewhat divisive reception.

_childDocuments_.review: It's still a great game but I do feel the first game is better. There are goal indicators but these are often false friends as the way forward is obstructed by an ability you don't yet have.I still did enjoy it, overall, but not quite as much as the original AV

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game. It takes place in the same universe (heh), and follows the ideas of the original Axiom Verge with a new protagonist. The first hour or so was very familiar, but the game takes you on a new adventure that is a little uncomfortable once you think you get your bearings. This is a good thing. This is not a carbon copy of the original, but follows the ideas set up in the first game and just runs with it. It is not a long game, my first run took me just under 12 hours… but I don’t know where the time went. If you like a good platformer, a good metroidvania, do give this a shot. It will not disappoint.

_childDocuments_.review: i loved it. a lot of people say the first game is better. and, while i do agree, i feel like this game might be overlooked because of that. it shouldn't be. this game is VERY MUCH worth playing. it's story is a lot less confusing as well.another difference is the first game focused heavily on ranged weapons. this game has one or two ranged weapons, but it's focus is mostly on melee weapons. which means you're going to have to get a lot closer to your enemies. so, it's a good thing that the game's movement is very fluid. it feels so buttery smooth.another big difference is this game's greater reliance on the controllable drone. you'll face some bosses with it this time. and surprisingly, it feels pretty good. you only get one main attack with the drone, but it's pretty versatile in how you can use it. especially with some upgrades.there's even puzzles to solve here. not that the first game didn't have them, but here, they're a part of progression. not just stuff you do for hidden items. though there's plenty of that too.there's a lot to love about this game, and i'm glad i gave it a play instead of continuing to ignore it due to hearing people complain about how it's not as good as the first game. i do still prefer the first game. but this one is a worthy sequel, and i still love it. honestly, the main reason is the atmosphere. the first game is a lot creepier and twisted, the music fits that tone too. the music in this game fits as well. but i'm not as big a fan of it. i love that dark creepy tone. it's what hooked me on the original metroid, and it's what i wanted from the first game because it sought to recreate that feeling. and it did. the atmosphere of this game reminds me more of Zelda II the adventure of link. there's even a hidden powerup for one of the weapons that makes you fire beams from the dagger weapon, just like link in zelda 2.the TL;DR though, if you liked the first game, you'll probably like this one too. maybe you'll like it even more. maybe not. but it's worth playing. it's just, good.

_childDocuments_.review: Truly awful, an absolute disappointment of a sequel.If you liked Axiom Verge 1 you will probably not like Axiom Verge 2. Not long after you start the game you will get your first two weapons that are to put it charitably bad. A climbing axe which is your main damage dealer, and a boomerang that never ceases to disappoint. Neither of them will ever do enough damage to justify their existence outside of the fact that they are your only options.Axiom Verge 2 is a departure from the first game in that the first had combat as part of the focus of the gameplay. In this game you should avoid combat if you can (you can't, most enemies will chase you to the ends of the earth if they are capable). When you do have to fight (which will be often) you will find yourself without the tools for the job, enemies will get hits on you and you will find it hard to avoid that, and enemies hit rather hard for a game that seems to want you to explore and search for things rather than fight. In the end you will find that you actually don't want to explore anything because death lays just around the corner at all times, and unlike souls like games where this is also the case, the combat systems in this game aren't made to deal with the enemies.Siliconera stated in their review blurb that axiom verge makes every upgrade feel like a game changer, this is a lie. You will get upgrades to your skills, and outside of one of them, they don't seem to have any noticeable difference on your character. Perhaps I missed some, perhaps there were loads more upgrades out there for me to get, but after playing for an hour and a half I realized I wasn't going to make it to two hours. I wanted to put the game down, the game felt like it was wasting my time and it was already asking me to go through a water level for it. I wasn't about to brave the frustrating enemies that had large area of effect attacks or the small hard to hit surprisingly tanky robots that waited for me, or the mines (THOSE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ HOMING MINES) again just to find that another piece to a puzzle I wasn't interested in. My story with this game ends with a rich heartless CEO trapped in another dimension miserable and without the ability to ever truly die and quite frankly I'm happy with that.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not Metroid."Blasphemy!" I hear you cry. "Axiom Verge 1 was the best Metroid since Metroid, praise be unto it for how good a Metroid it was. A sequel does not need to follow, footprint by footprint, the path of its predecessor, no matter how good of a Metroid it was.If you are looking for Metroid and  Metroid, I implore you to look someplace else. If you wished that this game was just more Axiom Verge 1 (i.e. Metroid) and are upset that it is not, then you are upset at a car for not being a fast horse.

_childDocuments_.review: The original Axiom Verge was a surprisingly solid Metroid-like for a one-man project, with tight gameplay and juicy lore, but I felt it was held back by a couple of frustrating design decisions.  The sequel fixes literally everything that I disliked about the original, while deepening gameplay and leaning more heavily into the "breach" mechanic by having you explore two parallel worlds in tandem.  Easy recommend.That said, it's still not perfect.  The compass and quest destination system reduces a LOT of the first game's necessity for playing with a guide, but because the quest destinations show you the location of your next computer terminal and not the location of the tools you nbeed to get there, there are a few chokepoints where you still find yourself at a loss for what to do other than explore the entire (TWO entire) maps and look for spots where your most recently acquired ability might let you make progress.  I gave up and searched the Internet a few times on hitting these walls.  The game also springs a nasty surprise on you halfway through which might screw you over depending on the skill build you were using -- and because one of the aforementioned choke points is right after that surprise, you might spend much longer than you're comfortable with playing a crippled build.  On a personal level, the 8-bit music for the alternate world began grating on me pretty quickly, and short of going into settings and cranking the music down, there wasn't much to be done about it.  Little irritations like that will keep this game from going into my S-ranks (Castlevania SOTN, Hollow Knight, and Thunder Lotus' magnificent and underrated Sundered) but it remains a strong A and I'll be eager to see if the developer releases a third.Also, fans of the first should note that this has transformed from a gun-based game into primarily a melee-based game.  I thought this was fantastic, but YMMV.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game because I loved the first one but soon realized the first one is far superior. Cons: 1. No guns meaning each enemy needs to be fought in close quarters. This wouldn't be an issue if the enemies didn't kill you in 2-3 hits.2. Cheap and overpowered enemies. With only being able to melee you are severely limited with how you can approach enemies and often dying in cheap and unsatisfying ways. The enemies will often take out 75% of your health before you even get close enough to hit them. 3. This game punishes you for exploration due to problems mentioned above. This game is a huge disappointment compared to the masterpiece that was the first game. If you are enjoying this game, more power to you. But if you are expecting a similar experience to the first game, you might be in for a disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: There are some really cool ideas and mechanics in this sequel, and it's great that the series gets a chance to grow beyond the Axiom Verge 1, which seemed to build a lot of its identity around Super Metroid in terms of gameplay. If Axiom Verge is to be its own franchise, I think this is important, but I have really mixed feelings about the execution. Calling this Axiom Verge 2 seems like a mistake. It should have been marketed as a spin-off or reimagining to separate itself from the original while still connecting lore as a spiritual prequel.  Here, you get something very different, more akin to a fusion of the first Axiom Verge game, Breath of the Wild (stealth elements), and to a weird degree classic NES sequels (a complaint I have seen elsewhere about this game in terms of how different it is from the first game). Progression is still metroidvania, but it feels really weird, in the sense that some items are just in plain site (e.g., the water mobility item is just found immediately with no effort at all traversing in the water beforehand). Nothing wrong with doing metroidvania differently, but its a number of moments like this that make the game feel lazily strung together in some ways. To enjoy the mechanics, you really need to experiment with items, and recognize that combat is often not the answer. Often, hacking (a cool mechanic) is the best way to move forward (which is probably one reason why others expecting more Axiom Verge find the combat janky), so there is some interesting choice-making when navigating through areas with enemies.That being said, the combat clearly has flaws, feeling very hit or miss because of inconsistencies in difficulty progression. Random difficulty spikes occur, most frustatingly with the enemies that break out from floor tiles prior to the drone-only section of the game. The drone-only part will feel frustrating at first, but it becomes a test of your understanding of the mechanics you learned up until that point. That said, it still seems that the large reduction in health from specific enemies should have been taken into account better when designing the difficulty progression, it just seems all over the place. Late game becomes a pushover, which makes the experience feel pointless. Items are pretty cool, and after familiarizing with the inventory and skills system, I don't really have complaints about them, besides the fact that some items don't contribute much to the progression. Some of them end up being very forgettable. This actually got me stuck looking around the map for a few hours picking up extra items before the next morning when I remembered the homing boomerang and a suspicious upward tunnel I could not climb. That speaks to the beauty of the genre more than anything.What makes things particularly iffy is the "bosses". This game has a series of large enemies that serve as optional bosses, as in the case of breath of the wild, but they play out like bosses from Castlevania 2, in that they kind of just stand there and are either too OP or too easy depending on where you are in progression. There are only 2 main boss encounters otherwise, and the way they are done requires no skill whatsoever. Having infinite respawn in the fights makes them completely pointless, regardless of whether that is an element of the plot or not. The stakes feel minimal (despite the story actually having high stakes). I am not sure why this was chosen as the way to design these sections, but I have a feeling it has to do with the massive amount of health that is lost when taking damage from enemies, which would make boss fights miserable in the game's current state.I like the main map a lot, and I think the breach as a "B side" is cool, especially since they make an effort to distinguish the environments from how they are the main map (unlike Castlevania SOTN and Harmony of Dissonance alternative castles, and other instances of the alternative dimension trope in many metroidvanias). It doesn't end up being too confusing here either. That said, the execution still feels iffy. It just doesn't feel like a cohesive universe, but rather disjointed. It doesn't help that music genres are all over the place in terms of volume and style, and rather tone-deaf to the heavy subject matter of the story when you enter many areas of the breach. Some of the vocals also seem way too loud compared to the rest of the music, but maybe that is sound system dependent. Even though that took me out of the experience, there are a few tracks I loved from the OST, particularly the base camp area below the glacier, the first climb on the mountain (breach version is a little obnoxious though), and underwater breach version. What makes this sad is that the core story idea was really interesting, but the endings come across as rushed and uninteresting. I remember seeing this game release to immediate backlash, followed by a more recent surge of people defending the game without much constructive criticism. I think the backlash is fair as a response to what seemed to be promised as more Axiom Verge. That's what happens when you put a 2 in your title. That said, I think a real identity for this franchise is starting to shape here beyond Metroid-inspired gameplay, and I really hope the ideas excel in future Axiom Verge titles!
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Now that I've done everything the game has to offer I can give a full review.1. AtmosphereThe world doesn't feel alien except some small segments. This may be a draw for some, but for me it feels off-putting since I was a huge fan of the aesthetics of the original. The seemingly Indian inspired music really never sat well with me personally. Didn't like it in Axiom verge 1, don't like it here. A bad experience with a stalker puts me off of it. May not be an issue for some.2. CharactersNo Trace. Not a fan of the new protagonist. She's a major global corporate CEO buying out people who are actually talented, and she seems to hate people in general. What's there to love? 3. Skill tree May not be something which is well liked by many who play metroidvanias. I like to explore so I can unlock new things to explore more (creating a nice and simple feedback loop), such as the original or hollow knight. Much less a fan of unlocking a base ability and upgrading them like in this game and Ori and the blind forest (the latter of which is more forgivable). The only things that are substantial for upgrading with skill points are the hacking strength and max health.4. Exploration Level design feels bland simply because there are so few tools to explore with for a huge portion of the game. The mobility in this game is interesting for a metroidvania, but it isn't great or terrible.The early game exploration options are not good, but they expand and become somewhat satisfying in the late midgame and on. The drone is the most entertaining tool to explore with and hacking is not particularly interesting, other than the fact you can't hack things as much as you want as it takes ammunition to perform certain hacks which is probably off-putting to many.5. Bugs Lots of crashing. (Edit: patch fixed as of 8/12/22)6. The weaponry and combat. There are only two bosses you need to fight and only one of those you fight traditionally.The combat in this game leaves a LOT to be desired. Few weapons, fewer weapon upgrades, and almost everything requires you to get in the face of enemies which can sometimes literally snipe you from across the room. Boomerang, while mid-ranged, is not a great weapon even using its nanite abilities. Your character has very little health naturally and until you get most of the upgrades or backtrack the whole map every time you get a major exploration upgrade you will be weak until near endgame.7. StoryThe story is pretty unsatisfactory. The main character swears in practically every other statement she makes and she gives off the whole "I want to be a man with breasts" vibe for most of the game rather than leaning into ANY feminine traits.  The only decent parts of the story are how it relates to the first game, and those references aren't particularly prevalent.8. MAJOR GRIPEAccessibility options. the only thing in there which I can see as being not made to detract from the game is upping contrast for platforms to make them easier to see. If that was the only thing I wouldn't care. That said, there are three other options. Alter damage your character takes, the damage your character deals, and the speed of the game. You can turn off taking damage. You can make most enemies die without effort. You can slow down the game to the point reflexes of a sloth can still let you play perfectly. AND YOU CAN EARN EVERY ACHIEVEMENT WITH THEM ON. In fact there's an achievement for actually USING one of these options.It kills any sense of achievement if a literal two year old with no effort and a lot of time on their hands would be able to get every achievement...Speaking of which, the speedrun achievement Overclocked gives you 6 HOURS to beat the game when even playing casually you can beat it in two.Final judgement. Not the worst game I've played, but I know what Happ is capable of, and seeing this just makes me feel like his heart wasn't really in it. I would call this a definitive disappointment. Combat particularly.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- Controls are great.- The game is rock solid (aside from some issues on Steam release which were fixed the same day).- Exploration and "puzzles" are enjoyable.- More world-building with some cross-over with the first game. There's some Weird S**t going on! It makes me want another sequel just for more story.Neutral:- Bosses don't gate progression. You can ignore them if you want.- Hacking doesn't feel as important as you would think it should be, and straight up doesn't apply to about half the game.Cons:- Almost all of the secret items are just multiple copies of the same exact item, which stops being exciting quickly.  The first game had a TON of weapons in the secret areas that made looking for secrets a lot more fun (even if a lot of those weapons weren't particularly useful, they were different).- Dark areas aren't fun except in horror games. This isn't a horror game.- Remember that one song with the "singing" (annoying wailing) in the first game that didn't fit with the other songs?  This game inverted that pattern; it's mostly (slightly better but still annoying) singing and only a few chiptune songs.

_childDocuments_.review: Axiom Verge 2 does not get as much love as Axiom Verge, for a variety of reasons, but the game does not deserve the hate it gets from some of the other reviewers. It is quite good and worth playing.First off, as everyone points out: this game is very different from its predecessor. If you only want to play a continuation of the first game, you will be disappointed. But by not following in the direct footsteps of its parent, the developer has made a much tighter game with better pacing and plot, while at the same time making the world more open. The world is easier to navigate and feels more lived-in due to the more detailed backgrounds and the interactions with other characters. Additionally, you can play AV2 without having played the first game (all the allusions to the first game are basically Easter eggs).The game is very exploration-heavy, moreso than AV1. The world is both easier and harder to navigate: it's easier to get around, but there're more nooks and crannies to search. Combat has been replaced from run-and-gun to a more leisurely hack-and-slash style. *I* think this is mostly an improvement, because the multitude of weapons in AV1 was ridiculous, but YMMV based on preference. The boss battles are also both better and worse: there are more minibosses, but fewer big baddies. This is a consequence of this game being much more open-ended than the first. If Axiom Verge plays primarily like classic NES Metroid, then Axiom Verge 2 plays primarily like an 8-bit Hollow Knight.Axiom Verge is well worth playing for Metroidvania fans, even if you haven't played the first game. If you like your metroidvanias to mostly be an adventure game with occasional boss battles, you will enjoy this. But, if you are a die-hard fan of the first game, you may be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Axiom Verge 2 is a litte bit shorter than Axiom Verge 1 but I still think I got my money's worth. Axiom Verge 2 is the right game for you if you enjoy Metroidvanias (2D platformer with a focus on exploration and finding pieces of equipment / abilities so you can cross into new territories... and if you don't mind a bit of running into (temporary) dead ends and having to do a bit of backtracking).There are references to AV1 but you don't need to have played it to enjoy AV2. Combat has more focus on melee and is easier than in AV1.Some said they liked AV1 better, but I think that can mostly be explained with different expectations. Coming into AV1 nobody knew what hey could expect, coming into AV2... well, some things are similar but some are different and so is the general vibe, but it's still great.Thanks, Tom Happ, I really enjoyed it.

_childDocuments_.review: Gonna paraphrase Red Letter Media here: Is it as good as the first? No. Should you still play it? Yes.It fixes some of the first game's (admittedly minor) gripes, like how the different areas all looked more or less the same, and how you could only bookmark two points on the map per area. As far as improvements go, that's really about it.It carries over a lot of the good points of the first game as well. Most of the power ups aren't just there to help you pass a barrier or two--you'll use them extensively for the rest of the game. Some castletroid games mess this up. On your first playthrough, there will be times when you aren't sure where to go, and then you get that wave of satisfaction when you finally figure it out. Happ's outstanding retro graphics and sound shine as bright as they ever did. Not crazy about the vocals, though. New for this game is the parallel dimension mechanic, which requires you to think between two worlds to tackle some obstacles. This is implemented well, imho.The game's plot is engaging and leads *just enough* into the first while still being its own story. It's a little easier to follow this time, as it plays fewer mind games and doesn't hide 2/3 of the readables behind translation codes.As for where the game falls a little flat, the biggest problem, as you've probably heard by now, is the combat. Instead of offering you a crapload of guns, there are a handful of melee weapons and a boomerang that gets upgraded as you progress. A lot of the enemies take a stupid amount of hits from either weapon to go down until you upgrade your offense using upgrade points you collect around the gameworld, and sometimes you'll find yourself cheesing the boomerang's kind of half-baked midair guidance to kill them from a distance... which takes even more hits. Boring. The boss fights are the other thing that people criticize. All but two are completely optional, meaning you can just avoid them altogether if you want. And if you do fight these optional bosses, they really aren't that hard at all. Very little strategy or pattern recognition involved. The non-optional fights aren't exactly Dark Souls either. I should also point out that the hacking mechanic doesn't quite meet its full potential. It's not worthless, as you'll figure out which enemies are worth the time to hack and which aren't, but there are only a few times when hacking is necessary to progress. Overall, I still recommend the game. It's another slice of Axiom Verge pie, just with less-fresh ingredients.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I was hesitant to try Axiom Verge 2 due to its mixed reception, but grabbing it in the bundle with the first game (mostly played on Switch) I was pleasantly surprised with the game. Admittedly - I didn't enjoy the first hour or so due to how radically different it was from the first game, some decisions annoyed me (Skill trees - not a fan of them in Vanias.) Background rooms to explore, harder to see/navigate mini map. Eventually the game clicked and I found myself enjoying it a lot and beat the rest of the game in a single sitting, I have some gripes - Drone usage is a bit much, less interesting abilities in comparison to the first game, less weapons - Whilst for some this could be a good thing, I do prefer how many you had access to in AV1 and how unique some of them were - hacker gun, ion beam, flamethrower, SMG that shoots ice, richocet -focused gun, etc. They were neat, meanwhile AV2 is just 'Axe, Axe2 and Axe 3' with Axe 2 being the best out of the 3 due to its faster and more lethal attacks.Overall, yeah I'd say AV2's worth a buy - just hope that AV3 is a sequel to both games or something, I don't want another prequel I want to see what happened to Trace and Indra not a third entirely new protagonist.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming staright from Axiom Verge 1, at first this game felt a lot different, but the core gameplay is still the same.A lot of things improved overall. There is less weapon variety, but that makes getting each of them more important, and they feel more unique as well. Most of the abilities felt amazing to use. Secrets were a bit easier to find in my opinion, but that might be just experience from the first game.The map improvemet and the ability to fast travel made the experience way less daunting and much more enjoyable. The lore and story are very well written out, and there were lots of references to the previous game.What I missed were the bossfights. You can skip most of the bosses, and a lot of them feel more like minibosses compared to the ones in Axiom Verge 1. They were way too easy and not that imaginative.Accessibility settings are a cool addition, but I missed a set difficulty option that you can choose from at the start.Overall a really solid addition to the series, would highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I was initially not on board with the new direction this took compared to the first game, but that changed after I had found enough of the lore to understand the context of the new world and characters. Like the first one, incredibly subtle with the worldbuilding - I'm convinced that even most people who praise this aspect of these games don't even grasp half of what's going on. Heck, most people don't even realize what happened to the main character's own daughter. Not to mention endless fractal vassal universes, programmable afterlives, or the wide-ranging implications for what actually happens in the first game. Very postmodern in the sense that what is real is non-existent, or so far removed from what we see that it doesn't matter.At this point I don't even care if Tom Happ doesn't make any more games specifically, as long as he gives me more of this deranged multiverse abomination
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: The early game is a bit linear for my tastes, but the game isn't telling you where to go its just funneling you down a certain path and there is little that can be explored outside of the main objectives. It opens up a decent amount afterwards, but by the time things feel like they're just getting going you're 2-3 hours from beating the game. If you go for 100% then it'll take longer; however I didn't feel all that inclined to do so. Most of the collectibles are skill points which you can use to make upgrades to your character. Nothing on the skill tree is all that rewarding so I never felt too inclined to max it out. There are two weapons that you get to use, an ax and a boomerang. I couldn't figure out a way to really use these as you have to be pretty close to the enemy to use either and its almost impossible to dodge some of the attacks from certain enemies. By the time that they show up you have plenty of health but its still annoying. There are some interesting abilities, but the menu to switch between them sucks and you have to click down on the right stick to activate some of them which is a bit clunky (you can remap your controls, but I shouldn't have to, especially when the left trigger does not get used for anything until the last hour of the game). There also aren't that many of abilities. By the end of the game you don't feel that powerful like you do in other games of this style. I felt like I was in the late midgame when I beat the final boss.Speaking of bosses they are pretty much optional (except for the final and one or two others). This is not a bad thing, but they're either completely broken and annoying to fight or waaaaay too easy. That's also not the worst thing in the world because you don't play this sort of game for boss fights; however, I didn't feel particularly challenged by any portion of the game and I feel like a lack of competent boss fights was partially to blame.One thing that was not lacking was the story. The lore is pretty good and reading the logs lying around was enjoyable. It was interesting to learn more about the world and whatnot. I did feel that the ending was a bit lacking and it didn't really answer all of the questions that I had.I do recommend the game, but don't go into it expecting a metroid like experience or even an experience like the first game. It's a decent game and I enjoyed playing it a lot. It was the only game I played for the past week, just don't expect too much. Maybe wait for a sale rather than paying full price.
