_childDocuments_.review: Got around to playing Axiom Verge 2 on my Steam Deck. This game was originally an Epic Games exclusive, but is now available here on Steam and on other platforms. Axiom Verge 2 is another Metroidvania which continues to deliver the same otherworldly allure that the original game did. I do have a slight preference for the first game, but you do not need to play the first game to enjoy this one, as the story is not directly connected. You'll have to pay attention to the lore to see how the two games are connected. The lore man.... it's captivating.... it demands deep dives and game theory-style videos. I love it.Here you play as Indra who travels to the Antarctic to save her daughter, and gets entrapped into a huge mystery. Part of the mystery involves the dual world mechanic, as there is the main overworld, and the breach world, a world of NES-style graphics and banger 8-bit music. I liked the use of the two worlds with plenty of puzzles to solve that involve traveling between both worlds. I also enjoyed the expanded use of the drone, and found myself using that more than running around on foot.Even though this game is solid, I think this game needed to be given a subtitle instead of being labeled Axiom Verge "2". That could have helped temper fan exceptions while keeping the Axiom Verge name in marketing. Also, the combat is really awkward. It's hard for me to put into words what is awkward about it.Count me in the group of people ready to buy and play whatever Thomas Happ releases next.

_childDocuments_.review: The first game was remarkable in a lot of ways, setting high expectations for this sequel; so, how did it go? "Badly", many will say. By this, I suspect they actually mean "differently", as though some kind of human being designed this game, and did so with the intention of creating more than just a glorified level pack for the previous instalment.The map is supposedly more confusing now. I, upon playing, found it to be greatly improved. Instead of flat color, it now displays the actual features of the regions you've explored; if there was a big statue of a guy with the body of a lion, you'll be able to find it by looking. You also don't need to switch between regions before you can view them, they're all just one big, connected world. You can also place and remove map markers anywhere, not just at your current location... and as many as you like, not just two per area. How is this more confusing?Well, alright, it's not exactly one big, connected world... there are two big connected worlds, and you do switch between them; the Overworld (more or less regular reality) and the Breach (where things get weird)!Each has its own look, sound and feel: The Overworld being more somber, beautiful and relatively friendly to humanoid life, along with various hostiles... and the remnants of a culture resembling ancient Assyria or thereabouts, parallell development sort of thing. It's very sciencey and more importantly it has a cool, distinctive look, so why question it? Just let it wash over you.By contrast, the Breach requires a drone to explore, looks and sounds a lot more oldschool - as well as more chaotic - and occasionally teases you with glimpses of the familiar from Axiom Verge 1. Hints, suggestions...The game's lore is much the same. Perspectives, suspicions, beliefs. Very little is known to be factual. Which is kind of nice, really. People like Dark Souls because it doesn't just plainly state this and that; understanding what is going on is a much more active process of piecing things together from what you know and suspect.The combat is different now. I personally enjoyed it, though... some of the pacing could use work. Certain weapons are granted rather late in the game, with the unfortunate consequence that you barely get to enjoy them. This is not ideal. Other weapons, however, are in for a good chunk of the respectable run time (especially if you go secret-hunting a lot), and some of them are quite fun to use. Melee attacks are your mainstay now; at a distance, you get a boomerangy thing which isn't great, but has its uses.You get skill points you can use to upgrade various abilities, including health and the strength of melee or ranged attacks. There are a good number of skill point pickups strewn along your path - or hidden about it - and by the end, I felt more than powerful enough to deal with what dangers emerged. Translation: Game too easy? Rush through faster! Game too hard? Go find more power-ups. Or play however you like, but the wiggle room is there for enjoyment to occur.Some of the platforming (especially to reach tricky secrets) can be very nintendo-y, but that's understandable, given the series' deep roots in that sphere of game design from the era when people were convinced that "the harder a game is to get through, the better value for money it is". Thankfully, Axiom Verge 2 has checkpoints instead of the traditional blatant progress robbery of the original NES era. Sometimes you get bumped back a ways from where you were, but you can eventually unlock fast travel to any revival site - you may want to save most of your backtracking for after you get that.This game is not perfect, but I respect the changes made and the chances taken compared to the original. Whether you agree things improved, or feel they declined, or see it all as a "sidegrade" which is neither better nor worse, merely different - games will not get better if all the developers do, if all they are  to do, is copy-paste from the previous instalment(s).This game has its own story to tell, its own journey and experience to savor. It is a work of art, lovingly rendered, and imperfect as all of ourselves. It is a challenge to overcome, and a set of riddles to make sense of. It is a pleasant pastime. It is many things.In particular, it is a game I enjoyed and would recommend to platforming exploration fans and fans of the first game. If you go in expecting something different, you shouldn't suffer too much from the changes.

_childDocuments_.review: Axiom Verge titles are slowly becoming one of my favourite series to play, the world and it's soundtrack is just amazing, Axiom Verge really shows within it's story/gameplay and the world just how much time and effort Thomas Happ has put into Axiom Verge as a series and he really shows how much he loves creating MetroidVanias. I for one am a huge fan of these games and 2 whilst it might not be considered "Better" by a lot of players, it does however come with it's own set of perks that make this standout compared to it's predecessor. I really liked how Happ has made Axiom 2 feel like Metroid Prime 2: Echoes with the need of constantly having to enter the "breach" to continue further in the game and even for exploration purposes. Without spoiling anything I love that this game starts and instantly feels like it has nothing to do with Trace and by reading notes and stuff through exploring it is nice to see how Happ is world building for Indra and how it all adds together in the end by showing you where this game lies within it's timeline.Axiom Verge 2 in my opinion is harder than Axiom 1 because you are forced into Melee combat over ranged and that's okay imo, every enemy can be avoided and can be walked by, bosses are not mandatory and I liked that as I was aloud to come and go when I pleased to defeat the enemies in my own time. The one perk Axiom Verge 2 has is if you find yourself to be struggling at any point just access the Accessibility settings and adapt the gameplay to however you want, Do you want tough boss fights? Do you want them to be easy so you can just go to the next area? It's all there and I love that this is an option for anyone who isn't the best at either the combat or platforming, so that's a thumbs up from me.The music in this series of games are just inspiring to me, I really like how the style changes so heavily from the 1st game and it still feels like it fits the setting, some are annoying and I don't expect every piece of music to be amazing, but they all fit the environments they are in and I like that. I just love Techno and Happ really gets some good songs off throughout. Keep it up and i'll keep buying your games is all i'm saying. Really hope that there will be a Third game down the line, These are the type of gems that gaming needs and I think everyone should try them. 9/10 Really really enjoyed Axiom Verge 2 and I will encourage anyone to try them and to enjoy them!

_childDocuments_.review: I both Can and Can't recommend Axiom Verge 2.  The game has a tremendous amount of upsides... and a tremendous amount of downsides.                                                               Pros:+The Standalone Story is great!+-The super varied combat system lets you tackle situations in a good variety of ways... sometimes. The problem is that most enemy placements end up being very repetitive, and when they aren't then the enemies end up getting in guaranteed hits anyways. The game has such a huge problem with trying to make interesting enemy placements that the Devs gave THREE Mega-heals that heal 50% of your insanely huge health pool... Speaking of which...+The backgrounds and stage-art look significantly better than Axiom Verge 1.+Is a great Stand-alone game.                                                              Cons:-You are way too tanky for no reason. The game's combat is so poorly designed that instead of trying to fine tune it, the Devs went "screw it, the player won't care about taking guaranteed hits if they have a metric F**k-ton of health."-The story and gameplay pacing is bad in quite a lot of areas with not enough time given to certain aspects of Indra's character and *too* much time spent with little to no characterization of her.-Not a good sequel. The themes and world introduced in the 1st game are not expanded upon or hinted at. This game only shares a name and 6-ish journal entries about Trace and the themes present in Axiom Verge 1.-Very often there will be an upgrade and as a player you want to use this upgrade to explore the world more but that upgrade can only be used in specific areas that scream "USE ME, USE THE SUPER EXPLODEY BOMB". This would be fine, but there's so MANY upgrades like this that you'll very often run into every possible side-path before finding the ONE area that actually continues the story,-The enemy variety is weirdly lacking, even towards the end of the game. There are only 11 enemy types in the entire game:   1. drone that runs and zaps  2. Walker with big legs that shoots minigun... and sometimes zaps.   3. bird that shoots  4. Fake block Shuriken  5.Anenome Tendril Robot  6. Tentacle monster  7. Robo Spider  8. Spartan Drone spawner  9. Flying thing that shoots downward.  10. Things that stay on the walls and crawl around on them  11. BossesAnd until you get halfway through the game, most of these enemy types are **not** present. so as a player you better get used to killing #1 and #2 in most rooms... if you even want to do combat at all. Where A.V.1 made combat a forced part of gameplay(where enemies would outright stop the player if they weren't dealt with), A.V.2. makes combat... not even worth it. There is only one required boss to beat the game, and that's the final boss.-----------------Overall I would recommend the game, but not to fans of the original...

_childDocuments_.review: This game was 10x more enjoyable for me than the first game, the choice to focus more on exploration was the right choice in my opinion.  people on here are mentioning a lack of boss fights(which is true), but they were the worst part of the first game for me so i didn't mind the change at all. The melee combat is simpler than the ranged combat of the first game, but this was not a major downside for me because of the focus on exploration. all in all it is more castlevania than metroid, with a much heavier focus on exploration rather than combat, if you liked the first game for the combat and boss fights, you will be disappointed, if you enjoyed the exploration and world more, this game builds upon that wonderfully.edit: Just finished the game. The ending is sort of disappointing and abrupt, but i don't think it takes away from the overall experience much

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the game. Yes, it's different than the first one, but no less of an evolution of the games it was based on. Like others said, the first was more Metroid (combat and backtracking) while this one was more Zelda 2 and Castlevania (more exploring and less combat). Most modern "metroidvanias" lean heavily into the Metroid style, so I can understand why some people would be disappointed if they didn't play a lot of the older games.I think the negative reviews have some valid points, but I think many of them are overly dramatic and critical and might turn people away who would otherwise enjoy the game (like me). Here are my comments:• This game is not very hard; it's just very open and non-linear, allowing you to encounter areas you're not ready for yet. It's more Zelda 2 than Metroid. This is one of the things I actually like about the game, unlike most modern metroidvanias that lock off the entire world until you get the one magic upgrade that allows you to progress to the next closed off area. In Axiom Verge 2, you can explore most of the world, while the ugprades generally allow you to progress into areas of the game that move the story forward. I think this is a really underappreciated aspect of the game's design, and I wish more games did it.• If it is too hard in places, there are Accessibility settings that you can turn on and off at any time, to do things like crank your damage way up, or the damage the enemies do way down, or slow the game down. I wish more games did this (Rogue Legends 2, Hades, and this game are great for it.) My seven year old managed to beat most of this game because I set it 70% enemy damage. If he can do it, you can do it.• The game is also very generous with upgrade points, there's practically one or two in every room, so you can always explore a little to upgrade health or damage if you're having trouble. I had a lot of points left over at the end of the game, so it's not like you have to grind for them.• Despite its openness, I rarely was unsure what to do next (I had to look up how to get the last story upgrade though). I'm the kind of softcore gamer that likes quest icons and pathfinding, and I think this game had plenty. Any time you progress the story, it adds a new icon to the map so you know where to go next if you want to move the story forward. Almost every room has secrets or things in it that you can find through the game, and the map design is constantly steering you back towards revisiting places you've been before by unlocking shortcuts, but it never felt like "backtracking". There's also plenty of fast travel points, so you can move quickly around the world.• Melee is fine, and early in the game, you get upgrades for strong ranged charge attacks. Like the negative reviews say, there are a few enemies that are simply impossible to avoid taking damage from, but they're only in 3-5 rooms out of the entire huge game. It's 30 seconds of frustration out of an entire 10 hours of fun. If it bothers you that much, you can temporarily turn enemy damage down. The entire rest of the game melee is adequate; combat is not the focus.• I played on Steam Deck, which was great. No other technical issues, except for one crash. There's plenty of save points, so it was not a big deal.• My one minor complaint with this game (even more so than the first one) is that the creator came up with this absolutely brilliant and captivating scifi world and philosophical story about the nature of reality, time, and consciousness, but then makes it so subtle and hard to piece together that I expect most people will not get it. It also ties in very heavily to the first game's story, which I hadn't played in years, so that made it harder to track. I only understand the plot because I dug through reddit for timelines and supplementary material that others pieced together on Reddit. I'm not a big story person in games generally, but I love the concepts so much and would even read novels set in this world (Peter Watts could do it justice). I just wish the game itself did a better job of exploring it because it's so unique and fascinating.Overall, the price is worth it for 10 hours of compelling gameplay, and I loved it enough to 100% the items and map. If you're looking for another Metroid game, you might be mixed on it. If you were fond of old school Zelda 2, Castlevania 2+, or other games like that, I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Many consider Axiom Verge 2 inferior to the original. After playing both games back to back, I strongly disagree. AV2 is a big improvement over the original in many areas:- Very satisfying exploration. Original AV had many obscure hidden areas which you'd never find without a walkthrough. AV2's exploration feels much more logical, relying on observation and reasoning. Fast travel system makes the experience far less tiring compared to AV1.- Art style. Original AV had a distinct 8-bit style which was minimalist to the point of being jarring. AV2 upgrades it to 16-bit. The sprites and environments are more detailed. Color palettes masterfully use subtle colors. The cyber-Sumerian theme is awesome.- Music. Just like the art style, the music is much more lush and organic. The inclusion of traditional instrumentation fits the Sumerian theme well. 8-bit style music featured in breach is less memorable though.- Combat is a downgrade from AV1, true. Gone are the varied ranged weapons, you're basically stuck with a melee attack and the boomerang for the entire game. However, I feel that criticizing combat too heavily is unfair since it is not the game's main focus.- Boss fights. Another often criticized area. Bosses are optional and are sometimes too easy. But I must remind you that AV1's late-game bosses were a mindless button-mashing experience without any strategy involved. And if you played on hard and did not find certain weapons, you could even softlock yourself. With that in mind, skippable or easy bosses are actually a huge improvement.Bottom line: must-play if you enjoy exploration and willing to overlook simplistic combat.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: While not a Hollow Knight-level Metroidvania game, Axiom Verge 2 certainly is a noteworthy one. The story is one I wouldn't mind seeing adapted to the silver screen. The controls are easy to learn, given the rebinding feature within the game's options menu, granting you access to your favorite keyboard setup. The items given to you are an upgrade from the first Axiom Verge, which is not a low bar by any means, though I do wish there was a long-range weapon for some of the enemies. My biggest complaint would be the vastness of the map. It feels rather grandiose, and there were times where I found myself lost, merely to stumble upon the correct way, which I could have done all along if I had known the path was there. However, once I did find it, I found myself enjoying the new areas.All in all, I would give this game a solid 7/10 stars. A good game, but not quite great. I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the Metroidvania genre, lore-heavy story, and/or a good, solid 8-bit adventure.Looking forward to Axiom Verge 3, should there be one.

_childDocuments_.review: I think Axiom Verge 2 is just as great as Axiom Verge 1. It is also a VERY different game from the first Axiom Verge both in themes and gameplay. Axiom Verge 1 takes heavy inspiration from Metroid with feelings of loneliness and being in a very alien world with a biomechanical setting. AV1 also focuses more on ranged combat with different types of bullets.AV2's aesthetic is much more bright, with most of the map taking place outdoors in more Earthlike settings (snowy mountains, desert plains, etc.) and a Mesopotamian theme. The theme is more about creation and life, compared to the dead world of AV1. I think the music is great but is way more energetic and airy with a middle eastern/indian flair. The gameplay itself focus way more on melee combat with your main ranged option being a slower boomerang compared to a gun. The story itself to me was just a good as AV1's story, just as heavy and leaves you pondering and trying to connect the dots with the first game. I thought the map layout was also pretty good, with a fun swapping to different world maps mechanic to get around obstacles and find secrets. I don't believe the game is very hard, but AV2 also has some accessibility options like lowering the damage you take or increasing the damage you do if you find yourself struggling.If you go into Axiom Verge 2 hoping it will be exactly like the first you may be disappointed, but to me both games stand among the great metroidvanias and I look forward to the next one.

_childDocuments_.review: Axiom Verge 2 is an enjoyable game, it was relatively quick to complete with about 10 hours to get to the ending. In order to better convey my opinions about this game, I'll explain my thoughts through answering these questions:1) How does Axiom Verge 2 compare to Axiom Verge 1?AV2 has the same hallmarks as AV1 when it comes to theme and genre; its a metroidvania with a focus on unconventional power-ups. Much like its predecessor, Axiom Verge 2 also lightly explores the ideas of what it is to be human and uses its gameplay to convey that narrative.Graphically, AV2 has more elaborate sprite art and beautiful animation for the especially large creatures and bosses that roam the world. The Background vistas are also very well done, but pale in comparison to the abstract and otherworldly vibe that Axiom Verge 1 had set up as its alien world.The music also has shifted in tone, its more optimistic than eerie and has more use of instruments that add to the more naturalistic setting, though there are places where chip-tune music is present and a few melodies and remixes are used at key moments in the plot.2) What new mechanics are there compared to the original?AV2 seems to have taken inspiration from the Castlevania games in comparison to the originals homage to Metroid. Instead of relying on a plethora of ranged weapons like AV1, AV2 has a focus on melee weapons and later on uses a more conventional fast travel system that was absent in the first game.There is also inspiration taken from Guacamelee, where the protagonist gets to explore Two large and interconnected maps that interlink between themselves and the player can use this dimension hopping to reach more areas along the critical path.Beyond that, one of the most considerate things added to this game are the accessibility features; you can decrease or increase the difficulty in a manner of ways, varying from weapon damage to damage negation. Alongside this, the bosses you encounter across the game are optional - you do not have to fight them at all and can walk right past them and carry onwards.3) Can you Play AV2 without previously playing AV1?Yes. While the plot of AV2 does have a few minor ties to the previous game, the plot and world are largely self-contained, making a good game to enjoy if you're curious about trying it out. The plot feels more like a back seat focus, but that isn't really a problem in my opinion as the gameplay is enjoyable.Overall I'd recommend getting this, whether you're a fan of the first game in this series or wanting to find a Metroidvania to play that breaks the staple of traditional power ups.

_childDocuments_.review: Really solid game, one that I liked better than the first one. It's a metroidvania through and through, that's for certain. This does make the game harder, and at times you will get lost, but that is also what makes this game so enjoyable. Oddly, almost every boss in this game can be skipped. You can just run right past them if you don't want to fight. Just further proof that this game does things a bit differently. Obviously, I'm really waiting for part 3 now.

_childDocuments_.review: Before the proper review, let me preface this with something more related to the general identity of this series rather than the qualities of this game specifically: Axiom Verge is and always was supposed to be a series of games about individual stories that can stand out on their own while being a part of something bigger, each game expanding on a monumental amount of lore by making you rethink about any certainties you had about the rules of the extended multiverse this series takes place in. It might take a long while before we find out about what happens after the events of Axiom Verge 1; nevertheless, the events and notes in this game greatly expand on what Axiom Verge 1 had done, while being seemingly unrelated at first. If you only care about Doctor Trace's Silly Adventures 2, look elsewhere, but if the writing of Axiom Verge 1 entranced you into wanting to know more about the inner mechanisms behind all that is Axiom Verge, this game is for you.Now onto a proper review of the game: I'm with the majority of the people who prefers Axiom Verge 1 to this game, as it sits in my top 10 favorite games, but don't let anyone tell you that this game is anything less than phenomenal.The combat isn't exactly its strong point, but if you care enough to put an ounce of strategy into what you do rather than slamming your face onto each enemy's attacks, you may realize that there's often many, many different ways you could possibly go about every encounter in the game. More variety in weapons would have been greatly appreciated, but as it stands, fighting in this game is fun and by no means bad. That being said, all boss fights, except maybe the final one, are very underwhelming.The world is vast and connected in an innumerable amount of ways, with shortcuts appearing very often all the way to the end of the game, and while each room isn't as memorable as perhaps the ones in Axiom Verge 1 would be, the organic way Kiengir is built makes it always a pleasurable experience to explore its various locations - and while the Breach follows different design philosophies, its quality is no less. To wrap it all up is a beautiful map menu that makes sure you get a good feeling of how each different biome is shaped and connected to the others, making it hard to forget where each thing is.The pixel art in this game is some of the best I've ever seen in indie games, and because of it multiple times have I had to stop for a second and remind myself that only one person is responsible for the entirety of this game. The soundtrack is no less, and while it doesn't reach peaks as high as Axiom Verge 1's collection of absolute bangers, you'll find that this game's different approach to its OSTs has plenty to offer.When it comes to length, this game is admittedly not very long, so whether it's worth its value to you is very subjective to what you want out of a game. If you only care about beating the final boss and then never open it again, I strongly recommend against buying it, as it will last you very little, and you will miss out on most of the things that make this game as good as it is. If you care for a single 100% completion rate playthrough, keep in mind that it will take more or less 10 hours to complete, so whether you should buy it or not depends on just how much you're interested about what this game's has to offer, and if it's worth it for you to pretty much spend 2$ for each hour you play. If you're interested in getting all achievements (which realistically will take you at least 2 playthroughs, one 100% and another quick one), or if you simply care to play this game multiple times, whether to speedrun it, or just to replay it and doing stuff in a different order to have a different experience with it, then I fully believe that buying this game is more than worth it. And if you're interested in this kind of stuff, the community is working on all sorts of mods, and may one day create a randomizer just like they did for Axiom Verge 1! But that might take a long while, so you're free to not let that change your judgement for the time being.All in all, while I do agree that this game is imperfect, I fully believe that it is an incredible videogame experience. Is it one of the best metroidvanias ever made? That's hard to say - especially because the genre is full of earthshattering games that will always keep you wishing for more! But it's a hell of a good one, and no matter how long it takes until we get another game that takes place in such a complicated multiverse, I'm very excited to keep following this series, because if there's something I know, is that Thomas Happ always Axioms a good Verge.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is by no means a continuation of AV1, but is still an absolutely outstanding game by itself. You really dont need to have played AV1 to play this game, as there isnt really any continuation in the gameplay, more so just in the story. This game also has much more emphasis on drone gameplay than the first game, which i quite like. The combat has also changed from ranged to melee (most of the time anyway), which means this game's combat is also significantly harder. There are also no mandatory bosses (excluding the final one) and a lot less of them, which in my opinion was a little bit of a downgrade since I kind of liked AV1's bosses. The graphics are prettier (imo) and except for an area sort of early game that I wont spoil, significantly less retro. It also felt somewhat shorter, which could have just been me not really taking my time, and with the shift to melee combat there are a lot less weapons to pick up, and you can only differ between like 4 in total, which I didn't really like that much.TL;DR: Really good game, while not being a continuation of Trace's story, still an amazing game in it's own right. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: ***EDIT1:Huh,lots of negative reviews for some reason, so i decided to give some feedback on common complaints: "constant crashes" -  Idk what their problem might be, but in 12h of play the game didnt crash even once for me."not like the Axiom Verge 1" - imo its not a good idea for a game to repeat itself and use the same tricks over and over again. So i for once,glad that AV2 is not copy-pasted AV1 with different locations and characters"characters are humans,not interesting" - guys,this game was made literally by ONE person,not a big team with writers, scenarists and whatnot. Do not expect AAA-lvl stuff from an indie game. For its price its quite good***This is a metroidvania in a sci-fi style with all the usual stuff: non-linear exploration, different biomes, abilities that allow to access new parts of the game world, upgrades for main character, tonns of collectibles, etc. Combat is fast-paced, real time beat em up with a decent selection of melee and ranged weapons. Later in game you will be able to hack enemies,which affects their behaviour (stop using certain abilities, fight for player, move fast/slow,etc).PROS+interesting exloration abilities, not your usual double jump,dash,etc+good biom variety, no boring forests,sea,volcanoes,castle (and other typical biomes) levels+nice variety of enemies, many have unique abilities/movesets+decent artstyle, sprites are well-done+good plot and lore. not a masterpiece, but got me interested enough+fair amount of content for its price - ive finished the game with ~95% completion in 12h+custom markers on the world map! (so you will have easier time getting back for previously inaccessible stuff). Thats actually important, but few game devs bother to do itCONS-bosses are too few and very weak, they really could use some balancing or new weapons/tactics.you will kill most (if not all) of them on the first (mb second) try, if you are somewhat familiar with genre-some weapons are clearly inferior to others and make no sense to use. For example, the remote controlled boomerang is used exactly once in the entire gameTL;DRGood game for a couple of days. If you like metroidvanias - you wont regret playing it

_childDocuments_.review: I really hate the combat.  The lack of ranged options isn't the problem.  The problem is the enemy mechanics are NOT balanced around this fact.  Generally, enemies move quickly and don't have any kind of openings after they attack so you either have to attack from a direction they can't hit back or just tank hits and button mash to kill them as fast as possible.  The majority of enemies have frequent ranged attacks as well so you can't really approach safely for melee, which means you're either running away from such enemies or doing the brute force method I mentioned above.  Then there's enemies hiding in blocks, blocks which are IDENTICAL to normal blocks!  Like silverfish, except they immediately hit you because they only pop out when you're right next to the little bastards.  Cheap damage!  There are other enemies which will swoop in from offscreen and hit you unless you know it's going to happen and are able to hit them as they rush in.  I've fought a few minibosses and one of them just starts spamming missiles once it's at low health and there's no way to get close without taking damage.  Just awful, complete unfun garbage.  Thankfully you do get enough health upgrades after the first hour or so that you won't die too much despite that.So I don't think the dev really put much effort into making the combat fun.  Maybe even the opposite, some enemies seem designed to be as frustrating as possible.Combat complaints over.  Unfortunately I must also complain about the music.  MOST of the tracks are fine, good even.  Others are ill-fitting; like, why does it sound like mysterious hindu music in areas that are just normal wilderness environments?  And then one of the music tracks feels like the singer is howling into my ear.  No thanks!Oh, and the plot sucks.  At first it's fine, you show up and things immediately get weird, but the plot hasn't really done anything within the past 4 hours I've played.  I keep going to new locations and being told to go to a different one with no reason given.  It's like the developer had ideas for the start of the plot and the end but nothing for the middle!I do like the map.  Being able to see the shape of the environment clearly instead of a grid of rooms is very nice.  Then again I don't like that there's only one type of map marker you can place, and backtracking to use new powerups is annoying because there's so much ground to cover and the compass you get points at things you can't reach all the time so it's near-useless for the intended progression path.The graphics are fine, but you can see that from the trailer, no new information here.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: After playing Metroid Dread, being dreadful, Shine Spark Puzzles. I needed a good side scroller to wash that bad taste out. Verge 2 delivers in many areas. Overall I had a good time. It was a bit strange, as this is one of the easiest Metroid style games ever made. My fingers were especially grateful.There are downsides. What made the first game, so original; is lacking in it's prequel. To a point where I recommend playing 2 first and then 1. If you never played a prior Verge game or are revisiting them. Verge 2 has no major problems. It's a series of minor problems. Sadly I think this is why it will not sell well. The 1,000 paper cuts. The dialogue needs work. The music doesn't jive as well as the first game. The story is a bit of a mess. A lot of interesting stuff happens in the background, and we're forced to read documents hidden through the world. While a much easier game, it is one of the hardest in the genre to locate hidden items. Some you can only find by inputting button combos on statues. It's ironically incredibly easy to miss mission specific items. On two different occasions I was stuck for hours! The constant switching between dimensions to advance will get frustrating. Map indicators would have been great. Just so I know what I missed, instead of scouring. This is even harder when you never have full access to all 5 inventory maps! Top it off with not getting the best upgrades until the 85%/95% mark.The freedom to explore the world is mostly monotone in difficulty. This has a benefit most open world games do not have. The downside is being able to fully access the world. It will require you checking the maps constantly. At least on your initial play through. Tom put a lot more emphasis on the drone dungeons. It's not bad, definitely the more challenging part of the game. The bosses become a joke quickly once you get enough upgrades.I still had a good time! If Happ makes a third one. He badly needs to overhaul it with some beautiful hand drawn graphics like in Owl Boy, possibly show don't tell the story so much. I think he took the feed game from AV1 and went into a very different direction. It's not that Verge 2 is bad. It's that feedback dictated him down a path that most gamers will not follow. Tom should have stuck more to his guns, literally.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm gonna go ahead and save you some time reading the rest of the reviews. 99% of the negative ones are basically " waaa... it's too different from AV1 boo hoo ". Essentially a bad case of pearls before swine.The only two things wrong with this game are as follows:1. We had to wait for a few months for the steam release as opposed to epic. (this doesn't apply anomore... so i guess it's one.)2. the respawn animation could've been a bit faster.... ok 3... because i'm knit picking ... there's a bug where using the drone there are two key bindings for the attack, and for some reason the game prefers D over S. ... but this is a bug so ... yeah. doesn't really count.That's it.For those who're actually fans of the Axiom Verge games and are reading this for some reason ... here's the thing. It's just as good as AV1 and in some cases even better. There's clear evidence that Thomas, being the sole developer of this game has learnt what he's learnt in AV1 and applied it to AV2. Moreover, it's clear that he wanted a completely different main character which wouldn't feel different from AV1's protagonist. He pulled it off brilliantly. There's also many additional layers to the game, new mechanics, and a hell of a lot more work done on the graphics side.People who are fans of this series and not porcinely challenged will appreciate this game for what it is. A great game that improves on its predecessor while making a point of feeling like a stand-alone rather than a glorified expansion pack.Thank you Tom. Looking forward to AV3 ... and 4 ... and so on. Great work!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game. I think it suffers from Chrono Cross syndrome, though, what with it having big shoes to fill and deviating quite a bit from how the first game played.You will not be getting any wacky guns in this game, and I'm sure that'll be a turn off for a lot of people. This game does, however, find other ways to make up for that. It has a new core mechanic that I find very interesting, and one of the things I wanted most in the first game but didn't get: Fast Travel. There's a certain something you spend part of the game getting back, and by the time you do, I find that it feels mostly useless.100%ing this game feels a lot more fair than the first game, though I can still think of a specific collectible that I did not feel was fairly placed. The music is also a lot catchier than it was in the first game, and the story feels significantly more coherent. The graphics are very pretty, and the world feels quite diverse. I did feel like mobility was lacking at times, but overall it's a very fun game, and I'm glad I played it. I'd probably give it a B. Worth playing, but not something I plan to replay unless something new gets added.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing the original Axiom Verge, I was hesitant to tackle it's divisive sequel. Rather than continuing the story of Dr. Trace in his search of answers concerning the alien world of Sudra, Axiom Verge 2 barely has anything to do with the storyline of the first game, except for a few references here and there to characters and concepts. This time you take on the role of a millionaire technology mogul named Indra who is investigating the mass disappearance  of a team of scientists in Antarctica. Her involvement in the mystery is personal because she received an almost threatening message informing her that her estranged daughter was at the facility when the crew went missing. Shortly after arriving, she's pulled through an interdimisional portal and thrust into an alternate world that resembles ancient Mesopotamia with robots. The original inhabitants are long dead after a war, but their kill-bots are still active. To survive, Indra merges with Arms, the civlization's sentient super-technology, which also doubles as the power-ups and traversal abilities. Unfortunately, this also drags Indra into the conflict between the Lamassu, the god-computer controlling the kill-bots, and the Arms. As remnant of the last war, Lamassu believes they should be destroyed and the Arms, being self-aware entities that were once people before super-science made them something else, want to continue living. The running battle between factions will threaten the multiverse. It's not just the plot that's different. The look, feel, and combat goes in a completely separate direction. The first Axiom Verge felt like the original metroid game. It was set in a truly alien environment where nothing looked familiar. Axiom Verge 2 feels sort of like being an American in a foreign country. There's grass and trees and mountains but the architecture looks kind of funny. This is also reflected in the musical score. Those upbeat chiptunes from the first game only make an appearance when you are piloting a drone to explore the Breach, an alternate reality that functions as a second map and gets Indra to places she can't reach under normal circumstances. When she explores the 'normal' world, the music for each zone is very similar to that one track from the first game for the Kur zone. A vaguely middle eastern rhythm accompanied by a synthesized voice doing this ethereal chanting. I was unsure how I'd react to the music in this game since that was my least favorite track from the original. I found the computer voice grating. Here the voice is provided by an actual person and her vocals lend the soundtrack a mysterious, almost mystical quality. The original game's combat was all about those super-science guns. By the time credits rolled, I had about nine guns and that wasn't even close to being everything I could have found. The sequel feels like combat is entirely optional. Indra starts with a pick-axe for a melee weapon and later gets a boomerang for a ranged option. After a hour or so, she'll get the ability to hack enemies and turn them into friendlies. Theoretically, you could avoid combat altogether and do a pacifist run. The game doesn't even have traditional bosses. It has boss-like enemies you may encounter, you don't even have to engage with them as they can be skirted around. The only thing you are required fight is the final boss. As someone who struggled with the late-game bosses in the first game, I appreciated this approach in practice far more than I thought I would. So we've established these are very different games. When I saw the reviews for this game, they honestly sounded like every change was going to be for the worse. But after playing it, hands down, Axiom Verge 2 is the superior entry to the series, and if there is an Axiom Verge 3 I hope it follows the conventions of this game as opposed to its predecessor. The first game was very retro in the sense that it could be frustratingly obtuse and would have you combing the map looking for what to do next. Axiom Verge 2 is more streamlined in that it gives you quest markers to keep you on task. Don't think that this feature dilutes the exploration element. If you make a beeline for the first objective, you will find yourself blocked and will have to make a detour into some underwater ruins for a new ability. You might have to go off the beaten-path to get to the objective, but you always know where you are ultimately headed. There was only one time in the game where I felt like I was truly stuck, and that was only because I overlooked a platform on the corner of the screen even though I should not have. And this game has fast travel. Hallelujah. You can warp back to any save point at any time. All you have to do is open the map.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not Axiom Verge 1, and that's a good thing; both are fantastic in their own ways, and you should almost treat them as wholly separate.I found this one to be a much steeper wall to get over initially - especially given the map size, it was hard to not get thoroughly lost at first. Once you start getting your footing, though, it's incredibly satisfying.As others have said, the world is MASSIVE in comparison, and there are so many quality-of-life improvements (thank you, teleport to save locations), and you essentially get a 2-in-1 game with the heavy drone play and two maps.I genuinely think my only real critique is that I thought the music in AV1 was so good that this one just couldn't live up to the same legacy - no parts of the OST hit like they did playing through Kur for the first time.Summary: I absolutely loved AV1, but AV2 hit me in a way I wasn't fully prepared for and I couldn't put it down. It was 100% worth every penny, and I would buy it again in a heartbeat.

_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so much better than the first game, it's not even funny. Axiom Verge 1 was a good Metroid clone with unique touches, reminded me of Blossom Tales, which is a competent Zelda clone. This game changes up stuff, though, and is more part of the "evolved" Metroidvania group, which Metroid certainly is NOT. Areas are a lot more varied, traversal becomes much more satisfying, music is much better (believe it or not). There's less focus on combat, but the exploration is just so, SO much better. Many more shortcuts to unlock, so the map is more interconnected. Abilities are more fleshed out, the story is much more interesting. A lot more detail and context is added to the world, making things feel more real and "alive." Oh, and the game looks GORGEOUS. Oh also, the enemy placement is done better, less haphazardly. Metroid fans, stick your heads out of your asses please, and stop souring the reputation of this awesome game. Props to Thomas Happ!
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I really haven't played much yet, but everything vibes poorly so far. It started with the starting cutscene not being pauseable, and instead trying to pause it skips it. I then notice the controls haven't adapted to my keyboard layout (something that is becoming more common thanks to proton), so I go in to change my keybindings.They're... a bit of a mess. The items are in a really weird order for some reason, space is accept and enter is cancel, hitting the wrong button will leave the menu (resetting your changes), the keybinds aren't in a list (going down from item 2 doesn't loop to item 3), and so on. Home and End are bound by default?? Maybe it's designed for laptops?After rebinding, the controls feel alright, but melee and ranged aren't bound next to each-other (They're item 1 and 3...) so combat was a bit strange at first. You unlock wall-climbing very early, and it feels like old 90's games where you have to fall down such that your hands interact with the ledge before you can climb up it, making poorly timed jumps feel terrible. I think this might be a nostalgia thing, perhaps, so maybe It's fine. I found it jarring. They then spend the next hour or two showering you with upgrades, just barely introducing an item before giving you the next one. It's well possible this isn't really indicative of anything, but not having played more it's... at least unexpected from a metroidvania.Overall, I found many segments tedious, and the ones that didn't feel tedious were either mundane or over too fast. The respawn animation is insanely long, and some segments where you become a tiny little robot had a very long (30s and up) reset if you ever missed a jump or went through the wrong door at the wrong time.The speedrun leaderboards make no sense, the any% world record is 605h, the second place is 10 minutes. The second place any% is at 2.5%, the record low% is at 16%. The record 100% is 13 minutes, the second place is 3.5 hours. How have the devs not given a ♥♥♥♥ about this?The art is alright, the music varies a lot. Some tunes were cool, some really weren't.I loved the first game, I'm currently feeling like this one might not really be worth the money or my time.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a good portion of the first Axiom Verge game and I got to a point where I hit a wall. It wasn't too bad of a game, but it was not an easy one. Then comes Axiom Verge 2.Have you ever played a game that you already know in the first area that it will be completely exasperating to the point where even getting to the next save is a chore you don't want to bother undertaking?There..that questions sums up Axiom Verge 2 completely.Based on this game...I pray that the series dies. I wouldn't want to see how 3 turns out. In fact this game is so bad that it caused this series to get a treatment no game in my collection has done before? (And to give you an idea of my collection size...I have not reviewed all my games yet, but this review marks #150.) After this review I will be uninstalling this catastrophe of a game, hiding it...and taking the first one with it. I don't even want to see either of them on my list ever again.I stated in my Axiom Verge review that the first suffered from maximum effort/minimum gain. AV2 takes this to a new level: maximum effort/zero gain. Nothing I got was interesting. None of the weapons I used are a joy to wield. Its like going to work for 12 hours a day for 7 days a week, to get a christmas gift in the mail from your job...opening it...and see that they gave you a one year membership to the Jelly of the Month Club.But I don't like doing a review without saying at least one good thing about a game. So here goes:This game is uninstallable.There I did it. Skip this whole game series. (yes, skip the first one as well now.) Don't play 3 if it ever shows up. You have better things you can do in life....like working those 12 hour days for 7 days a week.Special note: Just to add insult to injury....I got the achievement for beating the first boss. Only 41.5% have this achievement. Let that sink in on how fast people quit this debacle.

_childDocuments_.review: The first Axiom Verge is one of best Metroidvanias out there.  This one took an entirely different turn, unfortunately for the worse.  The story is hard to follow and dull.  You mainly focus on melee combat, not a ranged gun.  The enemies are extremely annoying, it's like you said how can I make this AI behavior frustrating not fun.  They had to make accessibility features just to balance the combat system. The map is very all over the place.  The only positive I have to say about the game is that the music is good, and similar in quality to the original.  I wish devs would realize when they have a good formula they don't have to go and try to rearrange that formula in the next to just give us something different.  They should keep the formula and expand on it with more features, improved UI, system mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: After waiting so long for this game to finally come to steam, i am kind of disappointed. Its not a bad game at all, and im giving it a thumbs up because its not a bad game, i just am very disappointed its not more like axiom verge 1, because that game was a freaking masterpiece.Also, just throwing this out there, zero crashes so far, not sure what the deal is with some other guys here but maybe time to upgrade your PC or software.*update*  just finished beating the game and while ill admit it did get better and the storyline got more deep and interesting, it kind of fizzled out at the end. _childDocuments_.review: story: fantastic3 years since the release I'm still completely in love with the story.not gonna pretend I understand what the heck is going on, and that is the reason I want more. can't wait for AV3.visuals: sexyart style is quite different from what we've had in AV1, as Mr. Happ abandoned metroidish tiles.loving the fractal backgrounds just as much as all parallax prequel-like backgrounds.music: goodthe music is absolutely the selling point of this game for me.Jesu Christo, that's one hell of a soundtrack. had the first half of it on repeat for the better part of a year. unfortunately I can't say the same about the second half of the soundtrack, especially the Breach tracks. they reek of 'uninspired' despite my suspicion they are supposed to be the way they are.the 'final boss battle theme' with the funny name is also a huge turn-off for me. this track sounds intentionally bad. like you can't f up the mix this badly without trying to.gameplay: goodit feels considerably more engaging compared to the prequel. I don't mind melee focus, as the second game is barely has combat and emphasizes exploration over the former. moreover, you no longer get to choose between 20 gimmicky guns (which were not so different in practice) like in AV1.I can't say whether AV2's objectively well-made or not, but it's finger lickin good for me. however, the bold steps Mr. Happ took, are for the better, and that's 100% certain.Axiom Verge is my most favourite series, probably, ever. I hope I live long enough to see what happens next.

_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: A sequel that largely steps to the side instead of forward, for better and worse.There is now a focus on close-range combat rather than guns. There are fewer weapons which leads to a more focused experience.  Bizarrely, they took a step back on bosses, when they could have been made much more challenging with the limited moveset.  I still find the combat to be tighter and more engaging but YMMV.A lot of the style with the music syncing up to animations and with the health bar beeping is completely absent, which is apparently a limitation of the new game engine, but still extremely unfortunate.  The environments are a bit more varied and open, and there is a lot of room for exploration and fast travel as opposed to the more confined areas in the first game.I personally think everything, minus possibly the music, is an overall upgrade from Axiom Verge, but I can only say this with regard to my own tastes.  I think this is probably a pretty contentious sequel which is fighting the precedents the series prior set while also struggling to further innovate.  You could definitely argue they already blew their load, though I still found a lot to enjoy here.Good for a dozen hours or so.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I played this first on Switch when it originally released. I really enjoy it and the first game pretty much equally. 1 is like Metroid but with Contra guns, while 2 plays closer to Symphony of the Night.I think I prefer the story in this game to the first one. It's mostly because I think Indra is a lot more interesting protagonist, and I think the writing for the other major characters is improved a lot compared to Trace and the Rusalki in Axiom Verge 1.I totally get why some people prefer 1 to 2. This genre has a lot of games where the gameplay is similar to this but the exploration powers in 2 are really fun, and they feel different from the usual double jumps and dash moves of other games.I recommend this game if you like the genre and if you liked 1. I think it was really smart to go in a different direction with the sequel, and if you expect that I think you'll enjoy the game more instead of wanting it to be more of 1.

_childDocuments_.review: The game isn't horrible, but it is a disappointing sequel to Axiom Verge.One can't help but wonder if some DEI was involved in the making, considering the white young scientist was replaced with a black female scientist. Later the first npc you run into, is a woman who makes sure to not fail the bechdel test. The scientific alien technologies have also been replaced with folklore of indigenous people ground to powder and hidden in bottles.DEI aside, those changes do not really impact the game. What does impact the game is the changes from using space weapons to using pickaxes. So instead of being able to play safely shooting enemies at a distance, you have run through shooting enemies to whack them in melee range, making the game much harder. Alternatively using the new mechanic of hacking robots, which also requires running near melee range and capturing them as friends or trying to disable them.The minimap has also been updated to show exactly how each room looks like, which adds jitter and makes it harder to tell what is ground, what is background, what is platforms, and so on. On the bright side it does give you a hint of where the grounds and walls are, that may help you, even if it is a bit unclear. A middle version with just walls would have been superior, instead of the far too detailed background inclusion.For some unknown reason, the resolution has also been dropped from the previous game. With the breach sections seemingly dropping the resolution even more, making it feel almost like you are playing a game made to fit on a calculator screen. Potentially they want to make it look like you are following the drone in the breach on a screen, rather than seeing it in reality. But that just feels like an unnecessary effect, when the game could just remain at the same graphic resolution the whole time.The bosses guarding important items seem to also have been removed, and replaced with some kind of room roaming large monsters. Which are now optional to fight, but you get skill points if you defeat them.Speaking of skill points, this mechanic is also not a good choice compared to the Axiom Verge design of giving you health when the game wants to give you health and giving you power when the game wants to give you power. Now that choice is instead in your hands, meaning you have to guess what the developers think would be best. Are the enemies going to do more damage in the next area so you need more health? Are they going to be higher level so you need to upgrade your hacks? Are they going to have more health so you need more damage or attackspeed? Game doesn't help you at all, and you get to make that choice yourself. Probably nice for speed running and your second playthrough or so, but for a first playthrough it is a poor design.Overall the game is not bad. But it feels so far from Axiom Verge, that it is hard to see why they bothered to use the sequel name. Maybe they thought nobody would be picking up the game unless they tried to ride on the former fame. But far from a metroid game, this feels a lot more like an open world castlevania game. It is more unforgiving, more frustrating, more confusing, and I'm not sure if that is really what people wanted in a sequel.
