_childDocuments_.review: After the slap in the face that was Axiom Verge 1, I wasn't excpecting a second game. Heck, I've seen it like one year later.I am a huge fan of Axiom Verge 1, music was good, art was outstanding and deisng was just blowing my mind.Some areas feels pretty weird and sometimes you don't really know where too go or what to do but it is a metroidvania after all, you explore by yourself.And then, I've played the second opus. And what a disappointment, The game is full of new features, a new story, a new mode, new bosses, new enemies and new areas and a whole new world. And it can be awesome but I think it's just not clicked for me.Every now and then I was feeling: "Wow, this is so fun, it reminds me of the 1 so much", and I was wondering, why not playing the 1 instead?This is not a bad game at all, it is, I think a hit or miss game where for some people it will be awesome and for some it will not click.I do not understand the story at all, first English is not my primary language and it does not help, but I do not have the sense to achieve something in this game.Our character just walks from point A to point B without question, you follow your map and you kill a big dude, than you got to somewhere else and again.The final boss was meh, I mean, it is litteraly the first boss of Starbound but you loose nothing if you die. It feels pointless.A big no for me is the comparison to the first game. In AV1 you are being told to do something but not how nor where. Here you are told where and how and when. It means you have always a marker on your map to the next point.This is not abhorrent until you try to reach it.In AV1 (and lot of metroid vania) the path to an objective is never the shorthest one. But in all these MetroidVania (Super Metroid, Hollow Knight, Blasphemous, AV1 and many more) the objective is not shown (or partially) so you wander and you find your path. But here because the objective is marked, you search everywhere near this objective, but sometimes, it is not even remotely close to this place because a new power up is needed.I tend to never read a wiki before completing a game for metroidvania, but for this one it was mandatory, I was stuck 3 times on the course of 9 hours of play (and I was stuck for about 3 hours) this is not a good sign.Again, if you enjoyed this game, good for you, I am not saying this is a bad game, I am just saying playing with the map on the second screen is not for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: It was an OK game I guess. I loved it more than Axiom Verge 1, but it could really benefit from about 20% extra content and polish to really shine. As of now it is short and the pacing falls a bit after first half.It is less about boss fights and being super metroid clone and more about being it's own thing which definitely benefited it in my book. The combat, flow and traversal are super nice. One review mentioned that this game has no double jump and it sold it to me cause I was really curious how they make the overall traversal flow and it is super enjoyable.The story is nonsense and forgettable, core gameplay is solid though, there is a huge emphasis on hacking and upgrades and there are a few core mechanics that are implemented really well. But overall, as I mentioned, the game is underdeveloped, a lot of things are underused, and some things like breach portals kinda do nothing interesting the moment they start finally clicking in your head.The biggest gripe I have with AV2 is the same that I had with AV1. There is a point where you don't know where to go, and all interesting side areas are kind of dead ends with small meaningless upgrades. This game would really really need better pacing and some alternative routes and overall a bit of playtesting for the last stretch. It is not as egregious as, say, ESα, but I can see a consistent pattern here.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This review references and builds on the review I wrote for Axiom Verge 1. Find it .Axiom Verge 2 (AV2) is another excellent entry in the metroidvania genre from Tom Happ. It swaps the guns of AV1 for some melee+boomerang combat, but still stays heavily on the metroid side, due to emphasis on exploration and platforming. Pick it up if you enjoy the genre, or if you want a philosophical metaverse sci-fi story told through lore.It's good. I'm not sure what else I could say to convince you. I give it an unconditional 6/7 and will be watching for Happ's next game.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Many seem to consider this game to be worse than Axiom Verge 1. I agree - and I didn't even like AV1 to begin with.The only reason I enjoyed AV1 was due to the worldbuilding and lore. The gameplay was meh and I actively hated the music. From what I have seen so far, AV2 has prettier graphics, but less interesting worldbuilding with *significantly* clunkier gameplay. After the mind-numbingly easy boss fights, I had several powerups get stuck beyond reach, forcing me to reload and repeat. Movement has no "flow" at all, platforming is clunky, controls (especially menu controls) are awkward, sound design and especially balancing is jarring. It feels to me that a lot of polish is still needed to make this a half-way enjoyable game.Also, I still despise the music.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like it. It's a gorgeously designed game. But I just don't dig the combat system. I'm hoping for something that has some awesome guns or something a la Metroid, and the brief stint I had playing the original Axiom Verge already had some really cool combat and exploration. So what happened? I get it if the dev wanted to provide a different experience, and I'm glad a large number of people like it. Again, it's absolutely worth the experience, and is incredibly well designed. I personally don't dig the combat.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I feel pretty neutral about this game, it think its worth playing at least once.If you enjoy collecting items, exploring the map, and are deeply invested with the Story.Then give Axiom Verge 2 a try, just don't expect a full blown Metroidvania experience.The art and music is pretty great, but not enough to cover its inherent game design flaws.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game could have been as fun as the first one but the combat absolutely ruins it.You only have a short-range melee attack and a slow, weak boomerang. Most enemies fire projectiles, and many of them fly. Your options are: try to close in to melee range and most likely get shot multiple times; try to avoid them and most likely get shot anyway; try to kill them with the boomerang and spend 30 seconds dancing around trying to hit them with it (also probably get shot). It just feels . It doesn't feel like you're given adequate tools to properly fight the enemies that are in the game.I actually enjoyed the game during stretches when I was just exploring and platforming around, but then I'd inevitably encounter enemies and it would become horribly frustrating again.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I think The best way to describe Axiom verge 2 is to explain what i hope it becomes, rather than what it is. As I played my way through the game, It felt like I was playing its version of original metroid, but what i was really craving was the supermetroid version. Let me get a bit deeper into it to explain why.I originally played Axiom Verge 1 years ago, after being drawn in by a love of MVs and a desire to see the mechanic that allowed you to 'hack the game engine'. It was a novel enough experience to prompt me to play the second one, looking for an evolution on that premise. Instead, the game plays more like a platform version of Zelda: the dark world, where there are actually 2 maps and you slowly nurture the ability to jump back and forth between them to get around obstacles in your path. The different upgrades you pick up along the way can be used very creatively, which actually caused me a little pain- getting 'trapped' in a later area of the game that i figured out a way into but didnt have the right powerup to leave. I couldnt really tell if this was a QA failure or a desire to give the map a more open world feel without enough avenues back and forth. Ultimately i did figure out a way to get myself back on track and work my way through the story, And by then i felt like i had a pretty decent handle on upgrades.Conversely, the weapons system left a fair amount to be desired. I never felt pressed to try out any of the different weaponry at any point in the game. I just picked up the biggest axe i could find and bashed my way through the enemies. I rarely used the hacking mechanism, too. Its novelty wore off pretty early on and was relegated to opening doors, moving platforms, and fighting bosses. I used the boomerang so little i pretty much forgot i even had it. I feel like the hacking features could have really made the game far more exciting if deployed properly. I loved the idea of taking over a bunch of enemy bots and using them to fight a boss, or something similar, but the system really wasnt complex enough to make it work, and that level of hacking was so expensive to use it was cost prohibitive. And I want to make it clear: these werent systemic failures in my eyes so much as not using interesting concepts to their full potential. Pushing the game design a bit more could have fleshed these out better. Of course, none of these criticisms extend to the spider drone. Simultainiously adorable and effective, I found myself spending larger and larger chunks of the game in spider mode rather than humanoid. The buzzsaw style weapon reminded me of playing oldschool rygar from when i was a kid, and the grapplinghook made it delightful for platforming. In terms of gameplay, it was probably some of my favorite, but i think the game actually suffered a bit from making humanoid mode less useful overall. So you're probably wondering at this point: why the metroid/supermetroid comparison? Well, the aspect of the game where this one really takes off is the worldbuilding. Unlike the first game, this story had me absolutely sucked in on so many levels. I wanted to see more of not just the primary world, but the others too. I wanted the map to be 10 times as big, with the breach fulfilling its true role of interdimensional travel rather than a dark world under the primary world. The story kept me pretty engaged, and even eager to find new bits of lore that are stashed around the map for those up to the challenge. What i hope for in any subsequent sequel is for the map and gameplay to expand to fit the size of the story. I would absolutely love to see this game evolve into ''super axiom verge 2'' in the same way that metroid evolved into supermetroid by adding lots of new mechanics and increasing the map size. Over all: I had a good time playing it, and while i cant say i was wowed by combat, the game had plenty of other features and a great story to keep me entertained. I think for the price i got it, it's a worthy diversion.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is unbelievably better than the first one to me. Almost every one of my gripes was resolved immediately. The quality of life changes are excellent. The one major gripe I had with the first game is alleviated about halfway through the game or so. I was so happy when it happened that it was almost worth not being the default.My only real complaint I have about the game as it is would be the fast travel.Most metroidvania (SEARCH ACTION if you're a nerd) games make it so you can select around warp points with a single button press, rather than making you look around the entire map. It's not a HUGE complaint but it would have been nicer to expediate.I had a great time with this game and I hope the next one keeps the positive trend going.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's a quality metroidvania. Not outstanding, but worth your time if you are a fan of the genre.What you need to know:1. Barely any connection to the 1st game, for good and ill.2. Use your map, make reminders.3. Not a lot of secret, breakable walls for a metroidvania. Instead, you tend to access hard to reach areas by entering "the breach" a lower res world that overlaps with the main world. You can jump back and forth (with some limits. These form the more satisfying parts of exploration for the game.Some notes.1. Fast Travel. Dear devs, thank you for having it. However, the slow animation that plays every time you reform from your nano-cloud when you fast travel is not welcome. For emphasis, please watch the animation when you reach the end of a sentence. I expect you will be insane or patch the issue before Ishmael gets on the Pequod.2. Above, plus a slightly faster movement speed would go a long way making getting around more fun.3. Some abilities feel half-baked. In that they get used a bit then are forgotten. This can be late game abilities that don't really play into backtracking, or early stuff like the blast that makes some blocks break or fall. That get's used for a while then completely forgotten about. Even the final pass through gates ability felt lack-luster. There really weren't that many gates or that much reason to use it to fly.And at 13 hours it's pretty short. 100% would take longer but I'm not motivated to do so.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty conflicting because there are many good aspects to it and quite a few disappointing aspects depending on what your personal preferences are. I have to give credit to is the developer deciding to go a different direction then the first game and instead have more of an emphasis on exploration which is definitely risky considering that many fans of the first game may feel somewhat alienated playing this one. Overall though I think that this game is very different and special in a lot of ways and is a very artistic interpretation of a exploration Metroid esque type of game with more in common with Zelda than Metroid for sure and as an experience is completely worth the asking price.Coming from somebody who's played the vast majority of Metroidvanias that exist I can safely recommend this game even at full price for people who are looking for a somewhat more casual relaxed exploration experience with passable combat mainly melee focused, at least optimally. I think the third game is going to be very critical when determining how people look back on the second game. I really hope that the creator can find a way to tie together both styles of gameplay to where it makes more cohesive sense from a trilogy perspective. I have great faith in Thomas Happ and look forward to seeing how he continues the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome game! If you loved the original, well, you may or may not like this because it's completely different. The movement feels comparable and there are callbacks, but the similarities end there. What is similar, though, is the in-depth lore and worldbuilding which I can't wait to see expanded upon even further in future sequels, if/when those come. (Thomas Happ said he has ideas for 8 games total in the series, so I'm hoping!)This game's best strengths are interesting exploration, abilities that feel fresh without being annoying to use, and great atmosphere and music. The exploration does some things that really set it apart which I won't spoil here. I enjoy the moment to moment combat a lot, too, though it's a bit of a rough start due to the enemies dealing a lot of damage, having tricky patterns, and your attack range being very small. This quickly becomes a very fair and enjoyable difficulty curve, however.I feel that one of this game's biggest weaknesses are the way it handles boss fights. The boss fights are mostly easy and optional, and the few times a boss fight is required, you can't fail because it gives you a save point right in the middle of the fight, which I honestly think detracts from the satisfaction you get from beating them. It's ironic because I usually don't care about boss fights, but here I actually think this style hurt the pacing. In the end, though, that was a minor issue for me and I enjoyed the rest of the experience through and through.I strongly recommend this if you're fine with optional boss fights, and you don't go into it expecting something like the original in any way.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'm an old school gamer who remembers playing the original Metroid and Castlevania on my NES. I still love Metroidvanias, and I highly recommend Axiom Verge 1 & 2. I was blown away by their creativity, lore, and gameplay. While Axiom Verge 1 was a really interesting game, it had a few jagged edges in terms of gameplay that made it sometimes frustrating. AV2 smoothes out those jaggies. It was more fun for me, right from the beginning, and whenever I got stuck, I was able to figure out the next path on my own. The art style is a little different, and there is no gun arsenal like in the first one, but movement and exploration is much more refined. I highly recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: +++ Wonderful sense of exploration and discovery.+++ Novel combination of abilities.+++ Lushly detailed artwork.+++ Compelling story and lore.--- Disappointing boss fights.This title can offer 15 hours of pure goodness where exploration trumps above all, including combat. Every little nook and cranny appears to have been given more than its fair share of effort, and this attention to detail contributes to the making of an experience that feels like reading a page-turner novel. It will not make waves among enthusiasts of challenging battles — however, it is an excellent choice for those looking to get pleasantly lost into another world.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Axiom Verge 2 does not play at all like the original.Mechanically, it controls similarly, but the actual game play goals and loop are very different.Where Axiom Verge felt more like a Metroid game with dark corridors, minimal graphics and a very dark combat oriented tone, Axiom Verge 2 instead is a bright, colourful game where exploration is much more important than combat.The pixel art remains gorgeous and the music stellar, but the sometime punishing combat of the original is instead replaced with what is frankly very easy fights.If you don't come in with the expectation of playing more of the original Axiom Verge, you may enjoy the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Part of what makes metroidvania fun is revisiting old places, more powerfully, to unlock greater things. It's not fun in this game, imo. World traversal is pretty meh, and you don't get fast travel until halfway through - and that doesn't make revisiting places more fun. You get an indication of "you need to be here" next - but every avenue you want to try to get there is met with frustration and failure. It's literally whack-a-mole trying to find the one specific spot that you can use to break through to make further progress on an old area. On top of that, the controls are pretty meh - you have to "tap" to use the , not hold, and if you hold it doesn't work. You have to double tap to use  - it's like the dev thought "how does every other game's controls use this mechanic? Lemme do the opposite of that". Frustrating in so many ways.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: It has a few caveats, but it is a nice metroidvania. Really different to the first one, which is something to appreciate I guess.I would recommend it only for metroidvania fans though, who value exploration first and foremost. Combat is not good at all, but the dev obviously did not focus into it much - bosses are optional and the last one is more like a puzzle / sequence.The abilities you gather are really interesting, and the dual world is one thing I wish more games would do. That plus a very well crafted map makes it a interesting metroidvania.The story is nice, but the ending feels rushed in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Unwieldy, in short.My previous review was a bit harsh, so let me try again.The good:- Interesting visuals.- A lot of very cool ideas, like hacking and the breach.- Exploration and platforming is fun.- Odd weapons require a bit of getting used to, but once you get upgrades you steamroll everything, in typical metroidvania fashion.The bad:- The odd choice of weapons create unfair situations often.- No real boss fights required to progress, all of them are optional. Some scenes could be considered bossfights, but they're really just glorified cutscenes and you can't die.- The breach gets quite annoying after entering it for the 100th time, my ears are bleeding.- Biomes aren't nearly as interesting as they were in axiom verge 1.- The story is confusing, but the first half was great.- The ending is disappointing.I'd say a 7/10, purely because platforming and exploration is the entire game, and it's the most fun part. Also I might have missed some story related cues, or I just need to replay Axiom Verge 1 to understand it better.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I was unsure what to expect from the sequel before its release, but I ended up enjoying it immensely. It made for an especially fun game on the Steam Deck.The first game was essentially a 2D Metroid game with all the H.R. Giger-inspired flair cranked up to eleven, yet it still had enough cool, unorthodox ideas of its own to make it feel original.The sequel retains some of that inspiration, but adopts a much brighter art style, focuses on melee combat instead of shooting, and features more ancient ruins and Earth-like outdoor environments.The world map feels wonderfully varied, with each area boasting its own distinct mood, music, and atmosphere. There are usually multiple ways to get from point A to point B. All the areas are connected in a very organic way, and you unlock some pretty fun and creative traversal mechanics.Optional bosses are a new addition that I think could have been executed better. While their visual designs are good, they sort of just feel like regular enemies with extra health and larger hitboxes. Additionally, the lack of unique boss music fails to give them the fanfare they deserve.It is somewhat hard to pinpoint how it compares to its predecessor. While I prefer the shooting mechanics, plot, and darker tone of the first game, I believe the sequel made significant improvements in terms of exploration and how you move around the world.Positives:+ Varied and organic world map, with each area having its own distinct mood+ Fun, creative power-ups and traversal mechanicsNegatives:- The optional bosses felt somewhat underwhelming
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Even though most people like Axiom Verge 1 more, for me it was different. Maybe the first one didn't click with me at first and this one had a better timing for me, but I liked this game. This game made nearly everything enjoyable for me and I could explore, like I wanted to explore. I think, this is a good prequel to the first game!There are again some annoying achievements for Achievement OCD players, but these are not hard at all with a guide. Just annoying. Those are the speedrun achievements (even though they are easy) and the less then 40% of items achievements. Those just don't feel good for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Great second game: feels very familiar to the first which I appreciated, however there was plenty of new material, abilities, mechanics. The movement is also smoother (added bonus!) Great soundtrack, great designs/art, interesting story that also compliments the first game very well. All in all I think there's something for everyone in this game. Don't like combat? you don't actually have to fight things if you don't want to. Like combat? you won't feel like every battle is a grind. Like puzzles? There's plenty to solve! Or just wander around. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Things I love:- The story- The map- The music- The controls/traversal- The pace of upgrades- Ease of fast travel and how early it's unlocked- The pixel art/envsThings that bothered me- The bosses, utterly and intentionally skippable and not even remotely challenging- The weapons there are two kinds and just a few variations within those- The ending, if you can even call it that. Years since release and I keep looking for someone to find the true ending- Like the main character? Too bad you will be a drone 80% of this game learn to love it and it's one combat technique- Feels like it's lacking depth compared to AV1
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: A superb sequel, everything about this game improves and builds on the original. The world is much larger, the movement and combat are refined and the "boss" fights while optional are better designed. However, it is different, while the first game was purely Metroid this game adds a lot of Castlevania influence to the mix, there is a focus on melee combat and the world is a lot more open, this allows it to experiment with new mechanics and expand the gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Axiom Verge 2 is NOT Axiom Verge 1.  It's in many ways a very different way that takes some bold swings.  Some hit, others miss.  For one, I didn't like combat very much in this game, and I thought the bosses in this game being optional was kinda an odd choice.  I spared them all .I do think the exploration in this game is actually really cool.  I won't give anything away, but there's actually a lot to explore here and the mechanics are all in place to make traversal pretty fun.  On another note, this game took a while to really sink its hooks into me.  I don't know why, but this game didn't really grab me until 3 hours in.  However, once it did, it didn't let go.Overall, Axiom Verge 2 is a fun game although it does make for a game I enjoyed less than the first.  I am glad to see that Axiom Verge as a franchise continues to evolve.  I think that'll make for a more diverse series.8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: A divisive follow up to the beloved Axiom Verge that I enjoyed. It's been a long time since I played the original, but I remember liking the world quite a lot. In the sequel, there's more story and... that's good and bad. The babylonian future tech stuff is excellent - nanobots, clones, AI powered by ancient ghosts. The actual plot and how it connects to the original, I couldn't save.Gameplay-wise, this is all about exploration. There's a lot of abilites that revolve around the Breach, an alternative map that mirrors the main map. Cool stuff.Bosses were weak. All of them you can just walk past. I don't get this. Either make they required or don't have them in at all. They were so uninteresting that they were basically just giant enemies.Overall, a fun game that diverges from its predecessor in some interesting ways. A fantastic metroidvania if you like pure exploration.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed the first one, I don't know if I'd consider this better, but with a sale on the bundle it's more love letters to Castlevania to play through, so go ahead if you want. Axiom Verge 1 was very much on the 'Metroid' angle of the term 'metroidvania'. Axiom Verge 2 is certainly on the '-vania' part. A lot of the gameplay is based on exploration rather than combat, with boss encounters amounting to there being an enemy in a room you can either avoid or kill outright.Comparing the two, Axiom Verge 2 feels slower. The teleport animation is about 10 seconds long, so if you're hopping around frequently get ready to watch the same swirling graphic over and over. The unique exploration gimmick is very interesting, and leads to a satisfying amount of puzzles you can solve with some thinking.I don't know how they did it, but 2's story is infinitely more confusing than 1's. It's supposed to be in the same universe, but the amount of terminology and concepts thrown at you are really strange. Couple that with the flat ending and I don't really know if I could say this game is above average compared to the first, but I got it in a bundle with the first which is a really good game, so I'd say it's worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: *got this through humble bundle*great game! while Axiom verge 1 takes more inspiration from Metroid, Axiom verge 2 takes more inspiration from Castlevania. The games play very differently which was unexpected but very fun and a breath of fresh air.this is a prequel and the story is great and subject to interpretation which is very interesting. You have a sort of alternate would you transport to that is overlayed on the normal one (think Soul Reaver). I backtracked more in this one than the 1st one but it is still a shorter game.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a fantastic metroidvania.Although it maintains the side-scrolling format of its predecessor, it offers a distinctly different experience in terms of atmosphere, gameplay, and mechanics. The visuals are bright and the environments are richly detailed, moving away from the traditional Metroid mood.The game emphasizes melee combat with heavier, more substantial jumps compared to the first installment. The drone plays a significant role, and there's a skill system allowing you to level up various aspects of your character. With a vast map full of items and secrets to uncover, exploration is a major highlight.It also finally has fast-travel :)However, the game is quite easy; bosses, including the final boss, are straightforward to defeat. The most challenging part is how to get to where you need to go; I did get stuck near the end for a while trying to figure out where to go next.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I had played the first game years before, and so when this came out I bought it right away. Played for a couple of hours and for some reason it didn't click with me at all. I refunded the game. Thought it sucked.It's now 2024 and I've replayed the first game and loved it once again. Wanting more I decided to give this sequel another chance. I just finished it and I absolutely loved the heck out of it. Looking to 100% the game now. Appreciate this game for what it is, instead of comparing it to the first one, and it might have a lot to give you.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Axiom Verge 2 was a treat, wow.I replayed the first game just before jumping into this one, thinking they might connect... well kind-of but only in very obscure references left in the notes scattered through the game.This game brings the vania in metroidvania as you no longer have any guns like in the previous title but that's just fine.Axiom Verge 2 is also much more heavily focused on the exploration aspect of metroidvanias and oh boy does it do it well!I'll leave-out my commentary about other "Metroidvanias", Axiom Verge 2 leans so far into the "Action-Exploration" that the world starts to feel more like an open world but without becoming overwhelmingly open and pointless.Eventually you'll have to explore-it all (well most) but there's not just one "Sequence" of upgrades; you get to choose where you go and it'll always be rewarding to do so.Axiom Verge 2 is truly the epitome of what an action-exploration game should be.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game was excellent! There's some complaints about changes from Axiom Verge 1, but I do hope the developer doesn't get discouraged by them. The movement felt miles and miles better in this one, and it's an absolute joy to explore the world. This is a wonderful Metroidvania through and through. Some people might not like that the combat is less involved and more or less optional, but the platforming and puzzle solving aspects are top notch.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Axiom Verge 2 (AV2) is a side-scrolling Metroidvania with a focus on exploration, platforming, and little puzzle solving. While AV2 is a stand alone sequel and it is not necessary to play or understand the story of the first game in order to enjoy AV2. There are some references to concepts and characters mentioned in the first game, but it is not necessary to understand AV2's story. If you enjoy Metroidvanias, AV2 is a solid game that is worth your time as the platforming abilities, map, and exploration are all quite good.  The original AV was a straight Metroid-like with really none of the "-Vania" elements of a Metroidvania. AV2 incorporates more of those Vania elements with a greater focus on backtracking, exploration, and includes a skill point/skill tree system to level up your character. The focus on AV2 is more on puzzle solving to explore more of the map, where as AV1 was more focused on combat. Both AV games have a pretty light story that is mostly told through journals found throughout the world. I didn't find myself too invested in either game's story, but I will say that I do find the story of AV2 to be more enjoyable and a little easier to piece together.   The world in AV2 feels much more sprawling that AV1, which I enjoyed. The level/world design is good, as well as the enemy placement being pretty solid as well. After you get the ability to call a drone, you get access to an additional world where you can only enter with your drone. This is often required in order to get access to other areas in the main world, but the "drone world" is a fully fleshed world as well, but with a more low-res visual style. As the world is more sprawled out, the game added the ability to fast travel at save points - which is something I feel AV1 could have benefited from having some limited form of fast travel. However, you can only fast travel only between points in the world you are currently in, unfortunately. This means if you are in the "main" overworld, you will have to enter the "drone world" first before you can fast travel to specific point in the drone world. I don't think there is anything that would have broken the game by making able to fast travel between points in the different worlds, so it became a little tedious to have to find an access point to swap between worlds before fast traveling.  In the first game, there was about a dozen or so guns to choose from, where as in AV2 you have a melee attack and a ranged attack that you will upgrade by finding stronger versions of those weapons (there are a few different melee weapons you can choose from, but it was a hassle to swap between them so I just stuck with the one that had the longest reach).In AV1, you would spend most of your time in your human form for combat and use your drone just for certain platforming/exploration sections (or occasionally scouting). I would say I spent 80-90% of my time in human form in AV1. In AV2, there is a much stronger emphasis on swapping between human and drone form - both for combat, exploration, and platforming as each form as an exclusive set of ways to attack and platform. This adds plenty of options in order to explore the world and tackle obstacles. Though towards the end of the game, I feel the drone's later platforming abilities were superior to the human form, and found myself being in drone form for almost all of the back half or so of the game.  One of my favorite mechanics in AV1 was the glitch/hack mechanic where you could glitch out enemies and certain terrain. In AV2, instead of having a gun that shoots out this effect, now you hold a button to expand a circular area in order to hack an enemy or object within range. Depending on what enemy or object your are hacking it can have a number of effects:*Make an enemy become friendly.*Disable an enemy's weapon.*Slow down the enemy's speed.*Make the enemy emit healing drops.*Turn the enemy into a platform.*Overheat the  enemy to cause massive damage.*Certain doors will require hacking to open.Some things can be hacked for free (such as opening barriers), but most "offensive" hacks against enemies use up you nanotech bar, which acts as "mana" to use these hacks. This bar can be expanded with skill points found in the world and dropped by bosses. Hacking is particularly useful against bosses as they will often have multiple components/weapons that can be hacked. This mechanic added an interesting wrinkle to combat.  I beat both AV games without using a guide and found the game did a good job of guiding and teaching the player through the game's mechanics/combat/puzzles without ever feeling lost, stuck, or frustrated. The 2nd game has a greater openness with more branching paths/routes your can go down to explore the world in different ways, where the first game felt a little more straight forward. To help reduce some confusion with the openness, AV2 will put markers on the map to show the player where to go to in order to progress the story.The first AV took me about 13.5 hours to beat with about 84% of the items found and 95% of the map explored.AV2 took me about 12.5 hours to beat with 94% of the items found and 99% of the map explored.As I prefer the the "vania" elements of Metroidvanias instead of the pure Metroid-like gameplay of AV1, I found myself enjoying AV2 more than the original game. If you weren't a fan of the first game as it was a Metroid-like and enjoyed other games of the Metroidvania genre, then I would recommend AV2 even if you didn't like AV1 because it is quite a different game.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: This is a really creative and interesting metroidvania. You're likely to get stuck, Get a guide and don't feel bad about it if you do. Otherwise this is worth itAxiom Verge 1 had unique and interesting abilities, along side a distinct retro style, and the second game in the series keeps that innovative spirit up. It's 'navigation challenges are also unique, and I found to be very fun.The routing in this game is very circuitous and challenging. But it's also a very linear metroidvania. To take circuitous routing in a linear metroidvania means the author had to put up tons of impassable barriers and blockers. The world feels bizarrely locked down. Get used to running into a ping barrier with a switch on the other side. You will be seeing that a lot. In my playthrough I got stuck twice and needed to look up what to do to continue. In both cases, I failed to notice a hint the map was giving me. But when I did fail to notice it, I ended up concluding that "there must be another way around or another ability I need" and then explored every nook and cranny of the available map, looking for some clue that was staring me in the face right at the start. I think the problem here is this: Very often in metroidvanias they will tease you with area's you can't currently get to due to a lack of an ability or some kind of key, and the solution is to find some other route around. Axiom Verge 2 compounds on this challenge in a a few ways: 1. The unique traversal mechanics and abilities mean you really can't predict what you need for a given barrier, 2. AV2 does not make it very obvious that an ability is needed for a given blocked. eg. a 2 x 3 square block in the terrain.3. The complex navigational challenges in this game leave you wondering if there isn't some sneaky way to get the thing you're after with the abilities you currently have.4. AV2 has lots of different types of keys and locks, and instead of using them it will use switches and pink barriers. I suspect these all these facts will make getting stuck in this game pretty likely...One last negative. The game's a bit buggy. I experienced two hard crashes, and two softlocks. I never lost more than a minute of progress to these, but it was annoying.OK. despite all those negatives, I still recommend this game. Damn fine metroidvania. If you enjoy this genera you should check this one out, it's a creative entry to the category and worth having a look for yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is an exploration focused metriodvania that is set in the weird sci-fi multiverse of the axiom verge games. It does have a story, and it's not bad, but the joy of the game is definitely in trying to figure out how to get to whatever location.I enjoyed both Axiom Verge 1 and 2 enough to play them through to completion, but I don't remember enough of the details of 1 to compare this beyond I remember it being good too.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Where it's predecessor was on the Metroid end of the spectrum,  is very much on the Castlevania side of things. It's a melee-oriented game with modern affordances like fast-travel to save points, unlimited custom map markers and a late-game item that gives you a hint if collectibles are nearby.The plot is interesting and raises more questions than it answers, the sound track is once again great (the overworld is fairly chill while the subspace is filled with bangers), the pixel art is pleasing to the eye and once again the traversal upgrades do an interesting job of making the world explorable.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I have been a bit worried when starting the game considering that a lot of reviews mention issues with the combat system and the game generally being worse than its predecessor. Luckily, none of these applied to my experience in the end and I had too much of a blast with it up till the last %. In my opinion a solid 9/10 and a worthy sequel to the previous game. Not many Metroidvanias truly reach this level of quality imo and I am wish there will be a next installment as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: If the first game was a Man with a Gun, this sequel is Old Yeller. But with, yknow. Existenal/body horror, drone war crimes, and pissing off the PTSD riddled vet till she straps up a flashy boom vest.Oh, and the dog you put down via long nature hikes n poor decisions is yourself. Well your other self, but not THAT one ofcourse. Thatd be weird.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: If there was a "middle thumb" this would get it.It's not 'bad' but it's also forgetable. They do a good job with the story "meaning" something but it feels disconnected and in text boxes of "data logs". If they meant for the game to feel like I should be running from just about everything, then that fits, but otherwise I just feel underpowered after several hours of game play. The pixel grfx are 'fine', their art is nice but to me it just kinda looks like noise after a bit. Finally I think the biggest downside is the map. Sure it's pixel styled but it feels like it contains almost nothing and getting around just feels like such a chore. No teleporting (basically) and no good movement options outside of platforming. I know it's been some years but the original AV felt more connected, more of that "desperate loneliness" and the world felt so much more foreign. It's a design choice but it didn't resonate with me.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, I love the new map tracker and upgrade system for stuff we want to use. The different parts of the maps look great and the music is amazing. I will say though that this is a whole different plot than the first Axiom Verge game and not a sequel. I also miss the old chat dialogue like the first game because I honestly have no idea who was talking with those boxes. The head visuals + cutscenes in the first game were 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is a review from someone who DIDN'T like AV1, since this is a rather rare occurence, thinking someone might need said input. A lot of people in these reviews who liked the first don't like this, and I understand why - it's a completely different experience. I think making it its own title would have been better. It plays completely different. As someone who didn't like the first I consider it a good thing. This is an exploration-first title, in fact there aren't really any boss fights, it's all really exploration. I mean there's combat, but this isn't a combat-MV like HK, Ender Lillies or Blasphemous. And I approve of focusing on what the game is about, which is exploration. And it does so very well. This is honestly one of my favourite MVs.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the first game more but still enjoyed this one. Took me a bit longer to get into it than the first one. The soundtrack in this one to me isn't nearly as good as well which was one of the awesome parts of the first one. Graphics and game play are similar to the first game. As you progress in the game the use of 2 overlapping worlds are really cool though. That makes exploration through the map pretty interesting. If you enjoyed the first one you will most likely enjoy this as well. It's worth playing in my opinion and a third game would be welcome to the series.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Finished the game. I'll recommend this game for the exploration, the vast of weapons and items you can obtain during your gameplay. I also enjoyed the art style and the combat. The mechanics behind each item was unique and made me think outside the box. The story is also very good and worth your attention. I finished the game with 11 hours and only did 84% of the items and 91% of the map cause there's a lot of hidden stuff left to find out. (I know, noob stats) but this is a game to play at your own pace and dont rush.  Enjoy!Thank you for Axiom Verge 2 and this incredible experience Thomas ! <3
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Axiom Verge 2 in many ways is a direct continuation from the original, and should be played right after for the best experience. Despite this, it seems like a conscience effort has been made to innovate and change up the core mechanics - so different move systems, weapon systems and upgrade system.The ability to fast travel makes going back for upgrades considerably more enjoyable that the first one. What I would say is that while there are improvements such as this, the combat feels a little less tight than the original - and the ending surprised me with it's abruptness. Still well worth playing, but treat is as different than the original, rather than an outright improvement. But with the original being so good, that's not faint praise.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: My play time says only 5 hours but I also have a copy on my switch from a while ago.I love this game.  The combat and mechanics are different from the first one but the game is still a great game, even if it wasn't what I expected at first.  The lore and story are also some of my fav in any metroidvania (or even any game to be honest).  The art style and setting is amazing.  The music is on point and beautiful.Anyway if you love metroidvania style game play, please give this a try.  It's a great series.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: If you like metroidvania exploration, then this is a great game. Each area is distinct, and the breach crossing exploration hearkens back to LTTP. The weapons are less fun than the first game. This might be intentional from a lore perspective as the war is over and any powerful weapons have been eliminated.In terms of lore it builds on the first game; however, without that base it would feel somewhat empty. There are no more patternminds in 'this' world. The entire game felt like being manipulated in some direction. The internal motivation was there as a backdrop, and I could not help but be suspicious of every person. The notes carry a lot in terms of the character building. This was a great game for the most part. I'll be looking forward to Thomas' next grand adventure.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I really liked this game. It is a well-polished Metroidvania with an interesting world, interesting and mostly unique abilities (no double-jump or dash to be found) and mostly fun gameplay. I had a good time playing it. It took me about 14 hours to 100% it, and I recommend it.However, there are a few nits that I feel I must pick.1. By the time you enter the second major area in the game, there is a sudden difficulty spike, and the game becomes outright frustrating for a while. You are ill-equipped to fight the enemies who all take way too many hits. They either have super fast melee attacks or move fast and do contact damage, or they completely outrange you with projectiles that are difficult to dodge (or just have lasers that auto-hit you unless you are in cover). Your only projectile weapon is a boomerang that is rather slow and has a significant downtime between attacks due to the time it takes to return. As soon as you get a few key abilities and items and invest in a few skills, this gets better, and near the end of the game you become very powerful, but the phase during which your combat abilities just suck is just a tad too long. I can imagine some people just give up during that phase and miss all the good gameplay that happens later.2. The fast travel system just wastes too much of your time:a) You will dematerialize and then rematerialize at the destination in a very unnecessarily long animation (and, if you are not  during the travel, you will then have to watch your character get up from a prone position which tacks on another second).b) You cannot fast travel between Kiengar and , so every trip across tacks on another minute that will just be spent fast-traveling to a save point near a portal, entering it and then fast traveling again on the other side.It takes no additional skill, only time, and makes the late-game item hunt much more of a chore than it needs to be.3. Most of the hidden items are easy to mildly challenging to find, but there are a few stinkers that are completely invisible/unknowable with no indication whatsoever. The most ridiculous ones are: andFortunately, there are only a few hidden items like this, but it is still annoying.If you can look past these small flaws, the game is quite enjoyable for any 2D Metroidvania enthusiast.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: 7.5/10Axiom Verge 2 is a good sequel that can stand alone because of its plot. A lot of changes happened to the game but all of them are not good. Exploration is very excited, but fights are get very simple and there is no challenge even in boss fights. So Axiom Verge 2 is easy game unlike the first game, but it is deniable that exploration in its map is so good that with beautiful pixel art and perfect musics, Axiom Verge 2 became a metroidvania game that is wonderful in adventure but not in action.+:Beautiful pixel art with different environmentsAn adventurous exploration in a metroidvania worldVarious power-ups keep the gameplay enjoyable and didn't let it become repetitiveThe second world along with the variety of gameplay, has made the exploration more challengingAmazing musics-:Fighting enemies is very simple, unlike the first gameNo good or challenging boss fights, unlike the first gameFinding target can be very difficult at times
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Axiom Verge 2 throws you off initially if you played the first game. Then you notice that the design decisions are too deliberate to be a fumble by the developer Tom Happ. The protagonist in AV2 is Indra, a ruthless, middle aged tech company CEO searching for her daughter. Instead of a multitool-weapon you're handed an ice axe and a boomerang that are borderline ineffective against the enemies, which are fast and have access to guns, lasers and other ranged weapons. Combat is designed more about avoiding, manipulating or zipping past enemies, although you can take every fight with ease, face tank and trade hits after the first third of the game. The game contextualises more of the Axiom Verge Multiverse and starts off quite sluggish. In true metroidvania fashion you will unlock abilities that help you traverse the environment while you get stronger and find out more about the mysterious world Kiengir that you landed in. You acquire different movement abilities for your human and drone form and are encouraged to combine them to get around. Later, you also unlock an alternate world that is layered over the normal dimension and constitutes an alternate way of traversing.Overall, I think Axiom Verge 2 is a good game, but it is simply less fun than its predecessor. The combat element of the game is very simplified, all bosses but one are optional. The art style better rendered, but overall less intriguing and beautiful than the monumental Rusalki and the strange, alien world of Sudra in AV1. I think you should play this if you want to know more about the story of Axiom Verge, but if you are in for the metroidvania-gameplay there are many better titles for you. The game is also overall much shorter than AV1, I have reached the ending of the game with 98% map completion in only 10 hours, really taking my time to explore. It's not a fumble, it's deliberate. But it might not be your thing. If it was not named Axiom Verge 2, but something like, "An Axiom Verge Story", it would maybe set the expectations better. Proper titling is important.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: At first I missed the cool ranged weapons from the first game and had some problems to distinguish foreground objects (like platforms) from background elements. But after playing half an hour, the Axiom Verge magic kicked in again and I had a great experience which is absolutely on par with the predecessor. You get a mysterious world full of ancient technology and mythological beings. I really love the mesopotamia/sci-fi theme. The pixel art is lovely and the soundtrack (again) absolutely stunning. I hear the tracks in my head, even when I'm not playing. The hacking tools and the two overlapped world maps add some interesting new gameplay elements. To summarize - in my opinion Thomas Happ delivered a worthy successor and a must-play for all metroidvania fans.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: A worthy successor to the first one IMO. Plays quite a bit differently but "tastes" the same if that makes any sense, so if you liked the first one like I did its definitely a must play.Its worth noting that most of the bosses are optional, which is fine considering the bosses are probably the weakest parts of these games. You get rewarded for fighting them but they are easy to miss.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: A letdown from the first AV. Atmosphere is gone, story is tame and emotionally not engaging. The world is boring, the main protagonist of the first AV is absent and the new main character is an unsufferable, inhumane trope. The game is based around melee combat, shooting takes a siderole - do not buy if you like Axiom Verge.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I originaly wrote a long and detailed review but i think this sums it up more succinct.Graphics: Improved pixel art from the first one, the enviroments are more natural, i liked this but some don'tGameplay: turned ranged combat into melee focused, this includes adding a lot of health to the player so they can facetank. I prefered the old style since  this one felt more annoying than fun.Story: Descent though it feels like it could have used more time to develop the other characters in the story rather than just the protagonistScore: 7.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: While not as great as the first game, in my opinion, Axiom Verge 2 is still a good Metroidvania. And a quite good sequel.Whilst the first game was a very straight forward copy of Metroid, with dark and dank caves and alien life forms, the second game has a lot more variety in the environments, visuals and gameplay. This is a good thing, mostly, since it feels like something else. Something different. The areas are more varied, for sure, but also not quite as cohesive and feels a bit broken up. I still prefer the first game's vibe though. The map is better, and worse. Better as in that you can see more detail, and worse because you can see...more detail. It can become quite cluttered and annoying on the eyes at times to be honest. But it's somewhat easier to see certain paths and what not.The story is as always equally strange and a bit hard to keep track on, which is exactly the point. You do feel lost in an alien world. Music and sound design is fantastic, as per usual, and the atmosphere is great.The game focuses more on melee combat (and to some extent, more exploration), which differs greatly from the run-and-gun-approach of the first game. It mostly works fine, though I'm not completely sold on the action this time around. Mostly on account of there not being enough variety and ways to tackle it. It's not snappy enough to feel sublime as a melee platformer. Still, it gets the job done and is not an issue since most enemies and bosses are quite simple to overcome.Overall, I quite enjoyed this sequel. It might not trump the first game for me personally, but I do applaud and salute the change in style. It's still very solid as a Metroidvania, and well worth playing. Recommended for people interested in the subgenre. The fact that it's still made by pretty much one guy is as amazing as before.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: After beating Axiom Verge I was excited to see there was already a sequel to dig my freshly sharpened teeth into. Right away I was impressed with how different the two games were. The drone capabilities alone added so much depth and strategic thinking. Last but not least, AV2's story is much more pronounced which gave it a better feel overall. I'll definitely be adding the AV series to my play again playlist.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly the story of both games are really intriguing. This game is superior to the first in every single way except:- bosses actually worse (which is saying alot because they were bad in AV1)- the many various guns were actually fun in AV1, vs the static kit in AV2. Still a decently fun kit by end game thoughThis game is definitely easier, AV1 went for the NES old school game difficulty with obtuse secrets.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: amazing, creative game, one of the few metroidvanias which really leans into exploration over everything else, which makes playing this game a breath of fresh air when compared to most other games in the genre which tend to focus on combat, or at least that's what my experience has been. art style, world and music are fantastic, story is satisfactory, not too much, not too little. compared to axiom verge 1 it is quite different in some ways, particularly concerning the combat and weapons, 2 stand out elements in the original, which are both far less developed. The game, at least when in combat, is quite a bit easier as well. Many negative reviews of this game (from what I've seen) come from people who don't necessarily dislike the game, but would rather it be a more direct sequel to axiom verge, which is fair enough that game was great, but as someone who loves exploration I am very VERY happy with the direction this game has chosen to go in. 9.5/10 easily.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game! While Axiom Verge leaned heavily into the Metroid side of the Metroidvania genre, Axiom Verge 2 sits squarely on the Castlevania side. This is not a bad thing.Intriguing story. Memorable characters. Beautiful landscapes. Good music. Great gameplay.The lack of any sort of gun was unexpected, especially when many enemies can attack from a greater distance than you can. The weapons pretty much all feel the same; The only real difference is how quickly they can attack. This can feel clunky until you upgrade your attack speed. I found many enemies easier to fight as a drone, because of the hitboxes of the enemies and the player's attack.AV2 improves on AV1 in many ways. The mapping system is much better, including pins to mark places of interest for later (just be sure to do so! A few more pins would be nice, because you run out quickly). The drone is much more capable. The Breach is an interesting change of pace from the main world. The world is much more connected and easier to traverse, and there's a very much-appreciated fast travel option. A pacifist run (and achievement) is possible. The lore is expanded greatly, yet leaves plenty to speculation. Hacking and "secret" areas are much less obscured, making it much easier to figure out where to go and what to do next.I loved both games and am eagerly awaiting the announcement of an Axiom Verge 3, if one should come to be!
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Non 100% run clocked at almost 9 hours, gameplay start kinda restricted, but get very fluid after you get some movement upgrades, history is really nice, not a lot of exposition so you need to piece things together yourself, and even then a lot is left a mistery, which is not a bad thing in my opinionif you played the first axion verge, the melee focused combat will feel kinda strange at the start, but it gets really fun around the mid point of the game, game has a lot of places to visit and there is enough choice for you to get side tracked.i will give it a 8/10 - not amazing, but really, really good.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: AV2 switches up a lot of things while Sticking to a lot of things that worked well in the first one. You still get plenty of fun items  that radically alter your ability to navigate the world and get's way more inventive than just unlocking a double jump. I enjoyed the hacking mechanic and in terms of colours, lighting and music it's a bit more HiFi than the first one while still being true to the character of a retro style Metroidvania. Grab it, especially if you're a fan of the genre!
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Wow ok basically this is a really good game so far. It is NOT a copy of the first game, it is very different on its approach, but most of the feel of the first game is still in it. Most negative reviews are about the fact that it's very different and having difficulty increased. It is very different, combat is not that much difficult, as you have a new powerup that lets you 'hack' and work around said op enemies.Briefly, it is very good. This is a 90% review game downgraded to 80% because it is very different in gameplay. But the actual gameplay and map workaround is VERY nice. It is a solid metroidvania. _childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game thinking it wouldn't be as good as the first because of the lower score, but I was wrong.I agree that the combat is a little off but I think all that needs to be changed is adding a combat dash or dodge like many other metroidvanias with melee combat have (castlevania, hollow knight, blasphemous)Some combat encounters in this game aren't winnable through playing smart or agile and you end up just having to spend your health as a resource by using your damage i-frames to get in close and button mash, and the button mashing itself can use some qol tuning as well as it's easy to mistime it and have your inputs ignored from mashing too fast.However, everything else in this game is a 10/10. Amazing soundtrack, spritework, environments, and worldbuilding. I expected a direct sequel, but it's instead a prequel that provides more context to the overarching plot. The story isn't over yet so a third game is extremely likely.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended, with some caveats.I do miss the visual style from the first game, but the music is an unbelievable improvement with better sound design and melodies.  Movement is also a lot more enjoyable and unique than it was in AV1, though having to manually switch between upgrades rather than have them mapped to separate buttons is frustrating, especially when half of the tools in that sub-menu are borderline useless and there's plenty of room on the keyboard.  Level design also feels a lot cleaner, with the moments I got lost definitely feeling more like my fault (I have a tendency to halt progression to explore an area more thoroughly then forget where I was supposed to be going).  A likely factor in this is the map system--not only is it much more useful, but it displays an impressive amount of artistic effort.  The Breach sections aren't super fun to traverse, but the subworld makes for some fun puzzles getting to secret areas.Though some of my friends didn't enjoy the new combat, I actually rather liked it, though that may be because I prefer getting close and hitting things at a range I can't miss.  Likely as a result of that, I didn't get much use out of the boomerang.  The melee attack of the drone felt kind of unresponsive, as well.Unfortunately, the second game shares a major problem with the first, in that the story is essentially over once the final upgrade is collected, with a short stint down a previously-inaccessible corridor leading to an impossible-to-lose boss fight.  I think some sort of "final challenge" area that tests the player's skills would have helped the ending to feel more satisfying.  I'm also disappointed we didn't get much info directly addressing the events of the previous game, though I'm willing to concede that I might just have failed to connect the dots.  Maybe Axiom Verge 3 will tie up the stories of Indra and Chaudhari in a neat little bow, but on the other hand I'd also respect the decision to make the AV series a set of disconnected narratives in a vast and confusing universe--one that has been expanded significantly by this game's plot.Rambling aside, I recommend this game.  It doesn't get everything right, but it gets a lot more right than its predecessor and is genuinely enjoyable most of the time.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed playing this! loved the original one too, and I wish for more content in this universe.My favorite part:1. exploration and sense of place, the pixel art2. movement especially with upgrades3. cool drone and hacking upgrades4. story and how it ties in to the first one5. the protag (not a silent protag)6. convenient fast travel, esp. at the end when mopping up7. musicMy least favorite part:1. I have all the upgrades but no tough enemy to try it on! (endgame content)2. Need more bosses What changes the most from the first one:1. the pivot to melee combat and non-weapon upgrades
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Axiom Verge 2 is an incredible follow up to the first title and faithful to the Metroidvania genre.  Just with the first game, it has good visuals, cool abilities, and I daresay; a better soundtrack than the original.  This game does not hold your hand, so it challenges you to find a way to progress.  My one complaint is that the bosses are entirely too easy: no challenge, no need for strategy, just spam your attack away to victory.  Otherwise, this is a fantastic game, and I hope to see more from this solo developer.  Tom Happ, don’t ever stop making games.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Axiom Verge 2 has a great retro feel and offers alot of fun exploring the game world. It's a must have for metroidvania fans. The developer Tom Happ provides enjoyable pixel artwork, music and gameplay, woven into a solid level design. Some things feel a bit tricky, some parts are strange, but it's an overall great experience. The story itself is interesting and matches the sci-fi genre well. Collecting all the crumps of informations stored on collectibles is pretty time consuming, though. The replay value is mediocre for casual players because of its high emphasis of drone shape.Compared to the previous game "Axiom Verge", it feels like quite some technical improvements and functions found their way into the game. However, the style of the successor game "Axiom Verge 2" has completely changed. It's far less about weapons and shooting enemies and much more avoiding fights, because that consumes alot of time and fighting doesn't feel rewarding, most of the time. The content of the game is fair, although it seems smaller than the first game.Axiom Verge 2 has few downsides. None of these impose a reason for serious complaints, though. There are a few strange decisions regarding the gameplay. No matter what players fight, it takes plenty of hits. It doesn't make fights more interesting or difficult. It just takes time and most players will soon prefer to just jump over and past enemies.After a while, the most interesting shape to use is the drone for movability, speed, combat and almost everything else. Players will also find themself teleporting all over the place and worlds so often and so fast. This can pull a player out of immersion. It can also drop tension and excitement level to zero, because character death has pretty much no impact. This exposes etremely at the last "boss fight". That fight wasn't exciting or interesting, but it was stylish.Axiom Verge 2 has far less equipment and weapons than the previous game. In fact, it itsn't much but that's not a bad thing. The introduction of a skill system for improvements is simple and alright. It's nothing refined but it works just fine. A surprise is the limited utilization of equipment. At some point, players can optain a weapon (hammer) and an ability to slam down upon enemies or the ground. It could be great to break through walls but instead, the game is much more about teleporting around and switching between two world for limited puzzle solving. It's still great work but the game does not live up to its potential.To sum it up:Axiom Verge 2 has a few quirks and oddities but it's fun and stylish. If we disregard "graphic blenders", the game could easily challenge many top titles of genres "platformer" and "metroidvania" and beat them. I can't say it beats the first Axiom Verge game but it does a great job.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I have thoroughly enjoyed the game and that's the issue. _childDocuments_.review: This is a good game, but I wouldn't call it great. _childDocuments_.review: Thoughts after finishing my first play through of Axiom Verge 2. As someone who enjoys slower paced exploration and world building heavy games, this one was thoroughly enjoyable and engaging. As an older gamer with limited time for hobbies, I have a very low tolerance for games that waste my time, and tend to bounce off them fairly quickly. Axiom Verge 2 kept my attention however, and I saw it through to the end fairly rapidly.What It Did Well- The Mesopotamian influences made for a compelling backdrop, reflected in the writing, art and music. It felt like a cohesive and fascinating world to engage with.- Just the right amount of speculative sci-fi elements without leaning too much into exposition.- The body horror and existential dread themes were sold very well through a thoughtfully designed ludo-narrative dynamic. As the protagonist grew stronger and became more of a game character, they gradually lost their humanity in a sense.- Early on in the game, there was a real sense of tension and need to use stealth and hacking to manage enemy encounters. - Nicely crafted spritework and animations. Each area was well distinguished with stark color pallets and varied level layouts.- Catchy background music with a few true earworms that never got too obnoxious.- Several upgrades with unexpected and clever ways to interact with the environments and overcome obstacles. I loved every "aha" moment when you realized how to reach a previously seemingly out of reach spot on the map!- Mastery of the mechanics sometimes allowed you to make your own shortcuts, which is always fun.Missed Opportunities- Would have liked to see more aspects of the world anchored in lore. Who were the optional bosses, and their role in the ecosystem or history of their locations? How come the world was layered in the way it was, and the sky wrapping around itself when at the lowest layer?- Early on there were interactions between the Arms, but that was quickly dropped. Something like optional questlines for each Arm to develop their abilities and learn about their pasts would have been neat!- Nearly impossible to avoid taking damage from most enemies, since they had attacks with zero signaling or build up.- The combat became trivialized too quickly, with the lack of any real i-frames or stamina system making rushing in and spamming fast attacks the most efficient way to tackle 90% of combat scenarios. - Conversely, the hacking system felt underpowered and hardly worth investing upgrade points into. For instance, the (expensive) ALLEGIANCE hack would have the enemy stay at their current route rather than follow you around, which made it next to worthless.Nitpicks- In the back half of the game, opening up shortcuts was entirely pointless. - The wall climb ability was way too sticky. In tight situations, it was too easy to get stuck on the wall when you wanted to do combat or platforming.- The slow walk mechanic was pointless, and was sometimes detrimental when you tilted the controller stick in just the wrong way to trigger it when you wanted to actually run.- Similarly, even the slightest upwards angle to the stick would have you climb stairs when you actually wanted to walk horizontally.- The unskippable save point "fountain" animation became very old very quickly. Please allow us to skip or speed it up!

There were some big surprises that, blindsided, shocked, and delighted me.  The level design and various abilities you acquire to help you traverse the levels are both interesting and creative. _childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Axiom Verge 2 is just as fun, intriguing, and as great as the first game. I really don't mind the differences in gameplay, as it reminds me of the old NES days when Zelda 1, Zelda 2, Mario 1, Mario 2, were trying to be creative and innovative by making changes to the gameplay. I am only 25% in the game so far, and I love the story, the new style gameplay, and the exploration so far. It's the kind of game where I tell myself I am only going to play for 30 minutes and end up playing for 2 hours. The game remains fresh, and does not feel stale. I also get some major Pitfall 2 vibes from the Atari 7800. I really look forward in finishing this game, and I look forward in Axiom Verge 3 if it ever comes to fruition.

_childDocuments_.review: DON'T LET THE DIFFERENCES FROM THE FIRST ONE TURN YOU AWAY!!!When I first got the game, I was a bit put off by the differences. The artstlye and combat is different. And overall, many of the surface-level features are unlike the first game.I'm really glad I kept playing it though. The level design is great. The OST is really nice. I really love all the little upgrades and abilities you can collect. And its VERY much tied into the first game.My only complaint is that the bosses aren't that great or challenging.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: In my opinion, this is one of the best metroidvania games out there, although I personally would have preferred if the game's combat system was a gun-based ("metroid" style) just like Axiom Verge 1 rather than a melee-based ("castevania" style), especially since a lot of elemies fire projectiles at you.Aside from that, the game features a lot of interesting ideas, mechanics and useful upgrades, although I have to admit that I found the first 30% of the game a bit boring due to the lack of actual gear to use -- however, the game becomes more fun at the later stages -- at least if you do not mind backtracking to collect items that you could not reach before. The story is okay, although quite confusing, and it is not linked to the story of Axiom Verge 1, but I don't really mind that.If you like metroidvania games and don't mind the melee combat system, then this game is definitely worth trying out.Finally, I really hope that Axiom Verge 3 combines the ideas and mechanics from this game along the metroid-style gun-based combat.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: A sequel to a great indie metroidvania, Axiom Verge is as beautiful in its visuals, music, and overall glitchy posthuman aesthetic as the first one — but the gameplay is way less challenging, to the point where it feels more like a puzzle platformer than an action game. Most enemies are at worse a nuisance, but getting where you want to — that's the real challenge. Highly recommended for metroidvania fans who love the genre for its exploration aspect, rather than combat.
