_childDocuments_.review: This is the kind of game that makes me wish Steam had more than just a "thumbs up/down" review. This game is very different from the previous one and overall, I don't think it really holds up to AV1. Id give it probably a 7/10: Better than average, and outside the context of its predecessor, it was still a very solid game. Some of the best exploration in a MetroidVania I've seen in a while, satisfying traversal, fun and interesting power ups, satisfying story, great world design, great music, the works. The combat however was fairly mediocre. But that's really the only major flaw in the game.They took the foundation of the last game, being a 8-direction shooter, and all of the design that comes with that, and they turned it into a predominantly melee experience. The enemy design however was not sufficiently changed. The enemies still felt like they were designed around being able to fight them from a distance and kite them. The ground enemies were extremely fast or had extremely low cooldown ranged attacks, sometimes literally undodgeable, and the aerial enemies would always sit just out of range of your attacks while firing their own ranged attacks, meaning you could only damage them with your very weak boomerang attack. The melee attack also wasn't even particularly good at dealing with them when you could reach them either; it was fairly weak, didn't have much knockback, and the hitbox was fairly high up so you often missed short enemies unless you stood still to crouch or aim diagonally, but you usually got hit for doing that. There was also a hacking mechanic, which would allow you to slow most enemies, among other effects. While it was occasionally useful, sometimes even fixing the undodgeable attack problem, it was slow to use, required you to get basically into melee range to use, meaning you'd usually get hit anyways, and the effects didn't actually do enough to justify using it most of the time.It seemed like the best strategy in combat was almost always to just tank a hit, and then smack them to death during the invulnerability. This strategy worked quite well for the entire game; there was enough healing and checkpoints to generally negate the damage. But it led to a fairly disappointing combat experience when it felt like that was the only viable way to approach it that wouldn't take minutes per enemy to kill with your very weak boomerang and hacking.For the most part, it usually ended up being more enjoyable to just run past most enemies when you could, killing the few that were in your way. It became a lot more fun once I treated the enemies and combat as just a device to enhance the exploration by adding some stakes and mild danger, not so much an integral part of the game on their own like in games like Hollow Knight or Dark Souls. But seeing as the game seemed to be much more heavily exploration focused, that style of gameplay actually worked pretty well once I shifted my mindset, especially as it got later in the game where I had more abilities to facilitate the exploration. As with most games in the genre, towards the end of the game you are running all over the map completing various tasks and finding all the stuff you missed on the way, usually ignoring enemies anyways. The game shined best during the second half for this reason. In the same vain of exploration there were very few times where I had the classic Metroid moment of "where am I even supposed to go?" The world and minimap designs and the very generous fast travel system made this almost nonexistant. I only got totally lost 1 singular time at the very end of the game, but it was partially my fault:When you are looking for the last upgrade, there is a specific room you need to use a specific ability in to get to it (the "Goodbye" room). While there was a visual indicator in the room to use that ability, I somehow missed it and left that room without realizing what I needed to do. Due to the way the map and abilities work and happened to combine just right in that room, there was absolutely no indication on the minimap that I had missed something; no empty neighboring room, no unchecked doors, nothing. So I spent about an hour running around looking for where to go, completing a bunch of side content before I gave up and checked a walkthrough for how to get passed this one part. Annoying but I don't really fault it too much since it only happened once and I had missed a very obvious indicator of what to do. Maybe they could fix this in a patch with some sort of minimap indicator, but I'm not really sure how.Lastly, the lack of proper bosses was a bit unfortunate, but also I didn't really miss them that much. There were only 2 mandatory bosses and both of them were fairly trivial; if you die you literally respawned directly in the same room without losing progress, so you couldn't fail. There were also optional mini-bosses around the world, but they weren't anything super special, definitely didn't scratch the Metroid boss itch. It wasn't really a big deal though, there was at least a proper final boss and escape sequence, and with the combat being what it was, it might've been more annoying than good to have more classic boss fights. Not really sure what to make of it.Overall, solid game. As much as I did a lot of complaining, it's just because it got so much right and it was so close to greatness. I did actually have a lot of fun playing it. The exploration and atmosphere were really top notch; it absolutely nailed that key aspect of the genre in allowing yourself to seemingly get lost in an interesting world without ever actually getting properly lost and not knowing what to do or where to go next. The combat was really the only problem with the game and frankly, they could probably fix most if not all of the combat problems via a patch; there were no foundational problems with the combat, it just needs a little polish.

_childDocuments_.review: I've read a lot of reviews saying this game isn't as good as the first one. I honestly beg to differ. It's different with a stronger focus on exploration and less on combat. And this fits with the story. I'm having a ton of fun with it, just as much, if not more than, the first. Look, if you like the metroidvania genre, you'll like this game. 100% would recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Start with Axiom Verge 1; it's a better game and the two games tie together very well.Axiom Verge 2 is also a great game, with a cool main character, some really amazing lore, and a wild twist in the middle that genuinely makes one think.  I beat it in about ten hours (no idea why Steam's playtime for me is inaccurate) and I had a good time.  A lot of it was blindly feeling around for an upgrade; there's not a lot that points you in the right direction, and the bosses are basically just high-powered enemies you can ignore.  Still, it's super cool and interesting, and I loved all the nods to the original.

It does a superb job of playing with your expectations for how items and traversal mechanics are going to work just like the first game did with all the upgrades that worked like no other item in a metroidvania did the traversal progress before.

_childDocuments_.review: i played this first on epic. if we are speaking honestly. i liked the first game more. but i really like what was done here. it is very different and yet familiar. the change from gun to melee as the primary means of combat is quite a change but its easy to get used to. i found that i got a little lost in where to go(this happened in the first one too) but you know thats part of the exploration aspect of it. people love to say hollow knight is the best metroidvania of the current ages, but i feel like this series does all the right things and does right by the genre to such an extent i would wager it to be better than hollow knight.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game, it takes a while to get used to the new combat and might seem a bit unfair at the start, but once you get the hang of it along with a couple of upgrades the experience feels very smooth.Some of the item locations seem a bit cryptic, and I still don't understand why there are no item pointers in the map to know if you have collected everything there.The story is not the best but not the worst, and there does seem to be a nod to a sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Some say this sequel is not as good as the original. I mostly agree. That being said, this is still a solid metroidvania with polished mechanics, great graphics and music, and also deals with the same uncomfortable themes of transhumanism as the first game. All-in-all this is a great game. Definitely worth a play-through. Most conspicuously, the game lacks the engaging boss battles of the original and the variety of weapons. If you like the original, there is still a lot to like here, though. I bought this game on a Friday and loved it so much that I couldn't stop playing for the whole weekend!
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent sequel to Axiom Verge. The change in world and scenery makes the experience less grim than the first installment, and opens the worldbuilding instead of channeling it deeper in its previous direction. The story and exploration is fantastic--better than the first, imo--and I hope we don't have to wait another 5 years for the third installment.The combat is less Metroid this time around, and more Castlevania, but without as much distinction between weapon types. Weapons instead are replaced by Breach items, which add a fun puzzle layer to the exploration. I do have to say the boss design took a bit of a dive from the previous game; you can just charge and tank all of them except the final boss. Bonus points to improved level design and map usability. The music is exceptional. True masterwork, there.If you liked the first one, definitely check this one out. And if you like Metroidvanias and you haven't played either, well get both!
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Not as good as the first game, but "not as good as Axiom Verge 1" still means it's a good gameExploration's pretty fun and cool, but the combat is pretty lacking and I'd honestly prefer more traditional boss battles than the mostly-skippable ones. Music's not bad but it's kind of a downgrade and the sound effect balancing feels kinda screwy. I like the cool torus-world visuals and the story feels more involved and hits on some more sci-fi concepts that I enjoy.If AV3 ever happens I hope Tom takes the exploration, artstyle, and storytelling from this game and combines it with the solid combat and tunes of the first game
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I would give this game a neutral if I could. The game looks and sounds fantastic and besides one section ran flawlessly for me at least. My main problem comes from the story, gameplay and rewards for exploration. Firstly the story pales in comparison to the first game, the bleak atmosphere, interesting conversations and intriguing characters are gone. Instead you are left wanting more elaboration and depth from every conversation, it feels like you are given limited information for a potentially deep story, but the more you look the more you realise how shallow everything is. There are so many little details that lend to something really interesting but there is absolutely no payoff, to the point that I though there would be a few extra levels, or a secret final area instead of only a few things that change in the endings. This game would benefit hugely from and extra area/difficult level akin to Celeste's Farewell. Secondly the gameplay is not at all like the first game, which is fine. However you are given very limited options to handle enemies, leading to every combat encounter feeling the same. The hacking mechanic is simplified and there are very little changes between weapons meaning that despite all the upgrades you get you will be fighting enemies the same way from the beginning to the end of the game. My last issue with the game is the rewards for exploration. The map itself and the process of exploring is wonderful but nothing you gain makes you excited for the next reward. Skill points are an interesting concept but since you feel nearly the exact same with every upgrade they aren't very rewarding, getting a specific power upgrade or hacking boost would be preferable personally. In addition the "Bosses" you can find while exploring are underwhelming, since besides two, they feel very similar and meld together since they have no build up, music, or memorable aspects/patterns. All in all, I did enjoy this game as it is, but I understand the disappointment from fans of the first game. It's very pretty and fun but much more shallow than the first.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly, wow.  What an amazing game.  This was truly an enjoyable experience from start to finish.  I really don't understand some of the negative reviews here.  The combat is different, yes, but in no way "clunky" or "unsatisfying."  The primarily melee-based combat system makes for a unique challenge.  The story itself did a good job of being it's own unique experience while at the same time finding ways to tie into the first game with visual references as well as other clues hinting to events from the first game.This game is everything Axiom Verge was, and more.  It was truly worth the wait, and the $20 price tag.  Kudos to you, Tom Happ, for creating yet another phenomenal experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I think axiom verge 1 is a better game. 2 looks great, has a fantastic soundtrack and i enjoyed the story, which i felt was slightly easier to follow. But i found alot of the traversal and combat changes and differences, whilst novel and well thought out, i did not enjoy as much as the originals to play and use. Definitely not a bad game by any means, but dose not surpass it's original.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: I've played this game twice over before on other platforms! And I have to say, I absolutely *love* this game. It's such an amazing world to walk around in and just drink the atmosphere in, with so much to learn and piece together about the world you're in. It's one of the few ever pieces of media that I started right back up from the start after finishing it, and one of so few games I've put the effort in to try and 100% myself. The visuals, music and writing all leave such a mark on me: playing this game changes my dreams.The melee combat is absolutely brillant. You really learn how to use movement to close distance, throw yourself into the danger and take high risks to end the battle quickly! Don't hold yourself back -- there's so much to master with how you move and place your hits, so much to learn about how enemies behave and react to you, about how movement *is* combat here. One of my absolute favorite moments was starting a new game and realizing just how differently I fought compared to my first time through in those early areas!Maybe it doesn't capture everybody from the Axiom Verge 1 audience, but this game is something complete and special in its own right. I really connected with it, and it's okay if not everybody does.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Its a great Metroidvania.The art is pretty and the songs are pretty catchy. Item progression is constant so things keep interesting for the most part. Unfortunately combat is mostly melee, with a few ranged options but they're not very good.Fans from the first game however will feel a bit sad that the "Giger-esque" feel to the game is mostly gone. Still a great game and I can't wait for more from Mr. Happ.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: It isn't what you'd expect after Axiom Verge 1, but it's not bad either.The second installment of Axiom Verge takes place seemingly in a different time and location, and operates on different styles of action.  So if you were expecting a continuation of Axiom Verge 1, shed that thought.  It is different in terms of it's pacing, and expect to go back and forth a lot between areas as you progress (typical of a Metroidvania style game).However, the graphics still feel worthy of the Axiom Verge title when it comes to it.  The music is another set of bangers like AV1, the graphics are very similar in nature (old school pixel style), and the combat system definitely provides a slight challenge above run-and-gun as AV1 presented.A lot of people who were expecting a "proper sequel" may be disappointed here, but if you shed the expectation and dig in, you will find this possibly adds to the universe in such a way where you play and study both, it's probably leading to a culmination in a future title.I do highly suggest this title to anyone who loved the first entry.  I first bought on EGS, and finally have it on my preferred platform, and still worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really fun metroidvania that has the feel of AV1 without playing exactly like the original.While I would have liked a continuation of AV1's story, it's still a fun prequel.  The music in many areas and the sounds makes it really feel like an axiom verge sequel/prequel.The weapon system revamp and ability points are a nice addition, as well as the larger mini bot focus (I played as it a lot once I got a few certain upgrades).I didn't even know it was an EG exclusive until I read some reviews, thought it just came out recently (marketing clearly wasn't the best)If you are looking for a metroidvania with a focus on exploration and secrets this will definitely scratch that itch.The only downside I really have is that there are basically no bosses.  There are large enemies that seem like mini-bosses, but they go down as quick as some of the regular enemies.  Even the final boss doesn't really feel like one (think steamworld dig 1 last boss).
_childDocuments_.name: Axiom Verge 2

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, I started giving a negative review due to crashes, preventing me playing the game after waiting to play it for so long. Now that I have finished it, time to make it right.• Overall time to finish : if you are used to the genre, count around 8h. 10-11h if you aim 100%.• Like Axiom Verge, the game is a Metroidvania, with an emphasis on exploration, powering up and backtracking. Your loadout change compared to the first game to where you have a melee weapon as the primary way to deal damage, and secondary weapon to deal or poke damage from afar. • The game is incredibly tough when you start, due to your lack of range and power, and you quickly face enemies that can obliterate you, forcing you to use stealth, or just flee. This change as soon as you find the Infection urn, that allows you to hack enemies and get the upper hand. However, once you get past a game-changing point in the game, you can just start to "rofl into the enemies' faces" melee attacks and take damage without much of consequences, that is aggravated now since you can now store health in advance.• Controls are nice. Indra feels a bit clunky due to the fact she has more inertia than Trace, but I never had any issue when I wanted to go exactly to a specific spot.• You have less "weapon junk" compared to the first game, which is great. But you have still some : why would I play with a "late-found" dagger/sword when my axes have special/powerful moves for a while ?• Infection is the Address Disruptor of the game, but better.• The Breach is nice : it's a world itself this time and is interconnected to the overworld. You have to think in both dimensions to open new areas, or find secrets, which is really neat. But it doesn't feel anymore like a place where you shouldn't be, and lost what made the secret areas so dangerous and exciting in the first game. • Level design is excellent, with lots of shortcuts you can unlock, with or without upgrades . Moving through levels never felt like a chore, on the contrary of the first game where sometime, moving through Indi was the only way to go faster from one area to another.• Bosses are "non-existent", which is good and bad at the same time. You can also entirely skip them, which is a rather innovative way to progress in a Metroidvania, especially for people who struggle in this kind of fights. However, kudos to MUS A M20, which was really interesting to defeat. I wish all bosses had something similar to defeat them, instead of just hack/spam attacks. • Secrets and 100% hunting : the game is not as generous as the first one, and we even lost some "think outside the box" puzzles (those who needed cypher translation) from Axiom Verge, in exchange for some "Konami codes". But it's still enjoyable nonetheless, and for people like me who cannot play a Metroidvania without 100% the s*** out of it, the game will still combles you very well. Especially with the extra juicy addition of optional upgrades that will help you to track anything you potentially missed, which is something I really like to have integrated in the game, instead of just going into a wiki or solution on the net.• Color are less vibrant/flashy (except in the Breach), and all graphical elements have finer details. It lost the charm of the first game, but at the same time, it has another kind of charm to it. Ultimately, I like the pixel art we have in Axiom Verge 2 : you have so much details compared to the first game.• Still feels a bit off compared to the first game : you are in another world, but it's not as Alien as Sudra. It makes highly odd to see such advanced technology in general in a world where vestiges of civilization show more "Indian/Egyptian" ruins. However, this is not necessarily a bad point, since it serves perfectly the story, and you will still have some surprises, that will counter this very argument.• The Breach (inside) is less "glitchy" and more structured with "clean" pixel art. It was needed to make a new interconnected map that would not be a mess, but it lost what made this area special in Axiom Verge.• In Axiom Verge 2, you will have lots of "Indian tunes", which may not be to the liking of everyone. But it serves the gameplay/story : when you will find the Earth campement, you will have a music that is more like the first game, but once you go further, you will be immerged in Kiengir's culture that you know nothing of... Well, with the exception of specific places, where memories will instantly flow once you have reached them.• Like the first game, there is some tracks that I didn't like, others that are good, and specific ones that are outstanding (Ex: "").• I couldn't help but stupidly smile when I heard remix of the first game tracks. Best part ? It's intentional and has a meaning lore-wise when you "read between the lines", when you consider everything you read/see in those places while hearing those tracks.• I couldn't help but be stupidly exalted when I heard the final boss music. I would need some severe amnesia to forget such a track ! • You can play the game without playing the first one, but it will be better if you do.• The ambiance lost a part of the "glitch" feeling, that you "hack" through reality. It's still somewhat present thanks to the Breach, but it felt less impactful.• Like the first game, if you like to think about it, it will make you question about our relationship with certain themes, like machines, religion and evolution.• Right after starting the game, you will realize this is a prequel to Axiom Verge. So sadly, no. We will not know what happened to Trace we incarnate in the first game.• Story is not exposed and will be mediocre at best (like the first game) if you rush, don't care about notes, or don't pause a bit to think about what it implies.• If you paid attention to details, the story in Axiom Verge 2 will not quench your thirst on what will happen after the first game, but  gives you informations that will make several pieces of the first game fall into place, and will allow you to speculate on what will happen, in both games.• If you remember parts of Axiom Verge' story, you will get that Dr. Hammond is the link between this game and the first one, and that Trace's epiphany has triggered indirectly the events in Axiom Verge 2.• If you greatly remember Axiom Verge' story (or took an express wakeup call on the wiki, works fine too), you will realize, at some part or at the end of the game, that you are witnessing events that will lead to the birth of Axiom Verge story , and clues to what will likely happen if there is an Axiom Verge 3 .Axiom Verge 2 lost parts of the first game that made/felt it special, but enhanced lots of points that were defaults in my eyes. You will not get answers if you expected some for Axiom Verge's end, but you will get new keys to understand what happened, and what will probably happen next. The game is exactly like the first one : a solid Metroidvania that will reward exploration, and even more, since combat is not the main focus of the game, something that can be loved or hated, depending on what your preferences are. However, there is no reasons to not buy it if you like the genre, and if you didn't played the first one, you have now two incredible games to play instead of one.

name: Wizardry: Labyrinth of Lost Souls
detailed_description: An old-school challenge in a crisp and colorful package, Wizardry: Labyrinth of Lost Souls revitalizes the time-honored formula of the original dungeon crawler series with modernized visuals and sound. Choose each of your six team members’ class, race, gender, and moral alignment, then delve into one of several dungeons near the central town hub. Advance with caution — monsters are vicious, deadly, and attack in packs. Plan each expedition carefully, stay focused on your objectives, and know when to retreat to the surface. In between expeditions, chat with the locals, pick up new quests, pray for guidance at the temple, go bargain-hunting for new/rare equipment, and more. With patience, skill, and careful planning, your party will rise from a gang of paupers to a mighty force. The magic torches are lit, the monsters are ravenous, and the kingdom is waiting for a new hero. Enter the world of Wizardry: Labyrinth of Lost Souls and experience a classic adventure reborn. KEY FEATURES Your Party, Your Way Choose from eight classes and five races to build a six-person team with diverse but complimentary skill sets. Change their classes in mid-adventure to fit your needs, or focus on leveling up their primary class to earn bonus skills for the party’s benefit. So Beautiful and So Dangerous Tangle with a menagerie of over 100 distinctive monsters, from the traditional to the bizarre, all drawn by famed series illustrator Jun Suemi. The game also features character illustrations by renowned commercial artist Yuki Hayabusa. Conquer the Dungeons Every step through the underworld is fraught with danger, and one wrong move can end your adventure. But if you have the grit to withstand what the dungeons throw at you, both you and your party will gain enough experience to stroll through them like you own them. Wizardry’s Rebirth on PC The PC remaster of this classic originally released for PlayStation 3 features English and Japanese text with the original Japanese voiceovers, high-resolution graphics, and a brand new Turbo Mode to make exploring the game’s massive dungeons a breeze. All story DLC is included, and players can download the Growth Fruit DLC for free to give themselves a boost when creating characters.

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty much just a prettier Wizardry 1.  If you liked the original from the 80's, you'll be fine.  If you have no idea what the original from the 80's was, you're going to have a rough time with the game.Example:  Was trying to roll a Samurai to start. _childDocuments_.review: RECOMMENDED  Ratings 7/10I used to play Wizardry 1: Proving Ground of the Mad Overlord by Sir-Tech on the very first day of release. I bought the game in 5 1/4 inch diskettes in a black box with a green dragon. Inside the box, was also a pad of square paper for the player to do manual mapping.This new game is basically Wizardry on Steroids and Gift Wrappers !! The high resolution graphics are awesome, the characters are hot and sexy, the music comfortable, and it also included many "Quality of life" improvements. The QoL improvements like auto-mapping, auto-leveling inside dungeon, fast and convenient savings, etc all make life a lot easier.However, what I really love about this game is that it captures the "feeling of Wizardry 1" that I experience many years ago. It's hard to describe, but here are the feelings that I  experience1. Feeling of Fear and DangerThat is the my first impression of Wizardry 1 --- it was so very easy to die and your team can be totally wiped out anytime. When I go to a new floor, I always stay near the stairs, and will escape and run anytime things go wrong. You can never be too well prepared in this game. There are too many reasons why you can get a total party wipe. Monsters may be immune to non-magic attack. They may also be immune to magic attack, or  you might step into a non-magic area. Or you may simply step onto a mine. So I play this game in fear and trepidation in 1981 and also today. It's the same feeling that I like.2. Feeling of Surprise and UnpredictabilityYou cannot be too comfortable or confident in this game, as the game will always spring you a few surprises. You may have fought a lot of low level (Level 1-6) monsters on the first floor of the Trial Dungeon, and then enter a 1 way door to a boss who is Level 12. She wipes out your entire team, and you curse yourself for saving inside the one way door. Ouch. Surprises like this literally dotted the entire game, and you have only a single savefile which you cannot even rename. So if I make a save in the wrong place, I am gone. Oh... how I hate (and love) that feeling.3. Feeling of Trapped and HopelessnessThere are just too many instances where you will feel trapped and hopeless. You feel trapped when you pass through a one-way door, or step onto a one-way portal and cannot go back. You step onto an anti-magic room and now all your casters are useless. You step onto a dark anti-magic room with spinners, and you keep wandering for ages. Spinners keep you disoriented and you feel lost and trapped. Also in this game, you cannot camp or do anything to regenerate your magic. You are given a fixed number of mage and priest spells, and the only way to recharge them is if you get back to town. Now, can you get back to town alive? You will start getting that feeling of hopelessness when your healer dies, or if you are poisoned and know that you will meet monsters every few steps you take. Arrgh!!! That's a feeling I love to hate.This excellent game capture all those "feelings of Wizardry1" that I experienced many years ago. It enables me to re-live and re-experience my past. I love this game, and highly recommend it to all the old school gamers like myself.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tricky recommendation because it's not a bad game. I enjoy it and for the right players it's perfectly fine way to spend your time and money. I'd buy it again without a doubt. But at the end of the day, there's far better dungeon crawls for the average player.The biggest issue with this game is that it's old-school in ways that hurt the experience. It feels like it has been balanced for players that like to abuse mechanics. Re-rolling characters for hours, generator characters to steal their money to buy your party starting gear, and save scumming.  The UI is dreadful and takes alot of experimenting to understand.This game is RNG madness.  The first quest was downright rage-inducing. Between battles that range from 1 to 15 units and hoping to collect random drops that just wouldn't come for well over 2 hours. They dropped me plate mail and magic swords but lord help me I couldn't get the super common tutorial daggers.While it feels alot better when you have proper gear... the same issues pop up from time to time. I'll be an hour into a delve, three rounds into a combat. "1 damage, 1 damage, 1 damage," and out of nowhere "247 damage your tank is dead."  (With a chance of permadeath) This does add a surprising tension to every single battle which I like, but the combination of random drops, massive variance in attacks, potential permadeath is just overly frustrating.  Despite my complaints, I genuinely enjoy this game. It's perfectly decent and I'm happy with the money spent. The maps are a bit nonsensical and dull but they serve their purpose. The battles tactics can be entertaining in part because of the brutality. From the moment I step foot inside the dungeon to the moment I leave I'm holding my breath.But when it comes to recommending it... I'd list pretty much any other Dungeon Crawl first. The issues it has are front and center and, for most players, it's going to be unforgivable.But if you're like me, love Dungeon Crawls, own the rest, crave more and apparently have a masochistic streak I can fully recommend it even at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: : They have updated the game to add an option to toggle the Turbo mode, which makes navigating dungeons or speeding through (easier) fights less of a chore. Very quick and cool addition.This kind of game appeals pretty much to those who already know if they're going to buy it. It's an old-school dungeon crawler (not the Diablo kind; think SMT or Stranger of Sword City) that lacks a lot of quality-of-life features newer dungeon crawlers have. Even when you buy a map, you can't look at it at the same time you are moving, so if that is the type of hardcore experience you're looking for, this is it.As for the port: it's probably one of the best, most basic ports I've seen. There's nothing wrong with it at all. What you see is what you get. Surprisingly, menus offer full mouse support, so you can play the entire game almost solely with your mouse (camp menu and map still need button presses). There's also full custom keybind support. The game does NOT play in fullscreen, but rather borderless fullscreen. For this kind of game, that doesn't matter too much.Because the game is entirely 2D images and animation, it's capped at 30fps and probably wouldn't benefit much from 60fps animation. That said, someone might be able to unlock it in config files--I haven't tried.There's not much else to say. This is an extremely competent port. It's the original game with the expected 2020 controls of a PC title of similar gameplay. If it weren't a port of an older game, we might see increased framerate or more graphical options, but since it is, there's not much need. The artwork all looks just fine at 1080p, which is somewhat of a remaster considering the original probably ran at 720p on PS3.Recommended for hardcore fans of the series or genre, or those who like to explore and figure everything out for themselves; would -not- recommend to those not already familiar with the genre, or who have a preference for a more story-focused experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like grinding enemies over and over hoping for a 1% quest item drop?Do you enjoy having your party 1-shot do to unlucky RNG?Do you enjoy going back and forth between 2 tiles hoping against hope that one of the enemies will drop a map for the next section?Do you enjoy making your own maps out of pen and grid paper?If you answered yes to these you will love this game.  If any of these things seem terrible and tedious, then stay as far away from this game as possible.The game is stable, runs fine.  Zero documentation, so  you'll have to look it up yourself.  It's a classic Wizadry dungeon crawler.

_childDocuments_.review: Wish I could recommend this one, since I really enjoyed most of my time with it, but unfortunately the difficulty ramps up about 2/3 into the game in a way that's making me give up on it. Until that point, I felt able to adapt to most of the new enemies and situations the game threw at me, and the exploration loop felt pretty good. I wanted to push myself as far as I could into the dungeons to unlock the next elevator before heading back to town, and the gradual difficulty creep with monsters provided a really good feeling of tension. The beginning of the game is super well balanced and pushing myself to explore despite the danger felt rewarding.Then, at some point, you gain access to the "free warp spell", which while super convenient, totally destroyed any feeling of tension. You can essentially warp back to town, rest to get all your spells back, and then warp back to the exact spot you just were, elevators and shortcuts be damned. The game doesn't really give you a good reason not to constantly do this, so the feeling of risk/reward was gone.To compensate, what the game does next is start to throw enemies that are just absurdly overpowered. Every encounter will feature enemies that always go first, have attacks that instantly kill one or more party members, inflict multiple status effects, drain multiple levels, drain your magic, and on the off-chance they just do a basic physical attack, will do at least 75% damage even to my strongest characters with equipment I've found that's far better than anything you can buy in the shop. The only way I can continue to make progress is through aggressive save scumming. I save after every battle and if the next encounter has more than a couple enemies in it, I hit alt-F4 and just load my save again.The strategy at this point, I imagine, would be to re-class my characters into something that gains agility so you have a chance of buffing your party and debuffing the enemies before they can instakill everyone. I've done a little bit of re-classing, and the game really feels like it punishes you for experimenting. Changing a character's class drops them back to level 1, and although they keep their stats and spells, they take such a massive HP loss that they're guaranteed to die in 1 hit. You can convert gold into XP to get their levels back up, but because characters have a chance of *losing* stat points every time they level up, this feels like a crapshoot, too.For example, I wanted to get my bishop's agility up so they have a chance of getting an action before the enemy. So I temporarily changed them into a thief. I got their levels back as high as I could with the gold I had on hand, which didn't bring them up to the level of the rest of my party, didn't give them enough agility to start going first, and also caused them to *lose* so much piety that I wasn't able to turn them back into a bishop. So I loaded my save, and realized I would just have to repeat the process and save scum until I got a more desirable outcome. And finally I realized that this is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and stopped playing.So yeah. Can't see any way to proceed without hours of grinding or save scumming for better die rolls. Maybe I ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up by not being diligent enough by re-classing my characters more frequently when the game was still "easy", but the game never stresses this as an important mechanic and by reducing your characters to level 1, massively disincentivizes you from doing so. That said, for 15 bucks I still got a lot of enjoyment out of it, and if you go into it knowing what to expect, it might be possible to have a party capable of dealing with the high-level threats, but unfortunately it's too late for me. Maybe I'll revisit the game in a couple years and start fresh, but for now, I can't recommend it after seeing the late-game balance changes.

_childDocuments_.review: **DISABLE VSYNC TO ENABLE 60FPS!!!***Labyrinth of Lost Souls a legitimate old-school Wizardry in the vein of Code Abyss or Elminage. It does not have an in-game help, so READ THIS if you are not sure what's up! If you are familiar with Muramasa-style blobbers, you can skip to the end...CHARACTERS:The game splits your saves into one slot for one each of every race and gender. There are achievements for completing every gender and race's story scenario, but they aren't super deep - the majority of the game is simply dungeon romping.There are four base classes and four advanced classes. Races have set starting stats, so not every race can start as every class. You can change classes at any time as long as you meet the stat requirements - you'll probably level someone up to 10-15 before changing to a Lord or Ninja, but Bishop and Samurai may be available at the start. (Growth seeds are available to make this happen for you earlier). Additionally, leveling happens on a curve, so you may lose points when you level in stats you want because of your race and class.Be aware of everyone's class skills, what they do, and spells when they learn them - they can make a big difference. ITEMS:-Range is the most important thing for weapons - only "L" weapons can attack from the rear row. This is why Slings are so expensive - they give your back-row Thief and Bishop a free moderate attack. -Many weapons are cursed or have hidden effects, or can be equipped in the off-hand. Examine every item after identifying it. -Identifying items can only be done by Bishops, or very expensively at the item shop. If you fail to identify an item, the Bishop will be Afraid. This is healed cheaply at the Temple, or over time.EXPLORATION:-Torches and maps are invaluable until you can reliably maintain the respective priest and mage spells with the same effect.-When opening chests, only Thieves can correctly identify and remove traps manually, everyone else will give you wrong info. Your only other option is the Priest spell when identifying a trap.-A "locked door" can be picked by a Thief. Press the examine button in front of the door. Also "Search" whenever anyone "notices something".-Return to town frequently and rest your mages at the stables when their MP is out. Only rest your fighters in the expensive rooms if you don't have healing magic. -Check your map often!=Is it for me?=YES. This game has tons of gameplay, and its mobile origins belay its depth of character. Beneath a less ostensible veneer is a tried and true dungeon romp. If you enjoy Elminage, Wizardry Xth, even Demon Gaze, you'll love this -- Just know what's up, first! Pros: +Great art and music+Customizeable gamepad icons and mappings+Classic Wizardry gameplay+Lengthy adventureCons:-Not as deep as the later Wizardry entries-Some translations obviously done out of context-No inline helpBasically,BUY IT, but be sure you learn the mechanics before giving your recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: "Modern" Wizardry games are often met with criticism for one reason or another. Old grognards often shun the new anime-style artwork, while younger players often complain about the brutal difficulty. But if we are able to look past these two viewpoints, there's actually quite a lot of love about these Japanese Wizardry releases.For starters, and you can argue this all you want, but they are pretty true to the original five games in terms of design and gameplay mechanics. Yes, they are more colorful, and there's certainly a Japanese-spin to them. But, both the Japanese audience and developers LOVED those original games. They have made it their goal to preserve that design while adding a few modern touches here and there. My favorite addition that Labyrinth of Lost Souls brings to Wizardry is the inclusion of quests. These side tasks are often optional, but they help give a little meaning to a game that (if we're being honest) is mostly walking around an empty maze and mindlessly killing monsters. If you're an older gamer that cut their teeth on Mad Overlord or Knight of Diamonds, and you look back on those games with fondness, you owe to yourself to see what these newer titles have to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first Wizardry game that I have played through. What I have learned in finally getting around to playing a Wizardry is it feels a lot like Dungeons and Dragons and required a bit of game research before making my characters. I ended up beating the game with a Lord, two Fighters, Thief, Mage, and a Bishop.   I also did a lot of class swapping even in researching things on the game to make better characters. Even with the guide and money to level up the class swaps it did take a bit of time and I over leveled on some of them not quite grasping how the spells carried over. It was a tad confusing.    I would say the biggest thing someone should know playing the series for the first time is when you die even if you get raised in the battle you lose 1 point in Vitality! So basically I ended up reloading anytime I went someplace that was too challenging. Bad part was I found that out so late in the game even on doing tons of research and my Porklu race character felt quite useless and is my least favorite race by far.I turned her into a Fighter at one point to give her more health and she still died so often even with good gear and everything. The Porklu race seem to mainly do well as thieves or ninjas but I still find them a bit undesirable after my first playthrough.  Also too there are monsters who have instant death spells so be prepared to save quite a bit.    All in all this is a game not for the faint of heart and you should figure out what you want to be before you play it but there is a sense of accomplishment when you beat it. I had a bit of ahh lemme just beat it already and work on the next  playthrough.  My Biggest complaint though is actually something that can be easily fixed. It wasn't the confusing stats or class swapping, random stat points going up or down on level so if you got something bad you wanted to reload. No my biggest complaint I guess was something that affected me personally. The game even though it has a dark backround which is easier on the eyes has a lot of flashing lights when attacks go off or spells. A lot of them are white flashing lights. This can even with the base attacks make me feel ill and have nausea. I wish the game had an option to turn off the attack moves and spells because then I would play the game more now that I know how the characters should be built and can enjoy going through it with other hopefully better built ones.   I did enjoy the art style of the game and some of the creatures were well designed. I also like how you can carry the characters over and there is a universal storage. _childDocuments_.review: Wizardry and Zork were the two very first RPGs I ever played back when I was barely old enough to read in the early 80s. I remember playing one of the Wizardry games on the NES, and Heart of the Maelstrom on the SNES, followed by Crusaders of the Dark Savant on DOS/Win95. I've never even seen another Wizardry game until this showed up on my recommended list in Steam. I saw the reviews calling it insanely hard, which seemed bizarre to me, but after seeing from the screenshots that it looked just like an updated Heart of the Maelstrom, I decided to go for it. The game is incredibly easy if you're used to old-school Wizardry. It's a lot like playing old-school Dragon Quest insomuch that as long as you grind your ass of early, the rest of the game is really easy. You need to get a few hundred thousand gold, a few dozen to a few hundred gold at a time. I'm averaging about 2000-3000 gold every hour or so, so you do the math on what the grind is like. Once you get your team outfitted and leveled up the game is a cakewalk though.This is a 1980's leveling engine in a first person perspective dungeon crawl. It lacks the puzzles that make games like Dungeon Master & Legend of Grimrock 2 so very fun, but it has a charm that reminds me of watching Anime like Grimgar,  or even the first season of Sword Art Online (before it turned into a s***y harem anime). The guild master offers you quests from other townsfolk, you talk to them pick up the details of the quest, go into the dungeon and do the fetch quest or whatever, and come back, and talk with the guildmaster again. The whole thing gives me two differently levels of nostalgia, one of watching those anime with my kids, and the other of playing the old-school dungeon crawlers from when I was a kid.It's a simple game, but it's not hard at all, just very grind intensive. I find it quite addictive though. Wish there were more character portraits to choose from for my party members though.

_childDocuments_.review: When I was a kid I played Wizardry 5 for the snes and there was something magical about that game. The graphics were grainy and the distorted midi music chimed along in the background in that way that only dated games did but there was something compelling about it that kept me playing long into the dark hours of the night; mystery. Old dungeon crawlers always kept you guessing gave you tons of random encounters that made you feel like the game had even more things to do and explore and never fully revealed all of its secrets even after playing for hundreds of hours. Sometimes you would get really lucky with loot drops even in early areas and get an awesome item but much of the time awesome items would be cursed and you could never tell until it was too late. They were painful, cruel, but also mysterious. The mystery of these old dungeon crawlers isn't in Labyrinth of Lost Souls. It's soulless. I can't recommend a modern gaming title that is barely more appealing in terms of visuals or audio than an snes title and isn't as good in terms of overall quality. If you are old like me and actually enjoy dungeon crawlers there are better modern titles to choose from and lots of older games.

_childDocuments_.review: Wizardry Labyrinth of Lost Souls is a spiritual successor to the classic Wizardries, 1 through 5. This game is difficult, unforgiving, and very punishing. Vampires will drain your levels, mages will wipe your entire team with one spell... regardless if everyone is at full HP, and vorpal bunnies will cut your heroes' heads off. The game truly is as hard as its predecessors. Yet, this is where its beauty also lies.Class changing mechanics are present, so you can level your characters in the spellcasting classes, then change them to a fighter-type like a Samurai or Ninja and they'll still be able to cast spells. You will find powerful weapons in the game that can even allow you to one-shot bosses. There is a great satisfaction in choosing the strategy your heroes will execute, from casting the incredible NAL Burst (an obvious throwback to Tiltowait), guarding themselves with the almost game-breaking Magic Wall, or having your Ninja hide and decapitate your enemies.You'll really feel your heroes' strength as they level and upgrade their equipment. Your fighters will attack five or more times per round, and your mages will advance from only being able to cast a few spells to teleporting around the dungeon and wiping the entire opposition. The enemy art is incredible, and you'll feel great as you progress from fighting small kobolds and goblins to demons, demi-gods, and dragons.The interface could definitely be a lot better, and the storyline is almost nonexistent, but I suppose for a dungeon crawler, that is to be expected. It's still interesting, despite being incredibly short. The DLC story is much more interesting and involving, however, so after you beat the main game, definitely give it a try.Wizardry Labyrinth of Lost Souls is for those that are experienced with Wizardry, or those that really love the old-school dungeon crawling style, but I believe its lack of a manual or tutorial, coupled with how difficult it can be, won't earn it many new fans. I love this game very much, but I can see how many would not.

_childDocuments_.review: Others have said it before, I'll repeat it - I'd rather give a neutral review, but not recommended will have to do.This game is unbelievably tedious, even for a remake of an early Wizardry game. There are remasters, such as the Bard's Tale Trilogy, which keep the core of the original experience and improve the overall quality of life and experience of the game, then there are games like Wizardry: Labyrinth of Lost Souls that believes tedium is a game feature.Want to heal your party at the inn? Every character has to rent a room separately. But wait, you don't have enough money on someone in your party? You have to constantly shift money from party member to party member rather than drawing from one single "party" pool of gold. You could also choose to use the free room that restores MP, then singly go through your entire party as you use heal spells, and then use the free room for MP again. Everything you want to do no matter how simple is an exercise in boredom and menus. This game is almost more menu than game. Combat... I don't have the same issue with combat speed as others but I have a huge issue with thee absolute randomness of it. Fighting a level 2 bat? Swing for 4 points of damage and it's defeated. The bat next to it, you swing for multiple turns with your whole party finally doing 22 damage and it's defeated. Both level 2 and enormous HP differences.This is the same for enemy damage. You'll feel pretty safe noticing most attacks miss or deal 1 damage... then suddenly that same enemy that's been doing 1 to you all combat suddenly does 30 on their next hit. No rhyme or reason. Either that's the largest critical bonus I've ever seen in an RPG or there's something wrong with their numbers. Anyways... this game is for someone. It's an old-school, traditional, slow as molasses dungeon crawl with no frills and no story, no depth, and no character growth beyond the basics. Some people enjoy that. I'm still spending time with it as something to do on my second monitor. But still, it's NOT good. It just exists.

_childDocuments_.review: I have fond memories of playing the original Wizardry in green and black, and then the next seven over the years. Most people don't understand the legacy of these games, games which today many would consider quaint at best, but they set standards and tropes for everything from anime to Final Fantasy to Doom. Its hard to understate the influence that games like it, Ultima, Rogue, and others had on the industry, so I was excited to learn that a Japanese company had picked up the IP and carried it forth.Wizardry: Labyrinth of Lost Souls is a faithful successor to the storied games that it descends from. Because it is so faithful, many modern audiences will no doubt consider it "quaint" or run away in horror. Where I still found aspects of it enjoyable, one downside is that the game's mechanics are so faithful to the original Proving Grounds that it inherits some of the less desirable aspects - character creation is a matter of assigning a random # of points to you attributes. That RNG can be, from my experience, anywhere from 6 to 40 (the max I recall getting in the original was only 20 something). This encourages you to waste time just rerolling your character until you get something awesome. That's not actually fun, and a niche of game design that most folks have moved past.Unfortunately, this iteration of Wizardry has extremely swingy RNG ranges. By way of example, I had one character gain only 4 hp when they went up a level, while another gained nearly a hundred. When you have foes that can smack you for for anywhere between 1 and 1700+ at a time, that range becomes significant. The game encourages scrum saving when you are near going up a level, and that's just an annoying feature.The dungeon design is straight out of the originals: each level is a square and there are many levels connected by stairs and elevators. Fortunately, there's not much grinding, except to fulfill quest requirements, and boy do some require grinding, particularly the collect X number of items quests. Where Labyrinth of Lost Souls lacks the depth of story and additional mechanics of Wizardry 6-8, it packs in more story than the original. That's not actually saying a lot, and the storytelling here can actually pretty frustrating. You can easily explore an entire dungeon only to learn you have to run through it again because a quest demands that you find something somewhere in it with little direction, and you must complete these quest check points in sequence. That becomes both boring and monotonous.I am pretty sure its just nostalgia talking, but despite its flaws, I still had fun. That's also why I can't recommend it. It's niche. If you like that so old school its ancient feel, if you want a nostalgia binge, then this is for you. Otherwise, skip it.

_childDocuments_.review: Labyrinth of Lost Souls is an extremely niche game.  Fans of old dungeon crawlers will likely love it, but most others will likely hate it.  It's one of several sister clones of Wizardry V: Heart of the Maelstrom that's been US-translated.  Given that, my review will be mostly about how W:LoLS differs from Wiz 5.+ XSeed has brought back a lot of what made old Wizardry great.  Rolling time and time again for bonus points, with 5 races and 8 class options.  Plenty of ways to go crawl around in the dungeon successfully... and unsuccessfully.  + Multiclassing has been reworked, but it's still awesome.  Upon multiclass, rather than dropping stats to racial base, stats remain the same and HP is about halved.  All spells learned are kept, but MP is halved.  No skills are kept, however.+ Hardcore dungeon crawling without hand-holding.  Some early monsters are capable of auto-kills.  Later monsters can petrify the entire party with a breath weapon.  Groups of enemy mages left unchecked can cause untold devastation to HP.+ Traps everywhere.  Chests can be deadly, and any mistake can cause a party wipe.  Dark zones, anti-magic zones, electric floors and walls are all commonplace.  Spinners are around but aren't much of a threat, unfortunately, as I found maps to be fairly easy to acquire. + It's as hardcore as you want it to be.  If a wipe occurs, you have the option of doing the old Wizardry thing and going back into the dungeon with another party to rescue them and their gear (take too long though, and they'll become ashen or lost forever). The Temple will also bring them back for you for some gold, or you can simply reload.  For those not wanting a hardcore experience, save-scumming is an option.  All up to you. - I don't mind the anime characters as much as some, but yes, some characters (especially the gnomes) look really cutesy.  It'll be a drawback to hardcore fans.  And that dwarf male is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tall.- Character portraits are far too large.  They inhibit my view of the dungeon substantially, so much that without a light spell active it's difficult to see doors and hallways without turning.- Wizardry 5 spoiled me a bit with it's awesome dungeons.  The SNES version really brought them to life for me.  While the dungeon wasn't terribly deep, getting through each floor really felt like an accomplishment.  Here, the dungeons just aren't as awesome.  Each floor fits nicely on a 20x20 grid, as opposed to the rough and chaotic layout that made Wiz 5 amazing.  And there's wraparound.  I hate wraparound.- No required items to find.  For every floor, it's the same formula.  Find the switches to the door for the next floor and public elevator, move on, rinse and repeat.- No NPCs to chat with (or steal stuff from and kill).  Boo.- In some ways this reminds me more of Class of Heroes than old Wizardry.  Mostly in the numbers.  Damage and HP are a bit inflated as compared to Wizardry of old.  For instance, my Wizard elves ended up with more HP than my human Fighter and Samurai.  There's no way that's happening in old Wizardry.*MURMUR**CHANT**IMPLORE**INVOKE*Does Wizardry live yet again?I can only hope.  Maybe we'll someday get PC Wizardry to the awesomeness of the PS2 Wizardry - Tale of the Forsaken Land.

_childDocuments_.review: It seems like many people got confused by the controls and gave up early.  I'd say it's an improvement over the older Wizardry formula.  If you like the old formula, like I do, you'll like the game.  If not, well, the game probably isn't for you, I hope you find something else that you do enjoy.   Here's a quick FAQ for people getting stuck.- The controls are fairly inscrutable but standard for Japanese games.  You can camp (press s) in town as well as the dungeon to manage items, cast spells, etc.  Press z for the menu where you pick locks, search, etc.  Removing magic seals requires flipping switches on the level.  Look at the keybindings at the start for a list, but seems like you can't remap arrow keys for movement.  They're mostly printed on the screen but not always.- There are some new features you may not remember from old Wizardry, so look around shops in town:  * The Inn has a vault for items, bestiary and stats.  * The Temple can recover people lost in the dungeon for a fee.  * The Guild has an item trading feature, often crap but sometimes good.  'Wanted item' is what they're requesting, the translation is kinda wonky there.  * Talking to the shopkeepers basically replaces the help feature/guide, get advice if you need it.  * You can see item stats by pressing the button indicated (default: s).  Same is true for character skills.- Yes, the first character you create has to be in the party, that's what that L is for on their portrait.  You can recruit that character from the Guild by making a different character.  You probably want to use the bonus fruits to make a lord and/or ninja if you're not going to class change, then send them with the party via this method to avoid rerolling for hours to get a 40 roll.  I use a Porkulu ninja to get high enough luck & agility that they don't suck at thief skills, but the choice is yours.- Stat requirements are standard for Wizardry games, look at the Steam guide for details.  There are a few new class skills.- Ninjas don't get the free long range attack when unarmed.  You'll have to wait until level 8 when they get hide/assassinate.  They do get evade per level via 'Abandon' starting at level 2.- You can make evil & good party members venture together the same old way as always:  go to the dungeon, save the game (press s for the camp menu), then pick another MC and search for party members and add them.- As always, Bishops have identify (appraise) as a skill.- Yes, chests can be empty, it does kinda suck, but blame your bad luck stat.- Yes, you have to deal with some bad insta-death monsters and level loss if you're not prepared, but resurrection is pretty cheap.- Items, meanwhile, are far more expensive than you might be used to.  Yeah, I know that a sling is just a strip of leather with a few rocks for ammo and has no business being more expensive than leather armor, but things are roughly priced according to how powerful they are.- There's a higher level mage spell to warp home, but it will take some leveling to get (~lvl 8 or 9).  Try switching dungeons if things are too hard, just don't go to the deep levels until you're quite high level and well armed, or you'll die quickly.- There's also a spell to replace the map items (which do not get consumed), but honestly I don't find that many items that I can't hang onto them.  It's more useful if you can't find the relevant item.  You can drop the ones for other dungeons into the inn's vault.- There are consumables to cover many common spells, many of which are quite cheap and useful.- The higher level mage spell for light doesn't get dispelled by dark zones, unlike the torches & basic spell.- Cast those priest buffs & levitate out of battle.  They leave little icons on screen while active.- Be warned that fleeing is a PARTY action.  So if you fight with 5 people and just one person chooses flee, everyone will do nothing and try to flee.  This sucks if you misclick, because fleeing almost never seems to work.  Or maybe it's just based on level and that's why you never seem to be able to get away from the monsters when you've wandered too deep, I dunno.- That rotating skull thing on level 1 is a miniboss.  If you haven't gotten many levels and are armed with daggers, you'll probably wipe on it.  It's farmable later (it will respawn if you save/load) and it has nice items once you can farm it.  Be warned that it can drain levels, which sucks.  The only cure for that is to get more XP.  Don't bother trying to flee.  Technically, it can be taken down with daggers (and a few mage spells) but you'll probably lose most of the party and maybe even a level or two.  Yeah, I found out the hard way.- Keep a bit of gold on the party leader.  If you wipe, he has to resurrect everyone.  He revives with 1 HP in the temple for free.  You can also keep a valuable item or two in the vault at the inn just in case.- You can buy things back from the shop after selling them as usual, but they don't keep any +x bonuses.  So if you sell a +2 dagger, for example, you can't buy it back at +2.There are a lot of convenience features that were added if you look around, like pooling gold in the temple, the elevator system and maps, etc. but much of this is faithful to the old Wizardry, for good and for bad.  I happen to like the old Wizardry back to playing the very first one so it's nice to play a nicer looking one.  But people who don't like that formula in the first place aren't going to be won over by this, they'll just get annoyed by splitting and pooling gold or forgetting to save and getting wiped out by a pack of BS monsters because fleeing never seems to work.  My only real complaint would be that I wish they'd put Hide as the second action after Fight in the ninja's command list, but that's pretty minor.

_childDocuments_.review: Wizardry: Labyrinth of Lost Souls is a Japanese remake of the original Wizardry game from 1981, originally being released on the PS3 in 2009 but making its way to PC in 2020. This is a first-person dungeon crawler in the same vein as the Wizardry games as made by Sir-Tech, but works somewhat faster than the original Wizardry games.You will make up a party of 1-6 characters using a combination of 5 races and 8 classes. You've got the traditional classes, Fighter, Thief, Priest and Mage. But there are the tertiary classes as well of Bishop, Samurai, Lord and Ninja. Every class has its own special skills as well as there being five spell casting classes (Priest and Mage who cast their respective spell types; and Samurai and Lord who cast Mage and Priest spells but with a more limited spell selection, you can think of the Lord class as Paladins) with the Bishop being a special mention because they have the exclusive class skill to identify items and ability to cast every spell in the game, so you should always make sure you have one if possible.In the original release the game was like the original version of Final Fantasy for the Famicom, having a level cap of 50, but this version has the DLC included which increases the level cap to 99 and adds in a bunch more to the dungeons of the game, giving the player much more to do. The end goal of the game is to put an end to the machinations of the wizard Werdna, which could prove more challenging than you might think.This is a grinding game, there's no way around it. You could easily spend 100 hours in this game and still not finish it. You will get a lot of gold and you will kill a lot of monsters. That gold is not really meant for buying equipment, but instead tithing at the temple which gives you 1 point of experience per gold spent. You can swap out your characters at any time in town (other than the currently selected hero), but you can also change character classes at any time in town. When doing so your current hit points will be retained (but halved), so if a character were to change class with 600 hp, they would become a level 1 with 300 hp. You should use this information to power up your characters and obtain thousands of hit points.This is the kind of RPG that I love, it's simple and focused. When looking at items, always note that red is bad and blue is good. And if you're color blind, then I'm sorry, but this game does not have a color blind mode. Perhaps there's a guide that will help you out.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game, and a good entry point for newbies to the Wizardry series. Not perfect, but a 7 / 10 and pretty laid back to chip away at. It gets kinda zen to delve down and explore or grind.Gameplay is the essential Wizardry experience. Make a party of six, enter the dungeon, grind a little bit to be competent. Go in and explore, killing monsters and claiming loot, deciding when to turn back (or doing so if a character gets taken down). Return to town, rest and recover, then go back to the dungeons to explore and slay s'more. All the best items are found by exploring and as monster drops; after a certain point, those pricey items at the shop will become purchasable, only to be resold back once you find duplicates, or items that outclass them. There is a certain rush of endorphins when you identify a cool new weapon or armor that gives your characters the boost they need. There's a little story here and there, but nothing special. Just set dressing to give you a reason to dungeon crawl. All in all, it's the quissential dungeon crawling blobber experience.Labyrinth of Lost Souls (LoLS, if you will) does some stuff to stand out compared to the classics, however. You can tithe excess gold at the church to get XP on a 1:1 ratio, kinda like old-school D&D. Useful to aid grinding, or help a recently-revived character get back up to speed. Either way, a good use for gold that would otherwise do nothing. There are item trades that show up now and again at the tavern, as well as some sidequests to do there. The inn also holds a bestiary to peek at monster stats, art and lore. and also item collection records.You'll also notice that each of the ten characters (male and female each for the five races) also act as their own save file each. These heroes each have their own specific quest in the game, and IIRC items in the shop can be bought and stocked across these heroes' journeys. Be warned that if your main character is permakilled for any reason, it's game over. That said, LoLS is surprisingly forgiving for a Wizardry game because it doesn't auto-save. This means that if reviving a character fails and they'd be gone for good, you can reload your save. Just don't forget to save periodically from the pause menu, and be warned that each hero can only have one version of their save file at once. There's no saving in multiple slots this way.Now, some personal gripes. The dungeons are pretty basic compared to others in the series, or with other spinoffs. No real puzzles, other than finding switches to open gated rooms. Mages' spell lists feel a little too Final Fantasy Black Mage -- that is, mostly elemental spells and that status ailment spells are pointless. Classic Wizardry gave the mages more varied spells. Likewise, priest spells are also mostly pointless tiers heals, and the first half of their light-elemental damaging spells are utterly pathetic. If you encounter a treasure chest in the dungeon that isn't a monster drop? Be prepared to run into the same lame pairs of shoes and torches. The optional sidequests are very RNG-based, having to do with drops from specific enemies (albeit, more than one enemy can drop the needed items). Those optional ones are mostly for extra gold though, so they aren't urgent. The dungeons themselves don't have puzzles or riddles to speak of, either. Pretty barebones, though the later levels in the Dungeon of Trials start to feel like a proper maze. Shiin's Dungeon is fairly challenging and labyrinthine from the get-go.I also cannot stand the Japanese voice acting, particularly the female voices. The screams and shrieks of running into shock floors, shock walls, bumping into walls or getting hit in battle make me want to claw my eardrums out. I always turn Voice Volume down to 0% in the menu immediately.Lastly, the game has something of a W-shaped difficulty curve. Most blobbers start out hard, forcing you to grind for a little while before things get easy. Around the middle floors of the Dungeon of Trials, things get stupidly easy before long. Once you get to the later floors there, the challenge returns. Shiin's Dungeon is usually one you chip away at, and is tied to the plot. It's one you venture to after getting your feet wet in the Dungeon of Trials first. And unless you have a death wish, avoid the Deeper Levels until you're in late-to-postgame content. Those levels were a DLC expansion that are included for free in the PC version.Oh yeah, you also get five "growth fruits" as free DLC as well, built into this version. They give a stupidly good boost of stats when creating a character. Once each fruit is used up though, it's gone for good and cannot be restored.All in all? Like I said, it's not perfect, but is a good starting game for the fledgling Wizardry fan. A pretty fun labyrinth to get lost in.

_childDocuments_.review: *** Good Old School Fun ***I was initially on the fence on whether to buy this or not. Now, I am glad I did. This Wizardry game is rather pleasant to play, and exceeded my expectations rather quickly. I used to play the old versions years ago, and it's nice to enjoy it once again.First, it's really not that hard of a game to understand. After an hour or two, you'll be fine. If you can figure out how to change some settings on your phone, you can handle this no problem. It's simple enough that you can play easily with a game pad. Sure there's no tutorials or manual. Don't let that frighten you. There isn't as much of a learning curve as their is just a discovery process. There's no rush. Just figure it out as you go.It's a turn based game, so don't worry about the 30 FPS lock. You won't even notice unless you are one of those types that stares at your FPS display, and it makes you panic. it will not effect the game play or your experience whatsoever. The graphics are nice. The artwork is pleasant to look at. Sure, it's anime-ish, but I wouldn't let that get to you, either. The way things are going these days with censorship creeping in to games, and some games having graphics approaching odd non-specific character models, you might as well give it a chance. Anime artwork may be the only thing left that doesn't look bland and gross.As far as sound, it has nice music and general effects. You may, however, wish to turn down the voices a bit. Having a full group poisoned running for the exit will get on your last nerve if it's too loud.A good comparison would be to The Bard's Tale remake. I have that game, and this game is much better. It's better done, and the mechanics are much more interesting in Wizardry.Frustration will only be an issue if you are impatient, and just want to rush. Wizardry is best played with a mindset opposite of being in an absolute hurry. Pretzels, peanuts, and some beers are great with it. Just chill, and think a little. Stats are pretty basic, and easy to understand. Don't worry about them too much. It all balances out when you level.RNG is a strange beast in this game. It can vary to extremes on occasion. Hit points on a level up can feel absurd one way or another. Don't let it bother you. It won't ruin anything. It's nice to have a surprise now and then, and that's how you should see it. If you get obsessed with one fighter getting 10 hit points, and the other getting 20, you will drive yourself nuts. My fighters at level 5 were quite different, but by the time level 10 rolled around, it balanced out just fine. It didn't have a really perceivable effect on game play.Combat is also fun. The strange critters you face will do all sorts of things. Some will panic and run. Some will wonder where they are. Some will chew your face off and others will light your pants on fire. There's just enough variety to keep it interesting.It's not game of the year, sure. But the asking price is fair enough. It's a good value for your gaming dollar. It's not for everyone, but can satisfy your curiosity of how early RPGs used to be made without making your eyes bleed.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely more for hardcore Wizardry fans, but I am one of those, so this hits the spot for me. The main issue is a lot of QA & QoL are desperately needed as I can't see non-blobber fans tolerating the hosts of issues ranging from utterly bizarre keyboard/mouse input, bad sound/voice quality (peaking and turning distorted in your ears, ugh), atrociously low RNG for items and chests, a weirdly abrupt ending and more. But one very positive aspect is save anywhere, which saves me from trekking all the way back to town to save. But having just one save slot also means it is very easy to mess things up with your save file as well (like accidentally saving when your whole party is wiped, whoops! The unsubtitled Japanese voices and anime-ish aesthetic also don't bother me. IF all of these don't seem like big issues to you, then give this a try, as the underlying core mechanics of Wizardry is very addicting and fun, and the sheer pleasure of the combat is just unmatched in RPG-dom, IMO. The monster art are quite compelling too, even if they don't animate. Just don't expect something of the level of Crusaders of Dark Savant/8/Tales of the Forsaken Land and you'll have fun.

_childDocuments_.review: It is fascinating how Wizardry, not only inspired lots of other games in Japan, but how there it continue to exist.When they say this a old school games, they aren´t playing around. Save some minor changes, this game is very faithful to the "ruleset" of early Wizardry games for both good and bad, and what this means? If you familiar you can easily get used, since it follow almost all classic "rules" of early games, but if you not, I can see things get a by confusing, but don´t worry, it fairly simple:- Here you first create a initial character, a leader, and then you can create a party on the Guild (under Register)- Certain classes require minimum stats (and they are the same as in the original games) and some of them, such as Lord and Ninja might be only accessible later when you get enough levels and use the class change.- When you level up may gain or lose stat like old Wizardry games.- Here spell have descriptive names, which make everything more clear.But that said, the games does have the tension of know when keep exploring dungeons (often doing quests for npcs in the town) or when you should retreating to the city to rest and recover. The game is overall very good, the menus/ui is a bit clunky but nothing too bad, there isn´t much tutorials or tooltips, but save that the game is pretty good if you want a classic wizardry game.

I did enjoy it for the most part, but it sorely lacked any story elements, NPCs and boss fights through the levels. The gameplay consists of wandering through the level to find the switch to unlock the elevator and then find the stairs to the next floor.
