_childDocuments_.review: This review can take two paths: one leaning towards recommendation with caveats, and the other leaning away but acknowledging potential. So, let’s dive into both perspectives with a warming tale of urban simulation:Comparing my initial experience with the predecessor at its launch to this sequel’s debut, the latter is significantly enhanced. How so?The first Cities: Skylines emerged as a beacon of hope for disenchanted SimCity aficionados, establishing itself as the new pinnacle of city-building games. It fostered a vibrant community of players, designers, and modders whose contributions have shaped its evolution. It surpassed SimCity in innovation, breaking away from traditional grid-based layouts, and introduced players to sophisticated urban planning concepts, sparking a niche for urbanist content creators online. Yet, when comparing the original titles in their base forms—sans mods and additional content—the first installment feels somewhat lacking. Features like the day-night cycle and diverse transit options were absent at launch, only introduced through subsequent updates and expansions.Cities: Skylines 2, in contrast, launches with a comprehensive suite of features. From day-night cycles and seasons to mixed-use zoning and a nuanced economy reminiscent of the depth in SimCity 2000, it offers a richly detailed urban simulation. Transportation options are expansive, and city planning tools are versatile, allowing for intricate road layouts and efficient traffic management. The sequel also introduces environmental considerations, such as pollution and disasters, enhancing the game’s realism and depth.So, why do some hold reservations with a "Yes, but ..." stance?Without delving into widespread criticisms already familiar to those reading multiple reviews, the crux of hesitation stems from misaligned expectations regarding performance, game mechanics clarity, and content depth. Initial performance issues and a UI that some found obtuse have overshadowed the game’s ambitious improvements. Despite these challenges, the game has undergone extensive patching, with more updates on the horizon.A key point of contention has been content. Having been part of the original game's journey from its 2015 release, I witnessed its evolution and the explosion of community engagement it spurred. This set high expectations for the sequel’s content offerings, leading to disappointment for some at launch due to perceived insufficiencies and aesthetic choices.However, the potential for improvement is evident. The current drawbacks—performance optimization, UI clarity, resource demands, tool refinement, and the absence of mods and editing tools—are all addressable. The development team’s commitment to resolving these issues suggests a bright future for the game.In essence, if you’re considering the game, know this: "I recommend, but ..." be aware of the ongoing fixes and adjustments, and you might find much to enjoy. "I don't recommend, however ..." if you temper your expectations, you can appreciate the sequel’s vast potential to redefine city simulation games. The first game claimed the genre’s throne by merit, and its successor is poised to defend it, even if it faces challenges along the way.Acknowledging the game's current state, it's clear that there are specific areas needing attention:-Further performance enhancements are necessary to ensure smoother gameplay.-The user interface requires more intuitive indicators to better understand the game mechanics.-The game demands a significant amount of computational resources, which might limit its accessibility.-The existing tools could use refinement for a more polished experience.-The absence of additional options such as props, prop tools, and decorative items is felt.-The game currently lacks mod support, a feature eagerly awaited by the community.-Essential editing tools, including map and asset editors, are not available yet, limiting creative freedom.-The console version's release is still pending, leaving a portion of the audience waiting.-Bug-related issues have led to delays in the release of the Ultimate Edition and its first two DLCs.-Some major bugs still require thorough investigation and resolution.

_childDocuments_.review: Big fan of the first Cities Skylines game and was excited to try out the second installment. My specs are - i7-10700kNvidia RTX 2070 Super32GB of DDR4 RAMI was a little worried about the game's performance after reading some reviews that complained about the game's optimization issues. However, after tweaking some settings like depth of field, sync, and motion blur, I was able to get decent FPS. I could run the game at 40-45 fps in the menu and 70-75 fps on an empty map. _childDocuments_.review: If they really needed money, they could have at lease labeled this early access.Performance issues aside, the game takes 1 step forward and 1 step back. The building system is more in depth, but road and building placement is finicky. Some buildings are incredibly large for no apparent reason (colleges and universities are 80% gardens) and service / infrastructure buildings like power plants have a very rigid placement as to where you must connect the roads and power lines. Small power lines and pipes are difficult to place because they will not snap / connect, and water / sewage plants are ineffective even after upgrades.The first game was already running terribly, at about 40 FPS, with under %50 CPU and GPU utilization, because it runs on Unity. The sequel also runs on Unity but it's much, much worse. On first start, the game defaults everything to max and runs at 6 FPS on the main menu, with drops to 3. When loading a NEW EMPTY MAP, with just a road and a power line, the game runs at 13 FPS. NOTHING IS BEING SIMULATED! The game is empty, save for some trees and empty terrain. The game also seems to render everything, all the time, because FPS remained the same even when fully zoomed in, staring at a blank patch of earth,  with GPU utilization at 98%, and CPU at 18%.Depth of field is truly broken, and disabling it immediately doubles your framerate, so listen to the devs and do that. On physical, the depth of field simply does not exist, despite tanking performance, and on tilt-shift it's more for a diorama/ photo mode, as you can't see things clearly outside a narrow field of view.While you're at it, disable shadows, as they are constantly flickering and look terrible.Overall, the game looks worse and runs worse. This was a great opportunity to build a base and framework for what might become a greater game than the first, but considering the fact that CS1 still runs poorly after all these years, I have little faith that this one will be any better.Ran on an RTX 4080, AMD 7600x and 32 GB RAM, with updated drivers, at 4k. First refund I ever requested on Steam...

_childDocuments_.review: Cities: Skylines II is a game developed by Colossal Order Ltd. and published by Paradox Interactive and is the sequel to Planet CoasterBefore I carry on with the review, I have to stress that I absolutely love both Colossal Order and Paradox as companies, they've developed and published games that are near and dear to my heart, especially when it comes to the simulation and strategy genreTherefore it pains me to, at least for now, give their recent release of Cities: Skylines II a not recommended. I've been delaying writing a review for this sequel hoping that the game would find it's redemption and perform a No Man's Sky mega-patch and fix some of the horrendous issues the game is plagued with, but after constant delays and slow progress - not entirely blaming the developers but then again, I  pay 90 EUR for the Ultimate Edition expecting a high-level quality product but received absolute junk instead and this is more because of what I feel is becoming the new norm of modern videogames, the "release it now, fix/update it later" mentality. I might have tolerated it for a while, but with more and more of my beloved franchises and genres going down this route, I just can't tolerate it anymoreWith the sequel to Cities: Skylines II, it seems like Colossal Order took two steps forward but four steps back, while the there are some great additions to the game that made it better than the original, with the game's current state, I do not personally feel that this game should be considered "complete" and the game still feels like it is an Early Access game rather than a fully-fledged 50/90 EUR gameLet's get the positives out of the way first:As mentioned before, it's great that they added some great new features such as the road building tool and the game itself offers some wonderful looking graphics (when it runs properly and doesn't hard crash your PC), although some ugly glitches here and there, it is pleasant all the same and really shows off the Unity Engine to it's fullest potential, there are definitely points in their Cities: Skylines series of games where I just literally place the game's camera somewhere and let the simulation run itself and the sequel is no exception, so props to the developersNow to the negatives:Cities: Skylines II right now (still) feels off, even a year after the game's release (i.e. October 2023) and a few patches here and there, it's as if Colossal Order still haven't finished this game completely and are rushing to make the game at least playable, hence the "release it now, fix/update it later" mentalityAdding onto my previous point, whilst the game looks really pretty at points, right now, the game's optimisation is horrendous, which is quite the nagging point of players with this game. I have somewhat of a beefy PC and can play modern games on quite high quality settings but with Cities: Skylines II, even after some patches trying to fix these awful optimisation issues, either the game just straight up crashes or hard crashes my PC, which is absolutely infuriating, especially when you've spent ages trying to perfect your cityNow, I'm no developer, so I cannot truly understand the intricacies (and let's face it, hardships) of game development but how could a game like Cities: Skylines, which was released in 2015, done by the same developers and that's almost 10 years old (at the time when this review was written, i.e. 2024) run better even when you build such a (no pun intended) colossal city which again brings me back to my point of the "release it now, fix/update it later" mentality. I'm sure Colossal Order will continue to release patches fixing this issue that will make everybody happy and jump for joy, but this should have not been an issue in the first place!Certain content that was previously available on Cities: Skylines have also been mysteriously taken out with Colossal Order either promising it through a free update or patch or through the (no doubt) ridiculous amount of DLC - which is probably a mandate from Paradox themselves - that will be released for this sequel, it frankly pisses me off that developers are doing this tactic more and more and although I am not accusing Colossal Order of cutting out content for the sake of free updates and/or DLC, it certainly feels like it...Adding onto this are certain things that are missing or straight up broken like certain gameplay mechanics being straight up broken or the traffic AI and path finding being absolutely horrendous makes me wonder why on earth Colossal Order felt the need to release this game now and in it's current state - which again, i put some blame on Paradox for probably pushing Colossal Order to release it when it was released to appease shareholders and make some green...I, frankly, cannot stand this mentality anymore of "release it now, fix/update it later" and too many modern games have done this and especially games and franchises that I have loved over the years, where they think it's totally fine to release a mid-tier state of a game and then make it better later - if at all and then players would later on rejoice and say, "it's all better now, it's been fixed!"In that case, I will be treating Cities: Skylines II as Colossal Order and Paradox seemingly have treated me and other lovers of this franchise and say that at it's current state, I cannot recommend it. Oh for sure they will release patch after patch after patch fixing the seemingly obvious "missing" features, releasing "free" content for us players, heralding to us that they "are listening" and "want to make it the best possible experience for our players", whilst also charging us MORE money for crap DLC and maybe one or two "good" DLCs in the mixColossal Order and certainly Paradox would probably never read this review or if they do, they'll probably just answer back in some corporate speak about how they're "sorry that the game didn't live up to your expectations" and "we are working tirelessly to make the game better" but in all honesty, I'm getting older by the minute and my patience is running thinner and thinner by the daySo to wrap up, Cities: Skylines II overall, is indeed a fun game to play (at some points) but if you were expecting a sequel that betters the original in various ways, then I'm sorry to say, this ain't it chief... I'm not sad or angry or upset, this is becoming an occurrence upon every single game release, I'm just - yet again - disappointedWait for a sale or for a few "updates" then see how it is, if you can't wait, play the first one - Paradox seem to want players to continue playing the first one anyway, they're still releasing PAID DLC for it...

_childDocuments_.review: Its the little things in lifeOne of the most appealing aspects of City Skylines is its impressive scale. Players can build expansive and intricate cities, complete with detailed road systems, zoning options, and even public transportation. The game provides a level of creative freedom that few other city-building simulations can match. The graphics are visually appealing even at 30FPS on a RTX 4070. Nothing like focusing on a vehicle and just watch your city go byHowever, the grand potential of City Skylines is undercut by its tendency to feel lifeless and barren. While the game provides the tools to create thriving metropolises, it often fails to deliver the bustling, dynamic cities you might expect.Schools have no childrenParks have no peopleSoccer fields and Football stadiums have no gamesUniversities of 1000+ people have empty parking lots and barely anyone walking aroundFire helicopters fly 10 map blocks to a forest fire just to turn around when they were 2 blocks away to put out a house fire 8 blocks awayThe water park "tourist attraction" has 1 pool and 2 water slidesFire engines put out fires by just driving up to the house. they don't even spray waterThe lack of attention to detail is disappointing compared to the first game. _childDocuments_.review: The game has 2 main issues:- It lacks basic city-simulation systems, like proper path-finding. The raw game is already there, but there are so many issues regarding the actual simulation of the city that to anyone that's looking to spend dozens of hours designing and detailing a complex city the result will be unsatisfying- It is very poorly optimized. In my case (R5 5600X, 32GB, RX6750XT), I get roughly 30fps in 2k with medium settings (as of March 2024, at launch it was closer to 20fps), and not even going to 1080p and low settings I don't get to 60 fps. That's simply unacceptableAs far as I can see, for whatever reason the management of either Colossal Order or Paradox has decided to rush the launch of this game, instead of giving the time it needed to stand up to Cities Skylines 1, which truly was a great game.Simply put, if you want a city builder sim, you're far better off buying CS1 for cheaper, download the more popular mods and maybe even get some DLCs if you like, and you will have a much better experience

I was a day 1 preorder, and I held off on leaving my review with the expectation that things would improve with updates, however at this point, there has been much less progress than I expected, and we are still left with a fundamentally broken game. _childDocuments_.review: I'm no stranger to buying early access games that are riddled with bugs. Most of the time, my interest in the game lets me overlook the early access bugs and other shortcomings, knowing that it will eventually get fixed. Problem here, is CS 2 is not an early access game, it was marketed, and sold with the price of a full, finished game, and it's anything but. I knew there were issues, and I tempered my expectations as such, knowing the game was going to be nowhere near as refined as CS1, and to be fair, the first couple hours of the game I was genuinely enjoying it! I thought everyone was being overdramatic... and then I hit 50k citizens, and the cracks started to show (as well as my performance taking a horrendous nose-dive). I'm no city-planning genius, I play the game just to design pretty looking cities and relax watching my cims drive around my spaghetti-mess of roads, but the economy makes little sense, the simulation of resources doesn't seem to actually make a difference, almost every building looks the exact same, and nobody wants to move into anything but a little house. "Just don't zone low residential", ok cool then I'll just sit here for several ingame years as my city growth comes to a stop. Service vehicle animations are gone, park animations are gone, cims don't seem to do anything but go to work or sleep, and I've heard the same radio announcement a dozen times in the last hour now. Was holding out hope that the game was going to improve, and maybe it will someday, but going on 7 months now after release with still no mod support (one of the biggest draws to me of CS1), unreliable performance even on a 3080 and i7 10700k, and overall very little improvement in the quality of the game is quite frankly embarrassing to me. TLDR: The game is in early access at best, the game feels like it needs at least another year in development. Steer clear of this game and just go play CS1 again until they get this Colossal disappointment in order.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the massive quantity of outrage that seems to have accumulated surrounding the game, I find it to be a huge improvement over the original and probably a massive improvement in the city builder genre. To make a comparison, this game should be as significant to the genre as SC4 was. It certainly has given me the same sense of magic that SC4 did when it released. Is the game perfect? No, not at all.  Are there major bugs? Yep. Is performance really awful at the moment? Yes again. Does this stop people from having fun while playing this game? I would say absolutely not. The game is headed in the right direction and the issues that people are complaining about at the moment will be fixed. In the meantime, it's really worthwhile to appreciate this game for what it is. You can enjoy the next gen road tools, amazing visuals, and much better asset scaling. It's really hard to get tired of looking down at your city and watching the insanely fine details that have been put into the game. There is no other city builder that has this level of fidelity yet.  It's really impressive, and it's worth buying even in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the bad performance reviews put you off, its largely a settings issue.When i first loaded the game up and played on the default settings, which were all set to high automatically. I totally understand the disappointment many people are voicing. Everything was flickering, worse than CS1.So i watched a couple of YT vids, and got some tips on what was worth lowering in the graphics settings. 80/90% of the issues i had were FIXED just by entering into the advanced graphics settings, and switching the AA to the TAA setting. Then there were a few other tweaks, such disabling some of the lesser obvious options such as dynamic resolution (which was counter-intuitive due to the CS1 mod). But it was only about 5 settings i changed, and the game seems to work perfectly. It looks great, no FPS issues so far, But admittedly, i'm only on a lvl 6 city so far i think. It may get worse with a bigger city.The game works fine if you can be honest about your rigs capabilities, and accept that you will need to tweak the settings a bit to start with. I'm looking forward to future updates, where i can crank everything up to max, add some mods, and build a city with 1mil+ citizensIts not perfect, but if you want perfect, you are better off getting a console, as they have standard hardware so easier to optimise for. But i'm finding the game fully playable. Its not perfect, but its playable.I'll update this with a gameplay review once i feel i have played enough to give an honest opinion.For reference, i do have an upper end rig: ROG STRIX RTX4080, 32GB DDR4 RAM, AIO cooled i7 7800k, Installed on an SSD. The minimum specs, really are the very minimum i would suspect. so make sure you at the very least meet them.

So it hurts to give up on C:S2 after less than a year.I built up my first city in the month after it came out, and stopped playing because I got bored. After the recent Economy 2.0 patch, I thought I'd try again, but my second city has played out exactly like my first city. My thoughts now:• C:S2 is rather disappointing. It is now an OK city building game. But it doesn't move things forward for the city builder genre.• If I had to pick my biggest issue, it's that nothing happens. The gameplay for a city of 500 is fundamentally the same as the gameplay when you reach 50,000 - build roads, zone, repeat. Every neighbourhood you build ends up the same. Compare a game like Civilization where gameplay cycles through exploration, expansion, offense, defense, building wide, building tall, etc., or Anno 1800 where there's always something new to build or tweak.• The player has no meaningful restrictions - lots of space on every map, money is easy to come by (Economy 2.0 just made it a bit slower), there's no political restrictions on what you can build, no real consequences for bad decisions. You never have to think, or make a hard decision - almost all the challenges in the game are solved by "build more". Everything feels so dead and flat.Like - let me go off on a bit of a tangent. Real-life cities are fascinating things, because like biological organisms they grow and decay, thrive or die. They have complex problems with no easy solutions, except C:S2 has an easy solution for every problem.If we look at some real life cities through a C:S2 lens:Tokyo - hemmed in by mountains with no flat land. C:S2 solution: Just buy more tiles.Los Angeles - too many highways. C:S2 solution: Delete half the city and build a mass transit system.London - not enough highways. C:S2 solution: Delete half the city and build more highways.Mumbai - smog and pollution. C:S2 solution: Delete the industry and re-zone it downwind of the city.San Francisco - rent is too high. C:S2 solution: Buy more tiles and zone more residential.And so on. These are all interesting, realistic challenges that a better game would simulate better and would be really fun to solve creatively. The closest the game gets is the rather intricate traffic and transit system - it is great fun to, for example, create a "park and ride" system that really works - but this kind of thing is missing from the rest of the game.Following on from that, the mechanics and art style are entirely focused on a very specific type of American grid-based urban sprawl. If you try to do anything else the cities you get just don't look right, in a way that's hard to pin down, but is so obvious when you look at real cities on Google Earth:• Look at real towns and cities and immediately you notice angles, spaces, historic buildings, and green spaces, nothing conforming to an exact grid - even in the USA. The way zoning works though, you end up with this ugly crammed-together cities all at the same angle, all with the same repeating ugly assets, and tiny square-shaped parks. Again, I can't help but compare to games like Manor Lords (which has beautiful, sprawling, freeform towns and plots) or Anno 1800 (which is even more grid-based but manages to look great anyway).• There's just something so bland and ugly about some of the buildings in particular, which gets worse when they start repeating.• Special mention to the absolutely terrible-looking specialised industry zones that are just a rubbish low-res texture painted on the terrain.• The C:S1 Parklife parks, which were a great idea to make more realistic cities, are gone and it's back to tiny square ploppable parks.• Big flat ploppables (the cemetery, power stations etc.) must be on perfectly flat ground or else you end up with these really ugly cliffs dug out of the ground.• You have to zone so much industry that it takes over half your city, and for some reason all the industries in this game are burning asbestos 24/7 so you end up having to put them all in one spot downwind of the residential areas. Most modern real-life industry in cities doesn't create air pollution.• Likewise, the simulation encourages you to create endless grids of boring suburbia. There isn't really any incentive to, you know, build a city.•  Of course with mods you can paint the city of your dreams, but I want a city builder where realistic-looking cities emerge from the gameplay and the simulation factors. (See Songs of Syx for a great city builder where the aesthetics and layout actually fundamentally affect gameplay.)• On a positive note, the way highways work now is so much better (e.g. you can build a proper 3-lane highway where one lane turns into a slip road, have 2 2-lane roads merge into a 4-lane highway, etc.) and I wish they had used that same approach for the rest of the game.I don't really mind the bugs or performance issues because those can be fixed. What concerns me is that these issues all come from fundamental choices that can't be fixed now until Cities: Skylines 3. The grid is a fundamental part of the game engine and it will be hard to introduce a more dynamic form of gameplay now. I will probably keep coming back because unfortunately there is no other modern city builder out there apart from the original game, but I think C:S2 has missed the mark by a great deal.

_childDocuments_.review: Much like Cities: Skylines, the initial release is a bit bare bones. My performance overall is superior to the first game. I run low 30 fps most of the time in Cities I, in Cities II, i hit mid 30s most of the time. I call that improvement. (People expecting 60fps in a simulation game are idiots.) Overall this is an improvement to the launch version of Cities Skylines, I am most excited by how the city feels more alive and less like a simulation. _childDocuments_.review: This game has a LOT of flaws.I get it, the performance issues are extremely obvious, so they easily grab most of the attention. But these issues can and, I'm confident,  be fixed. What should be much more concerning are the countless other game design decisions taken here, most of which are fundamental to the game itself. Though there are clear improvements, it all just leaves a bitter taste in my mouth.Starting with the good:- Road tools. They are vastly improved, no doubt. The modular system, while very lacking at the moment, I think has a lot of promise for the future. Now, of course it doesn't give you all that much control in the end, compared to CS1 with mods such as TMPE, Node Controller, IMT, etc. but it's a good start.- The awful cartoon look is gone, and the buildings look (generally) much more to-scale. Huge improvement.- Dynamic seasons. An obvious improvement over the static winter of Snowfall, and it brings some variety to the city's looks. - The economy is... better, I guess? It feels more detailed, and the customisable taxes are a welcome edition.- No more radius for service buildings! They seem to work more like how you'd expect; they serve everyone, but prioritise the vicinity. You can also restrict their reach to specific districts, which can be useful. - The reward buildings you get are basically built-in RICO buildings. They're cool. There needs to be  more of them, however.- Bigger maps.The thing is, as much as I appreciate the improvements, many of these aspects are band-aid fixes, not solutions, and they reveal some of the larger, overarching issues with the game.Zoning:- The grid. Keeping the original grid system is easy, so I get it. However, with the revamped road tools it quickly starts to clash with what the game supposedly wants you to do. The tools encourage you to make dynamic, free-form roads, which is great; however, the zoning grid is so ridiculously finicky and unintuitive that even making perfect 90 degree roads still manage to screw it up. There's no control over zoning , and there's no real way to predict how it'll change whenever you build in the vicinity. Sometimes I build a path next to a building and nothing happens; other times it removes half the cells and marks the building for demolition. This is even worse when dealing with roads, since the node generation seems to do its best to sabotage you. - The buildings. I'm not gonna go into the repetitive looks of them. Instead, the issues lies with their design. So many of them are now wall-to-wall, which just  with the unreliable grid system. It makes any city that isn't a perfect grid a complete eyesore, unless you spend hours on end trying to fiddle with the road configurations. To top it off, a lot of the buildings are comically disproportionate with each other. The mixed use buildings have no backyards; the low density commercial buildings are ; the high density ones are giant blocks that take up 99% of the lot, making commercial zones look like some kinda claustrophobic, dystopian hell; the other high density zones are literal skyscrapers that don't fit at all in , and ofc whose bases are way too small.- The types. They're bad. The distinction between commercial and office always baffled me, but in this game it just shows how much of an active detriment it is. There are...  types of goods an office can make. Why even have this zone at all? Not to mention how all zones except residential still lack medium density. Industry has . SC4 did it perfectly 20 years ago. The zones only regulated density (low/mid/high); the demand regulated . Despite having twice as many demand bars as CS2, it was far more dynamic and intuitive. - Mixed use. It's great that it exists, but it seriously shouldn't need to be its own type. Whether row houses or apartment towers, these buildings should already have the possibility for ground floor shops! Grocers, dentists, doctor offices... these all pop up organically, unless you specifically outlaw them (which, with the game's district policy system, would be easily implementable). Now, the other pervasive issue this game has is its blatant "americanisation". This is also clearly visible in the zoning, but I figured I'd put it in its own point.- Scale of buildings. The service buildings are all , which make them completely unsuitable for small towns. And even in large cities, their ridiculous footprint make them impossible to retroactively fit in a neighbourhood. I mean, come on, a primary school would require me to demolish housing for over a ? To make it worse, most of this footprint is made up of . There's a single bus terminal in the game with the size of an entire block--yet  of its footprint has nothing to do with buses--and it offers pedestrian access only on a single side!- Parking. It's great that it's simulated! But they really didn't think this through. Every building comes with their own massive parking lots. Why is this not  choice to make? Since they also only allow "customers", they end up remaining empty while I have to build three whole blocks nearby dedicated to public parking. - Parking (2). The game's ploppable parking lots only come in a few sizes that are all overly large, making it impossible to use them to fill in the inevitable gaps in zoning. Then what about highly compact parking garages? Nope, the lot is twice as large as the garage itself, and I could easily fill the same area with twice as many parking spots by just paving the entire thing with asphalt. Then what's the point of it?!- Parking (3). In real life, most new building complexes of course have underground parking for its residents. So why do zero buildings in this game have this? Instead, the underground parking garage the game offers covers an entire block.Okay, this is all getting very long already, so I'll just wrap it up with some remaining minor points.- The progression system. Thanks, I hate it! I'll be turning it off. - No filler zones. Anyone remember CitiesXL? It had this neat little feature that let you easily fill in the gaps between lots with various parks, plazas, etc. This would've at least alleviated the eyesore that CS2's grid system leaves.- Parks. Why do they look so... ugly? The fake grass, the paths, the assets... not to mention they are only accessible by a single side. Now, the vanilla CS1 parks weren't exactly beautiful, but many of the ones added in expansions actually looked pretty decent! So how did they manage to  in this regard?- Plazas/Squares. There aren't any of them. Just... none.- The fake grass. Sorry, but these fake grass lots that every single building has, that violently clash with the real grass, and that don't always even fill the entire lot, they look ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awful.- The modular building system, since it doesn't allow free rotations or adding extensions across roads, ends up just being a chore to manage.- How can a city of 100k+ have no more than ?- The specialised industries look hideous. All farms have a , really??- The lack of Steam Workshop isn't really a problem with me... except that there's . So people can't even fix the game with mods.I have so much more I'd like to have said about this game, but Steam doesn't allow me any more words. So I'll just say this: Yes, the game has improvements over launch CS1. But that doesn't excuse  I've mentioned. It's almost a decade old, guys! Are we really not meant to expect more from a full-priced title? Truth is, once I feel done with my current city, I'll probably just go back to CS1, because I frankly don't see any replay value in the game's current state.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is definitely in a better state than it was in at release, it's nice to see that CO is actively working on improving the game, the economy update is definitely a good start. At the moment it feels very similar to the early days of CS1. However, like in CS1, this game still needs a decent amount of fixing, although it's fun to play now especially in early cities when you're figuring out how the game works, or how the new update works depending on your expertise, the game shows it's cracks once again in late game. Things like the mass homelessness, where you just have homeless people roaming around your town, they don't get moved or deleted, even though the game supposedly has a mechanic for it, but supposedly only counts homeless people as homeless if they are in a park, otherwise they're just empty shells? not too sure what happened there but it sounds fairly simple to fix.Another bigger problem is with high density offices where they get reduced in employees the longer these offices exist, maybe the companies are just profitmaxing :D, but this can be annoying for bigger cities.Road management and Traffic AI is another quirk I'd love to see improved and fixed, traffic is just as dumb as CS1, which I wish they learned from the mistake of that but I'd rather the developers improve road management tools to make traffic more manageable, the AI itself should work better according to road management, it's just that we don't have any tools without mods to work on fixing a city's traffic.Performance could still have a few quirks knocked out of it but it realistically can't be improved too much since this is still at it's very core a city builder simulation, and sim games are not exactly known for their amazing frame rates, especially cities skylines if your city grows to high levels of population, this was no different in cities skylines 1, it was just not as heavy as this game due to it being years old now, so of course it will run better on newer hardware.Otherwise the game is fun and is actually pretty playable with the economy update, which realistically if the game hadn't been rushed we would have had this at launch, but I'll take what they give at this point. It feels worth the money if you get it on sale, but I'd still avoid if you are thinking of buying it full price, just wait for a decent sale and you'll have fun without regretting your decision.

_childDocuments_.review: As a C:S1 player, I WOULD recommend this game based on concept alone. **My current play through is at Milestone 12, population 56,000**However there are a LOT of things wrong with this game, and a lot that they did right. 1. Performance is a huge issue and I've had to change settings far beyond recommended just to get it at a playable level. *As you get further into the game performance does drop further*2. There isn't much 'life' to the game. CS1 assets felt much more lively with kids playing in parks, firefighters actually hosed down burning buildings instead of just driving into them and back out, etc.  3. Public transport tools, in my opinion, were a lot easier and simpler to use. I have really struggled at times to use them.4. Glitchy as all hell.. SOOO many cosmetic glitches or glitches that simply don't allow me to destroy taxi or bus shelters from the side of streets without destroying the entire street and replacing. Why? Who knows.5. Every time I Shift+Tab there's a chance my keyboard randomly disconnects from Cities (and ONLY cities, still works on every other application) and I'm forced to completely reload. 6. "Rent Too High" as well as people complaining of low healthcare despite availability being through the roof - same with crime rate (had crime rate of 1% and full coverage, they still complain of it being unsafe). How to fix any of these things? No clue. The game doesn't tell you so you're left with abandoned buildings and complaining citizens. 7. A lot of the assets have the same skins. There isn't much diversity and can look quite boring.8. Really inaccurate info. Clicked on a household and the only residents were a pet and a child. ?? Have seen other reviews saying there was a child CEO.Things I DO enjoy1. updated road tools are great! easy to use and much more functional.2. Assets feel a lot more true to size.3. New progression system feels a lot more rewarding. Having to unlock with progression points is a good take on it.4. Info panels and UI feels easier to navigate once you get used to the change from C:S1. A lot more info and stats available too which makes it feel more like a management game rather than just a city builder.5. Really enjoy being able to import and export water and power. Great way to make extra money later in game or save money early game.6. Water is both better and worse at the same time. Have weird water rising glitches out of nowhere that don't go away or dry up, but it also doesn't freak out when you terraform  causing mini tsunamis now like C:S1 did.Game needs a LOT of polishing but at it's current state it's good. Could be a lot better but it's good.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT 2: I am actively experiencing new bugs regularly so im probably missing someTLDR for those wanting "quick" points-Pros:+can look pretty from some angles and settings+new road tools are the best part+progression system is neat (but only the points system, actual progression sucks)+has an initial enjoyment+some fun small details, cars doing 3 point turns with reverse lights, etc   -semis still clip through themselves+volumetric clouds do look pretty!+the music is good!  -ads and hosts repeat themselves often and too frequently. also hardly any songs IN those stations. they repeat fast.+the new zoning types are also niceCons:-unfinished game-runs quite bad, and changes wildly depending on system hardware-settings made fps worse-parks are almost always empty-AI still sucks at higher pops-an overabundance of visual bugs, things loading and unloading in front of me regardless of distance and never sharpening back up-cars have orange windows from a distance-ray tracing turns cars fuzzy when they move-balancing isnt great-no real punishment for maxing out taxes?-the economy is made up and fake-industry zones suck, no other way around it, the weird (or lack) of texture variation and random building placement sucks and looks weird-Ultimate Edition does not include any actual expansions, just assets and radios-Tornado textures are a joke and thats putting it mildly. At least its not just a spinning repeating smoke texture like in the early trailers-for touting how you should support local business and industry, the lack of trucks, vans, etc let alone planes or boats or trains having those brands on them feels like a miss.-the most colorful things in this game are the cars and even thats unrealistic in this day and age-ships feel comically too large, and having to build these insanely tall bridges that dont look great doesnt help-terrain tools are a joke-devs and community need to stop making excuses for performance as a game in 2023 at minimum should be able to hit 30fps let alone 60-buying a new GPU should be factored into the game price at this rate-for also gloating about no population cap it seems the game cant even handle 50k for me-insane amount of land is rendered outside of the visible play area, even if low poly-no shared bus/taxi and traffic roads and same with bicycles-theres almost a lack of ambient sounds? feels ironically almost too quiet compared to CS1 which I think doesnt help with it feeling empty-locations dont seem to make sense for maps. Barrier Island is North American themed and vaguely resembles NYC yet its in the southern hemisphere?-map variety is pretty boring-LOTS AND LOTS AND LOTS AND LOTS OF VISUAL BUGSEDIT 1 OF MORE NEGATIVE CRAP HAPPENING:So after playing a bit more, the cloud layer that exists above the volumetric clouds (still don't get why they even exist if they don't move) started going faster and faster to the point that if you have epilepsy I would not recommend the game until this is fixed ESPECIALLY. It causes rapid flashing during the daylight hours from the shadows and they only stop moving after the game has been paused for a solid bit. My session was ended by the game crashing when placing a building then it soft locked my computer because it still thought it was running. I also eventually tried to lower the graphics after 10k population because it became substantially worse, but it didn't fix fps! Performance definitely got worse the more I keep playing.I can also sufficiently say the terrain tools SUCK. The flattening tool doesn't pick the point at which you clicked from and stick with it, if you move the mouse too quick it WILL snap to the next elevation, up or down. Every other game can seem to get this right.The economy? Seemingly made up. I maxed out residential tax to 30% and got constant single family home demand indefinitely. CO made mention that they changed the hourly money ticker to up/down arrows because it "isnt important to know how much you're making" but I believe its to hide the fact it just doesn't work at all. Consistently would go from -40k an hour to -1,000 in minutes of just sitting there and doing nothing. Once I backed off my insane taxes the game thought I should've been losing 1 MILLION per month and yet my money kept going up.Parks stay empty while random apartment blocks will have about 40 people doing yoga in the front yard, insane that pedestrian paths exist but you cant place parks on them.Traffic AI was the biggest letdown as my city got bigger (about 50k). They do exactly the same crappy moves as the first game after a certain point and still consistently pick the shortest route rather than the quickest leading to impossible to solve backups even with using almost all of the transit available to me minus trams.I would also consistently have tunnels filled with water when placing them. Be it roads or trains. My biggest gripe with transit is if you want to use ships you better have thought about unlocking every single tile in the ocean then manually connect everything back up. Good luck if you already built them and then have to wait for the next milestone just to use them. Not sure why we need to create routes to giant ugly floating arrows at the map edges. Same with airports.I appreciate that there are small details in this game that do make it fun but the game itself feels lifeless and bland (dare I say repetitive) after 15 hours. I want to see my Cims doing things. Feels like more effort was put into all these "unique buildings" (the ones that can only be plopped once) and graphics that dont even work well and small details most will never see; than anything that matters.Unrelated to playing the game itself and more of an overall critique, im quite annoyed and disappointed to see the only actual "expansion" we are getting is.... bridges and ports... everything in the Ultimate Edition is just asset fodder and radio stations, and id argue bridges and ports arent new gameplay features like an expansion should be, so just dont buy it. Its already a crime that the DLC individually + the game itself it will cost you $165 if and when they do that. Seems were getting the Victoria 3 treatment of being given a game devoid of features but immediately dumping out DLC. Paradox greed knows no bounds since they also seem to keep f-ing up Stellaris gameplay too. But I digress.Dont buy this currently. Give it 6 months. Minimum.

_childDocuments_.review: Since writing my original review the game has been extensively updated. Key improvements are:- Mods- Map Editor- Smaller service buildings- Revamped Economy- A lot of optimisationsMods are probably the key one here, they can ameliorate a multitude of issues the game has or add new features, some which feel like missed opportunities. This lets each player play the game they want to. I think C:S has broad player base, people who want to make as big a city as possible, people who want to make the most intensely detailed copies of real places, people who want to simulate (some of) a city with the strategy that involves. There is a lot of overlap here but CO have a hard time balancing a game that is playable by everyone and enjoyed by them too. Mods made C:S and I think they will make C:S II. The community have already produced absolute game changers like road builder, move it, and anarchy.This game has a bright future, even if it had teething issues and it is now very much in a state where I can recommend it. I thoroughly enjoy the game and its core mechanics are a vast improvement over the original. At only the start of this year I was apprehensive about updates, now I'm looking forward to the coming months with CO back from Summer holidays. Keep up the good work! TLDR:The game is now fully playable, go enjoy it----------------------------------------------------------Original review at 38.7 hours on 13/11/2023I think C:S II has some great improvements over the first game, new tools and systems can be interacted with and overall I enjoy creating and designing cities and towns within this game. I'm saddened by a number of features that are missing from the game that existed in C:S (without DLC) such as road signs which are placed on road ends rather than entire nodes, decorative props, and Cim animations (such as firefighting, playing sports etc). I'm also upset that many DLC features were not included in the base game, notably city parks which were fundamental to the creation of beautiful and realistic looking cities. The game also has some bugs with its underlying simulation which others go into in more detail but I have only noticed sometimes. I think overall the game does not feel complete, as others mention it has the feel of a somewhat polished Early Access game. The UI and feel of the game is great but mechanics are missing and it doesn't feel like any playtesting has been done, at least not with people willing to push their cities and dive into min maxing the games mechanics.I don't think I would refund the game even if I had the ability to as I am enjoying it but I don't like the fact I have paid a premium price for an under optimised game that is still missing features the community would expect to release on day 1.I would like to say that I believe that releasing this game without an Early Access tag is an act of bad faith. If there were known issues and missing features from what the studio wants in the 1.0 version then what we have now is not 1.0. I also think that if this early release was financially necessary then being transparent with the player base would most likely reduce the large backlash that has occurred. I think this is especially the case given the Dev diaries leading up to the release were so promising and made me think that CO really was being transparent with the community and I am truly saddened this is not the case.I do look forward to the upcoming changes and improvements and I am excited to see where this game goes but for the moment. I cannot in good faith recommend this game.TLDR:Do I enjoy this game, yes, but I cannot in good faith recommend it at this moment in time.

_childDocuments_.review: OG Post (Jan 2024):After playing a bit, as a new player to the series, it started to make more sense than initial impressions gave. The systems are a little more complex than CO would like you to think & I do believe this is an attempt to be a simulation. However, you can tell that this was not their best effort. From a new player perspective, this game is not intuitive for a logical thinker & there are many systems, economic, physics, population, taxes, etc, that all have some level of buggy behavior that make things murky to understand at best. Additionally, this game is not optimized; I say this from someone using a 5900X & 6900X combo w/ 32GB DRAM & M.2 NVMe drives only. So, I do not suffer from an under spec'd system like many of the first cries about this game were caused by. To be fair, CO/Paradox did raise the required/recommended specs to run the game shortly after these cries started to decimate their Steam reviews. There are plenty of videos & articles out there proving that CO/Paradox has left it's customers wanting a better product than what they released; even w/ the best hardware out there this game doesn't perform well in terms of compute. Graphically, it could be better, but the compute issues far exceed the graphical ones IMO. As everyone has stated, including myself in the Steam forums, this game should've been labelled as "Early Access" by CO/Paradox. While it would be admirable to have a modding platform for cross-platform uniformity, CO has yet to do anything that remotely indicates that they will be going thru w/ this claim of supporting mods officially & pissed off the existing player base by taking the Steam Workshop option of modding away from PC Steam players. CO/Paradox is also wanting to push future updates, to correct core system problems & bugs they failed to either correct prior to release or in initial bug fixes, via paid DLC content releases. Core content fixes should be separate from the DLC; fixing the core game shouldn't be held behind pay walls.CO/Paradox, this type of business practice shows that the player base means nothing to you past the revenue & profit you make off the game. In short, CO, but mostly Paradox, do not practice ethical business &, as a first time buyer into the franchise w/ this game, I have been lied to & am deeply disappointed that another publisher is just trying to turn a buck instead of helping a developer make a great game/simulator. I'm not convinced I'll buy anymore from CO/Paradox & I don't recommend anyone else does either until they can make it up to their customers.Edit (July 2024):Massive bugs still being encountered as you can easily verify via forums as well. There are also some inconveniences & what I would call essential assets needing added to base game.Bugs/Issues/Gripes:- Graphic distortions of roads based on angles places.- Some assets, mostly roads, get stuck under buildings that you can place down, like harbors or your power generator buildings; you'll need to move or delete the building in order to access the stuck asset.- The massive tax bug rears it's ugly head w/ no indication as to what specifically causes it; had both Industrial & office taxes just default to 0% income & the sliders because unusable, even when you haven't been playing w/ the sliders.- Industrial productions just decline in output for no apparent reason when they're higher level buildings & have 100+% efficiency.- Industrial companies say they're understaffed, but then never hire more people regardless of education levels of your population.- Garbage still accumulates & piles up regardless of how many trucks you have collecting, I had over 1.5k trucks collecting from a 200k population city & never could make a dent. Looks like truck still never make it to their destinations or generate trash themselves.- Death care is terrible. With an abundance of crematoriums & graveyards & hundreds of hearses, bodies are still not being picked up from their residences.- Traffic intersections still greatly suck when auto-generated, the lanes generate traffic lanes that would never legally exist (based on USA traffic laws) that cause all different types of congestion & accidents; there is absolutely no reason to include U-turns going into every single lane, when it should be the inner most lane only & it's illegal to change lanes within an intersection, so putting this in the game for American maps at least is stupid, clutters the auto-generation, & makes the game traffic much harder to control.- Traffic lights need more granular control as there are multiple light change tactics used in traffic control, i.e. split phasing, dedicated pedestrian cycle, etc. I shouldn't have to add a mod for this functionality.- There are no "No U-turn" signs that can be added to intersections; they have "no left/right turns" & "no forward" signs, but not "no U-turns"? Dumb. There are tons of locations that do not allow U-turns because it is so dangerous to do at times. U-turns should not be default behavior w/o something to turn them off in base game.** Caveat: These issues/gripes that you can fix w/ mods if a mod is developed for it, but I shouldn't have to mod in order to get what should've been base game functionality. You can have all the same default behaviors there are not for players that don't care about being granular, but enthusiasts of this genre would seriously appreciate a game that works & one that offers the option to be me granular like I've mentioned above.CO/Paradox: You MUST include core game fixes to the base game for free. Some of the other stuff I've mentioned can be included in DLCs if you can't stay accountable enough, but at least fix the gods damn core game!

The good:There is a strong foundation here for a worthy sequel to C:S1. The simulation itself seems solid and the tools right out of the box seem great. The UI is nicely laid out and I do appreciate all maps having seasons and all weather types. The XP progression system is also nice though could make do with being a bit more fleshed out.The bad:I seem to have been lucky in terms of performance, maxed out settings at 1440p my machine (GPU: 7900XT. CPU: 5900X. RAM: 32GB DDR4) seems to handle it fine. However, the graphics do not seem a huge improvement over the previous title despite nearly a decade passing. It is not a bad looking game, but I expected a bit more of a leap. That aside, one area that needs improving is how the landscape is flattened when placing buildings, it is quite ugly and jarring. There is also a lack of map variety and certain game mechanics don't seem as deep or are absent, for example no heating to worry about for when it snows?I suspect in time after a number of patches and some DLC etc this game will leap past CS1. Right now it is solid, if not revolutionary. That said, it was always going to be difficult bringing a game out to compare to a predecessor that has nearly 10+ years worth of patches and expansions, but I do think a few more months of tweaking and adding some extra variety etc would have been better.I will update this review once I have put some more hours into the game

_childDocuments_.review: It’s clear that *Cities: Skylines 2* is taking the franchise in an ambitious direction, and for the most part, it delivers a satisfying experience. For those who thrive on city-building challenges, the new economy mechanics are a breath of fresh air, making the balancing act of revenue generation, population management, and infrastructure feel more dynamic and, dare I say, more realistic. The inclusion of milestone rewards, particularly when it comes to managing a city’s economic challenges in the vein of developing countries with booming tourist industries, is a clever touch, pushing players to think beyond just “building the biggest city” and focus on sustainable growth and complex budgeting.Visually, *CS:2* is a significant upgrade over its predecessor. The cities now feel alive with vibrant details, from the shimmering skyline to the hum of daily city life. It’s a far cry from the somewhat sterile feel of the original *Cities: Skylines*, which makes the experience that much more engaging. Props to the developers for creating a world that’s a joy to look at.However, the AI, or rather the *CIMs* (as they’ve been dubbed by the community), still leaves much to be desired. I’m not entirely sure what’s going on behind the scenes, but the routing behavior of these virtual citizens often feels frustratingly erratic. The pathfinding, particularly in terms of buses, trains, and other forms of public transport, feels less intuitive than in the first game. For a game that prides itself on the delicate dance of managing city systems, it’s baffling how often I find myself questioning why a bus is making a 10-minute detour when it could’ve taken a direct route. I can’t help but wonder if a collaboration with NVIDIA to harness more computational power could fix some of these issues. A little AI intelligence could go a long way here.On the subject of improvements, while the new modding interface is certainly a step forward, it doesn’t quite capture the user-friendly magic of the Steam Community Overlay. The process feels more cumbersome, and creators are left feeling like they have to jump through hoops just to get their content into the game. I still don’t even know my Paradox login, despite having a Steam account tied to it. That lack of streamlined integration is a headache, especially for those of us who live and breathe mods.Speaking of mods, one of my biggest gripes is the lack of backward compatibility with the DLC packs from *Cities: Skylines*. If I’ve already paid for creator packs and expansions in the first game, I shouldn’t have to pay for them all over again. Sure, the free tram DLC is a nice gesture, but I’m holding out hope that more updates like this will come for free in the future. If Paradox can tap into scenario-based monetization (such as natural disaster DLCs or city challenges), they might find a way to generate more revenue while keeping the community happy.After a certain point, the game feels like it’s all about creativity. You’ve figured out how to make money, you’re no longer in danger of going bankrupt, and now it’s just about creating the city of your dreams. The scenarios are a fun addition, but I can’t help but feel they need more depth—perhaps something like competitive multiplayer cities where you can challenge other players for population dominance. Imagine competing with neighboring cities on the same server, battling for resources and citizens, pushing the boundaries of city-building in a more social and competitive space. That would add a whole new level of excitement and community engagement.Ultimately, *Cities: Skylines 2* feels like a game that's still finding its footing. It’s clear Paradox is wrestling with how to evolve the game without falling into the trap of being a "pay-to-win" subscription service, but there’s a tension between monetization and delivering a wholesome experience that has yet to be fully resolved. Let’s hope they can find that balance before the community starts feeling too exploited.Despite its hiccups, though, I still love this game. It's a sprawling, intricate world that lets you live out the dream of being a city planner—one with the kind of ambition that’s hard to ignore. It’s a great foundation for something even better down the line. Keep the free updates coming, Paradox, and for the love of all things urban, get that AI sorted out.

_childDocuments_.review: Loved the first CS, but this one is kind of boring? The assets are really well done, but having little to no asset variety makes it hard to visually differentiate between "neighborhoods" in the city. I'm not a huge fan of how the demand bars are functioning currently, as the combination of one medium density building clearing the whole bar and the need for medium density coming so quickly feels like I'm being rushed to expand a city as fast as possible. Another thing adding to this expansion need is the economy, the budget is impossible to balance early on, if you want to be in the green, you have to grow (fast) in order to get milestones to keep you afloat until your tax base is big enough to sustain you. While somewhat realistic, small towns do exist and survive financially? I might not be very good at the game, but I shouldn't need to research actual economics in order to play a video game. The fluctuations in income with little to no explanation are hard to wrap my head around, and I'd like the ability to make a small town, 3-8k population, self sustaining before I start trying to add in massive city services with massive upkeep costs. If you grow as fast as possible, money's no issue. If you try to slow down and plan things out, you go bankrupt. As of now, I'm returning to CS1, which has more customization for neighborhoods and an economy I feel like I can influence. (I play both unmodded as everytime I try to mod CS1 my game stops working.)

_childDocuments_.review: A game with a much less steep learning curve for those who have played other city building games. Any addition of strong-medium density options and row housing also feels like such a huge upgrade from CS1. Citizen well-being and wealth mean a lot in this game, and although it has a greater impact, I find myself being less frustrated with it than I was in CS1. Obstacles in CS2 feel overcomeable, and *satisfying* to overcome. A lot of the new road building tools and guidelines are extremely useful, even though I hardly find myself using the much advertised grid-builder tool.Also, of my favorite features of SimCity 2013 was ploppables, or in other words the ability to add expansions onto existing service buildings- we got the mechanic in this game as well! I love the way they implemented service features in this game and I hope it gets expanded in a future content update so we have multiple/branching options! Overall, despite some performance issues, I am satisfied with my purchase- the amount of content that we have at release compared to CS1 feels like night and day, and I'm looking forward to what I anticipate will be a less aggressive and more value-per-dollar DLC release schedule if it is anything at all like Victoria 3 and CK3 have been aiming at. I have probably spent already over 20+ hidden hours on Xbox game pass, and plan to spend plenty more here on steam.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: After the post-release patch 1, performance improved a bit. I also found a Steam article on making textures look so much better. If you have the same issue as me with horrible textures, do the following "Go to advance graphic settings, scroll to the bottom, make sure mip bias is 3, and adjust your advanced "Level of Detail" settings - level of detail distance should be relatively short 25-40%, and your geometry cache limit should be at least 1GB (considering your card, I'd make it 3+ GB)". This improved my experience significantly. And after the patch, I am getting over 60 FPS and only dip down when I zoom in very close to a city of +5K. Performance can only go up from here. Cannot recommend CS2 as of launch. As with every other negative review, the performance is abysmal. I meet/exceed the recommended specs (5800x3D, 3080 10G, 32GB RAM) and after watching every Youtuber's graphics settings tips and even including CO's "optimization" post, the game barely gets 40 FPS. I know a city builder doesn't necessarily need 144 FPS but changing all the settings to be low makes the game look terrible. Hedge rows are like 5 polygons, trees in the distance are a single polygon, and when zooming out rooftops are black and there is no detail at all. For fun, I returned all the settings to high to see if the issues with zoomed in details would get better...nope, still looks horrible. There are times when the game looks great but Colossal Order are months away from having the game run smoothly and look as advertised. I would have refunded the game but spent about an hour of the 2 hr window adjusting settings on a naked map. After reaching 3k population, the game runs even worse. Here's to hoping the game will be as advertised by mid-2024 when they iron out the console optimization. The lack of Steam Workshop is a huge negative as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, the response to this game got me to write a review for the first time in my many years of Steam gaming, the only game out of 295 that I've ever written a review for. Normally I ignore it all and just play my games, but this is different. I'm emotionally invested, okay? Not in this specific game or developer, but the genre as a whole. I can't even begin to count the hours I've dumped into city builders over the years - SimCity, Caesar, Pharaoh, Cities XL, Banished, Frostpunk, Citystate, Timberborn, and everything in between - and I expect Cities: Skylines II will be no exception.Simply put, Skylines 2 is the most detailed, accurate, fully-simulated modern city builder that has been released to date. It represents the absolute state of the art in the genre. There were bugs, there still are some (none game breaking that I've encountered), performance was rough at launch but is greatly improved (and that happened quickly). Still no mods, but they're coming. I find it quite playable, to the tune of 157 hours and counting.The art style is greatly improved over Skylines I. Industry still isn't done quite right, especially the specialized industries. The graphics are great, and the game is using up to date techniques, although there are some issues with anti-aliasing and shadows, and a strange grain effect that makes things look a little gross, particularly in low light.The vanilla road system is light years ahead of any other city builder. The building expansion is a great inspiration taken from SC2013. The high/low voltage mechanic adds a nice splash of complexity to electricity. The different residential zoning types let you control much better how your city looks & feels. Overall, I would play this over Skylines I modded to hell and back simply for the improved gameplay systems.It's lacking in content. You'll find yourself zoning for specific lot sizes and there simply isn't an asset that fits. City services are 1 building per function, which is fine for buildings you only need one of, but you'll need to be creative to hide all those elementary schools. The radio stations repeat, so just turn them off.Despite some bugs, despite the dearth of content, despite the slightly rough launch, I was honestly blown away by this game the moment I started playing it. I'm 157 hours in and I see no end on the horizon, even if I didn't know mods and DLCs and content packs were coming. Yeah, there are 8 free content packs, each for a different part of the globe, coming with 2,500 assets, pretty soon it sounds like. Modding, again, soon.I'm having a great time with the vanilla game, and to think of what this game is going to be in 6 months or a year, or 5 years... It's good one already, and it's gonna be a banger, folks.

_childDocuments_.review: In terms of gameplay, the game is fun. They managed to integrate some lessons learned over the years and, while it's nowhere near the complexity that 10 years of DLCs added to CS1, this start to CS2 is very promising.Regarding performance issues, by using the Geforce Experience app to optimize the game I didn't encounter many FPS issues... at the expense of visual quality. Optimization is something that I can somewhat forgive for a new launch, even though companies are becoming more and more reliant on shipping features and then later concerning themselves with this. Optimization should be a core feature of a product at launch, not an afterthought.But what I cannot, and will never, excuse are game-breaking bugs that invalidate all of your progress and even threaten system stability. While in the process of saving a game and overwriting a save file, the game simply crashed. Upon reloading, I discover that my save file is nowhere to be found... 10 hours of city development thrown down the trash bin with no option of recovering it!But the most serious offense was when I relaunched the game again... and got a blue-screen-of-death, my FIRST and only instance so far since I have owned this PC system in almost 2 years.I cannot recommend a purchase of this game at this time, given the above bugs. Which is a shame, because the gameplay itself is FUN!

_childDocuments_.review: "Thanks for the chats all, but I'm moving on. :)EDIT: (Nov 17) I've heard from Paradox support to the query I logged. They confirm I was banned for this post, where I said "Publishing games as bare bones as possible (even removing content to plunder later, looking at you pre-release DLC that CS2 has), is customer abuse IMO.".The Paradox support person went on to state: "Frankly I would have issued a much sterner infraction than the minor "trollish comments" one you got for that!" (I can provide a screenshot of the email to those interested).My comment got me a one month ban. Proves my point.------------------------------------------------------ORIGINAL POST STARTS HERE:I love city building games. I mean the ones where you can build up massive modern metropolis's like in this game. I remember getting my hands on SimCity back in the old days, and instantly fell in love with it. I would lay down roads, zones, services for the city, and watch it grow at my hands. And I loved every single city builder that came along. The various SimCity versions (except 2013), Cities XL/XXL/all the versions, City Skylines, and Highrise City. SimCity 4 is definitely my most favourite of the city builders.When I heard that Cities Skylines 2 was being made, I got pretty excited. But also, pretty worried. I was really excited, because a new game in my second favourite type of game was coming out. And the videos made it look really good! But I was worried. Worried because Paradox was publishing it.When CS1 came out, it was an insta-buy for me. I really enjoyed the game. I was happily playing along, making cities, and then the DLC start coming out. Before CS1 came out, for years I had bought Paradox games and the DLC. However, I was really getting annoyed by the DLC policy of Paradox. CS1 came out on the heels of the 80th or something DLC for Crusader Kings 2. Not to mention the countless DLC for HOI and EU that I also played. So when the DLC starting coming out thick for CS1, I decided it was time to bow out of Paradox and put them on "the list". "The list" contains the publishers I will not buy games from. There's a few now, including EA for what they did to SimCity/Maxis. Paradox had joined them. I did not buy a single item from Paradox after June 2017. I wanted to, believe me. But this was my very minor protest against their DLC policy.And then came Cities Skylines 2. I actually held my ground, until the day before release. I knew if I bought in, I'd be buying into the DLC flood. I was really conflicted. I knew Paradox was going to DLC the hell out of the game, and there was the performance announcement before hand but I knew from experience (with my work) that performance can (and usually does) get fixed. But I REALLY wanted to play a city builder. So I caved, and bought the standard edition. Hey, at least I would minimise my losses to $70 (AUD).The day came, and I downloaded it, and started to play. After changing a few graphics settings, I was okay with sitting on medium graphics and tuning a few things like RPS suggested to. And I played.But it wasn't too long before I started noticing things. But I kept playing. I noticed even more things, and read about similar things others were noticing on the Paradox forum and here. I got to 25 hours and wrote my review. I didn't want to give a cheap 2 hours review, so I gave the game an honest shot. I was actually really shocked how popular my review became. I just wrote what I honestly saw in the game.Then the hostility began. I found myself banned for 3 days at Paradox forums for the most flimsy of reasons (the review was being discussed there and I commented on that thread). At around the same time, I started getting threats and hostile posts on my steam profile, my workshop items for other games, and ended up playing whack-a-mole deletion of posts. No point reporting as they were level 0 empty profiles just made to attack me. But I did keep playing, because maybe they had a point. Maybe I'd misunderstood some things.Anyways, eventually I hit 85 hours. I was done. I did an update to my review, and my 3 points that I feel kill the game for me stand. They are:1. Performance and bugs. Whilst performance had improved on the graphics side, over 250k pop my PC would start suffering from repeated stuttering. This was simulation, not graphical. _childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game. Not the excellent game of the year type, it just a fun game. Not a broken game like many review make it out to be.I have fun building big cites on this game more than original, since the scale of building and map make me feel like city I build is really big and I can actually feel good about making a sparsely city since it still have plenty of room to grow. And by having medium density as a middle ground it is also perfect. I really like making city with medium density while keeping only small hot spot as a high density area since it's far easier to make medium density fit it with all service building. And I like how the art direction in this game is going for more realistic look, I really enjoy 1st person camera mod in this art style.Road building tool is also easy to use, I don't need to concern over road node anymore (well, mostly) and type of road included with base game are also good for 2 lane road, for example,  we have 1u, 2u, pedestrian, etc. and it's really good since I no longer have to create pedestrian zone like the first game's expansion. Even on highway road is good, it's way easier to make merger lane to look good in this game no need to use mod to adjust it.Overall game system is good, easy to use and some room to build upon in later expansion. Since they already fix most of balance issue that this game has when it first come out. (like pedestrian has weight more on illegal crossing choice rather than walk a bit to nearby crossing, etc.).Performance is horrible, but I found that if I just set maximum frame latency to 3, I'll get much more smoother gameplay, since this game is a building game anyway a bit of input latency is not an issue comparing to get smoother picture. I just wonder why it wasn't set to 3 by default. And combine it with FPS limit provide me with a good and consistent frame rate and enjoyable playing experience.I don't know why they don't have that option without mod though. Come on if dev want to make a game targeted at 30 FPS at very least they should have added FPS limiter option, since what more horrible than 30 FPS is a swing FPS.Bucket tool for growable is horrible, I found that if I make city with bucket tool only, it will mostly look really bad since many assets in the same density category don't look well together or doesn't look good together without having some space between them. So, I have to manually paint growable in specific size to make it into the asset I want to avoid repeating assets or assets not fitting together. I wish there was an easy tool to exclude or include assets while painting it with bucket tool.  Since it's kinda tedious to paint building one by one or sometime even have to go back and demolish some building that happen to share some size length but doesn't fit well with others.Mod support and DLSS update are the 2 things that make me recommend this game now. With mod I can change the design that I disagree with how dev design it. Like the ability to aged up tree, I understand that aging up tree will make unbalance resource available, but come on I play this game more like a sandbox with a few restriction not playing it as a city management simulation, I want to make city pretty and I'm not enjoying waiting for tree to grow in order to get to look at my full vision. User custom map is also a nice addition. The maps selection that come out with this game.... to put it bluntly they're bad, there are only 2-3 maps that I like and only 1 map that I enjoy building on it. And I'm not going to rebuild the city over and over again on that 1 map which is why my playtime stuck at 60-70 hours for awhile before this mod support. In my opinion for the to take this long before adding mod and custom map support is a really big blunder move of this game. (bigger issue than performance)As for DLSS, when the game first come out the aliasing of building look really really bad, even at the native resolution. Back then the only way to fix this is either CAS scaling or TAA that was buried in advance option but both of them look too burry and in TAA case has horrible ghosting trail everywhere. With addition of DLSS, it fix all those aliasing even at the lower native res and make the game finally look good. This is a big reason why I recommend this game now. I wish they add support for FSR2 too, but since they already support DLSS I think it should be easy to use a external tool to insert FSR2 and XESS support to this game. Try it, I should make this game look much better.Add ability to turn off growable zone on the road, right now only workaround are either using path or using mod to make one side of the road become quay. It's rather annoying to not having building facing to the direction I want them to.Update building upgrade system, its has potential to be a good system but right now it's very limited and hard to fix. For example upgrade must be place at adjacent to original building only, I can't put it across the street which is rather anoying. If I can put upgraded across street and I have ability to remove only upgrade, it could open to more design I can use.
