_childDocuments_.review: -Carrion is a fun, well designed, game that is about ⅔ “puzzles” and ⅓ combat.-Controller is harder to control, but allows for twin stick style (move one way, interact another)-Can be 100%-ed in a single day. It’s really short.-The workshop has a custom campaign and a NG+ (new game plus) mode.-On sale it can be a good deal, but it's a bit too short to pay full price for.    Carrion is a fun, well designed, game that is mostly puzzle solving, partly combat, and story wise is compact, but perfect andThe puzzle solving is centered around dismantling the human's defences and moving your way through their facilities. The game gives you new abilities and then it teaches you the basics of your new toy. Over time you, the player, will learn new ways that your existing powers interact with the world. Once you see the unwritten ways your powers work, you’ll wonder “How didn’t I think of that before?”. It will seem so obvious, in retrospect. The combat plays a smaller part, time wise. The combat is very easy and you can brute force the combat for the first 60% of the game. Don't get me wrong, it's satisfying to tear half a dozen scientists and guards limb from limb in a matter of seconds. You really get to feel like an unstoppable murder machine. Eventually the combat does, ramp up a bit and you have to think critically about how to beat some encounters. Even with the rise in difficulty, successfully killing a room full of soldiers goes from feeling the joy of smashing pumpkins with a baseball bat, to the satisfaction of crafting the perfect warhammer, for smashing pumpkins.Spoiler tag, because I tagged it in the first paragraph.Carrion actually has, in my opinion, the perfect amount and layout of story for a game like this. The follows this basic flow:Seriously, this game is a lot of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Carrion is a unique experience.  You're just a writhing mass of tentacles, mouths, and hidden eyes.  You exist, you are suddenly where you are not supposed to be, people want to exterminate you, and you need to survive and get out.  No morals, no backstory, no quests.  A tempest must be.The gameplay is pretty linear.  You just move about in mostly one allowable direction, using your abilities to survive.  The more you branch out,t he more you uncover: new areas, new abilities, new perks, new buffs.  It's all a gradual progression with only the perks/buffs being "side quests".  Abilities are based around either exploration or combat.  The more you gain, the more you can do.  At times getting past an area requires you to "devolve" and lose access to higher abilities in order to use lesser ones you grew up with.  This sort of puzzle element is sprinkled around the game but never feels like too much.When you're not navigating around, you're in combat.  In a direct fight, you will lose quickly, especially with stronger enemy types or anyone with enough backup. Your early abilities focus on being small and sneaky. As you grow to the largest size, the odds dramatically shift in your favour.  By the end you are a terrifying monstrosity capable of mass death.The premise, visuals, mechanics, and progression are solid.  Where I find it comes up short is in navigation (no map at all), controls (very slippery until you adapt to them), and depth (creative uses fro the mechanics aren't as fleshed out as they could have been).  Length is just about right.. it took me about 5-6 hours to complete at my own pace without 100% completion.  Not much more to go back and polish it off.  There is also free expansion DLC included which I have jumped into but not gotten far... it may likely solve the problem of depth: it is far more puzzle-y, difficult, and varied in design.I recommend playing Carrion if any of what you see sparks your interest.  Full price is a little steep so weigh that with caution.  At less than $10 on sale, it fit the bill perfectly.  Once you've experienced it all, it's kind of done.  There is an editor but main game/DLC replayability is low.Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: Carrion is fantastic and original. From first appearances it looks fantastic. It plays fantastic. And finally as an end product its clever; most people would look at carrion and consider it a mince-a-thon of ultra-violence, but its actually a puzzle game at heart.There's so much to be said about carrion, but I will just say from the level design , to the music,  the art and atmosphere ,  everything seems to be really well executed.Don't forget the smooth gameplay too; and the odd gib shower. The game plays very nice and the UI is very good also.The game is intuitive, and does not restrict your gaming in anyway - its a breath of fresh air.What's more, you have many options to deal with the enemies, and in fact the most powerful weapons ones can be used against them - which is fantastic and so satisfying(When you get the skills!).As an omnivore careering though the tunnels of a grey existence, its also good to acknowledge that if you love those lovely meaty meat bags... Umm i mean humans, you can choose not eat ALL of them;  instead, only Eat those them if they light you on fire, shoot you and grind you up!  I felt guilty - but i blame the damn military!The end game can be a bit tedious however, as once you reach a point you will need to navigate back though the levels you have done to search I guess for hidden gubbins and eventually find your way to what is the end. It is easy to get lost, but its important to remember that (I spent a while snooping around at the end for collectables etc. ) - this is optional I suppose- but I got lost and so did it to get my bearings.In saying that , I get why some people complain about the price and the length, however the game is a labyrinth, and if you don't know what your looking for , your likely gonna be like me and find the main skills, then finally go back and  maybe look for the collectables.[NOTE: Workshop does exist and there are maps that are being added, so though I expect some of those maps to be  @%$£e, its at least possible to play the game past the single player vanilla campaign - or make your own if that's your cup of cheese]On a second play-through , it has also become very clear how it's very easy to stomp it, as oppose the first time pla‌ying; like any good puzzle game. Against that , the creativity and state of the game IMO is really unique and well done, so I think 10 quid is reasonable for this - if you are not broke, or generally like games ; I REALLY enjoyed BOTH my play - throughs!Played this previously on Xbox pass(PC) for 8-10 hours, finished and found everything.

_childDocuments_.review: Another amazing indie game added to my recommendation list. Carrion feels like such a simple concept on paper and it made me wonder why it took so long for someone to crack the code. Oh my, how the tables have turned. YES, YOU are the op boss villain mercilessly murdering every innocent scum in your path. But still...I agree quite diabolical. Don't worry they mentioned in the credits that no real humans were harmed. It's chill. Even though your character is a mindless killing machine, the game does manage to throw some interesting challenges, although once you unlock all the abilities, there's really nothing that can stand in your way. The core mechanics are so well designed and implemented, just traversing the levels using your prehensile limbs feels absolutely fluid and satisfying. The Metroidvania-style exploration with some minor puzzles and gut-wrenching (literally) combat scenarios are nailed to perfection. It's just a 4 hour game at max, but boy does it feel so wholesome in the end. It's a cliched and predictable plot but does enough to add that slight curiosity in you. Commendable level design using the environment to guide the player through the various convoluted regions of the lab without having the need to show a map. The only issue for me would be the nausea-inducing camera movement and the lack of enemy types and boss fights. Yes, you are the boss but would have been fun to fight a big-ass spider robot. Feels like a nitpick, to be honest. If you haven't played Carrion yet, I'd highly recommend it. It's undoubtedly a must-play. P.S. A symbiote-like creature that can shoot spider webs? Sounds very familiar hmmmm.....

_childDocuments_.review: Really stellar game. No matter the format of a game, one of the beautiful things good game design can do is make you take on the role of the character you embody. There is something about playing as Kratos or Master Chief that makes you feel like a badass. Well Carrion makes you feel like a disgusting, probing, undulating mass of gore straight out of a John Carpenter movie. The game rewards behavior that such a monster would perform; you need to get out of various stages, so you find ways intuitively. There are "levels" you sometimes have to attempt a few times but never did I feel like I needed to watch a letsplay or read a guide to crack some impossible code. With enough lunging about, using the various powers of the monster which you acquire over time, I explored every nook and cranny of a well-thought-out, visually impressive world. With a lack of dialogue and extremely minimal text on screen, you're left to sus out the world using your own tentacles. 10/10 this game knows what it is and knows what it wants to be and executes it perfectly.

_childDocuments_.review: Carrion : By Triple F"Carrion" is an indie gem that thrusts players into a spine-chilling, asymmetrical horror experience unlike any other. Developed by Phobia Game Studio and published by Devolver Digital, this game takes a bold leap into the unconventional, allowing players to become the nightmare itself. As you delve into the dark depths of this reverse-horror title, prepare to be both thrilled and horrified in a way that only "Carrion" can deliver.Set in a sprawling underground research facility, "Carrion" places you in the role of an amorphous, tentacled monstrosity with a single aim: to escape and unleash chaos upon the unsuspecting world above. What immediately sets "Carrion" apart is its reverse-perspective, turning the traditional survival horror genre on its head. No longer are you the prey, cowering in fear of lurking terrors – you are the predator, a relentless force of nature that grows stronger with each passing moment.The pixel art aesthetics of "Carrion" deserve a special mention. Despite its retro-inspired visuals, the game manages to create an incredibly eerie atmosphere, dripping with tension. The labyrinthine corridors, dimly lit rooms, and gory carnage are all brought to life with an impressive attention to detail. The animation of the titular creature is a highlight, as it squelches, stretches, and unfurls its gruesome form to navigate the environment in a truly unsettling manner.The game-play in "Carrion" revolves around mastering your unique abilities. From the start, you'll feel both powerful and vulnerable as you gradually gain access to an arsenal of gruesome tools. Your amorphous being can slink through vents, squeeze through tight spaces, and lash out with deadly tentacles to snare and devour your human prey. The controls, while a bit unconventional at first, quickly become second nature, allowing you to execute gruesome kills with precision.The level design is a mixed bag, offering a combination of intricate puzzles and intense chase sequences. While some areas encourage methodical exploration, others push you to use your agility and cunning to evade armed guards and security systems. The puzzles are generally well-designed, requiring a balance of strategic thinking and experimentation. However, there are instances where trial and error can feel frustrating, disrupting the overall flow.One of "Carrion's" minor flaws lies in its lack of a compelling narrative. While the premise is intriguing and the game's minimalist storytelling approach aligns with its retro sensibilities, a stronger narrative thread could have heightened player investment and motivation. That being said, the absence of an intricate plot doesn't detract significantly from the overall experience, as the game-play itself remains the central attraction."Carrion" also boasts a hauntingly atmospheric soundtrack that complements the game-play perfectly. The eerie ambient sounds and subtle musical cues enhance the tension and contribute to the overall feeling of dread as you navigate the claustrophobic corridors.All in all, "Carrion" is an electrifying journey into the unconventional, offering a fresh twist on the horror genre that fans of unique gaming experiences will relish. It's a testament to the creative potential of indie game development, delivering an immersive world, captivating mechanics, and a truly unforgettable role reversal. While a stronger narrative and some refining of level design could have elevated it even further, "Carrion" undeniably stands as a remarkable and nightmarishly fun title that dares to be different. If you're ready to unleash your inner monster and revel in a macabre adventure, "Carrion" should absolutely be on your radar.

_childDocuments_.review: A really cool unique take on a monster horror game, being the monster you find ways to have fun and recreate the gruesome kills that you usually see happen to yourself. _childDocuments_.review: Carrion is a short, yet incredibly entertaining experience.  There are too few games on the market which allow you to play the role of the monster, and I can say with confidence that Carrion allows you to engage in that role with confidence.  Whether you enjoy a bit of role-playing, are looking for a means to release some stress, or are looking to cause as much havoc as humanly possible, then Carrion is a no brainer.  The feeling of immense power as you stalk and disembowel your helpless prey somehow never grows old.The only real criticisms for the game is its length and endgame.  On your first playthrough, the game will probably take you anywhere between 3-5 hours, with subsequent playthroughs being around 2-3.  There also isn't much of an endgame other than trying to find all of the upgrades, which aren't really that necessary to complete the game.  Once you 100% the game once, you probably won't do it again.  Besides that, I don't have any issues with the game other than it's helped me discover that I may be psychotic and lack a deep sense of regret.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game to get on sale. It's unique, sometimes a little janky dealing with enemies, but otherwise good fun. 8/10. The only real complaint I have is it was way too short. I would've liked to see the game get developed into a longer title, or maybe a sequel that'll be at least 2-3x in length. Once you get proficient at the mechanics and puzzle-solving, it's over in a few hours. The extra holiday mission was a welcome extension, but was only an hour long. I finished the base game and the extra mission in a Saturday evening.The more minor complaint is the map got a little confusing after a while, and I had to find some guides for collecting some final achievements, because I had no idea how to reach the earlier zones once I was near the end. Clearing a level is relatively straightforward, and exploring the whole thing is somewhat of a requirement, because you need to hit all the "checkpoints" to open the door to the following zone, but the collectables were often blocked by tools/abilities you didn't have yet, in random parts of the level. So not only was it you had to go back to the previous zones after getting said ability, but you also had to navigate a majority of a level you hadn't seen for several hours to find the barred path again.Maybe this is more irritating than I thought, that I'm writing so long about it. Essentially, backtracking was a bit of a chore, and could've been done better. They had some exit signs for where the portals to next zones were, but the "hub" is a bit of a maze and you'll end up going in circles more often than you like. It would've been a simple thing to add more signposts or a mini-map. But the game is so short, this can be overcome in less than 20 minutes with a short guide.

_childDocuments_.review: Carrion is a "reverse horror" platformer (you play the monster) with puzzles and combat, but no jumping (you can move freely). It nails the atmosphere and provides smooth gameplay with several fresh ideas.You play as an amorphous mass of tentacles and teeth that has just broken out of its containment deep inside a military research facility. Throughout the game you will explore several areas of this facility, feed on humans, fight armed forces, and seek out well-guarded DNA samples that make you stronger and give you new abilities.Apart from 3 flashback scenes that let you relive previous events, that's all the story there is. You never find out what you are or how you came to be. While keeping things mysterious is not a bad choice for horror games, I believe that finding a few well-written notes, emails, or journals as a reward for exploration would have enhanced the experience.Nevertheless though, the devs nailed the "horror B-movie" atmosphere. The way you slither quickly through corridors and tubes, or how you lurk right next to a room of soldiers and plan your assault, feels unique and satisfying.The 3 main gameplay elements are puzzle-solving, combat, and exploration, which I'll address below.The game looks and plays similar to a 2D platformer, though there is no jumping involved. Your tentacles allow you to move quickly to any spot in a room, you can also hang from the ceiling. You move your mouse cursor on the screen and click on your destination - the game will then move you smoothly and quickly in that direction and automatically extend tentacles to support you. Controlling the monster felt amazing, it really captures the feeling of a powerful demonic entity slithering around. Contrary to other games that let you play a monster, but stick to traditional run-and-gun controls, the Carrion devs implemented a new, fresh control scheme that was designed around a character who can move lightning-fast, strike anywhere, wreck large pieces of furniture and throw them around, but can also hide just out of sight, sneak, and pick powerful enemies off one by one.Another fresh idea is the "body mass" mechanic. You discover various skills for offense, defense, or utility, such as throwing a web, sprouting temporary spikes, or crashing through barriers. Each of these skills can only be used if your body mass is within a given range. You can increase your body mass by feeding on humans, or by creating and revisiting a "hive" location that also acts as a save point. But for many puzzles, you'll need to apply abilities that require a lower body mass, so you'll also have to occasionally shed mass in pools of liquid.This body mass management is an integral part of the game's puzzles, which you often have to solve in order to progress further. Other puzzle elements involve switches, doors, water levels, and traps. I found them interesting and engaging, they also fit quite well into the setting. They are generally fairly easy, it never took me more than a few minutes to figure out a solution and I never needed to consult external resources.Let's address combat next. You can either engage in open fights, which are fast and visceral, or you can lurk in safety and pick enemies off piecemeal when they are vulnerable. Later on, you'll also develop a useful skill that lets you infect humans and control them, this includes using the weapons of any soldier you might have taken over. While you are very powerful and can kill most enemies quickly, their weapons can also cause a lot of damage if you don't get out of the way quickly. Some soldiers also have a shield that blocks any attacks from the direction they are facing.Combat is therefore often dangerous and feels quite intense, and my preferred tactic was to plan ahead while lurking in safety, and then striking fast according to the plan I had developed. Nevertheless, survival is pretty easy since you can usually retreat to the nearest hive and heal. Rooms do not reset when you leave them, so as long as you can kill at least one enemy between your retreats, you're making progress and that progress gets saved. There are, however, rooms that lock you in until you have killed certain groups of enemies, and these sometimes took several attempts with different strategies before I got through - but all in all, I found the game quite forgiving and the difficulty manageable.It's noteworthy that there are only 7 different enemies (not counting scientists who only run away), plus a "sticky bomb" type of trap. While that's not a lot, I liked that many enemies have different strengths and vulnerabilities and react differently to your various skills, thus giving you a reason to make use of your entire arsenal of skills. There are also no boss fights (which I appreciate as well).Finally, a word about exploration: The game consists of 9 different areas plus a large "main" area that connects them. The layout of the different areas is often convoluted, with lots of doors and barriers that block access, as well as tubes that move you around. I'm a fan of "oldschool" exploration and I appreciated that the game does not hold your hand or guide you, you'll have to master the complicated environment by yourself. That said, I can see this being a potential source of frustration for players who are used to compass markers and in-game GPS, as Carrion does not even give its players a map to orient themselves. If you belong to that group, you may want to consult Steam's guide section, where you'll find maps and walkthroughs.On a side note, the game is sometimes classified as a "metroidvania" due to fact that it takes place in a contiguous open world, and that you can backtrack to previous areas and apply new skills to find previously unattainable upgrades. While this isn't wrong, I'd consider this game a borderline case and would not use that term myself. The reason is that you're mostly just progressing through the areas in a linear fashion, and you can fully explore each area except one secret room that may require a skill that you don't yet have. While backtracking to that room later does give you a powerup, those are just increments to your stats, and you don't really need those to complete the game. All new _skills_ are guaranteed to be found at the end of their respective areas. If you explore each area thoroughly and don't need the extra power, then you never need to backtrack to previous areas.The game uses pixel graphics in a fairly low resolution, but the hand-drawn animations have enough frames to make movement look smooth regardless. The atmosphere is rather gritty, with blood splattering the walls and bodies being ripped apart, but the gore remains stylized and (in my opinion) never became egregious. The gore supports the game's atmosphere, it's not an end in itself.Sound effects and music are truly excellent. The sloshing sounds when you move around, the panicked cries of fleeing humans, and the dark, ominous orchestral music contribute a lot to the atmosphere.There is no voice-acting in the game apart from the aforementioned shouts and cries. I did not miss it.The game provides almost no options apart from a resolution selector, a fullscreen toggle, vsync, and separate volume controls for sound and music. As a game with 2D pixel graphics, it can get away with that, though more options wouldn't have hurt.Keyboard controls are fully rebindable, which I do regard as essential for a game with fast-paced combat action. A mouse sensitivity slider is unfortunately lacking.Saves can only be done at checkpoints, but those are usually less than 10 seconds away.I recommend Carrion to players who like 2D puzzle/action games with fresh ideas, and like the idea of playing a monster. It's a well-designed, polished, very enjoyable product.

What else can you do? Use your imagination!"The lack of a map is a bit tedious, but only lategame. _childDocuments_.review: This is an alright game, but ultimately it tipped the bar a bit to far into negative territory for a recommend.It's honestly pretty short and not much of a metroidvania. There are a few upgrades to find, but progression is very linear and the lack of a map makes it too much of a pain to backtrack and find the handful of extra goodies hidden in the environment. The game is a bit closer to something like Inside or Little Nightmares in terms of scope and progression, but unfortunately does not have the same skillful environmental storytelling and immersion those games did so well.The game also skews more towards being a finicky stealth game instead of a power fantasy, with your 'unstoppable apex predator' being easily obliterated by rent-a-cops with pea shooters.  Enemies can often sense you through walls or behind them and will throw up an impenetrable force field when they detect you, forcing you to run away and hide until their awareness resets. Due to the creature's large, irregular shape, movement is often clumsy, with the center of mass never seeming to be quite where you expect. You might go into this expecting to be a unstoppable killing machine, but you'll spend a lot of your time awkwardly humping wall vents, hoping you can shove yourself in there before mall security catches up to you.The aesthetic here is going to be down to personal taste, but for my part it actually makes me nauseous after a while. The creature seems pretty cool to look at in the beginning, but after a while it's irregular shape and movements just become disgusting to watch. It's not obscene or offensive, just thoroughly unpleasant to look at after a while, at least for me. Things aren't helped by the relatively bland environments and lack of memorable landmarks. Combine this with the lack of a map function and progress through the world can often feel directionless and monotonous. It took me less than four hours to beat this game, but I swear it felt twice as long, and not in a good way.If you decide to go for this one, maybe wait for a deep sale. It's certainly a unique game with an interesting perspective, but I just can't say I had much fun slogging through it. Your mileage may vary.
_childDocuments_.name: CARRION

_childDocuments_.review: As the game mentions, rather than being the prey, you play as the predator seeking to escape from containment underground. I would only recommend the purchase when Carrion is on sale as the game is too short and has one major flaw. Navigation. It's easy to lose track of locating discovered and undiscovered objectives as the game does not provide a map. You will get stuck. That's my biggest complaint, which other players have also shared. Memorize where you're going, or you must watch guides.Excluding the final enhancements given by the Containment Units, the powers never felt useless and definitely provided strategy (even in sections where it's not required). Overall, minus the navigation, the gameplay was an enjoyable and graphic experience.
_childDocuments_.name: CARRION

_childDocuments_.review: Upon making this review, I sat here for a long time debating on weather or not I should make this a thumbs up or a thumbs down.  I want people to know that just because I voted one way, it does not mean that the game is not worth the money.That being said, I can not condone the value of the game.  Worth the price? Sure, why not.  But *value* is not measured in money.  I have determined that the game is a very good template with a limited pallet of untapped potential.  The length of the game feels lazy and a simple money grab novelty.   I am not saying that game development is easy and I am not saying that everyone can deliver an epic saga of tireless content, and I am certainly not criticizing the team as a whole for the talents that they possess.  I am simply articulating that the value of the game is short changed by a lack of effort and design that could have been much better.Why do I say this?  Because here's the thing... the game's mechanics are unique and fun, the concept of playing the bad guy is a great idea, and the music is stellar on every level.  That means that the team involved with this have the capability to make this game longer, more dynamic, and alot deeper than what is presented.  For what ever reason, they stopped at a point where it feels like the game had just started... without spoiling the game, I will say that the ending feels like the start of something much bigger that never emerged from it's cocoon state.If the developed implied that the game will be worked on and expanded upon, I will change my tune greatly.  However, that does not seem the case and thus the negative review.6/10

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. Although it's a VERY bloody game the pixel graphics and sounds they used kept it from being over the top grotesque. _childDocuments_.review: The premise is pretty solid (you play the monster, trying to escape) and learn about what happened without much, if any, dialog. _childDocuments_.name: CARRION

_childDocuments_.review: Allows me to live my fantasies of being a monster in the ventilation shafts of an underground base, using clever tentacles to manipulate levers and absorbing DNA mutations from laboratory test tubes, pixels graphics style. Monster feel is smooth and natural using both Steam Deck or Keyboard/Mouse controls, they're both fun. It can get challenging at times, but eventually a way forward presents itself using the progression of abilities.
_childDocuments_.name: CARRION

_childDocuments_.review: Reverse horror is hard to do well, and so are horror puzzle games, but this game surpassed all expectations. Though you play as the monster, the defences the scientists have as well as their "kill on sight" mentality makes it much easier to see things from the monster's point of view. Each puzzle and fight has multiple solutions, and the puzzles are difficult without being "I want to destroy my computer" levels of frustrating. I also love that you get a power increase from getting containment units rather than it being a meaningless thing just to get the achievement like most games. Not to mention the unique mechanic of having different abilities based on your character's size, which I've never seen in any other game ever. Plus the way the levels are laid out make it so that there aren't a lot of ways to totally get stuck, and if you do totally get stuck the save points are in convenient locations. The one flaw is I do wish it was easier to move between levels. Other than that it's perfect, never ever change a thing, 10/10 would play again and again and again.
_childDocuments_.name: CARRION

_childDocuments_.review: It's not quite a puzzle game, nor a metroidvania or an action game.  It's a little bit of all these things but ultimately is just a game about being a hideous slob of deadly biomass chewing your way through an underground complex of hapless soldiers and scientists and you grow larger, deadlier and more tooled out for traversing the waterways, pipes and hallways in the facility.The sounds are great too.
_childDocuments_.name: CARRION

_childDocuments_.name: CARRION

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game, but with a caveat - it's extremely short, the 5 hours I spent on it contains around 2 hours of running around and looking for passages to get the last two upgrades. The game is definitely missing a more engaging end-game and official custom level support. It's got a very basic but still interesting story, very nice pixel art graphics (but you can see those clearly in the videos and pictures on the store page already, right? ;) ). Now - the mechanics of being the monster are quite awesome, I must say I enjoyed the systems that were put in this game. I wish there was more to all of it.Just to sum it up in one sentence:I recommend to get this game in a bundle, or on sale, play through it and just have some mindless fun, do not expect a complex reverse-horror-story game, it's more of a simple puzzle action game.BTW. I got the game as birthday gift, so technically - for free. :)

_childDocuments_.review: Just play it. It's short, I've 100% completed it in 7 hours and finished the game regularly in quite a bit less. This game does a truly magnificent job of making you feel like a force of nature; something unstoppable, something powerful, something truly terrifying. _childDocuments_.review: Do you ever feel like an amorphous sack of organs that's barely in control of its own existence, lost in a great big world and just trying to survive while people shoot guns at you?Okay, maybe not that last one, but it turns out I have a lot in common with a giant blob of murder meat.It's not a long game, but it's very enjoyable for what it is. The reactions of the NPCs are suitably panic-stricken, and the more power-ups you gain the more you really start to feel like an unstoppable wrecking ball of horror. Sometimes it can be hard to control your murderous appendages, but it actually feels in character to not be wholly in control of your flailing.On the downside, the lack of a map becomes really confusing, especially late in the game when you're trying to track down all the upgrades. _childDocuments_.review: Right off the bat, I'm going to say that I absolutely adore this game. My only con is that it's too short, as it took me around three and a half hours to complete. Maybe it's better off that way, though; better than being too long I suppose. CARRION is a game where YOU are the monstrosity wreaking havoc on humanity, YOU are the element of horror in this game. This is my first time ever playing a reverse horror, and it makes me sad that there aren't more reverse horror games out there. I love everything about this game: the music, the graphics, the design of the monster, I love it all. The story is told without dialogue (aside from the descriptions of things you can check in flashbacks) and I prefer it that way. You as the player get to interpret the story without it telling you anything, and I really liked that. I loved starting off small and becoming bigger, growing into something even more monstrous as before. The music and the atmosphere of the game really make you feel like the antagonist too, especially as you attack defenseless humans that cower before you. I cannot stress enough how much I loved playing this game, and I can't wait to see what else the devs make in the future. I'll definitely be looking for more reverse horror games to play as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Carrion is so much fun. It is a nice deviation from the classic survival horror game where you actually play as the monster or villain rather than some poor helpless human. The 8-bit graphic style just further proves the fact that games don't have to be in ultra HD and real-life graphics to be good.  Personal Score: 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: You like pulling people into a vent to eat them? You can do that.You wanna slam them against a wall? You can do that.You fancy drowning them inside water? You can do that.You desire ripping them apart with needle shaped tentacles?YOU CAN DO THAT.You're this spaghetti looking thing with those predator worm teeth trying to escape this lab that goes from underground, into a cave, forest and even literally in a skyscraper looking at the city landscape. So close, yet so far...The music in the game changes tensity based on what the human NPCs experience. If you're in a vent, just that eerie I-don't-wanna-die noises in the background. Once someone with a gun spots you, the music goes all dramatic until they're either dead or you went around the corner like the bowl of coward noodles that is your character.The game, however short, is somewhat of a a metroidvania; you unlock new abilities that unlock new areas or routes. An important note I should add: The ability locks that pretty much every metroidvania has, is hard to notice when you play the game. So there is basically no clutter when you roam around the facility. The game also makes you follow a route that 'automatically' puts you where you need to be. You'll be backtracking without even realizing it.The only downsides I can see is that once you run off of that route, it's hard to get back on it and, as former mentioned, the game is short. Some options to extend your playtime is to grab all the achievements (which is actually easy) or access the workshop and check out some community made maps.

_childDocuments_.review: So first things first about Carrion, the game is a bit higher price than what I'd recommend but I really appreciate the game for what it is. At the end of the day depending on how well you progress through the game it will take between 4-6 hours to complete, that is the only reason why I say the price tag is a good bit too high.Moving on to the gameplay, Carrion is absolutely at its core a Metroidvania game where instead of getting equipment to progress through the levels and barriers you grow and gain new grotesque abilities to tear, break, and rip your way forward. Its weirdly satisfying at a primal level where you get to inflict carnage as this mindlessly rampaging biomass. There were many times during the game I got mildly frustrated thinking that I had just progress locked myself by accident and would need to reload in order to actually continue. But then after a bit of looking around it seems the dev team had actually made sure that there is no way you can accidentally block yourself in without very much deliberately trying to do so, even then I wouldn't say it would be easy to do so. On the downside sometimes I found myself looking around wondering, "ok what do I do know?", as a progression map might be a helpful addition to those without good direction finding.As for combat the game's combat goes between easy and brutally punishing but in a weirdly well designed way. Yes you can tank your way through the gunfire to shred and devour your foes but it isn't nearly as efficient as playing the creature as an ambush predator, which it definitely seems to be designed as such. Regardless the game gives you the ability to do both methods at your discretion, though sometimes you clearly should do one over the other.So... the story. Not sure if you could tell but the story could be described as, you are raging biomass of tentacles, mouths, and soon to be various other deadly weapons KILL EVERYTHING. Beyond that the one sentence descriptions, if even that, for the abilities get a higher word count than the actual 'story' does. Which is rightfully so, the game set out to be a simple short story about a blood thirsty lab-experiment gone wild, and it did just that. The ending gave me a cool little gasp shock, but nothing more.All-in-all Carrion is a fun little game that set out to be a specific game and really nailed it. If you are concerned with money I would say wait for it to go on sale. Otherwise its a good grab for the 4-6 hours it would last you.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty unique and fairly entertaining,  is a game where you're a monsterous (presumably alien) creature that has escaped containment in what I can only describe as a ; the game has some optional backtracking, but is for the most part very linear. If you're interested in playing as an off-brand xenomorph from  or are looking for a fairly unique, short experience it'll probably be worth your time. I feel like this is one of those games where you'll only "love" it if you're interested in the core premise to begin with.'s gameplay and controls are pretty simple, with the majority of the game spent moving around and laying waste to humans. The "creature" (I'll just refer to it as "the Carrion") has multiple abilities that are acquired through the course of the game (roughly 6 hours) that are tied to size. There are three sizes for the Carrion, and each size has two size-specific abilities. Size is lost by being damaged or leaving "biomass" in pools for later recovery, and it can be gained by going to a save point or consuming slain, unarmored humans. There are a few other abilities, but with the game's length spoiling those ruins a little bit of the fun.The game isn't particularly difficult and has no difficulty settings. While it wasn't  much of a problem, there is no map in this game, meaning that getting lost can (and probably will) happen to some degree. There is also a notable lack of "help", so if you need a reminder on what something is, or how to use something, you'll have to figure it out. On the positive side of things, the ambiance and design of the Carrion is very well done, and the overall "feel" of the Carrion's abilities match expectations. There are some very fun moments in the game, and  ultimately is a power fantasy game about being an unbelievably powerful piece of nightmare fuel, which ends up being pretty fun though unchallenging.I had fun, but the shortcomings definitely started to pile up by the end. Some of the "containment" rooms ended up just being one-room non-puzzles, which is disappointing. The game also dangerously approaches "repetitive" by the end, and the game lacks any sort of difficult combat challenges or "boss" encounters. The majority of the appear falls squarely on the shoulders of the main "gimmick": playing as the "villain" which happens to be an extremely powerful meat creature. I think the game is good (for me), but it would greatly benefit the current game to have some additional expansion. Finally, for the devs:  Current defensive abilities, aside from the first one for the smallest form, are underwhelming; the second defensive ability doesn't even have a puzzle built around it, unlike the other two (both have several "puzzle" uses). Even worse, most of the optional upgrades are related to increasing the amount of energy available for these lackluster abilities. Cloak is the only one that feels like it has use outside of puzzles. There needs to be more variety in combat, and more opportunities for difficult combat scenarios; several enemy types in this game occupy the same narrow combat roles and thus combat can feel repetitive toward the end. This feeling is reinforced during the ending sequence. A "boss" encounter or event would be an acceptable compromise to diversifying the roster's roles. More emergent gameplay designs need to be in here. There should be more opportunities for traps, there should be more ways to sneak around, and there should be incentive for sneaking. More interaction with the environment would be a welcome addition, and there are plenty of opportunities for that in an update, dlc or sequel. The size mechanic needs more granularity. The health "bar" should be more akin to some sort of percent-based health bar. The bulb-body approach works okay, but toward the end of the game the design favored extremely long body compositions, so the Carrion ended up being about three-quarters of my screen in length. It would be better if the Carrion's shape was more like a blob (even a mostly oblong one) than a daisy chain, as there would be fewer situations where a sticky bomb hits the last rung of your body and still somehow instantly kills you. This would make more sense if your body was a slightly tighter form.

_childDocuments_.review: The sound effects absolutely seal the deal on the experience of playing as a monstrous fleshy blob-creature on the hunt for human prey, in Carrion, in between listening to people screaming or devouring their parts, this game is awesome. _childDocuments_.review: Basically lives up to the premise. You are a horror movie monster, and sneak around killing and eating people. The focus in combat is stealth, and you will rarely win a fight against any but the easiest enemies without using it. You gain a whole slew of iconic horror monster abilities, both offensive and defensive, which are fun to use. Controls feel fluid and fun, if a bit imprecise, though they can be a bit frustrating with the largest size monster (especially underwater).One neat feature is that the slew of abilities available to you changes as you gain/lose health; all 3 states are needed for puzzles and have their own use in combat (though in general the biggest form is way more powerful than the others in a fight). All puzzles that require a smaller form helpfully have pools nearby that you can use to temporarily shrink.The game is rather short (took about 5.5 hours to beat with more than half the hidden collectibles and to finish the the free Christmas DLC, and that's including time spent getting lost). But that's more because it moves quickly than a lack of content, and it's a unique experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Carrion is a game all about playing a monstrous abomination. You will track, hunt and completely annihilate your prey, as you break out of imprisonment.The movement system for your creature feels so fluent. You instantly zip back and forth to any surface seamlessly, and you really feel unstoppable. The situations the game allows you to take advantage of are genuinely terrifying, even if you are actually the monster. Pulling enemies around corners, throwing doors at people, eating their legs, and covering people in web all feels so cinematic and fluid.I think the game struck a perfect balance between giving you moments of feeling like an unstoppable, terrifying creature that rips and tears through all people and walls, while at the same time slowing you down in sections with more heavily armed guards.A lot of guards have stronger weaponry, like flamethrowers that force you to seek water, or energy shields that block a frontal attack.The game feels like a metroidvania, although there isn't much emphasis on backtracking. You will however, be constantly evolving, and earning new abilities that help you traverse to the next location, or deal with those pesky guards I mentioned.Interestingly, depending on your size, you will have access to different abilities.For example, at your smallest size, you can shoot out a cobweb, which can be helpful with trapping those guards from behind their shield.Or, if you're a bit bigger, you trade in that cobweb ability for a powerful charge that destroys any enemies and weak wooden walls in your path.As you take damage, you'll shrink down to the smaller size. On the other hand, if you eat your victims, you'll gain health and grow bigger.These abilities and sizes come in to play while exploring too. In between "combat" sections, you will traverse the labs, and solve short puzzles. I thought these were the perfect length, and didn't detract from all the killing that the player is no doubt itching for.You will infrequently have to play as a human for 1-2 minute sections that reveal a bit of the backstory. Again, luckily they were just short enough not be too tiresome, while at the same time feeding you a bit of intrigue.The game doesn't have a map, which I do think is a downfall and can lead to some frustration. It's not too bad, but there were 2 or 3 times where I got lost for a solid 10 minutes, but eventually found my way.Overall, I really, really love the game. The movement and killing mechanics just feel so intuitive, and make for seriously cool moments. I thought the game's difficulty was just right. You are forced to be creative with some harder enemies, while others can just be your toys to play with. The aesthetic, music and sound really add to the atmosphere. I've since 100%ed and gotten all the upgrades, so as you can imagine, I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: CARRION

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting concept and fun all the way through, it's exactly what it says in the tin. It's a metroidvania at its core, and many people point out the lack of a map as a big barrier to navigation, but the areas aren't particularly large, and exploration feels rewarding enough.The only negative this game has is the length: many late-game abilities have a lot of potential depth, but are barely explored, with only a few rooms where you're required to use them. But then again, mod tools are available, and there's a community-made campaign up in the workshop already, and I'm sure there's more to come.

_childDocuments_.review: CARRION (has to be in caps, no excuses) is a fairly short, but unique game, in which you take on the role of a sentient Spaghetti Monster that is on a quest for revenge against humanity, as we have mercilessly devoured its brethren for years on end. There's a bit of nuance to the story, but nothing that's too difficult to understand without a basic understanding of horror storytelling. Think 'The Thing', but from the perspective of the titular Thing.Are you an absolute psychopath with no sufficient outlet for your unending need to express your rage through violent, bloody murder? Well, this is the game for you! Your primary goal is to escape. Your other primary goal is to C O N S U M E every human you encounter. By doing so, you gain biomass, rendering you more resistant to death, which can happen very quickly in this game. As the game progresses, you also gain new abilities, as well as new, horrific ways to brutally kill your enemies and turn them into readily-consumable chunky salsa.Right off the bat, you can employ the classic consumption technique, grabbing a screaming, flailing human with your prehensile tentacle and dragging them into your waiting maw, severing them at the waist (or at the neck with a bit of finesse) with a single bite. But that quickly gets boring, and a bit impractical when the humans start trying to kill you in return. So instead of devouring that screaming, flailing human, you can use them, or any other pieces of debris, as a weapon. Your Spaghetti Monster is easily strong enough to dismember humans with sheer kinetic force, be it by hitting them with an object (including another human!) or by slamming them into a wall.If you want to play around, there are plenty of sections with vents or waterways, all of which encourage an ambush playstyle. You can hide in a vent, roar to taunt an oblivious soldier into running beneath an opening, before unleashing your inner Xenomorph and dragging them up into the vents with you. In certain situations, you can even pull vent covers out from beneath humans, causing them to fall into your lap and giving you ample time to C O N S U M E. This game is very open with how you murder your way through a room.As you gain abilities, you can really start to have some fun. Is there one soldier who just doesn't want to come out of his corner? Well, you can turn invisible and sneak up behind him, or combo invisibility with a web shot, pinning him to the ground and completely disabling him. Unfortunately, you can't eat soldiers (ew, Kevlar!), but you can perform a brutal grab-n-shake execution to put them down for good. Since they can't be eaten, their corpses make for excellent blunt weapons. I won't reveal some of the REALLY fun abilities though... I'll leave that to you.Fair warning, there is a bit of puzzle solving in this game, but this isn't Portal. You shouldn't need to look up any guides for the puzzles, but one little ♥♥♥♥♥♥ I have is that there's no map. You can potentially get lost for a while as you loop around the map, trying to find a place where you can use your latest ability. Still, aside from that, CARRION is an excellent outlet for when the red mist descends...
_childDocuments_.name: CARRION

_childDocuments_.review: A short, novel game where you play as this cute creature unfairly held against it's will deep underground in some secret lab.My favourite part of this game is the locomotion. It's so cool just watching how you actually move about in this game. They put a lot of effort making the weight and the suspension feel not only right but also easy to control. The controls are pretty easy to handle and everything just flows into place. At least until you grow large, then movement starts to feel a bit cumbersome as you kind of just clumsily flop your mass around. Still good to be big, though, as your abilities will generally be more powerful and you're more resistant to enemy attacks and traps. While a little annoying at times, it does really make you feel as this huge lumbering  creature.The lack of a map bugs me a bit, though, especially since the map layouts tend to be fairly abstract without much variation in how the corridors look. Especially when you are making that late-game lap to grab all the secret containment chambers.I'm also a bit bothered how you have to keep using these sort-of-conveniently placed pools of toxic waste to switch your size from large to small. I get what they're trying to do with offering some gameplay variety depending on your size, but outside of a few moments it just felt like an unneccesary hassle just to open some path.Not as tight as the demo (which featured very different levels, and included in the game) but still a pretty good experience where you can play something that isn't humanoid.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun but way too short for the price. I have 4.7 hours but that includes an hour or so when I went to go eat something. Get it if it drops to like £8* in a sale.*EDIT* Just to expand a little on the original review.*Amended to £8 from £5 after thinking about my time spent with this gameLike I said previously, it is a fun game but the length is severely lacking in my opinion. For the short amount of time I spent with the game, it wasn't tedious in the least. In fact I was ready for more by the time I made it to the final evolution. One thing that I had been hoping for during the majority of my playthrough, was when you escape, you would actually get to go around the city you see in the background on certain levels, just destroying and devouring everything in your path with a possible last stand against a military, but you don't. The ending itself isn't bad but isn't something special either. It's probably more my own fault for having a certain expectation for the game, but that kind of sequence could have left a better impression on me. When I first got the upgrade, I was  excited thinking about how I could use the ability to  and wreak some more havoc on the facility in some other ways. Instead there's just a minute of traversing a few more screens and then the end credits roll.I think a 4 - 6 hour campaign length is fine for a game, provided it can offer something on repeat playthroughs and depending on the price, but the only reason I could see someone giving it a second go would be to unlock the 9 optional upgrade chambers. I wasn't aware of these until I was already quite close to the end of the game and only unlocked one, so I can't really comment on how much usefulness they add or if they make the game any easier. I managed to finish the game just fine without them , so they're not necessary unless you want to unlock all of the achievements. Since the level design is relatively open, this might actually have been a way to reward players who remembered an obstacle in an earlier section of the game that they couldn't break through due to not having a specific upgrade but could also just be seen as padding.Some people have said that the game itself needs a map, which I don't wholly agree with. Considering how fast you move throughout the map and the nature of the game, it'd be a little jarring to have a map that you would be able to open on a moments notice, but perhaps it could have been added within the game world itself. At the start of each "stage" there's a giant billboard that tells you how many chambers and hulls/doors have been breached. The map itself could have been built into this billboard, which would make sense in the game world since I think even employees at this facility would be confused on how to reach different areas of the map. Or the sonar ability (left shift) could've been changed or had a possible unlockable upgrade to show a kind of fuzzy looking map of the surrounding areas as an overlay. I didn't need to use the sonar ability all that much, since I never really felt lost except for one of the small underwater sections where I didn't notice a one way tube. The game itself was a pretty smooth experience for me.The mandatory unlocks themselves are fine for the most part. Some can be great fun in combat, like shooting a volley of harpoons, dragging them back and splitting them in half in the process. The charge attack is fun to use bursting out of vents into unsuspecting victims and using the mind control parasite to take control of a human to either shoot guns, flamethrowers or jump in a mech and destroy everything within range is extremely satisfying. These are the most standout abilities for me, because they've got a viable use in combat as well as unlocking extra paths allowing you to carry on with the game.Other upgrades are a little underwhelming and only really serve as a way to progress instead of adding to your arsenal. The invisibility at the first bio mass level is used to get through motion lasers that would close doors or alert people to your presence. You can use it to sneak around briefly but it requires energy that quickly depletes and the punishment for being caught is rarely even a threat since most times you can just hide in a corner until everyone deaggros and forget you were a thing. Pretty much every section of this game has one of these hiding places that even flying enemies struggle to get to since they tend to bounce off of surfaces like ping pong balls, the only exception being the drones but at biomass level 1, you can just use the "web shot" ability (on E) to temporarily disable one and bash the group with the remains. Failing that, if a group of drones is closing in on you, you can just use the web shot to disable them one by one fairly quickly and pick them off in a pretty safe manner. The web shot is a decent addition but probably could have done with a cooldown of sorts. The first time I came across drones, I was being chased around a room where there were no real hiding places and you're forced into biomass level 1 beforehand, so it's quite intimidating. I spent about 5 minutes on that section trying to separate the drones and take them out one by one, attacking them head on and this was quite exhilarating. I died and had to redo this one section. I tried using the web shot and it completely trivialised the entire encounter. All I had to do was stand still in a vent and wait for them all to come at me so I could just web shot them.The shield ability at bio mass level 3 and the worms are basically just ways to unlock puzzles and progress. The shield itself is kind of pointless to use in encounters, since you have so much healthy anyway, and the harpoon ability wrecks almost anyone within range, provided they've not got a shield up. Since most of the game is about ambush tactics, I didn't have any use for the shield at all and I don't think anyone else would, aside from progressing through the facility. The spikes ability at biomass level 2, I have no idea what they do. I tried to use them on all enemy types but I didn't see any difference between using the spikes and the charge ability. I was able to take out mechs just fine with the charge ability and ambush tactics and I would even use the charge ability with the spikes for the extra movement speed. I did write a bit about the story but seems I hit the character limit with it. In short, I didn't find it added much to the game at all. . In short, I think of these sections as a little bit of a breather from the constant mayhem that you cause, but also feels like padding since they don't really add much to what's going on, there are breaks from the mayhem already with the light puzzle solving you already do,  and as I mentioned earlier, the ending isn't anything special and even a little anti-climatic. I played the demo before release and really liked what was on offer. Since the demo has a different layout, it's possible that the organism in that is the one alluded to in the flashback sequences, but I wasn't looking for any story in the demo, or in this game. As an absolute worst case scenario, if I spent 10 minutes each on these sections individually, then that's about 10% of my *recorded* game time on Steam. As I mentioned before, I'd left the game running for an hour or so while I went to go eat.That said, the demo is a really good representation and it doesn't actually spoil anything in the game, aside from some of the unlocks. With all that said, Carrion is by no means a bad or mediocre game. It does have flaws and I would be interested in a follow-up game, possibly with different organisms to choose from with their own unique unlocks. I just won't be rushing to spend £17 on it as I did with this.

_childDocuments_.review: -Aesthetically, CARRION is wonderful. The pixel art is gorgeous, the music feels like a horror soundtrack in all the right ways, the sound effects are suitable grotesque, it's all around a good package.-Movement is a joy, full stop. I think we all came to watch that blob of flesh zoom and bounce around, and I can happily report that  it's as wonderful to play as it is to watch. Things can get a little messy towards the end of the game as you grow in size, but 99% of the time I had no problems with the controls.-Mechanics are interesting and varied, with each 'tier' of size/health giving you access to different abilities. A lot of the most interesting puzzles revolve around strategically dropping off and picking up your biomass, or around the late game mechanic that lets you control certain enemies to press switches for you and so on. If you're a hardcore puzzle nerd, you probably aren't picking this game up for the puzzles, but there's a decent smattering of them, and they range from fairly effortless to tricky enough to make you feel clever when you finally figure them out.-Combat itself is a blast, chewing through enemies, picking them up and thrashing them around, hitting them with objects,  etc. There's a certain joy in using the level geometry to get the drop on your opponents as well, or clever use of your abilities. You die surprisingly fast if you're not careful, which I don't really mind, at least in the beginning. Later on, though, the game starts throwing larger groups of enemies at you in more open spaces, and I often found myself struggling to engage them without getting overwhelmed, with relatively few opportunities to pick one or two off and retreat before taking damage. I might have liked somewhat more detailed stealth mechanics, a few more tools to let me sneak around and pick off enemies. Also it took me like, 30 minutes to figure out that you're supposed to cobweb the drones and I'm still not over it.-Level design is actually really good. The game has no map, but for the most part this isn't an issue. The game makes heavy use of one-way paths and the like to guide you through the vast majority of the game. From what I can tell, the game is basically divided into a hub area (the Frontiers) and various facilities with the powerups and fights and so on, but the game is laid out such that this only really becomes apparent at the end, when you get an opportunity to revisit all of the old areas to pick up collectibles.  Backtracking is simplified by the fact that you reenter each area from where you exited, rather than going in the way you came, which usually puts you pretty close to that area's collectible. Still, by the time I'd wrangled the last collectible, I'd more or less forgotten where to go to progress the story again, and finding it took more than a few minutes. At that moment, I WOULD have really liked a map.-There's a fairly minimal backstory, told in playable human-form flashbacks. Honestly, I think they detract from the feeling of the game, just because the human you control is so slow compared to the sheer speed of the main character.  There's a little bit of puzzle solving, but for the most part it's just walking and waiting. I don't know that playing them added anything. Nonetheless, they get the point across. Sketchy science people dug up organism and took samples, organism is pissed now.-The ending is.... abrupt? It's well built up to, and then it just sort of ends, and it's very open ended. Some people probably like that, some people hate it, I'm not quite sure where I stand on it.-Replay value is probably nonexistent. 5 hours is probably about as much time as you can spend on it, maybe 6. Overall: it's just 5 hours, but it's a very good 5 hours. If you're looking for something to spend a lot of time on, CARRION is probably not for you. If you want a really good experience, don't mind it being 5 hours, and have 20 bucks to spare, I'd strongly consider picking up this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, the best thing about the whole game is the animated trailer.I was a little disappointed in the game, and I think it's because expected a bit too much. Let me explain.I was hoping the game would have a sort of "The Thing" vibe, where I'd be able to outsmart and sneak up on scientists and guards, slowly overtaking a facility. Instead, it feels more like a run and gun, but without any gunning, and a lot of just ramming into people.There are also just be some occasional mandatory busy work parts of the game when you play as a human, and you slowly walk/run around completing very small tasks to progress the story.I dunno. It was pretty boring in comparison to what I had hoped the game would be. That being, an intelligent creature rampaging throughout a facility and overtaking the guards and scientists, as stated before.I couldn't even try and get into the mindset of an evil thing, set on toying with its prey. The moment any person without a gun saw me, or heard me, they just ran around screaming, and then crouched into a corner. No attempting to fight back, just, freeze. If you expected what I expected out of the game, I wouldn't recommend it. Maybe look into some gameplay footage and then see if you're down.

_childDocuments_.review: awesome game! its short, but really, if it was a whole lot longer, i think it would feel drawn out. so good on the dev team for making it the length it is! simple game, simple story, a little bit of a challenge/puzzle solving which was enjoyable. if youre after a shorter game where you get to play as the monster, get it! as everyone else said, its kinda like "The Thing" where you play as the thing.

_childDocuments_.review: A short but very original Metroidvania lite. Took me about 4 hours to 100% it. There is only one secret per stage and the puzzles are usually pretty easy, two or three took me a minute to figure out but the rest were pretty straight forward, use the ability you just unlocked in a couple different ways. Progression is pretty good, you get abilities quite often and early on you have to be careful in fights while at the end you can usually destroy everything using all your abilities without too much thinking.I encountered no glitch or any problem beside sometimes getting stuck a bit moving around when too big. Most of the time moving around with the mouse is very satisfying, you feel like a "tentacle" monster, Graphics are great, sound and music are minimal but good and fit the setting. I found it quite easy, it's easy to die but you quickly get multiple ways to tackle an encounter and save point are plentiful.I recommend it but on sale because of how short it is.

_childDocuments_.review: I AM SHOGGOTH (well the closest thing to that) AND I WILL CONSUME THE FLESH AND BLOOD OF ALL THOSE WHO WRONGFULLY IMPRISONED ME!!!!Jokes aside, another game to unleash my anger on humanity by becoming the monster and eating everyone. It's easy to get lost in this game though and ♥♥♥♥ those guys with the electric shields and flamethrowers, that's my only complaint,
_childDocuments_.name: CARRION

_childDocuments_.review: So while Carrion isn't a bad game it certainly isn't spectacular either.As a small game which is a bit of fun where you get to be a cool monster with cool abilities, it's great.The art style, the general gameplay loop and the vague story are all good and make the game good enough to pick up on a sale.The bad things make it not worth it to get at full price. The main issue is backtracking without a map. While mostly it's just for 100% there are one or two times where you need to backtrack for the story. The problem is no map, it is really annoying to try and go back to a specific area you know you missed something when you have no idea where it is.Something I only found out in the last hour or two of the game is that the Hub world and the actual levels are completely separate, there is a point quite early in the game that makes it seem as if getting to the next level requires you to find the entrance to it in a previous level, but that is not the case. This might have been obvious in hindsight but I managed to miss it.Overall it can be pretty fun but if I had bought the game instead of getting it as a gift I might have liked it quite a bit less.

_childDocuments_.review: A game like skyrim is a buffet. Lots to eat, maybe the chicken is dry, but the mash and sausages are great.Carrion is something special. _childDocuments_.review: The premise in  is simple. You're meat. You eat. With such a concept, you'd assume there's not much else to the story, and yet there's a few surprises waiting for the unprepared.In  you play as a toothy mass of flesh, eyes and tentacles. For lack of a better name, let's call it . Creative name, I know.You start out in captivity and have to break out. Tiny, but not at all defenseless. The monster is a veritable killing machine from the get go, and the action never lets go. There's a problem though, and that's the fact that meat isn't particularily resistant to bullets, fire, or what have you. But it makes up for it by being a great electrical conductor, apparently.The monster moves around fluidly, guided by the mouse in a point and click fashion. Hold left click to wherever you want to move and off ya go.The fact that you have to move in such a way makes the monster's size have more weight when it comes to gameplay (pun not intended).A smaller monster can move around swiftly and hide more easily, but larger forms with their increased combat capabilities might have a harder time moving around tight spots.If videogames were food joints, then  would be an All-You-Can-Eat Buffet. And what you can't eat, you can at least bite like chewing gum or use it to tenderize meat. And this is a very good thing! As luck would have it, a well fed monster is a healthy monster. So get to eating your proteins and chew up that biomass to keep your health up.If you previously played  rest assured, while this might not have much in common with that action fest, it keeps the spirit of it alive.Instead of shooting you're now hunting, so a more stealthy approach might be in order.Instead of a chainsaw, you have tentacles and teeth, Instead of guns, you gain new abilities. Adapt and overcome. But be forewarned! If you bleed they can kill you. The monster is a glass cannon of the highest order and will die relatively easy to most attacks if you don't play it smart. is simply magnificent to look at. The way the monster moves, the pixelart environments, the colors and lights. If you enjoyed the gritty industrial look of something like , then this game  won't disappoint either.The monster moves fluidly and the various fleshy parts of the environment twitch and move around as if they're constantly pulsating. It really gives the biomass the impression of being alive.As for enemies, they have simple movement and patterns but it's always fun to see them panic and try to run.Overall the big moving parts like doors and such never fail to look convincingly mechanical.So in terms of visual presentation, the game passes with flying colors.The game is really entertaining for metroidvania fans and newcomers to the genre alike. It never felt too unfair or punishing, and some areas really feel more like puzzles than a stealth game at times.The main criticism I'd have to make to the game is that it's frankly a great experience while it lasts, but too short.I'm writing this review after getting 100% completion of achievements and beating the Christmas DLC, clocking in at 7 hours, so make of that what you will.If you decide to look past that issue, the game turns out to be a frankly unique and memorable experience that'll stick with you for years to come.

_childDocuments_.review: Expertly executed 2D horror game! The art style is brutally detailed and animated, and lends itself perfectly to this style of game. The puzzle-like style of combat can be a little overwhelming, but is very rewarding learning how to deal with different enemy types. Level design in Carrion is extremely well done, heaps of detail was put into every nook and cranny. One small gripe I have with this game is the movement. It can feel a little imprecise when in some of the tighter areas in levels but is overall a pretty small problem. Carrion is a relatively short game, between 4-6 hours, but it is consistently good through out the entire experience. Worth every penny!

_childDocuments_.review: Fine horrors are lacking nowadays. To my recollection, the last worthy one was Alien Isolation.So whenever something half-decent comes out it's already an event. CARRION is full feature reverse horror single player experience, where you as a player take control of a monster to destroy all humans and break free from the captivity. This is quite original - I don't remember any single player reverse horror whatsoever. But apart from being innovative this look and feel good! For indie title for sure.The gameplay delivers expected amount of fun and the game manages to keep the pace more or less giving new tools and the ways to keep a player engaged for the most part of the game.The score is very much appropriate for this kind of game.There are two drawbacks which I see: replayability and map navigation. This ain't that indie title that you can replay for 30 times with lengthy playtime per every playthrough. I finished it in 7 hours to get 100%. There is zero replay value. But to be honest, this would probably hurt this game with available amount of content, at some point the game becomes repetitive without any injections of new so you just drag through the local story to the end.To the second. Several times I found myself lost in this map without any proper navigation mechanism in place so I had to resort to lets plays to find where should I go. This is especially irritating if you want to back track in order to collect everything for 100%. This isn't a deal breaker if you ask me but it's without doubt a massive flaw and something to be aware of.I did enjoy this game for the most part, if you are hungry for some horror games - this is definitely a must-buy.

Even with a map it took me almost an entire hour to find one of the levels.Other than that, it's a very fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: Once you get your head around the occasional uncontrollably fast movement, Carrion delivers a short but sweet metroidvania that doesn't overstay its welcome. It even manages to provide flowing and enjoyably open level design without the need of a map, based entirely on how easy and fun it is to slip around every crevice of your surroundings, making all of your movements and position easy to remember. Gorgeously animated, fast-paced, brain-teasing, morbidly imaginative and utterly gross... there's no other game quite like it. You are the tentacle alien. You have a dozen mouths. People are food. The end.★★★★★★★★★✩

_childDocuments_.review: For the fans of horror science fiction, alien/tyranid/zerg whatnot, this is the THING (pun intended).Controls and gameplay feel very fluid, sound design supporting the mood perfectly.
