_childDocuments_.review: Updated 22.11.2019It's really hard to pin down exactly what this game really is. Yes it is short, but on sale you basicly pay 10 cent per minute of 1 playtime(unless youre a bit of a noob like I am, and die 6 times). There are some translation errors, and what little story there is so far is really confusing. But the gameplay is just so satisfying! Dodging, special skills and shooting feels solid, and the music and sound design works really well. It's quite obvious where some of the inspiration for this game comes from, and Im fine with it. It might just be a bit over a half hour at this point, but it has some replayability as you get to keep your skills for each playthrough. An update late november added some english and japanese localization. And while I don't speak japanese, hence not really able to say if it's any good or bad, the english localization is both better than what I expected, and just as charmingly translated as the original. Voice acting overall is a bit stilted, but suprisingly good quality. The self narration is cheesy at best, and it does not really help the player understand what is going on. The update itself has not changed my view of the game, and I would still recommend it to people. But for those who already played through it a few times.. Well, it still feels like the same game as before. Just that we now get Air serpent in english.

_childDocuments_.review: With combat being its only real promising trait, I'm not sold on what this game is trying to be. People have touted this game as a doom/tomb raider/shadow warrior and dare I say dark souls like game but I've seen the bare minimum for all those titles. Combat is about as rudimentary as shooters go with nothing to interesting about the weapons. The abilities have promise but between the lackluster AI and boss fights that are a more like a kiting mini game, they lose their appeal after the second "playthrough". By the third playthrough, I found that just by spamming the time sphere and blade ability, I could kite every mob. I found that fair considering their hitboxes and telegraphs were all over the place and the dash/dodge was a haphazard attempt to show evasion even though more often that not I'd get a sword to the face.I'm not even going to bother mentioning the story because it's nonsensical. Air serpents, Carter's men, the doctor and who the ♥♥♥♥ is Wake? I get a timesplitter/quatum leap kinda vibe in terms of story direction but other than that, it's just a spaghetti mixture of sci-fi/fantasy tropes.I don't care about game graphics considering a game could have cryengine, unreal, or just be procedurally generated. If the "game" is boring, big whoop on how "pretty" it looks (I'm looking at you, wonky ass Shiela with your weird spider walk and fake ass hair).I'm not trying to knock the game or it's developer. I know its a single man studio and it's hard to make something like this work but I can't in good conscience give a good review to a game that is a glorified tutorial that lasts 30 mins and asks for 7 dollars. I'm fine with a game like this being placed in an early access with a reasonable price (5 dollars maybe) and a time table or road map on when updates will follow and when additions will be made, allowing people to play along with the new developments. What I can't abide is a developer having that status and then releases it as a full "game" with the "promise" of getting the full game when it's finally ready. Does this mean I won't be able to play any of the recent additions to the game as it's developed? If so, then it's wishful thinking that I'll have any interest in this title when it comes out in a few years having not kept up with it for the entire time. If this changes and the game touts an actual plan to allow players to play through through the developments, I'll be liable to change my review.

_childDocuments_.review: This game honestly surprised me. I came across it by chance and bought it simply because it was on sale. I really enjoyed it especially for how short the game is. There were a few issues but most of the few that I experienced were minor such as bullets firing from where the enemies guns aren't(only one instance), and one crash(also only once) there was also a lot of times when the combat rating wouldn't show until I aimed down the sight of my gun. I really enjoyed the combat, however if I were to criticize it I would suggest that the player be able to dodge/dash in any direction, not just to the left or right and maybe also be able to slide. (SPOILER WARNING)Other than that the only other combat problem I came across was at the God XingTian boss fight which was environmental; I kept finding myself getting stuck on the dragon heads spewing flames due to running into them and getting trapped by enemies. However I don't expect it to be changed because it could simply just be due to me not being good enough. The other thing is I think the shotgun should be worked on because it doesn't feel like a shotgun. It seems to do less damage than the machine gun which isn't good since it already has less range and fire rate. I really think the damage should be increased for it. Right, now the compliments. I really like the combat, it feels very fluid and I like how fast paced it is. The abilities and powers are awesome, love the R.P.G. elements. The enemies look great and have decent A.I. movement and tracking. The boss fights are really cool, I like the difficulty and the fact that other enemies spawn during boss fights, it makes sense. I also really like the execution thing, wish that was a move I could do on other enemies perhaps after stunning them. I would like to suggest that a Horde infinite mode be implemented with infinite waves of enemies, that would be awesome. I enjoyed the landscape and environment of the game, it was beautiful. The soundtrack as short as it is is very cool and it made me feel awesome while playing. Speaking of the environment, I really enjoyed the Dark Souls Reference with the bonfire and the Forest Lord Boss Fight, it made my brother and I smile when we saw it. The voice actress for Sheila (I forgot her name) was great to listen to as well as the voice actors for Wick and Carter. The only problem I noticed was a few minor grammar errors such as missing spaces and lower case letters for the English subtitles. I like where the story is going, I really like the future setting mixed with the ancient/medieval one. I can't wait to see what this game is like once fully developed, I know I will be buying it.

_childDocuments_.review: Poor controlsThere is no way to perform dash while moving forward or at 45 degrees. And you frequently need it. Also it's hard to use grapple shot just in time. The icon allowing to use it on something appears too late, when you have already missed it and gonna die. Abilities usage is inconvenient because some of them are on the same button, but with cooldown.Fights are inappropriate for the gameplayIt's a first person shooter, not a third person hasck&slash or souls-like. How am I supposed to see if there's a wall behind me while being in a critical boss fight? Or sometimes there are flamethrowers around and you have to dodge them. And the arena is pretty tight. It wouldn't be a problem if there was a really good third person camera that would make walls invisible if the character hugged them (like in Dark Souls 2 for example). But there is none.Technical issuesThe game once froze deadly during a boss fight when the boss was nearly dead. That was incredibly frustraring.ProsIt's not some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ open world grind fest (the game industry degraded so much I praise a game for not being another ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ grindy open world crap LoL). I hope the developer fixed everything in the full version (apparently, this one is just a short technical demo, a teaser game).

_childDocuments_.review: While I enjoyed Bright Memory for a short time, I ultimately will not recommend it right now.It's currently very short, taking less than one hour to complete, and even in that short amount of time there is a lot of repetition.. The same 3-5 enemies, certain mini-boss like enemies being re-used as part of a later fight, etc.  There are a couple of puzzles, but they're nothing more than time-wasters to help break up the fights, and offer no real challenge of their own.. not even sure why it's in there.The final boss would not be challenging in the slightest, if he didn't spawn gobs of minions, and even then it's pretty trivial.  The biggest chance you have of dying in this game is if you let yourself get surrounded by enemies, without any of your abilities cooled down to help you get out.  So keep moving around and you'll never die.Visually it's pretty impressive, at least for an indie game.. there are some cool abilities that I wouldn't mind seeing worked into other games, but on its own it's fairly lackluster after you've been through it once.  Somehow despite all the action, I felt bored at what would be about the midway point, and only pressed on because I heard it wouldn't take long to complete.  I don't think I'd have very much fun playing the rest, despite the 'cool' factor of zipping around, blasting and slicing up enemies.This could have been a free demo.  I guess the price isn't too bad, but if you're a hours-to-dollars sort of person then you're lookin at a 1h / 7$ ratio.  I don't solely judge a game on that parameter, but I do factor it in with other praises and criticisms like the ones I've mentioned above.  About 2 more hours worth of gameplay are planned to be added by the time Early Access is concluded on this title.. but as we all know, early access includes no guarantee of a finished product, so I am reviewing the product as-is.Keys are currently not re-bindable either.  That's a bummer.  I'd expect that to be excluded from a free demo, but I expect key rebinding to be included when I'm paying, even if it's early access.Bottom line, it's neat.. it looks pretty cool graphics-wise, runs pretty well on my system, and you feel kinda cool for a while after you get a handle on the controls.. but at the end of the day, would I feel good about revisiting this at another time to play the other 2 hours if they're ever done?  Probably not, unfortunately.

_childDocuments_.review: As of early access I like this game a lot.So far i've only completed week 1 but i feel like the time invested has given me a reasonable grasp on the game and the way it works.So let's start with what drew me to the game, the combat. _childDocuments_.review: Game simply wouldn't start upon using "New Game/Load Game" features. After attempting to contact the developer, I was met with nothing but rudeness and unreasonable disrespect, leaving me no other choice but to get a refund. I was excited to play this game. Had it on my wishlist forever. Maybe it would've even been fun, had it worked, and had the dev not been straight up rude for no reason.UPDATE: So I got the game working after switching GPU's; This game seems to have a massive Nvidia bias. After playing for a bit, I decided to keep the negative review, as this game is infuriatingly inconsistent. As I will outline below:[Graphics] - The "human" models are fine, despite looking like stolen assets from the "Tomb Raider" games, and having the worst hair I've ever seen. The forehead down looks like Tomb Raider with RTX on, but the forehead up looks like GTA V on the lowest settings.The surrounding environments are extremely dated, most of it isn't even 3D upon closer inspection. The enemies are weird, because they don't necessarily look bad, it's just very apparent that little to no effort was put into their models, especially when compared to the models of the characters. [Gameplay] -So close yet so far. Some things are amazing. The general shooting is great, being the smoothest and most accurate feeling I've ever used (feels similar and a bit better than Rainbow Six Siege). The movement feels like any other shooter; works great, nothing special. The problems arise with the inconsistency. Switching weapons can only be described as annoying. Skills are over complicated, and can take way too many buttons presses for the simplest things (Coming from an mmorpg/moba enthusiast) and dodging, one of your only lifelines, just doesn't work half the time. The dodge mechanic was so wildly inconsistent, I took the time to test it, because I was temporarily convinced my keyboard was broken (it wasn't). Lastly, the game has a tendency to throw things at you without warning, causing a lot of confusing situations where you die to seemingly nothing, or have to spend 5 minutes trying to figure out what you are supposed to do. [Sound / Music] -The surround sound is pretty good, and more than usable for determining direction. The background music is nothing special, if not stereotypical. [Optimization] -Honestly kind of impressive. I was pretty easily able to run the game in high settings, 4K, on a GTX 1060; which is a reasonable GPU, if not dated. Though, this may be a moot point considering wonky graphics, and a complete lack of support for AMD GPU's. Overall, not bad if you get it on sale for around $5 (assuming you have a NVIDIA Card; As of time of posting, there is no fixes for the majority of AMD cards)

_childDocuments_.review: This is going to be quite a length review, as despite the brevity of the game there's a lot to unpack. I want this review to serve equally to inform potential buyer and give feedback to the developer.The graphics are easy to get out of the way - they're great, they all form a cohesive art style, and the environments don't look like they were made in a matter seconds. That having been said, the level of detail in its graphics that this game opts for can make some enemies hard to see with all the noise coming from the detail of the textures and the very fast pace the game makes you play at.The two pitfalls that are the reasons I refunded the game are the combat mechanics and enemy behaviour.The combat mechanics feel as if they were made as a developer's first outing into FPS design. You want the game to feel fast, so you speed things up - enemy attacks, player movement, etc. It feels like the intuitive solution, but this is not the way it works necessarily, a fast paced game can be made to feel fast without everything happening quickly. Take DOOM 2016 - you move fast, but your rate of fire is controlled, and enemies all attack relatively slowly, despite DOOM's branding and success in being a fast paced FPS. It allows for decision making and greater observation of the environment not otherwise possible if you're always hard-pressed by enemies. In Bright Memory, enemy attacks for the mob enemies are seldom telegraphable due to the speed of the animation. Bright Memory's intensity is then brought right down by the game's combat being in favour of kiting. Dashes only move you backwards, there is no cooldown (or if there is, I never noticed it), and no enemy moves faster than you can kite with this ability. From there, all you have to do is empty your magazine into the closest enemy, dashing further away again when they get too close. It is a boring gameplay loop which the game tries to break you out of by providing abilities, though the EMP's cast time still means you have to strafe and if you've kited a large group of enemies, it never seems to catch them all. My two sole deaths were environmental - once I accidentally backed into a fire and was unable to run out as I was being blocked by enemies, the other time I ran backwards off a cliff. If running backwards through every combat scene is going to be how the game is played, at least makes the walls smooth and environmental deaths like these harder to have happen.Next in combat mechanics is gunplay. In this preview, you get three guns, only two of which that are really worth using, being the SMG and shotgun. The game never provides an obvious enemy type or environment type to let you know which you should use, you kinda just have to pick one and use it. Neither gun feels like it does much damage and all enemies are bullet sponges. The fact that the shotguns rate of fire isn't fixed is down right broken the second you let anyone remap their keys (why you can't is beyond me, gotta wait for the full game for that). The fact that guns have an ammo limit feels incredibly pointless - I never noticed any ammo pickups and I never was short on ammo for either gun. The ability to aim down sights is difficult to use given the pace of the game and lack of stationary gameplay as there's never any cover, so I don't really see why it's needed/included with the rest of the game balanced as it is. The game's feedback with hitmarkers and incredibly drastic time slow downs never felt consistent to me - I didn't know whether I'd killed an enemy or scored a critical hit, or why I was getting the feedback I did.Enemy behaviour. First of all - why do I never die from enemy attacks? I never at once even reached a greyscale state from enemy attacks. Not that I know where/if I have a health bar. Enemy spawning is poor, the spawns seem fixed, meaning you won't always see enemies spawn in, or you can just farm where they spawn from a safe distance. To add to the first point, enemies will attack you even if they're off screen. This seems normal without considering the experience the player ends up with - you weren't even aware there are enemies and now you're being hit by them. DOOM 2016, by contrast, tries wherever possible to spawn demons in your cone of vision and ensures that for the most part, demons you can't see won't attack you. In Bright Memory, I can't recall any decent audio cues, and so the lack of visual information was very unhelpful and if there were directional damage indicators I didn't notice those either amoungst the rest of the HUD's clutter. What about the boss fights? Same as the rest of the game honestly, strafe and aim for the head, empty magazine, reload. The character's commentary doesn't match up with what's happening during fights I found (specifically the knight dude), and the enemy AI doesn't seem to know what to do against a strafe queen, which is weird considering that's what you spend 90% of the game doing. The knight fight I would literally just back strafe and shoot the knight in the head while he walked slowly towards me. For the whole fight. Even the extras that get spawned couldn't do anything because I was kiting them one and the same. Poor, honestly. Bosses, especially in large arenas, need gap closers (not smaller arenas, that makes everything worse). Bosses movesets are incredibly limited (I identified maybe 3 moves for each boss) and they don't perform any combos or anything, just dice roll which attack to do (or so it seems).If the above was fixed, I'd happily keep the game and be able to enjoy playing it, nothing else is so awfully wrong that it'd stop me wanting to play. That having been said, here are my nitpicks, in no particular order:* The HUD is awful, there is literally clutter in the middle of your screen that serves no purpose. The game was noisy enough alright* The style system seems pretty stupid honestly. It doesn't fit the game's genre and however the scoring is decided, it will nearly always be flawed. I didn't feel 'A' tier constantly back strafing, bumping into things, and getting hit by enemies I couldn't see* Buying the game on Steam might get you a copy of the full game, but I am very concerned by the explicit non-promise to release on Steam. I will not support an Epic Games accepting title/developer* The framerate isn't consistent enough. You can often get large FPS drops right after cutscenes and when initiating abilities. This preview isn't in early access, it should be better optimised* The story doesn't make any sense. Hopefully it will in the full game with more time to explain* There are very few enemy times. I think maybe 6 excluding bosses, but some are very similar despite being strictly different (just giving a dude a shield for instance). Once again I'd expect the full game to include more* They literally reused an area in the game. The character even calls the dev out on it* The one puzzle is pretty poorly done honestly, when you realise the solution it takes an incredibly long time to solve still. There is no clear correlation between the symbols on the floor and those on the wall either* An EMP does not (in real life) make enemies float, put out fires, or break wooden objects. In this game, and EMP is never used as an EMP. It is a vacuum creator with some gravitational pull to go with it and should be named more accordingly

_childDocuments_.review: EARLY ACCESS REVIEW WARNING:Ever wondered what would happen if Devil May Cry got married and had kids with Shadow Warrior?This child of love, is what would happen.Bright Memory is an FPS game with some Hack and Slash elements. Let's break it down for you:Gameplay:Game controls like any other FPS particularly from the Shadow Warrior franchise, due to the fluidity of shooting + movement. What I like about this game is how it gives you all these cool tools to fight enemies with. You will be dashing, dodging shooting and levitating enemies up in the air to rack up that style meter combo. Yup you heard me, you got DMC's Style Combo Meter rewarding you for using different abilities in conjuction with shooting. It's a dance macabre of style.Story:From what I can gather, your name is Sheila and you are an agent from an organization trying to find acient artifacts while chasing another evil organisation trying to beat you to it. Tomb Raider would be proud. Nothing more has been revealed in the gameplay trailers, so this is all we gotGraphics:This game is beautiful if you can run it at DX12. Even at DX11 it looks stunning with backdrops like the courtyard, the water effects in the tunnel sequence. Game looks every bit as beautiful as the chaotic combat and jt helps that you have 4K HD option, if you want to blow up your PCMusic:Music is very limited and by that I mean there's only 1 track on the game as far as battle sequences go, everything else is just ambience until the next shootout, but the track of the game is very DMC 5 inspired, with heavy percussion and bass outlining the intensity of the fight, just wish there was more than just one for the demo, but it's still pretty kickassFinal Verdict:If you like stylish action games which challenge your sense of cool and have $20 to spare, I would recommend this game. Especially since if you are an Early Access member, you get the full game for free as an upgrade. AAA corporations be damned.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool game, not bad. Only 30 minutes long.Best part is the combat. It's fresh and with some polish it could really shine.3 major gripes tho... 1. Story. It's bland and uninteresting. A demo should not only hook you with gameplay, but story as well. 2. Animation/Design. The enemy designs work well and their attacks are telegraphed nicely, but the main protagonist and antagonist designs are cringe. Their facial animations are uncanny and their looks are forgetful. And for goodness sake, put some armor/clothing on the poor protag. She could look much more badass and less like a horny teenager's late night fantasies.3. Optimization. I have a high-end PC running a RTX 2080. I couldn't play this game on 1080p at medium settings without skipping and major frame drops.I still recommend the game despite these major flaws. It has great potential that I look forward to seeing in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Bright Memory is a flashy first-person shooter that allows you to play as Sheila, a specialist warrior capable of stopping time, using abilities to hit enemies AOE, shift rapidly on the side, and use her sword to slash and bash enemies.It's a fun combat that hopefully is well-implemented for the real game. Very interesting and fun to play, but unless you want to try it, I'd suggest just getting the real game, where I believe the real fun lies.   Good visuals, with nice settings even for an early access or demo like game. Cinematics are poor though and that is to be expected after trying this game out.   Weapons sounds punchy and powerful, abilities do the same. My only complaint is that some voice-actors, like Sheila isn't that impressive or well narrated. Hard to say what this game really is trying to say. But it's basically portraying a mystery story about Sheila looking for an artifact that as a player you get no details on.You get no additional information on the game story, characters or events.   A very short game. It takes 30-45 min, depending how well skilled you are with shooters and beating enemies and bosses in the game.Difficulty wise can be rather challenging, especially at defeating the last boss. Dodging is your best friend, so learn to use it well. An interesting demo, that opens up more to want for the game. Luckily, we got the main game, Bright Memory: Infinite and it seems to hold up well. If you get this game for free and want to experience a bit of what the full game is all about, sure, play it. You'll only spend 30-45 to get the idea behind it. I only wish game devs would label this as DEMO by changing banners and stuff, because that's what this game is. I gave it a negative review not because I don't like the game, but because I recommend the full game, if it's as good, if not better than this.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Get it if you want to support a game with a lot of potential and help the guy who made this. It has flaws and is short, but it's a good experience if you want to see a game that has potential.Bright Memory - Episode 1 is honestly a rather short game with okay/good gameplay. That being said, there's a reason why this game is highly rated and enjoyed. If I could describe this game with one word, it's likely potential. It's a word that's thrown around by a lot of steam reviews easily, but I think it's never applied better to a game in recent memory. The game itself is a hybrid of a first-person shooter and DMC. This episode is rather short (30 minutes - 1 hour). The game itself has a few issues but the thing I'd like to focus on is the combat. This game surprisingly has good combat but it's just a little short of excellent in my opinion. Whereas Devil May Cry's control scheme allows for a large moveset, first-person games tend to already hog the controls a ton already with the controls. This game surprisingly pulls it off well by giving you several abilities. My problem with the combat currently is just the variety of uses the abilities have. Admittedly, I am not extremely creative with movesets so I may be at fault a bit here, but I found the combat to not have a lot of ways it could be manipulated to obtain better or varied outcomes. Some abilities I think have uses but they aren't really useful outside of a few sections. One that comes to mind is the grab ability. You use it throughout the episode akin to a grappling hook. However, in combat itself it isn't really useful. You have ranged weapons so there is no incentive to really get close, especially since your weapons don't stun the enemies (aside from the abilities, which all can be used at a distance still). While I don't have suggestions for abilities that could replace the ones we currently have or even expand them, one suggestion I do have is having different abilities for what weapon you have currently equipped akin to weapons in DMC. If you could switch out your weapons quickly and they had different abilities, I imagine you can have synergy between your abilities on each weapon. Outside of that, the combat performance grading scale needs some help. It's extremely easy to get SSS and as a result I don't feel like I earned it that much. The other thing is enemies are a little boring in my opinion. While some can be very deadly, they aren't very interesting either. The  comes to mind as an enemy that is very deadly if you get too close but also very easy to cheese. Some of this is due to the idea of combining a FPS with DMC. While my weapons don't do much, my incentive is basically keep running in a circle and just hit him with my abilities after they come off cooldown. It's a dumb way to win and maybe that's on me, but it felt like the fight could have been designed better. Overall, Bright Memory is a FPS and DMC combined with some synergy issues and design flaws, but overall a surprisingly solid attempt at it I think, especially when it's coming from just one guy.P.S. The bonfire system made me laugh. It really just looks like Dark Souls. It's not a bad thing, but it made me feel like it was either a parody joke for a split second or something. It has no use as far as I know.

You have so much freedom to fight your enemies and i've barely unlocked any of the skills! You wouldn't be able to tell this is an indie game because the presentation is very well polished. My only complaints would be to clean up the HUD and implement an option to remove some of the weird looking blood and water splatter on the screen. Since we don't know very much about Shelia, it would be cool to have a tutorial of her going through her first day of training. _childDocuments_.review: The game is chock full of serious bugs, is extremely poorly designed and the graphics aren't that great except for the effects. My experiences and the bugs I've encountered in less than 1 hour:-A giant rat boss didn't spawn in front of a closed gate until I killed myself and respawned at the same spot, then it was already standing in my face with other monsters-several times enemies got stuck in rock formations, in places unreachable to me, just standing still in the weirdest places-I lost all my experience/level-up points without a warning-I need to crouch in areas where I'd normally be able to walk through standing-I fell to my death from less than 2 meters high several times-The melee skill hits from so far away that it requires no distancing or skill, you just press the button and virtually the entire game area receives damage from your slashes - very immersion breaking and unrealistic-Your skills flow into each other like water mixes with oil - very poorly. The enemies you send into the air just float there for ages and it looks ridiculous-Even basic enemies take ages to go down-Elements in the environment don't merge into each other smoothly and stick out like a sore thumb, it looks very artificial-I keep bumping into invisible walls where I should be able to pass through-I get forced down a narrow path and can't access areas that seem totally accessible, plus I fall to my death from less than 2 meters, just terrible level designTL;DR The game is terribly unpolished, amateurish, bug-ridden, and if the play time is really as short as other reviewers say, I'd stay away from this title unless you're really bored and are hungry for something "different".

_childDocuments_.review: Bright Memory is one of the more perfect games I played this year. But really it is not fair to write a review for it at this stage as it is really more of a tech-test right now, But that wont stop me from praising it. No siree. The current Bright Memory, like a drunkard who wakes up in a jail cell, has no story, explanation or logic whatsoever. It breaks many of the trends of modern games by not only having tons of mechanics ,(this is sarcasm), but fun ones at that, (this is not). It is unquestionably intense and whacky and is not afraid to wear that badge proudly. There are Dark Souls- like bossfights (Yes there are bossfights in this 1.5-hour game. Deal with it) and turtle-lions for gods sake. The main plot is about as present and relevant as story in hentai and just like story in hentai, dosnt need to make sense for it to be fun and engaging. What I could glean from the singular cutscene is that you play as this generic military lady with bad VA called Shelia (Not Sheela, ♥♥♥♥ you.) And you are part of this good guy group investigating a break in- at their lab and it doesn’t matter at all. Fast forward literally 2 minutes of dialogue and you have been teleported to a floating island above antarctica where Shelia is apparently immune to cold and emotion in dialogue. The island is full of undead monsters, ruins, mech-soldiers and the literal God of War. No its not Kratos. ( A sad shout of "BOY" echoes across the room") (The thing that attracted me to this game, infact, was the advanced movement. (Quick note here. I am going to be comparing this game to Doom Eternal a lot so heads up for that.). The way you double jump above the head of the enemies and then light them up while constantly b-hopping across the arena. It really does make you feel like a highly armed pinball that is possibly on Ketamine. However where it differs is due to the fact that in Vaguely Dim Memory, combos are really the name of the game. ( {Soft snicker here] I changed Bright Memory's name thrice in a sentence. That has got to be some sort of an achievement) In addition to an AR/SMG hybrid that deals as much damage as a mosquito that is sarcastically trying to bite you. But hey at least it has a mag size larger than my life-size cardboard cutout of George Clooney. Wait. You weren't supposed to see that. You also have an Eva-8 is it was actually good and could have a theoretically infinite fire-rate. There is also a [barfs] pistol that you will forget after the first 30 seconds like the name of the med website after you confirm you don't have housemaids knee. You also have this glowy  sword thingy that deals insane amounts of damage and has a cooldown shorter than the pp of an average Call of Duty fan. Which is to say, not a lot. But when it comes to actually using the shining lightsaber of fwienshwip [“fwiendship” is supposed to be in the owo voice] is that just like the Crucible in Doom, you always forget you have it in the most inconvenient of times. Another thing is that both the shotgun and the sword are both capped by your fire rate. And so if you dont have good control over your fingers, both the game and your imaginary girlfriend are going to be very disappointed in you. Well boys, prepare to get let down as even though the game has a grapple, its basically useless and only works on certain. marked out portions of the map that are as frequent as bonfires in souls-likes. To make up for this, there is a double-dash that seems ripped straight out of Doom Eternal. Even the sound effect sounds similar.There are also like 5 different abilities and perks that could be unlocked though the course of the game but these are usually minor buffs and there is only one major ability that you unlock at the end. Frankly I never thought that spongy enemies could be fun but it somehow just.... works in White Memory. Sure it should take you about 450 bullets from the rifle to kill a boss and even the minor enemies take about 30 or so bullets to go down and so you really have to focus to stay alive. This does lead to the claustrophobia problem as fighting in enclosed spaces is a nightmare as you just get gangbanged with nowhere to run. Alternatively, open spaces lead to you cheesing the enemies by continually dashing backward and shooting which is exactly what I did against one boss and just like sex, I was finished on the first attempt. Another thing to add is that the game completely lacks a difficulty slider or option of any kind. Again, I cannot harp on it too much as it is currently a demo and most of these issues should be fixed by the full release. It is pretty much unheard of to have industry standard graphics made by one dude in china. Options and customisation is ok with several different outfits to choose from. There is even a schoolgirl outfit complete with skirt physics that the dev is proud to acknowledge and wank to. That is something I definitely did not also partake in.In conclusion, Bright Memory should be seen for what it is currently, a promising demo which, like an eager politician, promises a lot and only time will tell if the full game is actually worthy of such praise. I will reiterate that the current game is worth its price of five dollars and that the full release will be available to PC users who purchased the demo, free of charge. With such a low price and you already getting the value for your money with the demo, I would urge all of you to go and try it out. It only has one flaw currently which is that some abilities could have been more fleshed out. 9.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: The game feels really fluid, and it seems to know quite well what it sets out to do, and does it. There are some small QoL changes I would like to see, primarily allowing your weapons to reload themselves when you swap away from them. This would really improve the flow of the game play, especially since the Style/Score system encourages you to constantly swap weapons. I find myself in fights where I have to take a good 10 seconds to reload all my weapons, in order to keep going, and it just really, really breaks the pacing of the combat. The feel of the gunplay feels a little lackluster, like there isn't much kick. All three weapons feel exactly the same when you are firing them. However, since the game is mostly about combat pacing, rather than the feel of the FPS elements, it doesn't do much to detract from the experience. Other than that, I really think this game has a lot of potential. It's fluid, and feels good to play. Lots of great potential here to be a diamond in the rough.

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting mix of sci-fi and fantasy. Bright Memory has strong influences from several major franchises, resulting in something that is both familiar but also incredibly unique. I love the cooldown abilities that can be combo'd in different ways. I love the epic fantasy style bosses. I love the incredibly fast-paced gameplay. While incredibly short, I loved every minute of it.My only complaint is that the AI for some of the bosses and enemies seem really really dumb. The final boss of the chapter spent most of his time swinging at nothing and dodging him was incredibly easy. This is easily forgiven considering that this is being developed by one dude.Overall, this short early access demo is more innovative and fun than most full priced AAA games I have played recently.

name: Creaks
detailed_description: Meet Your New Neighbours The ground starts shaking, light bulbs are breaking - and something rather unusual is happening right behind the walls of your very room. Equipped with nothing but wit and courage, you slowly descend into a world inhabited by avian folk and seemingly deadly furniture monsters. From the creators of indie classics Machinarium and Samorost comes Creaks, an immersive puzzle game that delights the senses with its hand-painted visuals, precise animation, eerie sounds, and an eclectic original score from Hidden Orchestra. Proceed at your own pace at figuring out the solutions to dozens of carefully designed puzzles, explore the mansion for hidden paintings and uncover the great secret. Creaks is best enjoyed with a controller and a good pair of headphones.

short_description: The ground starts shaking, light bulbs are breaking - and something rather unusual is happening right behind the walls of your very room. Equipped with nothing but wit and courage, you slowly descend into a world inhabited by avian folk and seemingly deadly furniture monsters.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic puzzle adventure by Amaninta-Design, the makers of ,  and .Options include separate sliders for Volume and Brightness, and choice of Language and Resolution.  Using a controller is recommended, but keyboard is also supported.:You're just minding your own business when the room starts shaking, things begin breaking and your wall opens up to reveal a mysterious passage to a world unknown.  Here you will find dangers and mysteries surrounding birdfolk, killer furniture and a very dangerous, very large antagonist.Despite the fact that we can die -- and have a giant  trying to destroy everything -- I did not find this game to be creepy in the slightest... As a matter of fact, I found it to be absolutely delightful!  Throughout the game you will uncover the story of this place via well-placed animated sequences.  These scenes can be skipped, if desired, which is very helpful when you are replaying a scene.:Although  is often referred to as a puzzle-platformer, there is absolutely no precision-platforming involved.  You do have to time things just right, but that is just part of the puzzle process, rather than what I'd refer to as typical platforming.Gameplay consists of figuring out the environment in order to progress to the next scene.  The puzzling comes into play as you learn how monsters react to the presence of light and how to maneuver them into positions that will help open up otherwise-inaccessible areas.Along the way you will discover interactive paintings -- some hidden, some in plain sight.The "interactiveness" of these paintings ranges from pushing a button and watching a few things move around to full-blown mini-games.  Fair warning that at least one of these requires fast reflexes, and while completing the minis is not necessary to finish the game, it IS required if you want to get all of the achievements.All told, there are 28 Steam achievements, most of which are from finding/completing paintings and discovering hidden areas.Did I not mention the hidden areas?  Well I did now!  They're not hard to find as long as you're paying attention ;D:The graphics are very environmental, and although there is a lot of darkness in the color palette, they have their own beauty.There are a grand total of 61 scenes in the game, and we have not only a very convenient scene select area on the main menu, but a Restart Scene option whenever you pause the game.As for the audio, I can't imagine SFX and/or music that could be any more appropriate.:Overall I found  to be an engaging foray into another world, with interesting puzzles that were just the right difficulty.  The graphics and audio were perfectly matched, and the overall production value excellent.  Absolutely delightful and highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: While it departs from the point-and-click format that Amanita is best known for (in favor of more platformer-like gameplay), Creaks delivers all of the same charm and substance of their previous titles like Machinarium, Botanicula, and the Samorost Series. _childDocuments_.review: I didn't know what to expect from this game.  While the developer always has outstanding graphics and audio, some of the reviewers were unkind as to the storyline/gameplay.  I purchased it anyway as I have always liked Amanita games.  I was not disappointed.  The game's graphics, while dark and subdued, were beautifully rendered and lent the right tone to the story.  The music was lovely and not overpowering and sound effects did not distract from gameplay.  As to gameplay, I would describe it as Amanita version of the first "Rooms" game but with a better story, graphics, and gameplay.  Yes, the basic play is to escape from chambers (rooms) as you move through this fantasy world.  This type of gameplay has intermittent breaks when you get a periodically come across some artwork pieces that have their own puzzles to solve.  As your character makes his way through this world, you gradually realize the plot and the nature of the characters you find.  The puzzles are challenging and never boring.  It's not a violent game but gentle with a satisfactory ending.  I'm very tired of games that leave me in limbo waiting for a subsequent games to purchase in order to determine the fate of my character only to find out my doom is my inevitable future with no chance of salvation.  I'm sorry;  I need a little hope right now.  If developers have the power to create a world and story for others to enjoy, why not create one that inspires and doesn't depress.  Amanita games leave me inspired.  I hope to see more from them.  A sequel to this game would be welcome.  As for me, I intend to play the game again right after I finish this review to discover rooms and paintings I missed.  As for recommendations, if you want a fighting/battle game, move on.  If you want a thoughtful game with interesting puzzles and graphics and a charming story, this is the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Hmm, having finished Creaks now, I’m indeed a bit torn. It’s definitely atypical from everything else Amanita has done in the past. Hard to explain, but this time they obviously went for a kind of classic puzzle platformer approach, which means you got similar rooms with certain puzzles and limited mechanics that you have to solve. And yeah, thus the single elements can indeed get very stereotypical, repetitive and boring (there are just too many puzzles with those dogs in the beginning, and everything rather revolves around counting steps and turning off the lamps at the right time). But I guess that’s normal for that genre, and at least after around 1/3 to 1/2 there’s more variation, so all in all I don’t really blame them for the experiment.Anyway, in hindsight I truly understand everyone who might be disappointed. To be honest, I wouldn’t even rule myself out in that regard, can’t really say why. But I guess it’s because Amanita just raised their own bar so freaking high in the past ;) You know, I just loved their other games much more, e.g. the playfulness and musicality of Samorost, the diverse puzzles from Machinarium or the anarchic psychedelic drug-trip weirdness of Botanicula. I even liked Chuchel a lot (disclaimer, before anyone wonders, I played it before the change and still own it on GOG in the original version), pure comedy gold under the line.  And to stay fair, nevertheless, there’s still a lot of the old Amanita vibe present here. Animations are over the top awesome as ever, as well as the plethora of dynamical background tunes, or especially all the interactive paintings are a highlight in my opinion. And the overall dark style is also very fitting and highly imaginative in its details.So long story short, no no no, this game definitely still deserves its positive rating, still a great game all things considered. Just don’t expect anything like their other products. And best play it in bite-sized sessions (at least I did), so that the missing variety doesn’t get on your nerves too quickly, especially in the beginning.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Let me first start by saying that this game is different from Amanita's fantastic earlier point and click adventures. This time they came up with something completely different... a puzzle platformer, heavy on the puzzle side and far easier on the platforming part. The gameplay is somehow comparable with Limbo - you have no idea where you are, you control your character with the gamepad and (more or less) one button to interact with the environment (mouse + kb is also possible). Your aim is not to get killed and reach the exit of each room (or rooms). The graphic is far more detailled than in Limbo, but the use of color is rather sparse as well.While you were reading a book in your small and shabby apartement, the light bulb begins to flicker and the tapestry falls down, revealing a small tunnel. Following the tunnel you find a ladder, which leads down - very far down. It leads to  a large underground cave with an enormous house in it, which you enter at the top. And here the challenge begins. The house consists of many rooms, but it is in a bad shape. Also the house lacks a stairway, so finding your way down through the strangely interconnected rooms is a bit complicated. You often have to jump over or down cracks in the floor. And then you discover the first inhabitants... very aggressive mechanic dogs... that turn to nightstands when exposed to light. You can push the nightstands around to reach higher points. And this is only the beginning of a very weird story about exploration and discovery, everything told by environemental storytelling and without any written word (as always from Amanita). You can die in the game, but you are resurrected at the last automatic checkpoint, which is never far away. Most of the time in the same room.Character movement by controller works fine. There are timed puzzles, but the difficulty is far from Celeste-level. Most of the time just your brain is required to progress. Find hidden paintings in the building and find out what kind of monster is crawling around outside the house...Polished, relaxed puzzle platformer with great art style.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I definitely didn’t see the tremendous quality of this one coming. Creaks is Amanita Design at their finest, an absolute joy for puzzle-adventure game lovers.In this game, Amanita finally steps forward from their usual point&click adventures into a game with full control over the character. It draws gameplay inspiration from classics like Flashback or the Oddworld series, and more recent titles like Candle, games in which you must lead the character through a rather dangerous world while solving puzzles along the way.In Creaks, all the puzzles are environment-based, which means that every solution depends on the movement of the protagonist and how it affects the scenery and other characters/enemies. You will have to combine that with some classic button pushing, lever pulling, ladder climbing and simple items usage in order to progress. Also, in a very brave design choice, the entire world map is fully interconnected, and every room and corridor leads somewhere in a very organic way, in spite of the intricate first impression that it produces. All the puzzles have their fair share of difficulty, not overcomplicating them but providing a decent challenge and with a very well structured sense of learning and progression.Aside from that, the story and visuals both have that signature Amanita charm. I usually love what they achieve in terms of visuals and to me, games like Machinarium or Botanicula are absolute indie classics in that regard, but I think Creaks really went that extra mile, and it clicked with me a lot. Maybe it’s because they kind of go back to the hand-drawn style of visuals from Machinarium, or perhaps due to its darker and grittier twist, but I was praying for the game to never end.Linking the artstyle to the gameplay mechanics, there’s also the way in which Creaks treats secrets and achevements: during your quest, you will come across plenty of paintings with a distinct visual style (actual oil paintings!). All of them are quite beautiful and include some little funny animations, but some of them will also contain exclusive minigames for you to play (most of them won’t pose much of a challenge). Beating those will grant you an achievement, making for a nice, lovely pace break in your adventure.The music is also very high quality, as usual in the productions of this studio, and has similar vibes to games like Machinarium, Samorost or Pilgrims. It is also adaptative and changes to let you know that you’re on the right track while solving a puzzle. Sound design is also quite on point, very elegant specially with the audio direction for the mechanical enemies, which perfectly combine an organic and artificial feel that represents their in-game duality.As I said, I really enjoyed this experience and as soon as I finished the game I immediately wanted to play more. I hope that Amanita Design keeps exploring this gameplay and narrative road since to me this felt like their most ambitious game to date.Do not turn off the lights!

_childDocuments_.review: What is Creaks? Well, it's a puzzle game. It isn't revolutionary. It isn't infinitely replayable. It isn't particularly difficult. But here's the thing: it isn't pretending like it is any of those things. What you have here is exactly what's on the box... namely a charming, 5-6 hour adventure to a world hidden behind your wallpaper. It's the perfect example of a 7-8/10 game, so if you have some cash burning a hole in your pocket, this might be worth a look.

_childDocuments_.review: In a departure from point-and-click, Creaks is a side-scrolling adventure that follows a guy through a portal in his bedroom into a world filled with avian characters and assorted monsters. The game is richly detailed with the whimsical graphics and sound that Amanita Designs is known for.    There are 61 scenes and most require you to use the environment and your wits to figure out how to remove obstacles and move on to the next scene. Along the way, you find paintings and mini-games. The first 10 scenes felt a bit like Limbo... there were repetitive mechanics and I got killed by mechanical dogs over and over. I persevered and, suddenly, I found myself really enjoying the game. Levels became unique and additional mechanics were introduced. Your path crosses with the avian residents who are searching for a way to rid their world of a giant monster. At first, you observe them and, towards the end, you begin interacting with them. Their story is told through brief cut-scenes and all communication is with sounds (not words).   While some scenes are very complex, most are solved by a reasonable amount of observation and planning. The mini-games are small vignettes with puppet-like characters. They are charming and are sure to make you smile. You are given unlimited tries to figure out what is required to complete each one.   You get achievements for finding paintings and solving the mini-games. There is a 'scene' menu that allows you to go back and replay any area. The game automatically saves between scenes and at critical points during some of the lengthier scenarios. Although there is jumping and climbing, this is an easy platformer that does not require any precision. While some monsters will chase you, most can be avoided and all can be turned into furniture when they are hit by light.     Creaks is a delightful and fun game. It has some challenging moments but is definitely worth the time. It is a sweet story where the good guy wins and lives to see another day.

_childDocuments_.review: Listen, this game has a few thousand reviews, and the trailer pretty clearly tells you what it's about. Creaks is a puzzle platformer, but really it's about the puzzles. What else can I tell you that you haven't already figured out? Maybe not much, but here are the notable things:1) This game is well thought out, and respects your time. ---Puzzles are chaptered, if you decide you want to get 100%, it's easy to go back and do that without a full playthrough. ---The little mini-games along the way checkpoint you between tasks. That means you don't get stuck redoing the easy part over and over because you need more practice on the hard part. You just play the part you're stuck on.2) The art and style for the core game is up to Amanita's usual high standards. Charming, lovely, and full of life. But the collectibles along the way (clockwork style paintings, and clockwork style mini-games) are really nice. They are all unique, interesting, and fun to behold. Instead of 'collect XX of the same thing' you are given extra dimension to the game's story with each trinket you find. I am not one to complete most collectible tasks, but Creaks rewards you for doing so with more than a shot of dopamine.On sale, this is an easy recommendation. Even without that, it's still really nice.

_childDocuments_.review: I desperately wanted to like this game since I am a huge supporter of Amanita Design (especially Machinarium), but I just found myself bored to death with the puzzles in the game. 2.4 hours into the game the same puzzle is thrown at you in increased difficulty as you progress. I tried to power myself through the puzzles (where you basically only manipulate enemy movement to get further), out of curiosity for the story, but I will have to put this one aside now. The reward for completing a room/section was not big enough for me so I will probably watch a playthrough later for the story.If you are okay with repetitive puzzles in increasing difficulty you will probably like the game though, since the artwork is really good and the soundtrack is nice as usual for an Amanita game. But if you are going into this game hoping for a Machinarium-adventure like experience it is very possible you might be as disappointed as me.

_childDocuments_.review: What fun! I I played this game in two sessions. It took me approximately 8 hours  to get through it and I did it with no hints which is a huge positive for me. A few of the sections are pretty tough and they will definitely get the brain cogs turning.  The gameplay is mostly figuring out how to get from one screen to the next, finding new creatures and figuring out how they work to allow you to pass to the next area.  I love the art style!  The characters are awesome and the world that they are in is so appealing to look at.  The soundtrack is great and sets the mood of the game perfectly. _childDocuments_.review: In Creaks, you play as a teenage boy where his only plans was to read his book before going to bed. It was particularly late though, so maybe he got to a particularly interesting part that he just couldn’t leave himself on a cliffhanger, or he had to get it finished pronto for school. However, that night turned out to be one that would prove unproductive as his bedroom light starts flickering annoyingly and his wallpaper starts to peel off. It’s not until a strange, loud, creak shakes his room enough to fully explode his light bulb and the wallpaper curled up on itself to reveal a small hidden door that he leaves his book. With curiosity getting the better of him (though who could blame him, I’d investigate too), he decides to grab a flashlight and see where this door leads. Hey, maybe it’ll be like Coraline… except hopefully without the Other Mother being there.Well, it turns out to be kinda like that. After being forced to climb down an old ladder after the floor crumbles right under your feet, you’re created with a towering building resides in a cave that you didn’t know existed right under your house. Each area you’ll be going through requires you to navigate the environment as you climb ladders, jump through holes in the platforms, and figure out how to avoid and manipulate strange furniture creatures. Creaks does a wonderful job showing players how you’ll generally go about its puzzles. You start out simple with areas that lets you learn about the creature before it becomes complicated. You start with these guard dogs that will chase you if you get too close, but you can easily outsmart them as they’ll linger where you were last at even if you climbed a ladder to safety for a while, making it easier to go around them or blocking their path off with barriers. You’ll also learn that these dogs, as well as the other creatures, won’t step into light. You’ll often need to trick them to step into where the light shines before turning it on so they’ll turn into furniture. This will help you get to broken ladders that you can’t normally reach and have pressure plates be activated forever. As you get further in, you’ll come across floating jellyfish that you can guide by blocking off their path, spikey human-like shadows that mimic your movement, and skittish goats that are content with eating grass and can run on walls if needed to. Before you know it, you’ll come across areas where multiple creatures are placed and even ones that host multiple types.In terms of puzzle difficulty, I don’t think the puzzles are too hard nor too easy. This features puzzles that you can figure out by looking at it and all you have to outsmart the creatures, while also ones that take a while before you get an “Eureka!” moment as it all clicks. From my experience, you’re often on the right track and just overlooking something. The only time I was properly stuck was the puzzles that featured the human-like shadows that mimic your movement. For those that are worried about timing, it isn’t as bad here. You’ll need to run, but the creatures give you enough time to get out of their path and turn on a light. No puzzles requiring super precise timing here!Every so often you’ll come across a cutscene featuring humanoid avians. Unlike the furniture creatures, these avians are in the same predicament as their home is crumbling due to a huge creature (that is just out of your sight) wrecking havoc. As you’re going through each area, you’ll peek in to spy on them and see what they’re doing. Though, you can’t really understand what they’re saying. You’ll eventually team up with them in hopes to save their home.While you’re traveling through the tower, you’ll also come across paintings. Not only are they just paintings, but you can even pull the cord and have a little tune play as well as parts of the artwork move. You’ll come across the majority as you’re exploring, but some are hidden away in secret rooms. Creaks does alert you to them existing, putting you right in the path of one, and relies you on noticing areas that you can, indeed, pass through or hidden levers. There are also interactive paintings that will give you a break from the regular puzzles. I absolutely loved the interactive paintings. After winding them up and figuring out the controls, the painting is in a marionette style that lets you control someone or something. These range from jumping over obstacles to dancing.I didn’t notice this until later, but it does seem these paintings go with the game’s lore rather than just being something pleasant that you can look at. Creaks lets you see your painting collection at any time, which is mostly helpful in seeing how many paintings you might have missed, but also a way to view them all without replaying the section they appeared in and see what order they are really in. I noticed that many paintings are part of a series, clarified by clearly featuring the same avian and/or person. This is certainly interesting.If you’re a fan of puzzle games, especially ones that require you to use your environment, you definitely should play Creaks. It does a great job showing you how how each mechanic works, the difficulty is just right, has interesting paintings as its collectibles, features unique and beautiful areas, and a haunting soundtrack. While the story relies on you wanting to explore, it reels you in with a mystery on what exactly is happening here. I also appreciate that the achievements are easily achievable due to mostly being tied to paintings. The only negative I can really think of is that it takes a bit to get used to having to look down or to the side before jumping and as I played using a controller, I often had times where I passed by furniture instead of grabbing it and often made me grab onto a ladder if I tried to move while by one.

_childDocuments_.review: Creaks was a 2D platform adventure brimming with imagination. Its puzzles were satisfying—transitioning from screen to screen, all while outsmarting pesky furniture that kept coming to life. It was a prime example that dialogue isn’t required to tell a story, the environment and characters charming in their own way. The most striking thing was its beautiful hand-painted visuals that depicted a crumbling mansion in a subterranean world.There wasn't a great deal of variety as most puzzles involved manipulating light in some way, but I liked it and found it relaxing for the most part, outside of the moments where the trial and error puzzle solving got frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: «Creaks» offers exactly what you'd expect when hearing the name of game developer Amanita Design. The visual is fantastic in its elaboration, which, in combination with incredible music, works perfectly; great animations; an obscenely simple plot in which the Big Evil again threatens a small and cozy world and the eccentric cute muttering of the characters instead of voice acting. What you are unlikely to expect is that this is not a traditional point-n-click adventure, but a puzzle platformer. I'm a huge puzzle lover, so I didn't have any problems with this transition, but those who for some reason expect a new Machinarium from this game may not like this innovation.Of course, the atmosphere and the supernatural ability of the developers to create their own unique world, living according to their own laws and rules, play a major role in the success of the final result. It is they who help to perceive a simple story in some special way, forcing to vividly empathize with all the characters of the small bird world of inventors, in which, by chance, the main character finds himself. As for the level of riddles, they are good. In the first third of the game, it seemed that their development had stopped, the same techniques began to be repeated too often, but with the introduction of new puzzle elements, things quickly got better. For the most part, you will solve them by trial and error, gradually reaching an understanding of the mechanism for solving this or that puzzle. An additional bonus here are collectibles - wonderful paintings and mechanical puzzle paintings, located somewhere in an open area, and somewhere well hidden, which stimulate even better study of the world around.This game is handmade in every sense. Another outburst of incredibly inventive imagination that can easily take the player into incredible adventures, striking in its scope. It remains only to be surprised by the lively energy that is inherent in the games of this studio, each time offering something new, and not getting hung up on the exploitation of classic titles. So if you like puzzles or Amanita games, then you will definitely like this thing.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think Creaks meets the standard Amanita has set for themselves with their previous games. There are interesting gameplay ideas thrown in, and I liked the later puzzles, but I don't know if I can remember a moment where there were more than two unique enemies on the screen you had to deal with. I don't think that sacrificing many original tracks is worth having a number of ambient ones that only swell for a few seconds when you find the solution to a puzzle. I don't need or want a deep, complex story in an Amanita game, but this game's story is much too shallow for how much time it takes if cutscenes aren't skipped.Unfortunately, I think Amanita's extreme attention to detail ends up going to waste a lot of the time. The nature of Creaks means that you need to go out of your way to appreciate environmental details. If you think something stands out or looks interesting, you need to stop playing the game in order to appreciate it. This can lead to a lot of the areas, which are all amazingly detailed, going unappreciated when they aren't superficially interesting enough to catch the player's attention. The strength of Machinarium or Samorost's art is that you are forced to engage with it to play the game; no inch of art goes unappreciated in a point-and-click game when you need to look for things to point and click on.I was very interested in Creaks' development, and I checked every update Amanita gave for it leading up to its release. I have played almost every other Amanita game, and I have loved them all; many of them are some of my favorite games. If there was anyone who was going to defend and love this game, it would be me. Is Creaks a bad game? No, absolutely not. I still enjoyed my time with it, despite my gripes. If this were the work of an average studio, I would probably be praising it. Amanita Design is not an average studio, though. I hope that they can learn from Creaks and come back with another great game in a few years.

_childDocuments_.review: It has more artwork than any other Amanita game, but people expecting situational, -style point 'n' click puzzles  be disappointed, at least initially; the challenges are of the abstract and iterative kind, with the player learning the behaviors of photosensitive furniture monsters and applying this knowledge toward increasingly complex (and clever) solutions.  I'd encourage such folks to try it anyway -- the puzzles really are quite fun when you get into the swing of things, and the subterranean fairy world around them is certainly  made of tiled pieces, but so thoroughly, finely detailed that it boggles the mind.  Along the way, you'll learn something of the mechanically inclined bird people who live down there, help them in their struggles, and find mechanized paintings -- a good number of which are fun little video games themselves!

_childDocuments_.review: This was a birthday gift from a friend. :)tl;dr if you like your puzzle platformers heavy on the brainwork and feather light on the reflex platforming, this could be a game for you. If you're in the mood for a whimsy-filled Amanita "toylike" point-and-clicker, this may not be a good fit. Amanita's just got those aesthetics some (like me) find irresistible. Even if they're not day-one-must-buys for me, their entire back catalog is slowly filtering into my "bought" list, like video game osmosis. CREAKS' design sensibility is less SAMAROST (doodles + photorealism) and more MACHINARIUM (all pen and ink, all the time, baby!). That goes for the gameplay, too. I typically think of Amanita games as point-and-click "toylike" puzzlers: you point and click and whimsy happens, and eventually puzzle-solving. The charming BOTANICULA is the latest game of theirs I've played in this vein. But MACHINARIUM (if I remember right) was more of a straightforward point-and-click adventure, and now CREAKS has the studio branching out into straight up puzzle-platforming, with direct control of the character.It's an interesting change. And they seem to have gotten the balance right: if this were more platformer than puzzler (by which I mean, using twitch muscles to run and jump the character along quickly), I think I'd feel like the character is too slow and clunky. But it's really a puzzler with platform elements. (The main character doesn't move fluidly like Abe from the ODDWORLD series, but the way you can walk up to an edge, then consciously drop-down must be reminding me of that.)And the puzzles are good! I just finished the first set and had a good time. It's fun to just figure out a room or two for bite-sized gaming sessions, and the puzzles are clever!My biggest complaint is due to my OS (which is not officially supported): it runs on Linux (Mint 19.3) via Proton, but I have to kind of fiddle with it to get the game screen to actually, you know, pull up so I can start playing. (Fiddling = moving it to another workspace, plugging and unplugging the controller, minimizing things, etc. until it works). From the forums, though, it seems to work smoothly for others, so YMMV.Oh and the soundtrack's great, but that's classic Amanita for ya!

_childDocuments_.review: Creaks is just as good if not better than Machinarium, I'll call it tied for my favorite Amanita design game. It's one of their longer games with an incredible hand drawn art style and a gorgeous world. Taking place in a massive castle in an underground cavern with Bird-People dwellers, it starts you off in your room before a passage to another world, or the cave opens up and the protagonist crawls through. You slowly make your way from the top of the castle down, gradually discovering more mechanics and enemies. Instead of being a classic point and click as is typical of Amanita games, this game takes on a different form of puzzles where you must move around to avoid enemies, draw them towards you and turn on lights above them so that they turn into furniture that can then be used to climb on top of. This form of puzzles makes the world much more alive in my opinion, seeing as your character can die and there is risk involved. Something I love about the game is all of the sections that the castle is broken up into. As you explore this richly detailed world you move from a golden shaded servant region to a purple area with fascinating libraries, towers, and labs to a green region and finally end in a blue one at water level. Each of them introduce new enemies that behave differently and have amazing sound design. From robot dog guardians, to floating jellyfish, to two different shadow enemies to goats, the game's cast remains varied. I cannot express enough how well this game uses environmental story telling, implementing stunning views, mysterious and enthralling music and cool little interactable paintings to discover. There are tons of hidden nooks and crannies where you can wind up a surreal style painting and watch a little animation play or solve a mini puzzle or game incorporated into it for achievements. I love how the music will start out very subtle in a room and slowly build up as you start getting closer and closer to solving the puzzle. The mysterious world of Creaks is even further enhanced by the intriguing plot of a group of bird people scrambling around to find something. I really enjoyed seeing the animations and listening to the frantic jazz play as they argued and battled the monster in their desperate situation. As the game progresses, you slowly you see more and more of the monster causing the creaks and destroying the castle. Eventually you meet the bird people and help them out, ending the terror of the escaped monster. Creaks is an Atmospheric game with a gripping world, narrative, challenging gameplay and puzzles, and music that I would 100% recommend to any fan of puzzle games.

_childDocuments_.review: is a change of pace compared to previous Amanita installments. It's not a point and click adventure, but rather a linear puzzle-filled 2D scroller, placed in .Besides its simpler structure (which for me is a plus, but I'll get onto that later), everything is so well put together that there's no way you could look at it and say "what a bad game". In fact, I would even say that it's one of my favorites from this studio.Creaks' premise is , actually. You're an actual normal person, lost in its thoughts, when suddenly your house starts to shake and your walls start to creak. As everything goes down, you eventually notice a small door on your right. Upon entering, you crawl your way into a room with a ladder, and you start your descent. What I've found interesting is that you can see all the zones you'll eventually trespass in your walkthrough while descending.. You'll come across various simple but well thought puzzles as you make your way through this unusual place.While descending, you'll encounter a few "avian folks" that will make for the game's main storyline, which I will not get into as Creaks' main focus is to  more and more as you venture into this grand abyss.And that's about it. While its story doesn't call for spectacular events or life-changing plot twists, it surely does call for an  which, as Amanita has always taught us, can be achieved without any sort of dialogue. And that's still the case with Creaks. Characters don't talk, but rather try to express their motivations with funny verses, and they always make their point. As always, this makes a great example by building entire characters without an exhausting background story or boring, unnecessary dialogue.Someone in the reviews below said that this is a game with boring puzzles and, overall, a boring gameplay. I would disagree! Creaks, as other Amanita titles, doesn't revolve much on an cutting edge gameplay; it does on different elements, such as .As a result, Creaks' puzzles won't come off as difficult but, in fact, rather . You'll eventually solve them in a matter of minutes (if not seconds, sometimes); and I think it works beautifully in this case.How many times have you tried watching a walkthrough of a said point and click adventure just to find out illogical patterns made only to stretch the game's length? I think of Monkey Island, for example, as it  lacks some logical cues that prevent you from going forward. Making a puzzle game with rewarding, yet not frustrating levels is a lot harder to do, compared to having difficult spikes purposely made to fill in the gaps. Creaks just does it .I've remained stuck only a couple of times thinking about the solution, eventually going forward smoothly, feeling rewarded.And that's why we play games like this. I'm not searching for an absurd challenge from an Amanita game, nor do I expect to feel ashamed if I watch a solution for their point and click adventures. It's not what the devs want, and it's pretty clear from the start.With that said, there's a  difficulty curve which increases as you descent, introducing new mechanics until the end.It kept my experience fresh, and I've appreciated every design choice made on level designing and on the overall world design.Creaks is a joy to watch and hear. The world and music are so well-thought and passionately delivered that they become your biggest companion through the journey below. Everything is hand-drawn, pencil-styled like titles such as Machinarium, with a huge focus on medieval castles-like ambiance and metallic sounds. Visually, it's  and really . While playing, you'll come across various paintings. Some of which interactive, some with animated only. Each one is well-crafted and interesting, adding to the experience.Sound-wise, Hidden Orchestra made a  soundtrack which goes on par with the game's settings. It's a jazzy, electro-ambient style which uses many harp motifs through the various rooms, and various chimes, as well as violins and catchy drums. Each soundtrack can make you feel in different ways, from melancholic to strong and brave, or curious.They range from the medieval-esque songs to the more modern sounding tunes, all with an unusual combination of scales and instruments which let Creaks have its own atmosphere. Definitely one of the most important aspects and , personally.Masters of artworks and music.You could argue that Creaks is not a cheap game. I would agree, but Amanita Design is a well-established studio and has earned its own reputation through the years. You can tell that their quality increases as each title comes out, and .I recommend this, of course. I've bought it while on sale, but even at full price you wouldn't be disappointed. : :

Something to see in every corner and creak (ha!)What I enjoyed about this game:+ great design/illustrations.+ love for details and diversity (every room is different/various themes)+ No talking but you still understand everything (storytelling)+ fun puzzles+ hidden rooms (where you find paintings)+ riddles within the puzzles (fun & easy, sometimes annoying)+ characters are lovely + atmospheric (also nice music & sounds)Not fantastic:- the length (pretty short 5h fast and around 10h slow with all paintings/mini riddles)- After finding the first paintings it´s quite easy to guess where they are- Riddles can be a bit repetetive but I feel it´s still a good variationI recommend it wholeheartedly to you if you enjoy a game that pleases the eye and isn´t overflowing with colours, sounds and a bunch of movements.
