_childDocuments_.review: Never did I expect to play a game where dogs fight rabbits, pawns are motivated by a donkey playing the butt trump and that you would fear the snail. And this was only the tutorial. I'm interested to see what more I'll discover.Either way, though I've not played long, the early access game feels done-ish. Compared to other early access games I've experienced it as stable, didn't encounter any bugs myself and, if the developer is to be believed, this is essentially the 'ready'  base game upon which they'll expand.The tutorials prove the game is easy to learn, but hard to master. And the tutorials don't mess around, either. It's easy to lose if you don't play tactically. Still, you immediately learn the game through playing so there's no need to go through an hour long boring tutorial. And the hints are well written, while being able to optionally enable/disable them. About 30-45 minutes in game got me up to speed.When playing journey mode, you'll choose your own Tiny Inkulinati (essentially 'you' represented in the game; if you die, you lose) from a number of designs. You can assign one of several (team) colors. You'll select an initial set of monsters, with the available options being dogs or rabbits. Based on a 'Prestige required' there's content to be unlocked through playing. During the journey mode you'll unlock other monsters to add to your roster. Finally, there's a number of talents to choose from that function as special powers during play.Combat is heavily position based, with various units having various forms of attack (swordmen attack adjacent squares, spearmen attack two adjacent squares, bowmen attack lots of squares except those adjacent). Creatures also have special attacks with a cooldown. There's also battlefield obstacles (which can either be a boon or a hindrance), etc...Interestingly, you can push opponents 'off' the arena, instantly slaying them. Comparable to Worms, when the end draws near, hellfire appears which creatures can also be pushed into. You win by either eliminating the enemy, or their master.EDITED 1st of february 2023 to slightly improve to grammar and descriptive elements.The TL:DR of this game is: an early access, 2D tactical combat game whose visual style is based on medieval art. Plays like a finished product, and we mught expect the developer to expand the content in the (near) future.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are the type of nerd that is prone to heavily mulling over your next move like I do (apologies to anyone I ever played MtG with), and enjoy doing so when the opportunity arises, this game is very satisfying. The "Academy" tutorials might seem like a bit much at the get go, but they play less like tutorials and more like puzzles once you get into them- and this makes learning the gameplay and your critter abilities less of a chore. This a point in some games where I quit because the adhd brain just can't, so kudos for making the tutorials into fun and engaging challenges. With that said, the game won't appeal to everyone, but it will strike nicely with those that enjoy a turn-based strat. As another reviewer said, it's "chess-like". Strategy, challenges, cursing under your breath, thinking, time...and a lot of fun. The art is gorgeous and thematic (it was great to see an old friend added to the lineup- iykyk), the sound effects are neat, and I can't get over the legs/paws icon- little peets! It seems a lot of love went into this game, and it shows. I snooped around the Discord and devs are pretty active and responsive, so I imagine that with community feedback and player engagement, more improvements will come along in the future. Now for my gripes: One is the zoom out during chapter changes. I play on my Steam Deck, which makes this game **extra leisurely** for me. It's a dream on the SD, but that zoom out is a shock to my junk eyes as they readjust- maybe I am just getting old. And one other is the load time into the next chapter. This probably contributes to making the game feel, as some have said, like a slog. Maybe they will find a way to address it in the future, without sacrificing the regular animation speed, as I do prefer a quicker load up before I spend 15 minutes deciding whether or not I want to use "Here comes the butt".

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very quaint and interesting. However, one thing makes this review negative: the game punishes you for not reading, then punishes (or I suppose fails to reward) you for reading. The glossary rules are not organised in the same way as the tutorial pages (the latter are oftentimes split between the former or missing). The game is missing some user friendly popups (including in the tutorial menu if you are trying to dig out a rule you have to go off pictures only). A whole bunch of the popups are wrong; the same terminology can mean many different things. It is often lacks specificity; 1 ability will say it affects "x" whereas it actually affects "xy" and other times it says "xy" and instead affects "xyz". And finally, it is just clunky to try and read things in the first place when it comes to what you can read and when.It almost feels as if the people in charge of ability balance and the people in charge of UI haven't been talking. Like at one point it was accurate but as each unit has just had its own deviations from the baseline it hasn't been reflected in the description whether because of lag or nuance that cannot be conveyed in the old format.Much of what happens is blatantly unexplained. At no point does it ever feel like I am having a fun time making meaningful decisions because anything can happen no matter what the game says can happen - and I have lost all motivation to play further.Minor gripe: there was no more neat voice work like I thought there might be from the trailer. I'll change this review when they fix these up - it is early days. I recommend keeping an eye on this game - or buying on launch sale and then waiting a bit to fire up.

_childDocuments_.review: Inkulinati is a decent game, but it doesn't hook me the way other rogue games do.  The things you collect are beasts for your army, hand actions, and talents.  Both the beasts and hand actions are nice and can feel good to pull off some cool strategies, but the boredom mechanic discourages you from using certain beasts too much.  Progressing through the run felt more like I was getting more options for each encounter, rather than actually becoming stronger (a key component for a roguelike).  The talents after each boss are where you specialize, with some being better than others, and can be strong when you use your main beasts/actions to lean into them.  I enjoyed playing this game, but I think it needs more meaningful decisions when it comes to selecting your roster that can make each run stand out.  As it is, you get so many beasts in your army that it doesn't feel very unique when you see them again next run.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good turn-based tactics game. Would be super ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing if not for two things.My main gripe with it is that it is incredibly slow-paced there are so many animations and camera pans and zooms for every event that take forever to finish and that you can't skip, really slows down the pace of the game. The tutorial would probably be a lot quicker too if it weren't for that. (I only did the basic tutorials to get a grip with the fundamentals, which is highly recommended since many mechanics are pretty unintuitive at first but they to make sense eventually.)And the second issue is that the whole game is set up as 1v1 game, but the only way to play against another human is local play (I guess Steam Remote Play should work, need to find someone to try it with). And the whole campaign is balanced (in traditional strategy game fashion) by the fact that the AI is pretty basic and higher difficulties are achieved by giving the AI just way more resources. Which works decently fine, and creates some interesting situations sometimes, but it's mostly about hoping that the AI won't randomly do the smart thing this time around and just crush you. Or it might just blow up its own units, you never know. Like there are whole game elements the AI just doesn't understand how to play around (like bell towers or snails), which makes me wish to play it against an actual opponent most of the time.The single-player campaign is serviceable though, the "boredom" system is neat and makes you try to not use more resources for a fight than you need (because using more units now will make later fights harder). But don't be surprised if it's tricky the first time around, because some of the units that would counter some opponents are locked at first and unlocking those by completing runs (win or lose) will help massively.Other than that there are some quality of life pet-peeves, like one can't de-select an action, so once you've clicked on an action you need to be careful you don't accidentally commit something when you just wanted to click around the battlefield. Most egregious example was: at the beginning of a turn (or chapter as it's called here) a unit is pre-selected, but I wanted to select a different one, so I click on my other unit, but since the initial unit didn't have any free spaces in its range, instead of selecting the move action (which would just switch to another unit if you click on it) it pre-selected the attack action. And before I realized it, instead of selecting my other unit, I attacked it ...Having said all this: I complain so much, because I really really really like this game, it's got cool and fresh ideas, pushing units around as a core mechanic is fun and funny. Just wish it wasn't so sluggish and I could convince somebody to play a round against me.

_childDocuments_.review: Inkulinati looks great. The entire bestiary of hand drawn critters jumps off the page and feel right at home in a medieval manuscript. There are good bones here with plenty of fun and laughs to be had in the opening hours. As things ramp, the fun and laughs disappear as you’re overpowered by the flatulence of a donkey or the alluring tunes of a skeleton band. The balance problems are a blemish that keep Inkulinati from being an automatic recommendation. Yaza Games has already confirmed balance is on the way (they just released some fixes on March 13, as I’m writing this), but until full release, I have my reservations about Inkulinati being worth the paper it is written on.Full Review:

_childDocuments_.review: This game is endlessly stuffed with comedic moments. The designers clearly did their research, going for historical authenticity at every opportunity that manages to be simultaneously Shakespearean and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The animations are goofy and cartoonish, reminiscent of old Looney Tunes characters, but medieval manuscripts. The voice acting for "animal" noises is obviously just humans imitating real animal noises, which only amplifies the comedy of the animation. In short, the aesthetics and design are absolutely flawless.The gameplay is easy to learn, but with a high skill ceiling that has almost endless potential for shenanigans of all kinds. The various creatures you can command all have different powers, strengths, and weaknesses, allowing for a surprising amount of tactics. The turn-based style makes it a perfect game for those who like to multitask their fun with other things. The story is very straightforward and short, but its simplicity lets the characters you encounter shine in their perfectly absurd ways.TL:DR It's awesome, funny, and I'd give it a 9.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: is a roguelite combat-based game. You play as a Medieval scribe who draws beasts to battle enemies on a battlefield of parchment. The game has layers of strategy; you could draw a beast to help with winning the current battle, but doing so will increase the cost of drawing that beast in future battles. To become an Inkulinati Master, you will have to use a range of beasts and talents (similar to perks). You will also have to carefully manage and trade various resources throughout the game, such as ink, gold, health and prestige.Yaza Games had an excellent and original idea of setting a game in the pages of a Medieval manuscript. The charming, colourful drawings suit the game’s cartoonish humour. The soundtrack evokes tension and excitement as the player battles enemy Inkulinatis and races to finish a fight before bonfires consume their beasts. Gameplay is reasonably varied. The ability to unlock additional content provides incentive to replay journey mode.My main criticism of the game is that the duel mode feels underdeveloped. Players choose from somewhat limited options for their beasts, hand actions and talents. Hence, the story-based 'journey mode' is the main draw for this game. is very good overall. I recommend it to fans of roguelite games and turn-based combat.

_childDocuments_.review: Another game that would have benefited from a demo. I think the problem of squashing a tactics games from 2D to 1D is how brittle the range of successful moves are in a 1D environment. The user interface, and the tutorials explaining this user interface, are not nearly as effective as it needs to be for a game introducing innovative tactical presentation.The visuals get old fast; or at least the humor does. Pentiment was more graceful in how it presented the medieval period.I am somewhat loath to write this game off as basically a gimmick - but it wasn't fun and I never got the impression that I was understanding the tactical mechanics in a consistent organic way like XCOM or Invisible Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting premise for a game - comparable to chess in that each figure has special moves and abilities and the player has to also consider the opponents' beasts abilities before taking a turn.However, what is incredibly annoying and really takes the fun away is that each battle depends on the RNG and sometimes the AI is given unfair advantages - but since the premise is that you cannot "escape" the battle other than basically losing or forfeiting it and then giving up one of your "lives" (quills) to either try again or skip, the entire thing becomes basically a Las Vegas slot machine.The game is also horribly unbalanced. i.e. some levels or "chapters" are super easy and some others are total head-scratchers how it would be winnable even on Easy.Later, on a playthrough on highest difficulty, I had some levels were there was barely a challenge for me because the randomly generated level was super biased in my favour - that's not fun either.Also incredibly disrespectful I found is the game wanting you to play through THREE times to get to the "final Act" - what a lazy way of arbitrarily increasing the length of the game without actually adding extra content.Here are my tips to still have some fun with this game that could have used a couple more beta tester playthroughs before release to better balance out this mess of a difficulty level:1) If a level isn't going in your favour, just hit Alt-F4 to quit the game and then reload it - unless your "Tiny" figure has already been killed, it will set you back to the beginning of the battle.This is also extremely helpful when you enter a battle and notice that you've selected the "wrong" units.2) On Windows, find the savegame folder in C:\Users\YourUserName\AppData\Local\Daedalic Entertainment GmbH\Yaza Games\Inkulinati and just take copies of all the files in there - if you have selected a level from the multiple-choice path in the campaign and want to try a different one, this is a quick way to revert back.3) Forget about the more expensive (ink) units - most of them are so expensive that you won't be able to use them until much later in the game when you have more starting ink and by then, the enemy beasts are also incredibly overpowered even in Easy mode that you end up mass "drawing" lower cost units anyway.Too bad - the game concept has potential and the graphic style is certainly good and "something entirely different" but that's not enough to make me see past the significant issues with this game.I play games to have fun, not to have to mindlessly repeat levels over and over just to hope for better luck on the next reload.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Worms, but for medieval manuscript marginalia.The art is charming, mixing illustration and mocap in a way that caught me pleasantly off guard. The music and writing are decent enough---not the star of the show, but certainly not standing out as negatives. And the gameplay is a fun puzzle rpg. It's pretty accessible, and I cleared my first run on normal difficulty.There's unlocks for new units and collectibles, and the game incentivizes you to play again on higher difficulties, but I didn't personally feel super motivated to jump right back in and keep playing. If the gameplay clicks with you, though, you probably will.Ultimately, if you think the premise sounds cute and you want something that's very visually distinct from other puzzle roguelikes, you should give this a shot. If you're looking for a million hours of content and a high base difficulty, there may be other games that better fit your bill.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR in case you don't want to watch the video:1. Did I already mention the art in this game is absolutely amazing?  So is the writing and humor!2. The game is easy to learn, but difficult to master - it can get tough at times especially with its roguelike nature , especially prevalent in the campaign.3. You create / command units over  2D side scrolling levels and wage turn based warfare against either the AI, or other players.4. You can also use ‘artist hand’ skills and abilities (much like HoMM spells and buffs).5. The apocalypse mechanic is great at pushing fights to breaking point - forcing players to the center of the map.6. I wish there really was more to the gameplay - its fun for hours - but I truly wish there was something unique to really keep my attention going beyond just those few hours.There honestly isn’t anything super new with regards to the gameplay mechanics - but that said, it is  a very well executed entry, albeit perhaps it might be better to wait for either a sale, or for the devs to bring more content and gameplay elements once early access is completed.I would recommend Inkulinati either over a sale, or when it gets more content in the near future!

_childDocuments_.review: Better than expected.I picked up Inkulinati for its neat aesthetic, fully anticipating the depth of a Newgrounds time-waster from 2007. I've been pleasantly surprised by its classic turn-based strategy, and the charm of its presentation and unit design hasn't worn off after ten hours. I'm on my third campaign, each time with a different starter "deck" of beasts, and each run has felt meaningfully different.That said, adjust your expectations accordingly. It's early-access so some features are unpolished; and though I was surprised at how satisfying I found it, the gameplay is  more innovative than you will glean from the trailers. The writing in the single-player experience is also very unsophisticated and tacked-on, although the (very) occasional joke does land.If you're into the medieval manuscript presentation, and either enjoy or tolerate strategy games, Inkulinati is probably worth the asking price. If you're more of a strategy fan, and are indifferent to the aesthetic, you might find more depth or complexity elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: "A Medieval Adventure of Innovation and Humor."Inkulinati is a stunning game that exudes creativity and innovation at every turn. The art direction is truly the standout feature, showcasing a medieval manuscript style that feels both charming and meticulously crafted. It's not often you come across a game that looks like it was pulled straight from the pages of history, and Inkulinati does this with an impressive level of detail and flair.The gameplay is equally unique, centered around a clever ink mechanic that I've never seen before. You draw and command whimsical creatures on the battlefield, and the way this mechanic is integrated into the strategy feels fresh and engaging. It keeps you thinking and experimenting, which adds a lot of depth to each session.There were also plenty of moments that had me laughing, thanks to the game’s quirky humor and the oddball scenarios that can unfold. It’s a game that doesn’t take itself too seriously, and that’s part of its charm.However, there are a couple of minor drawbacks. The runs can sometimes feel a bit longer than necessary, which might test your patience if you’re looking for quicker sessions. Additionally, while the game is a blast on the first playthrough, I found the replay value to be somewhat limited. Once you’ve experienced the core mechanics and humor, there’s not a lot pulling you back for more.That said, for the price, it’s absolutely worth taking the plunge. It’s a game that offers a unique experience, beautiful visuals, and a good dose of fun—definitely an adventure worth embarking on."

_childDocuments_.review: Inkulinati can be a fun experience for anyone willing to give it a shot. The art style is incredibly charming, the gameplay is surprisingly deep, and its roguelite Journey Mode can be pretty engaging. However, the game also spends too much time telling players how to play it rather than letting them learn at their own pace. Additionally, lack of any online modes, and the fact it does not do anything truly groundbreaking with the concept may push some players away. But even with all of that, fans of the genre may still find something to love here.PROS:✓ Well balanced deckbuilding mechanic forces you to try different units✓ Tactical roguelite gameplay with combat twists✓ Great turn-based fun✓ Journey mode✓ Beautiful presentation that mimics the appearance of a medieval manuscript✓ Challenging strategic gameplay✓ Large variety of creatures✓ Classic hotseat multiplayer✓ A lengthy and humorous campaign✓ Excellent use of animals' butts for tactical advantages✓ Lovely music✓ Unlocking new things after each gameCONS:- Tutorial is excessively long and largely unnecessary- Lack of online multiplayer seems like a glaring omission- Boss battles can be gimmicky- The low variety and diversity of battlefield locations and their repetition with each successive game does not help

_childDocuments_.review: I'm super on the fence here, the game is fun, but I really don't think it's worth the price.  I beat it on normal and hard, and had less trouble on hard (because I was used to things by then).  I feel it's a bit of a stretch saying it's roguelike since it's actually quite easy to beat and while yes, you get access to new troops and abilities after the game is complete (live or die, I presume)  because it's so easy it doesn't have that rogue feel to it at allNow given that it has STS style paths you can select in each map, if you read the icons first, it's fairly easy to pick an advantageous path.  As for the battles themselves, depending on your skills, you can just sit back and lure the bad guys in and some battles you don't even need to move.  Others require some strategy, but having units that can attack above and below and from range (spears and bows) and use others as tanks you're good.  It's really not complex at all.I suppose it does get more fun once you unlock more units.  Pigeons and little exploding demon dudes a rabbit that throws cats (or is it a cat that throws rabbits?) give you more options but also make the game inherently easier because of their abilities.  I suppose I could handicap myself with the weaker forces to make it a challenge but I'm just not that concerned with it.  I guess the level fighting the dragons was tough, but only because they had so much health but a well placed snail or a swordsman attacking from behind makes it a quick fight.I guess I'd recommend because it was a fun game, but I don't think it is worth the price paid,  Wait for it to go on sale do you can get the value for your dollar (pound, yen, kroner, whatever...)

_childDocuments_.review: I have not finished the main campaign yet, but damn is it good so far. I have been waiting for this game to come out ever since I saw the charming art work from the trailers. Trying out different tactics will take up a good chunk of time whether you want to or not. Like I the game is tough. _childDocuments_.review: Inkulinati is a strategic treat that has some awesome head scratchers that unfortunately has tried to incorporate rogue-lite replayability into an otherwise great game. Unfortunately it also lacks that final game design care, just a bit of a push, to be propelled into being a great game, especially in the UX aspect. However, I think the quirky art style and the obvious love behind the design really makes it a unique and worthy experience.The massive unit variety, with each race having wholly unique mechanics that get crazier the further you go on, is of course key to a wide variety of levels. From simple "pray and get a buff at the end of turn" to more complex "create water tiles on the map that you can walk to without losing your action, suffocating enemy and ally non-water units alike", and a lot in-between, there is a lot to play around with here. However, the UX of learning about these is plain horrible (you dont hover over concepts, instead you peruse two lists at once and try to connect the dots), especially on controller. On top of that, with different races having a massive variety of units that can even fly things can get confusing AS THERE IS NO WAY TO PREDICT WHERE AN ENEMY CAN SHOOT WITHOUT COUNTING TILES YOURSELF AND GUESSING LINE OF SIGHT BLOCKERS (and no easy way to even predict movement on controller). As time went on I found myself cringing at times when a new enemy type appeared due to this, but taking a month long break from trying to 100% the game allowed me to enjoy Inkulinati greatly regardless. Regardless, Inkulinati is a strategic treat because of its wide variety of levels, made possible because of a large set of mechanics.  On top of the large variety of units you have actions your Tiny can take that you collect on a run, as well as passive modifiers/powers that are the staple of any rogue-lite, so you have many different ways of tackling these great levels. Unfortunately, the general campaign that these levels reside in is not so great. You have a boredom mechanic that punishes you for constantly using a unit (instead of a mechanic that would reward you for using seldom-used units), but I learned to live with an love that eventually as it made me discover different playstyles. A level selector with a lot of different forced builds would have achieved the same though. My biggest gripe is that you are expected to beat the same bosses and content multiple times in 6-7+ hour campaigns, with the first couple hours growing uninteresting as you get good at the game. The game is just not great for a rogue-lite campaign structure because every run is so long. Not to mention, there is a disconnect and a bit of an anti-synergy between the great levels and the mediocre campaign design. Since you are meant to protect your largely immobile Tiny, whose HP is carried over from your rogue-lite run, on rare but deeply annoying occasions it is simply impossible to win a fight. Or you forget about a mechanic of a unit, which is very possible since there are so many units and not so great UX, and your Tiny/MC gets oneshot, losing the level even if you were winning the fight. This doesn't always happen since you can hide behind doors, play around with verticality etc, but when it does happen it can be deeply annoying, especially since you are often against an army or a Tiny with triple your HP that can't be pushed / bled / infected / etc. This is balanced by "[[Revival|quills / revival mechanic]]", which you are given a lot of during a run, allowing you to heal back to full, replenish boredom, and thus repeat levels without losing the run. But when you do lose the run, it can often feel like you just got unlucky / managed your quills badly / didnt power through the UX enough instead of being bad at the game. And then you are back to beating beginner levels instead of tackling the so interesting levels later on (though there are some really elegantly designed levels at the start too ofc). Despite my many gripes with the game, I kept coming back simply because the core design is superb. There is grid-based movement with two ranges (walk and take action or sprint), and a good degree of verticality in levels that form chokepoint ladders or make certain flying units, shooting units, spears etc. an interesting choice. The fact that you can draw both next to you, but also above and below you, as well as a great variety of terrain features, movement ranges, mechanics like headaches that dont allow taking an action after moving, etc. all make for a great strategic experience. Not to mention, you can push units, so if you have a bunch of enemy and ally units lined up next to each other you can basically send units to the other half of the map! There is a lot to get excited about and you constantly discover new tricks you can pull. A small interesting thing is that the AI is slightly undercooked. Of course you don't want a god-like AI in a game like this that searches through every possibility, so I expect that they defined a bunch of good utility behaviors. It works great most of the time, but it can look really dumb when it pushes your fish unit into water, expecting it to drown but in fact moving it to safety etc. In other words, there are some edge cases that make the AI look dumb especially later on in the game, even though it really is quite fun to play against in most cases. The art and general quirky nature of the game though breaks the balance and makes Inkulinati wholly worth it. I hope [[Yaza Games]] will make more interesting games like this in the future! In a world where games weren't expected to be replayable to no end, and where rogue-lites weren't so popular, I think Inkulinati would have been able to push forward with its merits instead of incorporating these expectations, sullying an otherwise great meal.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fine, thumbs up tactical fighting game. Not a great example of the genre but not the worst. It's biggest weakness, in my mind, is that I never fully understood all of the features in play or there were features often seemed pointless in comparison. The 2D perspective is somewhat limiting in a genre where you usually get 3D isometric. Still, the rules are the rules for everyone so it works. There's a decent variety of choice in what soldiers you can select. The game does a better job of associating choices with costs than with providing variety of choice.I especially enjoyed it because of the setting; a medieval illuminated manuscript where the armies consist of animal-like doodles often found as marginalia in those manuscripts. The setup was nice and was true to the source with flatulent humor. Worth playing more if you appreciate the homage to history than as a tactical fighting game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is delightful tactical game. I am no doubt the target for it: a nerd and a theology professor. That said, I do think that the game stands on its own: the animations are of great quality, the humor is omnipresent, the gameplay is engaging, and the theme is integrated in every mechanic (I especially got a chuckle from the fact that hitting the cat bishop makes you a heretic; how fun!). I highly recommend this game. I am thankful for the rise of Polish video games and board games designers. Barzo dobre!

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a long time since Kickstarter... but its worth it! Great concept of "pushing character for relocation, damage or instant death!" Most of the times I have to use pushing or other instant kill mechanisms to defeat the bosses. And of course, the art concept is really refreshing.  Here are a few points where I think could be improved:1. in Beast vs Beast combats, can we arrange our beasts on the board, or at least select their relative positions? Its really frustrating when my archer has to be standing in the front of the row...2. in other rogue-like games, higher difficulty is often compensated with higher exp rate, better equipment, more rewards, etc. But not in this game. I need more incentive to choose difficulties other than Easy, especially when I am grinding for Prestige;3. speaking of Prestige... I feel like too much prestige is required to unlock the last few contents. It's too slow... I need spend a full day playing similar matches over and over again, just to unlock one Hand Action/Beast/Talent? Note that players also have Boredom! 4. I think there should be more ways to protect/replenish health of the Tiny. As there are too many damage types to avoid or block. How am I supposed to survive consecutive combats where they just shoot me from high above every Chapter since Chapter 1? Or if there are fire sparks/infections/tombs every where? Or if there are skeletons screaming from every corner of the board?

_childDocuments_.review: i have to admit that i bought inkulinati entirely on impulse. i saw a game stylized after medieval manuscripts and immediately added it to my wishlist. i'm not usually one for turn-based strategy games, but i think inkulinati is perfect for people who don't usually play this sort of game. i saw another review describe inkulinati as "easy to learn, hard to master," which i think is the perfect way to describe it. the extensive tutorial/academy mode is very helpful when it comes to learning the ropes- once i was shown that a real, strategic move in this game is to make a rabbit shake its ass to make your opponent fall asleep, or have a donkey play the ass pipe to produce a headache, i knew inkulinati was for me. overall, inkulinati is a charming, thematic, and at times comedic game. the central theme of medieval manuscripts is executed very creatively throughout. it is, at this moment in time, still in development, which does mean certain aspects of the game are still very elementary. the campaign structure leaves much to be desired. the only real indicator of progress is that the inkulinati masters you battle at the end of each map/level get progressively more difficult. you unlock more beasts as you progress through your journey, but they aren't necessarily upgrades or more powerful than what you may already have in your army. i also feel like the prestige asset could be utilized and given more of a purpose during your journey, rather than just allowing you to pick different dialogue options. also, random suggestion i'd like to see in possible future updates: at the end of each battle, your tiny inkulinati will talk smack to their opponent. it would be nice to be able to customize the lines/pick from a set. my tiny inkulinati was made from alewife's template since she's the only female one, and i'm conformed to making puns about brewing.

_childDocuments_.review: Inkulinati is a 2D turn-based strategy game finally coming out of Early Access after nearly a year of updates and content. The game features a pretty unique art style, similar to , using medieval manuscripts as a battlefield and colorful beasts as soldiers. After watching the first lovely cutscene, you are soon introduced to three different game modes: Academy (tutorial), Journey (single player) and Duel (local multiplayer or vs AI). Inkulinati immediately suggests that you start with the Academy tutorial in order to learn the gameplay mechanics, but doesn’t warn you that it will literally take hours to complete.  The tutorial is divided into two modes - Basic and Intermediate - each one consisting in a long series of missions to complete. You are not forced to do them all, but on the other hand, if you really want to learn every single move and become a skilled player, it is heavily recommended, even if it takes lot of time.When you start the Journey (single player mode), the game partially repeats the tutorial at random points, showing many messages that you have already seen. I guess developers wanted to be sure that the game mechanics could be understood even by those who would skip the tutorial, but it feels a bit redundant for those who didn’t. Maybe the game should ask if you have played the tutorial or automatically detect it and remove the repetitive tutorial messages. Anyway, if you want to try the game without the risk of passing the 2-hour refund window for Steam, I recommend jumping straight into the Journey mode and learning through it.The goal of the Journey mode is to save your master (Yoda) from Death but, before doing that, you need to beat different Inkulinati masters and their armies of beasts. These masters are represented by real historical figures such as Hildegard, Dante Alighieri, Saint Francis of Assisi and a few others. You will also have to choose your own Inkulinati, which influences the type of beasts you can have in your army as well your starting talents and actions. Once the journey starts, you will see a map with multiple paths, each one with a battle or a random event that can make you earn either new units, gold or prestige, depending on your choices. As mentioned, the battle takes places in a 2D map in which you can have max 5 beasts at one time. The turn-based combat may appear simple at first due to the artistic style of the game but trust me, it isn’t. You need to use your brain and all the skills at your disposal to prevail in battle. Your Inkulinati can summon beasts by using ink, which regenerates by positioning your beasts on spaces filled with ink. Each beast requires a different amount of ink in order to be summoned, so you need to choose wisely depending on the situation you are facing (you will discover that some beasts are more effective against other types). Positioning your units carefully is actually very important, because your Inkulinati must be protected, but at the same time you need to find a way to defeat all enemies and avoid too many losses. If your Inkulinati or your beasts are close to the edge, they can also be pushed off and die instantly. The more complex battles also include obstacles, doors, bells, poison barrels and other elements that can influence both yours and the enemy’s army. If a battle takes too much time to complete, then a random effect will take place on the map, like a hellfire spawning on both sides that spreads after each turn and instantly burns any character that stands on the fire (like in a battle royale). Last but not least, as you unlock more units by defeating the Inkulinati masters, you will gradually learn all their personal skills and, most importantly, their strengths and weakness. For those who want to play the game with a friend, there is also a Duel mode. Here you can challenge the AI or play locally against your friends. If you don’t have a friend sitting next to you, you can use Steam Remote Together to play against online friends on Steam (thank you, Valve). However, the local multiplayer mode feels rather limited and I don’t understand why online matchmaking wasn’t included in the final release considering that dueling is the main gameplay feature. Imagine a game like  not having any online mode, that seems like a missed opportunity and could have easily attracted more players. The gameplay is interesting and offers a decent challenge against the AI (especially at higher difficulties), but it can become infinitely better when played against real humans who can be unpredictable, create more strategies and even make mistakes. Inkulinati is a game that doesn’t take itself seriously, but at the same time offers deep and strategic turn-based gameplay with a particular Medieval art style. Too bad that, after such long period in early access, there still isn’t a 1vs1 online mode. Considering that after beating the single player mode there isn’t anything left to do, the game would have been a lot funnier and more replayable with a dedicated online multiplayer mode.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember when this game was first released on GOG. I tried the demo and wasn't really impressed. After that, I pretty much forgot about it. Months later, I was offered a review key and told that the game was receiving its 4th major update. I have to say that the game has improved considerably since that original demo I tried. What was an endearing, but mostly forgettable game has evolved into a solid turn-based roguelite. It's challenging, but fair. Strategy is crucial, but you can certainly come back from making mistakes. There's long-term rewards to work towards that motivate me as a player to stay in the game. Finally, there's a clear ending that you're working towards in the story mode. After spending 4 hours in the tutorial, I was hooked. Now, I'm currently playing the actual story mode, and I'm definitely motivated to try to reach the ending. I love the art style and the sounds effect. The writing, though ironically not super important to the experience, is funny in its own way. I can't say how much I'd pay for the game, but it's certainly worth picking up in a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start by saying that I am not normally interested in strategy games. That being said, I am so addicted to this game that I could barely bring my self to stop playing long enough to write a review! What first drew me in was the artwork. I have always been fascinated by marginalia, and why medieval humans were drawing rabbits with trumpets up their butts, and I love medieval aesthetic. The gameplay turned out to be quite accessible, even to those of us that aren't really the greatest at strategy games. I hate to make comparisons, especially with big names, but it's kind of like draw-a-medieval-Pokemon-battle. The music is top notch - I love medieval and Renn Faire music. Lots of hammered dulcimer! (Needs more recorder music though, in my opinion.) The only negative I have to say is that like many others have said, there is A LOT of camera movement, zooming in and out, but it seems the devs are aware of this feedback and are looking to make a change. Keep in mind, this is in early access, but I am very excited to see how this game grows!

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who actually  calligraphy and illumination, I fell in love with Inkulinati the moment it appeared in my Discovery Que. But I have a hard rule against paying more than $10 for a game (yeah, I'm cheap. I know). So I waited .  . . and waited . . . and waited . . . then I waitered for a change (the tips were lousy), spent some time watering, weaving, waving and other things starting with 'w' before going back to waiting again. Then Inkulinati appeared in the sale list at 40% off. $14.95. I pondered, pondered some more. Lord God how I pondered. I invited a friend over and we took turns pondering. All of a sudden it came to me in a flash, like a vision burnt across the clouds. BUY INKULINATI! an ethereal voice said. So I thanked my friend, sent them home and took the plunge, shattering my $10 rule (don't worry, I mended it. Some duct tape and superglue and it's almost as good as new). Was it worth it? Well yeah. I might have regretted it if I'd paid full price, but then again I might not. It's a clever game and entertaining to a fan of medieval manuscripts like me. The illuminations are well done (as is the calligraphy. It looks like a variation of Gothic Textura Prescisus) and the animations entertaining. I mean who doesn't love a rabbit stunning a fox by mooning him? Communists and Nazis, that's who.It's not perfect, I'm still confused about how the turn sequence actually works for one thing, but it is still Early Access.So if you're looking to satisfy a yearning for more medieval illustration in your life, this is absolutely your game. If you aren't, buy it anyway. I mean where else are you going to see a be-robed donkey farting into a bagpipe? Apart from Tijuana that is.Also, there's 5,000 Steam points to anyone who can correctly identify the two sources I reference in this review.
_childDocuments_.name: Inkulinati

_childDocuments_.review: Lets Talk about the Game Inkullnati. The Idea of the game is Fun enough but honestly it's just to slow. I love the idea of how the game gives you a tutorial to understand the beasts and stuff as well as strategies you can employ. But lets talk about this with some of my usual pros and consPros of the gameHas some really good art styleThe Sound track is enjoyable enough i could listen to it and not be bored or feel annoyed by itThe Character design is fun and interesting Mechanics of the game make sense or at least seem to make it workThe fact that they add the detail of you drawing the character when you summon them with your characters hand like it was on a page is interesting. Now lets deal with the cons Cons Slow pace the game is very slow pace and it feels like the mechanics they introduce you to just make it more of a annoyance to play.How to attack from someone who is below or above you doesn't make sense or isn't explained. I don't like the religious references that are made in a game now these are minor things but some of it just makes me feel like it's not working for that game. Sometimes these things work if they are not a direct reference for instance Tropico is a great example of a game that can get political but it masks it fairly well with all the other things and the comedy behind it.There is a story in the background going on but you can't take the time to read it or see what is happening there. The Final con ill give it is the fact that there is no turn order so you don't know let alone understand which characters go first and which ones go lastWould i recommend this game personally no but that is because i just didn't like it after getting into the game. _childDocuments_.review: I want to give Inkulunati a positive review because I think there should be more games like this and I don't want to punish the developers with a negative review, as clearly a lot of love, effort and hard work went into it. This is less of a customer review, and more of an UX / experience report for the devs, so I wish they can improve on these aspects later on.What's good about the game?+the visual representation+the animations+the sound design +production valuesWhat's bad about the game?-the pricing-the UX-the pacingThe Pricing:I was aware of this game for a very long time, I followed it since a GIC even before Covid, generally I knew that it launched and I didn't buy it back then immediately. I didn't buy it, because of the pricing, but not because I couldn't afford it, simply because for 25 US$ you either can buy high quality III games (e.g. Cult of the lamb) or AA products. I recently bought it for 50% off, honestly I already forgot about the game and I only got it because I was buying a bunch of games to try on travel and this one was on a big sale and steamdeck approved. I don't think Inkulunati neither can compete with anything else in the 25$ segment, nor can it compete with other 15$ round based indie games, just judging it by its game design merits, taking away the presentation layer and looking at the ruleset, UX and pacing. It's clearly overpriced for what the gameplay offers.The UX:The user experience is abysmal. I played on the steamdeck and I simply gave up after an hour. In the time I played I gave about 8 times the wrong command, and as there is no way to take back a command. I was playing on the hardest difficulty, which shouldn't be a problem for a veteran of both roguelite and round based games, however i did not factor in that the horrible controls would be the by far biggest enemy. Potentially the game might be better on desktop than on deck, however the way how the camera behaves, how the active unit is not framed by the camera when you choose other units and that the camera is not adjusting when the path the unit take sis going outside of the visible space is amateur. It's things you expect from student projects or forgive cheap 10$ games, however in a game which is priced in the 25$ segment the taking a step back feature and the camera adjustment has to be expected on a pure craftmanship level. I played the tutorial and there are also a bunch of UX problems with the tutorial. The writing in the tutorial is quite bad, with the most crucial information sometimes given in the third sentence of a 4 sentence text. Of which each of the 4 sentences explain some different aspect, while at the top a gif runs you then need to rewatch multiple times to get to the exact point the text describes. It wastes time, is confusing and generally badly done. Also I personally didn't like that heros are named "tinys" and rounds "chapters", while this is immersive, I think in an otherwise already confusing tutorila this layer of crafting immersion rather hurts than helps. Maybe I wouldn't care if the expperience would have been smooth, but bumpy as it is, it's not a favourable decision.Also the biggest plunder for the UX is imho that once you finish the tutorial the game tells you "the tutorial didn#t teach you everything", far more concerning was then the realization as i started the first run and my "tiny" took damage simply because of bad controls, that it didn't heal up, which is such a core element of the game which doesn't get a mention in the tutorial, that I wonder, then why the tutorial exists in the first place, as literally one of the most crucial aspects of the game is not even mentioned.Also in the tutorial it is shown that you can push other units, in my first run I must have chosen somebody who can "move" units left and right only but not push them, but I was utterly confused that while the tutorial taught me pushing off the units, then in the first round i was unable to select enemies, but I performed however another turn, moving (pushing?) some carriage which I owned? I dunno but both of these actions sounded/looked too similar that right out of the box I would have been able to distinguish them and there is a lot of this confusion in the game because:The UI:Is bad. It's mostly bad because of the way how the camera is incorporated. How the tooltips are given on the steamdeck is a chore and how many things you need to check when the game starts combined with the slow moving cursor and the switching between the tooltip mode and control mode, while the pointer is not also activating the closest field or omething if you switch it off is so slow and so much effort, that I wonder how this could get past any Q&A or testing. The UI generally is also bad in the way that it makes the game slow down to a crawl and because it's so slow in the pacing, all the fun is sucked out.Also the costs of new armies which came in steps of 100 unlock points, while a single battle rewarded me 5 seemed lika a crawl to unlock new things. THis gives the slow pacing the death stab as it seems to be even slower to unlock new things in the game and I am not invested after a botched first hour to even think about this. After 90 minutes with the game the experience has been so bad, that for the rest of my vacation trip I decided to play the other games I bought with which i had an excellent time. I wish the same would have applied to this game, as it's one of the ones I had hopes for, but I don't intend to come back to this one. I also don't think at this point it makes financial sense to overwork those aspects of the game, for any further project down the line, please employ next time some UX person which catches a lot of these fundamental issues and do a better job at the price estimation and you might have a success at your hands.There is nothing else with the same visual style and it's charming and I'd love to see you succeed.

_childDocuments_.review: My short 4 minute review can be seen here:Inkulinati is an early access 2D deckbuilding roguelike which sees you battle against medieval themed enemies on old parchment, with randomly generated maps, brilliant strategic tactics to master and more dancing skeletons than the movie from the 1920s. Equipped with a pen and paper we face off against inkulinati masters on a grid based battlefield. With freshly drawn creatures we see ourselves perform attacks, spells and other actions with our beasts with the goal to either clear the enemies line up completely or taking down their king like drawing called tiny. After a quick tutorial we are either shown masterful strategies via further courses or drop right into the journey mode.This mode sees us travel across a typical roguelike map with various encounters, shops, taverns and more. The enemy encounters vary from duels against other inkulinati masters or a face off with hordes of beasts. Each master has a tiny version on the battlefield which can draw up creatures called inkulinati with a limited number of ink at their disposal. Every battle is turn based on a 2D grid with one or more levels connected with ladders but not chutes and if you understand that joke congratulations, you´re old.  These turns allow us to use one of our creatures, by moving them closer to our target and perform one of the preset actions. These actions range from simple damaging skills and healing spells, to pushing our enemies off the page or  creating poisonous puddles, all the way to creative effects like the dance macabre seeing our enemies shake a leg. The possible effects each skill has are vast and can become overwhelming at first, but with a somewhat decent explanation we can toggle on and off we can always read up on what each creatures strengths and weaknesses are. These inkulinatis cute design can be deceiving since their attacks often are quite brutal. Most attacks require us to perform a quicktime event which indicates the dealt damage. This damage can be enhanced with temporary buffs or better positioning, with hits from the back ramping up the numbers quite nicely. Finishing off an inkulinati sees them dropping and dripping down on the page leaving behind an ink pool which can be consumed for more summonings. Apart from these savage puddles the battleground gets filled in with objects to interact with and dangerous zones to avoid, requiring us to meticulously plan out our characters position.Luckily our tiny is equipped with ways to move around characters close to it, as well as perform other actions with skills we pick up during our successful run across the roguelike map.These actions and newly obtained inkulinati can be swapped in and out for every battle giving us plenty of strategic ways to face off against specific enemies. The changing in our teams line up is especially necessary due to the boredom we obtain. Every time we draw a creature in a battle we ramp up the cost for this specific creature. Facing off every battle with the same inkulinati can result in overwhelming ink costs. One step at a time we edge closer and closer to every levels boss fight which has a small story linking them all together. This story sees us meet death itself at the end, which is a far more jolly character than one would imagine.Apart from the new skills and creatures we gain we also collect coins and prestige we can use at various shops or random events to enhance our tinies life or ink pool, lower the boredom counter or buy more actions and creatures. Finishing a run successfully or biting the dust by running out of lives, the prestige shows one further usage. With a completed attempt in the journey mode we collect the prestige and work our way up to milestones unlocking new inkulinati like sexually assaulting rabbits, musically inclined skeletons and... assfaced devils. With all the different creatures, the procedurally generated maps, four different difficulties and the huge catalogue of extra courses and riddles, Inkulinati offers a decent amount of replayability. The distinctive design paired with a charming background music and sounddesign deals with the small cracks the repetitiveness opens, leaving me with an overall great experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I begin I'd like to make it known that I played very little of PC1 and 2. This one looked genuinely good so I gave it a shot. I know very little about the other 2 games and therefore will not be comparing this one to them. Please keep that in mind.If you've ever heard the term "death by a thousand cuts" that's what this game feels like. The core gameplay is overall fun; but there are SO many things that make no sense and don't work right that it becomes an annoyance to put up with. Things like when customizing your car and adding patterns, if you put a decal on your hood/roof/back of the car, you have to exit the pattern selector, exit the customization menu, go to photo mode, and move the camera around there to see what it actually looks like. And you will have to do this multiple times if you want to change the colors of said patterns. Btw there are only like 20 patterns in total which gets old very quickly. Things like having a car at the top of the class that can win races on hard, yet CANNOT beat hot laps/pace setter events no matter how many attempts I put in. Even tried a different car at the top of the class. Still no way that's happening.The career mode feels like a constant grind. I just finished C class (other than pace setter events because screw those to high hell and back) and I am having to grind just to get enough money for a B class car. I've been extremely careful with money in this game and man it is just constantly tight. From the moment you start racing in one class you have to save as much as possible for when you get to the next one.These are just 3 of the issues I've found. There are many many more fundamental problems with this game, some bigger, some smaller, and I really do hope they get fixed soon, because this does have potential to be a really great experience. The racing is very fun. The graphics are good for a modern game, the AI is challenging, even aggressive if you want them to be. Overall I can't say it's a bad game, just a good game with a lot of flaws. I can't say I regret buying it, but I can't I'd buy it at launch again either.

_childDocuments_.review: This game… oh boy. Let me start off by saying this: For all intents and purposes, Project CARS 3 is NOT a sim, at all. The ‘CARS’ in the title is supposed to mean ‘Community Assisted Racing Simulator’ which in this game’s case, isn’t even remotely true. There’s no mechanical damage, tire wear, fuel loss, or pit stops, and I can’t imagine how the racing sim community was ever involved with this particular game’s development. Every race is punctuated with obnoxious drum and bass that you’re quickly gonna want to mute, the AI treat every race like it’s a demolition derby regardless of aggression settings, and the menus & race UI can sometimes feel like they’re ripped out of a phone game.Now that anybody looking for a proper sim racer has rightfully stopped reading and moved on from this game, let me also say that I’m not the biggest simulation racing fan. I’m more of an arcade / simcade fan myself, so the fact that this game isn’t a diehard sim actually drew me to it in the first place. That said, I noticed how rough this game was at launch last year, so after spending some time with Rivals events, I put it in the backlog for about a year, played some other games, and got back to it a couple weeks ago while waiting for Forza Horizon 5 to come out. Now that I’m done with the career and DLC packs, I can confidently say this:I kept notes during my playtime of things that were getting on my nerves, and as I went on, the list ballooned in size. The thing is, this game is just not polished or well thought out, period.That’s not to mention the completely random crashes, complete with BugSplat error report messages, that randomly pop up when you go to start a race. Reboot the game, do the same race again, and it’s fine, until a few hours later when it isn’t, and so on. This one gets me, because it’s pretty obvious to me, that all the devs wanted to do post launch was add more cars and tracks as paid DLC, rather than try to fix the base game and its many small nuisances that just add up and ruin the experience.It’s such a shame too, because up until that one Road A championship in the snow, I honestly was enjoying this game a lot. After that nightmare of a championship, all I wanted to do was get the rest of it over with so I could move on and never think about it again. My advice? Stay far away from Project CARS 3, unless you’ve played every other modern racer to death, and you don’t mind something painfully mediocre that you can waste around 60-80 hours of your life on, and even then, don’t buy this at full price.

The camera angle swings out from those "sick drifts" when in chase mode to make things feel "awesome" but its just awkward and annoying. Cars feel heavy and slow but bounce around on the road and look unsettled on what are perfectly flat roads. The graphics are fine but that's it which is disappointing, the background feels flat and dull compared to what would be expected from a new title. The whole thing has just given up on being a sim to be a mediocre attempt at being an arcade game but lacks fun or accessibility of an arcade game. I quickly checked out quick race and had no cars unlocked because I have to collect myself which is just crap. The game feels like it doesn't know what it wants to be any more, it ruins fun by having forced progression and ruins dedication by being a half arsed attempt of an arcade racer. If you like that then good for you but fans of Project Cars will not be happy and its only a matter of time until they betray the new fans they are getting off being an arcade racing game. Even the community seems worse now with a sudden injection of new moronic fanbois who are attacking those who voice any complaint at all, telling long time fans to basically ♥♥♥♥ off to other games because they are no longer wanted, how can you disagree, it's what the devs have basically done.My advice is not only avoid this game but avoid the developer.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game with satysfying handling, but there are still lot of stupid/unfinished/broken features:- XP counting system - dont know who tought, that when you complete 20/20 races require to get XXXX XP points... you get 0, yes ZERO XP. There are tons of such XP tasks after every race like "finish 20 races with D car" or similar - its just punch in player's face!- Mastering corners/perfect line on track. Thats what i really liked in Shift 2, there was sense of this, you could look at statistics, and check, which track you have mastered. Not a case with PC3. Here you need to master EVERY CORNER AGAIN with new race on same track - EVERY F**** TIME. Sense? Specially, that mastering corners is BROKEN (03/2023) on some tracks (where task says, you HAVE TO master them) and there is not gonna be any fix!- Terrible AI - one of the worst, or simply the worst - no penalities for them when they cross the line, or smash at you (happen very often, they even push you out of the track). Unnatural grip and acceleration on corners.- AI - Hockenhaimring (or some similar name) is one of most terrible track. AI is so uneven, that you can beat them on most of tracks playing on gamepad on LEGENDARY difficulty, but once you get on that gerry track... oh boy, you're fu***d. Corners - 10000/10, acceleration - 50000/10, random mistakes - 0/10 - thats ai. On GTO whem you face electric volxwagen, you can forget about win, you have ANY chances only, when you equip same car (345 000 KR)- AI STUTTER/LAG - dont know how to name it. Basicly whole game runs perfect, but ai stutter in random ocassions. Fix for Nvidia users is turning ON Low Latency mode to Ultra (in nvcp), but for AMD users there is no fix till today (since release!)- Most stupid and broken progression system ever made in racing games. On each race you can get 3 stars for completing additional tasks (for example driviing in tail of other car for minute, mastering all corners, or getting clean sectors in row) - but completing those task is BUGGED and you can master all corners in some races, or get clean sectors, no matter how perfect you drove the race. This is absurd and madness.Game look ok, but thats all, PC2 was looking better IMHO. Dont waste time with this unfinished and abandoned game, dont trust those devs.Its still unclear to me, what is gaining XP in races, how much XP i gained on each lap - there is no such info. Same race, but completed different car in same class gives more XP? There is no better game for gamepad from this studio than Shift 2 tho.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - if you’re a car enthusiast, this game is dope AF. If you’re looking for more of a competitive esports experience or true motorsports experience, I can see how this game could disappoint.I don’t usually review games, but when I do it’s because I got duped by reviews. I’m a long time car enthusiast who loves buying and modding cars, tracks regularly, but has no interest in real life w2w racing. Even if I did, my wife would divorce me and take the kids. So I have a good sim setup instead. PC2 has been great for scratching that itch. Really terrific game in my opinion. I was excited for PC3 when it was released, but then the reviews came in and I passed. Recently decided to give it a go anyway since it was on sale, and man do I wish I had bought it sooner. The progressive acquisition of cars and upgrades is well done. Rewards aren’t too quick to accumulate which makes decisions meaningful. If you spend most of your day thinking about what cars/mods your next real paycheck is going towards, then deciding whether you’re going to run a C8 vs 911 vs GT-R vs NSX for C class is going to feel ridiculously satisfying. Driving dynamics are less realistic than PC2, but I personally think the balance they struck between arcade and sim feels good. Oversteer and weight transfer in PC2 are more difficult than actually being on track, which I attribute to not being able to feel what the car is doing. With all assists off in PC3, driving feels fun. More forgiving than on track but doesn’t punish you for not being able to feel when a front corner is loaded up.The exclusion of things like tire wear and pits is I think the right decision for this game as well. NO ONE on track likes having to throttle back for tire wear. If one of your tires starts chunking on a track day, it sucks. Full stop. I’m not saying tire strategy isn’t interesting in motorsports. I think it is. But getting to just run your best lap in the car you picked and built is more fun.I do think they left some potential on the table, like acquiring sponsors, meaningful tire/rim choices, visually representing aero changes, etc. But if you’re a car enthusiast, modder, track junkie, etc. you’re going to have a good time. Both PC2 and 3 are great games IMO. In a perfect world they would continue to support and update both with modern cars and racing teams. If I had to personally pick one though? It would be PC3.

_childDocuments_.review: An arcade racer in the mould of Driveclub with sophisticated physics requiring technique and skill, all whilst supporting steering wheels and VR?  Yes please!  Includes daily, weekly and Monthly leader board challenges along with 20 minute rotating online races and a long single player campaign to work through.  It's all out fun, all the time.It's not going to simulate the dour and grueling 24 hours of LeMans, but it will fill that 40 minutes you can spare with sliding sideways in the rain and swapping paint at every corner, whilst grinning like a loon.  That being said the leader board challenges are the stuff of 'one more try' that'll happily eat an extra hour or more.Do you even drift Brah?

_childDocuments_.review: Okay. So this game is getting a lot of heat, and I can understand the frustration with those of you who are upset by the change of direction/demographic this game is targeting. The problem, however, is that SMS probably made this decision based on the fact that sim players were never satisfied with the offerings from Project Cars so with experience in creating more user friendly racing games (NFS) why wouldn't they take a stab at appealing to a more casual audience? In my opinion, this is the kind of game needed to fill the Forza Motorsport hole that has been empty for a couple years. Being able to experience the world of Project Cars as a more casual player is actually great. The amount of hate being thrown around is the reason why the gaming industry is in the state it's in. Slightly Mad isn't out to steal your money, they're trying to make a fun game while constantly being harassed by consumers who simply cannot be satisfied.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: If you like GRID, Dirt and other more arcade racing with an enforced CAREER MODE and limited custom event options with locked cars and tracks, this is for you.Positives:1. It's a fun game.2. Career mode is straight forward3. The assist and be customized so you can feel like a damn pro4. Understeer be gone.  No more sliding off the track.Negatives.1. Zero freedom.  Career mode is forced on you2. No variety.  All the cars are locked behind a progression system.3. The vehicle you buy at the beginning is ALL YOU HAVE, in ANY EVENT.  Expect to spend tedious hours in road vehicles before you get the opportunity to unlock more.4. SteamVR and Oculus - I had shakey environments when I was in the home customizing my avatar, vehicle and browsing the menus.  First game to ever make me sick when sitting in a menu..5.  Forcefeedback in my Fanatec setup was nice, but take the HMD off, or alt tab, and come back to the game and your FFB is gone.This is NOT Project Cars game.  This is something else entirely.  While its not bad, don't buy it based on your love of PCars 1 and 2.  You're not getting more of the same here.  It feels a bit more like Dirt Rally.  But with the attitude of Dirt 2. (not rally, the older game that had energy drink sponsorship posted all over it.I will refund because its not worth the money.  But I would recommend it at 50 to 60% of current asking price.

_childDocuments_.review: PC3 actually is the best Sim/Arcade racing game on a good controller. The responsiveness and feeling of the different cars is very well done. Think about Forza + it's "Horizon" spinoff but one step better in terms of joypad support. I played on an X-Box Elite 2 one but as long as you have a good one with analog L/R triggers you are good to go.After reading all those negative comments I was really surprised to get an awesome joypad/controller racing game with an oldschool single player campaign. If it's that what you want, go for it! The game is seriously better than what people say about it. I understand the anger of some PC2 players though,
_childDocuments_.name: Project CARS 3

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly, I don't own Project Cars 1 or 2. I have been playing racing games since Outrun as a stand up arcade game, the first Need for Speed, Carbon, Forza, Grand Tourismo, you name it.This is a very slick and fun arcade game with great graphics and great driving physics that gets you on the track within a minute.It's not a driving simulator, I have played my buddies PC 2 and I understand how that is different.If you want to experiment with ride height, dampers, toe in, gear ratios and down force that you analyse in telemetry, stick to Project Cars 2.If you want to have a giggle with immersive graphics whilst playing on a game pad and necking a beer between rounds, this is the game for you.I read a lot of reviews about how easy and lame it is and I just don't see it that way. Perhaps they didn't tweak the AI to high and aggressive?I'm guessing this has the same physics package as PC2? Tear off the training wheels and it is a lot of fun.The tracks are great, plenty of actual circuits and really scenic made up ones.Great mixture of classics and modern hyper cars.If you don't get excited by Jackie Stuart's 1971 Lotus, you need schooling, I wonder if it comes with a spanner taped to the steering wheel.Throw in the Quest 2 and...just take my money....although I coughed up for the £75 deluxe version, which is toppy.V happy with this purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: PC3 is basically SMS abandoning their playerbase. However with the bias aside, the game still isn't very good.Graphics look like it's from a mobile game. Gameplay is grindy and feels lackluster. The racing itself feels shallow, and most of the "career" consists mostly of time-trial, and you don't have much saying in which activities you get to do.While the car and track selection isn't bad, it doesn't make up for how boring and grindy the game feels.Obviously this game can't really be compared to the other Project Cars games that balance between sim and simcade. It's interesting to see SMS' twist on a full on simcade title (even if they mess it up). If the game worked on the content it had, it could maybe be good enough for me to reccomend it, but the game feels like a barebones attempt at a car game.Of course if you yourself find enjoyment in the game, there's absolutely no shame in that. But the main thing about this game is that it by no means deserves the Project Cars title, and will probably forever be a stain on the series.
_childDocuments_.name: Project CARS 3

_childDocuments_.review: Project CARS 3 is a slap in the face to the community that helped build the franchise. They over promised and under-delivered and then got mad when they were not getting the reception that they were looking for from their community. From the looks of things, they decided to over-swing to the "Arcadey side" and basically said "We're not wrong for abandoning our fan-base, you're wrong for getting upset at what we're doing!" I feel like Project CARS 3 would have been awesome if they fleshed out what was working for them (Check out Automobilista 2 if you're wanting more of what made Project CARS 2 work...)... But ultimately, Project CARS 3 is a bargain bin title at best, a total mess at worst. STAY AWAY!
_childDocuments_.name: Project CARS 3

_childDocuments_.review: Huge fan of PC2, very disappointed in this installment. PC3 ditches the in-depth and detailed experience of the previous game in favor of a very arcade-like approach. Much fewer options/settings available to the player. The UI is annoying at its absolute best and the HUD is just plain terrible. Useful information has been ditched in favor of pretty colors and flashing lights. You are forced into the story mode/progression system whether you want to be part of it or not. In-game currency is required to simply tune your car. For reasons I don't understand, this is the only game I've ever played that doesn't seem to understand how my Logitech G29 shifter works; it thinks the second gear gate is 6th while getting the rest correct, save for 6th which apparently just doesn't exist. The upshot is a pretty solid set of cars, a track list that is more or less the same as PC2, and half-decent customization. Unfortunately, there is nothing else positive I can say about PC3.If you are more into NFS style games, this might be a decent game for you. If you are a fan of the previous Project Cars installments, I would strongly urge you to avoid PC3 and the massive let-down that will inevitably follow. Hopefully my refund will go through.
_childDocuments_.name: Project CARS 3

_childDocuments_.review: So- I do like this game, but coming from Project Cars 2, I can see why people "hate" it.But since I play on controller rather than the wheel I also understand why they did the changes they did. Comparing difficulty of driving physics from PC1 PC2 and this one its like comparing Audi RS8 with Fiat Panda--- there are no similarities. First thing one will notice is when using cockpit/helmet cam, once you turn and start sliding, hands (wheel) will be automatically adjusted- basically making it more arcade than its predecessors. Also- in my opinion AI is more forgiving, even with 100% aggressiveness.Overall- its a good simcade, if you are fan of more realistic driving, but not too realistic I would recommend project cars 1/2, if you are fan of really realistic driving there are asseto corsa and iRacer... or event BeamNG.But- if you are like me, and like both some challenge, but fun as well, and additionally- you are using controller, this one is the right one for you :)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a very disappointing sequel to PCars2. I get that the devs wanted to make the game more approachable for new players, but despite their claims, this was done at the expense of realism and simulation quality. I ran the game in VR with a force feedback wheel and three pedal setup (HTC Vive, Logitech G920), and still I feel like I'm driving a car strait out of the Need for Speed series. Even with force feedback maximized I could barely feel the car.In the 1 hour I've played this game, here's a short list of my issues with it:- Right out of the gate you're thrown into a race - without being given the option to adjust VR settings. I had to do the whole tutorial race with my "head" sticking through the top of my Corvette - c'mon devs...- There all all these weird sound effects that happen when you crash/spin that you can't turn off, even if the onscreen messages that those sound effects are for are turned off - very immersion breaking- Force feedback is just bad - too weak to be even remotely realistic- Some of the crash sounds (while more diverse than PCars2) sound very cheap - again, big hit to immersion.- Cool "Extra" features like being able to turn on/off windshield wipers or press a button to restart the car don't exist.- You can't select a rolling start- menus don't give detailed car information, like transmission type (which I use to determine whether to use paddles or 6spd H-Pattern shifter)- The menu music transitions from calming jazz / epic orchestral (PCars 2 style) to ear bleeding techno - seriously, who made that decision? Pick one feel or the other and stick with it.- All of the options / setting seem "boiled down" as in, PCars2 gave you various race rules, penalties, etc. that you could adjust values for. PCars 3 gives you an on/off toggle. That's it. It doesn't even tell you what the rules are...I guess that list wasn't so short. If you're looking for a fun pick up and play game that looks great and requires little effort, you'll enjoy this game. But let's be honest, if you're already a fan of this game series, that's not why you're here...
_childDocuments_.name: Project CARS 3
