_childDocuments_.review: An interesting game premise and plot that is somewhat let down by bad controls and stereotypical representations, but it worth playing nonetheless :)The interactivity of the game gives the player a sense of authority in dictating the unfolding of the story, yet the way choices and decisions are presented often leaves you wondering if in fact your choice impacted anything at all. This is the aspect of the game I enjoyed the most! Being given autonomy in the game, but questioning just how much power you actually have.The controls of the game are pretty lacking, with sudden changes in camera perspective causing you to move in  the wrong direction. I was consistently annoyed by direction and movement in the game working badly.Something else that rubbed me the wrong way is the depiction of every character that is not a white man. Seriously, this entire game is completely in the male gaze, with extremely sub par representations of literally any and every woman. The same goes for any non-white characters (which the game seems to be chronically lacking), often resorting to stereotypes.Overall, a pretty interesting story that (although lacking in many areas) is a very entertaining use of 10 or so hours :)

_childDocuments_.review: I played this because I have played Detroit and thought the latter was a great engaging game. You can see a lot of common elements between the two games. In the narrative flow, the structure, the mechanics, the aesthetic... it feels like their first draft for it. It is not all bad. The atmosphere is good. It looks nice for the time. You've got the start of good characters and some creative ideas. Scenes which could have been very cool and the whole concept is a good one. The music and sound effects are globally pretty good. It starts extremely boring with very long slow introducing scenes where you perform actions which are one step away from the Sims and a very cookie-cutter 'afternoon made-for-tv' presentation of the happy family before tragedy strikes. Nothing compelling or new here and it fails to create any emotional investment from the player. The game gets more engaging as the action kicks in and other characters are introduced (the FBI agent in particular, in which you can clearly see the first draft of Detroit's Conner). I can forgive a slow-start, starting a story is not easy and you learn how to interact with the game. Problem is, as things pick up so do plot holes. The game is completely story-driven. You do very little as a player so it relies entirely in how invested you are in seeing where things are going and solving the mystery. Here you have a harsh reminder that scenarist is a crucial and often undervalued job in video games. And that this job is not as easy as one might think it is. Nothing in this story holds up if you look at it from a logical perspective. The game keeps tripping itself up trying to be clever, opening narrative gaps they can't close and adding things which are outright lies to the player or just get forgotten and never explained to muddy the waters. The ending is so outlandish it retrospectively killed the story for me. You are also supposed to solve the mystery but end up not doing a lot of solving, you just perform very obvious actions and the thing solves itself for all characters (the FBI agent is the only one actually analysing things but even there you get very little clues, all from two locations) so you have no sense of working towards the ending.If you are interested in that kind of gameplay and haven't yet, go play Detroit. It is not perfect but it does some things really really well. If you have played Detroit, I would suggest you pass on this one and go see what else these people have worked on... that's what I'm going to do.

_childDocuments_.review: Heavy Rain instantly gained a cult following, becoming the game that people think of when they hear the words "interactive cinema". Critics praised it with top scores, and the promotional materials promised a lot. "A movie you can control!" they wrote in the advertisements.The game was a success, leaving a noticeable cultural impact and making the name of its director and writer, David Cage, a household name. Heavy Rain stood out from other AAA games of the time, valuing cinematography above everything else and offering a minimalist gameplay based on Quick Time Events (QTE), which became the hallmark of Quantic Dream, the French game studio behind it.Even such a simple gameplay turned out to be more than enough to engage players in the story. Many people who had never been interested in games before became interested thanks to Heavy Rain. The emotionality, the plot, and the characters - all these elements played a role in this. Although the management can be unsettling at times, it has helped create a sense of presence.An impressive story and deep emotional immersion - Heavy Rain remains a masterpiece that deserves attention.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a latecomer to this game, but despite it being from 2011, it did not disappoint. Heavy Rain is a heavily story-driven game about an investigation on a serial killer known as the 'Origami Killer'. The story is a little slow to start and get going, but once it does, it keeps you hooked. It lets us witness the events from 4 leading characters, all of which are in some way affected by the unfolding events. The characters are well-developed and life-like in their motivations and behaviours. The game touches on some heavy themes regarding loss of loved ones and kids being hurt. And it does put us in situations where we sometimes have to make some pretty hard choices. Some of the choices also substantially change some of the scenes and could even lead to some characters dying before the end of the game.The gameplay mainly involves point-and-click interactions with the environment so to get the plot moving along. And during dialogues we can often choose what to say. During action scenes there are quick-time events, so we need to be alert. Most of the QTEs aren't hard, but they can at times be annoying as there are so many of them, and some feel a bit lengthier than they should be. So if you're going for this game, go for it mainly for the story, characters and difficult choices rather than the gameplay.Lastly, if you encounter a somewhat common glitch where the game freezes (or rather the visuals just freeze), there's an easy fix on the Quantic Dream website. Go to 'Section 4: MY GAME CANNOT RUN, EVEN THOUGH I HAVE A LAPTOP MEETING THE MINIMUM SPECIFICATIONS'.
_childDocuments_.name: Heavy Rain

_childDocuments_.review: I was happy to finally play some of these older previously Playstation exclusive titles on Steam, starting with Heavy Rain. The game is an interactive story (similar to Telltale Games) with a psychological thriller theme similar to the Saw films. Most of the game play consists of quick time events, interacting with objects in rooms and choosing dialogue.The story was good and keeps you interested in finding out more, even if some parts don't make perfect sense. It's a short game, took me about 10 hours to complete but I imagine this can differ slightly based on choices you make and depending on what ending you receive. I would expect somewhere between 9 - 13 hours total.Some parts of the game were quite annoying throughout, such as the lack of description on objects and choices as you interact with them. The game doesn't always make it clear which buttons perform each action which can lead your character to perform an action you didn't intend to. The fixed camera angles don't help with this and I could often find my character walking out of a room and then immediately walking back in as the camera changes but I'm still holding down the same direction on my controller. It's worth noting I was frequently having frame rate drops throughout the game (I'm running off a GTX 1070 and an i7 6700k which can handle much newer and more detailed games with no problems) I'm assuming this is due to the age of the game and the port but annoying none the less.Despite all of this the game was enjoyable and my girlfriend also enjoyed watching the story as a back seat gamer, the soundtrack was very well done and it's worth a playthrough just to hear Ethan shout "JAAAASON".

_childDocuments_.review: I seem to remember playing this game on PS3 12 years  ago, when it originally released.I bought it on Steam 2 years ago, "old time's sake" factor at play.I recall not enjoying all of the mundane  tasks you need to do, and the overabundant number of QTEs, some requiring perfect timing (the sword fight, for example). But the game has  a very good story, if you can follow it through all of the QTEs and pointless tasks you can or have to do."Old time's sake" is not making the game's PC version enjoyable. I am honestly not likely to complete it here on Steam.I am older now, and both slower reflexes and arthritis are making it difficult to play, even though I know what I need to do to get everything done. The kb/m controls are some of the most awkward and painful ones I have seen in a game for quite some time. The controller works much better (IF you know to disable Steam Input in the game's properties menu- this issue popped up with a number of games, once Valve started messing around with controller configs in advance of the Steam Deck release),Controls and far too many QTEs are really making the game far less engaging, immersive, and enjoyable- it should feel much better, and the story should be the focus- not "Oh, hell, what kind of clunky weird QTE actions am I going to have to do next?".Great story, animations (especially facial anims) were good in 2010 (when the game first released on PS3) but are a bit distracting 12 years later. The music is fantastic. The setting is good- it conveys the mood quite well, but is tough on the eyes if you have vision limitations or any form of color-blindness. But the controls on both kb/m and controller are killing the enjoyment for me, and taking me away from the story-building and character development- 2 things the game relies heavily on.I will keep trying to play it to the end, but I have to admit I should have let this one live in the memory of playing it 12 years ago.Maybe get it on deep discount, if you have never played it before, and want to experience a really moving and deep story. But if you have any Accessibility issues with hands, reflexes and/or low vision- probably best to skip this one.

_childDocuments_.review: First released for PS3 in 2010, Heavy Rain still holds up as a decent game—even in 2022. Naturally, it feels a bit dated but not nearly as much as it could be for a 12-year-old game. I had played through Heavy Rain multiple times close to its original release, greatly enjoying it. After all these years, I enjoyed playing it once again. If you're already a Heavy Rain fan looking to give it another go, I highly recommend it at a $10 price point when it's on sale.If you haven't played Heavy Rain but are familiar with it and a fan of similar games, I highly encourage giving the game a chance as well.If you somehow find yourself checking this review out with little to no prior knowledge of Heavy Rain, then you should expect a cinematic third-person adventure with quick-time events and dialogue choices. It has a good story, soundtrack and visuals and—in my opinion—holds a place in video game history as an influential title, helping propel this style of game to prominence. If any of that sounds appealing to you, then I highly encourage you to check it out when you can.

_childDocuments_.review: (forget my low hours on this game, I originally played it on PS3)Heavy Rain is one of one those games that makes me wish steam had a better review system than a dumb thumbs up/down, It has its pluses and it's negatives which entirely overwrite such an old binary yes/no system. Anyway that's my rant about steam itself being poor over, now onto the game itself.Gameplay:Heavy rain is game that's plays like a point and click adventure (think Monkey Island/Broken Sword) with the controls being QTE based (like some of my favorite games (Big Up Shenmue 1-2))I won't go into much detail of the story itself, so as to not spoil anything. Effectively, the game plays almost like a choose your own adventure, seeing the intersecting story from several perspectives to come to one of the multiple endings depending on your choices throughout the game. When this originally came out in 2010 that was a pretty novel idea, I don't think there's many games that play this way, outside of Quantic Dreams own releases, there's a few using multiple playable characters, but not many. Which gives them a point for originality.Controls:Unfortunately the controls are incredibly imprecise (or overly precise, I haven't really figured that out yet on this version) which ends up breaking your sense of immersion pretty constantly. (Opening a cupboard shouldn't really feel like your trying to climb a mountain) The semi tank controls also constantly bug out as the camera changes. (I'm an OG Resident Evil Player and I think that still had better movement controls).Sound:The sound effects and music of heavy rain are one of the best things about this game, and do a great job of creating an overbearing atmosphere of constant dread and unease. However, the English overdub is almost laughable, completely immersion breaking with speaking at times in a tone of voice that completely throws immersion out. Do yourself a favor and play in the original french with subtitles on (if you can manage to keep with the questionable controls for long enough to actually play the game).Graphics:I always leave graphics to last when I write a proper review, because it's what a care about the least. I've played everything from TextMUDS on Commodore 64, to the latest triple A titles and great game play will always, ALWAYS beat great graphics in every way. Which is something I feel is a negative about this heavy rain. I feel that Quantic put far more time and effort into the (admittedly great) graphics of this game rather than refining the far more important controls.In Conclusion, Heavy rain is a great game if you can struggle through the poor controls and play it in the proper language setup. 6.5/10 (Fahrenheit was better)

_childDocuments_.review: Quantic Dreams big interactive movie, originally released for the PS3 and now available for PC.The story: It is an interactive drama. You mostly play Ethan Mars whose son is abducted by the Origami-Killer, a serial killer and a bit saw-like he is send increasingly dangerous tasks to rescue him. All while he is on the run from the police who think Ethan is the culprit. The other playable characters are Norman a FBI profiler assigned to the Origami-Killer case and in constant clash with the local police who just want to present any culprit, Scott a private investigator working on the case and Madison a reporter and potential love interest for Ethan. Story and characters are a bit cliché and the writers use some cheap tricks to hide the identity of the killer till the end but it is still the story that kept me interested in the game.The gameplay: In short it is bad and I sometimes wished the game would be a visual novel so I could enjoy the story without the gameplay. On PS3 the game use the tilt the controller feature extensively which translates to draw stuff with your mouse on PC. And besides this it is quicktime events, lots and lots of annoying quicktime events. It took me a while to understand that the developers choose this on purpose. They want the possibility that a player fails a quicktime sequence and by extend fail a task maybe even have one of the characters die as a consequence which leads to a branching storyline.  The problem is this needs a certain type of players, one that is willing to accept failure and go on instead of simply loading a checkpoint.The graphic looks nice during the close-ups of the characters while the game loads. But the real game graphics can hardly hide the fact that Heavy Rain was released in 2010.The game does not include the DLC “The Heavy Rain Chronicles“ because it is not available for PC.

_childDocuments_.review: Always wanted this game when it first came out but did not have a PS3.  So was great to see it get a PC release.  Yes, was some slowdown and stuttering issues, but did not distract me too much from the game.  I say game, but really this is more of an interractive move.  The storyline is top notch and it has a Hollywood production like script.  If you are into Call of Duty like games, fast action, etc, I doubt this may interest you too much.  However if you prefer a great story, plot paths that you can dictate and the odd key press to perform an action - you cannot go wrong.  This is up there with the best (perhaps THE best) storyline I have discovered in a game and will stay with me for a long time.Only real downside (by some performance issues) were the controls for movement, but that is a minor issue when you take everything into account.Highly recommended

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to enjoy this Game very badly, since it came sooo well recommended. And since i love the idea of games which are not linear, but your choices matter.Unfortunately the controlling is so unforgivable clumsy and it happened too often, that the person starts walking into the wrong direction because the camera angle switches (which is soo frustrating when time is of the essence).The switching of the camera angle is such a nice cinematic tool, but since it does that, i ended up not always knowing all my options i had in desperate situations, because the button kept bouncing off screen.fights were no fun at all with that controlling and i think on a console it would be much more enjoyable.i also think the fact that you can't run, but only walk (at least in my controling i couldn't), takes a lot of the suspense away: "time is running out, but it's enough for walking"...I think this game was way ahead at its time and still stands with a few hence the storytelling and intertwining storystrings. this is now almost 11 years ago. i have the feeling a lot of its praises live from nostalgia. i also have games like that, which some might not consider playing, but i had my time with them.This game maybe also got a bad pc port.in the end i felt very unstatisfied because it seemed the controls took away some choices and abilities to solve some situations.

_childDocuments_.review: I swear I've never sweated so much while playing a game. Heavy Rain is definitely at the top of my ranking of my favorite games. What remains to be said is that David Cage is an absolute genius. He made a real masterpiece - a fabulous game, but also a great movie, a masterpiece that deserves to be played and watched by everyone.

Some scenes are really intense.	- Game looks good for its time, I thinkCons:	- The story changes slightly depending on the choices you make, but in the end it doesn't make a huge difference. There is no branching of the story (except at the very end), only scenes you might miss if you take the wrong/right decisions.	- The game relies a bit too much on QTEs.        - Story has some really big plot holes. From what I understand some part of the plot was dropped after the initial draft, and it shows. Kinda embarrassing for a story-focused game.

_childDocuments_.review: *Heavy Rain* is a masterclass in interactive storytelling, blending a gripping narrative with intense emotional depth. The game's plot is nothing short of phenomenal, weaving a complex web of intrigue, suspense, and heart-wrenching drama. Each decision you make feels weighty and consequential, pulling you deeper into the story as you unravel the mystery behind the Origami Killer.The drama is palpable, with every twist and turn pushing the characters to their limits. The emotional stakes are incredibly high, making it impossible not to get invested in their fates. What truly sets *Heavy Rain* apart is its ability to make you feel the pressure of each choice, knowing that a single misstep could lead to tragic outcomes.This is not just a game—it's an experience that challenges your moral compass and tests your emotional resilience. *Heavy Rain* is a must-play for anyone who appreciates a narrative-driven game with profound dramatic impact.

_childDocuments_.review: Story's pretty interesting, controls are annoying to deal with. And I was playing on a controller, I can't imagine how annoying keyboard and mouse must have been with this. Sometimes the quick time events aren't easily distinguishable from each other (do I hold the button? do i repeatedly tap? do i alternate? do i quick tap?), so you'll most likely fail and redo at least a handful of them, most sections. There are so many QTEs and they're Extremely fast, so I recommend to players who have a hard time with that, playing on an easier level of difficulty. Gameplay is basically: explore and find things, QTEs, dialogue choices, and character/story choices (the regular for Quantic Dream). Sometimes game directions weren't clear and I missed things because I didn't know what the game was asking for OR i /did/ know, but I couldn't figure out how the game expected me to do it. It's pretty clunky overall, but if you can get through it, the story's entertaining. The voice acting is really gripping at parts and then falls really flat at most other parts. The characters occasionally act so bizarrely/alien-like, that they'll pull you out of immersion. Graphics are pretty decent! You can tell the mistakes they made in this game, they tried to fix and smooth out in Detroit Become Human. If you enjoy Choices Matter games, you'll probably enjoy this, but I recommend getting it on sale bc the controls are a pain.

_childDocuments_.review: This review may sound negative.. and in a way it is.. but the game is actually really good as a interactive crime miniseries. So I will put all the bad out there so you know what to expect, but the game is entertaining. I'll probably never play it again after beating it once, but I rarely ever replay games.Game has great story and still impressive graphics as of 2023, but if you hate quick time events like me it will be annoying or even unplayable for some. Literally everything is a quick time event!!! A single fight scene can be upwards 20+ quick times in a row as that is literally the only control you have for everything. Not just one or two possible buttons to hit either, but every darn button on the gamepad is a potential QTE trigger. Personally I don't have every button memorised by name so occasionally hit wrong one while trying not to get killed in a QTE fight. RB, RT, LB, LT, X, Y, A, B, right joy up, left, right, down, in circles, in a specific shape!!! Seriously draw a scythe shape with the right joystick to avoid an attack or do an attack!! Good luck making that shape which is popular in the game for interacting with stuff unless you check the discussion forum and find out how to set your gamepad deadzone to a + shape instead of a O shape... Yeah I had no clue what that meant either until I read the instructions in the discussion. Either way before that the shape was quite literally impossible on an XBox Gamepad.Also the controls for everything that is not QTE is pretty bad. Walking is really janky and can take several tries to even line up with a light switch. Think original Resident Evil level of bad walking controls and then make them a bit worse. Some things require you to press and hold buttons until that button disappears on screen to do something. Occasionally this can be around 5 buttons at once in random orders that requires an impressive game of Twister with your fingers. For example... Press Y.. not while holding Y add LT.. now add RB... now add X... Add B... now while holding all those move the right joystick in a certain direction at a certain speed or start all over because you failed.. Luckily even though I loathe QTE in games and the controls are like a tank struggling in mud with a cross-eyed driver behind the wheel, the story is strong enough to keep me playing to the end.If not for the controls and never-ending QTEs I would give it a 10/10. Hating the controls and truly despising QTE in general I give it a 7/10 merely due to great story and acting.  Plus it only took 10 hours to beat. Most of that was like watching a miniseries. Luckily I got the best possible ending so will probably never play it again. Got it on sale for next to nothing so can't complain. Definitely got my money worth, but would have been less happy at full price when it was released given my complete disdain for QTEs. lolBasically it's an interactive movie with some walking around between scenes and a constant stream of QTE to determine the out comes of most of the scenes.  Oh also at times it is really hard to tell what the dialogue options are as they are swirling around and at times fuzzy/blurred/occasionally hidden by camera. If you don't choose one in time then they all go away and you no longer can continue the conversation to find out stuff like clues.  Still even with all that I still give it a 7 for story and acting. Was going to play Detroit Become Human next, but need a QTE break. Gonna be having QTE nightmares for the next week. lol Excellent story though! Worth it for that.

_childDocuments_.review: Starting with positives:- relation father-son is created well, they tried to build it (not that common),- main idea is good.This game has many small issues, but they are irrelevant and I will speak about them later. However, it also commits the biggest crime of story-based games. Your choices are ignored.I had situation - two times - in which in-game conversation implied that I made different choice than I made. I know that I made unpopular decisions, but hey, they were in game!Sometimes there is also illusion of choice (like in Fallout 4). You have two opposite dialog options, but no matter which one you choose, it ends in the same way.There is also many moments in which you have a choice to jump over or go around. For me, those choices are irrelevant. But I understand that they may increase immersion.There are immersion breaking elements, like "magic" glasses of FBI detective. It just does not fit.Story looks nice at the beginning, but with time it has less and less sense. Especially the very end makes no sense.There are also four playable characters, so there is not much time to develop them.  This game is QTE simulator, so it's also good to mention that without a pad controller, it's almost impossible to play that game.And small (imho, not breaking game) spoiler, but very big minus for me: And bigger spoiler: The game is also short.

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to QTE-Hell.  Shenmue 2 has nothing on this nightmare of awkward button presses.A game set in the depths of the Uncanny Valley where the controls are jank, the children are suicidally stupid, and the Origami Killer is the fat bastard Scott Shelby (haha!) .... and if you believe I've just ruined the game for you, don't worry. The game came pre-ruined. Let me just lay it out for you... Pros:+ This game is so bad it is sometimes funny. Like totally ridiculous, and most of it is because it is trying to be serious and failing.  And that is it.  That is the only pro.  A completely accidental one.  The only reason to play this game is to laugh at how bad it is.  At least every chapter tells you the size of Shelby's erection, but it never quite reaches average.Cons:- : The controls are janky as hell. It needs a steam overlay controller fix to even be playable at all, and even when you've got that, characters will repeatedly go in the wrong direction, get stuck on objects, or the wrong QTE trigger will be highlighted.  In fact, the QTE issues need a separate mention they're just that bad.- : Those QTEs... where to even start?  This game is full of them and most of them are unintuitive.  They're displayed in faded white on the screen, which is sometimes nigh invisible. The icons themselves are often difficult to distinguish, since left and right or up and down look near identical when you've got less than a second to figure it out (without getting it wrong).  And that is without considering that they're often bouncing around like a kid on red bull, occasionally upside-down, and it is hard to be sure whether the game wants you to push the button, hold the button, hit the button, let go of the button, etc   since the inputs look too similar.  Given the entire game is based on them, there is no excuse for them being so bad. - : Ah yes, and the "difficulty" settings being called stuff like "I play games occasionally" or whatever.  The hell does that mean?  I play TONS of games, but that doesn't mean I want extra-stupor level bullsh!t QTE crap thrown in my face.   Say what you fŭcking mean, Devs. - : I think they were trying to go for realism with the characters,  but instead they dived headfirst into the uncanny valley and never came back.   Ethan is like a robot in an awkward-fitting human costume and the other playable characters aren't really any better.  At least the silly sods at Quantic Dream realised they were incapable of making believable humans and decided to run with the robot thing. - : Extra robot-points for having no damned clue how children of 10 years behave.  Between the obsessive drive to kill themselves at any cost, the mental age of 5-year-olds, and the occasional recitation of the most cheesy and contrived lines imaginable, it is safe to say nobody at Quantic Dream was ever a human child.  Beep boop.  Be careful not to send them ReCaptcha tests. - : Ah, the "plot". I believe this is what most people like about the game.  Except it kinda shows when you try too hard but don't have the wits to back it up, nor bring an overly ambitious story to closure. Clearly someone had been watching the Saw films and decided to copy the idea,  but couldn't do it right.  The story really pushes hard on the angle that Ethan is the killer with the blackouts and waking up in the rain with an origami figure in his hand, so it was immediately obvious that he wasn't.  And sure enough, nothing ever game of those weird scenes besides convincing the world's worst psychopath in the police force that Ethan had to be killed at all costs (I hate the police as much as the next guy, but Blake is just ridiculous).  Then you've got Norman Jayden, who just seems to be a simultaneous shout-out to CSI Miami and the Matrix and is also a drug-zombie for some reason or other.  Never explained, never explored, just used for cool-dude scenes that utterly destroy any sense of tension (also apparently he looked very different in the original, but now he looks like Rick Astley, which just magnifies the silliness of everything he does).  OH... and have I mentioned Scott?- : Scott Shelby, i.e. the Zodiac Killer, that is the big freakin twist of the whole game,  except he was the most likely suspect right from the start (not being pushed by the story like Ethan, Norman and even Madison were), and it was proven beyond a shadow of a doubt in the clock shop (since there were only two people in the building and the camera was locked on the other one, with no way for anyone else to get in nor out). - : There is no skipping of cutscenes (including the ending credits), no skipping dialogue, no fast-forward past things you've already seen.  And the game requires repetition (for achievements, for endings, for the inevitable QTE failures).  This makes an already frustrating game all the moreso.  So yeah.   I'd heard good things about this game, but they were all wrong.

_childDocuments_.review: Heavy Rain revolves around a father's desperate search for his missing son, exploring themes of love, loss, and the weight of choices. The story unfolds through the perspectives of four playable characters, each with their own motivations and internal struggles, allowing players to deeply connect with their experiences.Character AnalysisEthan Mars: As the father, Ethan’s pain and desperation drive the narrative. His character development showcases the strength of paternal love and the trauma of loss, with players feeling the emotional conflict in his choices.Madison Paige: A journalist pursuing the truth, Madison’s storyline reveals her bravery amidst complex circumstances. Her relationship with Ethan adds emotional depth, enriching the overall narrative.Norman Jayden: An FBI agent, Norman represents the intersection of technology and humanity. His use of high-tech devices contrasts with his internal struggles, highlighting the moral dilemmas in the quest for truth.Scott Shelby: Initially presented as a private detective, Scott’s complex motivations are revealed, culminating in a plot twist that challenges perceptions of good and evil.Thematic AnalysisChoices and Consequences: Every decision significantly impacts character fates and the storyline. This mechanic immerses players in the gravity of their choices, particularly during critical moments where missteps can lead to character deaths, amplifying the tension.Love and Loss: The game profoundly explores paternal love and the anguish of loss, especially through Ethan’s narrative. His struggles encourage players to reflect on the fragility of familial bonds.Moral Dilemmas: Characters face moral choices that prompt players to consider the boundaries between justice and revenge. The different perspectives highlight the complexity of human nature.ConclusionHeavy Rain successfully crafts an emotional journey through its intricate plot and multi-dimensional characters. While there are some control issues, the engaging narrative and the emphasis on choice make it a highly recommended experience for players who enjoy story-driven games.
_childDocuments_.name: Heavy Rain

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. What a great game and incredible story. Although there is much to be desired when it comes to the acting, and sometimes, with the writing. (mostly the acting tbh)SPOILER ALERT!!!I actually got really upset about Scott Shelby because he was my favorite character throughout. And even after, I was so torn about fighting him. But damn.. I guess that says something about the writing.I don't really have any strong complaints about the writing, but I was definitely left questioning why so many voices sounded like foreign people whose first language was not english? Most notably, Lauren and Scott and John. Like why did it sound like the voice actors were foreigners whose second language was english? I don't mind if it plays into the story, but it didn't play into the story at all, so it was really just kind of off-putting.Otherwise, this was an intense game with so many moments that are memorable, and several times where it was a downright cliffhanger and I couldn't stop playing. I really really enjoyed the ARI technology, loved the mystery, was grateful for the brief romance moments, and overall I think it was well-written with characters I could actually care about. I loved the gameplay as someone who doesn't really enjoy action-heavy gameplay, but most of all, the writing was superb. I was left on the edge of my seat and shocked more often than not.8/10 for Scott Shelby alone. Before the final act, I was ready to say "I want Scott Shelby to adopt me" lol. But after the final act, I am ready to say "I want to have a beer with Norman Jayden." (maybe I still want Scott Shelby to adopt me, but that's something for me and my therapist to unpack)Great experience. Feels like a game that is required playing for anyone who enjoys story-rich games like this.

_childDocuments_.review: How Far Will You Go To Save Someone You Love? Experience a gripping psychological thriller filled with innumerable twists and turns, where choices and actions can result in dramatic consequences. Spanning four days of mystery and suspense, the hunt is on for a murderer known only as the Origami Killer - named after his macabre calling card of leaving behind folded paper shapes at crime scenes. Four characters, each following their own leads and with their own motives, must take part in a desperate attempt to prevent the killer from claiming a new victim. [Sony]

name: Beyond: Two Souls
detailed_description: Triple-A talent and storytelling brings you a video game experience like you’ve never had before. LIVE AN EXTRAORDINARY LIFE: ONE LIFE, TWO SOULS A unique psychological action thriller delivered by A-list Hollywood performances by Elliot Page and Willem Dafoe , Beyond: Two Souls™ takes you on a thrilling journey across the globe as you play out the remarkable life of Jodie Holmes. Born with a connection to a mysterious entity with incredible powers, Jodie is different. Your actions will determine Jodie's fate as she faces extraordinary challenges, danger, and heart-wrenching loss on a journey to discover the truth of who she is. Create an action-packed story through your choices and actions as you live her life – a girl born with a link to a supernatural entity called Aiden. By playing as both Jodie and Aiden, you will face spectacular physical and psychological challenges to understand what truly lies… beyond. TEST YOUR SKILLS WITH ‘ADVANCED EXPERIMENTS’ The original DLC mission from the PlayStation™ releases is included in the full PC game. The entire game is playable in two difficulty modes, and in Solo or Duo mode. PLAY THE STORY THE WAY YOU WANT Cinematic or chronological order? Select the way you want to experience the story, and even play in local co-op mode using two different controllers for each player – one to play as Jodie and the other to play as Aiden. Play the way you want to play. FULLY OPTIMIZED FOR PC Beyond: Two Souls is brought to PC with stunning visuals including 4K resolution, widescreen 21:9 compatibility, and 60 fps framerate.

_childDocuments_.review: For the intriguing story alone I can recommend to get this game.How you succeed in the action scenes and which dialog options you choose affect how the story advances. How much difference they make I cannot say for sure, unless I replay the game. The core story should remain roughly the same, since the story was originally designed to be played in unchronological chapters. There's an option to play chronologically. I personally chose to play the game as designed and it gave the fascinating feeling of building a puzzle to understand the characters and the events.I found that the controls fell short somewhat due to their clumsiness, but it's also possible that I'm just an inept gamer. The camera was all over the place in some scenes, adding its own unwelcome challenge to playing the game.The stealth scenes felt pretty ridiculous at times and did not seem to take into consideration how audible it is to slam someone against the ground and punch them dead, not forgetting the unlucky victim's groans. That's mainstream action movies for you, so I'll give the game a pass there.The game was released in 2013 and the graphics reflect that, but I would say they were decent and don't push the player away from the game.All in all, poor controls, tricky camera angles and some unbelievable action scenes, but incredible story that makes up for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Among all of the titles that Quantic Dream worked on, I knew the least about Beyond: Two Souls. It got some buzz around it due to very high profile actors before release, yet after the game was out not a lot of people seemed to care much about it. Even the biggest Quantic Dream fanboys seemed to be more excited about the potential for more Fahrenheit or Heavy Rain, or were raging about how good Detroit is. Heck, even a potential sequel to Omikron seemed more exciting to people then talking about Beyond. Granted, maybe that was only in the parts of the internet that I’ve frequented as it seems that the game actually won some awards on release and had quite a few positive reviews. Yet, all I knew about it was that it was somewhat passable and not particularly interesting, and that it had William Dafoe and Elliot (then Ellen) Page in main roles.And now that I’ve finally had a chance to play it for myself, I can kinda see why it had this weird reception.The main “gimmick” of Beyond is the presence of an Entity named Aiden tied to our main character Jodie that essentially gives her (or rather him, usually upon her request) special powers like telekinesis or reading the past events from people or items. As such, you often have an option to press a button and become this entity, who has his own way of interacting with the world, and many of the problems in the game are solved by the pair working together. While it feels like a really cool idea and is originally presented as this wonderful fully controllable floating ability, as the game goes on, the ability to play as Aiden becomes incredibly limited and often frustrating due to how terrible the controls are. And sometimes, against the narrative or gameplay logic, the ability to switch to Aiden is simply disabled because of some reasons.But let’s return to the issue of controls in the game, because somehow Quantic Dream managed to devolve them with each next title. What was novel (if often silly) and quite easy to understand in Fahrenheit, because every action was clearly labeled, became harder to understand in Heavy Rain, because the motion prompts were placed in some general vicinity of an object to interact with, sometimes leading to completely unexpected results. But Beyond: Two Souls goes even further and simply places some vague dots near objects that you interact with by pressing the right stick towards them. All while: a) keeping the control of the camera still tied to the same stick leading to constant accidental interactions despite most of the buttons being unmapped and b) sometimes the camera rapidly changes as it waits for the interaction yet only one of the directions is considered correct to start the interaction and you have to simply guess which one.In addition to that if you play on the default difficulty, the game doesn’t actually tell you the directions you must press in QTE segments and you have to just guess them based on the animations. Which is especially hilarious since the action sequences with QTEs constantly break the 180 degree rule almost mid-interaction so understanding the intended directions is even harder. And in addition to that, lots of these segments contain some sort of automated movement, but some don’t and require you to move. And there’s absolutely no tell. What’s amazing about this is that the “easier difficulty”, which I recommend switching to if you value your sanity (while being insane enough to choose playing this game), is called “I don’t play games often”, even though what it does is shows what buttons to press in this completely context-sensitive button game, which is what other games actually do because they know that expecting players to just “know” what your hidden intent with button presses was, that changes with every next scene, is simply disrespectful.Yet, people tend to be attracted to Quantic Dream titles for their “cinematic stories” and I must say that Beyond: Two Souls might be their best attempt yet (again, I’ve not played Detroit at the moment of writing this). It’s not great, in fact it’s not good, but it’s considerably better done than whatever they’ve attempted before. There’s more consistency in characters, more actual story-telling instead of the game being just a collection of barely related scenes and episodes, more of a central theme. Don’t get me wrong here, there’s still a fair amount of ridiculous, tone deaf moments, obnoxiously long episodes that barely have to do with anything at all and idiotic character writing. And the very-very end of the game almost gets to the levels of stupidity on the level of Fahrenheit. But it’s more consistent and… fine.Which, ironically, is somewhat to the detriment of the game. Omikron tried to be many things at once, just like this game, and also failed, but it was far more ambitious and still has some unique ideas in its non-linearity. Fahrenheit still has some of the best opening parts to any games and by the end becomes such a fascinating train wreck that it’s hard to avert eyes. Heavy Rain is a mix of idiocy and some genuinely memorable moments and this almost surreal mix of elements makes it interesting. But Beyond: Two Souls has some nice gameplay ideas, some nice segments, some nice acting, and some stupid elements, but most of it is just “okay”. Never absolutely horrible, even when it desperately wants to be a stealth game and fails. Never memorable either. It’s very reminiscent of Omikron, in that this constantly feels like a game that could be good, but just isn’t (and also thanks in many ways to its controls). Yet, if I’m honest, I’d rather see Omikron remade or continued than this.There are some absolutely bizarre decisions as well. The narrative, for example, is told in fragments that are told out of order. Which does help the story in that it creates mini-mysteries out of otherwise insignificant “revelations”, yet it’s clearly a crutch, because without it the story would be even less interesting. Yet, for whatever reason, the PS4 and PC version of the game allow you to play the game in the chronological order. Probably because the reviews criticized it and the studio thought that this is the solution? I haven’t tried it, but I doubt that it’d make the story more interesting instead of less. Also there was a DLC for the game that is included with the PS4 and PC releases, that is an attempt to make the game work like a puzzle game with a Portal-like vibe. Yet it doesn’t really work and also it’s clear that the actors weren’t involved at all, so seeing the digital body of Elliot Page smile to some terrible writing in this cash grab of a DLC felt kinda disgusting.Beyond: Two Souls is a really strange game to talk about. I cannot in good faith recommend playing it, because the playing part is absolutely terrible, the worst out of everything Quantic has done, including Omikron. Yet, I feel like watching someone play this isn’t going to be that interesting either, unlike their previous titles which are fun to watch. But at the same time, it feels like a game that had the most potential to be really good out of them. If it wasn’t written by people who can’t write for crap, if the controls were made with humans in mind, if it was shorter and tighter this could’ve actually been a solid game. Heck, at times it felt like Life is Strange 2 was basically ripping this game off and, somehow, often for the worst and people like that one. Speaking of which, it must be noted that this is the game where Quantic saw the popularity of Telltale’s The Walking Dead and decided to show the choices outright at the end of each chapter, something every game of this sort seems to do lately. Anyways, it’s hard to recommend this game, but I cannot really not recommend it at all either. It’s not fun to play and is kinda boring to watch, but it could’ve been something. _childDocuments_.review: An interesting interactive movie.I'm not a big fan of the Quantic Dream control scheme which combines mouse motions, press-and-hold, press-and-hold-multiple-keys, and rapidly pressing keys on the keyboard (or clicking the mouse). I was seriously repulsed by it in Heavy Rain, which I've given up after just 2 hours, but Beyond was significantly more "gentle" (since it's not a horror story unlike Heavy Rain), so I managed to complete the game in about 9 hours.The story is interesting and if you play it in the original way (with out of order chapters), you will really want to know how it all fits together.In Beyond, you play as Jodie, a girl/woman gifted/cursed by a connection with an entity named Aiden who can use telekinesis and mind control to disrupt the world, take control of people, or even choke them to death. This ability/connection puts Jodie on a collision course with spy agencies and secret research laboratories.There are apparently multiple ways you can play through the game - most often, it's about choosing one of several possible approaches to a given problem ("Do I spook the person by using Aiden's supernatural abilities, or do I talk my way through?"), but based on the statistics screens at the end of each chapter, some choices expand the chapters and open additional content which you might miss otherwise. This is an obvious motivation to play the game multiple times, trying different approaches.The game has solid production values, with full motion capture of all the scenes, with 2 Hollywood stars taking the lead. The game flows really well, there are not many  moments.

_childDocuments_.review: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ THAT WAS AMAZING. THAT WAS A LESSON TAUGHT FOR WHAT LIFE IS.Quantic Dream consistently crafts some of the most compelling narratives in gaming, and Beyond: Two Souls is no exception. This game holds a special place in my heart; I've become deeply emotionally invested in its story. The way it explores life on a grander scale—delving into the "beyond"—evokes emotions that words can barely capture. It feels like a glimpse into a reality we can sense but are unable to fully explore.The interactions with the dead, especially the moments involving loved ones, hit me hard emotionally. Those "crumbs" of communication always leave me feeling both grateful and overwhelmed. So, thank you—and curse you—Beyond: Two Souls for making a grown adult cry! I love everyone in the Infraworld<3That said, I’m glad they didn’t pursue a sequel, even though the epilogue teased the possibility. I feel like we’ve seen enough of this universe. Beyond: Two Souls already felt a bit longer than it needed to be, yet it masterfully orchestrated and concluded Jodie’s story.-"EXCEPT THE CONTROLS!!!! THEY ARE AWFUL"This game has profoundly shaped my perspective on life—a perspective I’ll carry with me forever. I’m incredibly grateful to have experienced it. Now, I'll be waiting for Quantic Dream's next banger after Detroit..

_childDocuments_.review: Before I write my honest review I have to preface by saying I played through the game one time on my own decisions and there will be spoilers. I will play through again to and choose different options for my pleasure and to get more information. My positives and negatives should be taken with a grain of salt since I don't know every outcome of every option. To start with the positives, I would recommend this game to everyone. It has a great story and replay-ability. The different environments and character development are amazing. The game has moments of beauty and moments of awe while at the same time making you feel like the small mapped environments have more to them than whats readily visible. Unfortunately, even though I loved the game I have more than a few negatives. To start, both Jodies parents were gifted with special abilities but not her? In my play through the extent of Jodies powers were one time when she took control of Aiden and opened a door. That alone is frustrating. Next, Aiden and Jodie have been tethered together since birth and he was stillborn, somehow this allowed him to have the powers of an entity? Doesn't make sense, or that they could be separated. Ontop of that, the father wasn't talked about at all. Speaking of fathers, Dawkens and Cole were implied as adoptive fathers but then Jodie and Coles relationship turns sour out of nowhere and he shoots her when she tries to turn off the black sun to save the world? Next, sometimes in my play though Jodie could understand Aiden but other times she doesn't understand what he's trying to show her? The amount of plot holes is ridiculous. Barely any information was given about the infraworld and the entities themselves. And why in the world do they look like fish and they are all evil? Why are lost souls sent there? Is it a type of limbo? Does anyone ever get to leave? Next, sometimes Jodie is hurt and Aiden is fine but towards the end when Jodie is tied up on level -4 Aiden is weak? Did they or did they not inject the neuro acid? Even if they did, he's a soul, he isn't limited to her mental state. And why at the end, for months Aiden was gone and then showed up out of nowhere and was back with her? Multiple times its said if he's too far away it hurts her and when you have the decision between light and dark, it said Aiden was in the light and not with her. Ontop of that, it makes zero sense why Jodie would begin to lose her memory from the loss of the black sun when she was perfectly fine before the DPA made it. And to top it off, the number one thing that frustrates me more than anything is that there wont be a second game after it ends in a cliff hanger of whats to come from the entities entering the world implied by Jodies nightmares and feelings from the connection to the infraworld. This game was amazing but had too many plot holes, too many unanswered questions and too many inconsistencies. I have more negatives but these are the main one for right now till I can play a few more times and get more information.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like this is really the first time that Quantic Dream have really pulled it off and fused movie and video game almost perfectly. Having played this directly after having played "Heavy Rain", I feel "Beyond: Two Souls" is everything its predecessor aspired to be in a much more polished and seamless fashion. The clumsy interface of Heavy Rain has been replaced by a much more intuitive and elegant interface that doesn't disctract from what's happening on screen, the writing is much less of a pastiche than in Heavy Rain, the acting/dialogues are much more convincing and even though having been published only 3 years after Heavy Rain, the visuals have evolved quite a bit since Heavy Rain.So, while Heavy Rain, when it finally came to PC, left me somewhat disappointed, I think "Beyond: Two Souls" may be the best example of this kind of interactive movie that I have come across so far (not having played Detroit: Become Human, which I'll likely check out next).While I did have some issues with the depiction of female characters in former Quantic Dream games, Ellen Page as the female lead finally moved their games away from the stereotypical hyper-sexualization that may have been lurking in some of their former games. Jodie clearly is a strong female character that does not serve the sole purpose of fulfilling the male leads romantic needs. Still, it felt a bit annoying that the game seemed to nudge you again and again towards a male character that behaves totally rotten and condescending towards her and obviously just uses her as a kind of tool. Still the game keeps asking you: "Don't you want to kiss him? Ah, you could really kiss him now! Oh, he's coming over to visit, how excited you are - maybe you can lure him into the sack? Oh by the way, he suddenly decided he loves you! Are you really sure you don't want to spend the rest of your live with him?"But in the end, as with many things, the game leaves the choice to you. 24 different endings seem quite impressive to me, even though I'm not the  type to replay games again and again.My conclusion: I cannot recommend "Beyond: Two Souls" highly enough for anyone interested in the fusion of narrative / movie and video game. If you're looking for hard-core, Souls-like permadeath powergaming, you might feel incliined to look elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: ★★★★★ Superb!Beyond Two Souls is a game/movie hybrid, it focuses on story and emotion more than gameplay. I can't remember a single moment where the music was not fitting for whatever event, good or bad, was transpiring. The preface of the story is the connection of Jodie to a spiritual entity: Aiden. During the game, you take control of both Jodie and Aiden, and are able to shape the story though each of them. As you are able to take control of either character, you can use Aiden to assist other desperate people, or to kill anyone who opposes you. Characters, despite other elements, are no doubt the most fantastic part of Beyond Two Souls. This is partially due to the Hollywood cast of Ellen Page and Willem Dafoe, who do an exceptional job of conveying character and expressing the director's vision.

_childDocuments_.review: I was quite on the fence about settling on this game as a thumbs up or down, and it honestly sits in limbo for me after having some time to think about it after finishing. I played this right after playing Heavy Rain (which I enjoyed) so my evaluation of Beyond is very much in relation to Heavy Rain. With that being said, objectively there were two main positive things I can say about Beyond. 1) It is very well acted and 2) It controls better than Heavy Rain (which is still NOT saying that it controls well...)The story will be the main attraction for a game like this and I have to say I found the story wildly inconsistent. The narrative is chopped up as we follow the life of Jodie bouncing back and forth in various stages of her life. We get chapters with her as a child, teenager and adult with various side characters coming and going for various appearances throughout her life. Jodie is "attached" to a supernatural entity everyone call's Aiden, and Aiden is able to "do" various things for Jodie essentially giving her powers. I put "do" in quotation marks because my next main complaint is how wildly inconsistent Aiden's powers are. Aiden can kill people, control people, knock things over, scout around the area, heal, and the list goes on - but all these powers are arbitrarily assigned at any given moment. Sometimes Aiden can protect Jodie from being attacked, but if the plot requires Jodie to be knocked out with a strike to the head Aiden is nowhere to be found. Sometimes Aiden can kill an enemy at will, but later on in a level where you are sent to kill one particular person Aiden cannot kill him and thus the game forces you to find another way of doing it. But why would you? Any rational person would just send Aiden to do it.  This also plays into another level where Jodie is homeless: I actually did enjoy this level for some of its character moments - I just found it impossible to believe that anyone with powers like her would be homeless. There are so many solutions to a dilemma like this. All this to say that the game never quite understands how to incorporate Aiden's powers in a meaningful way, in large part due to him being (arbitrary constraints aside) incredibly overpowered.The characters (though well acted) are the next issue. Firstly: I didn't find any of these characters likeable. No one in this game is particularly nice or worth cheering for. And that goes for the main character, though I will concede that is maybe realistic given that she grew up surrounded by jerks. Many of the secondary characters are just your everyday walking cliches with nothing original added. You find out one of the main characters has an "event" that happens to him which supposedly sets up his motivation as one of the main conflicts in the game. Chronologically this event happens very early the game's story, but narratively the game presents the event towards the end of the game. This results in a wild character flip for this person as, very late in the game, we are supposed to believe that for the entirety of the game this character has been working towards this particular goal - even though narratively there is nothing to suggest this in the first 90% of the games chapters. It is jarring and again just adds to the overall inconsistency, feeling tacked on for the sake of adding conflict. Also one more for the cliche strike: the ending I got was (out of absolutely NOWHERE) a page ripped straight from The Terminator. To be fair there are multiple endings so maybe some of the others were more grounded. Which leads somewhat into my last point - by the end of this game I had no desire really to go back and replay chapters to get other achievements or see other outcomes. With Heavy Rain I immediately went back to see how chapters might play out if you chose X instead of Y. Heavy Rain has its plot faults as well but I would argue it was always interesting and it has the "whodunnit" component that constantly had me going "just one more chapter". Nothing about the narrative of Beyond really generates enough interest to do so. Stuff just happens because the game says so, even if Aiden could solve the conflict with 30 seconds of critical thinking.In summary, being so narrative driven your enjoyment of this game will highly depend if you like the characters and are interested by the plot. The game never really intrigued me in this way, and so I have to settle on a thumbs down for this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Beyond: Two Souls is yet another example that David Cage and his team of talented developers truly know what they are doing when it comes to cinematic storytelling and consequential gameplay. The increased budget at developers' disposal is obvious right from the start from the quality of animations, graphical design, improved gameplay and, most importantly, famous and talented actors hired - from Willem Dafoe to Ellen Page to Eric Winter.Storytelling-wise, we can also see an interesting new direction devs have taken with a narrative that jumps from one point of time to another and while I wasn't a fan of that initially, over time I realized that for a new player, this is a perfect way to change things up from time to time and keep them in suspense as well as have the story retain some mysterious elements. Story itself, as per Quantic Dream's tradition, has it's strong parts full of emotional intensity as well as its nonsensical side made to create artificial tension but overall, it is a story with an incredibly interesting premise and with the help of excellent animators and amazing actors bringing its characters to life, it is a very enjoyable experience that, once again, outclasses its predecesor and its a joy to watch how innovative each new subsequent game from Quantic Dream is.+ Realistic and beautiful graphical style, improved by its port to PC + Selection of amazing actors who really manage portray emotions of their characters in a realistic and believable way which is also supported by them being written well+ Story, for the most part, is intriguing and well-written+ Choices and consequences on every step that have meaningful impact on the story+ Quality of animations+ Gorgeously modeled environments+ New gameplay that has been improved from Heavy Rain with fighting relying more on estimating and reacting to a direction protagonist is aiming towards rather than on simply pressing right buttons. It also, once again, complements story decisions as the game reacts to your gameplay choices as well+ Improved controls that do not feel as annoying and impractical as in Heavy Rain yet are still challeging enough to be enjoyable+ Length+ OST- Technical deficiencies – just like Heavy Rain, BTS is locked at 60fps max, even though it starts with unlocked fps initially, before it creates the configuration file but doesnt let you play it unlocked and the process of getting the fps to the value you’d like is more complicated and annoying that in the case of Heavy Rain where only one value needs to be changed. Stupid, considering that this is a remaster for PC – they could have ensured at least that. Additionally, there are those obnoxious black bars that are supposed to evoke more „cinematic“ experience even though its just plain pointless and can’t be turned off if you have the audacity to want to make them use more of your monitor’s real estate – once again, something you didn’t have to worry in the case of Heavy Rain – why did this have to be so complicated again? This is, however, also possible to fix with a bit of modding but after coming to this from HR, it feels unnecessarily obtrusive- Some parts of the story are completely illogical and are shoehorned in just to artificially create a shock value - this is a persistent issue in Cage's games and I really hope he'll be able to get over it one day

_childDocuments_.review: Another masterful story from Quantic Dream. Coming after Heavy Rain, but before Detroit: Become Human, Beyond Two Souls definitely does not disappoint. It has a great story, with some instances of the plot seeming to have been stolen from other works. If you have seen them, you will draw the comparison easily. However, thankfully this stands on it's own very well and captivates the player with it's mystery, characters and writing. It also features Ellen Paige and William Dafoe, with their characters modeled after them.This game will make you feel a wide range of emotions, much like any great story or film would. The visual style is more pleasing to the eye than that of Heavy Rain's and is good enough for what this game sets to accomplish, with just the right amount of detail in everything that is focused on. This PC version also has enhanced visuals, such as higher-resolution textures, like the other PC version of Quantic Dream's games. It controls well, even though it is not always clear if you should be blocking something or evading something. There are some frame stutters here and there, but it is not an often occurrence or nuisance. Overall, this is a great port and I will easily recommend this game to anyone who hasn't played it yet.Overall Rating: 4.5 of 5

_childDocuments_.review: A Captivating Masterpiece"Beyond Two Souls" is a truly remarkable and breathtaking game that effortlessly combines immersive gameplay, stunning graphics, and an emotionally gripping narrative. From start to finish, I was captivated by its enthralling storyline, complex characters, and its ability to challenge the limits of interactive storytelling.The game follows the extraordinary life of Jodie Holmes, portrayed by the talented Ellen Page, whose unique connection with a mysterious entity named Aiden provides an experience like no other. The seamless blend of action-packed sequences, intense drama, and supernatural elements kept me on the edge of my seat throughout the entire gameplay.One of the standout aspects of "Beyond Two Souls" is the meticulous attention to detail in its graphics and animations. The characters are brought to life with such realism that it is almost impossible to distinguish them from their real-life counterparts. The environments are intricately crafted, from stunning landscapes to hauntingly atmospheric settings, leaving a lasting impression on the player.What truly sets this game apart, however, is the emotional depth of its narrative. "Beyond Two Souls" explores heavy themes such as identity, loss, and sacrifice, challenging players to make difficult decisions that shape Jodie's journey. Every choice has consequences, weaving a branching narrative that keeps players invested and engaged. The moments of heartache, joy, and self-discovery left me emotionally moved and forever changed.The gameplay mechanics in "Beyond Two Souls" are seamless, offering a unique blend of exploration, quick-time events, and puzzle-solving. Interacting with the world through Jodie and Aiden's supernatural abilities offers a fresh perspective and keeps the gameplay engaging throughout. Controlling both Jodie and Aiden offers a duality that adds depth to the experience, allowing for creative problem-solving and strategic decision-making.The voice acting in "Beyond Two Souls" is absolutely superb. Ellen Page delivers a stellar performance, perfectly portraying Jodie's vulnerability, strength, and inner turmoil. The supporting cast also impresses with their exceptional performances, bringing the characters to life and further enhancing the emotional impact of the game.In conclusion, "Beyond Two Souls" is an unforgettable journey that pushes the boundaries of cinematic gaming and storytelling. It effortlessly combines stunning visuals, a gripping narrative, and emotionally charged performances. This extraordinary masterpiece deserves all the praise it receives, and it is an absolute must-play for anyone seeking a deeply immersive experience that will stay with them long after the credits roll.

_childDocuments_.review: Your opinion of this game will likely differ whether you played Detroit before or not. The game is not bad, and if you are new to Beyond games, you will likely be charmed by the wonderful graphics and the story line. Plus, I do see some improvements over Detroit, but there are two elements why I still give it thumbs down: controls and story choices.Controls really suck. Controls were not great in Detroit, but it has got worse. In Detroit you had to take certain actions at random times but the actions were consistent. In Two Souls you have 1 second to press random buttons at random times, and some control dynamics are not introduced properly so you are left with some 'WTF do I do?' moments. And when you have to move the mouse in a certain direction in combat scenes, you may still get a penalty if you did move in the right direction. Reason 1 why I give it thumbs down is because the worst of Beyond games, namely the controls, got worse. The game is so good however, that if this was the only problem it would get a thumbs up. Second bad thing though, and the main reason why I give it thumbs down is that you have a more limited choice of where the story goes. in Detroit you were the master of the story, but Two Souls is heavily scripted. For instance you may chose to kiss or not to kiss the guy but you cannot chose not to date him in the first place. You may chose what to say at the bar but you cannot chose not to go to the damn, obviously bad idea, bar. But also during movement and combat, where you have a predefined path and sequence of events to take. You cannot expect the game dynamics of a regular combat game where you chose the angle of attack and how and where you move... nah, you have to go this way or this way and that's the only way. And you have to go this way at this scripted moment in this scripted way. It doesn't matter if you used Aiden to make sure that there are no enemies around because it is scripted that you will be encountered by one anyway.  Detroit felt like you were indeed in charge of the story and the future of the characters, Controls are annoying. - I really enjoyed Beyond: Detroit. the controls were some times not great but mobility was usually fine. The story, the atmosphere; all great. But this game, 'two souls' is all about those "press this random button right now", and some times you have a dot in front of you to interact but nothing seems to make it interact. I just press my whole keyboard and move mouse randomly until something happens. Then, there are many parts in the game where there is really no clue on what to do. Two Souls is all about pressing random buttons at random times. That's all it is.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't know what to expect coming into this game. As I've been playing through all the Quantic Dream games on steam, I've had some interesting experiences. Fahrenheit was a beautiful mess of a game that i'll always hold in my heart. Heavy Rain is a true diamond in the rough with both awkward and fantastic moments.I can honestly say this has been my favourite game out of the Quantic Dream titles I've played so far. After reading the past reviews online and others opinions on the game, it kinda shocks me to see just how much hate this game has gotten over time, especially when compared to other games from Quantic Dream. Like all of their games so far, Beyond is flawed, but anyone who calls this game "Bad" needs to play more terrible games.Visually, Beyond still looks pretty great in most aspects. The characters have great attention to detail and the environments are really well detailed. Despite being on the same system as Heavy Rain, its a big step up visually. Sound wise, the game is also pretty great. Sound effects are solid across the board and I was never pulled from the game by odd sound effects. The original score by Hans Zimmer and co is also really great, but Quantic Dream games all have great music so this is to be expected.In terms of gameplay, Beyond plays mostly like their previous games, except with a stronger focus on linear gameplay and reduced onscreen prompts. This is both a good and bad thing. It serves the game well in some places, but hurts it in others. When just playing normally, I like that i'm not being harassed by onscreen prompts and that I just able to get into the world. In combat scenarios however, I would argue its a mixed bag. The idea is pretty straight forward, instead of combat prompts for most of your fighting, the game will go into slow motion and you must click and move your mouse in the direction of your attacks and dodges. Most of the time, this works fine, however there will be occasions where the onscreen attack doesn't always fully match your inputs, leading to some odd fails here and there. For some people, it will be an improvement and for others it'll be awful. For me? It rarely caused issues and thus I didn't see it as a huge problem.To enjoy this game, you need to temper your expectations early. In essence, this is a hyper-interactive movie. Gameplay is ultra-linear and the game is pretty forgiving. Large periods of the game will be spent in dialogue and interacting with your environment as opposed to action set-pieces or large open areas. If you go into this knowing what you're getting into and are able to lose yourself in the story, then you will enjoy it far more.My only genuine problem with this game comes from the way the story is presented. The story is presented in a non-linear fashion, which is not a bad thing, except in the case of Beyond, it is unnecessary. Certain events and connections often feel as if they would coincide far better if the story was just told in the right order.There is a lot to talk about, but none of it really changes my opinion on this game. As an interactive experience presented through the media of gaming, I found Beyond to be really great. Just like Heavy Rain, it has plenty of flaws, but none of them truly hindered my enjoyment, and really that's all that matters.If you enjoy linear story driven games, I honestly believe this game is worth a try.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adored this game. I've always been a fan of Elliot Page, especially in Juno and The Umbrella Academy, and his voice acting is absolutely stunning. All the characters have such moral complexities, and no one is completely perfect. They're written so realistically, and as the story progresses, you get to see deeper into the character development for even the small side characters. The story is compelling and so captivating, and even thought I beat this game in about 7/8 hours, I've replayed it three times now. The story can change depending on your choices, and you are free to make those choices. But when you make those choices? You live with the consequences. The other characters react to your choices, and sometimes your choices can kill another character if you aren't careful, especially in the Navajo chapter. Along with having great story and characters, the game is genuinely fun. Simple tasks like finding shoeboxes or playing with dolls or smashing your room in a teenaged temper tantrum are fun and meant to be fun. And combat can be difficult, but not overly so. It's mostly timing based, and seeing how you react quickly to visual ques. Quantic Dream has amazed us once again.

_childDocuments_.review: Beyond Two Souls offers an immersive and captivating story that kept me engaged from beginning to end. The unique gameplay mechanics, such as controlling both Jodie and her spiritual companion Aiden, added an interesting twist to the typical narrative-driven game. The dialogue and voice acting were impressive, and the player's decisions had a meaningful impact on the story's outcome.However, the game's reliance on quick-time events can become repetitive and disrupt the immersion at times. Despite this, I found the overall experience to be thoroughly enjoyable and would recommend it to fans of interactive storytelling games.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished Beyond: Two Souls, and I'm still reeling from the experience. It's one of the most emotionally powerful games I've ever played, and it's left me feeling overwhelmed by a wide range of emotions.The game tells the story of Jodie Holmes, a young woman who has been connected to a mysterious entity called Aiden since birth. Aiden is a kind of spirit, and he can interact with the physical world in ways that Jodie cannot. Together, Jodie and Aiden must use their abilities to survive a series of dangerous events, while also uncovering the truth about their past.The game is incredibly well-made. The visuals are stunning, the voice acting is superb, and the story is both engaging and thought-provoking. But what really sets Beyond: Two Souls apart is its emotional impact. The game deals with some heavy themes, such as death, loss, and identity, but it does so in a way that is both sensitive and impactful.I found myself deeply connected to Jodie's journey, and I felt a real sense of empathy for her. The game's emotional beats hit me hard, and I found myself crying at several points throughout the story.Beyond: Two Souls is not a perfect game. Some of the quick time events can be frustrating, and the game can be slow-paced at times. But these are minor flaws in an otherwise outstanding experience.If you're looking for a game that will move you, then I highly recommend Beyond: Two Souls. It's a game that will stay with you long after you finish playing it.If you're looking for a game that will make you feel something, then I highly recommend checking it out.
