_childDocuments_.review: A superb story-focused adventure game. One in which choices and actions abound.The combination of Jodie/Aiden presents interesting possibilities. On one hand, we have the utility of an extra set of eyes and a poltergeist like ability to manipulate the world. On the other, some highly specialized talents. Somehow it's not surprising that Jodie and Aiden end up becoming CIA and tasked with dirty work. So much as anyone is fool enough to keep the hunt going after the loss of a city block.In terms of the narrative, pieces shift between Jodie's childhood, becoming a CIA agent, the mission that changed everything, and the groups of people she meets along the way. In the end the choice really is in your hands.As a bonus points, while a pretty QTE heavy game, much like House of Ashes, not every event is a make or break fatal. Missing the event can alter the course of the story but it won't force you to constantly retry. Well, outside of the CIA training which was kind of fun ^_^.A single play through took me about 12 hours. I imagine in 20-25, you could get them all. The game even offers the option to roll in chronological order instead of the narrative's shifting backwards and forwards to tell the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Beyond: Two Souls

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, this game felt apart halfway through. Like REALLY fell apart. I don't know if that's a staple of David Cage's games, but the highs of the game weren't enough to balance out the abysmal scenes. The story was engaging, and I actually liked the out-of-order scenes, as it was compelling and I wanted to keep playing in order to piece together Jodie's story. It was neat that the developers included an option to play it chronologically too, depending on one's preference. The voice acting was convincing, emotional, and carried the script, despite some lackluster writing that could have been far more strong. The PC controls were a major issue. They were not properly thought out or user friendly. The gameplay was stilted, the directions confusing at times, completely taking me out of the game. Changing the difficulty helped, but it still was jarring to have to focus on understanding the controls rather than the story. There was also no option to run unless it was automatically done for you and countless scenes were slow and dragging as a result of this. In regards to controlling Aiden, or doing tasks as him, I got used to it as the game progressed, but it often felt awkward. A vast majority of the game is just looking for the white dots that indicate your next step. There was room, to some degree, to explore in several chapters, but you were limited and really didn't have much control or say in choices.This being my first Quantic Dream game, I wasn't too familiar with the style or direction. There were times where I shook my head in frustration as to why a certain part was included, and times when the interactive scenes felt pointless to the story (I shouldn't need to physically take each piece of food, cut it, drink water etc.) I would have liked more clues and detective work, instead of everything being handed to the player.I liked the emotional moments with Stan, especially in helping each other out and the dialogue between the group. There was a lot I related to, and though some people said it romanticizes suicide, I felt like it was a genuine portrayal of Jodie feeling alone and like she can't continue. I also liked the nuance between Dawkins and Jodie, in the sense that on one hand, they're trying to protect Jodie, (although we had little character depth or development from Cole aside from him helping us at the end) but at other times I was suspicious of Dawkins' intentions, and as Jodie grew older, it was clear she was continually being used as a pawn.Though I certainly enjoyed several aspects of this game, I can't easily ignore the valid concerns and blatant examples of David Cage's history of racism and sexism. Again, I personally have only played Beyond, but reading the context and discussion on Cage's previous games and Detroit is concerning. In Beyond, I was shocked at the number of sexual assault scenes and felt that they were not needed, at least not to that degree, especially in the bar scene where no one present tries to protect her. In regards to the "Navajo" chapter, many people pointed out there were stereotypes and, to my knowledge, the scenes were not written or overseen by Indigenous people. Add the images of tepees burning, which is inaccurate in regards to the Navajo, as well as the focus on mysticism. It felt tremendously icky that Jodie was the one to resolve the issue with the Ye'iitosh, as if she was the first to discover everything and understand the family's history. Oh and the developers including the option to kiss Jay (which forced romance and felt off since nothing led up to that). Then Jay and Cory giving her the bike and saying she spent so much time fixing it, when it really took minutes and there was no indication that any of the family had noticed since they didn't mention it or see her with the bike. Another example of lazy writing. And one of the achievements I received after finishing the chapter was titled "Medicine Girl".... Um no. Which brings me to the warlord in Somalia, and the white savior complex, yet again. Although it did very blatantly show US imperialism and the effects of the military industry, how the US normalizes invasions and murder. The game at least presented the idea of soldiers being manipulated or lied to, told to complete a mission only to benefit the US government.The more I played, the more I cringed at the writing. And found it absolutely revolting that Ryan Clayton was an actual character who told a young Jodie to "shut your mouth and do as you're told". Then later in the game, one whole chapter is dedicated to Jodie making dinner for Ryan, as we flip through pages of the cookbook and weigh our dinner options. THIS SERVED NO PURPOSE TO THE STORY other than the wasted gameplay and pointless tasks. Jodie is also shown in underwear walking around her apartment and that we're supposed to "make ourselves look good" for Ryan. Then the option to kiss him. Then cue to the third scene with Ryan in "The Mission" chapter, and again, we have the option to kiss him. Despite no character development. Despite the uneven power dynamics. It gave me another reason why I feel David Cage is a creep. Add that to the fact that Cage and the developers left a nude model of Page in the game, despite Page not consenting and apparently having a no-nudity clause in their contract. And let's not forget the unnecessarily long shower scene after Jodie met Paul and the family.The developers forced trauma after trauma on Jodie and used sexual assault to further the plot. There was nothing subtle, So many of the scenes could have been handled with better sensitivity and direction. There was also virtually no character development, aside from Jodie. With a game that comes off looking like a movie, I wanted more investment in characters. We only have a few scenes with Ryan, more toward the end, but he has a savior complex surrounding him, like in the last few scenes where he says he always figured he'd die a hero. The ending choices felt rushed, more forced romance with Ryan or Jay (despite only being with Jay and his family for a few days). I was happy with my choice of reuniting with Tuesday, Stan, Jimmy etc but even with that choice and telling Ryan that I don't see a future with him, he still says "I'll wait for you". Please don't.Cage tried too hard to come across as deep and emotional, in a hamfisted way, not to mention his replies to prior accusations: "You want to talk about homophobia? I work with Page, who fights for LGBT rights. You want to talk about racism? I work with Jesse Williams, who fights for civil rights in the USA... Judge me by my work." Not only does that reek of tokenism, but it seems Cage believes he can be exempt from being held accountable because he works with diverse groups. As if you can't still be homophobic, or hold racial biases or prejudices. While it's definitely possible to separate the creator from the content, and is completely up to the player, I can't look beyond Cage's treatment of Page, his tone-deaf statements, his obvious ego and the most recent allegations of Quantic Dream as a whole in regards to a toxic work environment. I'm sentimental about some parts of the game, but that doesn't automatically mean I think the game is overall good or can be recommended. Most of the praise I'll give is toward the voice actors and the gorgeous graphics. Certain scenes were gripping and handled well, but it did not feel consistent enough. It could have been far more polished, and I'm hesitant on whether or not I will continue playing other Quantic Dream games or support the developers.

That did not pan out well at all. I constantly struggled to make Jodie walk in the right direction. Without me touching anything on the controller, she'd walk around in circles or start walking in a random direction. I'd press up to walk to a door, the door opening animation would trigger, and when I pressed up again to go through the door Jodie would take a left or a right and miss the whole damn door. And the camera, oh my god, the awful camera.My take is that Beyond Two Souls succeeds as a story-telling device yet fails as a video game. Get if you want an engaging enough story and some pretty cool motion capture. But don't expect a good time if you're gonna play this with a keyboard or an Xbox One controller.

_childDocuments_.review: 3/5I've only had good memories about this game for the past few years, so I've decided to replay it. And I must say, time was not kind to it.It's clear this was a high budget game with a highly ambitious concept, but most of it just ends up being so annoyingly bland and characterless. Even though I still honestly love the story and the concept, most of the script is just poorly written and straight up boring. And I feel like the non-chronological storytelling only does it worse - most of the jumps in the story are just too far in-between and feel disconnected.And next to that, I can't say that how this game mechanically plays out helps it either. The camera jumps combined with that god awful movement is just so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ annoying. I see this as a valid reason why someone might just give up on the game. And switching from a keyboard and a mouse to a controller doesn't really make it any better. Someone also thought that not adding sprinting was a good idea... So most of the time you're just bored out walking to the next checkpoint. Hopefully not the same guy that had an idea of unskippable cutscenes and post-credits, so every time you quit the game and wish to continue, you have to play long ass cutscenes all over again.Now onto some of the highlights. I think the "The Mission" was a decent chapter. I was invested, and I honestly wish more of the game was like so. But what honestly impresses me, even to this day, is the ending. I'm not gonna talk about the annoying choice you're left at the end, but I still love the way the "Briefing", "Dragon's Hideout" and "Black Sun" chapters develop. It feels like it actually has some character and kind of impacts me even today.This actually reminds me to mention that I really appreciate most of the acting here, but ultimately the script kind of makes it uninteresting. So, it leaves me to wonder, what happened here? Was the budget cut because of all these actors and all the mocap performances (ironically most of the time animations are just buggy and they suddenly switch in-between different expressions) combined with some really impressive graphics for it's time, with a great soundtrack by the man Hans Zimmer himself?I don't know. My peculiarity of completing games kept me from all the boringness just to replay the final part once again, a part that kept this game in a positive light in my memory for all these years. And honestly I'm glad I did so. I still love it as the day I first played it.So is it worth playing? Yeah. Just keep in mind that there are some things that might irritate you.

_childDocuments_.review: So this is going to be a rather critical review of the game, but I cannot bring myself to not recommend it. The game is fantastic, even with it's flaws that I'll briefly talk about.The story of the game is its strong point. It's unique, original and most importantly well-executed. The characters are mostly likable, and the actors tasked to perform them did a perfect job of conveying them. All animations have been done through motion capture, and the game looks phenomenal for it's age, making everything feel realistic even among the more absurd parts of the game. The game was originally made for the PS3, and some the cutscenes of that version are used in the PC port as well. To be expected, those pre-rendered cutscenes distract from the ones that use in-game graphics, but they're less frequent than the more contemporary ones, so I can't fault them for being the crux of soon apparent negativity. There's two problems I have with the game: Replayability and the controls. First off, the controls are a little funky, even on their original platform. Since the game technically has two separate characters you need to control, there's also two different control schemes. The intended controller controls for one of them are ideal, but for the other the controller is unnecessarily difficult. Vice versa, kb+m controls for one of the schemes are obscenely sensitive, but makes the other a cakewalk. This results in switching between the two for most enjoyment, which is a little silly. The pacing of the game makes it so that it's still bearable to do, but the controls become an issue very early on. Make sure you have a controller shelved somewhere before getting this, just in case. The camera controls aren't exactly smooth either. It's very clear they took the more cinematic approach with it, but it just doesn't always work in tight spaces or slow scenes. I found my protagonist to be stuck in doorways, or lollygagging betwixt objects like a Sim in scenarios where I needed to be doing something. That said, the game is mostly cutscenes and building up the incredible story, but these little points make the gameplay sections between them a bit of a chore when they really shouldn't be. And the story. Oh my god, if it ain't one of the best ones I've seen yet. The passion behind it resonates through the entire game, with the pacing sharpening it with each plot twist, and making sure that it doesn't go dull. Where I found the problems with this was when I replayed the game, where I found something I like to call the "Telltale games syndrome". Basically,  But it really doesn't negate everything good the game is, since the game really is an interactive movie, as Heavy Rain coined some years prior. And it's one hell of a good ride at that. So I must recommend this game to anyone who likes stories, and good game design. Each first playthrough of this will be a guaranteed emotional wild experience, that can't quite be expressed in words. It's about ten hours long and can be completed in one sitting, but even with numerous endings it has it wasn't designed to be picked at and replayed. That's not to say it's still not a phenomenal game despite all this. It took all its strengths, fine tuned each one of them to near perfection, making it one of the better experiences I've had this year. But as with anything, it's not quite perfect. Some would say, far from it.

_childDocuments_.review: ★★★ (5-star scale)This was such a cool concept, but in the end felt empty and disconnected. I understand what the writers were trying to do - having the players piece together Jodie’s memory by playing chapters of her life in a random order. But it just caused confusion and room for plot holes. It left me asking question after question. (What is the origin of the Infraworld? How is Aiden able to control other human beings? How is Aiden/Jodie able to heal people? Where did Jodie’s powers (and her parents’) come from? Where do the Infraworld monsters come from? What happened to certain characters between chapters? SO many unanswered questions.) Also, the romantic interests felt so forced (especially Jay - I didn’t see any chemistry between them at all). I loved the Native representation in the Navajo chapter, but the story felt really odd to me. They did Nathan’s character SO dirty (who I thought was this game’s saving grace - until the end). The best part of this game though was the Homeless chapter (of course, depending on how you play). That group’s characters (especially Stan and Tuesday) felt so incredibly genuine. Seeing Jodie’s vulnerability in that chapter, and how she starts to really care about people for pretty much the first time in her life was so bittersweet. That chapter’s story will always stick with me (and the ending I chose). The art of this game is also really beautiful. Although I feel on the fence of whether or not to recommend it, I’ll personally say that - in general - I wouldn’t recommend it. BUT. If you’re a fan of Quantic Dream (like Detroit: Become Human and Heavy Rain), or you’re a big fan of Elliot Page and Willem Dafoe, I would recommend trying this out.

(How are users supposed to figure that out?)The worst part is if you screw up, you have to restart the entire chapter. You can't restart from a checkpoint mid-chapter, and you can't skip any of the cutscenes.The same company produced another game called "Detroit: Become Human", which was much better and resolved much of the above. Play that one instead.

I suggest other players make that same mistake because I did play through the original ordering on a successive pass and the story felt really disjointed and hard to follow. Remixed just makes more chronological sense. It took me 10-12 hours on my first pass taking my time to investigate. Another 40 hours to get all the achievements but looking back it can probably be done in 20-25 hours.If you're an achievement hunter, I'd advise you play Duo mode your first time. There's an achievement that you have to play start to finish in Duo mode. If you launch the game at any point in Solo mode, you won't get the achievement. You can still play the game however you want, just use either two controllers or mouse & keyboard/controller. _childDocuments_.review: Even though I ended up liking this game, I can't recommend it, at least not in the way it is advertised.Just watch Stranger Things instead, it's surprisingly similar, but a lot better than this game.The music is good, the graphics are great (especially for the time), but the gameplay is pretty non-existent and the story makes very little sense if you think about it. All that is to be expected from a Quantic Dream game. On top of that, the control scheme is unintuitive, even after two playthroughs I still don't fully get it.But I'm willing to look past flaws, because in the end I'm playing this for the choices. In Detroit: Become Human the choices and story tree made up for a lot of its flaws in my opinion, I was expecting a similar situation here, but ended up incredibly disappointed.This game is not what it says on the box. Your choices don't matter. Quantic Dream had a specific story in mind and allows very little deviation.David Cage said that he wanted choices to feel organic, you would play the game and make choices without even noticing, like you often do in real life. And yes, those implicit choices exist in the game, but the problem is that most of the time they don't make any difference.I've also seen people defend that your choices in this game aren't supposed to change the story, they are supposed to define what kind of person Jodie is inside of that story. Which is a nice sentiment, and I believe that's what the game was going for, but it falls flat when the character constantly makes choices that I wouldn't make at times when I'm not in control (cutscenes or between chapters), basically undoing all of my choices. And even when I am in control, it often feels like there is a right and a wrong choice.My first playthrough was boring and confusing. Then I played the game again, and I had a lot more fun. My second playthrough was in the remixed (semi-chronological) order, which improved my enjoyment because that order makes a lot more sense to me. It's a bit slower-paced at the beginning, which some people might dislike (I actually prefer the earlier chapters), but it gives a better understanding of the timeline. I wouldn't be surprised if they wrote the game in that order, but later shuffled the chapters to get some more variety in the gameplay. The fact that I already knew what to do also helped a bit, because I wasn't aimlessly looking around for things to do.But the biggest difference was probably that I knew what to expect. Instead of a choose your own adventure story, I played a linear story with a few choices here and there. That change in perspective doesn't make it a masterpiece, but at least it's fun.Honestly, I could ramble about this game for a while (spoilers).

_childDocuments_.review: While it's possible to complete Beyond: Two Souls in 8-10 hours for those seeking a quicker experience, the true essence of the game unfolds with a more immersive investment of time. Whether pursuing achievements or embracing the challenge of exploring various narrative possibilities, dedicating ample time to unlock the game's full potential ensures a more fulfilling and rewarding gaming experience.In terms of gameplay, this game offers a rich interactive experience best described as an engaging festival of interactivity. Beyond: Two Souls places emphasis on delivering a compelling narrative, resulting in a higher-than-usual number of interactive elements. What sets it apart is the thoughtful integration of interactive objects, each serving a purpose related to the overarching storyline. Unlike some narrative-driven games, there's an intentional absence of filler interactions aiming at extending playtime, as every interactive component ties to the narrative. It's worth noting that, in specific sequences, the game becomes nearly unplayable without a controller - an issue likely a product of the initial console release. While this helps better understand the approach and gameplay design choices for the console version, it's frustrating that the developers didn't adapt the mechanics for PC play.Considering that many PC players don't own a controller, it seems a missed opportunity to enhance accessibility and user experience. As previously mentioned, certain sections prove almost unplayable without a controller, and even with one, the controls periodically feel a bit clunky. Fortunately, these instances are few, minimizing their impact. While this may be a drawback for some players, considering the game's origin platform, it becomes more understandable. Despite this, understanding the game's console origins can provide some perspective on these design decisions. In summary, this counts as the only issue I have with the gameplay portion of the game.Despite being an older game, the PC release of Beyond: Two Souls doesn't feel significantly outdated. While it shows its age and shortcomings due to the reduced density of specific areas, its visual appeal remains impressive. However, a notable drawback is the anti-aliasing choice, which, even at the highest setting, leaves 'irregular' edges around objects near characters - a frustrating issue. On a positive note, the sound quality is impressive, contributing to an immersive experience. The casting in Beyond: Two Souls is a standout hit, showcasing an engaging collection of characters. Although the soundtrack doesn't break new ground, it effectively fulfills its role. An impressive thing to note is the absence of character animation issues. In a genre where such problems are not uncommon, Beyond: Two Souls distinguishes itself by maintaining smooth and glitch-free character animations throughout the gameplay.The story follows Jodie Holmes, who has a psychic connection with a mysterious entity named Aiden. Players navigate Jodie's life from a young age to adulthood, experiencing her struggles and supernatural abilities. The narrative explores government experiments, personal relationships, and the impact of Aiden on Jodie's life. The game's non-linear structure and player choices contribute to multiple possible outcomes, providing a unique and emotional storytelling experience.The narrative unfolds in two distinct modes, presenting players with a choice between the original storyline crafted by the developer and a remixed version. In the original mode, the story unfolds as initially envisioned, seamlessly transitioning between chapters as players progress. This mode enriches the storytelling experience, offering clarity and ease of understanding, making it an ideal choice for the initial playthrough. The narrative's non-linear structure encourages deep engagement, prompting players to reflect on past events and anticipate future developments.On the other hand, the remixed style rearranges the story chronologically, allowing players to follow Jodie's growth over time. This format proves perfect for a second playthrough, providing a unique perspective and filling in any narrative gaps from the initial playthrough. The game's rich content is underscored by multiple endings, encouraging players to revisit and explore different decision paths. Achievements add an extra layer of enjoyment, motivating players to invest numerous hours for a 100% completion.I encountered no performance or game-breaking issues during two playthroughs. The game's limited to 60 FPS, but there's an option to choose between 30 FPS or 60 FPS. Given that PC gamers typically prefer frame rates above 60, it's unfortunate that a higher FPS option, or unlocked FPS even, isn't available. Nonetheless, having a steady 60 FPS is considerably better than being restricted to a fixed 30 FPS found on the consoles the game launched on. Considering the type and genre of the game, it wouldn't benefit from higher FPS that much anyway. Yes, the camera movement would be more fluid, but that's pretty much it. It is the one and only major drawback from the technical standpoint.Beyond: Two Souls offers a captivating narrative with a rich and immersive experience. With a tempting story, multiple endings, and thoughtful gameplay design, it provides a rewarding gaming journey. While some technical limitations and controller-dependent sections hinder accessibility, the overall presentation, content, and storytelling make it a worthwhile experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Making a game like this is difficult, not only because you have ensure that every choice is meaningful, not only that the game functions like it should, not only so that it looks and plays well, or even anything else that is intrinsic to quality games. Rather, it is difficult primarily because you are turning a game into what is essentially an interactive movie. Thus, the question becomes one of "How do we make this feel like a game, while telling our story?" Let's talk about it. Beyond: Two Souls is best described as an adventure-narrative game with a heavy emphasis on player choice. It throws out a majority of gameplay in order to tell its story and immerse the player, which admittedly it does very well. However, in order to keep its namesake as a game, it has to engage the player. And how does it do that? Two ways: quick times events and object interaction. This, of course, excludes the existence of Aiden, who plays with absolute freedom of movement and whose gameplay extends to looking around for something to press. Games like this and other's of Quantic Dream's (Detroit: Become Human, Heavy Rain), or even those of Telltale (Walking Dead, Wolf Among Us) and DONTNOD (Life is Strange), have to utilize these features in order to feel like a game. Quick time events are a very dicey mechanic, because rather than favor traditional skills like timing, combat prowess, or critical thinking, it favors the idea of reflex. And that can be tricky because it does not, as said, favor any kind of capability. You either press a button and win, or fail and lose. That kind of extreme 50/50 can be very offputting, as it is for me. Thus it should be noted that for games such as this, one cannot expect gamebreaking combat or puzzle solving, as that simply isn't the point. What is, however, is the story. And that is where Beyond really pulls through. The story follows a girl named Jodie, through a spiral-like framework of storytelling which funnels through the years of her life one after the other, often bouncing between young and old. Yet throughout the entire duration of her life, she is bound inextricably to a spirit known as Aiden. It is this premise which fuels and propels the narrative. Beyond this, I shall say no more. What I will say, however, is that it is good. I watched a playthrough of this game many years back and still I remembered it fondly. It works well on Steam, too. It runs well, and although the keyboard can at times be a bit unruly it is by no means a monstrous task to get through by that alone. Beyond prides itself on its narrative, on its spectacle, on its music and its characters. The game uses motion capture from real actors (many of which you may recognize) to inject a certain degree of life into the characters. They talk and interact like people, have ideas and ambitions of their own, all with their own stories, and not a single one of them are unimportant. It is choice which Beyond expresses the most of, with you, as Jodie, getting to interact in whichever way you chose with whichever person (just about). And what you do affects what happens later. It is this core mechanic which makes Beyond so exciting, so nerve wracking. Because one wrong step could skew your goals. Beyond does not utilize gameplay, as said before. You go in between Aiden and Jodie, each playing differently. But it isn't horribly complex, which allows Beyond to be accessible even to the most uninitiated of PC or console players. Like Telltale and DONTNOD, you don't need to be cracked at video games in order to enjoy what it has on the table. But for veterans of gaming, like myself, it may be odd to play something with such a minimalist approach. But for what Beyond does right, its narrative and musical score most notably, it is well worth the purchase for anyone who wants to experience some of gaming's finest storytelling. 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most heartfelt, touching video game stories I have experienced in some time. I wouldn't say it is my favorite game story (that honor belongs to Life is Strange), but I can easily say Beyond: Two Souls is a close second. The performances are all movie-level quality, especially from Elliot Page, though even the less well-known actors are good. Despite the non-linear storytelling, the game is excellently crafted in its ability to form a connection between the player and the characters. All of the characters, including Aiden, who has no dialogue whatsoever or even a face to look at, are well-rounded individuals with desires and fears and hopes, and they all feel like genuine people. I will say that the controls are a bit unorthodox, but I would not say that they are the debilitating crutch that others have claimed that they are. Once you get used to them (which doesn't take too awful long), you'll hardly even notice how strange they are anymore. Yet still, even if the controls were absolute garbage, I would still recommend this game as the story is simply too good to pass up on.Overall, this game is definitely worth playing for any player seeking a good story. If you only play video games for some mindless fun, this might not be the game for you, but if you want an engaging, well written and well acted story, then this is most certainly one you ought to pick up.

_childDocuments_.review: Whatever anyone says, but it turned out to be another exciting adventure from David Cage, the creator of such games as Fahrenheit and Heavy Rain. His games have the appearance of the gaming industry. "Fahrenheit" was a breakthrough in the genre of interactive cinema in its time. It had high-quality implementation of both variability and an exciting plot. Heavy rain finally won my heart, that I did not calm down until I walked it along and across to see all the possible endings. Only it impressed me. Beyond Two Souls is a great game that brought me a lot of bright emotions. And during the entire test, it was required that it last as long as it was possible to linger. Not only the plot hooked me, but also the little things filled with a well-known story. The plot is built around a girl named Jodie, played by Ellen Page. In my opinion, she did it perfectly. And she managed to convey all the accompanying characters 100 percent. The game has collected a lot of cool things. There is a gripping plot and excellent graphics. Interesting gameplay (interactive cinema, diluted with action), cool characters and their dialogues, and even the secondary ones were worked out. Special awards are given to those who found themselves in the center of the plot. The work of William Dafoe and Ellen Page. They gave it all. At some point, you even forget that you are playing a game, and not watching a movie.The plot revolves around Jodie (Ellen Page), and we go through her entire path of development with her. Starting from her childhood, ending with her growing up. She is not an ordinary girl at all, because she has to live with Aiden (spirit), who lives inside her. From birth, he is always there, or rather is a part of her, since he is in an advantageous position with her. Moreover, he has supernatural abilities, one of which is telekinesis and affects other people. As it usually happens, other people became interested in this goal and wanted to use it for their own purposes. And then the idea of ​​having two souls in one body changes the gameplay in an unusual way, because you can always switch from Jodie to Aiden. And he leaves his body, for example, he can open a closed door from the back, passing through. Or create a danger ahead in advance, for example, armed opponents and neutralize them. Or even take control of one of them, and then neutralize the rest of the enemies with it, who are completely unexpected. A share of mysticism also makes the plot even more interesting. I have never regretted that I decided to play, and now I want to replay it, delving into the details.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked this game. I didn't know much before playing other than Page's and Dafoe's involment as actors and all the mo-cap techniques that were used. And that there was a second "soul" you could move around Jodie, which I saw in a short clip.I was pleasantly surprised to find out it was a much more ambitious project than I thought it would be. An interesting story, not shying away from certain topics and keeping the action and drama always interesting throughout many locations and time periods in Jodie's life.One thing that pleasantly surprised me, besides the amazing animations and facial captures (which were better than I expected as well) is how this game did not avoid what I commonly describe as "bothersome things to animate in a video game". Examples of this are: characters picking up objects and handing them to someone else, pulling a blanket over yourself, taking a backpack off naturally, a shovel going into a mountain of dirt and coming out with dirt that is then dropped somewhere else... and a long long etc. Games like Assassin's Creed for example always try to hide these things out of camera. It was a joy to see a game tackle each of these issues without fear and with a lot of technical merit. Things I didn't love about this game, there are a few.I'm not a fan of the controls. I understand the need for them to be that way, but it was still frustrating at times. Movement and camera movement are propbably the worst offenders. If you're used to running in games with a third person camera, this game rarely lets you do so. And the camera is not just restricted, but it actually was some bobbing and cinematic movement to it, which is jarring.Graphically speaking, I loved everything about the character models, but not so much the environments. They are well conceived, well designed and well executed, but at 2019 game with so good looking characters needed to be running on a PBR engine. I think the extra work needed to get the roughness textures etc would have been so much worth it. The soundtrack of the game is fine but not really memorable. Some of the tracks by Lorne Balfe are too reminiscent of Inception (Balfe worked with Zimmer in that film and other productions) which paired with Ellen Page and even a spies-in-snow-suit section made it seem too influenced by the 2010 blockbuster. If you don't mind games with limited movement and you ike games with several choices (Life is Strange for example) then you might really enjoy this one. It combines the supernatural and the mundane in a way that works and makes each of the carefully chosen story moments be satisfying in their own right.

_childDocuments_.review: I came from playing Detroit: Become Human, hungry for more. I tried Heavy Rain and hated it... you can read my review for that if you want to know why. Beyond: Two Souls is much, MUCH better... in every way. I actually like the characters, the writing is believable, the controls and camera work much better, there are far fewer mundane tasks and cut scenes. The controls still leave a bit to be desired, as there are some less intuitive actions and some awkwardness. The story has a few weak moments, but nothing I couldn't get past. All in all, it's a compelling game with superb acting and a convincing environment. Detroit is quite a bit better, but this game is at least on a similar level.... and it's got Willam f'n Dafoe in it! That's worth an extra few points for sure, right? :) I'd give it 7.5 out of 10.

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to Quantic Dream's previous work (Heavy Rain), buttons are more intuitive. _childDocuments_.review: An absorbing narrative game about a girl's life bound to a paranormal entity.Difficulty   ★★☆☆☆☆☆☆☆☆ (mainly QTE and the game does find ways to continue the story whatever happens)This game is more an interactive psycho-thriller Hollywood movie with great actors played by Elliot Page and Willem Daffoe. And they did their job very well. The main story is told in little story pieces and events during the lifetime of Jodie Holmes, who is bound to an invisible entity called Aiden. And this is where the story unfolds very well as you find out step by step what is going on and how Jodie and Aiden find their way. There are a lot of sad things in the game, but also action parts as well.What I really loved about this game:* the story is really intense and it takes it time (needed 12 hours for the first playthrough)* character details are one of a kind and visuals are very good* you can play the game in chronical order or in the original, disordered version (which I liked more)* can be played coop (one as Jodie and one as Aiden, though Jodie is the one with the most interactions)* the game does not stop narration whatever happens, like a movie* you can make different decisions and story follows your actions you take, for the worse or better* good replayability as you can replay chapters anytime to find new ways and watch other outcomes* it's great fun spreading havoc with Aiden when it gets unleashed* many tiny chapters which give you an insight on Jodies life and struggles* different endingsDownsides of the game:* camera control can sometimes be a little weird* the story segments and your decisions are consealed, means most things are not dragged over to other story parts, but important ones are* chapter select can be used to see other outcomes of the current chapter, but will not be permanently saved. For some (minor) endings you have to replay the whole game. * uses QTE a lot (Quick-Time-Events), which is not directly bad though as it keeps the "movie" rollingThe QTE and consealed chapters are gimmicks to make it possible to tell the story fluently and not to produce too much different timelines. I was absolutely able to live with it.In the end the game was a total blast to play. If you like stories about ghosts and stuff, the story will catch you. I am a big fan of the Life is Strange series and other narrative games, but Quantic Dreams showed me that not only Dontnod can make awesome narrative games. Though Quantic Dream focus more on a movie presentation. Beyond: Two Souls is a must play if you like the topic and such game types.

_childDocuments_.review: Beyond: Two Souls was a game that I've been looking forward to playing since the day it came out but not having a PS3 back then didn't help at all. So, I played the demo somehow and watched couple of videos about it and I instantly fell in love with it. I finally got around playing it since it came out to PC and I wish I could return to time where I was an ignorant teenager who had no capability of understanding the plotholes and inconsistencies. That could've also helped with the void I've felt after finishing the story due to not being able to feel like how I felt about it back then. I'll elaborate it a bit further...Unlike Heavy Rain, Beyond: Two Souls presents a great acting thanks to Hollywood stars with exceptional acting skills. However, it fails to deliver a powerful impact but it ultimately delivers what was intended. It's an emotional experience of a girl called Jodie who has a link with an entity called Aiden since birth and this entity is capable of possessing, healing and killing people as well as interacting with the environment. The dramatic story of Jodie for having a link with an entity that she doesn't have any control over and the anomalies caused due to presence of him is being handled perfectly. The price she has to pay for something she isn't responsible is heartbreaking. However, the focus shifts from Aiden really fast and most of the chapters show what happens to Jodie because of Aiden. There are only three chapters that we get to see Aiden at his full potential and one of them is a DLC. It's not a bad thing of course but the balance between Jodie's emotional state and Aiden's origins is not being handled properly. The story is also not being presented in a chronological order which makes things a bit confusing but I think it's alright since we witness every part of Jodie's life from her childhood to adulthood. There is an option to play the story in chronological order, but I wouldn't recommend it.Since it's an interactive movie, cutscenes naturally exceed gameplay and there aren't as many QTEs as Heavy Rain. However, there are stealth sections that give you full control over both Jodie and Aiden and the approach to the situation at hand is entirely up to you. This is what I meant by Aiden's full potential. You only get to see what he's capable of during these sections and sadly, there aren't many of them. Maybe it's just me. Maybe I wanted more gameplay rather than watching most of the time but it doesn't change the fact that Aiden's capabilities weren't really explored or presented outside of these sections.The last thing I'd like to point out is that David Cage needs to learn how to write a proper romance between characters. I've played three games by him thus far and the romance between the characters didn't make any sense in all three of them. They felt awkward and forced. It is also obvious that he is fascinated by the supernatural elements but he is very bad at using them. There are inconsistencies here and there but thankfully, Beyond isn't as bad as Fahrenheit when it comes to that regard.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy David Cage games although I don’t like him (the person) at all (although I don’t actually know him personally, obviously… He just comes across as being stuck up, arrogant and annoying).  I played everything from Fahrenheit to Detroit: Become Human but somehow missed this one.  I finally got around to playing it and… I loved it!!!For all those who don’t enjoy the mechanics:  Why are you playing these games if you want tight controls and mechanics?  This is not what David Cage games are about.  They are about the story, setting and atmosphere.  Sure the story itself is a little on the wild side and there are plot holes galore… but who cares?  The presentation is stunning… even for 2022.   The game is highly immersive and enjoyable.  Each chapter has its own feel and setting.  Sometimes it is thoughtful and emotional, other times it is nail bitingly intense.  There are some stand out chapters which really hit hard emotionally for me, such as the chapter where you go to a birthday party… man, that didn’t end well at all, did it?  :-)It was a good, standard David Cage game that I enjoyed thoroughly.  If you enjoyed Detroit: Become Human and / or Heavy Rain, then there is absolutely no reason why you won’t enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the story, it's really amazing, it feels like an interactive movie that keeps me wanting to see how the progress develops. I played the remixed version (chronological ordering), and I'm glad I did, people say the original ordering felt too random. Even though allegedly we are playing Jodie's memory, which are mixed up, I didn't feel like watching a movie like Memento (2000) again... This kept the story nice and easy for me.But for god's sake, those controls pissed me off! I am so angry that I wanted to do the better, longer outcomes, seeing the story in full, and not keeping getting rescued!! It takes a second to do the right thing but you are given no hints like, move the mouse up or down, left or right. Surely one can practice it, but I'm the kind of guy who has no patience for that! I get punished for one tiny moment done wrong in the game (actually, I'm given multiple chances, fair enough, but guess what, for some reason still too hard for me), and to hell with that! I won't replay whole chapters just because of these unforgiving, panic inducing controls I am supposed to get used to. No way! I just watched the better endings on YouTube, although I'm definitely not proud that I didn't get things right.So yes, probably I will regret this decision, but because the controls made me so angry, I won't upvote a game that is otherwise awesome. I'd say, yes, buy the game, but for the hardest parts, just save yourself the trouble and watch the missed scenes on YouTube. Now I'll go and channel my anger into a physical workout excercise.

_childDocuments_.review: Original Review (2.1 hours gameplay):Wow, this game is Hell warmed over. It looks story rich, aesthetically captivating, with a variety of branching paths to follow. The problem is the controls. They are auto-prompts, and change all the time. This makes them utterly reactionary, completely randomized, and so confusing that they totally ruin your getting into the story, the action, the settings. I finally quit in the forest outside the train because the controls are so ridiculously confusing and unforgiving. They say it's a 10-hour game; I made it for two. Better luck next time, Quantic Dream. Assign actions to keys so players don't have to keep re-inventing the wheel every time they want to make an action.Update (29 hours gameplay):I thought I'd give Beyond:TS another try. By cranking down the difficulty to primitive, I was finally able to see the story beyond the annoying controls. The story & characterization are phenomenal. Things that seems so annoying early on like shuffled chapters and a bewildering plot were actually intentional--meaning, they serve a purpose. In fact, the story had me crying several times in the last chapters because it's so well written. The controls GUI is still dreadful (at least on PC)--but Jodie's story and influence on characters around her (esp. Aidan) easily compensates. I'd now score it 4 stars, except the control interface might still drag it down to 3 or 3.5 stars.

_childDocuments_.review: KB+M controls are ROUGH, man. You need to spend quite some time to get the jist of it, some hate it, I did too until I started getting it. Game itself doesn't tell you in which direction to move your mouse, you actually have to observe the situation, your character and calculate the best move option in a very short time frame. I find this mechanic very unique and fitting but it's hella difficult too.There's lots of QTE, in my opinion they make the game even more intense along with the story - which is my favourite part, but if your reflexes are not that great then you'll be frustrated at times. I've seen people advising to play it in chronological order as it was too confusing for them, I have to disagree. If you're blessed with basic logical skills and can add 2+2 then playing this in original mode is for you. I find it way more intersting to shift back and forth in time throughout Jodie's story, witnessing it in retrospective mode. As if in real time Jodie is going back to her core memories, reliving them, like we all do sometimes. Playing as Aiden is awesome, his fluid-like movements and possibilities to do good and bad to people outside and it's host are what I think an entity could be. There's a fair share of paranormal stuff in here too, which I adore. Beyond: Two Souls is overall a heartbreaking story, so if you tend to really feel for the characters - prepare to bawl your eyes out and get angry af, cause the amount of betrayal in this game is insane. Emotions QD serves you are off the charts, great acting makes you feel like it's all real and you're in the middle of it, elements of horror keep you on the edge of your seat, tough choices make you feel responsible for Jodie.These choices are sometimes tricky and their importance may not be so obvious, therefore you don't even know that you ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up until later on. So choose wisely, always. ♥♥♥♥, man. If a game can make you feel so much then it's truly a work of art. However it's not really a game though, not really a movie either, it's hell of an experience. Sure has some technical flaws, but personally I don't dwell on them if the story has you in chokehold. Story-wise Quantic Dream never disappoints. So huge kudos to the creators, keep em' coming.

_childDocuments_.review: Paranormal Thriller:Very captivating story, good characters, and great performances. Not as many branching story paths as I wish there were, but there are enough to warrant multiple playthroughs to see variations. One playthrough will be around 10 hours, which I think is good. As for the scenery, pretty much all of the places in the game are packed with detail. You will likely find yourself wandering and flying around just to look all of the scenery.Some Control Problems:The controls are pretty clunky at times and you might find yourself getting stuck on walls and scenery, slowing progress down a bit. I would HIGHLY recommend using a controller. I couldn't get my xbone controller to fully function with the game for some reason, but my switch pro controller worked perfectly.Like Playing a Movie:There isn't really much to the gameplay here. Walk around, find stuff to interact with, make choices. There are collectibles to get that are mildly stimulating to look around for and find. These unlock concept art and other stuff like that to look at. Oh, and there are a LOT of QTEs here. I usually hate these with a passion, but if you play on the lower of the two difficulties, the commands are much more lenient and bearable.Worth the Buy?:If you want a solid, story-heavy experience, and don't mind the lacking gameplay, then I'd say give it a go. It is probably worth the full price, but I'd recommend trying to get it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Before you read my review, know that I haven't played the entire game yet. I have played maybe half of the game. TLDR;I only recommend this game because of the storyline. That's it. It's like the scenes going on in your head while you read a book, but you have control over two sentences on the page. The gamplay sucks, trust me, it will suck more than you think. In the beginning (even if you play video games 25 hours a day, 8 days a week) tell it you've never played games before, I think that will help. DO NOT pay full price for this game. Wait for it to go on sale. Play the demo!As everyone else has said, THE GAMEPLAY SUCKS. Trust me, I went in to this game expecting the gameplay to suck, and I was still surprised. You have to learn how to actually move the mouse instead of just tilting it. If you tilt it in the correct direction, the movement fails and you get punched in the face. How lovely. Sometimes when you move it in the correct direction, you still get punched in the face. Great, right?Anyway, the training chapter really sucks. It just stabs you in the gut with controls it doesn't explain, and if you don't get the hang of it in 0.2 seconds, it'll give you the "Jodie sucks" storyline and you just have to deal with it. Forget looking really cool in fights, you will never look cool, ever. Have fun moving your mouse in 20 different directions and pressing all 100 keys on your keyboard to figure out what the game wants from you. And don't forget that if you aren't looking in the right direction, it won't even display the little circle that signifies an action. The game makes negative effort to tell you what it wants you to do, you just have to walk around and hope you see an action marker. Oh, and did I mention that it also switches the camera angle every few seconds? And there is no button to stabilize it?Jodie really doesn't know how to pick up the pace (even by a little bit). My favorite chapter was the Navajo chapter just because you get a horse and Jodie learns how to speed. (but then she seems to immediately forget smh)IF YOU ARE LOOKING FOR A "CHOICES MATTER" GAME, DO NOT PLAY THIS. You're choices really don't matter at all. Everything is scripted, no matter what Jodie seems to make it out okay in the end. I'm not sure if Jodie can actually die, but I'm 90% sure she can't unless you really tryhard it. You just get to choose how she talks to people (it doesn't change what they think of her, though) and what minimal decisions she makes. (Maybe the choices do matter, but this game really doesn't give you that vibe.)Your favorite characters will probably be the exact same as the next guys'. Accept it. I've said a lot of negative things, so here's some positive stuff: > The storyline. Like I said, it's like reading a (minimally) interactive book. And it's a pretty good book.> The characters. The characters are extremely lovable (or hatable, depends what they were going for) the only thing that bugs me is that no matter what you do or say, their opinion of you is scripted. The only thing that really changes this is how Aiden acts. Also, it's kind of weird how fast the other characters come to like Jodie, but that's only a minor gripe.> The graphics, the scenes, the faces. Everything looks great. Really great. (Although some things do clip. It's inevitable for a game like this. A few times in some cutscenes her hand just goes right through her hair. Whatever.)> The main "conflict". About halfway through the game, or maybe at the very beginning, you come to love Aiden. The only thing I hate is that Jodie never starts (explicitly) liking Aiden though she relies on him. She always complains or argues with him although he's saved her life about a billion times. (maybe she starts liking him at the end, idky)If there was an option to both recommend and not recommend this game, I would choose it. I love this game, but I'm pretty sure I'm just grieving the loss of the 8 dollars I payed for it.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent story, there are a few holes in the plot but it was definitely entertaining the whole way through. What did ruin some things for me was the extreme amount of quick time events, where you have to rapidly press some buttons in order to make choices. This was really badly done in my opinion, I already dislike this mechanic because I'm not always very fast and it's very easy to mess up. Beyond: Two Souls takes it to another level by not even giving you an indicator and you have to predict how the character needs to move in order to succeed which isn't always clear enough which will 100% make you fail at some of the events causing major story changes for no reason, which is incredibly frustrating. That being said, the timeline approach to the story is very interesting although some of the short stories don't always feel like they're part of the same game, but I kind of liked the diversity. The game also feels very gamey in that there's usually very few ways in how to approach a situation, but overall I thought the characters were very well done. I also had to restart the game two or three times due to my player character or NPCs getting stuck and being unable to continue the story. Despite the flaws I would still recommend the game to people that are looking for a great story, however making choices you didn't want to in the QTEs will be nearly unavoidable.

_childDocuments_.review: With no gameplay I knew it would be a cinematic experience, but if you don't like the story. It is a  waste of time, I think when it comes to such games they need to get us hooked to the story since there is no gameplay. I recommend other games, unless you're getting this very cheap. Both The Medium (2021) and Plague Tale: Innocence do it better, they also focus less on gameplay (though far better than this) but at least your character can die, you at least have some puzzles? You can't die in this game and if you don't make a choice a choice is made for you, if you decide you could just sit back and relax with game picking default choices or Aiden saving you if you don't perform the QTE properly. There's also the fact that some very obvious choices don't really have a branch split from the main story, i.e. whatever you do either you protest, comply or reject your choice wont matter, I tested this trust me. The game forces you to have "relationship" with characters I hated. _childDocuments_.review: 📖 Narrative Depth and Storyline: [Rating: 10/10]☑️ The game presents a powerful main plot with rich themes and a well-structured narrative. The story's complexity, coupled with unexpected twists and pivotal moments, makes it compelling and truly unforgettable.👤 Character Development: [Rating: 10/10]☑️ The main and supporting characters are exceptionally well-developed and relatable. Jodie’s motivations and character arc evoke strong emotional responses, and certain characters stand out for their profound impact.💗 Emotional Engagement: [Rating: 10/10]☑️ The game excels at connecting with the player on an emotional level. Moments of empathy, excitement, and tension are interwoven throughout, leaving players deeply invested.🎤 Dialogue and Voice Acting: [Rating: 9/10]☑️ The dialogue feels natural and fitting to the context, enhanced by strong voice acting that adds depth to the characters and enriches the storytelling.🧩 Themes and Messages: [Rating: 10/10]☑️ The game tackles significant themes and underlying social commentary effectively integrated into the story, resonating deeply with the players.⏱️ Narrative Pacing: [Rating: 9/10]☑️ The pacing is generally well-maintained, balancing action and narrative. While there are moments that could feel a bit slow, the story’s development remains engaging throughout.🎭 Choice and Consequence: [Rating: 10/10]☑️ Player-driven choices are impactful and meaningful, shaping the story in significant ways. This depth ensures that decisions feel weighty and integral to the narrative.🔥 Overall Average Score: 9.71/10A beautifully crafted journey that stands out for its story, characters, and emotional depth. Highly recommended for those seeking an immersive, story-driven experience. 🌟Beyond: Two Souls is a deeply compelling interactive adventure game developed by Quantic Dream. Players follow the life journey of Jodie Holmes, witnessing how she navigates countless challenges to find herself and redefine her existence. Two key themes—the reshaping of life and love—left a lasting impression on me.The reshaping of life serves as the main thread throughout the game. From being abandoned as a child to becoming a subject of experiments at a research facility and later navigating her military career and life on the run, Jodie’s every step is marked by pain and trials. Players can feel how she gradually reshapes her identity and destiny, breaking free from external constraints to pursue true freedom and self-recognition. The game’s various endings allow players to see how Jodie’s pivotal choices contribute to the reinvention of her fate rather than passively accepting it.The power of love permeates Jodie’s life journey, acting as her driving force. Whether through her complex and profound relationship with Aiden or her connections with other characters, the game explores different forms of love. The bond between Jodie and Aiden is tense and multifaceted, representing a deep dependency and bond that feels akin to an inseparable kinship or partnership. Additionally, Jodie’s interactions with her foster parents, friends, and romantic interests highlight her warmth and selfless love, showing how love can sustain her through the darkest times.Beyond: Two Souls excels at pulling players into its narrative through outstanding storytelling and emotionally rich character development. It masterfully showcases how life can be reshaped in the face of adversity and how love provides hope in the bleakest moments. If you’re a fan of deep, story-driven experiences with captivating character arcs, this game is an emotional journey not to be missed.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I loved this experience. I found the story super engaging, and while it was a point of complaint for many people, I appreciated the "jumping timeline" style of storytelling, as it all comes together in the end.All of the actor's performances was also magnificent, from the voice acting to the mo-cap, to the facial animations, which really helped to draw me even further into the narrative.The graphics weren't too shabby at all, most of the time making me forget this came out on the PS3.Unfortunately, the parts which brings it back down for me was when the game forces you into some gameplay.The game tries very hard to feel like a movie. In gameplay sections, the camera continues to follow you in cinematic shots as you control Jodie, allowing for some beautiful shots that showcase how pretty the game can be at times.However, this means that you are continually fighting the camera when you are playing, as the camera keeps moving to show you the pretty sunset instead of where you need to go.Movement is also pretty jank, where tapping a direction means she will make an exaggerated turn and a few steps to make the movement look more "natural", but by then you've missed the damn door you were going for, and at the same time, the camera is trying to show you a damn picture on a desk.The many... Many quicktime events also serve to break the pacing of many scenes, and many of them are utterly redundant. As in the kind that just wait for you to press the button, with no consequence, while everyone awkwardly holds their animation.Other parts of "gameplay" sections also feels strained, like they remembered that this was supposed to be a game, rather than a movie, so they shove in a few stealth missions that combine your janky camera and janky movement with some janky cover-to-cover hiding system against fairly scripted enemies.The best fun you will have with this game is when you are not playing the game, and instead is just watching the cutscenes.Despite the high levels of jank, the story has enough intrigue keep you curious enough to pull you through, and the stellar performances of Ellen Page and co-stars definitely kept me hooked.In fact, I finished the game in two 5-ish hour sessions, so that has to tell you something (both about the game length and my life choices).Ultimately, if this game had been mostly cutscenes with no quicktime events for mundane/useless parts of the story, it would have made it infinitely better (literally, there are MULTIPLE quicktime events for you as you try to sleep. Like... Why?).TL:DRAwesome story, awesome cast performance, surprisingly decent graphics.But literally every gameplay part has a certain level of jank that just gets in the way of the narrative.If you like interesting, well performed, narrative based games, then this might be for you.If you like Ellen Page, then you will probably like this.If you are absolutely allergic to any levels of jank, then maybe just YouTube the story.Would give this movie 7 Ellen Page's out of 10

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to summarize what this game is like. It has bits of everything in it. The cinematography and action sequences feel like they're straight out of Metal Gear Solid 5, especially the Somalia segment. The early parts of the story are like the film "Carrie" (the original, not the remake), and the later bits feel like the 2019 video game "Control," except this one is a little more interesting. The gameplay is certainly unique, and occasionally hard to control, but it makes up for it in how fluid it feels. Granted, if you're playing on mouse-and-keyboard, be careful, because you'll have to fight the camera controls a number of times. The soundtrack is excellent, and the story is certainly powerful and full of twists and turns. If you're into complex narratives that weave action and clever storytelling with emotional moments, this is definitely a worthwhile pick. Granted, my only gripe with the story is the same one I had with Hitman: Absolution: The side-villains (you'll know them when you see them) in Beyond: Two Souls feel so two-dimensional, and are bad for the sake of being bad. Essentially, they're the bullies from "Carrie" with even less motivation.All in all, however, this is definitely a worthwhile game. If you're interested in long-term stories where your choices really matter when it counts, go ahead and pick it up. Is it worth full-price? I don't know. Is it worth it on sale? Definitely. Overall, it deserves a 9 out of 10.

_childDocuments_.review: The game from David Cage has been intriguing since its announcement. Still, Heavy rain and Fahrenheit are great games, of course. I expected a lot from this game. What came of it is described below.The game tells about the misadventures of a girl named Jody. From birth, she is associated with a certain creature from another world (here called the infraworld). Their bond is unbreakable and invisible. The creature's name is Aiden, he can influence the objects of this world, including electrical appliances, by moving tables, chairs, etc. He can also inhabit people and animals, controlling them. Moreover, he can even heal and kill people. The whole plot revolves around Jodie, from her early years to becoming an adult. The narrative will throw us from one time to another and back, thus showing the key events in the life of the heroine. By the way, the girl went through a rather difficult life path, managed to be a CIA agent, a homeless person, a farm worker and a fugitive criminal. As it should be in Cage's games, everything is shown in the most detailed and emotional way. There is enough drama in the game, but also enough different fight scenes and chases. Perhaps there is nothing in the game that would be worth cutting. Like past games by David, this one is a breeze. It is clearly longer than the same Heavy rain, although the narration here is from the perspective of one person, not four. We will face different people in the game. Both good and not so good. Someone will despise Jodie, someone will help, someone will want to kill, someone will save. Everything is as it should be. With all this, they still manage to shove us to different parts of the world, so there is plenty of variety in the game.The musical accompaniment in the game is on top, as always. Graphic too, especially people (review was written in 2014). Although some shortcomings are already being felt, perhaps the technologies of the set-top box, and possibly the algorithms that are written for it. This is especially noticeable in the absence of smoothing and in "square" vegetables. But these are the little things in life.The game is a beautiful and long movie in which we will worry about the main character in her difficult moments, make often difficult choices leading to different ends and, of course, fly Aiden and sweep chairs and tables. The game is very worthy, despite the fact that it is not highly appreciated by critics. It's just that, apparently, after heavy rain everyone was expecting something similar again, but more, but beyond two souls came out, sometimes a dashing action movie, sometimes a drama. Good in its own way, not requiring comparison with past games.

It swells and fades with the story's beats, intensifying moments of tension and adding poignancy to quieter, introspective scenes.While some critics argue about the balance between gameplay and cinematic experience, "Beyond: Two Souls" succeeds in offering a compelling narrative that grips players from start to finish. It challenges the conventions of what a video game can be, pushing boundaries with its ambitious storytelling and character-driven gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: I rate this game: I would definitely **recommend** grabbing this PC game. Especially on saleFirst off, I never played any David Cage games before. As a "First Playthrough" variety Streamer on , I am always looking for: 1. Great Story Based Games, 2. Visually and Immersive game play, and 3. A game that will bring new viewers to my Twitch channel. For me, it doesn't matter when the game was released, as I tend to play games that are NOT zero-day released games. I want to play games that have been released for a while so as many bugs can be worked out of them. My Journey started into Cage games began with Detroit: Become Human, then to Heavy Rain, and ended with Beyond: Two Souls. Beyond: Two Souls, IMO, is the best of the trio. I was so surprised by how I fell for this game. I totally knew nothing about the game's story and must say WOW. Get this game.  In  my past there was a time when i was interested in the  program of the USG and I found myself slipping in and out of that kind of mental space while playing this game. It was awesome seeing where this game's story goes from day 1. Again, no spoilers here... but it certainly was a bit of an emotional roller coaster ride.There are two choices of Play Order in this game. 1. Chapters in Remixed (chronological) order, and 2. Chapters in "Original" order. This in the initial game release mode; game's chapters in a non-linear narrative.My first or blind playthrough was in "Chronological" Order (I flipped a coin to decide). Then I played the game, again, in the Original order to to get a few more Steam Achievements. Another unexpected surprise. This 2nd playthrough was as interesting since it represented such an alternative view of the game.While playing this game, Twitch viewers, new to my channel, and definitely loyal to this game constantly mentioned having some confusion when trying to follow what was happening when playing in the "Original" mode. Again, wow! Props to Cage.I hope anyone reading this review who decides to dive into Jodie's travels and story puts it together. The revelation made it even more worth the $$ for this game. It's ingenious. - Developers: 	Quantic Dream- PC Release Dates: Windows - July 22, 2019- Perspectives: Third-person, First-person, Cinematic camera- Genres: Adventure, Quick time events- Theme: Sci-fi- Beyond: Two Souls is a single-player and multiplayer third-person, first-person and cinematic camera adventure and quick time events game. _childDocuments_.review: This is certainly worth a play through if you like Heavy Rain or Until Dawn type games - in fact, it improves on the formula while maintaining the strong point and click DNA of that genre.  The QTEs are forgiving and what it often lacks in intuitiveness (or occasional control/response issues), it more than makes up for in charisma, strong narrative and style.  It may be a tad shorter than the average triple A title, but honestly, this type of game cannot afford to overstay its welcome.  It varies things up with combat and navigation, but once you know the ropes, little is required while you push the plot forward.  For those that do want a longer run in this intriguing word, replay is present to see alternative conclusions from choices that do have a bearing at crucial junctions.  However, for the first run through, I heavily recommend avoiding spoilers and walkthroughs.  There isn't really a "wrong" path as such, but options that allow tremendous personal engagement with a relatable character in ridiculous circumstances.

It really is a game where the less you know going in the better the time you are likely to have. I do wish it had an option to alter decisions shortly after you made them. Even a sort of quick save system would be nice. I can understand why this isn't present but restarting chapters or quickly exiting the game to fix mistakes can be rather tiring. The controls felt quite odd a lot of the time when using a mouse and keyboard. I noticed this less so when using a controller. I only noticed a handful of glitches. All of which were in chapter 14. The game took me about 10 hours to beat. I could see myself replaying it to try out alternate routes. The DLC only added about 15 minutes of extra playtime. I was unable to get it working properly on Linux.

_childDocuments_.review: Willem Dafoe, Willem Dafriend, Willem Dafoe, Willem DafriendI do not recommend this game to others. While it has its strengths, which includes its voice acting, especially Willem Dafoe, the writing is cringy enough at times and overall over the top that it loses any relatability and makes the entire game tedious. The game is written to force emotional situations on a player rather than letting a player appreciate them organically, that makes it all tedious. As one who is in general a very sympathetic person, having the entire game be about how tortured the main character gets old fast even for me. While there are attempts at balancing this out, they too feel forced and unpleasant to experience as a player. I cannot recommend this game even on sale as they are 11 hours that I personally wish that I had back. A few choice comments on the game below:There are a number of "episodes" that the game could have easily left out and it would have been a lot better, such as the main character's "coming of age" experiences that were plain cringy. Despite this, the game made a callback to them at the end, which ruined a strong ending. A number of characters were just plain over the top, like the main character's father. It removed any sense of relatability, which Quantic Dream claims to seek to address.Finally, the game is just plain trying to force emotional scenarios on players. There were some positive game moments where the emotions of a given situation developed organically, but so much of the game is so clearly designed around trying to force a player to have a given emotion or feel a particular way that it is unpleasant to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, with interesting story and truly great acting by Elliot Page. I remember reading some bad press back when it came out, and started playing with low expectations, and was pleasantly surprised. The game let's the player choose, if they want to play the game's story chapters in a chronological mode, or the "original". In the original mode the chapters are not presented chronologically, but in a way determined by the devs, which actually makes sense from gameplay perspective, as it gives the action more variety and more breathing space. Some of the chapters are more about drama and discovery, some are action-packed sequences, with even a few sneaking parts, reminding me of Metal Gear Solid. The messy structure of chapters also makes sense through what is presented in the ending scenes. At the start, playing the game in the original mode, it was kind of difficult to follow and get invested, but it quickly starts to make sense and it's hard to leave the game before finishing the whole story. "Unfortunately" it takes about 10 hours to get through to the end, so you probably won't make it in one sitting.Throughout the game, there are dozens of choices to be made (and by that I mean these are mostly actions you can take, which you have to figure out by yourself, not just dialog options), and by the end of every chapter you are presented with statistics on how many people made the same choices as you. These are useful if you wish to replay the game, or specific chapters, making different decisions leading the story a little different. Whole game can be replayed multiple times thanks to this freedom of choice.

_childDocuments_.review: This was probably the most dramatic game I've ever played, (and I played a lot of story-wise rich games) the story of a problematic, abnormal (and mostly unwanted) girl with supernatural abilities she can't fully control. This is easily in top 5 for me (concept and storywise) even though there are some things that I'd like to add to/remove from the story. But still, could've been so, sooo much better even without altering the story completely, simply by making it with the better tech, experience and feedback that we have today.It's lacking the "multi-optioned dialogue choices that changes the story drastically" part that Detroit: Become Human has and you have very little to say about the story you're going through, which upset me to be honest.MINOR SPOILERS BELOW I'd have prefered an antihero (self-serving and egoistic) Jodie after some point of the story. I played it in the chronological order and the first couple hours, up to the point of being sent to the CIA, was extremely fun for me. I would have prefered to be able to not join the CIA at all and wreck sh*t up (like she ends up doing anyway, duh) if they try to force Jodie to join. Playing with litte/teenager Jodie was way more fun than having endless action sequences with terrorists or "entitites". I'd have preferred it better if they left Aiden and the "Infraworld" completely unexplained tbh, since the "explanation" they tried was pretty lame imho. Wanted to add, I'd just remove the desert sequence completely.By the way, I admire Elliot* Page for the great voice acting he's put in this masterpiece of a game. With a better storyline and better dialogue, he could've done much more better, I believe.
