_childDocuments_.review: A game needs two things to be good, a strong central narrative and a good core game play loop. Minecraft may not have a strong narrative but the game play loop is very engaging.  The Stanley Parable may not have much in terms of game play, the narrative is so strong you want to explore every possible path. Close to the Sun has neither of these and falls flat on it's face harder then Icarus.This review will contain spoilers for the game, if you don't want to know what happens then I recommend seeing a walkthrough for the game as opposed to playing the game.The game is clearly taking inspiration from Bioshock. However, where that game was able to use the flaws of human nature to demonstrate the down fall of the utopian society, Close to the Sun just has monster. The monsters in the game are described as the antibodies of time, which is a apparently a living organism. This is extremely stupid. First, it doesn't tie into what Bioshock was about. Second, the game never explains how or why time is a living organism. They talk about how they're tapping into other timelines and universes, so why couldn't they saw the creature came from one of these timelines or universes. What's more, the monsters never play a part in the main story. They only serve to be the center pieces of chase sequences. The central conflict of the game is nothing but a set piece.When it comes to the main characters there is nothing. The only thing you can say about them is just that they are what the game needs them to be. Your sister is a scientist and that's it. Nikola Tesla is a scientist and that's it. The voice on the radio is just a surprise villain and that's it. You are there to drive the plot and that's it. The game mentions how you're a reporter and when you find the interrogation room you even say how your editor would love this. You being a reporter is meaningless as non of that translates into game play or the narrative. Even the surprise villain is done wrong. Through out the game you learn that Edison had sent spies on board the ship. The surprise villain how ever isn't a spy, he's a disgruntled scientist that was knocked down a peg when your sister came on board. The entire cast of characters you interact with are nothing but hollow and empty.Finally what I want to talk about is the time travel. You first go to meet your sister after you get a letter from her only to realize she hadn't written it yet. As you go through the game you get notes in the pneumatic tubes that are letter revealed to be sent from your future self. When the game ends however, you never perform any action that would lead to those events happening. It's likely that it was kept that way to tease a possible sequel. As it stands, nothing about this game is worth your time or money.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has no save system. Repeat, this game has no save system. The only time the game saves is in the end of each chapter, so if you have to leave the game before that (and gee, people have lifes and stuff), you will have to repeat the whole chapter from the start.I quit the game because of this. This would be a somewhat decent walking simulator otherwise, but sometimes I do wonder what the hell developers think when they get ideas like making a game that does not have any kind of even half functioning save system.

_childDocuments_.review: is finally released in a right store so we can check it out! The story takes place in an alternative steampunk universe, year 1897 ("Experience a second era of scientific enlightenment, where the mind and inventions of the great Nikola Tesla have shaped the 19th century" while in reality he's often called "The Man Who Invented the Twentieth Century"). In this reality Nikola Tesla competes with Thomas Edison in a technological war and events take place on his huge "The Helios" ship that serves as a hub for the world's most successful scientists and inventors. Additional pieces of story could be gathered from various documents, such as letters and newspapers that are scattered throughout the ship.The Helios is really cool, detailed very well and atmosphere there slightly reminds Bioshock. In addition to nice environments, the story is interesting as well so both key aspects are totally fine (we have a walking simulator here after all). Horror elements are spooky at times but not scary enough due to obvious game design limitations (horror atmosphere is great where it needed though). Rare "chase" sequences are surprisingly refreshing and could bring some adrenaline. Essential puzzles are very simple but not annoying and fit well.While there's an achievement to complete the game in under 3 hours (that shouldn't be hard to do), an actual playthrough with exploration and reading interesting notes should take 4,5-5 hours.Fun fact: 1 year beta-test was not enough. My character got stuck in the end of 3rd chapter (that is a relatively long one)... and I had to replay it from beginning, yep. It was a HORRIBLE trap between a plant, sofa, chair and coffee table - my character was unable to jump over any of those :(To be honest it was the only technical hiccup that I've encountered, but jumps are ridiculous here - there's no real use for them and they are quite awful. I believe jumps were added "just to be added" so you may unbind jump button without hesitation.All in all,  is a solid and fun to play walking simulator with horror elements that reminded me Moons of Madness. These games are like twin brothers in almost every quality/gameplay/genre/technical aspects. At the same time Close to the Sun is unique in its own way and could definitely brighten a couple of evenings for any fan of such games. 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Close to the Sun

_childDocuments_.review: So let me fist say that I want to give this game a positive review, but there's too much here that I dislike that would need to change in order to give this game a thumbs up. Which is sad, because I really like the atmosphere and what story there is. The ship is incredible and there's a lot of time and thought given to the locations. So, spoilers ahead. First of all, the action scenes are annoyingly bad and consist of running aimlessly down corridors, and I say aimlessly because most of the running sequences do not tell you which direction  to go, you have to figure this out by dying repeatedly and being made to watch a horrible death animation. Run from the guy with the knife, run from the time monsters, run from explosions, run from lightning. There's one moment where you have to jump from a moving tram car, but there is no indication on which door is about to open or that you need to time the jump correctly. The voice on the com yells Jump, this resulted in me looking around to figure which door was open and then jumping into the fire. Next time I figured out exactly which door was going to be opening and when the voice said jump I jumped, into the fire. I finally figured out you have to wait to be right over this steel grate below the tram to jump.  With the time monsters (other than one exception by the Tesla elevator) you're told to run, but take a wrong turn, death animation, start sprinting too late, death animation, sometimes when you do everything right, death animation, and the darkness of the game does not help in finding your way while sprinting, or the fact that the sprinting animation narrows your field of vision. I had the gamma almost all the way up and it was still too dark in spots where I missed walkways multiple times while dying repeatedly.In another section, the player has to make their way across an bunch of walkways while I giant Tesla generator is sending out waves of death inducing electricity. You figure out quickly that you need to hide behind objects when the pulse goes off or you'll die, but the person asking you to run this gauntlet never tells you that, he just says, hey get over there and good luck. However, you also find out that not everything that looks like you should be able to hide behind it will protect you, so...death animation. Look, I don't mind dying, but at least give the player more means to succeed than to fail. As far as the puzzles go, they were alright. Most of them involve spinning things or pulling levers, or picking something up in one area to be used in another. Nothing game changing, and extremely simple. I was willing to overlook this to follow the story. I am generally willing to withhold my disbelief until a story is completed and I can see all of the parts. This whole story revolves around some experiment going horribly wrong and breaking time.  It starts off with a letter that you find out hasn't been sent yet and through your explorations you will find cryptic notes seemingly written by your future self. There's even a section where you see yourself doing something that you haven't done yet. Your immediate goal, however, is not to fix the problem but to escape the ship with your sister.  So, I was expecting some payoff where in the second half of the game you end up going back in time to fix everything that happened. BUT THE STORY JUST ENDS!!!! Obviously I hate cliffhangers, especially in video games, and especially where I have not been warned that this is one chapter in a larger series. Do not tease me with time travel and say "Oh this will make more sense when I'm looking at this from the perspective of the future." This is not Quantum Break. Though it may be, who knows. All I know is that I completed the game in 3 hours while being told the whole time that there was a larger payoff, and then at the end I get told, oh but not in this game. Note: Dev's put in the description or something that this is just part of a story before you pull people in expecting a full experience. I love what you've done here but ending the story on "I know how to fix everything" and then running Credits is kind of...I don't know...anticlimactic. Now I feel like playing Quantum Break again.  Overall, this is a good game, with an interesting story, and a great location to explore, but I'd have rather had a walking simulator with a story, like Pine. The monsters don't add anything other than annoyance, and the knife wielding murderer has some kind of motivation that apparently we won't be told in this game. I'd have loved to just explore these amazing locations and have the time to take everything in. I'd have also loved an actual ending to this story, but it's not really memorable enough to wait for a second game to fill in the blanks. This is an episode of television at most, and no one wants to wait years before the next episode.

_childDocuments_.review: is a decent horror walking simulator with an interesting yet predictable story, exceptionally beautiful atmosphere, gorgeous scenery, and fantastic audio design. Gameplay consist of traversing the spooky abandoned ship, solving simple puzzles, and surviving various scripted chase sequences. There are collectibles scattered throughout each section with a handy journal to keep track of how many more you need to find. Even though a small indie team created this title, the first thing you may notice is how similar the design elements are to  The game is rather short and can be completed within 3-4 hours. Only negatives would be having a forgettable story and having no manual save option which forces you to start from the beginning of the chapter again. I would recommend getting this game on sale [7.5/10]

_childDocuments_.review: So, this game had me intrigued all the way back when it was an exclusive on the Epic Games Store. Didn't buy it over there, though. Much later I got it here on a discount, but didn't get around to play it for quite a while - until now.Close to the Sun is an interesting game. At first glance, everything screams 'BioShock': the setting, the art style etc. Some environments could've been taken straight out of Rapture and put in this game - if it were the case, I would totally believe that. When you start getting a bit further into the game, you'll notice that this plays a lot different than Irrational's all-time classic, though. This plays more like SOMA or Amnesia: environmental puzzles combined with exploration. In fact, Close to the Sun has just a few puzzles, and they are not very hard to figure out. So, there's just a bit more to the gameplay to elevate this over a walking simulator. From time to time you're also tasked with escaping from enemies, and in this game you do one thing then: you run. And those parts are, in my opinion, the weakest sections of the game by far. One little mistake, and you're caught (and killed) - reload the last checkpoint. This can get very frustrating very fast. Other than that, the game is overall pretty uneventful. The story, as typical for these kinds of games, leaves a lot unexplained and especially the ending feels highly unsatisfying.On the technical side, the game has massive performance issues. The fps were mostly above 60 for me, but something seems to be up with the frame times: inconsistent frame rates and stuttering are pretty common. Graphically, the game is fine and looks good, the sound design is also done nicely.Overall, I would not recommend this game. There's not enough 'meat' here to keep your attention and leave a good impression, and the performance issues can be annoying. A playthrough should take around 5 to 6 hours. Unlocking all achievements during one playthrough is no problem.Recommendations for similar games: Among the Sleep, Call of Cthulhu, Firewatch, Master Reboot, INFRA

_childDocuments_.review: is a very mixed bag, and honestly, a game with a bit of an identity crisis, if you can believe that.First and foremost, this game does more than just wear its influences on its sleeves; it is directly trying to imitate way too many aspects of the  series. Just see what you think when I list some items:There's more to it than just that, not to mention some of the color schemes and even the game's font. But yes, this game was really going heavy on large aspects of the  series and it was way too noticeable for someone who loves that series.Besides that, I said "identity crisis" because, although a good amount of people said it is not in the horror genre, the game definitely feels like the developers wanted it to be for a while. The first few chapters of the game have quite a few slow-moving, eerie areas as well as many jump scares (visually and audibly). Probably halfway through the game, it kind of loses all of that, especially once you've been through a few chase scenes, which I'll talk about later.Now, the visual design is the best part of the game, but it is not consistent. You can see some very nicely made areas and then you look at other objects and they are poorly designed (especially any NPCs or bodies). There's graphical glitches too, in terms of rendering, and I had a couple of times where my character's head (or rather, lack of a head) came into view from above even though it was in first-person.Besides that, the general contrast/brightness is poorly done. The game's brightness screen suggests you to adjust until the rightmost logo is barely visible. That is horrible advice! As I tend to do with most games, I increased the brightness a bit instead. But even with that, the game has wide disparities between what should be dark or not. There'd be overly bright sections of the game, and other sections that have pitch black spots even though they should be visible. And adjusting your monitor/settings doesn't help; it's simply the way the developers rendered light inside of the game.On top of that, this game has one of those designs where black shading surrounds the edges of the screen. I've never understood why some games do that, because it's not even realistic. There's not large black spots in my peripheral vision in real life; my vision just... stops. The only way to simulate this in real life is to scrunch my face up so skin starts blocking the edge of my eyes! So... why do some developers surround your view with dark shading?Gameplay-wise, it's a typical walking simulator. With the exception of occasional side doors, the game is almost entirely linear. I think the first couple of chapters have "hub" areas where you go down certain halls and return afterwards, but otherwise you'll be walking straight ahead.Occasionally, the game throws in chase scenes, but with the exception of one of them, they're mostly tedious and not interesting. They start very quickly and you have to make sure you find the right path, as you die if you even fall behind one second. Oddly, some of the chases are trial and error because you might turn to find a door is closed, or something suddenly breaks to block the path. And despite that, there's never time to turn around and go another way. If you get blocked, you're dead, and that's it. Also, during some sections of the game, but especially during those chases, my frame rate sank, and I'm certain it is due to optimization issues in the game engine.My review's pretty long at this point, but I'll wrap it up by saying the story is nothing special. Besides the various notes it tries to copy from , the overall message of the story is too on-the-nose. Papers you find, NPC discussions, the name of the game and its chapter names, and even its credits song make it seem like it is the first time the writers have heard of metaphors.And its ending decides to cut off at the worst time. Instead of trying to wrap anything up, it continues repeating the same questions, insinuating some answers vaguely with little to no reason, and decides to just end at a moment that screams sequel bait.In the end, there's way too many weaknesses to recommend this one to anybody.
_childDocuments_.name: Close to the Sun

_childDocuments_.review: Fear, loss, pain, depression, loneliness, betrayal ... and now about the game Yes buy it if you like slow paced adventures that heavily depend on atmosphere First of all people should stop comparing this to bioshock because even though the art style might resemble bioshock it has exactly 0 as ZERO, NULL, NOTHING, RIEN, NICHTS, NADA common with bioshock.This game is very dark (both visually and tonally) and yet it manages to lean heavily to visual story telling thanks to the overall slow pace in conjunction with the very subtle yet disturbing ost and overall very good sound design I'm not afraid to say it creates atmosphere that would suit SCP title.It's not the longest of games and it's a good thing. You could probably run through it in about 4-5 hours yet I've spent twice as much there just to explore in detail what the devs crafted here. I won't go into detail to avoid spoilers but I can say that thanks to very sparingly used chase sequences they never overstay their welcome.The only thing I could blame devs for is optimisation, even on i7 and 3070ti I had to lower shadows from ultra to high to get stable 60+fps but to be honest you will probably never see the difference in shadows quality anyway and UE4 looks just fine on basically any setting.So the conclussion is yes support devs with actual vision not the corporate copypasta shills selling you the same thing for the 25th time.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a walking sim where the movement is agonisingly slow, the linear narrative is full of contrivances and loose threads, the story itself intentionally derivative, and the puzzles (if you can even call them that) few and far between. Probably the least interesting interactive narrative game i've ever played so far.The singular highlight would be the environment designs - which was the only thing that kept me playing and I can honestly say it's NOT worth it. Just find a Let's Play or just browse the image gallery on the store page or something.The plot is some wishy-washy-generic-science-experiment-gone-wrong-find-your-lost-sibling hogwash that has too little characterisation for me to care about anyone in the story and to make it worse none of the plot lines have a satisfying resolution - the game just abruptly ends when you escapes, and without answering any of the questions raised during the last two chapters.Suffice to say if I were to start again - I will most definitely refund this game before reaching the 2-hour mark. Absolutely not worth £16. If you REALLY have to find something to scratch that Bioshock 1&2 itch - be prepared to be thoroughly disappointed and wait for it to be at least something like 60% off.

_childDocuments_.review: To the developers (from a game developer):You've already proven you can create stunning visuals, an interesting and misterious story, and a dark and exhausting atmosphere. Period.However... there's plenty of room to improve in terms of gameplay.I've felt myself "claustrophobically trapped" while playing this game (and not in the good sense). No freedom to explore. Always driven on rails. Always everything too scripted. Allways very little to do, apart from search for newspapers and some collectibles per level. Lots of frustration for not being able to climb up these or those small piles of furnitures and check if some clue/information, or some useful object, or some alternative exit could be found beyond. Frustration turned into annoyance when discovering that you really can do that on some specific places... that has being chosen by the designer. A bit more on rails, and it could have been House of the Dead without shooting.I really see you all as a company with potential, and I really, really hope you can grow and improve your future games, fixing these game design flaws that make this game recommended only for those to want to focus on the story and nothing more (if you are one of them, go ahead, you'll love this game!). And please, don't forget to add a "Redefine Keys" menu option, there's still plenty of PC users out there that use keyboard + mouse, and want to remap the default game keys for playing.  I'll keep an open eye for your future projects, Im sure it'll worth the effort and you'll make "better" games.Kind regards,STM_User2

_childDocuments_.review: A steam-punk-ish alternate reality mystery thriller. You're about to visit your Sister at the Helios, Nikola Tesla's sea faring high tech lab. Surprise, something went horribly wrong and you're in for a rescue mission... Reminds me a bit of Bioshock (just way tamer, less crazy and without all the action).  I like the setting and the aesthetic, but hate how the controls feel - more like steering a sleepwalker than playing a person.  Is there any unwritten law, forcing walking simulators to proceed at the speed of a tortoise? Even "running" outside of chases feels less quick than I'd normally walk. And during chases, running feels like "a comical nightmare version of running", where you move your arms fast, but don't get much momentum forward. But, no spoiler: It's not a nightmare. The game would have been way shorter (and more enjoyable for me) if it wasn't that slow moving. And chases? Quite annoying, too. Rarely indicators where to go, no time to look around and make an educated guess, so you just die until you find a way that isn't a dead end. That is, if you can see the path in the dark. And even then I died quite a few times because our heroine didn't want to jump past an obstacle because... honestly, I have no clue ,,, she just jumped on the spot instead of over the obstacle and as time is very short on chase I died again.The story was OK, but leaves us with a quite a few plot-holes and mere hints on how the might get closed. Planned sequel, or just bad writing? I don't know.Wouldn't recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Close to the Sun

_childDocuments_.review: This was a hard call, but ultimately I felt the game was just too lazy to be fun. It seems like it was made by a team of talented graphic artists moonlighting as game developers. It's not that the gameplay was bad. It was just mundane. You just run around a ship. Literally. Except when you're walking. And you don't do it freely, but only as you're directed to by the NPCs. I mean, there are huge areas that you can walk around in and look at things, but it's all pointless until the game directs you to do something. (That's not completely true of the first part of the game, but it is completely true of the latter part; it's as if the devs changed their minds halfway through about how they wanted to proceed.)As for all the obligatory things lying around for you to read and look at: at first, you have the feeling that, just like with Bioshock and similar games, these are meant to unfold the plot for you. However, eventually you realize that all it's really meant to do is earn you (entirely optional) achievements. If you don't care about the achievements, about 90% of the crap you run across isn't worth wasting your time on (violating the initial spirit of the game--more on that in a moment). The plot itself unfolds more or less in realtime around you, with your responsibility being mainly to flip switches and run footraces with electricity monsters and the occasional knife-wielding lunatic (don't ask). There are lots of footraces, and they are all exactly the same: if you've played the game Mafia and remember the infamous car race, you know exactly what to expect. Luckily, these are not as difficult or as long as the car race, but they are every bit as pointless and off-putting. No one bought Close To The Sun because they wanted to play Achilles vs. the Hare. But you'll be playing that a lot, and when you lose--as you will often--you'll be yawning through unskippable death cutscenes.Now for the spirit of  the game: in the end, the game fails because its main reason for existing is the (Bioshockesque, Tesla-inspired) environment, which (notably, in the later stages of the game) the devs end up forcing you to race through without giving you any time to stop and smell the electromagnetic coils. It's like inviting someone to a party and then rushing them out of the house.  What exactly was the point? In this case, the point is that the devs seemed to run out of architectural ideas, so instead of putting any effort into designing several distinctive engine rooms and whatnot, they went with the one they had and relied on rushing you through it before you could realize that that was all there was.As for the plot, I'm still not exactly sure what was going on with some of it--the whole mad slasher thing came across as just ridiculous--yet at the same time it ended up being so simplistic as to be almost insulting. There was no real mystery surrounding any of it, other than how Nikola Tesla acquired the billions of 19th century dollars it would have cost to build such a mammoth ship in the first place. The ending, which was supposed to be the big payoff for the player's endurance of the game's many sins, was especially terse and unrewarding...almost a slap in the fact after all the teasing that preceded it.A word on the audio: the voice-acting was tolerable-to-good, but the volume level seemed to vary on its own at different points in the game. In the beginning, Rose can't whisper without hurting your ear drums, but then if you adjust the level in the options, you find yourself straining to hear her in the next section. I ended up surrendering and just taking the pain. The music, as little of it as there was, wasn't grating or intrusive, which is my gold standard for games, so chalk up a win here. And the graphics, of course, were...well, you've seen them, so you already know whether you'll like them or not. One thing to note, however: nothing much changes from what you've seen. In Bioshock, there was a general art deco theme, but different environments had their own visual "take" on it. In Close To The Sun, what you see at the beginning is pretty much what you'll see all the way through.The controls were simple: WASD + space + mouse. That's it. And that's a good thing, because it's all you need (there's exactly one spot where the space bar--bunnyhop--is needed, and I'm not positive it's needed; I just never tried not using it there). I wish the game had gone full SOMA and featured sneaking, in which case other controls would be necessary, but since it didn't, these minimalist controls are ideal. No fuss, no muss. In most cases, tricky moves like edging along a balcony or shimmying under things are accomplished by clicking on an icon, Okay, so that's all I can think of to tell you. I didn't hate the game, but it's not one I can unreservedly say was worth the time I spent on it. As always, YMMV.

_childDocuments_.review: This one is tough. I'm a big fan of indie games, and believe in supporting our indie game developers. However, I also need to be honest with this one. I was pretty let down. Leading up to the release of Close to the Sun, I was super hyped for its release. The visuals looked great, the story seemed interesting, and I liked the setting. However, once I got to playing the game, I began to realize how little "playing" there actually was. This game really is a walking simulator, with very minimal moments where you're given the opportunity to do anything significant or rewarding. Out of the 10 chapters, the first 7 were quite dull, with more exposition and build up than anything else. You do a few puzzles here and there, but you're mostly walking to your next destination while listening to someone talk to you. The final 3 chapters were decent, but couldn't save the game, for me. In my opinion, for a walking simulator to be good, the game needs to allow more interaction, whether it's with NPCs or the environment. A good example would be Norwood Suite. OR, for a walking simulator to be good, it needs to keep you emotionally or mentally invested. A good example would be most first person horror games. Unfortunately, for Close to the Sun, there weren't enough moments that kept you super engaged. More exposure to the monsters, and more chase / hide n' seek sequences could have helped fix this issue. Or, more interactivity with the environment could have helped. Close to the Sun fell just short in both of these areas.Close to the Sun had some good ideas behind it. But, I feel it could have been executed much better.

The atmosphere and environment are what really shine here but I wish there had been more to all of it. Nothing wrong with walking horror games that tell a story but there was something distinctly disappointing and lacking about Close to The Sun. It's all looks and no substance, like an overpriced 'gourmet' burger. During my first playthrough my enjoyment steadily decreased as it went on, and on my second I had quickly lost any interest. It's not horrible but its just not that great either. The only similarities with Bioshock are the failed utopia themes. But Bioshock is a gem, and this is fool's gold. Go play Bioshock again, because you won't find the scratch to that Bioshock itch with Close to The Sun.

_childDocuments_.review: The illegitimate lovechild of Bioshock and Amnesia. tl;dr Decent story adventure with a great atmosphere let down by some stupid chase sequences. 6/10In essence, Close to the Sun is a walking simulator punctuated with a some "chase" sequences taking place aboard a ship that could easily be mistaken for Rapture.  + Visually Beautiful (prologue made me seasick, but the rest of the game was fine)+ Eerie+ Eerie+ Eerie+ Aubrey. This guy says a lot of very funny stuff. Clearly insane and he knows it. At one point Rose asks Aubrey if he is alright.  Aubrey replies:- Puzzles are mostly just searching around to find a code to input into a lock. - Some of the chase sequences are ridiculously infuriating.  I must have died 10 - 15 times on Chapter 8 in the "10 second" chase which requires unprecedented precision to be fast enough not to get yourself skewered.  Almost rage quit because of this one scene. - Level design is generally very linear with the player constantly "railroaded" on a specific path.  You often need to go around stuff because Rose can only jump as high as a snail. Few jump scares, but mostly just an eerie and tense atmosphere. note: There are a lot of mutilated and gory corpses included for shock value, more than would seem plausible.Duration: 4.5 hours to complete, which is probably the right length for this style of adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: Close to the Sun doesn't come close at all.Set in an alternate history late 1800's, CttS takes place in a world where Nikola Tesla and Thomas Edison have become so powerful that they each more or less control half the world and are constantly warring with each other to get their hands on the other's half.  Tesla has created an utterly gargantuan ship out in the Atlantic known as Helios which acts as his home and the base of operations for his company's continued scientific endeavors.  Players take control of Rose Archer, a journalist who recently received a strange letter from her sister Ada.  Ada is a scientist aboard the Helios and has beckoned Rose to come find her, and so Rose does, but soon Rose finds herself trapped aboard an unfathomably massive vessel filled with corpses, failing ship systems, and something else stalking the halls while a strange blue energy fills the air and glowing apparitions move about as if everything is fine.All of this is a perfectly acceptable set up for what could be a thrilling story of mind bending discovery and cosmic horror.  Instead, the game only delivers a confused mess of a narrative that somehow manages to be utterly predictable in its twists while somehow also feeling incomplete enough to leave you scratching your head and wondering if you missed something major.  Unfortunately, you didn't, and worse yet, the game feels like it hopes to explain a lot of the nonsense in this story with a sequel that frankly doesn't deserve to become a reality.  Rose walks the line between boring and outright unlikable, while other characters are either predictably traitorous, confusingly helpful, or inexplicably monstrous.  Having a spooky knife wielding man stalking the halls and painting messages on the walls in blood is fine, but if the only explanation for why he's doing it is "he used to be Jack the Ripper", then don't waste the audience's time with his messages and ramblings that seem to allude to something more going on if you don't intend to explain it.  Add to that some genuinely terrible dialogue and a protagonist who constantly talks to herself in the most nonchalant way imaginable as she wades through death and horror, and a script that thinks pretty lowly of its audience's intelligence; and you've got a downright terrible story experience.There isn't any.  No, truly.  There's no inventory.  No combat.  No traversal or stealth.  The game never even bothers giving you a list of controls, as the only buttons that you'll need are your movement keys, sprint key, and use key.  The overwhelming majority of the game is nothing more than walking (or "running") around the Helios at an unacceptably slow pace.  You'll solve occasional "puzzles" such as flipping a switch to open a door or flipping a switch and then running through the door before it can close again.  Every now and then the game will throw some truly advanced puzzles at you which involve finding four symbols in a room and then matching them up on a spinning wheel device.  Exciting stuff.  Every now and then the game will throw a chase sequence at the player, likely to keep them from falling asleep, but given that these chases involve nothing more than holding down the sprint and forward key while occasionally making forty-five or even ninety degree turns; the risk of dosing off never really goes away.  The game also features some laughably rookie mistakes that even the most basic round of testing should have revealed when it comes to its world exploration, if one can call it that.  Every now and then, Rose can climb over objects if the developers designated that specific object as being something she can climb over.  But since the mass majority of objects in the game world, big and small, physically block her from getting around, players are quickly trained not to bother walking in any direction that has an object in the way.  This can lead to wandering around rooms completely unsure where to go for minutes at a time (made all the more infuriating by just how slow Rose moves) until players finally stumble across the one designated object in the room that the developers have so graciously given them permission to climb over.  Either give players the ability to mantle objects at will, or stop putting objects in their path on occasion.This is the only part of the game that has any merit to it, and even this doesn't escape unscathed.  Visually speaking, Close to the Sun looks rather magnificent.  The sheer scale and relatively high detail of the Helios is impressive, and public facing environments tend to be gorgeous places to be in which makes it baffling that the game spends as much time as it does shoving players into dimly lit metal grey corridors and back halls so often.  When you're free to walk around some of the Helios' larger rooms, it's often beautiful enough to briefly make you forget how bored you are as you admire the splendor.  Lighting is very high quality which gives the game a rich atmosphere early on before the mundanity of the gameplay settles in.  Sound is equally effective and the music usually does a great job of setting the tone of a scene when it comes bleeding in.  Animation is rather rough.  It gets the job done, but it is noticeably several tiers lower than the quality of the objects and people being animated.  The voice acting is largely terrible with only one stand out, though it's also hard to tell if some of the bad acting has more to do with the direction than the person delivering the lines.

_childDocuments_.review: I only suggest this game if you really enjoy a good story/setting over everything else. I wish we had the ability to rate somewhere in the middle, because that is where this game falls for me. Parts of it were so infuriating that I debated saying "no". It's a walking simulator, which I tend to enjoy as a casual gamer.Welcome to the Helios, a radio-controlled ship in the time of Tesla - who in this alternate reality, has become the main supplier of energy. In an effort to solve the world's issues and find an infinite source of power, Tesla has invited all the world's smartest minds aboard his revolutionary cruise ship. Here, while escaping the spies of Edison, your sister is working alongside Tesla. Tesla may or may not be an evil genius. It remains to be seen. Your sister has asked you to board the ship, and when you do, you find it totally empty with signs of struggle. You embark on a journey to figure out what has happened on the ship and find your sister. Pros:- Excellent story, would honestly make for an interesting film - Lovely soundtrack - A few decent jump scares - Interesting factoids and easter eggs throughout - Cool ideas and concepts- Amazing rendering and graphics/settings. I loved roaming the ship and looking at details - well rounded characters - The story and environment make up for it being a walking simulatorCons:- Though it auto saves, if you exit the game you'll start the chapter again regardless of where you auto-saved last. This is infuriating because if you die, or leave the game toward the end of a chapter, you'll have to restart it - running barely increases your characters speed- Respawn after you die during a chase scene usually only gives you 1-2 seconds to move before you die again - The chase scenes have no strategy in them, it's all about figuring out the pattern to escape and the difference of 1-2 seconds of the wrong direction or walking instead of running can be the difference in you dying- The ending doesn't really explain anything and feels anti-climatic - it's hard to know when chase or run sequences have ended, so you can accidentally run through an area you were meant to explore for collectables - Drawn out death scenes so when you do die you're waiting a long time to respawn and keep playing Tips:- Don't exit the game mid-chapter - Unless prompted to run on screen, regardless of what is happening around you, you have time to explore for collectables - if you're in a chase scene or a run scene you'll be told with text- Even after beating the game, you can go back and replay chapters for achievements - The game is mostly walking simulator with some escape and a little bit of puzzle - Always click ladders with the mouse or you can walk past them and fall, and die- The little green symbols that appear everywhere are an easter egg, not a collectable, don't worry about them- Look everywhere for collectables- there's a few jump scares and lots of flashing lights so be careful if you're prone to seizures - I found the controls required by mouse click (such as going over, under, or around an object) often didn't engage so if you're trying to use one while on a run sequence they can be the difference between you dying or not- It's good to look at every setting fully because if you do get to a run sequence you'll have a better idea how to escape - Not the game for you if you want shooting, combat, or more engagement or stealth I don't know how people manage to get the achievement for beating it in under 3 hours or beating it without dying - on their first play through. So much of it just seems random in terms of the attacks etc and it can take doing the run sequences a few times to figure them out through trial and error. I often rage quit and forgot about the save states and found myself back at the start of the chapter I had almost finished.
_childDocuments_.name: Close to the Sun

_childDocuments_.review: Close to the Sun is a horror walking sim where you play as journalist Rose Archer, as she travels to find her sister in the massive ship Helios, created by famed scientist Nikola Tesla as a utopia for researchers, scientists, and like-minded people away from the world. As you'd expect, the ship has fallen into ruin, and she must avoid dangerous beings and solve some light puzzles to reach her goal. I should mention for storage-tight people that the game is only 20 GB, not 50 GB as the sys-req states.What caught my interest in this game is because of another game: BioShock. Other than the Art Deco aesthetics on a ruined city with dangerous creatures, some story elements are similar, like the reasoning for Tesla's and Ryan's creation for their utopia in the middle of the sea, you being assisted by a man with a heavy European accent, and even Rose's name is usually associated with BioShock's protagonist name Jack, as in Jack-Rose from the Titanic movie, also set on a ship. The chapters are also named after Greek gods, which BioShock uses in naming their locations.The level design is beautiful and really screenshot material, with cool areas such as a theater and a Tesla museum. Although many parts of the game takes place in generic hallways and engine rooms, the areas not in those categories usually takes your breath away. The puzzles aren't hard as well, mostly you can get them right by doing a bit of exploration or trial-and-error. I never had to look at a guide to solve puzzles, only collectibles. And the collectibles are unique as well, each chapter has a thematic collectible. Like in one chapter it's passports, then masks, notes, blueprints, etc.However, CttS has some flaws as well. The most important one being the story. The big mystery teased in the beginning isn't even solved, only lightly referenced and touched upon. It's been almost 3 years since their initial release, and no signs of a sequel. The second issue is the FOV, it's too narrow, and even if you change it to a slightly wider value (I use 70) everything looks a bit stretched. Lastly, I don't really mind the game being too dark, but it also continues a feature I don't really like in BioShock 1 where the characters are almost never seen clearly, usually only from far away. Lastly it's mostly a weird marketing decision, but this game starts being sold on Steam a few weeks after it goes free on Epic. I got this as a gift from a friend, but honestly I was kinda unwilling to buy this here at first.Close to the Sun is a pretty great walking sim, although I wish it was longer and with the big mystery solved. Get it if you like horror walking sims or simply just a BioShock fan looking to fill that Art Deco hole in your heart. I will absolutely play the sequel if they made one, and hopefully it remedies the issues I addressed.
_childDocuments_.name: Close to the Sun

_childDocuments_.review: Set in an alternative version of the 19th century, the game takes place aboard a massive, mysterious ship known as the Helios. As Rose Archer, a journalist searching for her sister, players navigate the vessel to uncover its secrets and unravel a gripping narrative.Background:The game's setting is a key highlight, drawing inspiration from Nikola Tesla's work and envisioning a world where his inventions have had a profound impact. The Helios, a colossal floating laboratory, serves as the stage for a gripping tale of scientific ambition gone awry. The narrative unfolds through environmental storytelling, audio logs, and atmospheric exploration, keeping players engaged in the unfolding mystery.Controls:Navigating the Helios is done seamlessly with intuitive controls. The first-person perspective enhances immersion, allowing players to delve into the eerie atmosphere and uncover hidden details. The controls are responsive, ensuring a smooth gameplay experience. The incorporation of puzzles adds an extra layer of engagement, requiring both critical thinking and dexterity to progress.Graphics:"Close to the Sun" boasts stunning visuals that bring the oppressive ambiance of the Helios to life. The attention to detail in the environment is commendable, with intricate designs and atmospheric lighting contributing to the game's eerie atmosphere. The graphics play a crucial role in immersing players in the alternative history setting, making exploration a visually captivating experience.Audience:The game caters to fans of atmospheric horror, combining elements of suspense and narrative-driven gameplay. Players who appreciate a well-crafted storyline, along with a sense of isolation and mystery, will find "Close to the Sun" particularly appealing. While not overly reliant on jump scares, the game excels in building tension through its narrative and unsettling atmosphere.Fun Facts:The game draws inspiration from real historical figures, most notably Nikola Tesla, whose influence is woven into the narrative's fabric.The Helios is a fictional representation of Tesla's ambitious but unrealized plans for a global wireless power transmission system.The art direction in the game is influenced by the Art Deco and Art Nouveau movements, contributing to the unique visual style of the Helios.In conclusion, "Close to the Sun" offers a compelling blend of atmospheric storytelling, engaging gameplay, and captivating visuals. It successfully creates a sense of unease and curiosity, making it a must-play for fans of atmospheric horror and narrative-driven experiences.I would definitely recommend it for the mystery and the twist of a historical figure and the art alone.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, I recommend this despite some shortcomings. In doubt, get it on a sale. It looks amazing and I love the voice acting. (more on that later)But here's the worst of it: The chase sequences. Look at other reviews and you will understand. I didn't hate them too much but I could have done without them. Or a more polished take of them, at least.That you can't step over anything higher than an inch is also kinda dumb. You will circle around corpses on the floor the whole time, even if it's just an arm or something. There are invisible walls everywhere.Other than that it's a "walking simulator" with a few easy "riddles" thrown into the mix. The music is nothing to write home about, mostly simple non-memorable piano work or ambient stuff. I do like the main theme/song but it doesn't fit the setting in my opinion. The general sound design is good however.Where it gets really interesting is the art design. This game is unspeakably gorgeous. And I really mean it. Bioshock or not, some places on the Helios are jaw droppingly well made, begging for screenshots. I also like the atmosphere. It's not really scary but eerie I'd say. Especially with all those corpses lying around.Also, Emily Moment, who voices the protagonist Rose (in english). Most probably don't care much about it but she simply knocked it out of the park for me. She really sticks out of all the voice work I generally hear. I don't know if her voice direction was so fricking good or she's just naturally talented as hell, or both. Either way, that was some stellar voice work on her part and kind of the best part of the game for me, personnally. I have no idea how she manages to transport so much character in her lines.The other VAs are good too, being veterans of the profession and all. But not THAT good.tl/drIt's okay. It's not a masterpiece but it's far from being trash. You'll get over the chase sequences.Also, sequel bait. And I wouldn't mind another one.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw this game on Steam randomly and just about immediately wanted to get it, at least based on the screenshots and the description of the game on the storefront. I liked the premise, the bioshock-like setting, and I'm always down for a decently good horror game. The first few chapters were interesting enough, with a cool intro and some nice looking environments that reminded me of Bioshock as I hoped for. Even got caught by one of the game's early cheap jump scares, and while after I acknowledged it for what it was I hoped that since it managed to get me there it might give more interesting scares later on. After getting past the first of the game's many annoying chase scenes though, things went downhill for me. The only horror left was the various gore covered corpses, the occasional random jump scare (most of which didn't really add anything or build any tension), and the darkness of the environment. The last one got pretty severe at times, but not in a good scary way...more of a "I just can't see where I'm going" way. The initial story was interesting and I hoped the relationship between the sisters would get more development, but it got to the point where the story beats get pretty obvious and it became hard to really invest much emotion into it. I enjoyed some of the dialogue, but most of it felt just cookie-cutter. "You need to go here and do X! Hurry, I'm losing the communication signal and can't talk anymo-" is a good summary of a lot of it. There are ten chapters, and once I got to the 5th I just wanted it to end, but didn't feel like going through a lengthy second half. Luckily for me after chapter 6 the rest of them can each be completed in probably 10-15 minutes. I breezed through the second half just so I could say I finished it, but by then the game lost me. Overall, it's a game that I really wanted to like...but the lack of interesting gameplay and the weakening of the story as it progressed made it pretty difficult to do so. While I can't recommend it, it's still a decent enough effort that if the developers made another game I'd at least look into it to see if any improvements were made. Gotta give it a 4.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Close to the Sun

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Bioshock where Rapture is the Nautilus from The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen except with less dark satire of Atlas Shrugged and more Tesla vs. Edison feud, less genetic engineering science magic and more electrical arcing science magic, and all the dismembered and disemboweled corpses you could ever want but with no way to make more of them yourself. A walking simulator where you sometimes suddenly have to run for your life, which is still way better than QTE. It's a great first half of an entertaining story that will never get a second half. And don't even think about quitting in the middle of a chapter, because you won't have your progress saved. Not perfect but I had an enjoyable playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start off by saying that I do not understand where the negative, or even average, reviews for this game come from. I found this game when looking through the Wired Production franchise, and was intrigued straight away. I didn't look much into it, and simply bought it because it looked interesting. I have not regretted this at all. This games story, as well as plot and all around execution, is wonderful. Not to mention the absolutely breathtaking areas you can explore on the Helios. I must say, as someone who never takes screenshots in a game, I have probably taken around 50 in this one. This game, in its entirety, is one of the most beautiful and interesting games I have played, and I recommend it wholeheartedly if you adore exploring and walking simulators with beautiful design.The game is also incredible for achievement hunters, and you can get all achievements in one playthrough, or finish up getting them in 10 minutes afterwards (as I did).

_childDocuments_.review: I’m sure most of you have already heard/read/watched the reviews on the game and most of them have been negative. 6/10 is what most people award the game and let me explain, I do not recommend games that aren’t at least 7/10. At least according to me, so let me tell you why I think this game is better than most people give it credit for. Also, spoilers ahead.The best parts of this game are the first 3 hours and the last hour. I finished the game in 5 hours, although it should take normally 6 hours. Well the first 3 hours set up the game very nicely. The gameplay is as good as you would expect from an indie developer, but the game is graphically stunning. The blood and the art-deco design makes you remember BioShock and fits nicely with the theme of Nikola Tesla’s giant ship. You are quickly introduced to most characters in the story, who are all voiced well, except for maybe Tesla who sounds kinda funny with his overexaggerated Slavic accent, as a Slav I can tell it is overexaggerated. The atmosphere is great. You really get a feeling you are alone on a giant, creepy, cold ship. The plot is pretty nice, it isn’t unpredictable, but it does make you want to see the end of it, especially with all the other small stories supporting it, although the game would be even better with more of them. The first time you see Ludwig you get the creeps. I mean there is a lunatic linked to Jack The Ripper on board a giant ship, full of dead people. I must say I expected Tesla to be the villain and I hoped the game would give us more of a reason to the so. I basically thought he was the villain because he locked us up early in the game and because I played BioShock. I mean at least as much of a villain as Andrew Ryan was. It was really a surprise when Tesla suddenly appeared and saved me near the end of the game. What I think the game could’ve done better was the EXO enemies. They really aren’t much threatening because their blue cartooney appearance makes it less and less scary and more and more annoying as they appear more often. Ludwig though, that’s a missed opportunity too. As much as I love some of the scary parts where he tries to get you I see the problems with just running away and basically having to guess which is the right way, which is a problem, they could’ve come up with something better, but when you’re perceptive you can get all the chases on the first try. Now back to Ludwig, I wish, I wish they would show us  his backstory. Apart from the notes and the newspaper talking about how he is from Whitechapel there isn’t much backstory, which sucks because he’s got interesting design and interesting lines. It can be seen that this game takes some inspiration from Outlast with some of the environments and chase scenes. I wish there was more stealth sections and more backstory when it comes to Helios itself and Tesla. The game set’s up for a sequel, which I honestly hope happens because this story ends on an interesting note. Overall if you are willing to look past the chase scenes and the lazy monster design it’s a solid game. The story is nice, the atmosphere and graphics are great and the idea of the game is grand as well. It’s sad that it isn’t another BioShock, but I do think most people underrate this game a lot. 7.8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Close to the Sun

_childDocuments_.review: If I could, I would give this a mixed review. Close to the Sun does a lot right. I like the main character, I love the setting, the atmosphere, the art design, both visuals and audio. The game looks and sounds amazing, and the premise is tropey but intriguing.However, it doesn't quite know how to turn all of this into a functional game. I expected this to be a walking simulator, but unfortunately, it lacks everything that makes walking simulators so enjoyable.1) There is barely any exploration. The game is divided into several "chapters", all of which are constructed and scripted to accomodate for no more than one strictly linear path through it. There are meaningless collectibles to find in "hidden" corners, but no major revelations.2) There is no environmental storytelling. All of the lore and background story is conveyed through text or dialogue.3) There is no unspoken secret to uncover. Anything that could remain implied is blurted out by the protagonist in the tackiest way possible.Instead, the game features plenty of "mechanics" that do little more than pad out the experience. Under an onslaught of unengaging "puzzles" that rarely ever incorporate actual setpieces and are mostly confined to machines, and after what feels like dozens of frustrating chase sequences, I feel like all I am actually doing to engage with this world is listening to what the characters say and press buttons when I'm told to.Even the 7 hours that it took me to finish this felt like 3 hours too long. Worst of all, in the end there aren't even enough plot points to put the pieces back together in a satisfying way. There is no "Aha" moment, just: Yes, that's what I already knew, but what about X, Y, and Z?
_childDocuments_.name: Close to the Sun

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR at the bottom!It deeply saddens me but the time has come for my first negative review. And giving it to a young italian studio makes it even harder.But you know, this game caught my eye and my interest, and now it's time for me to take my well deserved revenge.I completed the whole game in less than 6 hours, and even if the first three hours felt great (a walking simulator with some creepy moments), it's clear that the second half of the game has been rushed. And then it suddenly ends, without giving you any answers or explainations.There are lots of ints teasing a sequel, but it's not what I wanted. I wanted to play the whole story HERE, in this game. I don't want to buy two different games to understand the plot.By the way, the game looks really good, it honestly looks astonishing, but in some of the latest chapters there are some huge drops in quality; and most of all it features some great voices and sounds. Its OST is perfect.Animations are really bad but you'll hardly see any of them, and puzzles are.. ok, you'll never get stuck, they are mostly enjoyable.Most of the characters are well written, even if they are a bit predictable. It's awful that those guys keep saying "Don't worry, I'll explain later" and they never do. You never really understand what's happening and this drives me crazy.P.S.Collectables are cool.TL;DR: It's the setting from the first bioshock in a creepy walking simulator where you never get to understand what the hell happened. It looks good and it sounds great.

_childDocuments_.review: This may be the most mixed review I will ever post. Since steam refuses to add a mixed opinion, I suppose for statistical reasons or whatever, I ultimately decided on a negative review and I will motivate why. But first, I wanna talk about what I liked about this game. The story is about Rose, who you play as, got a letter from Ada, her sister, to visit her (or help her) onboard the very steampunk ship, helios. Onboard helios you find that it is pretty much abandoned and in a total state of quarentine. And then, everything ensues. First and the best, the visuals are great. The lightning can be easily adjustable if you feel that it is too dark, but at the same time I feel that is rather cheating to do so. The place is emply and practically abandoned of life. Darkness should consume pretty much all. The models of these strange apparatuses scoured around the Helios really bring light to the world they live in. It's steampunk after all, you will expect odd machines and everything industrialized. Some of these machines and creations are based on real things that Nikolai Tesla was researching.The sounds are good, they really emphasized the barren hull that is the Helios. The clacking of Roses boots changes drastically depending on where you are and I feel that many areas are very well expressed. The chunking and clunking of massive machines brings light to the areas you visit. and.. a.. ok. I can't do this anymore. It's time to bring the ship down. Negatives.First, it is important to state that I have beaten the game. Not 100%, since I didn't get all collectibles, but I have gone through start to finish. This game is . Incredibly short.Second, The game starts good, but plummits REALLY hard. When you first realise what's going on and the first major encounter, things get interesting.. Until the chase sequences. They're incredibly boring and the developers are strangely proud of it. They go on and on and on, you will have to suffer multiple of them. You will die sometimes many times to figure out the very specific and linear route you will have to take to succeed. I cannot fathom how they stuck with this lackluster idea. It ruins everything the game has been panning for the majority of the game.Third, The ending is aweful. Aubrey is a confusing character and so is about everything else that is going on. There is no resolution and you will hate the game for it. The ending brings no solace or clarification on what is going on. So your will ultimately stick to "well, I guess all that happened" instead. I hate it, and I hate the game for it!Fourth, no manual ducking and no crosshair. The ideas were alright, they're not major like previous statements, but I couldn't stop thinking about it. Sometimes you need to be awefully specific where you stand to pull a lever. This happened to me multiple times during the aweful chase sequences. Instead it has some kind of automatic system where if you stand close, the icon will chance so you can interract. I didn't like it. Makes me even wonder why they added Jumping. You never use it and never will.As it stands, this game is ultimately a failure as a horror game. Horror is subjective, but I promise you that you will find this not scary at the end of the day. It shouldn't have focused so much on horror elements and perhaps stick to a thriller mystery game with minor puzzle solving. I believe that if they continued on that route, it could have made the game better and more appealing. So far, this will remain as one of the most below average horror game I have ever played.But, with the price tag, it was still an alright experience. It is not the worst game ever, or exatly bad either. It's just.. below average. It's not exactly in the middle 50%/50% range, it's like 60% bad, 40% good. What are your guys thoughts? Was I too harsh on a very obvious indie project, or am I objective enough to make it fair?

_childDocuments_.review: Primarily a walking sim with a very few, easily solved puzzles and a small number of chase sequences where you have to run for your life. There are collectibles that you find along the way, none of which are truly difficult to find. The story is presented in 10 chapters and the game automatically saves at the end each each chapter. If you need to leave the game in the middle of the chapter, you'll restart at the beginning of that chapter.I was drawn to this game by it's premise and by the look of the ship in the trailer. I was not dissappointed. The design and presentation of the ship that you explore is visually captivating, the voice acting and music were appropriate, and the story was intriguing. A well presented, immersive experience.I am not a fan of horror and gore, and I was relieved that those elements weren't over-the-top in this game. There were a few mild jumpscares and a pervasive tense atmosphere. I was disappointed that many of the mysteries raised in the story never seem to get resolved by the end of the game.Overall I really enjoyed this game and will replay it just to fully explore the environment. Recommended for fans of walking sims looking for something a little different.

_childDocuments_.review: "Close to the Sun" looked right up my alley. I love the semi-niche genre of first person adventure games, which there honestly aren't enough of. When I saw the setting, a turn of the century Tesla research facility on the high seas, I was sold.However, Close to the Sun isn't very good. This game has so few puzzles (or gameplay at all, for that matter) that it borders on being a "walking sim." Plus, the only puzzles that the game has are the most generic door code, pattern recognition baloney that you see in ever other game.The most annoying moment in the game came when I was introduced to what appeared to be a sort of cypher puzzle, with a message where normal letters were replaced with abstract symbols. While I knew I didn't need to solve the cypher to progress in the game, I chose to do so anyway. I sat down with a pen and paper and "cracked the code" after about thirty minutes. When I fully translated the letter, it revealed a message that said "Wow! We can't believe you actually translated it! Please enjoy the rest of the game." Well, I didn't. First and foremost because of the letter itself. It was legitimately some of the worst game design I've ever seen. What purpose is there in creating the illusion of an elaborate puzzle, more interesting than anything else in your game, only to spit in the face of the players that actually solve it?Just as solving the cypher was a waste of time, so was the game as a whole. The story wasn't terrible, but not all that interesting either, and ended on a cliff-hanger. Plus, despite looking just okay, the game ran poorly on my semi-expensive modern rig that doesn't struggle at all with modern AAA releases. Avoid this one or wait for a VERY deep sale if it looks interesting enough to you.

_childDocuments_.review: When does a homage become derivative junk? Probably when it replicates the original work without adding anything worthwhile. Close to the Sun, then, is saved from being derivative junk only by a few moments of visual flair. Obviously aping Bioshock, Close to the Sun retains the gorgeous art of that game, but brings an inferior script and sound design, and ditches the gunplay and exploration for jump scares and dismal chase sequences. This leaves you with a steampunk walking simulator that falls far short of its 2007 inspiration. Which is a shame, because Bioshock – for all the legitimate criticisms one could make of the series – did a lot to bring interesting and artistically-worthwhile excellence in visual design and thoughtful worldbuilding to the gaming mainstream. Its influence can be seen in the output of studios like Arkane and Frictional, but art-forward game design in the Bioshock style still feels like a fruitful avenue under-explored by artistically-minded devs.Close to the Sun dumps Rose, its strong female protagonist, aboard a fallen, ocean-bound utopia with little explanation. This time ominous radio messages from the setting’s vengeful founder are those of Nikola Tesla – doing a bad attempt at a Croatian accent – the scientific misadventure is time paradox something something physics, and the portentous references are to a grab-bag of Greek mythology. Don’t worry, though, there are still crazed killers to dodge, audio-logs to collect, and Art Deco splendours to glimpse – for all that that movement post-dates the game’s nominal 19th Century setting. Asking for historical accuracy from an “alternate universe” where Tesla is building death rays aboard an ocean liner the size of a city block might be a stretch, but it is disappointing that the script slips in anachronistic references to “nerds” and “high fives,” makes no mention of the sexism the two principle characters would likely have had to deal with, references physics that hadn’t yet been discovered, and generally fritters away an interesting idea with careless and uninspiring execution.In summary, Close to the Sun will supply a few hours of eye candy to those hungry for retro-futurist gaming, but no more. If you’re looking for more accomplished walking simulators, Firewatch, Gone Home, Edith Finch and Tacoma all feature much better scripts and more interesting design. If you’re looking for Steampunkish weird fiction, don’t miss Sunless Sea or – beyond the world of gaming – China Mieville’s fabulous Bas Lag trilogy. If you’re after Tesla-centric alternate history, of course The Prestige is superb. Finally – and again outside the world of video games – Netflix’s Arcane is a visual feast which marries stunning steampunk visuals to a satisfying drama, and is perhaps what Close to the Sun was reaching for.

_childDocuments_.review: A walking sim with a visual style reminiscent of Bioshock, a suspenseful atmosphere and a few chase sequences thrown in to prevent boredom. Beautiful use of the Unreal 4 engine (one of the best I've seen). Story is engaging, but without the sequel that is promised by the cliffhanger ending, much of it remains confusing even when it's over. Worth picking up for those who like to wander & explore without (too much) pressure. Be aware that some of the visuals are gruesome and the game is very demanding to run.Total size on my hard-drive: 20.4 GB

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game and while clearly inspired by Bioshock, it has a great setting. But that's all that the game has to offer. The gameplay is boring. You walk way too much and there's no puzzles to mix up the gameplay (except for one or two instances and they were painfully obvious to solve). The game tries to mix up a little with the horror elements but it's basically the usual basic scare jumps and the oh-my-god-he's-after-me-I-have-to-run sequences.But the worst offender is the writing. Oh God, the writing is so awful! The dialogues are not adequate to the era that it takes place and we get dumb jokes here and there while there's people dying (in horrific ways). Also, the story is equally dumb and there's a lot of things that stays unanswered (and yes, I did understood the stupid ending).This studio needs good writers and a new lead gameplay designer, then maybe, just MAYBE there's a good chance that a good game will come out of it.
